One important aspect of this description is that the name of the following metres are different in the NS, e.g. Drutavilambita = Harinapluta (NS), Bhujangaprayata = Aprameya (NS), Sragvini = Padmini (NS), Malini = Nandimukhi (NS), Harini = Vrsabha-cestita (NS), Mandakranta = Sridhara (NS), Prthvi = Vilambita-gati (NS), Kusumita-lata-vellita = Citralekha (NS).

Another difference between the respective experiences of natya- rasa and kavya-rasa centers on the definition of the term bhava (emotion) in dramaturgy. Bharata Muni says the word bhava is derived in the causative sense: A bhava is so called because, by means of speech, bodily movements and good vibrations, it brings to life the emotion that was in the poet’s heart.

By deriving the term bhava in the causative sense in yet another way (bhavayati rasam iti bhavah), Bharata Muni implies another distinction between natya-rasa and kavya-rasa:

*nana-dravyair bahu-vidhair vyanjanam bhavyate yatha \|*  
*evam bhava bhavayanti rasan abhinayaih saha \|\|*  
*na bhava-hino ’sti raso na bhavo rasa-varjitah \|*  
*paraspara-krta siddhis tayor abhinaye bhavet \|\|*  
*vyanjanausadhi-samyogo yathannam svadutam nayet \|*  
*evam bhava rasas caiva bhavayanti parasparam \|\|*

**“By means of acting techniques, the bhavas give rise to the rasas. There is no rasa without a bhava, and there is no bhava without a rasa. In a play, one effects the other. Just as the combination of vegetables and condiments make the rice tasty and the rice enhances them, so the bhavas give rise to rasa and the rasa enhances the bhavas” (Natya-sastra 6.35-37).**

Another great dissimilarity is that in natya-rasa there are four main rasas, and the other four proceed from them:

*srngarad dhi bhaved dhasyo raudrac ca karuno rasah \|*  
*virac caivadbhutotpattir bibhatsac ca bhayanakah \|\|*

**“Hasya-rasa occurs from srngara-rasa, and karuna-rasa from raudra-rasa. The origination of adbhuta-rasa takes place from vira-rasa, and of bhayanaka from bibhatsa” (Natya-sastra 6.39).**

In that regard, Dhananjaya wrote:

*svadah kavyartha-sambhedat atmananda-samudbhavah \|*  
*vikasa-vistara-ksobha-viksepaih sa catur-vidhah \|*  
*srngara-vira-bibhatsa-raudresu manasah kramat \|\|*  
*hasyadbhuta-bhayotkarsa-karunanam ta eva hi \|*  
*atas taj-janyata tesam ata evavadharanam \|\|*

**“Relishment takes place from the rise of the bliss of the self on account of the commixture of the meanings in the poetry. There are four kinds of relishment: cheerfulness, exaltation, agitation, and mental perturbation: They occur in srngara, vira, bibhatsa, and raudra respectively. These same kinds also relate to hasya, adbhuta, bhayanaya, and karuna, therefore the latter ones are occasioned by former ones.” (Dasa-rupaka 4.41-42)**

## The Theme of Each Chapter

**Chapter** **Topic**   1 natyotpatti (origin of dramaturgy)   2 mandapa-vidhana (description of the playhouse)   3 ranga-daivata-pujana (homage to the presiding deities of the stage)   4 purva-ranga-vidhana (rules for the prologue; description of the karana dance (gestures and postures: synchronized movements of hands and feet); when drums should be played)   5 purva-ranga-prayoga (performing the prologue)   6 rasa   7 bhava-vyanjaka (revealers of emotion)   8 upanga-vidhanam (gestures of minor limbs, of the head and of parts of the face)   9 angabhinaya (gestures of the limbs)   10 can-vidhana (the procedure for cari movements)   11 mandala-vidhana (the mandala movements)   12 gati-pracara (different gaits)   13 kara-yukti-dharmT-vyanjaka (zones and local usages)   14 vacikabhinaye chando-vidhana (the denotation of vowels and consonants; the meters; rules of prosody while reciting)   15 chando-viciti (metrical patterns)   16 vag-abhinaye kavya-laksana (diction of a play; characteristics of poetry in words and in drama: 4 figures of speech, 10 dosas, 10 gunas, and 36 characteristics of fine dramatical poetry)   17 vag-abhinaye kaku-svara-vyanjana (a lengthy discussion on Prakrit languages; using Prakrit in the metrical patterns; vowels and consonants pertaining to a change in the tone of voice while reciting, i.e. 4 varnas, 2 kakus, 6 alankaras and 6 angas)   18 \>dasa-rupa-nirupana (ten kinds of plays)   19 sandhi-nirupana (description of intervals)   20 vrtti-vikalpana (styles)   21 aharyabhinaya (costumes and make-up)   22 samanyabhinaya (harmonious performance)   23 (no name) (dealing with courtesans)   24 pum-stry-upacara (the conduct of men and women on stage)   25 citrabhinaya (amazing dramatic gestures)   26 vikrti-vikalpa (types of changes of emotions)   27 siddhi-vyanjaka (indicators of success)   28 jati-vikalpana (differentiation between the seven notes, etc.)   29 tatadodya-vidhana (the procedure for stringed musical instruments; the jatis called udatta, lalita, ribhita, and ghana)   30 susiratodya-laksana (the characteristics of hollow musical instruments)   31 tala (musical rhythm)   32 dhruva-vidhana (the rules for the introductory verse of a song, often repeated as a chorus; dhruva is also the name of a tala)   33 guna-dosa-vicara (considerations of qualities and faults)   34 puskara-vadya (the musical instrument called puskara)   35 bhumika-vikalpa (the types of introductions)   36 natya-sapa (the curse related to dramaturgy)   37 guhya-tattva-kathana (a discourse about a secret topic: the descent of dramaturgy on Earth)

Thousands of details are discussed in Natya-sastra, but the major topics in the thirty-seven-chapter recension were mentioned above. The thirty-six-chapter recension combines chapters 36 and 37 of the other recension, but from chapter 10 the two recensions are dissimilar in point of sequence. For the details of the thirty-six- chapter recension, consult Ghosh (1951: Vol. I, pp. 17-36) or Kane (1998: 29-39). In addition, the number of verses per chapter in each recension varies and some topics differ.

Vishnu is the presiding deity of srngara, the Pramathas are the presiding deities of hasya, Rudra is the deity of raudra, Yama of karuna, Mahakala of bibhatsa, Kala of bhayanaka, Indra of vira, and Brahma of adbhuta (Natya-sastra 6.44-45).

Bharata Muni lists three kinds of srngara (related to words, attire, and deeds), three kinds of karuna (from violating a code of dharma, from a loss of wealth, and from sorrow), three kinds of vira (dana- vira, dharma-vira, yuddha-vira), and so on (Natya-sastra 6.77-79).

The eight states of a ladylove are mentioned, and so are these categories of speech: alapa, pralapa, vilapa, anulapa, samlapa, and apalapa (Natya-sastra 22.52).

Moreover, at the outset of the fourth chapter, Bharata Muni says Brahma and he went to Siva’s abode, in the Himalayas, and showcased a play that Brahma had composed. After the perfor­mance, Siva praised Brahma for the play.

The Natya-sastra recounts the origin of dramatugy:

*mahendra-pramukhair devair uktah kila pitamahah \|*  
*kridariiyakam icchamo drsyam sravyam ca yad bhavet \|\|*  
*na veda-vyavaharo ’yam samsravyah sUdra-jatisu \|*  
*tasmat srjaparam vedam pancamam sarva-varnikam \|\|*  
*evam astv iti tan uktva deva-rajam visrjya ca \|*  
*sasmara caturo vedan yogam asthaya tattva-vit \|\|*  
*neme veda yatah sravyah stri-sUdradyasu jatisu \|*  
*vedam anyat tatah sraksye sarvasravyam tu pancamam \|\|*  
*dharmyam arthyam yasasyam ca sopadesyam sa-sangraham \|*  
*bhavisyatas ca lokasya sarva-karmanudarsakam \|\|*  
*sarva-satrartha-sampannam sarva-silpa-pravartakam \|*  
*natyakhyam pancamam vedam setihasam karomy aham \|\|*  
*evam sankalpya bhagavan sarva-vedan anusmaran \|*  
*natya-vedam tatas cakre catur-vedanga-sambhavam \|\|*

**“Indra and other gods approached Brahma and said: “We want enter­tainment than can be seen and heard. The Sudras are not allowed to hear the Vedas, therefore kindly create a fifth Veda, one for all the castes.” Brahma told the gods that he agreed, and dismissed Indra. Situated in yoga, Brahma remembered the four Vedas, and thought to himself: “I shall make a fifth Veda, called Natya, which will comprise the histories (Itihasa). It will be a compendium where there will be no deviation from moral ethics (dharma) nor from prosperity (artha). The purpose of that compendium is fame and the teachings of moral instructions. It will illustrate all the activities of the world in the future. It will include the purport of all the scriptures. It will propound all the crafts.” Lord Brahma took recitation from the Rg-Veda, music from the Sama-Veda, dramatic gestures from the Yajur-Veda, and rasas from the Atharva-Veda.” (Natya-sastra 1.11-16)**

In Natya-sastra, the philosophy is this:

*dharmartham hi tapascarya sukhartham dharma isyate \|*  
*sukhasya mulam pramadas tasu sambhoga isyate \|\|*

**“Performing austerities is for the sake of dharma. Dharma is desired for the sake of happiness. The root cause of happiness is women. Sex with women is desired.” (Natya-sastra 22.148) (24.147 in the thirty-six-chapter recension)**

Many deviations from Vedic culture are expounded in Natya- sastra. For instance: (1) “A king unites with a woman who stays indoors, whereas a common man may unite with a woman who goes outdoors. The king can have union with a heavenly courtezan,” (2) “Due to respect for the queens and out of fear of his favorite women, a king should secretly make love to the queens’ maids,” (3) The qualifications for being a concubine of a king are stated (Natya-sastra 34.40 in the thirty-six-chapter recension), (4) The abhisarika ladylove can be either a courtezan, a well-mannered wife, or a maid, and (5) “The king’s union with the women of the inner palace is allowed in daytime, but in dealing with external women the union should occur at night.”

## Bharata’s Sons Are Cursed and Come to Earth

The thirty-sixth chapter relates that in an assembly, the foremost sages, such as Narada, Brhaspati, Angiras, Vasistha, Kasyapa and Visvamitra, addressed Bharata, praised him, and asked him how dramaturgy could be expanded from heaven to Earth. They also inquired about his offsprings, renowned actors. Bharata replied that his sons were staging morally degraded dramas and mocking the Rsis. The sages became furious, addressed his sons and cursed them:

*nirahuta vina homaih sudracara bhavisyatha \|\|*  
*apankteyah kutsitas cavama eva bhavisyatha \|*  
*yas ca vo bhavita vamsah sarvasauco bhavisyati \|\|*  
*ye ca vo vamsa-jas te ’pi bhavisyanty atha nartakah \|*  
*paropasthanavantas ca sastra-panyopajlvinah \|\|*

**“You, who were not invited, will undergo the conduct of Sudras, without performing fire sacrifices. You are out of line. You will become despised and inferior. Your future lineage will be impure, and your descendants as well will become actors. They will wait on others, and their livelihood will be the trade of weapons.” (Natya- sastra 36.39-41)**

Hearing this, Indra and other gods became dejected. They besought the Rsis, complaining that dramaturgy would come to an end. The sages denied it. Later, Bharata told his sons to promote dramaturgy to disciples and others just as they were taught, and to practice atonement (Natya-sastra 36.42-51).Afterward, since Indra was absent due to practicing penance after killing Vrtrasura, Nahusa was appointed king of heaven. Seeing the dramas, he desired that the art be taught on Earth, and asked Bharata about it. Bharata said:

*tathastv iti maya prokto nahusah parthivas tada \|*  
*sutas cahuya samprokta sama-purvam suraih saha \|\|13\|\|*

*ayam hi nahuso raja yacate nah krtanjalih \|*  
*gamyatam sahitair bhumim prayoktum natyam eva ca \|\|14\|\|*

*karisyamas ca sapantam asmin samyak-prayojite \|*  
*brahmananam nrpanam ca bhavisyatha na kutsitah \|\|15\|\|*

*tatra gatva prayujyantam prayogan vasudha-tale \|*  
*na sakyam canyatha kartum vacanam parthivasya hi \|\|16\|\|*

*asmakam caiva sarvesam nahusasya mahatmanah \|*  
*atmopadesa-siddham hi natyam proktam svayambhuva \|\|17\|\|*

*sesam uttara-tantrena kohalas tu karisyati \|*  
*prayogah karikas caiva niruktani tathaiva ca \|\|18\|\|*

*apsarobhir idam sardham kridariiyaka-hetukam \|*  
*adhisthitam maya svarge svatina naradena ca \|\|19\|\|*

*tatas ca vasudham gatva nahusasya grhe dvijah \|*  
*strmam prayogam bahudha baddhavanto yatha-kramam \|\|20\|\|*

*atropabhogatas te tu manusisu mamatmajah \|*  
*baddhavanto ’dhika-sneham tasu tad dvija-sattamah \|\|21\|\|*

*putran utpadya vadhva ca prayogam ca yatha-kramam \|*  
*brahmana samanujnatah praptah svargam punah sutah \|\|22\|\|*

*evam urvi-tale natyam sisyaih samavataritam \|*  
*bharatanam ca vamso ’yam bhavisyam ca pravartitah \|\|23\|\|*

*kohaladibhir evam tu vatsa-sandilya-dhurtitaih \|*  
*martya-dharma-kriya-yuktaih kascit  kalam avasthitaih \|\|24\|\|*

*etac chastram pranitam hi naranam buddhi-vardhanam \|*  
*trailokyasya kriyopetam sarva-sastra-nidarsanam \|*  
*mangalyam lalitam caiva brahmano vadanodbhavam \|\|25\|\|*

*ya idam srunuyan nityam proktam cedam svayambhuva \|*  
*kuryatprayogam yas caivam athavadhitavan narah \|\|26\|\|*

*ya gatir veda-vidusam ya gatir yajna-karinam \|*  
*ya gatir dana-silanam tam gatim prapnuyad dhi sah \|\|27\|\|*

*dana-dharmesu sarvesu kirtyate tu mahat phalam \|*  
*preksaniya-pradanam hi sarva-danesu sasyate \|\|28\|\|*

*na tatha gandha-malyena devas tusyanti pujitah \|*  
*yatha natya-prayoga-sthair nityam tusyanti mangalaih \|\|29\|\|*

*gandharvam ceha natyam ca yah samyakparipalayet \|*  
*sa isvara-ganesanam labhate sad-gatim param \|\|30\|\|*

*evam natya-prayoge bahu-vidhi-vihitam karma-sastram pranitam \|*  
*noktam yac catra lokad anukrti-karanat \|*  
*samvibhavyam tu taj-jnaih \|\|*  
*kincanyat samprapurna bhavatu vasumati nasta-durbhiksa-roga \|*  
*santir go-brahmananam bhavatu nara-patih patu prthvim samagram \|\|31\|\|*  
*iti bharatiye natya-sastre guhya-tattva-kathanadhyayah sapta-trimsah \|*  
*natya-sastram sampurnam \|\|*

**““I replied to King Nahusa: “So be it.” Then I summoned my sons and addressed them with conciliatory words in the gods’ presence: “Joining both hands in respect, King Nahusa is begging us. Go to Earth and implement drama, and we will make the curse come to an end when drama will be properly implemented; you will not be despised by Brahmanas nor by kings. Once there, promulgate theatrical representations. King Nahusa’s command cannot be transgressed. Brahma said to all of us and to Mahatma Nahusa that dramaturgy becomes established by the instructions of qualified persons. Kohala will do the rest—the representations, the definitional verses and the etymological explanations—in a subsequent treatise. Dramaturgy is a reason for entertainment with courtezans, and I, along with Narada and Svati in heaven, preside over dramaturgy.”**

**“Thereafter, O Brahmanas, they went to Earth and, in Nahusa’s dwelling, sequentially put together the manifold representations of women. O best of twice-borns, in that place, my sons developed great affection for those women, as a result of enjoyment. They fathered sons and did representations with their wives. Authorized by Brahma, the sons went back to heaven. In this way dramaturgy came to Earth through the disciples. The future dynasty of bharatas (actors) thus came into being. This scripture, which increases the intelligence of humans, which reflects the deeds of the three worlds, which illustrates all the scriptures, which is auspicious and charming, and which arose from Brahma’s mouths, was composed by Kohala, Vatsa, Sandilya and Dhurtila, who, staying for some time, were engaged in actions dealing with the mortals’ dharma.**

**“A person who continuously hears this treatise, spoken by Brahma, and makes a representation, or else any person who studies it, attains the destination of the knowers of the Vedas, of the performers of fire sacrifices, and of those who are generous by nature.**

**“In all the ethical codes for giving, a great result is glorified: Among all gifts, providing a theatrical representation free of charge is praised. The gods are more pleased by a play than they are by worship with flower garlands and sandalwood paste. One who financially supports dramaturgy which is accompanied with music achieves the highest destination.**

**“Many types of books dealing with day-to-day life are used in a play. Whatever remains unwritten should be conceived by dramatists by observing people. In addition: May the disease of famine cease, may the earth become fully enriched, may cows and Brahmanas live in peace, and may a good government run the country. Here ends Natya-sastra. ” (37.13-31)**

Dr. Kane comments:

The Natyasastra, as narrated in its last chapter, knew well that the drama and actors had come into great disrepute for their loose character and tries hard to raise the status of both. This work is probably unique in the world’s literature on dramaturgy. Hardly any work on dramaturgy in any language has the comprehensiveness, the sweep and the literary and artistic flair of the Natyasastra. It is sad to note that in spite of the noble words of the Natyasastra, dramatic artists descended to very low depths in a few centuries after it as attested by Damodaragupta in his Kuttanimata (latter half of the 8th century A.D.).

A few words must be said about ancient writers on dramaturgy as their works have not yet been found. \[...\] Kohala is one of them and a good deal has already been said about him above (pp. 24-25). He appears to have written on all topics of Natya-sastra especially on music, acting and dance. \[.\] Mr. Kavi (in J.Andhra H.R.S. vol. III. at 24) says that the Sangita-meru of Kohala is not now available except the chapter on tala and abhinaya. It was Kohala who started the definitions of Uparupaka like sattaka \[...\]. The Rasarnava- sudhakara of Singhabhupala (p. 8 verses 52-54) states that the sons of Bharata, viz. Sandilya, Kohala, Dattila and Matanga wrote works on Natya-sastra. In Kama-sutra (I.1.11, VI.2.55, VI.3.44) mention is made of Dattaka who at the request of the Ganikas of Pataliputra expounded the vaisika section of Kama-sastra. The Kuttanimata (verses 77, 122) mentions Dattakacarya (v.1. Dantilacarya). The Abhinava-bharati (vol. I. p. 205, chap. 4. 326-327 on dhruva) quotes a sloka from Dattilacarya.

Dr. Sushil Kumar De writes:

Kohala, side by side with Bharata, is recognised as an ancient authority as early as the end of the 8th century A.D. in Damodara-gupta’s Kuttani-mata (verse 81). It is interesting to note in this connexion that Abhinavagupta, commenting on Bharata vi.10, says that although Natya is usually said to consist of five angas, the enumeration of eleven angas in the text is in accordance with the view of Kohala and others, to whose opinions the commentator makes many other incidental references mostly on the topics of Natya and Geya. Kohala is cited also by Manikyacandra on Mammata, \[...\] and by the authors of the Natya-darpana, while Singabhupala (i.51) acknowledges him as an authority on drama and allied arts. Hemacandra, with reference to the classification of the drama, says: prapancas tu bharata-kohaladi-sastrebhyo ’vagantcvyah.

Kohala is credited by most writers on Dramaturgy with the introduction of Uparupaka. Mallinatha on Kumara VII.91 quotes Kohala on the subject of Tala. A work on music called Tala-laksana, probably a late compilation, is attributed to him, and a Kohaliya Abhinaya-Sastra purporting to embody his views, is also known. A work called Kohala-rahasya in at least thirteen chapters, dealing with musical modes, is ascribed to the sage Kohala (described as a son of Bharata) who reveals the subject on being requested by Matanga. The description that he was a son of Bharata is perhaps due to the indication in Natya-sastra i.26 (ed. Chowkhamba 1929, ed. GOS, Baroda 1956; but not included in the NSP ed. 1894) that Kohala, along with Sandilya, Dhurtila and others, are spoken of as sons of Bharata. Since Abhinavagupta says (Abhinava- bharati p. 25) that Kohala describes the verse jitam udu-patina from Ratnavali (i.5) as an example of Nandi in accordance with the rules of Bharata, P. V. Kane is of opinion that Kohala was later than Ratnavali, i.e. than 650 A.D. But this conclusion cannot be very well reconciled with the fact that Bharata and Kohala are already recognised as ancient authorities in the 8th century A.D. From Abhinavagupta’s references and citations, Kohala’s lost work appears to have been mostly in verse. A work on music, entitled Dattila-kohallya, is mentioned by Burnell, apparently a compendium of the opinions of Kohala and Dattila. The latter, whose name occurs variously as Dantila and Dhurtila, is mentioned by Damodara-gupta (verse 123) and is cited as an old authority by Abhinavagupta (as Dattilacarya, chiefly on music) who quotes (on Bharata xxviii) a verse of his in Anustubh \[...\] and by Singabhupala (i.51), as well as in various works on music. A work called Dattila on music is also published.

In the same way, Sandilya is mentioned as Natya-sastra- kara by Singabhupala (i.51). Kasyapa or Kasyapa as a muni who preceded Bharata and his opinion on Ragas is cited by Abhinavagupta (on xxix), as well as by Nanyadeva. Satakarni is cited as a writer on dramaturgy by Sagaranandin (on Sutra- dhara, 1.1101). Visakhila is also cited as an authority on Kala- Sastra by Vamana (i.3.7), by Abhinavagupta (on xxviii, xxix 31-33) and by Nanyadeva as an authority on music. Parasara or Parasara, mentioned by Rajasekhara, is also cited as a Bharata-putra in Natya-sastra (i.32); his views on Nandi and Totaka are quoted by Sagaranandin (II.1091, 2770, 3202-3). Similarly, another Bharata-putra is Nakhakutta, who is also cited by Sagaranandin (II.2668, 2994).”

From these indications it is likely that between Bharata’s original text and its existing version, there came “Kohala and others” whose views found their way into the compendium, which goes by the name of Bharata and which indiscriminating posterity took as genuine and unquestionable. \[.\] The process of incorporation must have occurred very early and was apparently complete by the end of the 8th century, when the work assumed more or less its present shape.

P.V. Kane specifies: “It is possible that Parasara in the above passage of Kavya-mimamsa means Badarayana, who is mentioned as a Bharata-putra in Natya-sastra I.32 (Badarayani in Ch. ed.) and whose views on nandi and totaka are quoted by Sagaranandin (in na. la. ra. ko. II.1091, 2770, 3202-3).” Dr. Manomohan Ghosh adds: “Sagara quotes from Badarayana twice and possibly names him once as Badari, and from the extracts quoted it seems that this early writer discussed dramaturgy.” Dr. Ghosh says this about Satakarni, a son of Bharata:

Satakarni (Satakarna, Salikarna). Satakarni as a proper name is found in inscriptions from the first century B.C to 149 A.C. Hence it is possible, though not quite certain, that Satakarni the writer on drama flourished about the first century A.C. Like kings in later times who were sometimes found to take interest among other subjects in drama and poetics and to write treatises on them, this Satakarni might well have been a king or a person of royal descent. From the quotations made by later writers, it appears he wrote on dramaturgy.

Dr. Manomohan Ghosh calls Bharata’s sons “the so-called sons of Bharata.” He doubts the attribution of authorship. He writes: “.. Muni Bharata, the supposed author of the Natya-sastra,” and: “Kohala has been mentioned as one of the hundred sons of Bharata and as such he was anterior to the author of this work.”

## Two Recensions

Dr. Ghosh, whose translation of Natya-sastra contains thirty-six chapters, states:

Dhananjaya the author of Dasarupa quotes from the shorter recension, while Bhoja, who closely follows him, quoted from the longer one. Abhinava in his commentary on the Natya- sastra, however, used the shorter recension as the basis of his work.

The thirty-six-chapter recension is the long one. Depending on the editions, the recension of thirty-six chapters contains 5615 or 5633 verses whereas the version of thirty-seven chapters has 5499 or 5624 verses. Another difference between the two recensions is that in the thirty-six-chapter version, Nahusa says dramaturgy had already been expounded on Earth: He told Bharata that dramaturgy and Pururavas’s work on it had been explained by Urvasi, the latter’s wife, to their entourage, but that after Urvasi’s death, Pururavas, Nahusa’s grandfather, became insane, their entourage became distressed, and eventually the art of dramaturgy was lost. In Dr. Ghosh’s opinion, the thirty-six-chapter version is the long one:

Ramakrishna Kavi, who has examined no less than forty manuscripts of the text, is of the opinion that the longer recension (which he calls B) seems to be ancient, although it contains some interpolation (pointed at by him) going back to a time prior to Abhinava. Mr. Kavi, however, does not try to explain the origin of the shorter recension which he calls A. This view regarding the relative authenticity of the longer recension seems to possess justification. Reasons supporting it are to be found in the tests differentiating the two recensions, which are as follows:

(1) Chapters XIV and XV of the shorter recension dealing with prosody introduce the later terminology of Pingala (ra, ja, sa, na, and bha ganas etc.) while the longer recension uses terms like laghu and guru in defining the scheme of metres.

(2) The shorter recension in its chapter XV gives definitions of metres in Upajati, while the corresponding chapter (XVI) of the longer recension gives them in Anustup metre and in a different order. Considering the fact that the bulk of the Natya- sastra is written in this (Anustup) metre the longer recension in this case seems to run closer to the original work.

Though Ramakrishna Kavi has overlooked it, there is yet another point which may be said to differentiate the two recensions. The chapter dealing with the Natyagunas and Alankaras have nearly forty slokas differently worded in the two recensions. These slokas in the longer recension (ch. XVII) are written in the usual simple language of the Natya- sastra while (ch. XVI) in the shorter recension (the slokas) betray a later polish. The opening stanzas of the chapter (XVI) in the shorter recension are in Upajati metre while in the longer recension (ch. XVII) they are in the sloka metre. This points to the earlier origin of the latter, for the bulk of the Natya-sastra, as has been pointed out before, is composed in the sloka metre.

Now the shorter recension, which appears to be of later origin, does not seem to be totally devoid of worth. It appears that this has in certain cases preserved what once existed but are now missing in the longer recension. The cases in which the shorter recension gives in a different language the corresponding passages of the longer recension may be explained by assuming that the passages in question were probably written from memory of the original in the prototype of the recension.

## Commentaries and Tradition

The most famous commentators were stated by Samgadeva:

According to the Sangita-ratnakara of Samgadeva the expounders of Bharata were Lollata, Udbhata, Sankuka, Kirtidhara and Abhinavagupta (vyakhyataro bharatiye lollatodbhata-sankukah \| bhattabhinavaguptas ca srimat- kirtidharo ’parah \|\| I.19). A separate section will be devoted to Udbhata, but here a few words may be said about his commentary on Bharata. Udbhata is mentioned by Abhinava on the following points: (1) On Natya-sastra VI.10 (quoted above) the views of Audbhatas are quoted and Abhinava says that Lollata did not accept them (vide Abhinava-bharati G.O.S. vol. I. p. 266) \[...\] (4) Udbhata appears to have criticized Bharata himself as to the four vrttis, Bharati, Satvati, Kaisiki and Arabhati. \[.\] For this and other reasons Udbhata gives up the four vrttis and proposes only three vrttis viz. Nyaya-cesta Vrtti, Anyaya-cesta Vrtti and Phala-samvitti Vrtti (for murcha and marana) or Phala Vrtti.

Bharata Muni only mentioned the four Vrttis—Bharati, Satvati, Kaisiki and Arabhati—by name twice (Natya-sastra 1.41-42 and 6.24). In Bhakti-rasamrta-sindhu, Rupa Gosvami said they are only for dramaturgy (4.9.42). He defined them in Nataka- candrika. Specifically, according to him Satvati is used for vira- rasa, adbhuta-rasa, and so on, Kaisiki for madhura-rasa, and Arabhati for vira-rasa (Nataka-candrika 243-255). Dhananjaya stated that Kaisiki is used in srngara-rasa, Sattvati in vira-rasa, Arabhati in raudra-rasa and bibhatsa-rasa, and Bharati in all the rasas: srngare kausiki vire sattvaty arabhati punah, rase raudre ca bibhatse vrttih sarvatra bharati (Dasa-rupaka 2.57). Bharata Muni mentioned that he had observed Kaisiki in Siva’s dance. He added that without women, Kaisiki cannot be properly practiced by men. Therefore Brahma mentally created Apsaras, and handed them over to Bharata.

The names of the four Pravrttis show that some knowledge of dramaturgy was already present on Earth when Natya-sastra was composed: bharati satvafi caiva kaisiky arabhati tatha \|\| catasro vrttayo hy eta yasu natyam pratisthitam \| avanti daksinatya ca tatha caivodhra-magadhi \|\| pancala-madhyama ceti vijneyas tu pravrttayah \| (Natya-sastra 6.24-26).

Rajasekhara explains the difference: tatra vesa-vinyasa-kramah pravrttih, vilasa-vinyasa-kramo vrttih, vacana-vinyasa-kramo ritih, “The Pravrttis concern accouterment; the Vrttis concern bodily movements; and the Ritis relate to sound” (Kavya-mimamsa 3).

According to Singabhupala, the Bharati is so called because it is used by actors (bharata): prayuktatvena bharatair bharatiti nigadyate \| prastavanopayogitvat sangam tatraiva laksyate \|\| (Rasarnava-sudhakara 1.261)

Moreover, Dr. Manomohana Ghosh gives details about the antiquity of Indian music, in reference to the dating of Natya-sastra:

Narada, mentioned repeatedly in later literature on music, seems to be the earliest writer on the subject, and the Siksa named after him appears, apart from its interpolated passages, to be a very old work, and it may be as old as 600 B.C., and its teachings may be earlier still. \[...\] The fact that it describes the Gandhara Grama in detail (together with its Murchanas) shows clearly that it is much anterior to the NS which ignores altogether this Grama and was written when they became obsolete. The NS quotes the NaS (1.2.13) at least once (XXXIII.227) without naming it. As this Siksa discusses the seven notes in the three Gramas and the Murchanas and Tanas connected with them, the Indian Music seems to have been pretty advanced at the time when this work was composed.

srngara-rasa-sambhava \|\| asakya purusaih sa tu prayoktum stri-janad rte \| tato ’srjan maha-teja manasapsaro vibhuh \|\| (Natya-sastra 1.45-46)

In Natya-sastra, many names of Indian places are listed: pancala saurasenas ca kasmira hastinapurah, bahlika salyakas caiva madra-kausinaras tatha (13.48). The term Bharata-varsa is stated: punas ca bharate varse tams tan varnan nibodhata (21.104). And names of tribes or groups of people are mentioned: kirata- barbarandhras ca dravidah kasi-kosalah, pulinda daksinatyas ca prayena tv asitah smrtah, sakas ca yavanas caiva pahlava vahlikas ca ye (21.110-111).

Dr. Ghosh notes that although Bhasa and Kalidasa indicated their knowledge of Natya-sastra, such as using technical terms seen therein, they disregarded several rules and invented novel methods of presentation (Ghosh (1951) Vol. I, Introduction, pp. 82-86).

## 2. Visnu-dharmottara Upapurana

This work is not easily available: “It is a matter for some surprise that, though the Agni Purana has come in for treatment at the hands of several scholars, this Purana, which contains very valuable material on Dramaturgy and Poetics in its third section (khanda) has not been thoroughly studied by any scholar so far.” P.V. Kane expounds upon the chronology:

There is another very important consideration which weighed with me in placing Visnu-dharmottara even before Bhatti. According to the commentators, Bhatti gives examples of about 38 figures of speech. Dandin, Bhamaha, Vamana and Udbhata all mention between 30 to 40 Alankaras, while the Visnu- dharmottara enumerates and defines only 17 alankaras in chap. 14, all the verses of which are set out here. \[...\] The figures are: anuprasa, yamaka, rupaka, vyatireka, slesa, utpreksa, arthantara-nyasa, upanyasa, vibhavana, atisayokti, varta, yatha-samkhya, visesokti, virodha, ninda-stuti, nidarsana, ananvaya. It must of course be said that it knew upama also. So at the most eighteen Alankaras were thought worthy of being mentioned by the Visnu-dharmottara.

If we hold that the 2nd section of Visnu-dharmottara is of the same date as the 3rd section, then it would follow that the Purana is later than Varahamihira. Visnu-dharmottara II.176.9- 11 are borrowed from the Brhad-yoga-yatra of Varahamihira, since the Adbhuta-sagara pp. 494-5 quotes seven verses from the Brhad-yoga-yatra of which Visnu-dharmottara II.176.9- 11 are three. Besides, Visnu-dharmottara II.124.15-26 are identical with Brhat-samhita 45.82-94 (Dwivedi’s ed.) on utpatas. So the Visnu-dharmottara (3rd part) will have to be placed between 575 to 650 A.D., the period during which Bhatti most probably flourished or a little earlier.

Dr. Sushil Kumar De provides other details:

In some of these verses reference is made to older authorities (puratana orpurana). Ch. 15 speaks of Kavya and distinguishes it from Sastra and Itihasa. The Mahakavya is then defined and characterised; it should contain nine Rasas, namely, Smgara, Hasya, Karuna, Raudra, Vira, Bhayanaka, Bibhatsa, Adbhuta and Santa; there should be description of towns, countries etc ; it should have a Nayaka and Pratinayaka, but it should not describe the death of the Nayaka. Ch. 16 names, defines and classifies Prahelikas. Ch. 17-31, based mostly on Bharata’s Natya-sastra, deal generally with dramaturgy.

\[...\] The section is essentially a rapid compilation and presents no definite system. The date of the Upapurana, however, must be early. It is later certainly than Bharata’s Natya-sastra which is used as a source, but it is earlier probably than Bhatti and the works of Bhamaha and Dandin, who enumerate a much larger number of poetic figures. Its internal evidence as a whole indicates that it cannot be earlier than 400 A. D. and later than 500 A. D. It was composed either in Kashmir or in the northernmost part of the Panjab; but its date is too early for any reference, direct or indirect, to the Kashmirian Dhvani school.

Dr. Lele adds:

The compiler of the VDP is of the opinion that the poetic compositions are written artistically, that they describe only two purusarthas, namely dharma and artha and that they give no advice: tad eva kavyam ity uktam copadesam vina krtam I kavyam kala-kausala-samprayuktam dharmena carthena tathopapannam \|\| (VDP 1.15). Thus the VDP looks at kavya as a work of art carried out with great skill but not burdened with advice.

## 3. Bhatti

Bhatti flourished between 590 and 650 CE. He wrote Bhatti- kavya, also called Ravana-vadha. Some scholars classify it as the sixth maha-kavya. This work is not a poetical treatise per se: It is a grammar-based epic: On the theme of Ramayana, Bhatti exemplified Panini’s grammatical rules. Other famous works in this genre are Halayudha’s Kavi-rahasya, which illustrates Sanskrit verbal forms by a eulogy of King Krsna III, and Hemacandra’s Kumarapala-carita, which exemplifies Hemacandra’s Sanskrit grammar and Prakrit grammar by recounting the life of King Kumarapala. In Hari-namamrta-vyakarana, Jiva Gosvami quotes Bhatti-kavya several times to exemplify grammatical rules. Further, Dr. De writes:

At one time it was believed, on the indication given by the Jayamangala on Bhatti, that the Alankara chapters in that

Kavya, especially canto x, was meant to illustrate the rhetorical teachings of Bhamaha in particular; but the date now assigned to Bhamaha will re-adjust his relation to Bhatti in a new light.

Bhatti was himself no theorist but only professed to illustrate the poetic figures popular in his time and presumably based his treatment on some standard treatise. The conclusion, therefore, is likely that Bhatti made use of a text unknown to Bhamaha but not materially differing from Bhamaha’s own sources.

Dr. Kane expounds:

This poem of 22 cantos was composed mainly for illustrating the rules of Sanskrit grammar. \[...\] In the tenth sarga (75 verses, 74 in Mallinatha) he gives illustrations of 38 Alankaras (including the two sabdalankaras of anuprasa and yamaka). The 11th illustrates madhurya-guna (in 47 verses); the 12th illustrates the figure bhavika (which is said to be prabandha- visaya by Bhamaha II.53 and Dandi II.364) in 87 verses and the 13th elucidates bhasa-sama in 50 verses (where the same verse may be regarded as composed in Sanskrit as well as in Prakrit). On account of these four sargas Bhatti deserves at least a passing notice in the History of Alankara literature. It will be seen from the comparative table in section 13 below that Bhatti illustrates almost the same figures as are defined by Bhamaha and Dandi.

\[.\] From this it is clear that Bhatti does not follow either Bhamaha or Dandin, but bases his examples on some other work or works that were prior to both of them. It may be stated here that Bhatti (in the 10th sarga) does not expressly name any figure of speech. It is the mss. that mention the several figures over the verses and the commentators differ among themselves as to the figures of speech in several verses. K.P. Trivedi in his Introduction to Bhatti-kavya mentions thirteen commentaries on it.

The commentary Jaya-mangala is comparatively an old one. It quotes only such Alankara writers as Bhamaha and Dandin, but does not quote Mammata. So the author who had three names (Jayesvara, Jayadeva, Jayamangala) flourished after 800 and before 1050 A.D.

Mallinatha who flourished in the 15th century and who often relies on such late works as the Pratapa-rudrlya differs about 20 times at least from the Jaya-mangala and sometimes very harshly criticizes the latter.

For instance, Jayamangala says verse 10.50 is an example of paryayokta, whereas Mallinatha says it illustrates bhrantiman, invented by Rudrata. Regarding another verse, P.G. Lalye says: “It is thus obvious that Jayamangala is following Bhamaha whereas Mallinatha is following Ruyyaka, the author of Alankara- sarvasva.” Mallinatha superimposed on Bhatti’s poem concepts of ornaments that did not exist in those days, whereas Jayamangala revealed what Bhatti had in mind:

As far as the alankaras in Bhatti-kavya are concerned, some special points are worth noting. Jayamangala, another commentator, has pointed out figures of speech in the tenth canto of Bhattikavya whereas Mallinatha has pointed them from all the cantos. He has defined about twenty-five alankaras (arthalankaras). He has adopted the definitions of Prataparudriya of Vidyanatha for about twenty alankaras. Mallinatha has pointed out some alankaras, six to be precise, which were not very much in currency in the days of Bhatti. They are karana-mala, kavya-linga, pratipa, bhrantiman, sama, and drstanta. \[...\] In Bhatti-kavya verse X.22, the figure of speech is Adi-dipaka and verse X.24 is Anta-dipaka, according to Jayamangala. But Mallinatha identifies them as karana-mala and kavya-linga respectively.

Mallinatha has a wide renown. He was a master of poetic theory: “Mallinatha, as a learned rhetorician, has pointed the figures of speech, virtually in every verse of the five maha-kavyas. ” Among the works of the great poets, Bhatti-kavya stands out because one whole chapter specifically illustrates ornaments and because no poetical treatise between Natya-sastra and Kavyadarsa has been recovered.

Of the seventy-five verses of chapter ten, the first twenty-two, except the first one, are examples of the ornament of sound called yamaka (word rhyme); the other verses mostly illustrate ornaments of meaning. In his commentary on Bhatti-kavya, Sesaraja Sarma relates Jayamangala’s interpretations: Jayamangala says this verse illustrates taddhita upama (a simile expressed with a taddhita suffix) (in atma-vat). It is in the category of elliptical simile. The context is: Hanuman returned from Lanka, brought back Sita’s crest jewel, and handed it over to Rama:

*avasanna-rucim vanagatam*  
*tam anamrsta-rajo-vidhusaram \|*  
*samapasyad apeta-maithilim*  
*dadhatam gaurava-matram atma-vat \|\|*  
*(sundari)*

**Rama looked upon that jewel as if it were Himself: Its splendor had faded, it was vanagata (it had come from a grove: Asokavana in Lanka) (as a pun: He had entered the forest), it was greyish with a film of dust that had not been wiped off, it had been separated from STta, and it was merely worth its intrinsic value (gaurava-matra) (or: all He had left was His venerability). (Bhatti-kavya 10.34)**

Jayamangala says the following verse is an example of arthantara- nyasa (corroboration). The verse also features yamaka (word rhyme) (in bold type). Hanuman speaks:

*ahrta dhanesvarasya yudhi yah same****ta-mayo dhanam***  
*tam aham ito vilokya vibudhaih krtot****tamayodhanam*** *\|*  
*vibhava-madena nihnuta-hriyatimat****ra-sampannakam***  
*vyathayati sat-pathad adhigatathaveh****a sampan na kam*** *\|\|*  
*(nandanam)*

ahrta—he stole; dhana-isvarasya—of Kuvera (“the master of wealth”); yudhi—in battle; yah—who; sameta-mayah—he with whom magic is connected; dhanam—wealth; tam—him; aham—I; itah—returned; vilokya—after seeing; vibudhaih—with demigods; krta-uttama-ayodhanam—he by whom a great fight was done; vibhava—due to might; madena—with arrogant pride; nihnuta- hriya—\[pride,\] by which shame is suppressed; atimatra—with exorbitance; sampannakam—endowed; vyathayati—makes one go astray; sat-pathat—from the good path; adhigata—obtained; athava—at all; iha—here (in this world); sampad—wealth; na— not; kam—whom?

**I have returned after seeing Ravana. He has magical powers. He stole Kuvera’s treasures in battle. He has an exorbitant attitude with the pride of his might, which suppresses his sense of shame. Who in this world is not driven from the right path by acquired opulence? (Bhatti-kavya 10.37)**

This is a twist on the nidarsana ornament (illustration):

**na bhavati mahima vina vipatter**  
**avagamayann iva pasyatah payodhih \|**  
**aviratam abhavat ksane ksane ’sau**  
**sikhari-prihu-praihiia-prasania-vicih \|\|**  
**(puspitagra)**

**As if making the onlookers understand that there is no greatness without adversity, the ocean gradually decreased the intensity of its mountain-like waves. (Bhatti-kavya 10.63)**

Jayamangala says the verse illustrates nidarsana (also called nidarsana). However, Bhatti uses the word iva (as if), a charac­teristic of utpreksa (fanciful assumption). Bhamaha says that in nidarsana a word such as iva should not be used. Similarly, Dandin makes no reference to such words (Kavyadarsa 2.348), and Vamana follows suit (Kavyalankara-sutra 4.3.20). Udbhata and Rudrata do not acknowledge nidarsana. For Bhatti, Bhamaha, Dandin, and Vamana, nidarsana is so called because it illustrates a moral precept.

Jayamangala says this is Bhatti’s example of the ananvaya orna­ment (self-comparison): viyati ca vilalasa tad-vad indur vilasati candramaso na yad-vad anyah, “In the sky, the moon shone that way. No one else is resplendent like that” (Bhatti-kavya 10.69). In Mammata’s terms, the verse features an elliptical simile characterized by the absence of a subject of description (upameya- lope luptopama).

According to Jayamangala, the next verse is an example of utpreksavayava (an utpreksa with additional aspects (rupaka and slesa)). The moderns call this a samsrsti (combination) of utpreksa (fanciful assumption), rupaka (metaphor) and slesa (pun) (literal double meaning):

*saranam iva gatam tamo nikunje*  
*vitapi-nirakrta-candra-rasmy-aratau \|*  
*prthu-visama-silantarala-samstham*  
*sa-jala-ghana-dyuti-bhtta-vat sasada \|\|*

saranam—to a shelter iva—as if; gatam—went; tamah—darkness; nikunje—in an arbor; vitapi—by trees (“they have branches”); nirakrta—are excluded; candra-rasmi—\[in the form of\] the rays of the moon; aratau—\[the arbor,\] in which the enemies; prthu—broad; visama—uneven; sila—of rocks; antarala—in the intermediate spaces; samstham—a presence (or a location); sa-jala—which has water; ghana—in a cloud (or of a cloud); dyuti—of the glimmer (or \[the location\], which has a glimmer); bhita-vat—as if afraid; sasada—obtained.

**The darkness as if went for shelter in the grove where its enemies the moonbeams were excluded by trees and, as though it were afraid of lightning in a rain cloud, took refuge in the interstices of large uneven rocks (or: as though it were afraid, took refuge in the interstices of large uneven rocks which looked like rain clouds). (Bhatti-kavya 10.70)**

Bhatti invented what is now called ekavali (modified series):

*na taj jalam yan na sucaru-pankajam na pankajam*  
*tat yad alina-satpadam \|*  
*na satpado ’sau jugunja yah kalam*  
*na gunjitam tan na jahara yan manah \|\|*

**A pond not graced with a beautiful lily is not a pond. A lotus without a bee inside is not a lotus. A bee that does not hum sweetly is not a bee. And a humming that does not charm the heart is not a hum. (2.19) (Kavya-prakasa, verse 549)**

## 4. Dandin

His treatise is called Kavyadarsa (the mirror of poetry). Dandin is also famous for his Dasa-kumara-carita. Whether Dandin lived before Bhamaha is a subject of controversy. In their works, many specific topics are similar, and many passages are exactly the same. The date of Dandin is one of the most difficult problems in the chronology of Alankara literature. In short, Dr. Kane writes: “Dandin, the great-grandson of Bharavi’s friend, should have his literary activity placed 75 to 90 years later (i.e. between 660 and 680 A.D.)”. Dr. Keith states:

If, for reasons which will be given later, we place the Kavyadarsa definitely before Bhamaha (c. A.D. 700), there is no reason to assert that he wrote much earlier.

\[...\] The matter is not indeed, of the highest importance, for it is not supposed in any case that Dandin lived long after Bhamaha, who certainly used the works of Udyyota-kara (c. 650) and probably knew the Nyasa of Jinendra-buddhi (c. 700). On the whole, having regard to the facts regarding the Dasakumara-carita, which suggests that it precedes Subandhu and Bana, we may place Dandin some generations before Bhamaha.

Dr. Kane remarks:

Vide Prof. V.V. Mirashi’s paper on the ‘Historical Data in the Dasa-kumara-carita’ in ABORI. vol. 26 pp. 20-31, where he arrives at the conclusion that the political conditions described in the 8th Ucchvasa of the Dasa-kumara-carita point to the inference that Dandin must have flourished not long after 550 A.D.

The sixth century had been accepted by many scholars as the date of Dandin. Vide Max Muller (India; what can it teach us; 1st edition p. 332

\[...\] Bhamaha himself says that Medhavin enumerated seven upama-dosas (vide II.40). So this was an ancient topic. One may rather use this as an argument for Dandin’s priority. Dandin names only four upama-dosas (II.51) while Medhavi knows seven and Bhamaha follows the latter. So Dandi was the pioneer. Vamana speaks of six upama-dosas.

Another subject of controversy regards a verse by Rajasekhara, which states that Dandin is famous because of three works. Dr. Kane comments:

All that the verse means is that three compositions of Dandin are well-known in all the worlds and not that Dandin wrote only three works.

Considering all that has been said by many scholars I am inclined to hold on the whole (though with some hesitation) that the Avanti-sundari-katha is a work of Dandin (though not the Sara) and constitutes the prelude to the current Dasa- kumara-carita.

\[.\] The third work of Dandin is the Dvi-sandhana-kavya ascribed to Dandin by the Smgara-prakasa. Dr. Raghavan kindly informs me that the Madras ms. of Smgara-prakasa vol. II. p. 444 mentions the Dvi-sandhana-kavya of Dandin as an illustration of prabandha-visaya-dvi-sandhana (presenting in the same work the stories of both epics viz. Ramayana and Mahabharata).

Ironically, Avantisundan is the name of Rajasekhara’s wife. Dr. Keith states his opinion:

The effort to strengthen the case for dating Dandin later than Bhamaha by using the evidence of the Avanti-sundari-katha and its Sara is clearly a complete mistake. The Katha should never have been published from one mutilated manuscript, whose readings, even if correctly stated, have already been proved wrong by other manuscript evidence. Even, however, from the mutilated text it was clear that Bharavi was not made out to be the great-grandfather of Dandin, who is given as Damodara. But, as Dr. De has pointed out, even the most careless reader of the Katha and the Dasa-kumara-carita should have been struck by the extraordinary difference of style between the two works, the Katha rivalling unsuccessfully the worst mannerisms of the Harsa-carita and the Kadambari. If a Dandin wrote the work, he was assuredly not the author of the Dasa-kumara-carita, and its date may be centuries later than the great Dandin,

Dr. Kane says perhaps Dandin originated from the middle part of India: “Apart from the statements in the Avanti-sundari-katha, he appears to have belonged to the Deccan or to some part south of the Narmada.” Still, as shown ahead (verse 3.114), it is obvious that Dandin was very familiar with Kanchipuram, in modern-day Tamil Nadu. According to Sesaraja Sarma, Dandin resided in Kanchi, although some say he lived in Berar (eastern Maharashtra, south of the Narmada).

Dr. Sushil Kumar De writes:

The conclusion is very probable that Dandin was familiar with the text ofBhamaha whom, as a notable predecessor expressing contrary views, he could hardly ignore. On this point we have the almost unanimous testimony of Dandin’s commentators, who expressly state that in most of these disputed passages Dandin controverts the earlier opinions of Bhamaha.

Dr. Kane responds:

The commentator Taruna-vacaspati distinctly says that in some places Dandin criticizes Bhamaha (e.g. on Dandi I.23, 29; II.235, 358 and III. 127). Taruna-vacaspati is comparatively a late writer. He quotes from the Dasa-rupaka (on Dandi II.281) \[...\]. So Taruna-vacaspati flourished in the first half of the 13th century i.e. about 6 centuries after Dandin. He found conflicting views and thinks that Dandi criticizes Bhamaha. A similar example will illustrate how unsafe it is to rely upon later commentators in the matter of chronology. Cakravarti- bhattacarya in his commentary on the Kavya-prakasa thinks that Mammata criticizes the view of the Alankara-sarvasva on the verse rajati tatiyam (10th ullasa) and so says Nagoji also; while Jayaratha (who wrote about 1200 and was very near to both Mammata and the Sarvasva) thinks that the Sarvasva criticizes the Kavya-prakasa (p. 250 of Sarvasva). Therefore Taruna-vacaspati’s remarks should carry hardly any evidence with us in the absence of other very cogent evidence.

\[.\] Before proceeding further three points must be made clear and emphasized. One is that both Bhamaha and Dandi have several passages in common as specified above. The second point is that both expressly say that they had before them the works of older teachers on Poetics and Bhamaha actually names one of them viz. Medhavin. This should warn us against jumping to the conclusion that one necessarily borrows from the other when they have identical verses or one appears to criticise the other when their views conflict. This fact and our ignorance of what went before Bhamaha and Dandi should make all of us reluctant to dogmatise and should dispose us to regard as probable the hypothesis that both are quoting from or criticizing older works now lost. The third point is that both are comparatively very early writers and very near to each other in point of time.

\[...\] It seems that Bhamaha and Dandi follow independent traditions, the former having more affinity with the Alankara school and the latter with Bharata’s school. \[.\] I hold that the reasons so far assigned for Dandin’s priority are far more weighty (though not thoroughly decisive) than those assigned for Bhamaha’s priority.

But if the account of Dandin’s life in “his” Avanti-sundari-katha is accepted as genuine autobiography, it follows that Dandin was a great-grandson of a certain Damodara, a poet from Vidarbha patronized in Kanchi; Dandin was born there, and left Kanchi because of the threat of invasion. Yigal Bronner explains:

In the late 1920s scholars such as Keith and De argued for the existence of wide stylistic gaps between the Avantisundari and the Dasakumaracarita and claimed that the two could not have been by the same author, let alone parts of the same work.

I find all this odd and indicative of a deep-rooted suspicion of any biographical testimony supplied by the relevant texts and later tradition. Indeed, this suspicion paradoxically stands in inverse relationship to the elaborateness and dependability of the testimony, so that the richer and better the data, the more profound the doubts. But the fact is that in the Avantisundari, a work unmistakably ascribed to Dandin by its colophons and by later sources, the author provides uniquely ample information about himself and his surroundings. With the exception of Bana, whose Harsacarita likely served as Dandin’s model here, no early Sanskrit writer ever provided such a detailed autobiographical account. Dandin begins with a lengthy description of the city of Kanci and of a Pallava king named Simhavisnu. When Simhavisnu holds court one day, a musician sings a beautiful verse blessing the presiding king; the singer of the verse then informs the king of its author, Damodara, hailing from the city of Anandapura. This up- and-coming poet, the king is told, came in contact with the great poet Bharavi. He also received patronage from a prince named Visnudharma. This relationship ended on a sour note, however, when the prince offended the vegetarian Damodara by offering him meat during a hunting expedition, after which incident Damodara joined the services of King Durvinita from the Ganga lineage. On the basis of this recommendation, which included a sample verse and a short but impressive resume tying Damodara to some of the leading poets and royal houses of his time, Simhavisnu invites Damodara to join his court in Kanci. The 20-year-old Damodara is promptly recruited and enjoys a successful and fruitful tenure under Simhavisnu’s generous patronage. At this point in the narrative, Dandin turns to detail his own ancestry as the great-grandson of the young court poet: Damodara was married in Kanci and fathered three sons; his middle-born, Manoratha, had four sons; Manoratha’s youngest son, Viradatta, married a Brahmin woman, Gauri, and they had several daughters and, eventually, a son, Dandin. Dandin then reports that he lost his mother at the age of seven and his father shortly thereafter, and that as an orphan, he had to flee Kanci because of an enemy invasion and was able to return only once peace was restored. \[...\]

Also significant is the mention of a disruptive invasion of the Pallava kingdom, which is likely the Calukya sacking of Kanci described in the Gadval inscription of Vikramaditya I Calukya (dated to 674 CE). These details all suggest that Dandin’s active career took place around 680-720 CE under the auspices of Narasimhavarman \|\| Rajasimha in Kanci (r. 690/1-728/9). In all the scholarship written on this topic, I have not found a single good reason that we should dismiss this godsend of good and rich data.

## Sequence of Topics

Dandin’s Kavyadarsa is a very original work with short yet charming examples. Dr. Kane notes:

The Kavyadarsa is throughout written in a flowing, mellifluous style. As compared with Bhamaha, the palm of superiority in the sphere of poetic excellence must be given to Dandin, though as regards precision and logical acumen Bhamaha stands higher than Dandin. Dandin’s examples bear the stamp of originality.

Dandi has not been shown to quote any verse from another author except limpativa.

The Kavyadarsa consists of 660 verses in three chapters: (1) The two styles: Vaidarbha (the southern style) and Gaudiya (the eastern style), (2) Ornaments of meaning, and (3) Ornaments of sound, and literary blemishes. In some editions, the section on literary faults forms a fourth chapter. Dandin’s literary faults (Kavyadarsa 3.125­126) are the same as Bhamaha’s ten faults (in the group of eleven) (Bhamahalankara 4.1-2), but Dandin added that pondering whether pratijna-hetu-drstanta-hani, the eleventh fault in Bhamaha’s list, is a fault is useless (Kavyadarsa 3.127).

Dandin established a difference, in name and principle, between ornaments of meaning (artha alankara) and ornaments of sound (sabda alankara): sabdarihalankriyah (Kavyadarsa 3.186).

This is Dandin’s definition of poetry: sariram iavad istariha- vyavacchinna padavali, “Poetry is simply a body which is a series of declined words taken separately from the intended meanings” (Kavyadarsa 1.10). Dr. Belvalkar comments: “Kavya, according to Dandin, is istartha-vyavacchinna padavali, that is to say, he gives more prominence to the word-element in poetry as compared with the sense-element.” Dandin and Vamana valued sound over meaning.

For the most part, Dandin reiterated Bharata Muni’s interpretations of the ten gunas. One peculiarity of Dandin’s and Vamana’s systems is that the gunas are types of alankara (ornament) in the broad sense of “embellishment”. At the outset of his treatment of figures of speech, Dandin draws a distinction between them:

*kascin marga-vibhagartham uktah prag apy alankriyah \| sadharanam alankara-jatam anyat pradarsyate \|\|*

**“Some ornaments (the gunas) were mentioned earlier (in the first chapter) to differentiate the two styles. Now the rest of the category of alankara is shown: Those ornaments apply to both styles (marga = riti).” (2.3)**

Dr. Sushil Kumar De expounds:

It must be distinctly understood that the word alankara is used by Dandin in the general sense of that which causes beauty in poetry: kavya-sobha-karan dharman alankaran pracaksate (ii.1). \[...\] In other words, poetic figures are Alankaras common (sadharana) to both Margas, while Gunas are Alankaras as belonging exclusively to the Vaidarbha.

It must also be pointed out that some of Dandin’s Gunas refer to sabda (word), some to artha (sense), while others to both these elements.

Jacobi points out that the Gauda Marga, long before Dandin, could never establish for itself a good reputation, and Bana had already condemned it as aksara-dambara (Harsa-carita i.7). Dandin, on the other hand, attaches great importance to Riti in poetry, which, under the name marga, occupies a considerable part of his treatment. \[.\] He himself prefers the vaidarbha.

Bana had mentioned four styles: The North Indian style was mostly based on slesa-guna (coalescence of words), the West Indian style merely on artha (meaning), the South Indian style on utpreksa (poetic fancy), and the Gauda style on aksara-dambara (bombastic sounds). Dr. Sushil Kumar De explains:

This disparaging observation regarding the Gaudas is explained by the suggestion that it reflects a partisan spirit on the part of the court poet of Harsa-vardhana, which is also clear from the feeling which he displays towards his patron’s rival, the unnamed but much maligned king of Gauda.

Shashanka (c. 600-625 CE) was the first independent king of Bengal. He established himself in Gauda, the north-western region of Bengal, and made Kornosubora in Murshidabad his capital. He gradually extended his authority in Orissa (Odisha), in parts of Central Provinces and in Bihar.

Dandin selected the southern style and the eastern style, especially since they are poles apart, and detailed the methodology:

*asty aneko giram margah suksma-bhedah parasparam \|*  
*tatra vaidarbha-gaudiyau varnyete prasphutantarau \|\|*  
*slesah prasadah samata madhuryam sukumarata \|*  
*artha-vyaktir udaratvam ojah-kanti-samadhayah \|\|*  
*iti vaidarbha-margasya prana dasa gunah smrtah \|*  
*esam viparyayah prayo laksyate gauda-vartmani II*

**“There is more than one path for words. The differences are subtle. In that regard, the Vaidarbha is polished whereas the Gaudiya is bombastic. The ten qualities are: slesa, prasada, samata, madhurya, sukumarata, artha-vyakti, udaratva, ojas, kanti, and samadhi. They are the ten life airs of the path of the Vaidarbha. For the most part, their opposites are perceived on the path of the Gauda” (1.40-42).**

## Dandin’s Ten Gunas

anayor anavadyangi-stanayor jrmbhamanayoh \|  
avakaso na paryaptas tava bahu-latantare \|\|

*‘O maiden with faultless limbs, there is not space enough between thy creeper-like arms for the expansion of those swelling breasts.’ The Gauda exaggerates:*

alpam nirmitam akasam analocyaiva vedhasa \|  
idam evam-vidham bhavi bhavatyah stana-jhrmbhanam \|\|

*‘Surely the creator hath made this world too narrow, fore­seeing not so great an extension of thy breasts.&rsquo*

madhuram rasa-vad vaci vastuny api rasa-sthitih \|  
yena madyanti dhlmanto madhuneva madhuvratah \|\|  
yaya kayacic chrutya yat samanam anubhuyate \|  
tad-rupa hi padasattih sanuprasa rasavaha \|\|

*“Intelligent bees, those dedicated to nectar, are mad about sweet words. Such words have a relishment—the relishment of the sounds and of the idea conveyed by them. Sruti anuprasa (alliteration for the ears), a series of words by which a similarity of sounds is perceived, conveys the relishment” (1.51-52).*

## Ornaments of Meaning

At the beginning of the second chapter, Dandi lists the ornaments of meaning (thirty-four in total, excluding samsrsti):

*svabhavakhyanam upama rupakam dipakavrttih \|*  
*aksepo ’rthantara-nyaso vyatireko vibhavana \|\| samasatisayotpreksa hetuh suksmo lavah kramah \|*  
*preyo rasavad urjasvi paryayoktam samahitam \|\| udattapahnuti-slesa-visesas tulya-yogita \|*  
*virodhaprastuta-stotre vyaja-stuti-nidarsane \|\|*  
*sahoktih parivriiy-as'ih-sank'irnam atha bhavikam \|*  
*iti vacam alankara darsitah purva-suribhih \|\|*

**“These ornaments of words were shown by previous scholars: svabhavakhyana (svabhavokti), upama, rupaka, dipaka, avrtti, aksepa, arthantara-nyasa, vyatireka, vibhavana, samasa (samasokti), atisaya (atisayokti), utpreksa, hetu, suksma, lava (lesa), krama (yatha-samkhya), preyas, rasavat, urjasvin, paryayokta, samahita, udatta, apahnuti, slesa, visesa (visesokti), tulya-yogita, virodha, aprastuta-stotra, vyaja-stuti, nidarsanam, sahokti, parivrtti, asih, sankirna (samsrsti), and bhavika” (Kavyadarsa 2.4-7).**

Dandi used some synonyms to fit the meter. Moreover, the figure called asih (blessing) was dropped by most rhetoricians although it is often seen in religious poetry. His example is: patu vah paramam jyotir avan-manasa-gocaram, “May the topmost effulgence, beyond the range of word and mind, protect you all” (2.357). Dr. Belvalkar comments:

The figure asih recognised by Dandin is recognised by no other Alankarika except Bhamaha and Vagbhata the author of the

Kavyanusasana. It should be noted, however, that the name occurs amongst the 36 effective literary devices mentioned by Bharata in the beginning of the 16th Chapter.

Bhamaha mentioned aslh in passing, by saying that some consider it an ornament: aslr api ca kesancid alankarataya mata (Bhamahalankara 3.55). Rupa Gosvami says aslh is used at the beginning of a play (Nataka-candrika 15) (Lalita-madhava 1.1).

In Dandi’s system of ornaments of meaning, svabhavokti and vakrokti are the two most important concepts. The svabhavokti ornament (a special characteristic, lit. “a mention of the nature”) stands by itself, and all others are in the category of vakrokti (poetic expression). In that regard, Dandi highly valued slesa (literal double meaning):

*slesah sarvasu pusnati priyo vakroktisu sriyam \|*  
*bhinnam dvidha svabhavoktir vakroktis ceti van-mayam \|\|*

**“ Slesa is precious. It nourishes the resplendence in all the vakroktis. The realm of words is separated in two categories: svabhavokti and vakrokti.” (2.363)**

Dr. Sushil Kumar De explains:

The term vakrokti is used only once and is reserved by him as a collective name of all poetic figures barring the svabhavokti. According to Dandin’s scheme (as indicated in ii.363), the whole realm of poetic figures can be divided into two distinct groups, consisting of svabhavokti, on one hand, and vakrokti, on the other. By the former, which he characterises as the first or primary figure (adya alankrtih), he implies a plain and direct description of things belonging to a genus (jati), or of an action (kriya), or of a quality (guna), or of an individual (dravya). In this so-called natural description, there is apparently no scope for any artificial or ingenious mode of expression, and it should, therefore, be distinguished from all other poetic devices, figurative or otherwise, collectively designated as the vakrokti.

Hence, the word “poetic figure” or kavyalankara, \[is used\] instead of “figure of speech.” In a formal scheme of Poetics they no doubt correspond, but this point of view of its involving poetic charm would be entirely omitted in a treatise of rhetoric. It is, therefore, misleading to translate Sanskrit Alankara as Sanskrit Rhetoric.

Dandi did not define vakrokti. The term was used by Bana. The svabhavokti was also called jati by Dandi (2.8), Bana, and Rudrata. One might think that Dandi should not have classed asih as a vakrokti. In usage, however, the poets used asih in a crooked way: By using a present participle on that occasion, the poet says the blessing, in the form of the Deity’s protecting the readers, should occur while the Deity is performing the action which is the subject of description. An example is incidentally shown in Ratnakara’s verse at the end of Appendix I.

Dandi innovated in many ways:

He mentions by name (ii. 4-7) only thirty-five poetic figures; but the special feature of his treatment, as contrasted with those of Bhamaha and Vamana, consists in his attempt to make a large number of subordinate varieties, the most remarkable instance being that of upama, which has thirty-two subdivisions, of which eight at least have the value of independent figures to later writers.

Some say this proves Dandi lived before Bhamaha, because Bhamaha stated that aside from these varieties of upama— lupta, ninda, prasamsa, acikhyasa, prativastupama and upameyopama— malopama and other subcategories of upama are useless elaborations: malopamadih sarvo pii na jyayan vistaro mudha (Bhamahalankara 2.38). The malopama was illustrated by Dandi, who specifically used that name (Kavyadarsa 2.42).

Dandi indulged in hair splitting by creating numerous subcategories of simile and metaphor. This is Dandi’s example of atisaya upama (excessive simile): tvayy eva tvan-mukham drstam drsyate divi candramah, iyaty eva bhida nanyety asav atisayopama, “Your face is only seen in you. The moon is seen in the sky. That is the only difference” (2.22). Still, Dandi subsumed ananvaya (self­comparison) and sa-sandeha (poetic doubt) in the upama ornament (simile): ananvaya-sasandehav upamasv eva darsitau (2.358).

His tattvakhyana upama (a simile that says the truth), the reverse of the modern apahnuti (poetic denial), was renamed the niscaya ornament by Visvanatha Kaviraja, but Kavi Karnapura lists it as an additional variety of the sandeha ornament. Dandi gives this example: napadmam mukham evedam na bhrngau caksuslime, iti vispasta-sadrsyat tattvakhyanopamaiva sa, “This is not a lotus, it’s your face. And these are not two bees, these are your eyes” (2.36).

The modern pratlpa ornament, so called by Rudrata, has two main subdivisions, based on two subcategories of Dandi’s simile: viparyasa upama (reverse simile)—for example: tavananam ivonnidram aravindam abhut, “The open lotus looked like your face” (2.17)—and prasamsa upama (a comparison for the sake of a praise): brahmano ’py udbhavah padmam candrah sambhu-siro- dhrtah, tau tulyau tvan-mukheneti sa prasamsopamocyate, “The lotus, Brahma’s place of birth, and the moon, held by Siva on his head, are like your face” (2.31).

Dandi lists four kinds of faults in a simile (upama-dosa): linga- bheda (difference in gender), vacana-bheda (difference in num­ber), hlnata (deficiency) and adhikata (excess). He says they are not faults if they do not disturb a connoisseur: na linga-vacane bhinne na hinadhikatapi va \| upama-dusanayalam yatrodvego na dhimatam \|\| (2.51). This is the seed of the notion that a literary fault is not invariably faulty.

Dandi says the rupaka ornament (metaphor) has twenty-one varieties. Dandi’s hetu-rupaka is the prototype of the ullekha ornament (angles of description) (invented by Ruyyaka), according to Visvanatha Kaviraja. Dandi’s tattvapahnava-rupaka (a metaphor in which there is a concealment of the truth) (2.94-95) is the same as the modern apahnuti, so called by Bhamaha. Dandi’s apahnuti is a poetic denial that does not involve a similarity (an instance of the modern apahnuti is: “This is not a face, it’s a moon”). For example: apahnutir apahnutya kincid anyartha-darsanam, na pancesuh smaras tasya sahasram patrinam iti, “Cupid does not have five arrows; he has thousands of victims” (Kavyadarsa 2.304). Furthermore, this is Dandi’s example of upama-rupaka (a metaphor with a simile):

*ayam alohita-cchayo madena mukha-candramah \|*  
*sannaddhodaya-ragasya candrasya pratigarjati \|\|*

**This moon face whose splendor is red due to passion rivals the splendor of the moon which has the redness of sunrise. (2.89)**

It is an upama-rupaka because the moon face is compared to the moon. Dandi does not define the ornament. This is Bhamaha’s definition: upamanena tad-bhavam upameyasya sadhayan, yam vadaty upamam etad upama-rupakam yatha, “When the poet describes a simile while accomplishing the existence of an upameya (subject of the comparison) with an upamana (standard of comparison), that is upama-rupaka” (Bhamahalankara 3.35). Vamana defines it in this way: upama-janyam rupakam upama- rupakam, “An upama-rupaka is a metaphor generated from a simile”

(Kavyalankara-sutra 4.3.32). Bhamaha listed upama-rupaka as an ornament proper whereas Vamana said it is a kind of combination of ornaments (samsrsti). In modern theory, upama-rupaka no longer exists. In the verse, the verb pratigarjati (it rivals) expresses the simile. In that regard, Dandi spiced up simile: He listed words (such as iva, vat, va, yatha, prakasa, sama, anyuna), suffixes (such as kalpa and desiya), verbs (like spardhate, jayati, dvesti, druhyati, pratigarjati, akrosati, nindati, vidambayati, anveti), phrases (e.g. tulam tenadhirohati), and certain bahuvrihis, all of which are expressive of a simile, for a total of sixty-seven terms (Kavyadarsa 2.57-65). Nowadays, however, half of those locutions express the vyatireka ornament (contrast), which, as Dandi points out, involves a similarity, stated or implied, between the two contrasted things: sabdopatte pratite va sadrsye vastunor dvayoh \| tatra yad bheda- kathanam vyatirekah sa kathyate \|\| (2.180).

At first, Dandi states three categories of his avrtti ornament (repe­tition): (1) The repetition of a meaning: vikasanti kadambani sphutanti kutaja-drumah, unmilanti ca kandalyo dalanti kakubhani ca, “The Kadamba trees blossom, the Kutaja trees bloom, the Kandali plants flower, and the Kakubha trees effloresce” (2.117), (2) The repetition of a word (noun or verb): utkanthayati meghanam mala vrndam kalapinam, yunam cotkanthayaty eva manasam makaradhvajah, “The clouds make the peacocks have a longing, and Cupid makes the girls’ hearts have a longing” (2.118), and (3) A combination of both. According to Dandi, yamaka (word rhyme) is a special type of avrtti: avyapeta-vyapetatma vyavrttir varna- samhateh, yamakam (3.1).

Dandi’s arthantara-nyasa (corroboration) has eight varieties (2.170). This is his example of the subvariety based on slesa:

*utpadayati lokasya pritim malaya-marutah \|*  
*nanu daksinya-sampannah sarvasya bhavati priyah \|\|*

**The breeze from the Malaya Hills gives pleasure to all. Indeed, a person with southern manners (or with skill) (or with straight­forwardness) is dear to everyone. (2.174)**

Moreover, Dandi’s vibhavana ornament (an effect without a normal cause) is the same as the modern vibhavana. Dandi’s samasokti corresponds to the samasokti variety of aprastuta-prasamsa, whereas Bhamaha’s samasokti matches the modern understanding of it (Bhamahalankara 2.80). Moreover, Dandi exalted the atisayokti ornament (statement of superexcellence):

*vivaksa ya visesasya loka-simativartirii \|*  
*asav atisayoktih syad alankarottama yatha \|\|*  
*mallika-mala-bharinyah sarvangmardra-candanah \|*  
*ksaumavatyo na laksyante jyotsnayam abhisarikah \|\|*

**“Atisayokti is a description of a special entity, and that description goes beyond normal standards. It is the best of ornaments. For example: “Young women who are going to a tryst, who have garlands of jasmines, who have sandalwood paste all over their bodies, and who wear white linen clothes are not perceived in the moonlight”” (2.214-215).**

That example was taken by Mammata to illustrate his own samanya ornament (sameness).

In citing the verse that begins limpativa, Dandi established that when the word iva (like, as if) refers to high-flying imagination, the statement is classed as an utpreksa (fanciful assumption), otherwise it is an upama (simile).

Bhamaha rejected hetu, suksma and lesa, but Dandi calls them the topmost ornaments of words: hetus ca suksma-lesau ca vacam uttama-bhusanam (Kavyadarsa 2.235). Since Bhamaha mentions his rejection of those ornaments immediately after extolling vakrokti (poetic expression), Bhamaha implies that his reason for rejecting them is that he thinks there is no poetic expression in them. For his part, most likely Dandi reasons that in suksma, and occasionally in hetu and in lesa, a subtlety is involved.

Dandi divides hetu in four categories: karaka-hetu (a fully effective cause), jnapaka-hetu (a subtly informative cause, such as: smoke indicates fire), abhava-hetu (a nonexistent cause), and citra- hetu (an amazing cause, beyond the laws of nature). Each has many subvarieties. Dandi says citra-hetu takes place by qualitative figurative usage: citra-hetavah. te ’mi prayoga-margesu gauna- vrtti-vyapasrayah (2.253-254). In the context of subdivisions of karaka-hetu, he states three kinds of karmas (nirvarttya, vikarya, and prapya) (2.240), which are taken from Bhartrhari’s grammatical treatise called Vakya-padiya (3.45). This is Dandi’s example of pradhvamsa abhava-hetu (a cause that does not exist because it was brought to nil):

*gatah kama-kathonmado galito yauvana-jvarah \| ksato mohas cyuta trsna krtam punyasrame manah \|\|*

**The rapture of passionate talks is gone, the fever of youth has dissipated, bewilderment is utterly diminished, and cravings have vanished: The mind has found a place in the virtuous stage of life. (2.248)**

Visvanatha Kaviraja modified Dandi’s theory of hetu as follows: hetus tridha bhavati, jnapako nispadakah samarthakas ceti. tatra jnapako ’numanasya visayah, nispadakah kavya-lingasya samarthako ’rthantara-nyasasya, “There are three kinds of hetus: jnapaka, nispadaka (also called karaka-hetu), and samarthaka. In poetics, the jnapaka-hetu (subtly informative cause) is in the sphere of anumana (inference), the nispadaka-hetu (effective cause) belongs to kavya-linga (explanatory reason), and samarthaka- hetu (justification) relates to arthantara-nyasa (corroboration)”’ (Sahitya-darpana 10.62). In modern terms, the above verse is classed as the kavya-linga ornament.

Thus for the most part, Dandi’s hetu became known as kavya- linga. The hetu ornament of Rudrata, Visvanatha, and Baladeva, however, is a cause expressed as its effect, as in: yuva-jana-manaso vasi-karanam, “She is the subjugation of the minds of young men” (Sahitya-darpana 10.63), meaning she is the cause of the subjugation.

Pandita-raja Jagannatha says that although kavya-linga is nothing but the absence of the literary blemish called nirhetu (lacking an explanation), he acknowledges kavya-linga only because it was propounded by the ancients.

This is Dandi’s illustration of the subcategory called anyonya abhava-hetu (a reason which is a mutual nonexistence):

*vanany amuni na grhany eta nadyo na yositah \|*  
*mrga ime na dayadas tan me nandati manasam \|\|*

**These forests are not houses. These rivers are not women. And these deer do not need an inheritance. Therefore here my mind is at peace. (2.249)**

In modern poetics, the verse cannot be classed as the kavya-linga ornament because the word “therefore” is used. It cannot be classed as the anumana ornament either, because the reasons stated for the conclusion are not logically flawless. Rather, it can be classed in Ruyyaka’s and Visvanatha’s category of arthantara-nyasa where an effect is justified by a cause due to a contrast.

Further, Dandi’s suksma was accepted as is by Mammata and others: It involves a first-rate implied sense. Dandi’s lesa (lit. fraction) has three subdivisions. This is the definition of his first variety: leso lesena nirbhinna-vastu-rupa-niguhanam (Kavyadarsa 2.265). Ramacandra Misra elucidates: lesena svalpa-bhavena nirbhinnasyaprakatatam gatasya vastunah kasyapi rahasya-vastu- visesasya yad rupam svarupam tasya niguhanam pracchadanam, “Lesa is the concealment of the nature of some special secret idea that has become manifest with just a slight emotion (lesa = su- alpa-bhava).” This is Dandi’s example:

*raja-kanyanuraktam mam romodbhedena raksakah \|*  
*avagaccheyur a jnatam aho sitanilam vanam \|\|*

**By the visible manifestation of horripilation, the guards of the palace might understand that I am enamored of the king’s daughter. Aha, I remember: Everyone knows that a cool breeze blows in the forest. (2.266)**

In Mammata’s system, Dandi’s first lesa corresponds to the milita ornament (indistinct) only because of the concealment. The second and third varieties of Dandi’s lesa are stuti-ninda (criticism in the form of praise) and ninda-stuti (praise in the form of criticism) (2.268-272): Those two are the same as the two subvarieties of the modern vyaja-stuti. However, Dandi says vyaja-stuti is based on slesa (2.347). Another difference is that in lesa there is a fraction of a bhava. Dandi does not claim to have invented those two varieties, because in the definitions he writes: eke viduh (some know) (2.268). Bharata Muni had listed lesa among his thirty-six kavya-laksanas. After Dandi, the name lesa was ignored by almost everyone in poetics, or else it was interpreted differently. Rudrata’s definition of lesa is that either a fault has become a quality or a quality has become a fault (Kavyalankara 7.100-102): Bhoja and Jagannatha accepted this.

Dandi’s rasavat ornament includes the eight rasas. The old guard of poetical rhetoricians, most of whom lived before Anandavardhana invented the Dhvani theory (c. 850 CE), explained instances where a rasa occurs by only categorizing them as the literary ornaments called rasavat, preyas, Urjasvi, and samahita. In Dandi’s and Bhamaha’s methodologies, rasavat refers to a rasa, preyas to bhakti, and urjasvi to arrogant words or to any improper procedure in the scope of a rasa. Their samahita is the same as Mammata’s samadhi ornament.
