In the Alankara school, the concept of implied idea (vastu-dhvani), one of three types of implied meaning in the Dhvani theory (in addition to alankara-dhvani and rasa-dhvani), corresponds to Dandi’s paryayokta ornament (circumlocution). This is his example and explanation:

*dasaty asau parabhrtah sahakarasya manjanm \|*  
*tam aham varayisyami yuvabhyam asyatam iha \|\|*  
*sangamayya sakhlm yuna sankete tad-ratotsavam \|*  
*nirvartayitum icchantya kayapy apasrtam tatah \|\|*

**“\[A sakhi said:\] “That cuckoo is biting the buds of the mango tree. I’ll stop it from doing that. Both of you should stay here.” \[The explanation is:\] Some confidante had made her friend meet her lover in a secret place, then she departed, desiring to bring about their love fest.” (2.296-297)**

Dandi’s slesa ornament (double meaning) has two categories: abhinna-pada (not a different word) and bhinna-pada-praya (almost a different word) (Kavyadarsa 2.310). These varieties are now known as abhanga-slesa (the double meaning does not involve a different breakup of syllables) and sabhanga-slesa (the double meaning is achieved by separating the letters in a different way). Besides those two main categories, Dandi invented seven minor kinds of slesa: abhinna-kriya, aviruddha-kriya, viruddha-kriya, sa-niyama, niyamaksepa-rupa, avirodhi and virodhi (Kavyadarsa 2.314-315). This verse illustrates viruddha-kriya-slesa (a pun in which the actions are contradictory):

*ragam adarsayann esa varuni-yoga-vardhitam \|*  
*tirobhavati gharmamsur angajas tu vijrmbhate \|\|*

**While manifesting a redness (or a fervor) that has increased due to a connection with varum (the west) (or with liquor), the sun disappears, but passion thrives. (2.318)**

The following verse shows niyamaksepa-rupa-slesa (a pun in the form of denying what has just been affirmed):

*padmanam eva dandesu kantakas tvayi raksati \|*  
*athava drsyate ragi-mithunalinganesv api \|\|*

**When you are protecting the country, a thorn is only seen on the stems of roses. Or else it is also seen when two lovers are embracing. (2.320)**

When slesa is secondary, it is classed as a subvariety of the pre­dominant ornament. This is Dandi’s example of slesa-mula-virodha (seeming contradiction based on a double meaning):

*krsnarjunanuraktapi drstih karnavalambim \|*  
*yati visvasaniyatvam kasya te kala-bhasini \|\|*

krsna—of Krishna (or black); arjuna—and of Arjuna (or white); anurakta—passionate (or reddened); api—also; drstih—a sighting (or the eyes); karna-avalambini—relied on the ears; yati—attains; visvasaniyatvam—the state of being believable; kasya—by whom?; te—your; kala—is soft and sweet; bhasini—O you whose speech.

**Sweet-talking woman, who is going to believe that you had a passionate sighting of Krishna and Arjuna which caught your ears? (or Who is going to believe that your eyes are black, white and red and reach your ears?) (2.339)**

The contradiction is that a sighting cannot take hold of the ears. Moreover, Dandi defines visesa, also called visesokti, as follows: guna-jati-kriyadinam yatra vaikalya-darsanam, visesa- darsanayaiva sa visesoktir isyate, “Visesokti is that in which a defect of either a quality, a category, an action or a unique entity is shown for the sake of illustrating a specialty” (2.323). Only Bhamaha’s example corresponds to the modern visesokti (no effect in spite of a cause) (Bhamahalankara 3.24) (cited by Mammata and Visvanatha as an instance of visesokti). Dandi’s examples of guna- visesokti and hetu-visesokti are very similar to vibhavana (an effect without a normal cause). This verse illustrates guna-visesokti:

*na kathoram na va tiksnam ayudham puspadhanvanah \|*  
*tathapi jitam evasidamuna bhuvana-trayam \|\|*

**Cupid’s weapon is neither hard nor sharp, yet the three worlds were conquered with it. (2.324)**

This is Dandi’s example of dravya-visesokti:

*na ratha na ca matamga na haya na ca pattayah \|*  
*strinam apanga-drstyaiva jiyate jagatam trayam \|\|*

**The three worlds were conquered, not by war chariots, nor by elephants, nor by cavalry, nor by infantry, but only by the side looks of young women. (2.327)**

This exemplifies hetu-visesokti:

*eka-cakro ratho yanta vikalo visama hayah \|*  
*akramaty eva tejasvi tathapy arko nabhas-talam \|\|*  
*saisa hetu-visesoktis tejasviti visesanat I*

**“There is only one wheel. A charioteer is wanting. The horses are gone. Still the sun, being effulgent, keeps its pace in the backdrop of the sky. This is a hetu-visesokti because of the adjective: tejasvi (effulgent, powerful).” (2.328-329)**

Dandi’s tulya-yogita (connection with a similar attribute) is pecu­liar: It has two varieties: stuti (a person is praised as being equal to others who are praiseworthy) and ninda (criticism in terms of being compared to someone whose similar attribute poetically fits the reproach) (2.330).

Dandi’s nidarsana ornament (illustration) has two varieties. It is so called because it illustrates a similarly good result or a similarly bad result. This verse shows the first variety:

*udayann esa savita padmesv arpayati sriyam \|*  
*vibhavayitum rddhmam phalam suhrd-anugraham \|\|*

**While rising, the sun gives splendor to lotuses to make people realize that the result of good deeds is the favor of a friend. (2.349)**

The above alludes to the pun that in the masculine gender, the word mitra (friend) is a synonym of sun; here Dandi used the word suhrt (friend) instead. This illustrates the second variety:

*yati candramsubhih sprsta dhvanta-rajiparabhavam \|*  
*sadyo rafa-viruddhanam sucayanfi durantatam \|\|*

**Touched by moonrays, the mass of darkness at once vanishes to hint at the dire end of those who oppose the king. (2.350)**

Here the paronomasia is that the word rafan (king) also means moon: raja mrganke ksatriye nrpe, “Rajan means moon, Ksatriya, and king” (Amara-kosa 3.3.111).

The model of Dandi’s example of sahokti (conjoined statement) was copied by Mammata (Kavya-prakasa, verse 495). A young woman feeling the pang of separation speaks:

*saha dlrgha mama svasair imah samprati ratrayah \|*  
*panduras ca mamaivangaih saha tas candra-bhusanah \|\|*

**The nights are long, and so are my exhalations. Adorned by moonrays, the nights turn out whitish, and so do my limbs. (Kavyadarsa 2.352)**

## Ornaments of Sound

In the third chapter, Dandi discusses yamaka (word rhyme), citra- kavya (amazing placement of series of syllables), and prahelika (conundrum). Dandi expounds yamaka in 72 verses. A yamaka is a repetition of sound with a difference in meaning. These seven verses are the best:

3.16

***maninima nini****sus te nisangatvam ananga me \|*  
***harini harini*** *sarma-****tanutam tanutam*** *yatah \|\|*

maninl—a woman in a pique; ma—do not ; ninlsuh—desire to bring; te nisangatvam—your being a quiver (for arrows); ananga—O Cupid; me—my; harinl—ravishing; harinl—she has a necklace; sarma—of happiness; tanutam—the thinness; tanutam—she should make (or sarma-tanutam tanutam—she should make the condition of having a body of bliss); yatah—because.

**Cupid, my ravishing girlfriend has a necklace. She’s in a huff. For the time being, stop your habit of becoming a quiver for the bow of her eyes, because she should render the usual happiness a trifle.**

3.18

***ramaṇī ramaṇī****yā me*  
***pāṭalā pāṭalā****ṁśukā \|*  
***vāruṇīvāruṇī****-bhūta-*  
***saura-bhā saurabhā****spadam \|\|*

ramani— ladylove; ramaniya—pretty; me—my; patala—pink; patala— \[endowed with\] trumpet flowers; amsuka—has a blouse; varuni—the varuni liquor; iva—like; aruni-bhuta—which has become aruna (dawn; or the saffron-rose color at twilight); saura—relates to liquor (sura); bha—\[varuni,\] whose splendor; saurabha—of fragrance; aspadam—a place.

**My sweetheart is gorgeous. Her pinkish blouse, a locus of fragrance, has designs of trumpet flowers. It’s as if varum, a splendid liquor, has become aruna.**

3.20

*madhur ena-drsam manam madhurena sugandhina \|*  
*sahakamdgamenaiva sabda-sesam karisyati \|\|*

madhuh—springtime; ena-drsam—of doe-eyed girls; manam—the pique; madhurena—due to sweetness; sugandhina—which has a nice fragrance; sahakara—of assistance; udgamena—by the rising; eva—only; sabda-sesam—the rest of the sounds; karisyati—will make.

**Due to a very aromatic sweetness, with just a little cooperation spring will turn the pique of doe-eyed damsels into the rest of the sounds.**

3.23

*svayam eva galan-mana-kali kamini te manah \|*  
*kalikam adya nipasya drstva kam nu sprsed dasam \|\|*

svayam eva—automatically; galat—is dissolving; mana-kali— \[her mind,\] because of which Kali’s pride (in inducing a quarrel); kamini—O amorous girl; te—your; manah—mind; kalikam—the buds; adya—now; nipasya—of the nipa tree; drstva—after seeing; kam—which; nu—at all; sprset—might it touch; dasam—stage (condition).

**Amorous girl, naturally your mind causes Kali’s pride to melt. Which condition might your mind reach now, upon seeing the red blossoms of the asoka tree?**

3.29

*kam aleh sama-kesam te*  
*kamalersya-karam mukham \|*  
*kam alekhyam karosi tvam*  
*kamalevonmadisnusu \|\|*

kam—head; aleh—to a bee; sama-kesam—on which the hair is similar; te—your; kamala-irsya-karam—which makes the envy of a lotus; mukham—face; kam—which \[person\] (kam = kam janam); alekhyam—one who cannot be written (counted); karosi tvam— you make; kamala iva—like Laksmi; unmadisnusu—among those who are mad.

**Your face makes lotuses envious and your tresses are similar to series of bees. You’re like LaksmT: Who does not become mad by seeing you?**

3.45

*sarayantam urasa ramayanti*  
*sara-bhutam uru-sara-dhara tam \|*  
*sarasanukrta-sara-sakanci*  
*sa rasayanam asaram avaiti \|\|*  
*(svagata)*

sarayantam—is making him go out; urasa—because of the breast; ramayanti—is causing amorous pleasure; sara-bhutam—who is the best; uru—much; sara— \[breasts,\] which have firmness; dhara— she has; tam—him; sarasa—by lotuses; anukrta—is imitated; sara—she whose power (liveliness); sa-kanci—she has a girdle; sa—she; rasayanam—a tonic; asaram—which is not the essence; avaiti—understands.

**While giving him pleasure, she, who has very firm breasts, makes him go. He is the best. Her liveliness is imitated by lotuses. She, who has a girdle, knows a tonic, which is not essential.**

3.71

*sa-manayasamanaya samanayasamanaya \|*  
*sa ma na ya sa-ma-naya samana-yasa-manaya \|\|*

sa-manaya—\[with her,\] who has pride; asamanaya—\[with her,\] who is unequalled; samanaya—make \[me\] unite; asama—O you who are unequalled; anaya—with her; sah—he (her husband); ma—me (ma = mam); na—is not; ya—\[she\] who; sa-ma-naya— \[she who\] has splendor (ma) and wits (or good behavior); samana—is the same \[as mine\]; yasa—of whose efforts (yasa = ayasa); manaya—\[with her,\] the measure.

**Unequalled companion, he is not there, so lead me to that proud woman who has resplendence and wits. She is unsurpassed, and is making just as many efforts as I am.**

In Kavi Karnapura’s methodology, the above verse is called sarva- yamaka (each line is a yamaka and each line is the same).

Dandi composed many tri-pada-yamakas (a yamaka in three lines): An instance is in the first example above (3.16). Mammata considered them faulty simply because they fell out of usage: yamakasya pada-traya-gatatvena yamanam aprayuktatvam dosah (Kavya-prakasa verse 583 preliminary).

The only other theorists to endorse tri-pada yamaka are Bhoja— catus-tri-dvy-eka-padesu yamakanam vikalpanah (Sarasvati- kanthabharana 2.61)—and Krishna Kavi: pada-traye yatha (Mandara-maranda-campu, KM p. 41).

Dandi also composed three types of palindromes:

♦ pada-pratiloma, a verse where the second and fourth lines are the reverse, syllable by syllable, of the first and third lines respectively,

♦ slokardha-pratiloma, the second half is the reverse of the first, and

♦ sloka-pratiloma, one verse is the reverse of another.

Dandi calls them pratiloma-yamakas (word rhymes in reverse) (3.73), but nowadays palindrome is included in the category of Citra-kavya. This is an example of the first category:

3.74

*yamatasa krtayasa sa yata krsata maya \|*  
*ramanarakata te stu stutetakaranamara \|\|*

ya—which; amata-asa—O you whose wish is unacceptable; krta- ayasa— \[thinness,\] in relation to which efforts were made; sa—that; yata—was obtained; krsata—thinness; maya—by me; ramana—O lover; arakata te astu—your being one who goes should take place; stuta-ita—O you who were praised and went; akarana- amara—O god in the matter of not doing.

**O lover who went elsewhere and were praised there, now your desire is unacceptable. I made many efforts and became thin \[in separation\]. You can leave. You’re only a god in the matter of not doing anything.**

These two verses illustrate the repetition of a verse in reverse (syllable by syllable):3.76-77

*yd na mdna-ya-mdrdvi-kasondna-jandsand \|*  
*ydm uddra-saiddhlndm dyam dyamanadi-sd \|\|*

*sa dindmaya-mdyamd nddhitd saraddmuya \|*  
*ndsandjanand soka-virdmdya na mdna-yd \|\|*

yd—\[she\] who; na—not; mdna-ya—who obtains pride; mdra—in the form of Cupid; avi—for the sheep; kasa—she has a whip; una— is deficient; ana—whose breath (life force); jana— \[me,\] a person; asana—she pervades; yam—whom; uddra-sata-adhmdm—\[her,\] who is submissive to hundreds of illustrious persons; dydm—I fully obtained; dyamana-ddi-sd—she brings restraint and so on to an end; sd—she; dina-dmaya-md—she knows day is a disease (whereas night is the cure for the pain of separation); aya-amd—she obtains good fortune; na adhlta—she was not studied; sarada amuya— by that autumn; ndsana—the ruin; djanand—she fully generates; soka-virdmdya—for the cessation of sorrow; na—not; mdna-yd— she attains pique.

**She has a goad for proud Cupid, who has become a sheep. I did not quite win her over, though she is submissive to hundreds of illustrious friends. She fills me whole. My life force has become deficient. She puts an end to self-control. She knows daytime is an ailment. She has good fortune. She reaches the state of pique. She is not a subject-matter of autumn (her intentions are not limpid). She is going to finish me off. She is not conducive to the cessation of my affliction.**

Next, Dandi illustrates citra (citra-kavya), which he also calls duskara (hard to make). He also uses that term (3.28) for certain yamakas and alliterations. Dandi exemplifies go-mutrika (syllables in a zigzag diagram), ardha-bhrama (a kind of incomplete sarvato- bhadra), and sarvato-bhadra (good on each side). This is the example of sarvato-bhadra (the second half of each line is a mirror of the first, syllable by syllable):

3.82

*samayamamaya masa*  
*maranayayana rama \| yanavararavanaya*  
*mayarama marayama \|\|*

sā mā yā mā   mā rā nā yā   yā nā vā rā   mā yā rā mā

sa-ama-ayama—she has the broadening of the disease; amaya— she is not deceitful; masa—along with the moon; mara-anaya— brings Cupid; ayana—she whose arrival; rama—a beautiful woman; yana—the feet (“the means of going”); avara—covers (surrounds) (“that by means of which there is the covering”); a-rava—of proper sounds; anaya—she whose net; maya-arama—she whose pleasure is magic; maraya—for the sake of Cupid; ama—with (Medim-kosa 2.50).

**Her ailment (the fire of separation) is expanding. That beautiful woman is not deceitful. Her arrival with the moon fosters Cupid. Her pleasure is magic. The sound of her anklebells surrounds her feet and is a net for Cupid’s sake.**

The above verse is also Dandi’s example of a verse made with only one vowel (3.87). In the category of duskara, Dandi illustrates three kinds of alliteration:

- svara (a verse is made with one, two, three or four vowels),
- sthana (a verse corresponds to one, two, three or four places of pronunciation) (sets of consonants are grouped according to their place of pronunciation in the mouth), and
- varna (a verse is made with one, two, three or four consonants). He does not use the term anuprasa (alliteration) in that respect, but niyama (restriction): yah svara-sthana-varnanam niyamo duskaresv asau (3.83).

This verse illustrates the repetition of four vowels (catuh-svara- niyama) (each line has only one vowel):

3.84

*amnayanam ahantya vag giti ritih pritir bhitih \|*  
*bhogo rogo modo moho dheye vecched dese kseme \|\|*

amnayanam—of the Vedas; aha—talks about; antya vak—the last speech; gitih—songs; ritih—methods; pritih—affections; bhitih— fears; bhogah—enjoyment; rogah—a disease; modah—pleasure; mohah—a bewilderment; dheye—\[the Lord’s two feet,\] which should be meditated upon; va—possibly; icchet—one can desire; dese—in a place; kseme—for the purpose of security.

**The Upanisads, the end of the Vedas, mention songs, methods, affections, and fears. Material enjoyment is a disease: The pleasures are delusions. For prosperity, one should desire the Lord’s feet, which are to be meditated upon in a lonely place.**

Dandi and Bhoja were the only rhetoricians to value the alliteration of a vowel. This is Dandi’s illustration of the repetition of one set of phonemes (eka-sthana-niyama) (gutturals):

3.91

*aga gam ganga-kakaka-gahakaghaka-kaka-ha \|*  
*ahahanka khagankaga-kankaga-khagakakaka \|\|*

agah—You went; gam—to Earth; ganga-ka—O You to whom the water of the Ganges is related; a-ka—\[of persons,\] up to Brahma; aka—of the hearts (“they go crookedly,” from the root ak kutilayam gatau); gahaka—O penetrator; aghaka—in the form of sins; kaka—of crows; ha—the killer; ahaha-anka—O You whose characteristic is not sounds of desperation (haha = haha-sabda ) (as contrasted with Rama); kha-ga—the sun (“it goes in the sky”); anka-aga—to Sumeru (“the mountain which marks,” from the root ak\[i\] laksane); kanka—which goes (from the root kak\[i\] gatau); aga—\[long like\] a tree (“it does not move”); khagaka—O You who have a bird (ka is a bahuvrihi marker); akaka—O You who are not fickle (from the root kak laulye).

**O You to whom the water of the Ganges is related, O You who penetrate the hearts of all and even of Brahma, O You whose characteristic is not sounds of desperation, O You who are not fickle, and whose bird, long like a tree, can go to Sumeru, the mountain that marks the movement of the sun—You, the killer of the crows of sin, went to Earth.**

The following verse is made with three consonants (tri-varna- niyama):

3.93

*devanam nandano devo nodano veda-nindinah \|*  
*divam dudava nadena dane danava-nandinah \|\|*

devanam—of gods; nandanah—the delighter; devah—God; nodanah—He drives away; veda-nindinah—one who criticizes the Vedas; divam—the heavens; dudava—He scorched; nadena—with a sound; dane—at the time of the tearing apart (from the verbal root dan avakhandane); danava-nandinah—of he who delights the demons.

**Lord Nrsimha delights the gods and drives away the blas­phemers of the Vedas. When He tore apart Hiranyakasipu, who gratifies devils, the Lord tormented the heavens with His roar.**

A verse of two consonants:

3.94

*surih surasurasari-sarah sarasa-sarasah \|*  
*sasara saraslh sm sa-sUruh sa sura-rasl \|\|*

surih—a pandit; sura—unto godly persons; asura—and unto un­godly persons; a-sari—properly goes; sarah—He whose power; sa- arasa—are greatly crying (“are endowed with shouts”); sarasah— \[the lakes,\] where the cranes (or sarasa-sarasah—where there are lotuses and cranes); sasara—He went; saraslh—to the lakes; sir!— He who has the plough weapon; sa-su-uruh—He is with Revati (“she has nice thighs”); sah—He (the well-known one); sura— which is heavenly liquor; rasi—He has the liquid.

**Baladeva, a pandit, has heavenly liquor in His possession. His power properly goes both to the godly and to the ungodly. Accompanied with RevatT, who has nice thighs, He, the wielder of the plough weapon, went to the lakes where lotuses and swans abound.**

Next, Dandi illustrates prahelika (conundrum). He says prahelika serves three purposes: to provide entertainment, to increase the proficiency of those who know how to entertain, and to be a means of verbally confusing others: krlda-gosthl-vinodesu taj-jnair aklrna-mantrane \| para-vyamohane vaci sopayogah prahelikah \|\| (3.97). Dandi specifies that there are sixteen good varieties and fourteen bad ones, all illustrated by previous teachers: etah sodasa nirdistah purvacaryaih prahelikah \| dusta-prahelikas canyas tair adhitas caturdasa \|\| (3.106). These two verses feature prahelika:

3.114

*nasikya-madhya paritas catur-varna-vibhusita \|*  
*asti kacitpurlyasyam asta-varnahvaya nrpah \|\|*

**Some town around the middle of Nasikya is adorned with the four varnas. There, the kings are called with eight varnas.**

The town is Kanci and the kings are called Pundraka, which has eight letters (varna). The following is the variety of prahelika called pariharika (a series of words whose meanings are simply etymological):

*3.120 vijitatma-bhava-dvesi-guru-pada-hato janah \|*  
*himapahamitra-dharair vyaptam vyomabhinandati \|\|*

vi—by a bird; jita—\[of he who was\] defeated; atma-bhava—of he who took birth from himself; dvesi—of the enemy; guru—of the father; pada—of the rays; hatah—oppressed; janah—a person; hima-apaha—of fire (“it takes away cold”); amitra—of water (the enemy); dharaih—by torrents; vyaptam—pervaded; vyoma—the sky; abhinandati—praises.

**The person oppressed by the rays of the sun, which is the father of the foe of Arjuna, who was born from Indra, who was defeated by a bird, Garuda, praises the sky, which is filled with clouds: Clouds have water, the enemy of fire, which dispels cold.**

The meaning at a cursory look is: “The person oppressed by the feet of the guru of the foe of him who is self-born and was defeated praises the sky, which is filled by those who support the enemy of that which dispels cold.” Bhamaha cites the second half of the verse as an instance of the fault called avacaka (inexpressive). However, Bhoja shows the verse as an illustration of the fault named klista (hard to understand) (Sarasvati-kanthabharana 1.9). Mammata would agree with Bhoja. Further, in Mammata’s methodology, Dandi’s variety of prahelika called vyutkranta (Kavyadarsa 3.110) corresponds to klista occurring in a sentence where the proper order of the words is jumbled up. Similarly, the prahelika called samana-sabda consists in a verse that is hard to understand simply because rare synonyms are used (Kavyadarsa 3.118). Dandi’s prahelikas called eka-cchanna and pariharika correspond to the fault called neyartha (the meaning can only be guessed).

Dandi does not categorize the paronomastic prahelikas as slesa (double meaning) probably because they have no great literary charm. However, Dandi’s prahelika called samana-rupa (Kavyadarsa 3.112) is exactly the same as what Mammata calls the slesa variety of the aprastuta-prasamsa ornament, whereas Dandi’s and Bhamaha’s aprastufa-prasamsa literally consists of praising the aprasfufa (what is not the actual topic) for the sake of finding fault with the prastuta (the actual topic, the subject of description) (Kavyadarsa 2.340).

This is the opening verse of Dasa-kumara-carita. It illustrates lata anuprasa (repetition of the same word in a different clause):

*brahmanda-cchatra-dandah sata-dhrti-bhavanambhoruho nala-dandah ksom-nau-kupa-dandah*  
*ksarad-amara-sarit-pattika-ketu-dandah \|*  
*jyotis-cakraksa-dandas tribhuvana-stambha-dando ’nghri-dandah*  
*sreyas traivikramas te vitaratu vibudha-dvesinam kala-dandah \|\|*

**The pillar in the form of the three worlds is the danda (the handle) of the umbrella which is the universal shell. Lotuses in Brahma’s abode have a nala-danda (a stalk). There is a ksonl- danda (a tree), a nau-danda (an oar) and a kupa-danda (a stick used to hold the rope in a well). There is the danda (a tusk) of Him from whom the Ganges flows. There is a pattika-danda (a pole to weave cloths) and a ketu-danda (a comet, or a falling star). There is a jyotir-danda (a lightning flash) and a cakraksa- danda (the rims of a wheel, and the shaft). There is also an anghri-danda (a walking stick). But the best danda is kala- danda, Trivikrama’s rod of Time used for the gods’ enemies. May it take you across. (cited in Sad-ukti-karnamrta 217)**

## 5. Medhavin (184)

Bhamaha referred to Medhavin as a previous authority: ta eta upama-dosah sapta medhavinoditah, “These seven faults in a simile were stated by Medhavin” (Bhamahalankara 2.40).

Similarly, Bhamaha wrote: yatha-samkhyam athotpreksam alankara-dvayam viduh, samkhyanam iti medhavinotpreksabhihita kvacit, “Scholars know that yatha-samkhya and utpreksa are two more ornaments. Somewhere, Medhavin mentioned samkhyana (a synonym of yatha-samkhya) and utpreksa (fanciful assumption)” (Bhamahalankara 2.88). Medhavin did not invent utpreksa, but included it in poetical theory. Previously, it was classed as a simile. Therein the term iva means “like”, but if the sense of iva is “as if (as though)”, it is classed as an utpreksa.

Bhamaha mentioned several books and persons, including Medhavin: Asmakavamsa (1.33), the Acyutottara of Rama Sarma (2.19; 2.58), Medhavin (2.40; 2.88), Rajamitra (2.45; 3.10), Sakha-vardhana (2.47), Ratnaharana (3.8), Kanabhaksa (5.17), Nyasa (6.36), and Salatunya (another name of Panini) (6.62-63).

Naganatha Sastry comments: “Bhamaha mentions Medhavin and Rama Sarman whose work was known as Acyutottara, Sakha- vardhana and his two works Raja-mitra and Ratna Harana.”

The seven possible faults in a simile are: hmata (deficiency), asambhava (impossibility), linga-bheda (discrepancy of gender), vacana-bheda (discrepancy of number), viparyaya (unsuitability of the standard of comparison), upamanadhikatvam (the standard of comparison has an additional element), and asadrsata (non- similitude).

To prove the exclusive validity of Rudrata’s list of four faults in a simile, Namisadhu wrote Madhavin’s verse about the seven faults and showed all seven examples given by Medhavin. P.V. Kane remarks:

On Rudrata (XI.24) Namisadhu again quotes Medhavin about the seven dosas of simile and the manner in which he deals with this topic suggests that the examples he gives are taken from Medhavin’s work, ‘atra svarupopadane saty api catvara iti grahanad yan medhavi-prabhrtibhir uktam yatha linga-vacana-bhedau hmatadhikyam asambhavo viparyayo ’sadrsyam iti saptopama-dosah ... tad etan nirastam.’ Namisadhu quotes seven verses illustrating the seven faults of Upama mentioned by Medhavin. Five of these seven occur in Bhamaha’s Kavyalankara II.40, 47, 55, 58, 63. \[...\] Namisadhu mentions the seven examples immediately after mentioning Medhavin and does not name Bhamaha with regard to them.

Namisadhu mentions Bhamaha by name on Rudrata 8.84. If the verses were Bhamaha’s he would have probably so stated. Therefore Bhamaha should be taken as quoting five verses from Medhavin.

Of those five examples cited, Bhamaha specified that verse 2.47 was composed by Sakha-vardhana and verse 2.58 by Rama Sarma. Bhamaha’s example of asambhava (impossibility) is blazing gushes of water emanating from the sun (2.47); it is cited in Kavya- prakasa (verse 598) as an illustration of the same.

This is Bhamaha’s example of the fault called hinata (deficiency) (the standard of comparison lacks an element) (now called nyuna- pada), cited by Medhavin:

*sa marutakampita-pita-vasa*  
*bibhrat sa-lilam sasi-bhasam abjam \|*  
*yadu-pravirah pragrhita-sarngah*  
*sendrayudho megha ivababhase \|\|*

**With His yellow garment fluttering in the wind and with His Sarnga bow, the hero of the Yadus, playfully holding the moonlike conch, was resplendent like a cloud with Indra’s bow. (Bhamahalankara 2.41)**

Indra’s bow is the rainbow. The deficiency of the comparison is that there is no equivalent for His garment (lightning). Nevertheless, since the analogy that His yellow garment resembles lightning is obvious, the verse can be classed as an eka-desa-vivartini upama (partial overall simile), invented by Visvanatha Kaviraja. Pandita­raja Jagannatha’s example of eka-desa-vivarti-rupaka (partial overall metaphor) follows a similar construction (rupa-jala etc., in Rasa-gangadhara, KM p. 232, cited in Appendix \|\| on p. 716).

## 6. Bhamaha

He wrote Kavyalankara (the ornaments of poetry), which is always called Bhamahalankara to distinguish it from Rudrata’s Kavyalankara. The title Kavyalankara is an instance of the punar-uktavad-abhasa ornament (semblance of a repetition), because in other contexts the word alankara can be a synonym of kavya (poetics). Bhamaha flourished sometime after 700 CE. Dr. Kane expounds:

Bhamaha is deemed to be the oldest extant exponent of the Alankara school of Poetics. Of his personal history we know next to nothing. In the last verse he tells us that he was the son of Rakrilagomin: ‘avalokya matani sat-kavmam avagamya sva- dhiya ca kavya-laksma \| sujanavamaya bhamahena grathitam rakrilagomi-sununedam \|\|’. This name Rakrilagomin has given rise to a heated discussion whether Bhamaha was a Bauddha.

\[...\] So here we have ancient evidence to show that Gomin was not a purely Buddhistic appellation as early as the 4th or 5th century A.D. \[...\] The first verse salutes Sarva Sarvajna. Sarvajna is an appellation of Siva as well as of Buddha, while Sarva simply means ‘sarvasmai hita’ and is not given by Amara as an appellation of Buddha. \[.\] The fact that Bhamaha discarded the theory of apoha and was branded as duratman by a staunch Buddhist like Santaraksita is one of the strongest arguments against holding that he was a Buddhist on the ground that he paid homage to Sarvajna just as Candragomin did in siddhampranamya sarvajnam jagato gurum I.

It is possible that Bhamaha lived at a time when Gautama, the Buddha, had come to be regarded as an avatara and wrote a mangalacarana verse which has two meanings, one applicable to Siva and the other to Buddha. He was probably a Hindu steeped in all the ancient Sanskrit culture but with an admiration for Buddha’s noble life and therefore indulged in a double-meaning opening verse and also probably he had learnt Buddhist logic that was very much esteemed from the 5th to the 8th century.

In the fifth pariccheda Bhamaha devotes some verses to the elucidation of blemishes resting upon logic and philosophical doctrines. \[...\] I was probably the first Indian to point out that Bhamaha quotes in this pariccheda the words of Dinnaga and probably of Dharmakirti.

Anandavardhana implies that Bhamaha cannot possibly have lived after Bana (c. 640 CE) because he says a text of Bana is an improvement upon one of Bhamaha. Dr. Kane responds:

Supposing for the sake of argument that the Dhvany-aloka meant that Bhamaha’s verse is earlier than a passage from the Harsa-carita, there are obvious replies. Bana flourished about two hundred and fifty years before the Dhvany-aloka and it is quite possible that the author of Dhvany-aloka had no correct chronology about the two authors before him. He was more familiar with Bhamaha who was his countryman and a rhetorician, while Bana hailed from distant Pritikuta on the banks of the Sona river and was only a poet.

The name ‘Bhamaha’ is derived from the verbal root bham krodhe (to be angry). Naganatha Sastry, a translator of Bhamahalankara, says this about the author:

The root “Bhama” means “to be angry” and the word “Bhamini” (one who is angry) as applying to women in general is referable to this root, though perhaps it is neither chivalrous nor just to do so. The derivative meaning of “Bhamaha” would be “one who has killed or given up anger.” That meaning will fit in excellently with one of the very few personal traits of the writer which we can gather from this work; for Bhamaha seems to have been an extremely modest person who had great respect for his predecessors (vide 4.51). That it may be a pen­name is also gatherable from the following considerations. His father’s name is given as Rakrila Gomin. The second word ‘Gomin’ has been understood to be a contraction for ‘Gosvamin’, a family name which exists in its original form among many Mahratta and Bengali families of today. It is unlikely that this writer dropped his family name and adopted that of “Bhamaha” as his name for his everyday transactions. Further, his true name must bear some resemblance to that of his father and to a host of similar names such as Rahula, Ramila, etc.

All critics are however agreed that Bhamaha was a Kashmerian. Mr. Narasimha Iyengar’s conclusion that he was a Buddhist is analysed and examined by Mr. Trivedi who concludes that he was a Brahmin. Mr. Kane does not agree with Mr. Iyengar although he does not express himself definitely on the point.

## Sequence of Topics

Bhamaha’s treatise consists of 398 verses in six chapters. He says that for the most part a poet is a writer who has creative intelligence: kavyam tu jayate jatu kasyacitpratibhavatah (1.5). Bhamaha sheds light on the background that can turn a potential writer into a poet:

*sabdas chando bhidhanartha itihasasrayah kathah \|*  
*loko yuktih kalas ceti mantavyah kavya-hetavah \|\|*

**“A good wording (grammatically and phonetically); prosody; knowledge of dictionary meanings; stories based on the histories; the ways of the world; logical reasoning; and the arts are the causes of poetry” (1.9).**

Next he states his definition of poetry and the categories of poetry:

*sabdarthau sahitau kavyam gadyam padyam ca tad dvidha \|*  
*samskrtam prakrtam canyad apabhramsa iti tridha \|\|*  
*vrtta-devadi-carita-samsi cotpadya-vastu ca \|*  
*kala-sastrasrayam ceti caturdha bhidyate punah \|\|*  
*sarga-bandho ’bhineyartham tathaivakhyayikakathe \|*  
*anibaddham ca kavyadi tat punah pancadhocyate \|\|*  
*sarga-bandho maha-kavyam mahatam ca mahac ca yat I*

**“Poetry is sounds and meanings together. It has two varieties: prose and verse. There are three sorts: Sanskrit, Prakrit, and Apabhramsa. There are four kinds: A narration of events; a praise of the deeds of a king and so on; a product of the imagination; and poetry founded upon the arts and the scriptures. Poetry has a further five varieties: sarga-bandha (composition in chapters), abhineyartha (for a theatrical representation), akhyayika (historical narrative), katha (novel), and anibaddha (single verse). A masterpiece (maha- kavya) is a sarga-bandha, a great one of the greats.” (1.16-19)**

Modern historians of poetics add a sixth category, stotra (hymn), such as an astakam (set of eight verses). Bhamaha’s definition of poetry is the origin of the term sahitya (literature, lit. togetherness). Dr. Sushil Kumar De expounds:

... sabdarthau sahitau kavyam (Bhamaha i.16), from which, as Kuntaka indicates, the name sahitya was probably given to poetry. The earliest use probably ofthis term sahitya in Sanskrit Poetics occurs in Mukula and in his pupil, PratTharendu-raja, while Rajasekhara expressly uses the term sahitya-vidya. The orthodox etymology of the term, which derives it from the above definition of poetry as the union of word and sense, is thus put by Rajasekhara: sabdarthayor yathavat saha-bhavena vidya sahitya-vidya, an interpretation with which Kuntaka agrees.

Exactly when and how the term Sahitya came to be employed for Poetry we do not know, but the concept is acknowledged from the very beginning. We find, however, that it is no longer a grammatical, but a poetical concept in Rajasekhara, who mentions Sahitya and Sahitya-vidya as Poetry and Poetics.

The term Sahitya implies that Sabda and Artha are inseparable and go together. Kuntaka describes this Sahitya as Anyuna- anatiriktatva or Paraspara-spardha; but Kalidasa conveys it more beautifully by his well known comparison of poetry to Ardha-narisvara, in which Parvati is Vac or Sabda and Paramesvara is Artha. That the poets and not only the theorists were aware of this idea is also clear from Magha’s declaration that the discerning poet pays equal regard to Sabda and Artha in the well known line: sabdarthau sat-kavir iva dvayam vidvan apeksate.

This means: “A scholar pays attention to both sound and meaning like a good poet does” (Sisupala-vadha 2.86). Rupa Gosvami and Kavi Karnapura implicitly accept the concept of Ardha-narisvara: dehardhe dayitam vahan bahumatam atrasi yan nagatah (Ujjvala- mlamani 5.36); umayai dattvardham vapuh (Alankara-kaustubha 3.23).

Samudrabandha, a commentator on Ruyyaka’s Alankara-sarvasva, explains Bhamaha’s definition from another perspective: visistah sabda visista arthas ca militva kavyatam yanti, “Special sounds and special meanings that come together become poetry.”

**Ardha-narisvara**

The above reference to Kalidasa points to the opening verse of Raghu-vamsa:

*vag-arthav iva samprktau vag-artha-pratipattaye \|*  
*jagatah pitarau vande parvatl-paramesvarau \|\|*

**“For the proper ascertainment of words and their meanings, I praise Parvati and Siva. They are eternally connected like word and meaning and are the mother and the father of the universe.” (Raghu-vamsa 1.1)**

Bhamaha considers that poetry is a harmonious togetherness of ornaments of sound and ornaments of meaning. His definition is a roundabout way of rejecting the Sausabdya theory (the state of su-sabda): In poetry, sound, including a good stringing of words, is more important than meaning. This theory was promulgated by Dandi and developed by Vamana and Mangala (ninth century).

It reached its apex in Vamana’s concept of paka (maturity): Mangala says paka means parinama, the proficiency in the usage of nouns and verbs, whereas Vamana says paka means sabda- paka: The words are so well-placed that they cannot be changed: yat-padani tyajanty eva parivrtti-sahisnutam \| tam sabda-nyasa- nisnatah sabda-pakampracaksate \|\| (Kavyalankara-sutra 1.3.15)

According to Bhamaha, a composition that is clear, straightforward and elegant in conformity with the Sausabdya theory differs from ordinary language only like music does, in terms of only delighting the ears. Mammata included Bhamaha’s definition of poetry in his own and cited Bhamaha’s elucidation:

*rupakadim alankaram bahyam acaksate pare \|*  
*supam tinam ca vyutpattim vacam vanchanty alankrtim \|\|*  
*tad etad ahuh sausabdyam nartha-vyutpattir idrsi \|*  
*sabdabhidheyalankara-bhedad istam dvayam tu nah \|\|*

**“Some scholars hold the opinion that in poetry, the ornaments, such as a metaphor, are extrinsic. They insist that proficiency in the usage of nouns and verbs is the real ornamentation. They call this Sausabdya. They say a distinct construction of meanings is not so important. We, however, say that both are important, otherwise there might be a discrepancy between an ornament of sound and an ornament of meaning.” (Bhamahalankara 1.14-15) (Kavya- prakasa 6.48)**

Regarding the Gaudiya and the Vaidarbha styles, Bhamaha remarked that the distinctions drawn between them by some scholars are pointless: gaudiyam idam etat tu vaidarbham iti kim prthak \| gatanugatika-nyayan nanakhyeyam amedhasam \|\| (1.32).

Bhamaha says the Gaudiya style that has an ornament, is devoid of vulgarity, is properly meaningful and is not too complex is just fine and is not different from the Vaidarbha style: alankara-vad agramyam arthyam nyayyam anakulam \| gaudiyam api sadhiyo vaidarbham iti nanyatha \|\| (1.35)

He propounded ten literary faults: neyartha (the meaning can only be guessed), klista (hard to understand), anyartha (another sense), avacaka (inexpressive), ayuktimat (improper), gudha- sabdabhidhana (using a mysterious word) (1.37); sruti-dusta (indecent), artha-dusta (unpleasant meaning; the modern aslila), kalpana-dusta (difficult to understand, because of an unwanted pun), and sruti-kasta (hard on the ears) (1.47).

In that regard, Bhamaha says the fault called ayuktimat occurs when either one of the following is used as a messenger, because either they cannot speak or they cannot distinctly speak: a cloud, the wind, the moon, a bee, a harita bird, a cakravaka bird, or a parrot (1.42-43). As such he disagrees with Kalidasa’s usage of a cloud messenger in Meghaduta.

Bhamaha added that in certain contexts a fault is not a fault, and sometimes it turns out as a quality:

*sannivesa-visesat tu duruktam api sobhate \|*  
*nilam palasam abaddham antarale srajam iva \|\|*  
*kincid asraya-saundaryad dhatte sobham asadhv api \|*  
*kanta- vilocana-nyastam malimasam ivanjanam \|\| (1.54-55)*

In the second chapter, Bhamaha says the gunas are only three: madhurya, ojas and prasada. Bhamaha says madhurya means the sounds are pleasant to hear, the composition has either few compounds or no compound, and the sense is not too terse; prasada consists in the absence of compound and in an ease ofunderstanding; and ojas means there are many compounds. Afterward, he begins his disquisition on ornaments, which continues throughout the third chapter.

Bhamaha’s fourth chapter mostly consists of an explanation of another set of ten faults: apartha (the meaning does not jell), vyartha (meaningless), ekartha (redundancy) (lit. the same meaning) (also called punar-uktam, in the two categories of word and meaning, 4.12), sa-samsaya (ambiguity), apakrama (lack of symmetry), sabda-hma (grammatical mistake), yati-bhrasta (a caesura in the middle of a word), bhinna-vrtta (violation of the metre), visandhi (awkward euphonic combination), and virodhi— desa-virodhi (inconsistency of place), kala-virodhi (inconsistency of time), kala-virodhi (inconsistency related to the arts), loka- virodhi (inconsistency related to the ways of the world), nyaya- virodhi (inconsistency related to books on either dharma, artha, or kama), and agama-virodhi (inconsistency related to Dharma- sastras) (4.1-2). Those literary faults are similar to Bharata Muni’s list of ten blemishes.

Bhamaha devotes the entire fifth chapter to an eleventh fault: pratijna-hetu-drstanta-hina (lacking the threefold syllogism: the proposition, the proof, and an example).

In the sixth and last chapter he discusses grammatical details: He emphasizes the value of Panini’s grammar and states his own preferences of usage especially as regards technical grammatical rules.

## Ornaments

Bhamaha wanted that poetry be understandable without a com­mentary. He greatly expounded upon ornaments and thus justified his approach:

*rupakadir alankaras tasyanyair bahudhoditah \|*  
*na kantam api nirbhusam vibhati vanita-mukham \|\|*

**“Ornaments, such as a metaphor, were described in many ways by other scholars. Indeed, a woman’s face without an ornament is not resplendent even to her lover” (1.13) (quoted in Kavya-prakasa 6.48).**

Bhamaha lists and exemplifies ornaments group by group, thereby indicating a sequential progress in the field since the time of Bharata: “The way in which Bhamaha successively enumerates and groups these figures probably shows that to the original five mentioned by him at the outset, others were added in course of time as the study itself advanced.”

- At first he only elaborates upon these five (2.4): anuprasa (3 kinds), yamaka (5 kinds), rupaka (2 kinds), dipaka, and upama (3 kinds: two taken from Bharata: ninda (criticism) and prasamsa (praise), with the addition of acikhyasa, a comparison which can be taken as either criticism or praise: 2.37);
- Then he mentions luptopama (2.33) and prativastupama (2.34);
- He further states these six (2.66): aksepa, arthantara-nyasa, vyatireka, vibhavana, samasokti, and atisayokti;
- Next he defines yatha-samkhya and utpreksa (2.88);
- In the third chapter, he lists and illustrates twenty-three more ornaments: preyas, rasavat, Urjasvi, paryayoktam, samahitam, udattam, slistam (slesa), apahnuti, visesoktam (visesokti), virodha, tulya-yogita, aprastuta-prasamsa, vyaja- stuti, nidarsana, upama-rupakam, upameyopama, sahokti, parivrtti, sa-sandeha, ananvaya, utpreksavayava, samsrsti, and bhavikatvam (bhavika) (3.1-4).

This amounts to two ornaments of sound (anuprasa, yamaka) and thirty-five ornaments of meaning (not counting samsrsti). Bhamaha mentioned svabhavokti in passing: svabhavoktir alankara iti kecit pracaksate, “Some say svabhavokti is a literary ornament” (2.93).

Bhamaha expounded three types of alliteration:

- The first one has no name. The example is: sarupa-varna- vinyasam anuprasam pracaksate, kim taya cintaya kante nitanteti yathoditam, “Darling, why are you going overboard with that anxiety?” (2.5).
- His second type of alliteration, called gramya anuprasa (homey alliteration), is almost the same as Dandi’s example of alliteration in Gaudi and was renamed komala (soft) by Udbhata; Mammata accepted Udbhata’s term. Bhamaha’s example is: gramyanuprasam anyat tu manyante sudhiyo ’pare, sa lola-malanilali-kulakula-galo balah, “Bala’s neck is swarmed by dark bees, on account of the dangling garland”” (2.6).
- He invented the term lata anuprasa, his third variety: latiyam apy anuprasam ihecchanty apare (2.8).

In conformity with Dandi, Bhamaha’s vakrokti is a charming mode of expression: vakrabhidheya-sabdoktir ista vacam alankrtih, “The expression of words with a twist in the denotation is their desired ornament” (Bhamahalankara 1.36). The word vakra literally means crooked. Das Gupta notes:

Probably the word vakra has been suggested by the amorous glances of women. The glance made in a straightforward manner is simple vision but an arch-glance signifies the whole situation of mental complex and emotion that fills us with a thrill.

Bhamaha equated vakrokti with the term atisayokti (superexcellent expression):

*sarvaivaiisayokiis tu tarkayet tam yathagamam \|\|*  
*saisa sarvaiva vakroktir anayartho vibhavyate \|*  
*yatno ’syam kavina karyah ko ’lankaro ’naya vina \|\|*

**“Atisayokti is all in all. One should ponder over it in a manner that follows the tradition. This all in all is vakrokti. A meaning is made to be felt (vibhavyate) by means of it. A poet should make an effort to bring about vakrokti, without which there is no literary ornament” (2.84-85) (cited in Kavya-prakasa, verse 562 vrtti).**

Dr. Kumar De remarks:

Commenting of Bhamaha’s central verse on vakrokti (ii.85), saisa sarvaiva vakroktir anayartho vibhavyate, Abhinavagupta attempts to read into it his own idea of the importance of Rasa and interprets vibhavyate technically as: pramadodyanair vibhavatam myate visesena ca bhavyate rasa-mayi-kriyata ity arthah \[“A meaning is vibhavyate, i.e. it turns out as a vibhava (stimuli) along with a young woman, a garden, etc., and in addition it is felt (bhavyate) in a special way (vi = visesena), i.e. it is made to be imbued with a rasa” (Locana 3.37),\] he apparently makes Bhamaha mean that by vakrokti, the sense of poetry is rendered into a suitable factor of Rasa, so that by using the word vibhavyate with the technical meaning given to it Bhamaha would imply that the Rasa as well as Alankara originates in vakrokti.

Moreover, Abhinavagupta kept Bhamaha’s usage of the term atisayokti as the underlying principle of all ornaments: atisayoktih sarvalankara-samanyam (Locana 3.37). Mammata used the word vaicitrya instead: vaicitryam alankarah, “A literary ornament is amazingness” (Kavya-prakasa, verse 383 vrtti). Visvanatha Kaviraja stated: vaicitryasyaivalankaratvat, “Only amazingness makes an ornament” (Sahitya-darpana 10.62).

Like Dandi, Bhamaha also used the term atisayokti as an orna­ment of meaning (statement of superexcellence). He defined it as otherworldliness: nimittato vaco yat tu lokatikranta-gocaram, manyante 'iisayokiim tam alankarataya yatha, “There are words which, for some reason, go beyond the scope of worldly norms. Scholars consider that atisayokti a figure of speech” (Bhamahalankara 2.81). Bhamaha said atisayokti is so called because it is a statement of the supereminence of a quality (atisaya = gunatisaya): ity evam adir udita gunatisaya-yogatah \|sarvaivatisayoktis tu tarkayet tam yathagamam \|\| (2.84). This atisayokti, which often amounts to the svabhavokti ornament (a description of the nature) when there is a description of Radha or Krsna, matches the second variety of the modern atisayokti because the essential characteristic is otherworldliness. For instance, Jagannatha’s definition of the second variety of atisayokti is: atha prakarantaram, yatrabhede ’pi bhedo lokottaratva-pratipatty- arthah, idam eva prastutasyanyatvam ity anenoktam (Rasa- gangadhara, KM p. 311).

Bhamaha did not accept the plain description of things as poetry: “Why do they call a varta (plain talk) such as this ‘poetry’: gato ’stam arko bhatmdur yanti vasaya paksinah, “The sun has set. The moon shines. The birds go find a place to stay”?” Dandi includes the same example under the figure hetu, specifically in the subcategory of jnapaka-hetu (an informative cause), and says it is useful for letting one know of a particular activity done at that time of day. In other words, the statement hints at a rendezvous at dusk. In that line of thought, Mammata showed that the sentence “The sun has set” can have many implied meanings depending on the suggestive specialties such as who is talking and who is being addressed (Kavya-prakasa 5.47).

Bhamaha’s slesa (literal double meaning) must involve a similarity between the two things: upamanena yat tattvam upameyasya sadhyate \|guna-kriyabhyam namna ca slistam tad abhidhlyate \|\| (3.14). Vamana accepted Bhamaha’s interpretation of slesa: upamanenopameyasya dharmesu guna-kriya-sabda-rupesu sa tattvaropah. tantra-prayoge tantrenoccarane sati slesah. (Kavyalankara-sutra 4.3.7). For example:

*chayavanto gata-vyalah svarohah phala-dayinah \|*  
*marga-druma mahantas ca paresam eva bhutaye \|\|*

**Great persons and wayside trees exist only for the prosperity of others. They provide shelter (or shade), they are not wicked (or they have no snake), they are accessible (or they are easy to climb), and they give results (or they give fruits). (Bhamahalankara 3.18)**

The similarity is implied. Nowadays, however, the verse is classed as a tulya-yogita (equal connection with an attribute) based on slesa. Moreover, Bhamaha was the first to state the notion of artha- slesa (one literal meaning applies to both subjects of description): slesad evartha-vacasor asya ca kriyate bhida \|tat sahokty-upama- hetu-nirdesat tri-vidham yatha \|\| (3.17). For instance:

*ratnavattvad agadhatvat sva-maryada-vilanghanat \|*  
*bahu-sattvasrayatvac ca sadrsas tvam udanvata \|\|*

**Due to being dark like a jewel, due to being deep, due to going beyond limits, and due to being the support of many beings, you resemble an ocean. (3.20)**

Nowadays the verse would serve as an example of the fault called padamsa-gata sruti-katu (hard on the ears, in parts of words: tvat tvat tvat).

Bhamaha’s tulya-yogita ornament is this: One of the subjects is notably inferior, and the intent is to express its equality with the others as regards a special quality: nyunasyapi visistena guna-samya-vivaksaya \|  
tulya-karya-kriya-yogad ity ukta tulya-yogita \|\|

(3.27). For example:

*seso hima-giris tvam ca mahanto guravah sthirah \|*  
*yad alanghita-maryadas calantlm bibhrate bhuvam \|\|*

**Sesa, the Himalayas, and you, O king, are great, heavy, and steady, because all three hold the moving Earth without going out of bounds (or without transgressing etiquette). (3.28)**

Bhamaha’s aprastuta-prasamsa literally is “Praising the aprastuta ”: adhikarad apetasya vastuno ’nyasya ya stutih \|aprastuta- prasamseti sa caivam kathyate yatha \|\| (3.29). For instance:

*prmita-pranayi svadu kale parinatam bahu \|*  
*vina purusa-karena phalam pasyata sakhinam \|\|*

**Look at the fruits of trees. The fruits delight those who gladly take them, are sweet, ripe at the proper season, abundant, and produced without human endeavor. (3.30)**

Commenting on this verse, cited by Udbhata, Pratiharendu-raja says the implied sense is that everything happens by fate. Alternatively, by compounding the words as prmita-pranayi-svadu-kale, the verse means:

**Look: After the delectable occasion of the gratification of lovers, the fruits of trees become big and ripe without any man around. (3.30)**

The speaker hints at this meaning: “Similarly, your breasts have become big since your lover fondled them, but he remains unseen.” The fruits grew although there was no visible sprinkler.

Moreover, Bhamaha spoke of a poet’s legacy:

*upeyusam api divam san-nibandha-vidhayinam \|*  
*asta eva niratankam kantam kavya-mayam vapuh \|\|*

**Upon ascending to heaven, those who had written a good literary composition leave behind a healthy and beautiful body con­sisting of that poetry. (1.6)**

## 7. Udbhata

Udbhata flourished around 800 CE. He was the chief pandit in the court of King Jayapida of Kashmir (779-813 CE). His treatise is named Kavyalankara-sara-sangraha. It is also called Alankara-sara-sangraha, Kavyalankara-sangraha, and Alankara-sangraha.

Udbhata’s treatise was found in Kashmir by the German scholar Buhler. It was transliterated in 1897 by Col. Jacob. Udbhata’s commentary on Natya-sastra is lost, and so is his commentary, called Bhamaha-vivarana, on Bhamaha’s treatise. Dr. Kane expounds:

The work Bhamaha-vivarana seems to have been an elaborate one and it appears that the Alankara-sara-sangraha was only a summary of that work, as its very name indicates. Later writers very frequently refer to the Bhamaha-vivarana of Udbhata \[...\].

Udbhata exercised a profound influence over the Alankara- sastra. He eclipsed Bhamaha and it is probably owing to his great fame that Bhamaha’s work remained in the background and was rarely to be had up till a few years ago. He is always quoted with respect by his successors, even when they differ from him. He is the foremost representative of the Alankara school and his name is associated with several doctrines in the Alankara-sastra. In several important points he differs from Bhamaha.

Udbhata’s Kavyalankara-sara-sangraha consists of seventy-five definitional verses (karika) and ninety-five illustrations. He was the first to break up a karika into sutra portions: One verse that defines two ornaments, for instance, is separated in two in the text either to add an explanation or to insert an example.

Udbhata does not concern himself with a definition of poetry nor with any other detail of poetic theory except ornaments: He defines and illustrates them from beginning to end, probably because he gave the details in his Bhamaha-vivarana.

Udbhata discusses thirty-six ornaments of meaning (not counting sankara and samsrsti) in six chapters:

(I) punar-uktavad-abhasa, cheka anuprasa, anuprasa (three vrttis), lata anuprasa, rupaka, dipaka (3 kinds), upama, and prativastupama,

(II) aksepa, arthantara-nyasa, vyatireka, vibhavana, samasokti, atisayokti (4 kinds),

(III) yatha-samkhya, utpreksa, svabhavokti,

(IV) preyas, rasavat, urjasvin, paryayokta, samahita, udatta (2 kinds), slesa,

(V) apahnuti, visesokti, virodha, tulya-yogita, aprastuta-prasamsa, vyaja-stuti, vidarsana, sankara (4 kinds), upameyopama, sahokti, parivrtti, and

(VI) ananvaya, sa-sandeha, samsrsti, bhavika, kavya-linga, and kavya-drstanta.

Dr. Sushil Kumar De comments:

Udbhata seems to have taken over almost verbatim from Bhamaha the definitions of aksepa, vibhavana, atisayokti, yatha-samkhya, utpreksa, paryayokta, apahnuti, virodha, aprastuta-prasamsa, sahokti, sa-sandeha and ananvaya. The poetic figures are enumerated almost in the same order as that of Bhamaha. But Udbhata omits a few Alankaras defined by Bhamaha (e.g. yamaka, upama-rupaka, utpreksavayava) and adds a few not defined by the latter (e.g. punar-uktavad- abhasa, kavya-linga, drstanta, and sankara). \[...\] Udbhata’s three Vrttis, on which the classification of Anuprasa proceeds, are absent in Bhamaha.

Udbhata is the only older writer who entirely omits the treatment of yamaka.

PratTharendu-raja (c. 925 CE) wrote Laghu-vrtti, a well- known commentary on Udbhata’s treatise. In his introduction, PratTharendu-raja says Udbhata composed a literary work called Kumara-sambhava, from which the illustrations in Alankara-sara- sangraha were taken. Dr. Kane explains:

The Kumara-sambhava of Udbhata from which the examples of Alankaras are cited seems to have been a poem resembling the famous mahakavya of Kalidasa. There is a close correspondence between the two works not only in phrases and ideas, but even in incidents.

## Ornaments of Sound

Udbhata invented the punar-uktavad-abhasa ornament (seeming redundancy). For example:

*tada prabhrti nihsangi naga-kunjara-krtti-bhrt \|*  
*siti-kanthah kala-galat-satl-sokanala-vyathah \|\|*

**Siva’s throat is dark blue. He has snakes and an elephant skin. On that day, he was alone. In separation from SatT, who was squandering time, he felt the pain of the fire of sorrow. (Alankara-sara-sangraha, illustration 1.1)**

The instances of punar-uktavad-abhasa are “naga-kunjara” (in other contexts, naga, snake, can mean kunjara, elephant) and “siti- kanthah kala-gala”: The actual words are kala-galat (squandering time), but kala-gala (dark-blue neck) seems to be a repetition of siti-kantha.

Udbhata invented the term cheka anuprasa, but he says cheka anuprasa is a repetition of syllables, regardless of the order: chekanuprasas tu dvayor dvayoh susadrsokti-krtau (1.3). In modern poetics, alliteration where the letters are repeated out of order is classed as a vrtti anuprasa.

Udbhata did not accept the ritis nor the gunas, but he propounded three modes of alliteration: parusa (harsh), upa-nagarika (sweet like a city girl) and komala (soft).

The term parusa is taken from Dandi, whereas the komala is the same as Bhamaha’s gramya.

In that regard, Udbhata was the first rhetorician to categorize the phonemes. Inparusa, the phonemes are the letters s, s, t, th, d, dh; any consonant with r; and hl, hv, and hy.

In upanagarika, the sounds are: kk, cc, pp, and so on, as well as nk, nkh, ng, ngh, nc, nch, nj, njh, nt, nth, nd, ndh, nt, nth, nd, ndh, mp, mph, mb, and mbh.

Udbhata says the komala vrtti anuprasa includes the rest of the phonemes: sesair varnair yatha-yogam kathitam komalakhyaya \| gramyam vrttim prasamsanti kavyesv adrta-buddhayah \|\| (1.6).

Mammata’s three kinds of vrtti anuprasa are exactly the same as Udbhata’s three modes of alliteration, but Mammata slightly altered the categorization of phonemes in deference to Vamana, who started the theory that conjunct consonants such as nd pertain to an alliteration of harsh sounds, thereby contradicting Udbhata. In that regard, Vamana attacked his nemesis: ulbanas tu na sreyan, yatha valll-baddhordhva-jutodbhatam atati ratat- koti-kodanda-dandah, “The alliteration called ulbana (the same as Udbhata’s parusa) is not the best. For instance: valli-baddhordhva- jutodbhatam atati ratat-koti-kodanda-dandah, “The punishment of a million twanging bows goes to Udbhata, whose dreadlocks are high and are bound in a creeper-like fashion”” (Kavyalankara- sutra 4.1.9).

Mammata categorized a single n as well as a single r in madhurya- guna, based on Vamana’s examples, whereas in Udbhata’s methodology they fall in the category of komala. In addition, Mammata transferred sounds such as kk, cc, pp from upanagarika to ojas. Dandi perhaps indicated that the sounds k and kh are harsh (parusa), whereas Udbhata, Mammata and later writers implicitly included them in the category of soft phonemes (komala).

Mammata correlated the types of alliteration with the rasas: harsh phonemes express the rasas based on the modern ojas (raudra, bibhatsa, vira), and sweet phonemes evoke the rasas based on madhurya (srngara, karuna, santa)—whereas Udbhata, like Vamana, mostly had sound in mind. For example, Udbhata’s illus­tration of parusa vrtti anuprasa has no connection with the theme, serenity:

*tatra toyasayasesa-vyakosita-kusesaya \|*  
*cakase sali-kimsaru-kapisasa-mukha sarat \|\|*

**Autumn is resplendent. The directions are reddish because of numerous parrots, and all the lotuses in the ponds bloom. (1.3)**

Udbhata illustrates upa-nagarika vrtti anuprasa:

*sandraravinda-vrndottha-makarandambu-bindubhih \|*  
*syandibhih sundara-spandam nanditendindira kvacit \|\|*

**Sometimes a bumblebee buzzes with bliss because of the oozing honey-like drops of water from clusters of lotuses. (1.4)**

This is Udbhata’s example of komala vrtti anuprasa:

*keli-lolali-malanam kalaih kolahalaih kvacit \|*  
*kurvati kananarudha-sri-nupura-rava-bhramam \|\|*

**With the melodious humming of bees that thirst for games and sometimes with the cacophony, now that she is in the forest she is causing a dizziness with the sound of her beautiful ankle bells. (1.5)**

Mammata said that some scholars equated Udbhata’s vrttis with Vamana’s ritis: kesancid eta vaidarbhi-pramukhya ritayo matah (Kavya-prakasa 9.81). Still, the only similarity between Udbhata’s upanagarika and Vamana’s Vaidarbhi is sweetness, because the Vaidarbhi contains all the gunas of Vamana. Vamana propounded two types of alliteration (one matches Udbhata’s upanagarika and komala and the other matches his parusa), which he did not correlate with the ritis.

Abhinavagupta wrote:

*nagarikaya hy upamitety anuprasa-vrttih srngaradau visramyati, paruseti diptesu raudradisu, komaleti hasyadau, tatha “vrttayah kavya-matrkah” iti yad uktam munina tatra rasocita eva cesta-viseso vrttih. yad aha, “kaisiki slaksna- nepathya srngara-rasa-sambhava” ity-adi.*

**“The vrtti of alliteration named upa-nagarika, so called because it is compared to a young woman living in a city, is based on srngara and so on; parusa is based on raudra and other blazing rasas; and komala depends on hasya and so forth. In that way, a particular mode that is only suitable for a rasa is a vrtti, in reference to Bharata Muni’s statement: vrttayah kavya-matrkah, “The vrttis are the matrixes of poetry.” Bharata stated: kaisiki slaksna- nepathya srngara-rasa-sambhava, “In Kaisiki, which originates from srngara-rasa, the bodily decorations are slack” (Natya-sastra 1.45), and so on” (Locana 3.48).**

If the same phoneme is repeated, Udbhata’s vrttis as modified by Abhinava and Mammata are in the categories of guna (quality of the rasa) and alankara (anuprasa, alliteration) simultaneously.

## Ornaments of Meaning

Udbhata expounded Bhamaha’s two varieties of metaphor (rupaka)—samasta-vastu-visaya (complete set of metaphors) and eka-desa-vivarti (partial set of metaphors) (Bhamahalankara 2.22)—and invented mala-rupaka (series of metaphors) (Alankara- sara-sangraha 7.13). This is Udbhata’s example of samasta-vastu- visaya:

*jyotsnambunendu-kumbhena tara-kusuma-saritam \|*  
*kramaso ratri-kanyabhir vyomodyanam asicyata \|\|*

**The garden of the sky, variegated because of the flowers of the stars, was sprinkled in sequence by the venerable girl in the form of night with the waterpot of the moon, from which issued the water of moonrays. (1.11)**

Moreover, Mammata’s subdivisions of simile originate from Udbhata, who listed purna upama (complete simile) and lupta upama (elliptical simile), with the manifold subdivisions of the suffixes kyac, kyan, kvip, namul, vati, kalpap, and the like (Alankara-sara-sangraha 1.15-21).

Udbhata copied Bhamaha’s definition of atisayokti, but he made four varieties (2.11-13): They were reiterated by Mammata. Bhamaha was the first to use yadi in an atisayokti (Bhamahalankara 2.83): It is the same as Udbhata’s third variety.

Udbhata further innovated by including santa among the rasas, for a total of nine (4.4). They are only in the scope of his rasavat orna­ment. Dr. Kane writes:

From the Vikramorvasiya II.18 and the Kavyadarsa II.392 and the text of Bharata (VI.15-16) it follows that there were originally only eight rasas. As Udbhata (IV.5) and the Visnu- dharmottara-purana (p. 68 above) mention nine rasas it follows that santa-rasa was certainly included from about the 7th century. The Bhava-prakasana p. 47 states that it was Vasuki who first recognized santa-rasa. Some hold that Santa may be a rasa in poetry but not in dramas; vide Dasarupa IV.35.

Udbhata’s preyas consists of either a bhava or an anubhava. His example illustrates vatsalya (parental affection). His interpretations of urjasvi and samahita were accepted by Mammata.

Udbhata said that a rasa can be expressed by the use of its name (srngara, etc.). This view was criticized by Anandavardhana.

Mammata classed such an occurrence as a fault (rasa-dosa): vyabhicari-rasa-sthayi-bhavanam sabda-vacyata (Kavya-prakasa 7.60).

In addition, Udbhata invented the second variety of the udatta ornament. And what is known nowadays as the two main varieties of tulya-yogita was first stated by him (the things enumerated are either all contextual or all noncontextual).

Udbhata follows Bhamaha by listing slesa (pun) among ornaments of meaning. He also states two varieties: sabda-slesa and artha- slesa. Udbhata’s sabda-slesa corresponds to sabhanga-slesa (double meaning achieved by separating the letters in a different way), and his artha-slesa matches what is now called abhanga- slesa. Udbhata propounded the extreme theory that slesa is always conducive to another ornament and therefore in every instance the whole text is only classed as a slesa. Vamana implicitly rejected this. Mammata reiterated Vamana’s attack by stating that in a slesopama (simile based on a double meaning), the simile is predominant. In addition, Udbhata followed Bharata Muni in terms of accepting the application of Vedic accents (svarita, udatta, anudatta) in poetry, specifically in making a double meaning, such as taking a compound either as a tatpurusa or as a bahuvrihi, based on Panini’s rules. Bhoja accepted the usage of Vedic accents in poetry: svaras tridha—plutadayah, udattadayah, pragrhyadayah. \[...\] adi-grahanenanudatta-svaritaika-srutayah sangrhyante (Srngara-prakasa 7.145-148). Mammata refuted any such usage: “kavya-marge svaro na ganyate” iti ca naye (Kavya-prakasa 9.84).

Mammata defined artha-slesa (one word applies to two nouns in the text) in conformity with Bhamaha’s example; one characteristic of artha-slesa is that the pun is not altered by using a synonym: artha-slesasya tu sa visayah, yatra sabda-parivartane ’pi na slesatva-khandana (Kavya-prakasa, verse 377 vrtti). In addition, he criticized Udbhata for classing sabda-slesa as an ornament of meaning: sabda slesa iti cocyate, arthalankara-madhye ca laksyate, iti ko ’yam nayah. (Kavya-prakasa, verse 383 vrtti).

In poetics, the issue whether sabda-slesa is an ornament of sound or an ornament of meaning has not been settled: Ruyyaka, Jayadeva and Jagannatha follow Udbhata, although Jayadeva accepts Mammata’s two varieties—abhanga-slesa and sabhanga- slesa—and his interpretation of artha-slesa (Candraloka 5.63-65).

Udbhata’s vidarsana (nidarsana) is the expression of similarity between two things when in fact there may or may not be a connection: abhavan vastu-sambandho bhavan va yatra kalpayet \| upamanopameyatvam kathyate sa vidarsana \|\| (5.10). For example:

*vinocitena patya ca rupavaty api kamini \|*  
*vidhu-vandhya-vibhavaryah prabibharti visobhatam \|\|*

**Though she might be beautiful, an amorous young woman without a fitting husband assumes the lack of resplendence of a moonless night. (5.9)**

Night is the moon’s ladylove, especially because in Sanskrit the word for moon (candra) is masculine and the word for night (nisa) is feminine. Mammata and others accept that to assume a quality of another constitutes a subvariety of nidarsana insofar as the sense culminates in a simile (she is like a moonless night): atra katham anyasya lilam anyo vahatiti tat-sadrsim ity upamayam paryavasanam (Kavya-prakasa verse 436 vrtti).

Further, Udbhata created the term sankara. He says it has four categories: (1) A doubt regarding which ornament is actually occurring (this is the modern sandeha-sankara, according to Pratiharendu-raja, which Kavi Kamapura calls aniscaya-sankara), (2) An interdependent mix of an ornament of sound and an ornament of meaning: sabdartha-varty-alankara-sankara, (3) Many ornaments are in the same sentence: eka-vakyamsa-pravesa- sankara, and (4) A mix of ornaments that assist one another: paraspara upakara alankara sankara (Pratiharendu-raja calls it anugrahya anugrahaka sankara, which corresponds to Mammata’s angangi-bhava sankara) (Alankara-sara-sangraha 5.11-13).

Udbhata originated the theory that samsrsti is simply a combination of two or more ornaments that are not mutually connected, whereas in sankara the ornaments are intermingled. Visvanatha Kaviraja accepted this principle of differentiation between sankara and samsrsti (Sahitya-darpana 10.98), whereas Mammata says that a sankara has three varieties: (1) Udbhata’s first variety, (2) Udbhata’s fourth variety, and (3) Two ornaments are in the same compound (Kavya-prakasa 10.140-141).

Udbhata invented the term kavya-linga (poetic causation), but his definition does not quite match Mammata’s interpretation (explanatory reason). Udbhata says the kavya-linga ornament is this: A thing, whether heard or perceived, causes either a remembrance or an experience (such as a feeling).

By definition, Mammata’s bhavika (seemingly present occurrence) is the same as that of Udbhata, who modified the ancients’ interpretation that bhavika only signifies “the poet’s feeling” and is only in the scope of a prabandha (anything more than one verse): pratyaksa iva yatrartha drsyante bhuta-bhavinah \| atyadbhutah syat tad-vacam anakulyena bhavikam \|\| (6.6). For example:

*karosi pidam pritim ca niranjana-vilocana \|*  
*murtyanaya samudviksya-nanabharana-sobhaya \|\|*

**With this body of yours, on which the splendor of ornaments is worth continuously gazing at with awe, you of special eyes without eyeliner induce pain and joy. (6.7)**

Pratiharendu-raja comments that she induces pain because she took off her ornaments—this is indicated by the fact that she has no eyeliner—and she induces joy because the speaker is fully gazing at the ornaments in the form of her natural beauty. In bhavika, a past or future thing is perceived as if it were directly present. At best, the verse is a bhavika-dhvani (implied bhavika), if it is understood that the male speaker is mentally visualizing the ornaments. Or else, the remembrance of the resplendence of ornaments on her body is a smrti-vyabhicari-bhava-dhvani in the form of kavya- linga because it is the reason he feels pain. In addition, the virodha ornament (oxymoron) takes place since an action (giving pain) is seemingly contradicted by another (giving joy).

Bhamaha had mentioned drstanta (exemplification), but only in the sense it has in Nyaya philosophy, not as an ornament (Bhamahalankara 5.26). Udbhata was the first rhetorician to define drstanta as an ornament. He renamed it kavya-drstanta (6.1). He illustrates it:

*kincatra bahunoktena vraja-bhartaram apnuhi \|*  
*udanvantam anasadya maha-nadyah kim asate \|\|*

**You should attain the master of Vraja with many utterances. Do great rivers become idle when the ocean is not reached? (6.9)**

In this regard, Udbhata’s drstanta (example) and prativastupama (two sentences have an implied similarity) correspond to Mammata’s prativastupama and drstanta respectively (Kavya-prakasa 10.101­102). According to Udbhata, drstanta is an exemplification that does not mirror every aspect: istasyarthasya vispasta-pratibimba- nidarsanam, yathevadi-padaih sunyam budhair drstanta ucyate (6.8). In this matter, for the most part Ruyyaka, Jayadeva, Visvanatha and Jagannatha followed Udbhata. In addition, Mammata invented the vaidharmya variety of drstanta (contrasted example) and Ruyyaka the vaidharmya variety ofprativastupama.

Dr. Sushil Kumar De writes:

To later writers, it is not Bhamaha but Udbhata who is the authoritative exponent of this system and whose views are entitled to great respect from all schools of opinion. Bhamaha indeed commands veneration due to his antiquity; but he was, in course of time, eclipsed by his commentator, and later theorists turn to Udbhata’s work as embodying the standard opinions on the subject. We have the testimony of Anandavardhana, Abhinavagupta and Ruyyaka that some of the later speculations and controversies (e.g. those regarding upama divisions, and slesa) started from Udbhata’s time; and Udbhata (as also Dandin and Rudrata) probably showed the way to minute analysis and differentiation of poetic figures, which play such an important part in later theories. We can understand what influence Udbhata’s teachings exerted in this respect when we bear in mind that they guided very considerably the enquiries of two important later lawgivers in Poetics, Mammata and Ruyyaka, who fixed for the last time the definitions of most figures, analysed and arranged them on some general principle, and systematised their underlying doctrine.

Although Kuntaka elaborated one part of Bhamaha’s teaching which he took as the basis of his own peculiar system of vakrokti, it was Udbhata who properly carried on Bhamaha’s tradition and gave a systematic exposition of his work. Along with his contemporary Vamana, Udbhata may be taken without exaggeration to have been the founder ofthe Kashmirian school of Poetics, which produced its finest fruit in Anandavardhana; for Udbhata in Kashmir established the alankara doctrine in Poetics at a time when Vamana was skilfully constructing a theory of nti on the basis apparently of Dandin’s teachings, and both of them prepared the way for Anandavardhana.

PratTharendu-raja’s commentary is the oldest extant commentary on Alankara-sastra. Another commentator on Udbhata’s treatise is Rajanaka Tilaka:

Jayaratha, commenting on Ruyyaka’s Alankara-sarvasva, refers in more than one place to an Udbhata-viveka or Udbhata-vicara by Rajanaka Tilaka, and states that Ruyyaka generally followed the views propounded by Tilaka. We know that a Rajanaka Tilaka was Ruyyaka’s father.

In addition, Udbhata began the discussion on denotation and figurative usage, which he calls abhidha and guna-vrtti respectively: Abhinavagupta quotes Udbhata’s Bhamaha-vivarana, where Udbhata writes “Abhidhana is the significatory usage of words which is called the function of primary meaning (abhidha) when the sense is primary, and which is called the function of secondary meaning (guna-vrtti) when the sense is secondary.” In modern poetics, however, the broad category named abhidhana no longer exists, Denotation is called abhidha (or mukhya-vrtti), and guna- vrtti (gaunl-vrtti) is a category of figurative usage (laksana-vrtti).

Moreover, Visvanatha implicitly referred to Udbhata when he said that metaphor and most other figures of implied similarity are based on gaunl-vrtti (qualitative figurative usage), although in that connection Visvanatha quoted Vacaspati Misra’s explanation of Sankara’s commentary on Vedanta-sutra.

## 8. Vamana

He was Udbhata’s arch-enemy at the court of King Jayapida: “Vamana flourished between 775-810 A.D.” Vamana was the protagonist of the Riti school (style is most important). He wrote Kavyalankara-sutra and his own commentary, Kavyalankara-sutra-vrtti. Vamana was the first writer to profusely illustrate his theories with existing literature instead of composing his own.

The divide between Dandi’s and Bhamaha’s methodologies was accentuated by Vamana and Udbhata. Taking inspiration from

Dandi, Vamana expanded the concept of riti by adding much complexity to Bharata Muni’s ten gunas, whereas Udbhata discarded any notion of riti and emphasized alliteration.

## Sequence of Topics

Vamana’s treatise has twelve chapters in five cantos. The definitions are in the sutra style. The treatise consists of 317 sutras and approximately 250 examples. Ruyyaka and Jagannatha were the only other well-known rhetoricians to write in the sutra style.

In the first canto, Vamana says the goals of poetry are pleasure and fame: kavyam sad drstadrstartham, priti-kirti-hetutvat (1.1.5). Moreover, Kavi Karnapura reiterated Vamana’s twofold classification of poets—those who have no taste for vulgar things and those who consume whatever they get even if it has grass in it—as well as Vamana’s standpoint that only the poets in the first category are real poets: etena dvaye kavayah sambhavanti, arocakinah sa- trnabhyavaharinas ceti vamanah, tatra sa-trnabhyavaharinah kavaya eva na bhavanti, anadrtatvat. arocakina eva kavayah (Alankara-kaustubha 1.11). According to Vamana, only the first kind of poets should be taught: arocakinah sa-trnabhyavaharinas ca kavayah (1.2.1);purve sisyah, vivekitvat (1.2.2).

Vamana described his three ritis. Then he elaborated on the three main categories of poetry (gadya, padya, misra): He invented three styles of prose and gave names to them: vrtta-gandhi (some phrases follow a meter), curnam (no long compound and no boastful sound) and utkalika-prayam (the opposite of curnam) (1.3.22­25). He writes: yathahuh, gadyam kavinam nikasam vadanti, “For example, they say prose is the touchstone of poets” (1.3.21). In addition, he mentioned the types of knowledge that a poet must have: Among them, he says a poet must be familiar with erotica (kama-sastra). Dr. Krishnamachariar expounds:

Kama or love is the third Purusartha, that is, the third object of a man’s life. From the remotest ages the idea that enjoyment of pleasures is as much necessary for a man’s salvation as Dharma and Artha, virtue and wealth, has been prevalent in India, and tradition attributes the first treatise on these three objects of life to the Creator himself in 100,000 chapters.

Dr. Keith writes: “There is no question of the importance of knowledge of this topic for the writers of erotic poetry, and there is abundant proof that the Kama-sutra was studied as eagerly by would-be poets as were grammar, poetics and lexicography.”

Vamana adds a list of miscellaneous factors that make a poet good: The knowledge of poetics, practice, learning from authorities on poetics, the proper placement of words (including the concept of paka), creative intelligence (kavitva-bijam pratibhanam, 1.3.16) which he says is a special subconscious impression from a previous life, and one-pointed concentration: laksyajnatvam abhiyogo vrddha-sevaveksanam pratibhanam avadhanam ca prakirnam \|\| (1.3.11). An unspoken factor, illustrated by Vamana’s and Udbhata’s lives, that contributes to being productive is competition. Another example is the rivalry between Appaya Diksita and Pandita-raja Jagannatha.

In the second canto, Vamana discourses on literary faults. He was the first rhetorician to make categories, four in total: Those occurring in a word (pada-dosa), those in a meaning of a word (padartha-dosa), those in a sentence (vakya-dosa), and those in the meaning of the sentence (vakyartha-dosa). He invented the concepts of apratita (not understood, due to being a technical term), aslila (unpleasant) in three divisions (vrida-dayi, jugupsa- dayi, amangalatanka-dayi), and aprayukta (not in use).

The ideas that the redundancy in the words karnavatamsa (ear ornament on the ears), sravana-kundala (earrings on the ears), sirah-sekhara (crest on the head), and so on is acceptable (2.2.14) and that the word puspa, in puspa-mala, is expressive of super­excellence (2.2.16) (Kavya-prakasa 7.58) originate from him.

In the third canto, Vamana defines and illustrates his ten sabda- gunas (quality of sound) and ten artha-gunas (quality of meaning). Each of Bharata Muni’s ten gunas is defined in two ways: as a sabda-guna and as an artha-guna. Vamana kept the names of Bharata’s gunas, but changed some definitions.

In the fourth canto, Vamana treats of ornaments. He also explains six faults to avoid in a simile: (1) Inferiority of the standard of comparison, (2) Great superiority of the standard of comparison, (3) Disparity of gender, (4) Disparity in number, (5) Absence of similarity, and (6) Impossibility of the events described.
