Notably, the first two categories have three subvarieties: jati (category), pramana (size) and dharma (attribute of comparison) (4.2.11). Mammata’s six upama-dosas and Kavi Kamapura’s thirteen upama-dosas are based on Medhavin’s varieties and on Vamana’s subvarieties.

His fifth canto resembles Bhamaha’s six chapter: Vamana elaborates upon the proper usage of words: He discusses syntactic and grammatical details, such as:

♦ (1) Using certain words, like khalu, at the beginning of a line is improper (5.1.5);

♦ (2) If the existence of the noun is easily perceivable, only use an adjective (5.1.10);

♦ (3) The loose sasthi should be used only occasionally: sambandha-sambandhe ’pi sasthi kvacit (5.1.12);

♦ (4) For the words breasts, eyes, hands, etc., the singular, which signifies the category, should be used instead of the dual (5.1.17);

♦ (5) Substituting te and me in place of tvaya (by you) and maya (by me) is acceptable (5.2.10);

♦ (6) The verb asa is made from the verbal root as gati-dlpty- adanesu, not from as bhuvi (5.2.27); and

♦ (7) The verb aha (he speaks), a replacement by the rule bruvah pancanam (Astadhyayl3.4.84), is ordained in the present tense but can be used in the past tense (5.2.44).

Vamana also expounds upon the proper usage of rare terms. Dr. Kane writes:

In the vrtti on V.2.1 he says the forms indrau, bhavau, sarvau are not proper. This appears to be aimed at Bhamaha VI.32 (sarupa-sesam tu puman striya yatra ca sisyate \| yathaha varunav indrau bhavau sarvau mrdav iti \|\|). In V.2.15 Vamana says that the word bimbadhara frequently used by poets should be adhara-bimba if we consider Pa. II.1.56 (upamitam vyaghradibhih samanyaprayoge), but that word can be justified if it is taken as a madhya-pada-lopi-samasa (bimbakaro ’dharah bimbadharah).

Some surmise that Vamana is the same as the Vamana who co­wrote Kasika. Most scholars do not agree with this. It is generally accepted that Jinendra-buddhi, who commented on Kasika, lived around 700 CE. The Chinese traveler I-tsing mentioned Kasika and said that Jayaditya, the other co-writer of Kasika, passed away thirty years before. Dr. Kane comments: “I-tsing wrote his work in 691 A.D. So Jayaditya died about 661-62.” (1998: 118).

I-tsing did not mention Vamana. The consensus is that Vamana worked on Kasika after Jayaditya’s departure. Still, Jinendra- buddhi mentioned Vamana: nasti virodhah bhinna-kartrkatvat. idam hi jayaditya-vacanam tat punar vamanasya. (Nyasa 3.1.33)

## Ritis and Gunas

Vamana follows Dandi in terms of defining a guna in the broad sense of alankara (embellishment). He explains this term alankara as literary beauty—saundaryam alankarah (1.1.2)—and specifies: sa khalv alankaro dosa-hanad gunalankaradanac ca sampadyah kaveh, “A poet produces embellishment by avoiding faults and by adding qualities and ornaments” (1.1.3). He derives the word alankara which means “ornament” in the instrumental voice: “that by means of which there is embellishment”: karana-vyutpattya punar alankara-sabdo ’yam upamadisu vartate (1.1.2 vrtti).

Unlike Dandi, Vamana stated a distinction between gunas and alankaras: tad uktam, kavya-sobhayah kartaro dharma gunah, tad-atisaya-hetavas tv alankarah, “It is said: “The attributes that make the resplendence of the poetry are the gunas. However, the causes of the eminence of the resplendence of the poetry are the alankaras ”” (3.1.1-2). Therein lies the essential difference between the Riti school and the Alankara school: Vamana says an alankara is not necessary, and moreover an alankara without a guna cannot produce literary beauty:

The Riti and its constituent Gunas come in as a sine qua non in the production of this beauty, but the poetic figures only contribute to its heightening. This distinction between the Guna and the Alankara as to their respective position in a formal scheme of Poetics, which is vaguely hinted at by Dandin, is fully developed for the first time by Vamana (iii. 1.1-3). The Gunas, being essential to the Riti, are defined as those characteristics which create the charm of poetry (kavya- sobhayah kartaro dharmah)—a function which is assigned to both Gunas and Alankaras by Dandin—but Alankaras are such ornaments as serve to enhance the charm already so produced (tad-atisaya-hetavah).”

Vamana, who systematically established the Riti-theory, goes further and lays down that the Gunas are essential (nitya) excellences, while the Alankaras are not essential (anitya) but serve only to increase the beauty of a poem already brought out by the former.

In the world of style, Vamana represents a giant step forward. He is famous for propounding the theory that riti is the soul of poetry: ritir atma kavyasya (Kavyalankara-sutra 1.2.6). Thus for the first time, a poetic theorist officially talked about the soul of poetry. However, by stating that vakrokti (poetic expression) is all in all, Bhamaha had stated in a roundabout way that vakrokti is the soul of poetry. Dr. Dasgupta writes:

When Vamana said, ‘ritir atma kavyasya’ he probably simply meant that kavya necessarily implies a bandha or arrangement of sabdartha. Though he uses the word atman yet by that word he really means deha (body) of kavya, which is really sabdartha. But Bhamaha was shrewd enough to perceive that it is not merely the bandha that constitutes a kavya but the expression must be out of the commonplace. It must be vakra.

Therefore, when Anandavardhana stated that the connoisseurs of poetry say the soul of poetry is a first-rate implied sense, he added, as a tacit reference to Vamana, that the connoisseurs also say the soul of poetry is the literal sense of the text. Anandavardhana avoided the inconsistency of “two souls” by defining soul as essence. To illustrate that poetry has a twofold essence, Anandavardhana gave the example of a beautiful woman: She has a directly perceivable charm, with her limbs and her ornaments, and a subtle charm, her nature.

In addition, Anandavardhana created the third category of poetry with respect to poets like Vamana, for whom a rasa is not essential: Anandavardhana’s term citra (amazing) was used by Vamana in this context: etasu tisrsu ritisu rekhasv iva citram kavyam pratisthitam iti (Kavyalankara-sutra 1.2.13). Anandavardhana himself did not accept it as true poetry. Visvanatha Kaviraja agreed with Anandavardhana. Mammata, however, considered citra a third kind of poetry proper: sabda-citram vacya-citram avyangyam tv avaram smrtam (Kavya-prakasa 1.5). Kavi Kamapura followed Mammata in principle and changed the name citra to vaicitrya in order to differentiate third-rate poetry from its subcategory called Citra-kavya (picture poetry, etc.), but his sole example of third- rate poetry is classed as second-rate by Ananda’s and Mammata’s standards.

Vamana defined the term riti (style): visistapada-racana ritih, “Riti is a specific arrangement of words” (1.2.7). Thus although Vamana created the concept of artha-guna (quality of the meaning), he preferred sound over meaning. Vamana did not invent the term riti, because in introducing one verse about riti, he wrote atra slokah (a verse in this regard), a formula which refers to a previous authority: atra slokah—samastatyudbhata-padam ojah-kanti- gunanvitam, gaudiyam iti gayanti ritim riti-vicaksanah (1.2.12 vrtti). In his writing and in his citations, Vamana also mentioned these synonyms of riti: kavya-paddhati, bandha, kavya-bandha, pada-nyasa, racana, pada-racana, and marga.

The specificity stated in the above definition “Riti is a specific arrangement of words” (1.2.7) lies in the attribution of specific gunas to each of his three styles: Vaidarbhi, Gaudiya, and Pancali. The Vaidarbhi is the riti that has all the gunas at once (samagra- gunopeta vaidarbhi, 1.2.11). The Gaudiya has the sabda-gunas called ojas (denseness of the arrangement of words) and kanti (no vulgar word) (ojah-kantimati gaudiya, 1.2.12). The Pancali has the sabda-gunas called madhurya (no long compound) and saukumarya (absence of harsh sounds) (madhurya-saukumaryopapanna pancall, 1.2.13). He adds that the richness of the artha-gunas is to be savored in the Vaidarbhi. Vamana went over the top regarding the Vaidarbhi: He said only the Vaidarbhi is acceptable since it has all the gunas. Not only that, he propounded a pure Vaidarbhi, characterized by the absence of compound. Dr. Waman Keshav Lele comments:

Kalidasa is considered the best representative poet of the vaidarbhi riti. Vamana has quoted a few verses from Kalidasa’s different works to illustrate some theoretical concepts. But if we go through these verses we come to realize that even Kalidasa’s compositions do not represent the suddha-vaidarbhi variety. \[...\] Thus even Kalidasa, the Lord of the vaidarbhi riti, could not write suddha-vaidarbhi ! All in all the suddha-vaidarbhi conceived by Vamana as a category of the vaidarbhi riti is an imaginary and impractical concept. It, therefore, cannot be accepted.

Singabhupala accepted Vamana’s interpretations of Vaidarbhi: samasa-rahityam yatha (Rasarnava-sudhakara, illustration 1.149), and so did Kavi Kamapura: avrttir alpa-vrttir va samasta- guna-bhusita \| vaidarbhi sa tu srngare karune ca prasasyate \|\| (Alankara-kaustubha 9.3); samasta-guneti gunas trayo va dasa va (9.3 vrtti).

At the end of the chapters on the gunas, Vamana quotes verses which class poetry in two: amra-paka-kavya (development like a mango) and vrntaka-paka-kavya (development like an eggplant, which needs to be cooked to become edible). The first one has all the gunas. However, Vamana does not say what he means by “all the gunas. ” The same ambiguity applies to his definition of the Vaidarbhi. Perhaps it refers to any ten gunas among the twenty. The second type of poetry, vrntaka-paka-kavya, is so called because the phraseology is grammatically flawless yet the meaning is complicated.

Vamana’s gunas are literary qualities in the true sense because he includes all types of literary embellishments, such as an implied sense, in his gunas. Bhoja and Vidyanatha followed this principle. On the other hand, Anandavardhana and Mammata used the term guna both in the conventional meanings of “quality of sound” and “quality of meaning” and in the technical sense of “a rasa’s quality” (sweetness or melting for the rasas with madhurya, and vigor for the rasas with ojas): guna-vrttya punas tesam vrttih sabdarthayor mata (Kavya-prakasa 8.71).

## Vamana’s Twenty Gunas

**Guna** **Definition as a sabda-guna** **Definition as an artha-guna**   ojas Compactness of the arrangement of words (they seem to form one block) Five categories: One sentence expresses the meaning of a word; One word expresses the meaning of a sentence; The exact same purport is repeatedly stated in many ways; Several short sentences are tightly grammatically constructed into one sentence; And one word is very purposeful   prasada Relaxed structure: the words are spaced out, but this must occur with ojas, yet without a sequence Clarity of the meaning by avoiding superfluity   slesa Coalescence of words resulting in smoothness: masrnatvam slesah (3.1.11) Coalescence of ideas: A construction which is a mix of krama (sequence), kautilya (cunningness), anulbanatvam (nonexcessiveness, absence of extravagance), and upapatti (likelihood)   samata No change of riti throughout the verse Sameness: The absence of a lack of correspondence with the meaning by not changing the suffix or word that had been used   samadhi Crescendo and decrescendo (a long compound and a series of single words, in sequence several times) Grasping a meaning as a result of mental concentration; this guna is called samadhi because it is a cause of samadhi   madhurya Single words (no coalescence), and no long compound Poetic expression   saukumarya Softness (Mammata says this is only the absence of harshness) No harsh or inauspicious meaning   udarata Sprightliness (this is the origin of the purposeful usage of ojas-guna in the scope of srngara- rasa) Exaltedness: the absence of a rustic meaning   artha-vyakti The meanings are clear because the words are separated and are placed in proper order (this is the modern prasada- guna) Explicitness of ideas which makes the nature of things clear (this is the same as the svabhavokti ornament)   kanti Elegance (Mammata says this is only the absence of a rustic word) A rasa is prominent (dipta- rasatvam) (3.2.15)

On the whole, Vamana did not follow Dandi’s gunas:

Vamana’s Gunas differ considerably from those of Bharata or Dandin. Vamana’s ojas, for instance, would correspond to Dandin’s slesa, while Dandin’s madhurya is split up into prthak-padatva and agramyatva.

It appears that Dandi seized upon one part of Bharata’s definition of ojas (viz. samasavadbhir bahubhih) while Vamana relied upon two others (viz. sanuragaih and udaraih) in defining ojah as sabda-guna and artha-guna respectively.

Although Abhinavagupta, in his commentary on the sixteenth chapter of Natya-sastra, explained Vamana’s gunas by defining and illustrating them, Mammata made short work of Vamana’s gunas by reducing them to three steps. He accepted only three and repudiated the rest either by showing that a guna of Vamana is nothing but the absence of a fault, by subsuming one guna in another, by classing a guna as an alankara, and so on. Mammata points out that, as sabda-gunas, slesa, samadhi and audarya are partially included in what is known nowadays as ojas; the artha- vyakti corresponds to the modern prasada, whereas saukumarya and kanti are essentially the opposites of the literary defects of harshness (parusya) and vulgarity (gramyatvam) respectively.

Visvanatha reiterated Mammata’s refutation of Vamana’s gunas. Nonetheless, although he follows Mammata in this regard, Pandita-raja Jagannatha perfected Vamana’s definitions of gunas and gave outstanding examples. Mammata would have to explain how he includes the smoothness of multiple phonetic combinations (Vamana’s sabda-guna slesa) in the modern ojas. Moreover, Vamana’s sabda-guna udarata (sprightliness) is a noteworthy category of poetry that Mammata failed to acknowledge. Pandita­raja Jagannatha supported Vamana in this matter. Jagannatha says ojas can suitably occur in the context of madhurya if there is some purpose that justifies it, such as an intensity which is not in the scope of ‘sweetness’ per se.

In Vamana’s system, the notion of rasa-dhvani is called artha- guna kanti:

Vamana’s artha-guna kanti corresponds to figures like rasavat of the Alankara system, therefore he does not define rasavat. \[...\] Bharata’s udara differs considerably from Vamana’s udarata, which does not comprehend, as Bharata’s udara does, the Rasas and Bhavas in its scope; but it corresponds partially to Vamana’s artha-guna kanti. At the same time, it would seem that, in spite of such minor discrepancies, Bharata’s scheme of the Gunas as a whole is developed to its furthest possibilities by Vamana.

In Vamana’s methodology, the notion of vastu-dhvani (implied idea) is included in his artha-guna samadhi. In that regard, he states two kinds of meanings: vyakta (obvious) and suksma (subtle) (3.2.9). He subdivides the latter in two: bhavya (perceivable) and vasaniya (pertaining to a subconscious predisposition) (3.2.10).

He defines them: suksmo dvedha bhavato bhavyo vasamyas ca, sighra-nirupanagamyo bhavyah, ekagrata-prakarsa-gamyo vasaniya iti, “A bhavya meaning can be quickly understood from the description. A vasaniya meaning can be understood by the eminence of one-pointed concentration” (3.2.10 vrtti). This verse illustrates a bhavya meaning:

*anyonya-samvalita-mamsala-danta-kantih*  
*sollasam avirala-samvalitardha-taram \|*  
*lila-grhe pratikalam kila-kincitesu*  
*vyavartamana-nayanam  mithunam cakasti \|\|*

**In a dwelling for love games, the gracefulness of a mutually connected fleshy tusk, a shrill half-murmur enthusiastically occurring every now and then, and eyes that are revolving in emotions of kila-kincita at every moment make a splendid intercourse. (Kavyalankara-sutra 3.2.10)**

Dr. Sushil Kumar De remarks:

Vamana’s systematic formulation certainly obtained for it a large number of adherents and followers, so that important later authors like Rajasekhara, Hemacandra and Jayaratha, cite with respect the opinions of the Vamaniyas, just in the same way as they cite the Audbhattas, the followers of Vamana’s contemporary and rival Udbhata.

But the Riti-system, in spite of Vamana’s well-reasoned formulation and the advocacy of his followers, never appears to have wielded very great influence, and its existence was comparatively short-lived. There is no doubt that like the

Rasa and the Alankara systems, it left its impress on later theories, but it never found a serious champion after Vamana among latter-day writers, and its theories never found unqualified acceptance.

Although he greatly favored ornaments and is thus classed in the Alankara school, Rudrata developed his own concept of riti, and so did Bhoja, but Mammata demolished the Rlti school. In Kavya- prakasa, the style of compounding is included in the definitions of madhurya-guna and ojas guna.

Mammata criticized Vamana for using phonemes without considering a rasa. Vamana would say that the poetry is sweet simply because it has sweet phonemes. According to Mammata, Vamana opines that the poetry is not sweet if there is no sweet phoneme, even when there is srngara-rasa.

Still, Mammata and others accepted Vamana’s selection of phonemes of sweetness. And in his definition of poetry (tad adosau sabdarthau sa-gunav analankrti punah kvapi, 1.4), Mammata reiterated Vamana’s and Bhatta Nayaka’s emphasis on the necessary presence of a guna, although Mammata said that for the most part a guna is so called because it is an attribute of the rasa.

## Ornaments

Vamana discourses on two ornaments of sound (yamaka, anuprasa) and thirty figures of sense (not counting samsrsti) in this order: yamaka, anuprasa, upama, prativastupama, samasokti, aprastuta- prasamsa, apahnuti, rupaka, slesa, vakrokti, utpreksa, atisayokti, sandeha, virodha, vibhavana, ananvaya, upameyopama, parivrtti, krama, dipaka, nidarsana, arthantara-nyasa, vyatireka, visesokti, vyaja-stuti, vyajokti, tulya-yogita, aksepa, sahokti, samahita, samsrsti, upama-rupaka, and utpreksavayava.

Vamana does not fall short of expounding alliteration: It has two modes. They are not inherent in his gunas because his sabda-guna madhurya is simply the absence of a long compound and his sabda- guna ojas is a tight phonetic construction, therefore Udbhata’s vrttis (modes of alliteration) cannot be equated with Vamana’s ritis. Vamana’s alliteration called anulbana (not excessive), which he says is the best (anulbano varnanuprasah sreyan, 4.1.9), corresponds to Udbhata’s upanagarika and komala, and his ulbana matches Udbhata’s parusa. But Vamana innovates by showing that the anusvara (m), a single n, and a single r, severally, belong to an alliteration expressive of sweetness (anulbana). For example:

*kvacin masrna-mamsalam kvacid ativa-taraspadam*  
*prasanna-subhagam muhuh surataranga-lilankitam \|*  
*idam hi tava vallaki-ranita-nirgamair gumphitam*  
*mano madayativa me kim api sadhu sangitakam \|\|*

**Some particularly excellent music as if maddens my mind. The music, repeatedly marked by the playfulness of godly waves (sura-taranga)—or by a playfulness that sets the stage for amorous sport (surata-ranga)—is clear and lovely, due to being emanations from the sounds of your lute, and is sometimes smooth, at times strong, and occasionally the form of intense high notes. (4.1.9) (Sad-ukti-karnamrta 1065)**

Vamana was the only poetical theorist to say that all ornaments of meaning are based on simile: prativastu-prabhrtir upama- prapancah (4.3.1). Dr. De expounds:

The importance of upama, involved in other figures, is recognised from Bhamaha’s time; and consequently this figure, which is the source of all the figures grouped together by later writers as sadrsya-mula or aupamya-garbha Alankaras is always given a place of honour at the beginning of most treatises on Sanskrit Poetics; but Vamana goes to the extreme of defining all figures with reference to the idea of comparison, or in terms of the relation of the upamana and the upameya. On account of this fundamental postulate, his definitions of some of the figures differ widely from those given by other writers; and he has also to exclude such figures as paryayokta, preyas, rasavat, urjasvin, udatta, bhavika, and suksma which he does not define. He gives a peculiar definition of the figure vakrokti as a mode of metaphorical expression.

Vamana’s simile proper is only based on the similarity of a quality, not on the similarity of an action: upamanenopameyasya guna- lesatah samyam upama (4.2.1). He specifies that by definition a standard of comparison is superior to the subject of the comparison. The two broad divisions of Vamana’s simile are laukik (commonplace, i.e. well-known) and kalpita (imagined). The next two subdivisions are padartha-vrtti and vakya-vrtti (4.2.3), with the subcategories of purna (complete) and lupta (elliptical): He specifies that an elliptical simile is a simile where one of the four constituents is absent: upameya (subject of comparison), upamana (standard of comparison), attribute in common, and a word expressive of the comparison (4.2.5-6). Vamana’s kalpita upama, taken from Bharata Muni, is the same as utpreksa, but his utpreksa corresponds to Udbhata’s and Mammata’s first variety of atisayokti (introsusception): atad-rupasyanyathadhyavasanam atisayartham utpreksa (4.3.9).

Vamana subdivides simile in three categories: stuti (praise): “A loving wife is as good as the Nectar”, ninda (criticism): “An unchaste wife is like poison”, and tattvakhyana (it says the truth). The first two are taken from Bharata Muni.

Some of Vamana’s ornaments do not match modern ornaments though the names are the same. Vamana defines his aksepa in two ways: The first one is the modern pratipa, and the second one is the modern samasokti. His samasokti is the modern aprastuta- prasamsa: upameyasyanuktau samana-vastu-nyasah samasoktih, sanksepa-vacanat samasoktir ity akhya (4.3.3 vrtti). And his aprastuta-prasamsa involves a slight mention of the prastuta (subject of description): upameyasya kincil-linga-matrenoktau samana-vastu-nyase ’prastuta-prasamsa (4.3.4 vrtti).

Vamana’s visesokti is a kind of metaphor where the subject of comparison (upameya) does not have one of the said qualities of the standard of comparison (upamana). He says it is almost a metaphor: rupakam cedamprayeneti (4.3.23). Vamana’s visesokti is the same as Dandi’s viruddha-rupaka. This is Vamana’s example: dyutam hi nama purusasyasimhasanam rajyam, “For a man, gambling is a kingdom without a throne” (Mrc-chakatika) (4.3.23). Visvanatha Kaviraja accepted this concept and renamed it a metaphor involving a dissimilarity (vaidharmye rupaka) (Sahitya- darpana 10.33), whereas Jagannatha renamed it drdharopa-rupaka (Rasa-gangadhara, KM edition, p. 439).

Vamana’s krama ornament, another name of yatha-samkhya (parallelism), is based on relations between many upameyas and upamanas. Vamana’s interpretation follows Bhamaha’s example of yatha-samkhya. All other writers list yatha-samkhya as an ornament while tacitly admitting that it is simply the absence of the fault called bhagna-prakrama (broken symmetry) (anacoluthon).

Vamana renamed Bhamaha’s vakrokti as artha-guna madhurya (poetic expression) and defined vakrokti as an ornament of meaning: sadrsyal laksana vakroktih, “Vakrokti is figurative usage that takes place because of a similarity” (Kavyalankara-sutra 4.3.8). Dr. De explains:

Bharata’s prasada, corresponding to Dandin’s samadhi, is a metaphorical mode of expression, which Vamana would include in his peculiar definition of the vakrokti figure and which comes generally under laksana or upacara of later theorists.

According to Ruyyaka, Vamana’s vakrokti involves an implied sense: vamanena tu sadryya-nibandhanaya laksanaya vakrokty- alankaratvam bruvata kaycid dhvani-bhedo ’lankaratayaivoktah, “Vamana mentioned some particular variety of dhvani (laksana- mula atyanta-tiraskrta-vacya dhvani) as an alankara by stating that laksana founded on similarity is the vakrokti ornament” (Alankara-sarvasva, introduction, KM p. 7).

Vamana invented the term vyajokti (artful concealment), as an ornament. For example:

*sarac-candramsu-gaurena vataviddhena bhamini \|*  
*kasa-puspa-lavenedam sasru-patam mukham krtam \|\|*

**Passionate girl, your face, pale due to the rays of the autumnal moon, has become the backdrop of a downpour of tears because a portion of a full-blown flower (without a stem) was not pierced even by the wind! (4.3.25)**

Vamana defines vyajokti as a similarity by the truth of a disguise: vyajasyasatya-sarupyam vyajoktih (4.3.25); vyajasya cchadmanah satyena sarupyam vyajoktih (4.3.25 vrtti). In Mammata’s methodology, the above verse is classed as an atisayokti (introsusception).

Vamana’s atisayokti corresponds to Udbhata’s and Mammata’s third variety of atisayokti, characterized by the usage of the word “if”. Vamana writes: sambhavya-dharma-tad-utkarsa- kalpanatisayoktih, “Atisayokti is the imagination of an honorable attribute and of its supereminence” (4.3.10). For instance:

*ubhau yadi vyomni prthak-pravahav*  
*akasa-ganga-payasah patetam \|*  
*tenopamiyeta tamala-mlam*  
*amukta-mukta-latam asya vaksah \|\|*

**If the flow of the celestial Ganges and a flow of milk would somehow run separately in the sky, then His chest, dark like a tamala tree and graced with a loose creeper in the form of an elephant-pearl neacklace, could be compared to that. (4.3.10)**

## 9. Rudrata

I Ud udrata (c. 850 CE), a Kashmiri, wrote Kavyalankara. IK It consists of 16 chapters and 734 verses (definitions and examples) mostly in the arya meter. He composed all his illustrations. Rudrata belongs to the Alankara school: Arguably, Kavyalankara excels Dandi’s Kavyadarsa as the best treatise outside the scope of the Dhvani theory. His definitions are sharp, his examples original and delightful. As regards sabda-slesa, vakrokti, ornaments of meaning, and so on, Mammata took inspiration from him. Rudrata also had a profound influence on Ruyyaka. In addition, Rudrata was keen on rasa, and showed his mastery of alliteration in almost every example in his treatise.

The contents of the sixteen chapters are: (I) Respects to Ganesa and to Gauri, the purpose of poetry, and the essential requisites of a poet (sakti, vyutpatti, abhyasa, along with definitions), (II) Definition of poetry, enumeration of ornaments of sound (vakrokti, anuprasa, yamaka, slesa, citra), the ritis (four kinds), the six languages in which poetry can be composed (Prakrit, Sanskrit, Magadhi, Pisaci, Sauraseni Apabhramsa), definition of vakrokti (two kinds: slesa and kaku), and the details about anuprasa (5 vrttis), (III) Yamaka, (IV) Sabda-slesa (nine varieties, adopted by Mammata and Visvanatha: varna-slesa, pada-slesa, linga-slesa, bhasa-slesa, bhasa-sama- slesa, prakrti-slesa, pratyaya-slesa, vibhakti-slesa, and vacana- slesa), (V) Citra (citra-kavya), (VI) Sabda-dosa (in two major categories: in a word (pada) and in a sentence (vakya)), (VII) Twenty-three figures based on vastava, (VIII) Twenty-one figures based on aupamya, (IX) Twelve figures based on atisaya, (X) Artha-slesa (ten varieties); moreover, ornaments of meaning are either suddha (single ornament) or sanklrna (mixed), also called sankara (10.25-28), (XI) Nine artha-dosas and four upama-dosas, (XII) Ten rasas, and an elaboration on srngara, (XIII) Sambhoga- srngara, (XIV) Vipralambha-srngara, (XV) Characteristics of other rasas, and (XVI) The definitions of other types of poetic composition, such as katha, akhyayika, maha-kavya and laghu- kavya.

## Vakrokti

The modern concept of vakrokti (ambiguous speech) originates from Rudrata and Ratnakara:

Rudrata’s definition of the figure replaced that of Vamana’s metaphorical vakrokti, survived Kuntaka’s broader inter­pretation of vakrokti, and established itself as the only recog­nised figure of that name in later literature from Mammata onwards.

It will not be wrong if we accept the most plausible date assigned to him by Pischel, viz. the middle of the 9th century. The date makes him a contemporary of Anandavardhana, who never cites or refers to Rudrata, as he does to other well- known predecessors, and by whom this peculiar alankarika connotation of vakrokti, if known, was not apparently recognised.

We need not go so far as to hold with Jacobi that Rudrata derived his idea of vakrokti from Ratnakara’s well known poem Vakrokti-pancasika, and therefore was later than Ratnakara, son of Amrtabhanu, who lived under Brhaspati and Avantivarman of Kashmir; bit it is clear that if this new idea of vakrokti did not originate with Ratnakara or even with Rudrata, it was defined for the first time by the latter and illustrated by the former as a particular poetic figure. This verbal figure is described as resting on slesa (paronomasia) or kaku (intonation).

Anandavardhana mentioned the concept of kaku (implied sense based on a modulation of the voice): He classed it in the category of second-rate implied sense (Dhvany-aloka 3.38).

Rudrata, Mammata and others do not include slesa-vakrokti in sabda-slesa because slesa-vakrokti only occurs in a dialogue. Rudrata defines it: vaktra tad anyathoktam vyacaste canyatha tad- uttara-dah, vacanam yat pada-bhangair ya sa slesa-vakroktih, “When one speaker says something one way and the other person gives a reply by interpreting the speaker’s words differently by separating the letters in another way, that is slesa-vakrokti” (Kavyalankara 2.14). Later writers said it can also be based on abhanga-slesa (the double meaning is achieved without separating the letters in another way). Rudrata, however, followed Udbhata in terms of defining abhanga-slesa as artha-slesa. This is Rudrata’s example of slesa-vakrokti:

*kim gauri mam prati rusa nanu gauh kim asmi*  
*kupyami kam prati mayity anumanato ’ham \|*  
*janamy atas tvam anumanata eva satyam*  
*ittham giro giribhuvah kutila jayanti \|\|*

**Siva: GaurT, why are you angry at me?**

**Uma: (thinking he said: kim gaur imam prati rusa, “O Cow, why are you angry at her?”): If I’m a cow, why would I be angry, and at whom?**

**Siva: You’re angry at me. I know this by inference**

**(anumanatah).**

**Uma: That’s because you bow to women who are not Uma (anuma-natah).**

**Uma’s crooked words were victorious that way.**

**(Kavyalankara 2.15) (cited in Sad-ukti-karnamrta 32).**

An example of vakrokti by Ratnakara is shown at the end of Appendix I. The difference between vakrokti (ambiguous speech) and vyajokti (artful concealment) is that in vyajokti a speaker construes his or her own statement in a tricky way afterward.

## Ritis and Vrttis

Rudrata discourses upon riti. He expounds four varieties, but they are only based on the style of compounding, not on the type of phoneme: In the Pancali the compounds are made of two or three words, in the Latiya the compounds have five, six or seven words, in the Gaud! the sky is the limit, and in the Vaidarbhi, the best one, there is no compound (Kavyalankara 2.3-6). Rudrata matches ritis and rasas as follows: vaidarbhi-pancalyau preyasi karune bhayanakadbhutayoh, latiya-gaudiye raudre kuryadyathaucityam, “Vaidarbhi and Pancali are used in preyas, karuna, bhayanaka, and adbhuta, and Latiya and Gaudiya are for raudra, so long as there is appropriateness” (Kavyalankara 15.20). There is no rule for the other rasas.

Rudrata’s alliteration has five modes (vrtti) (2.19):

- madhura (sweet),
- praudha (mature),
- parusa (harsh),
- lalita (charming), and
- bhadra (gracious).

Rudrata ignores the topic of guna. He does not correlate the rasas with his vrttis. He divided Udbhata’s parusa in three: praudha, parusa and bhadra. His lalita corresponds to Udbhata’s komala. He rejects Vamana’s rejection of Udbhata’s inclusion in madhurya of sounds such as nt and nd (Kavyalankara 2.20). This is Rudrata’s example of madhura:

*anuranan-mani-mekhalam*  
*avirata-sinjana-manju-manjiram \|*  
*parisaranam aruna-carane*  
*rana-ranakam akaranam kurute \|\|*

**While moving about, your gem-studded girdle is always resoun­ding and your charming anklebells are constantly tinkling: They make a sensual desire for feet that are merely reddish something for which there is no valid reason. (2.23)**

The distinctions between Rudrata’s praudha, parusa and bhadra are subtle. The parusa is used for harsh meanings. This is the example ofpraudha:

*karyakaryam anaryair*  
*unmarga-nirargalair galan-matibhih \|*  
*nakarnyate vikarnair*  
*yuktoktibhir uktam uktam api \|\|*

**Dishonorable persons do not give ear to the difference between good and bad, even though the differentiation is properly reiterated time and time again. Those persons, whose intelligence is ebbing, are unimpeded on the wrong path in life.(2.25)**

Rudrata defines his alliteration of softness: lalitayam gha-dha-bha- ra-sah laghavo las caparair asamyuktah, “In lalita, the sounds are short gh, short dh, short bh, short r, and short s, as well as l, but not if l is conjoined with another phoneme” (2.29). For example:

*malayanila-lalanollala-*  
*mada-kala-kala-kantha-kalakala-lalamah \|*  
*madhura-madhu-vidhura-madhupo*  
*madhur ayam adhuna dhinoti dharam \|\|*

malaya-anila—of the Malaya breeze; lalana—due to the play ( the movement); ullala—\[the cuckoos,\] which are enthusiastic; mada- kala—\[which are endowed with\] rapture and sweet tones; kala- kantha—because of cuckoos (“they whose throats are melodious”); kalakala—of a cacophony; lalamah—\[spring,\] in which there is a predominance; madhura-madhu—by sweet nectar; vidhura— are impaired (intoxicated); madhupah—\[spring,\] during which the bees; madhuh—springtime; ayam—this (the well-known); adhuna—now; dhinoti—pleases; dharam—the Earth.

**Spring is mostly characterized by a cacophony engendered by rapturous and sweet-sounding cuckoos enthusiastic due to the play of the breeze from the Malaya Hills. At this time the bees are intoxicated by sweet nectar. Now spring delights the Earth. (2.30)**

## Yamaka

In the third chapter, Rudrata turns on the jet engines of his genius and expounds yamaka (word rhyme) in fifty-nine verses: “Rudrata perhaps ranks next to Dandin in the fulness of his treatment, though there is considerable divergence in the details of classification of these two writers.” Here the first line is repeated in the fourth, and the second in the third:

3.14

*muda ratasau ramam yata yam*  
*smarasy ado ’lam kurutena vodha \|*  
*smara-syado ’lankuntte ’navodham*  
*udaratasau ramamyatayam \|\|*

muda—owing to joy; rata—is enamored \[of you\]; asau—she; ramanl—a beautiful woman; yata—was held back; yam—whom; smarasi—you remember; adolam—doubtlessly; ku-rutena— with contemptible sounds; vodha—a leader; smara—of Cupid; syadah—the impulse (Amara-kosa 1.1.67); alankurute—adorns; a-nava-udham—an unmarried woman; udarata—exaltedness; asau—that; ramanlyatayam—in being beautiful.

**That beautiful woman whom you subjugate with socially reprehensible sounds was held back. She is enamored of you out of joy; there is no doubt. You remember. The impulse of Cupid adorns an unmarried woman. That is exaltedness in being beautiful.**

3.17

*nanama loko vidam anavena*  
*mahl na cari-tra-mud-ara-dhlram \|*  
*na namalo ’kovida-mana-venam*  
*ahlna-caritram udara-dhlram \|\|*

(repetition of a half verse)

nanama—bowed; lokah—people; vidam—to a knower; anavena— by praising (from the prefix a\[n\] and the verbal root nu stutau); mahl—\[people,\] who have festivals; na ca—never; ari-tra—\[a knower,\] who delivers enemies; mut—because of joy; ara-dhl— the intelligence of a multitude of enemies; lram—\[a knower,\] who impels; na—not; na—not; amalah—not dirty (or nama-lah—people give names); akovida—of fools; mana—the conceit; va—of those who deride (or of those who take away); inam—\[a knower,\] who is the master; ahlna—is not deficient; caritram— \[a knower,\] whose behavior; udara-dhlram—who is exalted and intelligent.

**People only care to have a good time. They do not give respect to smart persons, much less pay them a compliment. A smart person is pure, delivers foes, joyfully stimulates their intellects, is a master among those who dispel the conceit of fools, does not lack good behavior, is exalted and is witty.**

3.42

*yasam citte mono ’mano narir bhuyo ’ram ta ranta \|*  
*sara-prema san-nasanna jayetaivananta nanta \|\|*

yasam citte—in whose minds; manah—pique; amanah— immeasurable; narih—women; bhuyah—repreadely; aram— quickly; tah—those women; ranta—he who nicely takes pleasure; sara-prema—he whose love is the best (sara = vara); sat-na— an eminent man (or san na); asannah—\[women\] who are near; jayeta—might become; eva—only; anantah—unlimited; nanta— submissive.

**An eminent man whose love is the best and who repeatedly enjoys sensual pleasures with many closeby women in whose hearts the pique is immeasurable quickly becomes submissive.**

3.45

*santo 'vata bata pranan*  
*iman iha nihanti nah \|*  
*sad-ajano jano ’yam hi*  
*boddhum sad-asad aksamah \|\|*

santah—O saintly persons; avata—all of you should protect; bata— alas; pranan—life airs; iman—these; iha—at this time; nihanti— hurt; nah—our; sat-ajanah— \[people\] drive away good persons; janah ayam—these people; hi—because; boddhum—to understand; sat—good; asat—and bad; aksamah—unable.

**Alas, sadhus, save our lives. These people are oppressing us. Since they cannot understand the difference between right and wrong, they drive away the righteous.**

3.54

*ghanagha nayam na nabha ghanaghanan*  
*udarayann eti mano ’nu darayan \|*  
*sakhe ’dayam tam avilasa khedayann*  
*ahiyase gor athava na hiyase \|\|*

ghana-agha—O you whose sins are thick; na—not; ayam—this (the well-known); na—not; nabhah—the month of Sravana (July- August); ghanaghanan—thick raining clouds; udarayan— while causing to move; eti—goes; manah—the mind; anu— afterward; darayan—while tearing apart; sakhe—O companion; adayam—mercilessly; tam—her; avilasa—O you who have no fun; khedayan—while causing \[her\] to be dejected; ahlyase—you act like a snake; goh—than an ox (because of words); athava—or else; na hlyase—you are not less (or you are not hurt).

**Thick-skinned offender, the month of Sravana is not going away. It brings clouds and then clouds the mind. Dear companion, you’re not enjoying yourself while hardheartedly making her dejected. Either you’re acting like a snake or you’re no more than a bull.**

3.57

*kamalimm alim dayitam vina*  
*na sahate saha tena nisevitam \|*  
*tam adhuna madhuna nihitam hrdi*  
*smarati sa rati-saram ahar-nisam \|\|*

kamalinim—a lotus; alini—a female bee; dayitam vina—without her beloved; na sahate—does not tolerate; saha tena—and so was he; nisevitam—\[the lotus,\] which was served; tam—him; adhuna— now; madhuna—by spring; nihitam—him, who was put; hrdi—in the heart; smarati—remembers; sa—she; rati-saram—him, who is the best in love; ahah-nisam—day and night.

**Without her beloved, the female bee cannot tolerate the lotus: Her beloved and the lotus gratify each other. The she-bee remembers him day and night: He is the best in love, and because of spring she holds him in her heart all this time.**

## Citra-kavya

In the fifth chapter, Rudrata illustrates picture poetry. Dr. Kumar De observes:

There is no reference to citra in Bharata, Bhamaha or Udbhata, although Magha says (xix.41) that it was in his time a figure indispensable in a Maha-kavya; Dandin dilates upon some of its varieties, but Rudrata gives a much fuller exposition; and it is noteworthy that although Mammata does not attach much value to such verbal ingenuity, yet in his discussion of this figure he quotes almost all the illustrations from Rudrata.

Rudrata was the first poetical theorist to compose a verse in the lotus diagram:

*ya paty apaya-patitan avataritaya*  
*yataritavapati vag bhuvanani maya \|*  
*yaman ina vapatu vo vasu sa sva-geya*  
*yage svasasura-ripor jaya-patyapaya \|\|*

ya—who; pati—protects; apaya—in adversity; patitan—those who have fallen; avatarita—comes down; aya—\[she because of whom\] good fortune; yata—goes away; arita—\[she because of whom (or from whom)\] enmity; avapati—she pervades; vak— Sarasvati (personified language) (the material Sarasvati is Brahma’s daughter; the transcendental Sarasvati is Narayana’s wife); bhuvanani—the worlds; maya—Maya; yaman—\[pervading the eight\] periods of the day; ina—the female master (Gauri); vapatu—may she sow (generate); vah—to you all; vasu—wealth; sa—she; sva— \[by means of\] herself (in the form of sound); geya—who is praised; yage—in a fire sacrifice; svasa—the sister (as Yogamaya, Devaki’s ninth daughter); asura-ripoh—of Vishnu (“the demons’ enemy”); jaya-pa—she safeguards victory (or she safeguards a mode of eminently existing); ati-apaya—she by whom adversity has been overcome.

**May SvaminT generate wealth for you all during the whole day. She protects those who have fallen into adversity. She causes good fortune. She dispels enmity. She pervades the three worlds: She is Maya. She is SarasvatT: In a fire sacrifice she is praised by means of herself. She is Vishnu’s sister; she safeguards a mode of eminent existence, and is beyond all kinds of misfortune. (Kavyalankara 5.21)**

**The Lotus**

![рис-001.jpg|678](<Versified History of Sanskrit Poetics/рис-001.jpg>)  
The example of the sword diagram consists of two verses:

*marari-sakra-ramebha-mukhair asara-ramhasa \|*  
*sararabdha-stava nityam tad-arti-harana-ksama \|\|*

*mata natanam sanghattah sriyam badhita-sambhrama \|*  
*manyatha sima ramanam sam me disyad umadi-ma \|\|*

mara-ari—by Siva (“Cupid’s enemy”); sakra—by Indra; rama— by Rama (Parasurama); ibha-mukhaih—and by Ganesa (“who has the face of an elephant”); asara—of a hard shower \[of sounds\]; ramhasa—with the impetuosity; sara—in the best way; arabdha— is begun; stava—she the praise about whom; nityam—always; tad-arti—their pain (or his pain); harana—to dispel; ksama—she is able; mata natanam—a mother to those who bow; sanghattah sriyam—the amalgamation of splendors; badhita—are annulled; sambhrama—she because of whom delusions; manya—worthy of honor; atha—completely; sima ramanam—the limit of beautiful ladies; sam—auspiciousness; me—to me; disyat—may she bestow; uma—Uma; adi-ma—she whose splendor is foremost (or the primeval mother).

**May Uma bestow auspiciousness to me. Her radiance is foremost. Prasing her is always begun in the best way, as a flowing momentum, by Siva, Indra, Parasurama and Ganesa. She can dispel the pain of Indra and others. She is a mother unto those who bow. She is an amalgamation of splendors. Illusions are dispelled by her. She is worthy of honor to a high degree, and is the foremost lovely lady. (Kavyalankara 5.6-7) (Kavya-prakasa verses 384-385)**

**The Sword**

![рис-002.jpg|500](<Versified History of Sanskrit Poetics/рис-002.jpg>)

This is the verse for the drum formation:

*sarala bahularambha-taralali-balarava \|*  
*varala-bahulamanda-karala bahu-lamala \|\|*

sarala—simple; bahula—much; arambha—speed; tarala— fickle; ali—of bees; bala—of an army; arava— \[autumn,\] during which there is the noise; varala—of geese; bahula—in which there is a multitude; amanda—are not idle; kara-la—during which the kings (“they take a tax”); bahu-la—she gives much; amala— dirtfree.

**Autumn is simple. At this time there is a noise of an army of bees that are fickle and have great speed, there are many geese, and the kings are not idle. Mud-free autumn has much to offer. (Kavyalankara 5.19) (Kavya-prakasa verse 386)**

Commenting on Kavya-prakasa, Nagesa Bhatta says sarala (simple) means megha-nirmukta (cloudless) (Uddyota).

**The Muraja Drum**

![рис-003.jpg|916](<Versified History of Sanskrit Poetics/рис-003.jpg>)

Rudrata also wrote verses for other diagrams: the cudgel (musalam), the bow (dhanus), the arrow (Sara), the pike (sulam), the weapon (sakti), and the plough (hala). For his wheel diagram, he used eight verses: these six and the two for the sword illustration. In addition, he exemplified sarvato-bhadra (diagram of squares), pratilomanuloma (palindrome), and so forth.

In addition, Rudrata expounded poetical games such as matra- cyutaka (omitting a matra), bindu-cyutaka (omitting an anusvara or the like), prahelika (conundrum, riddle), karaka-gudha (concealed by a case ending), kriya-gudha (concealed by an action), and prasnottara (question and answer; the answer is hidden in the question; etc.) (Kavyalankara 5.24). Bana (c. 620 CE) had mentioned bindumati (a verse is shown as a puzzle by writing a circle in place of each consonant, but without deleting the diacritics), gudha-caturtha-pada (the syllables of the fourth line of a verse are also in the first three lines) and so on. For more details, consult the eleventh chapter of my translation of Baladeva Vidyabhusana’s Sahitya-kaumudi.

Rudrata’s treatise is known among chess historians too because it contains one of the earliest references to chess in India. Dr. Macdonell notes:

Chess in Sanskrit is called chatur-anga or the “four-limbed army,” because it represents a kriegspiel, in which two armies, consisting of infantry, cavalry, chariots, and elephants, each led by a king and his councillor, are opposed. The earliest direct mention of the game in Sanskrit literature is found in the works of Bana, and the Kavyalamkara of Rudrata, a Kashmirian poet of the ninth century, contains a metrical puzzle illustrating the moves of the chariot, the elephant, and the horse. Introduced into Persia in the sixth century, chess was brought by the Arabs to Europe, where it was generally known by 1100 A.D.

This verse illustrates turaga-pada-patha, also called turaga-pada- bandha (arrangement in the steps of a horse, in chess) (5.15). The same verse, of four lines of eight syllables each, can be read from left to right or by following the movements of a knight on tour:

*sena lililina nali linana nanali-li-li \|*  
*nalinalile nalina lilili nana-nanali \|\|*

Separation of words: senah, lililinah, na, ali, linanah, nanali-li-li, na, alinali, ile, na, alinah, lilili, nana-na, anali.

Syntactical connection (prose order): (yah aham) linanah nanali- li-li lilili nana-na anali na lililinah alinah senah ile, (sah aham) ali na (bhavami), na (va) alinali (bhavisyami). senah—the armies; lili-ili-inah—\[the armies,\] whose master habitually praises those who have fun; na—not; ali—one who has deceit (ala); lina-anah—\[the man,\] whose carts are close together; nana-ali-li-li—\[the man,\] whose men are nana-ali-li-la— they take the embrace (the connection) (li = li\[h\] slesane + kvip) of various groups; na—not; alina-ali—one whose enemies (alin = arin) (ari = enemy) are not gone; ile—I praise (from id stutau); na—\[I\] a man; alinah—\[the armies,\] close together; lilili—\[the man,\] whose man (the king) is lili-ila—he due to whom the Earth (ila) has playfulness; nana-na—he has various types of men; an- ali—he does not melt.

**The Knight’s Tour**

![рис-004.jpg|533](<Versified History of Sanskrit Poetics/рис-004.jpg>)

**I praise the compact armies whose commanders compliment those who divert themselves. My chariots are aligned, my men are backed up by manifold units, my superior is the reason the Earth has an amusement, and I have various types of soldiers: I do not melt. I am not deceitful, and my enemies shall perish.**

## Ornaments of Meaning

Rudrata was the first to propound a basis for the classification of ornaments of meaning. They are divided in four groups:

(1) Vastava (based on fact): sahokti, samuccaya, jati (svabhavokti), yatha-samkhya, bhava, paryaya, visama, anumana, dipaka, parikara, parivrtti, parisamkhya, hetu, karana-mala, vyatireka, anyonya, uttara, sara, suksma, lesa, avasara, milita, and ekavali (23 figures),

(2) Aupamya (based on similarity): upama, utpreksa, rupaka, apahnuti, samsaya, samasokti, mata, uttara, anyokti, pratipa, arthantara-nyasa, ubhaya-nyasa, bhrantimat, aksepa, pratyanika, drstanta, purva, sahokti, samuccaya, samya, and smarana (21 figures),

(3) Atisaya (exceeding worldly norms): purva, visesa, utpreksa, vibhavana, tad-guna, adhika, virodhabhasa (virodha), visama, asangati, pihita, vyaghata, and ahetu (12 figures), and

(4) Slesa (artha-slesa = abhanga-slesa) (pun) (ten kinds).

The total is fifty-seven ornaments of meaning. Although six ornaments (sahokti, samuccaya, utpreksa, uttara, purva, visama) have the same name in two groups, they are actually different ornaments since they are differently defined.

Rudrata invented ornaments that have remained the same, in name and definition, in the pantheon of modern poetics: paryaya, visama, anumana, parikara, parisankhya, karana-mala, anyonya, uttara, sara, samuccaya, ekavali, pratipa, bhrantiman, smarana, visesa, tad-guna, adhika and asangati. Moreover, Rudrata’s hetu ornament (the cause is expressed as its effect) (7.82) was accepted by Ruyyaka and Visvanatha. This is Rudrata’s example of sara (climax):

*rajye saram vasudha*  
*vasundharayam puram pure saudham \|*  
*saudhe talpam talpe*  
*varanganananga-sarvasvam \|\|*

**In a kingdom, the essence is the land, in the land the city, in a city a mansion, in a mansion a couch, and on a couch the best woman, the all in all of Cupid. (7.97)**

All the subvarieties of Rudrata’s vastava samuccaya (sad-yoga, asad-yoga, sad-asad-yoga, and guna and kriya) were accepted by Mammata. This is Rudrata’s example of kriya-samuccaya (conjunction of actions): daivad aham atra taya capalayata- netraya viyuktas ca, avirala-vilola-jaladah kalah samupagatas cayam, “By fate, I became separated from that woman whose eyes are fickle and wide, and the darned time when the clouds are thick and unsteady arrived in full force” (Kavyalankara 7.29).

Rudrata mentioned kriya-dipaka (one verb for many subjects): In addition, he invented karaka-dipaka (one noun connected with many verbs). Rudrata’s dipaka does not involve the notions of prastuta, aprastuta, upameya, or upamana. As regards dipaka, Kavi Kamapura is Rudrata’s most loyal follower. Rudrata’s aupamya- samuccaya (conjunction based on similarity) is the same as his kriya-dipaka, except that some similitude is involved. Mammata merged both concepts to make his own dipaka. This is Rudrata’s example of aupamya-samuccaya:

*jalena sarasi mina himsrair ena vane ca vaguraya \|*  
*samsare bhuta-srja snehena naras ca badhyante \|\|*

**Fish in a lake are caught with a net, deer in a forest by mischievous persons with traps, and men in material life by the creator by means of the affection of people. (8.104)**

Rudrata invented the paryaya ornament. Mammata’s paryaya is the same as Rudrata’s first variety, whereas the second variety is the same as the ancients’ paryayokta which involves an implied meaning that is neither a cause nor an effect (7.42). The concept of implied sense also constitutes Rudrata’s bhava ornament:

*grama-tarunam tarunya*  
*nava-vanjula-manjari-sanatha-karam \|*  
*pasyantya bhavati muhur*  
*nitaram malina mukha-cchaya \|\|*

**The splendor of the face of the young woman who is continuously looking at that youthful man, the village Don Juan with new asoka blossoms in hand, becomes even more tarnished. (7.39)**

The verse is cited by Mammata as an instance of second-rate implied sense where the implied idea is not as beautiful as the literal meaning: atra vanjula-lata-grhe datta-sanketa nagateti vyangyam guni-bhutam, “Here the implied meaning, which is secondary, is: She, who set up the rendezvous with him, did not go to that place abounding in vanjula creepers” (Kavya-prakasa, verse 3 vrtti). She missed the rendezvous.

Rudrata changed the name of some of his predecessors’ ornaments: He does not mention rasavat, urjasvi nor samahita, but the concept of rasavat is included in his theory as the second kind of his avasara ornament, whereas his first kind is the same as Udbhata’s and Mammata’s second udatta. Rudrata classes preyas among the rasas. In addition, Rudrata’s mata is similar to Udbhata’s first variety of atisayokti (introsusception) (Kavyalankara 8.69). His purva is based on the model of Udbhata’s fourth variety of atisayokti (a change in the sequence between a cause and its effect) (9.3). His vyaghata is the same as visesokti (no effect in spite of a cause) (9.52).

Dandi’s first variety of lesa was renamed milita by Rudrata and Mammata. Rudrata’s lesa is that a fault becomes a quality (his illustration amounts to: Ignorance is bliss) or vice versa (7.100­102).

Rudrata’s upameyopama (reciprocal comparison, 8.9) and ananvaya (self-comparison, 8.11) are two of his six kinds of vakya upama, which is one of his three types of simile (8.4): The two other categories are samasa upama (a simile in a compound) and pratyaya upama (a simile with a suffix). Dr. Sushil Kumar De comments:

We have already noted that Udbhata enters rather minutely into the grammatical subdivisions of upama, but this finds no place in Rudrata’s treatment, which includes them in a lump in samasopama and pratyayopama.

Rudrata invented rasanopama (a series of similes where one upamana is the upameya in the next clause) (8.27), rasana-rupaka (a series of metaphors where one upamana is the upameya in the next clause) (8.50), and paramparita-rupaka (one metaphor causes the other) (8.51). This is Rudrata’s illustration of rasana-rupaka:

*kisalaya-karair latanam*  
*kara-kamalaih kaminam jagaj jayati \|*  
*nalimnam kamala-mukhaih*  
*mukhendubhir yositam madanah \|\|*

**Cupid conquers the world with the hand shoots of creepers and with the shoot hands of Don Juans, as well as with the face lotuses of lotus ponds and with the moon faces of women. (Kavyalankara 8.50) (Kavya-prakasa verse 429)**

Some of Mammata’s ornaments are sourced under different names among the subvarieties of Rudrata’s ornaments. Rudrata introduced the term tad-guna in poetic theory (9.22-25): He coined the term tad-guna, but the concept is first seen in Magha’s Sisupala-vadha (2.21; 4.14). Rudrata’s tad-guna has two varieties: The first one, called atisayokti by Dandi, was renamed samanya by Mammata. The second variety corresponds to Mammata’s tad-guna. This is Rudrata’s example:

*kubjaka-malapi krta kartasvara-bhasvare tvaya kanthe \|*  
*etat-prabhanulipta campaka-dama-bhramam kurute \|\|*

**The garland of white kubjaka flowers you placed on your golden neck reflects the luster of your neck and looks like a garland of campaka flowers. (9.25)**

For the most part, Rudrata’s artha-slesa is the same as the modern abhanga-slesa. Although Rudrata classed sabda-slesa as an ornament of sound, he followed Udbhata in terms of equating sabhanga-slesa with sabda-slesa and abhanga-slesa with artha- slesa. The ten subcategories of Rudrata’s artha-slesa, some of which are taken from Dandi, are ingenious: avisesa (the usual double meaning), virodha (contradiction), adhika (some words are Mammata’s artha-slesa and some others are Mammata’s sabda- slesa), vakra (a crooked pun in the scope of srngara-rasa), vyaja (praise is implied from words of criticism or vice versa), ukti (the double meaning adds weight to the first meaning), asambhava (impossible pun, though apparent, based on a renowned idea), avayava (partly a pun), tattva (real), and virodhabhasa (semblance of a contradiction) (Kavyalankara 10.1-2). This is Rudrata’s example of avayava-slesa (partly a pun):

*bhuja-yugale bala-bhadrah*  
*sakala-jagal-langhane tatha bali-jit \|*  
*akruro hrdaye ’sau*  
*rajabhud arjuno yasasi \|\|*

**As regards both arms, that king was bala-bhadra (a gentleman because of strength). In traversing the whole world he was bali- jit (he defeats powerful ones). In his heart he was akrura (not cruel). And in fame he was arjuna (white). (10.19)**

Visvanatha Kaviraja classifies a format like the above as the ullekha ornament (angles of description) founded on slesa (double meaning).

This is Rudrata’s illustration of tattva-slesa (true pun):

*nayane hi tarala-tare*  
*sutanu kapolau ca candra-kantau te \|*  
*adharo ’pi padmaragas*  
*tri-bhuvana-ratnam tato vadanam \|\|*

**Slender girl, your eyes are two fickle stars, your cheeks are lovely like two moons, and your nether lip is a red lotus, there­fore your face is the jewel of the three worlds.**

**Alternatively: Slender girl, your eyes are two silver gems, your cheeks are two moongems, and your lower lip is a ruby, there­fore your face is the jewel of the three worlds. (10.21)**

The following verse exemplifies virodhabhasa-slesa (a pun based on a semblance of a contradiction):

*tava daksino ’pi vamo*  
*bala-bhadro ’pi pralambha eva bhujah \|*  
*duryodhano ’pi rajan*  
*yudhi-sthiro stity aho citram \|\|*

**This is quite amazing, O king: Your arms are expert (daksina) and beautiful (vama). They are hanging down (pralamba) though gracious with strength (bala-bhadra) (or: Your right arm and your left arm are hanging down although gracious with strength). And even though you are hard to fight (duryodhana), you remain steady in battle (yudhi-sthira). (10.23)**

Rudrata’s virodhabhasa-slesa and virodha-slesa were renamed slesa-mula virodha by Pandita-raja Jagannatha (RG, KM p. 428) and Baladeva Vidyabhusana (Sahitya-kaumudl 10.133). Jagannatha points out that if the word api (although) is not used, then Rudrata’s virodhabhasa-slesa is the same as Anandavardhana’s sabda-sakti- mula virodha-dhvani (implied semblance of a contradiction by the force of unchangeable words).

## Rasa

Rudrata discusses rasa in four chapters (12-15). He lists ten rasas: To Udbhata’s nine, he added preyas (12.3). He says sneha is its sthayl (15.17). His disquisition on rasa greatly differenciates him from his predecessors. Rudrata laid emphasis on rasa: tasmat tat kartavyam yatnena mahlyasa rasair yuktam, “Poetry endowed with rasas should be done with the greatest efforts” (Kavyalankara 12.2). Dr. Sushil Kumar De writes: “Although influenced considerably by the Rasa doctrine, Rudrata belongs properly to the Alankara school.”

Kavyalankara is the first poetical treatise to include topics of kama- sastra (erotics). Rudrata states a lover’s qualities (12.7-8), four types of lovers (anukula, daksina, satha, dhrsta) (12.9-12), the three types of companions of a lover (plthamarda, vita, vidusaka) (12.4), the types of ladyloves (12.16-40), four states of a ladylove (12.41-46), the four kinds ofvipralambha (prathamanuraga, mana, pravasa, karuna) (14.1), the ten stages of vipralambha (14.4-5), and six means of pacifying an angry ladylove: sama (conciliation, i.e. catu ukti, flattery), dana (offering a gift, etc.), bheda (creating a difference in opinion, i.e. bringing one of the woman’s friends into the discussion), pranati (being submissive), upeksa (neglect), and prasanga-bhramsa (falling at her feet) (14.27-32). Bharata Muni mentioned these means: sama, dana, bheda, danda, and upeksa (Natya-sastra 35.66 in the thirty-six-chapter recension). In the fifteenth chapter, Rudrata gives technical details about each rasa. In those four chapters, however, he does not provide illustrative examples. Still, Rudrata’s disquisition on rasa was a great source of information for Bhoja, who in turn had a great influence on the theory of rasa. Dr. Kumar De says there are spurious verses in the twelfth chapter:

While Rudra describes at some length the eight conventional avasthas (conditions or situations) of the nayika (i.131-132), Rudrata mentions only four (viz., abhisarika, khandita, svadhma-patika, andprosita-patika, xii.41), although to make up for this unwanted divergence there is in some manuscripts a long passage (between xii.40 and 41) describing the usual eight conditions but irreconcilable to its context, and rightly stigmatised by Rudrata’s editor as interpolated.

They are not commented upon by Namisadhu. Dr. Kane agrees that they are interpolations (1998: 151).

## 10. The Dhvanikara (and Anandavardhana)

In the history of Sanskrit poetics, the impact of Dhvany-aloka was as colossal as that of Natya-sastra. Dr. Kane writes:

The Dhvany-aloka is an epoch-making work in the history of Alankara Literature. It occupies the same position in the Alankara-sastra as Panini’s sutras in grammar and the Vedanta-sutra in Vedanta. The work shows great erudition and critical insight. It is written in a lucid and forcible style and bears the stamp of originality on every page. As the Rasa- gangadhara remarks (p. 425 dhvani-krtam alankarika-sarani- vyavasthapakatvat), the Dhvany-aloka settled the principles to be followed in poetics.

There is a controversy regarding the authorship of the definitional verses (karika) and of the elaboration (vrtti). In his History of Sanskrit Poetics, Dr. Kane expounds the matter in thirty-seven pages (1998: 162-198). In short, the author of Dhvany-aloka was a man who had the epithet Sahrdaya (esthete); and the author of the vrtti (elaboration) on Dhvany-aloka was Anandavardhana. For practical purposes, elsewhere in this book the name Anandavardhana refers to the author of Dhvany-aloka, but in this chapter the author of Dhvany-aloka is called Dhvani-kara. In the terminology of many historians, Sahrdaya is referred to as the Dhvanikara (or Dhvani- krt, the author of Dhvany-aloka) and Anandavardhana as the Vrtti-kara. In the first publication of his book, P.V. Kane stated that Anandavardhana is the author of Dhvany-aloka. This is often said for the sake of convenience. In a reedition of History of Sanskrit Poetics, however, he remarked:

The evidence so far advanced for holding that Sahrdaya was the author of the karikas is quite inadequate. But there is more evidence, which as far as my knowledge goes, had not been relied upon by scholars before I wrote in 1923. The Abhidha- vrtti-matrka, which was composed about a hundred years earlier than the Locana, distinctly says that dhvani, which had been propounded as a new doctrine by the respected Sahrdaya, does fall within the sphere of laksana ‘laksana-margavagahitvam tu dhvaneh sahrdayair nutanatayopavarnitasya vidyata iti disam unmilayitum idam atroktam’ p. 21. So also on p. 19 Mukula says ‘tatha hi tatra vivaksitanya-parata sahrdayaih kavya-vartmani nirupita’. This clearly shows that when Mukula wrote (about 900-925 A.D.) dhvani was a new doctrine and that Sahrdaya propounded it.

Lastly, it has to be remembered that the Karika-kara and Vrtti- kara had come to be identified, as shown later on, even before Abhinavagupta. So Abhinava did not harp every now and then upon the difference between the two.

So the Karika-kara briefly described the essence of poetry, which Ananda explained at great length.

Similarly, Dr. Keith and Dr. Sushil Kumar De agree that the author of Dhvany-aloka and the author of the vrtti on Dhvany-aloka are two different persons. P.V. Kane explains the usage of the plural in the name sahrdayaih in the abovementioned text by Mukula:

The general practice seems to be that ancient authors were mentioned in the singular while those that were elderly contemporaries or flourished just a little before the writer are mentioned in the plural. For example, Mammata mentions Bharata (an ancient muni), Rudrata (from whom he quotes probably more verses than from any other single author) and Dhvanikara in the singular, while he refers to Abhinava a commentator of Bharata and of the Dhvany-aloka in the plural. Sankaracarya refers to Bhagavan Upavarsa and Acarya Sabara in the singular. For this reason Mukula who as will be shown below was almost a younger contemporary of Ananda spoke of the latter’s teacher (if he was called Sahrdaya) in the plural.

Apart from the use of the word sa-hrdaya or sa-cetas in the Ramayana (adhyaya 13.22) and Kalidasa (sacetasah kasya mano na duyate in Kumara-sambhava V.48) in a general sense (viz. one who has a feeling or sympathetic heart), the word sahrdaya in the technical sense occurs more than a hundred years before Anandavardhana in Vamana’s Kavyalankara- sutra-vrtti (1.2.21) where the following is one of two verses quoted with the caption “tathahuh— ‘ vacasi yam adhisayya syandate vacaka-snr vitatham avitathatvam yatra vastu prayati \| udayati hi sa tadrk kvapi vaidarbha-ntau sahrdaya- hrdayanam ranjakah ko ’pi pakah \|\|’”. Therefore, the emergence of the word sahrdaya in a technical sense must be placed long before Vamana. There is nothing unusual in a person being called by a word that has a general sense (such as Sahrdaya) as we have authors in the Alankara-sastra itself named Medhavin, Dandin, Dhanika and so on.

I do not profess that I have completely proved my hypothesis. The remarks of Mukula cited by me above indicate that Sahrdaya was in the opinion of Mukula the author of the Karikas or of the whole work and according to Pratiharendu- raja, of the whole work.

Sahrdaya said that a connoisseur is a person whose heart does not feel joy by only understanding the surface meaning and who is able to grasp a first-rate implied sense. Or else Dhvany-aloka was written by several connoisseurs.

Anandavardhana was in the court of King Avantivarman, who ruled Kashmir from 857 to 884 CE. Anandavardhana wrote three works from which some of his illustrative examples are sourced. Dr. Kane expounds upon the chronology:

According to Raja-taranginl V.34 the poet Anandavardhana became famous as a poet in the reign of Avantivarman. The Visama-bana-llla, the Arjuna-carita and the Devl-sataka were, it appears, composed before the Dhvany-aloka. That means that the Dhvany-aloka was a work of a man of mature years and so Anandavardhana as a critic (not as a poet) should be held to have become well-known probably about or after 875 A.D.

Anandavardhana’s work cannot be placed earlier than about 875 to 900 A.D.

The Dhvany-aloka expounds the Dhvani theory in 116 definitional verses, in four chapters punningly called uddyota (light, illumination): In the causative sense, the verbal root dyut diptau (to shine) often means ‘to hint at’. Anandavardhana uses the words dyotana and dyotaka in the sense of “suggestive” (Dhvany-aloka 2.3 vrtti; 3.4 vrtti). Abhinavagupta explains the word uddyota in karika 2.2 as uddyotana-vyapara, a synonym of vyanjana-vrtti (Suggestiveness) (Locana 2.2).

Even in the vrtti, there is no substantial discourse on ornaments of sound nor on ornaments of meaning: The Dhvanikara said that the ornaments which are only based on the literal sense, such as simile, had been expounded by other rhetoricians, and so there was no need to elaborate on those ornaments in the book. At the outset, the author claims that the Dhvani theory is not a new mental concoction:

*kavyasyatma dhvanir iti budhair yah samamnata-purvah*  
*tasyabhavam jagadur apare bhaktam ahus tam anye \|*  
*kecid vacam sthitam avisaye tattvam ucus tadiyam*  
*tena brumah sahrdaya-manah-pritaye tat-svarupam \|\|*

**“Scholars say that Dhvani is the soul of poetry. It had been told before (by a tradition). Some opponents say Dhvani does not exist, others say it is in the scope of figurative usage, yet others proclaim it is not in the scope of words and is a principle related to their own hearts. Therefore we shall explain the nature of Dhvani to please the minds of the rasikas” (Dhvany-aloka 1.1).**

Dr. Sushil Kumar De comments on the above:

This implies without doubt that the school existed from a very early time, but some unknown writer gathered together, summed up, and fixed the theory in a form which obtained considerable literary esteem for his work and the honoured but somewhat vague appellation of the Dhvanikara for himself.

Dr. Kane expounds:

If the author of the karikas be different from that of the vrtti and one had to make a choice between the two as to who should be called Sastra-karapar excellence there is hardly any doubt that most scholars would bestow the palm of superiority on the Vrtti-kara.

Additional arguments for asserting that the theory of dhvani in poetry had been propounded before Anandavardhana may be set out. Ananda quotes a verse which the Locana ascribes to Manoratha, a contemporary of Ananda, in which the theory of dhvani is ridiculed ‘kavyam tad-dhvanina samanvitam iti pritya prasamsas jado \| no vidmo ’bhidadhati kim sumatina prstah svarupam dhvaneh \|\|’. \[...\] If this Manoratha is identical with the Manoratha who flourished in the reign of Jayapida and Lalitapida the dhvani-karikas were composed between 800-825.

Anandavardhana said he is the Vrtti-kara. At the end of the vrtti, he wrote:

*sat-kavya-tattva-naya-vartma-cira-prasupta-*  
*kalpam manahsu paripakva-dhiyam yad asit \|*  
*tad vyakarot sahrdayodaya-labha-hetor*  
*anandavardhana iti prathitabhidhanah \|\|*

**“For the purpose of ensuring the rise of esthetes, he who has the designation Anandavardhana explained the precepts of the path of the methodology of principles of good poetry. The precepts had slept a long time in the minds of those of mature intellect” (Dhvany-aloka 4.17 vrtti).**

According to Abhinavagupta, the invocatory verse in the treatise was written by the Vrtti-kara: vrtti-karah svaccheti (Locana 1.1). The verse features a cheka anuprasa (the repetition of two or more phonemes in sequence):

***sveccha****-kesarinah* ***svaccha-sva-ccha****yayasitendavah \|*  
*trayantam vo madhuripoh prapannarti-cchido nakhah \|\|*

**May the nails of Madhuripu, who is a lion by His will, protect you. They make the moon dejected because of their limpid shadow, and cut the pain of those who have humbly approached Him. (Dhvany-aloka-vrtti, mangalacarana)**

In that regard, Dr. Sivaprasada Dvivedi comments: yady ubhayor bhagayoh kartarau bhinnau syatam, tada mangala-slokav api bhinnau syatam, “If there were two different writers for the two portions (karika and vrtti), there would have been two invocatory verses.” P.V. Kane refutes this assumption. He says there is no rule; for example, Udbhata did not write an invocatory verse (1998: 176).

Dhvany-aloka is also called Kavyaloka and Sahrdayaloka, as well as Sahrdaya-hrdayaloka. There is something magical about it. The Dhvani theory is the foundation of modern Sanskrit poetics. Anandavardhana defines a dhvani as follows: vyangya-pradhanye dhvanir ity uktam, “When the implied meaning is predominant (it is more astonishing than the literal meaning of the statement), it is called dhvani” (Dhvany-aloka 3.33 vrtti).

The word dhvani thus has the technical sense of “first-rate implied meaning.” Kavi Kamapura popularized the usage of the term dhvani in the general sense of “implied meaning”: vyangyam eva dhvanih (Alankara-kaustubha 1.14). In his treatise, the usage of that term takes place according to the context.

This is the Dhvanikara’s dictum: kavyasyatma dhvanih, “A first- rate implied sense is the soul of poetry” (Dhvany-aloka 1.1). This statement became the cornerstone of modern poetics.

The Dhvani theory, perfected by Abhinavagupta and Mammata, says an implied sense can only be accounted for by a function of words that is beyond Denotation (abhidha) and Indication (laksana). That function is called Suggestiveness (vyanjana).

The Dhvani theory is partly based on the school of Purva-mimamsa called Abhihitanvaya-vada, in which the rule of semantic analysis is that a literary function can only be used one time; Sabara Svami wrote: amuni padani svam svam artham abhidhaya nivrtta- vyaparani, athedamm padartha abhihitah santo vakyartham avabodhayanti, “Once the words of a sentence have denoted their respective meanings, their function ceases. Thereafter the words’ meanings, having thus finished with abhidha, make one understand the sense of the sentence (by the function called tatparya)” (Purva- mlmamsa-sutra-bhasya 1.1.25).

Thus, the function called Denotation cannot account for an implied sense. Abhinava explains: ‘visesyam nabhidha gacchet’ ity- adinabhidha-vyaparasya viramya vyaparasambhavabhidhanat, “Denotation cannot be used twice for the same word, by the rule: visesyam nabhidha gacchet ksma-saktir visesane, “After its power has been used up as regards the qualifying characteristic (the jati, the category denoted by the word), abhidha does not reach the individual thing \[denoted by the word\] (lit. that which is qualified by the jati)”” (Locana 1.4).

The same applies to Indication. Abhinava writes: viramya vyaparah sabda-karma-buddhy-adlnam padarthavidbhir nisiddhah, “After it has been used up \[one time\], a function that relates to either a word, an action, or a means of knowing is stopped by those who know the meaning of words” (Locana 1.4).

Nonetheless, Suggestiveness can be used unlimitedly, precisely because it is not in the scope of words per se, thus one implied sense can automatically suggest another.

There are three kinds of dhvanis (implied sense): (1) rasadi-dhvani, (2) vastu-dhvani and (3) alankara-dhvani. Each is either first- rate or second-rate. A rasa is a vastu-dhvani (implied idea) in the form of a rasa. A rasa is implied: A rasa is always a rasa-dhvani because a good poet never uses the name of the rasa to signal its occurrence. And just as a vastu (idea) which fits in a definition of alankara is called alankara (ornament), so a vastu-dhvani which implicitly fits in a definition of alankara is called alankara-dhvani (implied ornament).

The first category is called rasa-adi-dhvani because it includes the nine rasas, the sthayi-bhavas, the vyabhicari-bhavas, rasabhasa and bhavabhasa. According to Abhinavagupta, the dictum “kavyasyatma dhvanih” means only a first-rate rasadi-dhvani is the soul of poetry, since implied ideas and implied ornaments are meant to enhance a rasa.

The sum and substance of the Dhvani theory is that the highest experience of poetry is one where the pleasure is almost like a trance. This means the rasa in a technical sense (aesthetic delight, i.e. a sthayi-bhava is implied by vibhavas, anubhava, and vyabhican and has thus become relishable) becomes a full-fledged relishment, or rapture. Dr. Kane expounds:

Bhamaha, Dandi, Udbhata, Vamana and Rudrata expatiate on sabda, artha, guna, alankaras and dosas. The school of dhvani regarded these as of secondary importance, they are only the external appearance of poetry and it holds that we must look deeper into the inner or implicit meaning viz. the emotional atmosphere or mood that underlies the best poetry. As in Vedanta objects of experience are held to be not the ultimate reality but only manifestations of Reality, so words and the expressed meaning came to be regarded as the mere external appearance of poetry and the emotional mood which a poem communicates to those who read it came to be regarded as the essence of poetry. Poetry came to be regarded as having a double purpose viz. giving the highest delight (sadyah para-nivrti) and also contributing towards a higher mode of conduct and character (upadesa) in a subtle persuasive way. When dhvani or rasa is said to be the soul of poetry (kavyasyatma dhvanir iti) it is virtually employing the language of the Upanisads about atman and ananda (anando brahmeti vyajanat). There is a remarkable similarity between the aesthetic experience on reading a poem or on seeing a good drama and the spiritual experience derived from the Vedanta discipline by one who has realized and contemplates upon the one Reality. It is therefore that Mammata speaks of rasa as ‘ brahmasvadam ivanubhavayan ’. But there are differences between the two experiences. Art experience does not last long, vanishes when the stimulus is withdrawn, while the bliss of one who has reached the brahmi-sthiti is permanent. Art experience does not necessarily require moral elevation, while blissful spiritual life is not possible without moral discipline. Before the theory of dhvani secured general acceptance, it had to pass through an ordeal of fierce criticism at the hands of Pratiharenduraja (pp. 80-86, Nir.), Vakrokti-jivita, Bhatta Nayaka and Mahima-bhatta.

Anandavardhana invented the term dhvani-kavya (first-class poetry, lit. poetry called Dhvani): vyangyasyarthasya pradhanye dhvani-samjnita-kavya-prakarah (Dhvany-aloka 3.41 vrtti). Abhinavagupta comments: dhvanir eva kavyam iti, atmatminor abheda eva vastuto vyutpattaye tu vibhagah krta ity arthah, “The term dhvani-kavya means Dhvani is poetry. This is said in the sense is that there is no difference between the soul and the body (poetry has a body of sounds and literal meanings), but in truth a differentiation is made for the sake of etymology” (Locana 3.41).

Alternatively, “Dhvani is poetry” in the sense that a Dhvani is the cause of poetry, since the Dhvanikara did not accept that a text without a Dhvani can be called poetry: pradhana-gunabhavabhyam vyangyasyaivam vyavasthite \| kavye ubhe tato ’nyadyat tac citram abhidhlyate \|\| (Dhvany-aloka 3.41). Visvanatha Kaviraja, however, says the word dhvani in dhvani-kavya is derived as: “echoing is done in this”. For his part, Visvanatha Cakravarti says it is derived as “the poetry from which there is the origination of a first- rate implied sense.”

Further, the term madhura-rasa (a synonym of srngara-rasa), made famous by Rupa Gosvami, originates from Anandavardhana: srngara eva rasantarapeksaya madhurah prahlada-hetutvat. tat- prakasana-para-sabdarthataya kavyasya sa madhurya-laksano gunah (Dhvany-aloka 2.7).

## First-rate Poetry

Anandavardhana illustrates implied ornaments (alankara-dhvani). His examples are first-rate because the implied meaning is more charming than the literal sense.

**Rupaka-dhvani**

*lavanya-kanti-paripurita-din-mukhe ’smin*  
*smere ’dhuna tava mukhe taralayataksi \|*  
*ksobham yad eti na manag api tena manye*  
*suvyaktam eva jala-rasir ayam payodhih \|\|*

**Beautiful woman with fickle and wide eyes, this smile of yours fills the directions with loveliness and splendor. Since the ocean does not become even a little agitated about your face on this occasion, I think that obviously the ocean is an inert mass (jala- rasi = jada-rasi). (2.27).**

An ocean becomes agitated during a full moon, and so the speaker implies that her face is a moon. The verse also features the slesa ornament: Abhinavagupta glosses jala-rasi (a mass of water) as jadya-sancaya (a mass of inertness) (Locana 2.27). For the purpose of slesa, yamaka and citra-kavya, the letters l, d and r are interchangeable. In Sanskrit, they sound similar because their place of pronunciation is the same.

**Virodha-dhvani**

*sarvaika-saranam aksayam*  
*adhisam Tsam dhiyam harim krsnam \|*  
*caturatmanam niskriyam*  
*ari-mathanam namata cakra-dharam \|\|*

**All of you should bow to Hari, Krishna, the imperishable and sole shelter of all, the overlord, the master of various kinds of intelligence. He is quick-witted by nature and is actionless. He thrashes enemies and has the cakra. (2.21)**

Abhinavagupta expounds:

*saranam grham aksaya-rupam agrham katham. yo na dhisah sa katham dhiyam Tsah. yo harih kapilah sa katham krsnah. caturah parakrama-yukto yasyatma sa katham niskriyah. arTnam ara-yuktanam yo nasayita sa katham cakram bahu-manena dharayati.*

**“The word sarana (shelter) is a synonym of house. How is it possible that He is an imperishable house? Moreover, how can one who is not a master of intelligence (adhTsah = na dhT-Tsah) be the master of various kinds of intelligence (dhT-Tsah = dhiyam Tsah)? \[...\] How can one who is quick (catura) by nature be actionless? And how can one who injures those who have spokes of a wheel (ari = arin = ara-yukta) hold up a wheel (cakra) with high regard?” (Locana 2.21).**
