Mahima-bhatta cites the verse as an example of the fault called vacyavacana (the improper usage of an ambiguously double­meaning word). Dr. Kane writes: “The piling up of slesas for their own sake and for no other purpose is vacyavacana. He finds this fault (on p. 95) in the verse sarvaika-saranam aksayam adhisam, which is Anandavardhana’s own”.

**Aksepa-dhvani**

*sa vaktum akhilas sakto hayagrivasritan gunan \|*  
*yo ’mbu-kumbhaih paricchedam jnatum sakto mahodadheh \|\|*

**A person who is able to know how many waterpots would be needed to contain the water of the ocean would be able to say how many qualities Hayagnva has. (2.27)**

Anandavardhana explains:

*atratisayoktya hayagriva-gunanam avarnaniyata-pratipadana-rupasyasadharana-tad-visesa- prakasana-parasyaksepasya prakasanam,*

**“By the atisayokti here (a statement that exceeds worldly norms), there is a manifestation of aksepa (hinting by negating): It takes the shape of propounding the notion that Hayagnva’s qualities are indescribable, and its purpose is the manifestation of that extraordinary particularity” (2.27).**

This negation is implied: No one can possibly count God’s qualities. It implies that God has innumerable qualities. That constitutes an implied aksepa ornament (hinting by negating) (paralipsis). Ruyyaka stated that Anandavardhana’s example is not a proper aksepa-dhvani because what is implied is only a negation, whereas by Ruyyaka’s definition, accepted by Visvanatha, what should be implied is a semblance of a negation.

Ruyyaka’s interpretation is in line with Mammata’s: nisedho nisedha iva (Kavya-prakasa 10.106 vrtti). Pandita-raja Jagannatha defended Anandavardhana by emphasizing that firstly aksepa should only be characterized by a suppression of the meaning, secondly Anandavardhana is the founder of modern poetics, and thirdly the ancients should be respected as authorities otherwise everything crumbles.

**Rasa-dhvani**

*raktas tvam nava-pallavair aham api slaghyaih priyaya gunais*  
*tvam ayanti silimukhah smara-dhanur-muktas tatha mam api \|*  
*kanta-pada-talahatis tava mude tadvan mamapy avayoh*  
*sarvam tulyam asoka kevalam aham dhatra sa-sokah krtah \|\|*

**You are red (rakta), on account of new buds, and I am in love (rakta) because of my ladylove’s praiseworthy qualities. Bees (silimukha) assail you, and arrows (silimukha) released from Cupid’s bow assail me. The strike of a woman’s foot makes you happy; it is like that for me too. O asoka tree, everything about us is the same, except that only I was turned sa-soka by the creator (Providence gave me the blues). (2.19)**

Anandavardhana comments: atra hi prabandha-pravrtto ’pi sleso vyatireka-vivaksaya tyajyamano rasa-visesam pusnati, “Although slesa was begun in the composition, it is given up with the intent to express a contrast (vyatireka), and enhances the particular rasa (the vipralambha)” (2.18-19).

At the beginning of the verse, the slesa was implying a simile, but the words “everything about us is the same” made it obvious and thus downgraded that upama-dhvani to an expressed simile, which only culminates as the similarity inherent in the vyatireka ornament. Anandavardhana lists six ways an ornament accompanies the rasa, and this downgrade of an ornament from being implied to being expressed is the fourth kind. The verse features a vipralambha-srngara-rasa-dhvani, arisen by sabda- sakti (the force of the word sa-soka, sorrowful), along with slesa and vyatireka.

## Second-rate Poetry

In Dhvany-aloka, rasavat is the only ornament defined. The ancients’ rasavat corresponds to a rasa-dhvani which is either first-rate or second-rate. The Dhvanikara says that in the Dhvani theory, the term rasavat only means a second-rate rasa-dhvani: Rasavat occurs when the astonishment generated from the rasa is secondary compared to that of the meaning of the statement. Anandavardhana adds that rasavat also takes place when, on the topic of madhura-rasa, and so on, a mode of being of a conscious entity is attributed to a non-conscious one, or when a non-conscious entity is prominently involved. For example:

**Rasavat**

*taranga-bhru-bhanga ksubhita-vihaga-sreni-rasana*  
*vikarsanti phenam vasanam iva samrambha-sithilam \|*  
*yatha-viddham yati skhalitam abhisandhaya bahuso*  
*nadi-rupeneyam dhruvam asahana sa parinata \|\|*

**The curves of her eyebrows are waves. She grew agitated, foam developed, and due to a series of arrows her girdle slackened like a garment becomes loose because of running. Withdrawing within herself, she went on recalling his blunder again and again, with a broken heart. Unable to tolerate it, she forever became a river. (2.5)**

**Rasavat**

*tesam gopa-vadhu-vilasa-suhrdam radha-rahah-saksinam*  
*ksemam bhadra kalinda-saila-tanaya-tire lata-vesmanam \|*  
*vicchinne smara-talpa-kalpana-mrdu-cchedopayoge ’dhuna*  
*te jane jarathi-bhavanti vigalan-nila-tvisah pallavah \|\|*

tesam—of those; gopa-vadhu—with the wives of the gopas \[was happening\]; vilasa—when a playful enjoyment; suhrdam— the well-wishers; radha-rahah—of the secret dealings with Radha; saksinam—the witnesses; ksemam—a happy tranquillity; bhadra—O good friend; kalinda-saila—of the mountain named Kalinda; tanaya—of the daughter; tire—on the banks; lata- vesmanam—\[of those\] abodes in the form of creepers; vicchinne— is nil; smara-talpa—a bed of Cupid; kalpana—for the sake of fashioning; mrdu-cheda—for the soft picking; upayoge—when the use; adhuna—now; te—those; jane—I know; jarathi-bhavanti— have become old (or are stooping); vigalat—is evanescing; nila— of a deep color; tvisah—whose splendor; pallavah—the blossoms.

**\[Krishna speaks to Uddhava, in Dvaraka:\] My good friend, those abodes in the shape of creepers on the banks of the Yamuna had an elated tranquillity. They were well-wishers when a playful enjoyment with the gopis was going on, and they were direct witnesses of My secret dealings with Radha. I know the blossoms there are stooping and their deep colors are evanescing, now that there is no use for softly picking them to fashion a bed for lovemaking. (2.5)**

## The Origins of the Concept of Implied Meaning

In the first chapter, the Dhvanikara refutes the opinions of the opponents of the Dhvani theory. In short, a new literary function had to be accounted for to explain the existence of an implied sense: Denotation is insufficient because a subtle implied sense is only perceived by a connoisseur, someone who has the required predisposition. For instance, the implication in the sentence “The young man goes to the young woman’s residence” is not understood by a child. An implied sense cannot be explained by Indication either: The Dhvanikara stated that Indication is applied when the meaning obtained by Denotation does not make sense. However, Kumarila Bhatta’s definition of Indication allows figurative usage to take place even when the main meaning is not blocked. In the Mimamsakas’ methodology, an implied sense is classed as a form of figurative usage (laksana-vrtti).

Suggestiveness is not a new literary function because it was dormant in the ancients’ categories of poetry, meaning it was being used although it was not acknowledged as a distinct function. Ananda- vardhana pointed out that the notion of rasa-dhvani is sourced in Natya-sastra. In addition, he explained that many ornaments inherently contain an implied sense, although in most cases the implied sense is only second-rate, as in samasokti, aksepa, the anukta-nimitta variety of visesokti, paryayokta, and aprastuta- prasamsa of the cause-and-effect variety. If aprastuta-prasamsa is only based on paronomasia, it might fall in the category of dhvani (first-rate implied sense). Anandavardhana says there is no automatic inclusion of a dhvani elsewhere: tasman na dhvaner anyatrantar-bhavah (Dhvany-aloka 1.13 vrtti). Still, Mammata mentioned that suksma inherently contains a first-rate implied sense, and Ruyyaka added that the same applies to vyajokti and vakrokti. The verse cited by Mammata as an illustration of suksma was classed in the category of second-rate implied sense by Anandavardhana. Further, Abhinava, like the Dhvanikara, added that kaku (modulation of the voice) involves an implied sense. Ananda illustrates the samasokti ornament (concise statement):

*upodha-ragena vilola-tarakam*  
*tatha grhitam sasina nisa-mukham \|*  
*yatha samastam timiramsukam taya*  
*puro ’pi ragad galitam na laksitam \|\|*

**The front part (or the face) of Night, in which the stars are fickle (or in which the pupils of the eyes are fickle), was taken by the Moon, who had assumed redness (or who was in love). Thus the entire darkness, in the form of the dress, in the east (or in front) was imperceptibly slackened by her due to redness (or out of love). (1.13)**

The stars represent the eyes. The moon was in the middle of the eastern sky at dawn: The implied sense is that the moon is like a lover and the night is like his sweetheart. The astonishment produced by this implied similarity does not exceed the astonishment generated by the literal meanings, and so there is no dhvani (first-rate implied sense). Samasokti occurs because the behavior of the aprastuta (what is not the subject of description; a lover) is superimposed on the prastuta (the subject of description, the moon).

Thus Visvanatha’s three constituents of samasokti take place:

- Gender: The moon is masculine (sasin) and the night is feminine (nisa),
- Action: Their respective actions resemble the behaviors of a lover and ladylove, and
- Paronomastic modifier. (There is no paronomastic substantive: If the main noun were paronomastic, the text would be classed as an implied simile founded on slesa.)

Several other ornaments of the ancients are based on an implied similarity, as in rupaka, tulya-yogita, dipaka, apahnuti, and vyatireka. But it is only second-rate. Ananda illustrates dipaka (one verb for many nouns):

*canda-mauehim nima nalini kamalehim kusuma-gucchehim laa \|*  
*hamsehim saraa-soha kavva-kaha sajjanehim kara-i garni \|\| (Prakrit language)*

*candra-mayukhair nisa nalini kamalaih kusuma-gucchair lata \|*  
*hamsaih sarada-sobha kavya-katha saj-janaih kriyate gurvi \|\| (Sanskrit rendering)*

**Night is enhanced by moonrays, lily pads by lilies, creepers by flowers, autumn by swans, and poetics by the righteous. (2.27)**

Abhinavagupta comments: saj-jananam api kavya-katham vina kidrsi sadhu-janata, “What would sadhus be like without the righteous’ discourse on poetry?” (Locana 2.27)

Ananda shows the above verse to illustrate that the implied similarity in dipaka is only a part of the scheme of the ornament itself, therefore the text is only classed as a dipaka, not as an implied simile. Still, exceptions are possible, if the beauty of the literal meaning of the text is meant to evoke the beauty of the implied sense. Thus Ananda gives an example of an upama-dhvani (first-rate implied similarity) in the scope of vyatireka (contrast with similitude):

*viranam ramate ghusrnarune na tatha priya-stanotsange \|*  
*drsfi ripu-gaja-kumbha-sthale yatha bahala-sindure \|\|*

**The eyes of warriors do not take as much delight in the upper part of a ladylove’s breasts reddened by saffron as they do in the deep vermilion on the temples of an enemy’s elephant.**

Moreover, Ananda specifies that those who say a first-rate implied sense cannot be defined (in relation to the body of poetry: sounds and expressed meanings) are right if they mean to refer to the quintessential nature of Dhvani due to poetic expression. Abhinava gives this example:

Those syllables sweet arouse in my heart  
Something beyond my descriptive art!

## Dhvani in Grammar:

## The Kashmiris’ Burden of Proof

The Dhvanikara introduced the notion of poetical suggestiveness: ukty-antarenasakyam yat tac carutvam prakasayan \| sabdo vyanjakatam bibhrad dhvany-ukter visayi-bhavet \|\| (Dhvany- aloka 1.15). He started the usage of the word dhvani as “implied sense”. From that, he defined first-rate poetry: yatrarthah sabdo va tam artham upasarjam-krta-svarthau, vyanktah kavya-visesah sa dhvanih suribhih kathitah, “Scholars stated: Poetry is called Dhvani-kavya when a meaning, and/or the sound, is suggestive and is subordinate to the implied sense” (1.13). This definition is called Dhvani-karika and is the basis of modern poetics. Abhinavagupta explains that the poetical term dhvani (implied meaning) is sourced in the grammarians’ usage of the term dhvani which has the sense of vaikrta-dhvani (echo):

*sruyamanesv iti, srotra- saskulim santanenagata antyah sabdah sruyanta iti prakriyayam sabda-jah sabdah sruyamana ity uktam. tesam ghantanuranana- rupatvam tavad asti, te ca dhvani-sabdenoktah. yathaha bhagavan bhartrharih, “yah samyoga-vibhagabhyam karanair upajanyate, sa sphotah sabda-jah sabda dhvanayo ’nyair udahrtah.” evam ghantadi-nirhlada-sthaniyo ’nunaranatmopalaksito vyangyo ’py artho dhvanir iti vyavahrtah.*

**“Regarding sruyamanesu (in the vrtti), the last sounds arrive in the ears as a continuity and are heard. In this manner it is said that sounds originating from sound are being heard. Those sounds are simply the form of the echo of a bell, and they are expressed with the word dhvani. For example, the highly venerable Bhartrhari said: “The propagators of another school say: What is produced by the organ of speech by means of contact and disjunction \[of the tongue with the places of pronunciation in the mouth\] is called Sphota. The dhvanis (vaikrta-dhvanis) are sounds originating from sound” (Vakya-padiya 1.102). Dhvani is thus used in the sense of being a meaning, an implied one, which is partially indicated, which has the nature of an echo and which is akin to the resonant sound of a bell” (Locana 1.13).**

te ca srttyamanesu varnesu dhvanir iti vyavaharanti (Dhvany-aloka 1.13 vrtti).

The Dhvanikara used the word anuranana (echo) as a synonym of dhvani (implied sense): avivaksita-vacyasya pada-vakya- prakasata \| tad-anyasyanuranana-rupa-vyangyasya ca dhvaneh \|\| (3.1). All the major poetical theorists after him did so too.

Abhinavagupta was referring to Anandavardhana’s vrtti (elaboration). Ananda sought to prove that the usage of Suggestiveness (vyanjakatva, or vyanjana) is sourced in the grammarians’ methodology because, he said, the grammarians are foremost scholars and because the Dhvanikara alluded to scholars: “suribhih kathitah” (1.13) iti vidvad-upajneyam uktih, na tu yatha-kathancit pravrtteti pratipadyate. prathame hi vidvamso vaiyakaranah, vyakarana-mulatvat sarva-vidyanam. te ca sruyamanesu varnesu dhvanir iti vyavaharanti. tathaivanyais tan-matanusaribhih suribhih kavya-tattvartha-darsibhir vacya- vacaka-sammisrah sabdatma kavyam iti vyapadesyo vyanjakatva- samyad dhvanir ity uktah. (Dhvany-aloka 1.13 vrtti).

But here Anandavardhana says the word dhvani in the Grammarians’ system is a revealer (vyanjaka) (i.e. the prakrta-dhvanis reveal the sphota). There is a similarity in name only: There is no suggestiveness proper in grammar, because the grammarians do not acknowledge the function called Suggestiveness.

Abhinavagupta too said an absurdity: He defied all logic by stating that in Patanjali’s theory of Sphota, the word dhvani signifies not only vyanjaka-sabda (prakrta-dhvani) but also vyanjaka artha (a meaning that reveals).

According to Nagesa Bhatta, the concept of Sphota originates from a sage called Sphotayana, a grammarian mentioned by Panini: avan sphotayanasya (Astadhyayi 6.1.123). There are two main theories of Sphota: external (Patanjali’s theory) and internal (Bhartrhari’s theory). They have very little in common. Dr. Subrahmania Iyer writes: “The word sphota occurs already in the Mahabhasya of Patanjali on P. I.1.70; but there it is not applied to the meaning-bearing element.” In Vakya-padiya, Bhartrhari mentioned many Sphota theories and propounded his own. Since the Kashmiri Shaivites disagreed with Bhartrhari’s philosophy at large, they only referred to Patanjali’s theory.

## Patanjali’s Theory of Sphota

In this theory, the term Dhvani has two meanings: prakrta-dhvani (phoneme) and vaikrta-dhvani (prolongation, echo). The prakrta- dhvanis are the audible form of the sphota, i.e. the word that the speaker has in mind and utters. And if those prakrta-dhvanis are prolonged, they become vaikrta-dhvanis.

Patanjali propounded his Sphota theory in his commentary on a sutra by Panini: tat-paras tat-kalasya (Astadhyayi 1.1.70). That aphorism only refers to the length of the sounds of vowels (hrasva, dirgha, pluta). Patanjali comments:

*evam tarhi sphotah sabdah, dhvanih sabda-gunah. katham, bhery-aghata-vat, tadyatha bhery- aghato bherim ahatya kascid vimsatipadani gacchati kascit trimsat kascic catvarimsat, sphotah ca tavan eva bhavati, dhvani-krta vrddhih, dhvanih sphotas ca sabdanam dhvanis tu khalu laksyate, alpo mahams ca kesancid ubhayam tat-svabhavatah.*

**“Thus, sphota is sabda (sound, word). Dhvani is the quality of sound. How is it so? It is like beating a kettledrum. That is as follows: Some drummer beats a kettledrum and goes for twenty steps. Some other drummer beats a kettledrum and goes for thirty steps, and some other drummer beats a kettledrum and goes for forty steps. The sound (sphota) is just to that extent (beating the drum one time) (it remains unchanged); the increase was done by the echo (dhvani, i.e. vaikrta-dhvani). Dhvani and sphota take place, but only the dhvani of the sounds that is noticed is little and great. In intelligible sounds, both sphota and dhvani occur, owing to their nature” (Mahabhasya 1.1.70).**

Commenting on this, Nagesa Bhatta explains that Patanjali used the term dhvani in two ways: the phonemes and their prolongation: dhvanih sabda-guna iti bhasye dhvani-sabdena varna vaikrta- dhvanis ca (Mahabhasya-pradipoddyota 1.1.70). Kaiyata says the phonemes are the revealer and the sphota is the revealed: dhvanih sphotas ceti, vyanjako vyangyas cety arthah (Mahabhasya-pradipa 1.1.70).

The difference between Patanjali’s theory and Bhartrhari’s theory can be illustrated as follows: The word kamala (lotus) occurs after hearing the six phonemes k-a-m-a-l-a. The sphota is revealed after the pronunciation of the last letter (although sometimes a person gets the sphota before hearing the last letter, especially when a word in the Vedas is incomplete, as in the word srnga in the Rg- Veda verse that begins catvari srnga, cited ahead, where srnga stands for srngani). In Patanjali’s theory, sphota means sabda (the word in the speaker’s mind which becomes audible). In Bhartrhari’s theory, however, the last letter activates—in the mind—an ethereal thing (which he calls sphota) from which the meaning of the sound kamala comes forth. In Bhartrhari’s theory, the sphota of kamala is called a pada-sphota (the sphota of a word). Still, Bhartrhari specialized in expounding the vakya-sphota (the sphota, “flash of insight”, of a sentence). Sometimes, both sphotas occur at the same time: When we speak, we know what we are going to say, obviously, but on occasion we grasp another sense of our words upon hearing them. That second sense is a khanda-vakya-sphota, whereas Bhartrhari’s sphota is the akhanda-vakya-sphota.

Dr. Korada Subrahmanyam explains Patanjali’s theory:

Dhvanis manifest the Sphota. There are ten dhvanis in the sentence ‘ghatam anaya’ (fetch the pot).

In truth the Sphota-sabda is partless and has no sequence whatsoever.

Since Sphota-sabda is eternal, the qualities of time won’t / cannot create any distinctions in it. It is manifested by the dhvanis. The qualities of dhvanis reflect in Sphota-sabda. Prakrta-dhvanis manifest the Sphota. Since the Sabda is mixed with them it attains the time distinctions, i.e. ekamatra etc.. Since Vaikrta-dhvanis are external their qualities won’t reflect in Sphota. Rather, they can cause the existence of Sphota for some time.

The Prakrta-dhvani is the cause of the manifestation of Sphota-sabda. Prakrta-dhvani and Sphota-sabda are mixed like milk and water. It is impossible to separate them. Since both are inseparably mixed, the qualities of the Dhvani are reflected in the Sphota-sabda. It is due to the Dhvani that the Sphota-sabda appears in the form of ka, ga, etc. The form of Prakrta-dhvani itself looks like the form of Sphota-sabda. It is due to the hypothetical attribution (aropa) that we notice the difference caused by time as ekamatra, dvimatra and trimatra in a Sphota-sabda. That is how the Sphota-sabda differs.

Patanjali’s Sphota theory only accounts for the usage of the term dhvani in the sense of echo, which the Kashmiri rhetoricians stretched to mean “implied sense”.

The poetical function called vyanjana (Suggestiveness) was in fact invented by Abhinavagupta: ekayabhidha-vyaparam karoti dvitlyaya vyanjana-vyaparam (Locana 3.33). Anandavardhana used the term vyanjakatvam.

In the Dhvanikara’s methodology, however, Suggestiveness is nothing but the Abhihitanvaya-vadins’ tatparya (the Drift) (the meaning of a sentence is more than the sum total of the meanings of the words). The Abhihitanvaya-vadins are Kumarila Bhatta and his followers. Their tatparya is the equivalent of Bhartrhari’s Sphota, although the latter has a wider scope. The Dhvanikara only hinted at the origin of the usage of the term dhvani: He did not source the origin of what Anandavardhana and Abhinavagupta call Suggestiveness, because he implied that the Abhihitanvaya-vadins’ tatparya is a form of Suggestiveness. Anandavardhana followed the Dhvanikara’s methodology on the whole, but in one instance he showed that he was not happy with it: He indicated that the tatparya cannot account for an implied sense: na ca padartha- vakyartha-nyayo vacya-vyangyayoh, “The methodology (the Drift) between the meanings of the words and the meaning of the sentence does not apply to the methodology between a literal sense and an implied sense” (3.33 vrtti). Abhinava comments: nanv evam ma bhud vacaka-saktis tathapi tatparya-saktir bhavisyaCHy asankyaha na ceti, “He makes this statement suspecting that someone might reply: “Fine, the power of literally expressive words is insufficient to accomplish an implied sense, but the power of the Drift will be sufficient”” (Locana 3.33).

In that line of thought, Anandavardhana pointed out karika 1.10 of the Dhvanikara and politely stated that he is wrong in equating Suggestiveness with the Drift. Anandavardhana said that Suggestiveness and the Drift are merely similar in some way. It was Abhinavagupta who clearly established the theory that Suggestiveness is distinct from the tatparya and occurs after the tatparya has been applied: asmabhir api prasiddhebhyo sabda- vyaparebhyo bhidha-tatpayra-lakana-nipebhyo tirikto dhvanir ity uktah, “We say dhvani is entirely distinct from the well-known rhetorical functions called abhidha, tatparya, and laksana” (Locana 1.13). Abhinavagupta even corrected the Dhvanikara by saying that in an analysis of the derivation of an implied sense, ultimately only Suggestiveness is referred to, not the Drift: svatas tatparyenety abhidha-vyapara-nirakarana-param idam padam dhvanana-vyaparam aha na tu tatparya-saktim (Locana 2.22). Abhinava seemingly reproached Anandavardhana for the same reason: vacyeti, tatparyena visranti-dhamataya. prayojanatveveti yavat. prakasanam dyotanam ity arthah (Locana 1.14).

Abhinavagupta explains that the term sva-samarthya in Dhvany- aloka 1.11 (cited in the footnote) denotes the Drift: sva-samarthyam akanksa-yogyata-sannidhayah, “The term sva-samarthya means akanksa (mutual requirement of words), yogyata (congruity) and sannidhi (proximity, i.e. uttered without delay)” (Locana 1.11).

Abhinava used the Abhihitanvaya-vadins’ tatparya (the Drift) and applied it before using Suggestiveness. According to him, when an implied sense is based on abhidha, three functions are involved: abhidha, tatparya, and vyanjana. And when an implied meaning is based on laksana, all four functions are involved, since even then abhidha is somewhat taken in consideration insofar as the main meaning is judged incompatible before laksana is applied.

In truth, the Dhvanikara’s “Suggestiveness” is the Purport (tatparya) based on the Drift (tatparya)! It will be shown ahead that Bhatta Nayaka and Dhananjaya agreed with this, according to Dhanika (p. 384). The ‘Purport’ denotes the Anvitabhidhana- vadins’ concept of tatparya. It’s the same in English. Bhoja said that what is called the purport in general language is called dhvani in poetics: tatparyam eva vacasi dhvanir eva kavye (Srngara- prakasa 1.5). In essence, the Dhvanikara used Bhartrhari’s Sphofa and changed the term.

According to Nagesa Bhatta, the poetical function called Sugges­tiveness is sourced in Bhartrhari’s methodology in two ways: (1) In grammar, a preposition such as iva (like) is called dyotaka (suggestive) in the sense that it suggests a similarity (but the Naiyayikas and the Alankarikas call it vacaka, expressive), and (2) The Sphota is revealed (vyangya) by the phonemes. Bhartrhari mentioned it in his reiteration of the external sphota theory

(Patanjali’s Sphota), where the sphota is the revealed (vyangya) and the prakrta-dhvanis are the revealer (vyanjaka): grahana- grahyayoh siddha yogyata niyata yatha \| vyangya-vyanjaka- bhavena tathaiva sphota-nadayoh \|\| (Vakya-padiya 1.97). But there is no Suggestiveness per se: Nagesa Bhatta clarifies that in grammar vyangya stands for abhivyangya (manifested): atredam bodhyam, eka eva sphotas tat-tad-varnais tad-tad-rupenabhivyajyate (Mahabhasya-pradipoddyota 1.1.70).

The poetical concept of suggestion is vaguely sourced in Bhartr- hari’s system: A word ‘suggests’ its meaning, so to speak. Dr. Subrahmania Iyer notes:

The two, sabda and artha, stand in relation to each other, they face each other, and it is then that they are said to be vacaka and vacya, the expressive word and the expressed meaning. They are also said to be cause (karana) and effect (karya). That is why Bhartrhari has declared that the relation in which they stand towards each other can be looked upon as that of illuminator and illuminated (prakasaka-prakasyatvam) and as that of cause and effect (karya-karana-rupata ).

For example: apoddhara-padarthah ye ye carthah sthita-laksanah \| anvakhyeyas ca ye sabda ye capi pratipadakah \|\| karya-karana- bhavenayogya-bhavena ca sthitah \| (Vakya-padiya 1.24-25). This is like the aforesaid dynamic of vyangya and vyanjaka. However, the grammarians did not acknowledge “suggestiveness” per se (although Bhartrhari did in some way: p. 304). Dr. Kumar De writes:

It is well known that the philosophers refuse to recognise the vyanjana as a Vyapara sui generis, and even after it was put forward by the Alankarikas, they would explain it by another recognised function as anyatha-siddha; it is not surprising, therefore, that orthodox grammarians or philosophers should entirely ignore it.

Dr. Keith explains the Dhvani theory by connecting it with Sphota:

The theory finds its origin in the analysis of language and meaning. The phrase, a herdsman’s station on the Ganges, is obviously as it stands absurd ; the denotation (abhidha) gives no sense, and we are obliged to find a transferred sense (laksana) which gives us the sense of a station on the bank of the Ganges. This shows the incompatibility of the literal sense as one factor, and the possibility of giving an allied meaning as another. But this is not all : there is brought to us by such a phrase deliberately used in poetry a sense of the holy calm of such a station situated on the sacred stream with all its associations of piety. This, it is contended, is not given by implication, but by the power of suggestion which is derived from the poet’s purpose (prayojana) in applying the phrase. This doctrine of suggestion which the grammarians did not accept could be based on a philosophical opinion of the grammarians themselves. They recognized the Sphota, a mysterious entity, a sort of hypostatization of sound, of which action sounds were manifestations, and the same idea of the revelation of something inherent (vyanjana) is found in the Vedanta, where all is a manifestation of the underlying reality, the Brahman or absolute.

Dr. Sushil Kumar De adds:

This brings us to the consideration of the views of those who accept the concept of vyangya artha but dispense with the necessity of such a separate and unauthorized Vrtti as vyanjana, which is regarded as included in other functions of sound and sense. Some Mimamsakas hold, for instance, that the so-called suggested sense is conveyed by the abhidha- vrtti or the denotative power of a word. In this connexion, the dlrgha-vyapara-vadins  are said to have maintained that as a single arrow, discharged by a strong man, destroys by a single movement, called velocity, the armour of the enemy, pierces through his body and takes away his life, so a single word, used by a good poet, brings before us by a single power, called abhidha, the sense of the word, teaches us its logical connexion (anvaya) and makes us apprehend the suggested sense.

Ironically, the grammatical term jnapaka is the same as the poetical theorists’ term vyanjaka (suggestive word or phrase). Not only that, on the one hand Anandavardhana upholds the notion that poetical suggestiveness is sourced in the grammatical system, but on the other, poetical rhetoricians rebuke dry philosophers such as grammarians and Mimamsakas for being unable to relish an implied sense in the scope of a rasa, especially implied meanings in the scope of bhakti. Dr. Kumar De remarks:

The unexpressed meaning is bound up by means of definite links with the expressed, without which it cannot exist; but it is wrapped up in such a manner as to make it possible only for the initiated in the poetic hieroglyphics to comprehend it in its subtlety. The unexpressed is not understood by those who know grammar and lexicon, but only by men of good taste and literary instinct who know the essence of poetry. It is the province of the sahrdaya, the connoisseur, who is expert in discerning through the intricate meshes of veiled word and sense into the aesthetic relish of deeper significance, in which the pleasure of the beautiful is mixed up with the pleasure arising from the fineness of the problem itself. \[Sometimes, analyzing a verse is a challenge.\]

The Kashmiris never mentioned that Suggestiveness is sourced in Bhartrhari’s Sphota theory, for two reasons:

1\. Bhartrhari says the phonemes are unreal, in the sense that only the meaning of the sentence counts, whereas the Kashmiri Shaivites say the phonemes (Sanskrit phonemes) are real;

2\. The same basic principles occur in the respective philosophies: Bhartrhari’s world view conflicts with Kashmir Shaivism: Bhartrhari says the world is different from Brahma whereas the Kashmiri Shaivites say the world is real.

The Kashmiris gave their respects to the Grammarians in name only: They ignored Bhartrhari, one of the chief grammarians. Whenever Abhinava quoted Bhartrhari, the citations were only about Bhartrhari mentioning a Sphota theory of another scholar; and elsewhere in the book, when Abhinava mentioned the grammarians, he implicitly referred to Bhartrhari and considered him an adversary. This cover-up reached the peak of ludicrousness: Ananda, Abhinava and Mammata exalted Patanjali’s Sphota theory to the point of saying that in poetics, even the literal meaning can be called dhvani. The Dhvanikara never allowed such a usage.

He established that the word dhvani means “implied sense”. Dr. Sushil Kumar De writes:

The word dhvani itself, as Anandavardhana pointed out, is sometimes used by the grammarians for the word or letters which reveal the sphota. Mammata’s remarks in this connexion are pertinent. In his Vrtti on the definition given by him of dhvani (i.4), he says that the dhvani is, according to the grammarians, that word which reveals the all-important sphota, inasmuch as through it arises the knowledge of the word’s meaning. Others, by whom he signifies the writers on the dhvani theory in Poetics, carry this doctrine of the grammarians a step further and apply the term dhvani to the meaning, as well as to the word which is capable of suggesting a meaning superseding the one which is directly expressed. Intrinsically the two theories have scarcely any mutual connexion; but what the Alankarikas really wanted was an authority for their assumption of the power of vyanjana, which the great grammarians did not acknowledge.

Kavi Kamapura indicated that the poetical function called Suggestiveness is validated by ‘the’ Sphota theory. Combining the linguistic concepts of Patanjali’s Sphota with those of Bhartrhari’s, Kavi Kamapura stated that this is what Mammata had in mind when he referred to “the Grammarians”.

In expounding the Sphota theory, Kavi Kamapura incidentally criticized Pratyabhijnana: pada-janya-pratitir janyate, sahakari- dardhyena pratyabhijnana-vad eva. pratyabhijnane pratyakse ’pi atitadi-purvavastha sphuraty eva, tena krtam sphoteneti, tan na. tatha hi pada-vyutpadana-samayo hi sphota-krta eva, “\[Someone might argue:\] ““In a recognition (knowledge which is a mixture of direct experience and remembrance), the previous situation, even an old one, comes to mind even when there is the direct perception, so what is the use of a Sphota theory?” That is wrong. The explanation is this: The time when it is known that “This meaning of the word is taking place” is made by sphota.” (Alankara-kaustubha 2.5).

Kavi Kamapura did not see through the Kashmiris’ cover-up, but his opinion that the concept of vyanjana is sourced in the Sphota theory hits the bull’s-eye. The similarity between Suggestiveness and Bhartrhari’s Sphota theory is that each involves a flash of insight. It is high time to do justice to Bhartrhari.

## Bhartrhari’s Theory of Sphota

Bhartrhari lived around 500 CE. His theory of Sphota treats of linguistics and philosophy. In linguistics, the Kashmiri Shaivites adopted the standpoint of Kumarila Bhatta, but in philosophy they developed their own system: Pratyabhijna, or Recognition. It involves this sequence: vismrti (forgetfulness), pratyaksa (direct perception), and smrti (remembrance): In a flash of insight, the soul remembers its nature, and regains knowledge of itself. The term abhijnana in Kalidasa’s Abhijnana-sakuntalam refers to a similar process: Sakuntala went to meet Dusyanta, but he did not recognize her. Much later, all of a sudden Dusyanta remembered that he had married her. The term abhijnana denotes the transition from forgetfulness to remembrance. The prefix prati emphasizes the notion of “return”.

Bhartrhari’s philosophy is a form of sonic theology and is based on this aphorism by Vyasa: sabda iti cen natah prabhavat pratyaksanumanabhyam, “If someone says this contradicts the validity of Vedic word, the reply is: No, because the universe originates from it, and this is proven by direct perception and by inference” (Vedanta-sUtra 1.3.28). This sutra does not mean that sabda-brahma is the ingredient cause of creation. Rather, the purport is that meanings and other kinds of ideas did not originate with this creation, since they are archetypes that have always existed. For instance, what is said of Indra in the Vedas is said in reference to the category (jati) of Indra and does not necessarily denote the Indra of this universe, because if it only referred to the Indra of this universe, Vedic words could not be said to be eternal. Consequently Vyasa concludes: ata eva ca nityatvam, “For this reason also the Vedas are eternal” (Vedanta-sutra 1.3.29).

Jiva Gosvami rejects the Sphota theory: ata eva sphoia-rUipaivad vedasya nityatvam \[...\] vedantinas tu varna eva tu sabda iti, “\[The followers of Bhartrhari say:\] “Therefore the Vedas are eternal because they take the form of sphoia.” The proponents of Vedanta, however, follow this principle: “The phonemes themselves are the sounds”” (Sarva-samvadim 11 of Tattva-sandarbha). In other words, the Sphota-vadins presume that what is eternal in the Vedas is not the individual words but the overall meaning of a sentence. This eternal meaning, they say, is recollected every time the Vedas are recited. The Mimamsakas and the Vedantists, however, accept that not only the meanings but also the phonemes and the words of the Vedas eternally exist. Nonetheless, Bhartrhari’s viewpoint is substantiated by looking at the variant readings of the same hymn, Purusa-sUkta, in each Veda although the meaning is the same: mukham kim asya kau bahU ka UrUpada ucyete (Rg-Veda 10.90.11); mukham kim asyasit kim bahU kim UrU pada ucyete (Sukla Yajur- Veda 31.10); kav UrU padav ucyete (Taittiriya Aranyaka 3.12.13); mukham kim asya kim bahU kim UrU pada ucyete (Atharva-Veda 19.6.5).

Yaska stated Audumbarayana’s opinion that words only exist in the mind and senses: indriya-nityam vacanam audumbarayanah. (Nirukta 1.1)

Kavi Kamapura accepts the Sphota theory and adds that the phonemes are eternal (Alankara-kaustubha 2.1-5). However, if it were said that the phonemes are necessary to convey a meaning, there would be no scope for the concept of understanding a meaning by means of telepathy, not to mention the concept of intuition. The language of the heart is universal:

Poetry is the universal language which the heart holds with nature and itself. He who has a contempt for poetry cannot have much respect for himself, or for anything else. (William Hazlitt

Patanjali stated that the perception of a meaning can occur by intui­tion, not necessarily by means of properly pronounced phonemes:

*sabdartha-pratyayanam itaretaradhyasat sankaras tat- \|*  
*pravibhaga-samyamat sarva-bhuta-ruta-jnanam \|\|*

**“A word, its meaning, and a person’s perception of the meaning are intermixed because they are superimposed on each other. By yogic concentration on their differentiation, a person obtains the knowledge of \[the meaning of\] the sounds of any being.” (Yoga­sutra 3.17)**

Sankaracarya did not accept Bhartrhari’s Sphota theory: sphota- vadinas tu drsta-hanir adrsta-kalpana ca, varnas ceme kramena grhyamanah sphotam vyanjayanti sa sphoto ’rtham vyanaktiti gariyasi kalpana syat, “Those who adhere to the Sphota theory reject something obvious (words directly express their meanings) and imagine something imperceptible (sphota). Moreover, that doctrine assumes too much: “These phonemes, heard in sequence, activate the sphota, and then that sphota reveals the meaning”” (Sarlraka-bhasya 1.3.28). Similarly, Bhamaha rejected the Sphota theory: sapathair api cadeyam vaco na sphota-vadinam, “The words of the Sphota-vadis cannot be accepted even if they were to swear the Sphota theory is true” (Bhamahalankara 6.12).

Bhartrhari says Sphota is both the revealer and the revealed, a cause and an effect: prakasaka-prakasyatvam karya-karana-rupata, antar-matratmanas tasya sabda-tattvasya sarvada (Vakya-padiya 2.32). In like manner, Nagesa Bhatta derives the term sphota as: sphutaty artho ’smad iti sphotah, vacaka iti yavat. evam ca varna- sphotadi-padanam varnadayo vacaka ity arthah, “Sphota is that from which a meaning bursts forth. Sphota amounts to being a vacaka (an expressive thing, i.e. by means of phonemes) (Kumarila Bhatta disagrees with that). This means the phonemes of the words of a varna-sphota and so on are vacakas” (Sphotavada 2). Visvanatha Kaviraja stated: vaiyakarana hi prathame vidvamsah, tan-mulatvac chabda-vyavaharasya. pradhanatvam ca sphotasyartha-pratyayana-rupa-phala-pratyasatya sphutaty asmad artha iti sphotah, “Only the grammarians are the primary scholars, since grammar is the root cause of the usage of words. The fact that sphota is all-important is because it approximates the result which is the suggestion of a meaning. Sphota is so called because a meaning bursts forth from it” (Kavya-prakasa-darpana 1.4). The verbal root is sphut visarane (to burst, be manifest).

Nagesa Bhatta enumerates the types of Sphota: (1) varna-sphota, (2) pada-sphota, (3) vakya-sphota, (4) akhanda-pada-sphota, (5) akhanda-vakya-sphota, (6) varna-jati-sphota, (7) pada-jati- sphota, and (8) vakya-jati-sphota (Sphotavada 1). Nagesa Bhatta says a vakya-sphota is the most important sphota because the meanings of words culminate in a sentence.

In Vakya-padiya, Bhartrhari stated various interpretations of Sphota-vada, but his own Sphota theory is the akhanda-vakya- sphota  (the meaning of the sentence is one and is more than the sum of its parts). Dr. Subrahmanyam explains:

When the earlier dhvanis are emanated, then that was phonemes and words which are felt and not the Akhanda- vakya-sphota-sabda. Rather, the Sphota-sabda itself is felt not in its real form but in the unreal form of phonemes and words. It was through the last dhvani that the form of phonemes and words is gone and the real Vakya-sphota is manifested. \[...\] The Vaiyakaranas believe that the phonemes and words are artificial. In fact they do not exist. Sentence is the real unit. The same is Sphota-sabda.

The theory of Naiyayikas that a group of phonemes is a word and that of words is a sentence, cannot be substantiated. Therefore, phonemes are genuine and words and sentences are nothing but illusion. \[.\] Therefore, neither the theory of Mimamsakas that only phonemes are real, nor that of Naiyayikas that words only are real can be taken for granted.

Dr. Subrahmanyam adds:

All the Vaiyakaranas have accepted that there is an entity called Sphota and it’s the origin of all Sabdas, and therefore they became famous as Sphota-vadins. \[.\] The roots of Sphota- theory were already there in ancient times, rather Bhartrhari can be considered to be the first to elaborate, propagate and accentuate the theory. The famous Mimamsaka, Kumarila- bhatta and the Naiyayika of similar fame, Vacaspati-misra have vehemently refuted the concept. In his work ‘Sphota- siddhi’, Mandana Misra strongly advocated the theory of Sphota.

Kumarila Bhatta disagreed with Sphota-vada. Still, Mandana Misra, who defended Sphota-vada, was a disciple of Kumarila Bhatta. Sankaracarya defeated Mandana Misra in debate, though the legend does not say whether Sphota-vada was a topic.

Sabara Svami (fourth century) invented tatparya-vrtti (the Drift) in principle. Bhartrhari’s Sphota, called akhanda-vakya-sphota, is practically the same. It seems that Sabara Svami endorsed Sphota-vada: purva-varna-janita-samskara-sahito ’ntyo varnah pratyayaka ity adosah (Sabara-bhasya 1.1.1). The Drift became the essential aspect of Kumarila Bhatta’s Abhihitanvaya-vada: Abhidha-vrtti can only be used one time: It ceases to function after giving the meaning of each word; then tatparya-vrtti is needed to make the syntactical connection of the words, which amounts to the meaning of the sentence.

While discussing the different viewpoints in analyzing a sentence, Bhartrhari mentioned the views of the two Mimamsa schools that later became known as Prabhakara’s Anvitabhidhana-vada (abhidha-vrtti has the power to effect the meaning of a sentence) and Kumarila Bhatta’s Abhihitanvaya-vada.

Purva-mimamsa and Vyakarana have much in common: Both stress the importance of faultless words. Kumarila Bhatta orchestrated the decline of Buddhism by propounding the notion that Buddhist scriptures cannot be logically correct because they contain grammatical inconsistencies. On the other hand, the Sanskrit in the Vedas is irregular. Moreover, the Grammarians and the Mimamsakas (athato dharma-jijndsa, Purva-mimamsa-sutra 1.1.1) agree that life should be based on dharma (moral ethics) and that dharma is expounded in the Vedas: dharmo jnanasya hetus cet tasyamnayo nibandhanam, “If dharma is the cause of knowledge, then the Vedas are the root cause of understanding dharma” (Vakya- padiya 1.135). The Grammarians say the practice of dharma is conducive to liberation:

The purpose of Vyakarana is claimed to be two-fold: Artha- jnana (cognition of meaning) and Dharma (a virtue useful in attaining Moksa—salvation). The latter is, in truth, of two types—Pravrtti and Nivrtti. The former is useful in attaining comforts in this world whereas the latter is for Moksa. Two kinds of relations and two types of purposes are proposed in verse 25.

In addition, Bhartrhari expounded figurative usage. He even acknowledged the concept of implied meaning: ya pravrtti-nivrtty- artha stuti-ninda-prakalpana, kusalah pratipatta tam ayathartham pratiyate, “A clever person understands that praise and admonition as incentives to action and inaction respectively are unreal praise and unreal admonition” (Vakya-padiya 2.318).

In that regard, Bhartrhari said that sometimes the Vedas make false statements to prevent people from committing bad deeds, like a mother might tell her baby to stop crying or else a tiger will devour the baby. Punyaraja comments that Vedic statements which tell people that they will go to hell if they commit a prohibited act fall in that category, consequently such statements should not be taken at face value.

Thus Bhartrhari nowhere stated that his Sphota only involves the literal sense of the words. According to him, sometimes the sense of a sentence is not obtained from its form: Logical reasoning— especially the line of reasoning in Purva-mTmamsa—facilitates the understanding of the real sense. Bhartrhari even says that the power of words is nothing but that logical reasoning: sabdanam eva sa saktis tarko yah purusasrayah, sa sabdanugato nyayo ’nagamesv anibandhanah, “Human reasoning is the power of words. That logical reasoning is in accordance with the scriptures. The reasoning of those who are not in line with the scriptures is invalid” (Vakya-padiya 1.138).

This is an example of figurative usage in the Vedas:

Rg-Veda 4.58.3, which begins: “It has four horns, three feet, two heads,” is taken to be a series of metaphors: by the four horns are intended (abhipraya) the four priests, by the three feet the three pressings of soma, by the two heads the patron of the sacrifice and his wife. It is, Sabara adds, “like praising a river by saying that a pair of water birds are its two breasts, a line of snow geese its brilliant white teeth, the silvery rushes its garment, and the dark seaweed its flowing hair.” See Sabara-bhasya on Mimamsa-sUtra 1.2.46. The distinction between sruti and laksana is drawn by Sabara in his comment on Mimamsa-sutra 6.2.20. Kumarila’s analysis of metaphor and metonymy is found on Tantra-varttika on Mimamsa-sUtra 1.4.22.

The whole verse reads:

*catvari srnga trayo asya pada dve sirse sapta hastaso ’sya \|*  
*tridha baddho vrsabho roraviti maho devo martya a vivesa \|\|*

**“He has four horns, three feet, two heads, and seven hands, and is bound in three ways. A bull (the best of men) intensely recites. The great Lord enters humans that way.” (Rg-Veda 4.58.3)**

The first half of the verse is rendered in Bhagavatam 8.16.31 and the second in Bhagavatam 11.12.17. Commenting on Bhagavatam 8.16.31, Sndhara Svami cites the verse, ignores Sabara Svami’s above interpretation and quotes Yaska’s explanation. Yaska writes: “The four horns are the four Vedas. The three feet are the three parts of the day. The two heads are the introductory portion and the concluding portion of a sacrifice. The seven hands are the seven meters. He is bound in three ways, by the mantra portion of the Vedas, by the Brahmana portion, and by the kalpa portion (the rules for a sacrifice). “A bull intensely recites” means men invoke Him with hymns of the Rg-Veda, perform sacrifice to Him by means of hymns of the Yajur-Veda, and praise Him with hymns of the Sama-Veda” (Nirukta 13.7).

In the form of transcendental sound, the Lord enters the body of a reciter of the Vedas (Bhagavatam 11.12.17-18). This refers to the four phases of Vedic sound: Para, Pasyanti, Madhyama, and Vaikhan (Rg-Veda 1.164.45). The above text from Rg-Veda involves figurative usage, and it occurs twice. These two separate Sphotas of the text constitute a khanda-vakya-sphota. The same occurs in verses of Purusa-sukta and so on. Therefore Bhartrhari’s theory that Sphota is one and undivided does not hold here.

In addition, Patanjali’s interpretation of the above verse constitutes a third application of figurative usage. According to him, the four horns represent both the four phases of speech and these four: noun, verb, prefix, and preposition. The three feet are the three phases of time: past, present and future. The two heads are the two forms of Sabda (sphota and audible phonemes). The seven hands are the seven types of case-endings. He is bound in three ways: on the chest (the origin of vowels), in the throat (where the consonants are pronounced) and at the head (where the anusvara is made; or else in the nose).

Over and above that, Patanjali cites the verse to illustrate that one purpose of studying Sanskrit is that a similarity between the Lord and us may take place: mahata devena nah samyam yatha syat iti adhyeyam vyakaranam (Mahabhasya, preliminary). Nagesa Bhatta says this is actually the Purport (the implied sense); in other words, he says, the verse signifies that God makes a pure reciter of the Vedas non-different from Him.

Another example of Suggestiveness in the Vedas is in: sarvam khalv idam brahma, “Indeed, the entire universe is Brahma” (Chandogya Upanisad 3.14.1). This is figurative usage, by the logic that duality does not exist: dvaitasyavastunah (Bhagavatam 11.28.4). The real meaning is: “Brahma is the cause of everything.” That indirect meaning occasions an implied sense: The universe is pervaded, in potential, by transcendental potency: etat sarvam idam visvam jagad etac caracaram \| para-brahma-svarupasya visnoh sakti- samanvitam \|\| visnu-saktih para prokta ksetra-jhakhya tathapara \| avidya-karma-samjhanya trtlya saktir isyate \|\| (Visnu Purana 6.7.60-61). In that sense the world is transcendentally real (in part): This is the true meaning of Parinama-vada (Brahma / Vishnu transforms as the world). Vyasa states: atma-krteh parinamat, “\[Vishnu is both the ingredient cause and the instrumental cause of the world,\] because of a modification, on account of making Himself (the world is His body)” (Vedanta-sutra 1.4.26). Pradhana, a material potency of Vishnu, is the ingredient cause (upadana- karanam). Baladeva Vidyabhusana states that Vishnu, in the form of transcendental potency, is the instrumental cause (nimitta- karanam).

Time has a dual nature: It is a transcendental potency and a potency of Maya (Bhagavatam 3.26.15-16): tam evakalam dvedhalaksayati (Bhavartha-dipika 3.26.16). But since transcendental potency is not always present, the world is fundamentally unreal because the three gunas are unreal in the sense that they are not transcendental.

Similarly, Bhartrhari says his Brahma is both different from and not different from its potencies: ekam eva yad amnatam bhinna- sakti-vyapasrayat \| aprthaktve pii saktibhyah prthaktveneva vartate \|\| (Vakya-padiya 1.2). This is the same as Gaudiya Vaishnava philosophy, called acintya-bhedabheda-tattva (paradox; the principle of inconceivable, simultaneous difference and non­difference) (the universe is different and not different from God, a soul is different and not different from God, and God’s attributes are not different from Him). The philosophy of Paradox is substan­tiated as follows. This is a verse of catuh-sloki:

*yatha mahanti bhutani bhutesUccavacesv anu \|*  
*pravistany apravistani tatha tesu na tesv aham \|\|*

**“Just as afterward the five elements both entered in large things and in little things and did not enter them, so I am in them and I am not in them” (Bhagavatam 2.9.35).**

At first the outer coverings of the universe were created, therefore the subsequent entrance of the five elements inside the universe is not really an entrance because they were already present, by taking the coverings of the universe to be part of the universe. That verse has its counterpart in Bhagavad-gita:

*maya tatam idam sarvam jagad avyakta-murtina \|*  
*mat-sthani sarva-bhutani na caham tesv avasthitah \|\|*  
*na ca mat-sthani bhutani pasya me yogam aisvaram \|*

**“I pervade all this world by My unmanifest form (Brahma). All things and all beings are in Me, but I am not in them, nor are all of them in Me. Behold My godly might.” (Bhagavad-gita 9.4-5)**

The theory of paradox is also substantiated in the very first line of Bhagavata Purana: janmady asya yato ’nvayad itaratas carthesu, “\[We meditate on Him\] from whom the creation, the continuation and the destruction of the universe take place because of His connection (anvayat) in things (arthesu) and (ca) because He is altogether distinct (itaratah) from them” (Bhagavatam 1.1.1).

In the fourth verse of catuh-sloki in Bhagavatam, Krishna sum­marizes His teachings:

*etavad eva jijnasyam tattva-jijnasunatmanah*  
*anvaya-vyatirekabhyam yat syat sarvatra sarvada*

**“The inquiring by one who seeks to know the truth about the Soul should be done to this extent that it occurs in regard to everything at all times both in terms of connection and in the opposite way.” (Bhagavatam 2.9.36)**

In terms of connection (anvaya), the Absolute is in the world in the form of transcendental energy, or the Absolute communicates by symbols and by implied meanings, along the model expounded in Purusa-sukta. And by the negatory process, the opposite of a connection, nothing in the world is the Absolute: neti neti (not this, not that) (Brhad-aranyaka Upanisad 2.3.6). The concept of negation is exactly what is meant here. For instance: nisedha- seso jayatad asesah, “Glory to Asesa, who is the remainder of the negation” (Bhagavatam 8.3.24).

Sridhara Svami says “in terms of connection” means God is present in the effects, and “in the opposite way” means He, the cause, is completely distinct from the effects: anvayah karyesu karanatvenanuvrttih. karanavasthayam ca tebhyo vyatirekah (Bhavartha-dipika 2.9.36). This philosophy does not only relate to the Absolute: In everyday life, for instance, we examine a situation by assessing the pros and the cons, the qualities and the faults.

The philosophy of Paradox amounts to what I call the Unified Theory of Vedanta: The two theories, Parinama-vada (the world is a transformation of God: the world contains transcendental energy) and Vivarta-vada (the world is unreal: the world is distinct from God and consists of material energy), are valid. This dual approach is substantiated in Bhartrhari’s philosophy, according to Gaurinatha Sastn (pp. 330-331 ahead). Practically speaking, the paradox is this: There is a God. There is no God. Both propositions are true. Although Brahma is a form of God, Brahma has no bearing on the world per se. Moreover, those who only say there is a God have not lived much, and those who only say there is no God have not lived much. As the British Empire sent India’s precious stones back to England and hence became rich, let the intellectual gems of India enrich the minds of scholars all over the world.

Thus, Bhartrhari’s Sphota-vada is a primitive yet complete theory, for it includes all the literary functions of the poetical theorists: Denotation (abhidha), Indication (laksana), the Drift (the Abhihitanvaya-vadins’ tatparya), the Purport (Mammata’s tatparya, which is the well-known tatparya of the Mimamsakas), and Suggestiveness (vyanjana). For this reason Abhinavagupta says Sphota-vada is not a valid methodology of interpretation: According to him, a cause-and-effect relation between literary functions should be established, based on specific rules, like in Purva-mimamsa philosophy these six are sequentially less important in determining the sense of a sentence: sruti (a statement from a sruti scripture), linga (the conventional sense supersedes the etymological meaning), vakya (the agreement in case ending), prakarana (the actual context), sthana (proximity to another context), and samakhya (the etymological meaning). Still, Bhartrhari mentioned such factors that narrow down the possible literal meanings down to one (VP 2.315-316). Mammata and many other poetical theorists cited him in their respective sections on abhidha-mula-vyanjana (Denotation-based Suggestiveness).

Bhartrhari says the meaning of a sentence is understood by means of a flash of insight (pratibha). This flash joins the meanings of the words, once those meanings have been severally understood. Bhartrhari said the flash is obtained either: (1) by means of one’s nature, (2) by good conduct, (3) by practice, (4) by contemplation, (5) by the result of performing good deeds, or (6) by being bestowed by a special person.

In conformity with Anandavardhana, Mammata used Bhartrhari’s concept of “a flash of insight” to explain how the readers perceive an implied sense, such as a rasa. Commenting on this, Baladeva Vidyabhusana says “the flash of insight” refers to the specific predisposition (e.g. only a grown-up can understand about srngara- rasa): pratibha vasana-visesah (Sahitya-kaumudl 3.2). Therefore sphota is of the nature of a flash of insight. Suggestiveness is dhvany-aloka (the light for an implied sense). In other contexts, the term pratibha means creative intelligence. Thus, Rajasekhara explained the two meanings of the term pratibha: karayitrl (creative intelligence) and bhavayitrl (the cause of appreciation).

Ultimately, Bhartrhari’s Sphota is Sabda in the highest sense (Sabda-Brahma). The scriptures say there are two Brahmas: dve brahmanl veditavye sabda-brahma param ca yat, sabda-brahmani nisnatah param brahmadhigacchati, “Two Brahmas are to be known: Sabda-Brahma and Para-Brahma. A person learned in Sabda-Brahma attains Para-Brahma” (Visnu Purana 6.5.64).

Bhartrhari, however, made no difference between the two: anadi- nidhanam brahma sabda-tattvam yad aksaram, vivartate ’rtha- bhavena prakriya jagato yatah, “Brahma, the Imperishable, has neither beginning nor end and is the Word Principle. The ways of the world revolve by the existence of meanings from that Brahma” (Vakya-padiya 1.1).

In this verse, the verb vivartate (it revolves, i.e. it manifests as an illusion) was the precursor of the term Vivarta-vada, a doctrine propounded by Sankaracarya. Bhartrhari comments on his opening verse: tathedam amrtam brahma nirvikaram avidyaya kalusatvam ivapannam bheda-rupam vivartate (Vakya-padiya 1.1 vrtti). Nonetheless, Bhartrhari’s concept of vivarta refers to Sabda- Brahman: The world is a modification of the Word (omkara):

For the first time in the Vakya-padiya of Bhartrhari the theory of Sphota and modification of word (sabda-vivarta-vada) has been established and discussed in detail. Really speaking, the theory of sphota is a unique achievement of Indian grammarians and as such it forms India’s outstanding contribution to the philosophy of language.

Later in his introduction, Bhartrhari says the Veda, which branches out as various Vedas according to the tradition, is a resemblance of that Brahma and is the means to achieve it: prapty-upayo ’nukaras ca tasya vedo maharsibhih \| eko ’py aneka-vartmeva samamnatah prthak prthak \|\| (1.5).

The Sphota theory is sourced in this Vedic verse:

*catvari vak parimita padani*  
*tani vidur brahmana ye manisinah \|*  
*guha trim nihita nengayanti*  
*turiyam vaco manusya vadanti \|\|*

**“Speech is divided in four stages. Wise Brahmanas know them. The first three stages appear only within the body. They do not occur externally. The fourth stage of speech is the sounds spoken by humans.” (Rg-veda 1.164.45)**

The Bhagavatam refers to Bhartrhari’s Sphota:

*disam tvam avakaso ’si disah kham sphota asrayah, nado varnas tvam om-kara akrtmam prthak-krtih (10.85.9). Commenting on this, Sndhara Svami mentions the four phases of speech, equating Sphota with Para Vak: disam upadhikrtakasa-pradesanam avakaso disas ca tvam. kham samanyakasas tad-asrayah sphotas ca sabda- tan-matram paravastha vag ity arthah. nadah pasyanti. omkaro madhyama. varnas cakrtmam padarthanam prthak krtih prthak karanam abhidhanam yasmat tat padam. varna-padady-atmika vaikhari ca tvam ity arthah. (Bhavartha-dipika 10.85.9).*

The Bhagavatam equates sphota with sabda-brahma (srnoti ya imam sphotam, 12.6.40), according to Kavi Karnapura, or, according to Sridhara Svami, with omkara: ko ’sau paramatma tam aha, srnotiti. imam sphotam avyaktam om-karam (Bhavartha- dipika 12.6.40). Elsewhere, however, Sndhara Svami says sphota means sound in the form of Para Vak; nada denotes Pasyanti; and omkara denotes Madhyama: kham samanyakasas tad-asrayah sphotas ca sabda-tanmatram paravastha vag ity arthah. nadah pasyanti. omkaro madhyama (Bhavartha-dipika 10.85.9). Still, even in this context sphota denotes sabda-brahma, an extremely subtle form of sound.

Dr. Sukla writes:

Nagesa believes in four types of vak viz. Para, Pasyanti, Madhyama and Vaikhari and shows a vast difference between Para and Pasyanti. In this way Nagesa identifies Para with Sabda-brahma. The process of creation (srsti-prakara) described by Nagesa is completely explained in the treatises of Tantra, and according to them this Para or Sabda-brahma is the product of bindu which itself is the product of Maya and Purusa created by Bhagavat.

Dr. Srinivas Murti expounds:

The doctrine of the Eternity of Sabda (the Word) has a most fascinating and ancient history having its roots in the well-known Rg-vedic hymns to the Goddess of Speech— Vagdevi. The traditional formulator of this theory according to grammarians is Sphotayana Rsi, as referred to at the end of the present publication. As developed by grammarians like Bhartrhari, the theory of Sphota links up the transient phenomenon of the pronounced word to Brahman as Sabda- Brahman, the eternal Noumenon of every form of significant sound or word and indeed of every manifested object of creation. This is a view which strikingly brings up to our mind the conception of Platonic Logos (the Word) and the saying of the Christian scripture “In the beginning was the Word (Logos); the Word was with God; and the Word was God.” \[...\]

Sanskrit grammar is not merely a Science of Linguistics or an Art of correct speaking and writing. It is far more than mere Science or Art. It is also a Philosophy with its own Metaphysics. It is even more than this; for it is also a moksa- sastra—a religion pointing a way to Moksa (Liberation) through the discipline or upasana of Sabda-brahman (Word­Brahman) conformably to the text “he who is well-versed in Word-Brahman (Sabda-Brahman) attains to the Supreme Brahman:

*sabda-brahmani nisnatah param brahmadhigacchati I*

\[.\] The transition of the eternal Sphota or Sabda-Brahman from the highest level to the form of the spoken or audible word or sound at the lowest level is described as occurring in four stages technically known as Para, Pasyanti, Madhyama and Vaikhan. Para and Pasyanti are too subtle to be comprehended by our sense-organs except by the yogins. The Madhyama stage may be comprehended through practices like japa while the Vaikhari is what is uttered by the vocal organs and is capable of being heard by ordinary folk. Para is the Eternal Noumenon—Sabda-Brahman originating from Kundalini in Muladhara-cakra. This is also referred to as Nada. Pasyanti originates from Svadhisthana-cakra in the navel region. Both Para and Pasyanti are classed as Suksma (subtle) Sphota. Madhyama originates from Anahata-cakra in the region of the Heart where the voice of the silence is heard. It is also referred to as Antara (internal) Sphota. Vaikhan originates in Visuddha-cakra in the region of the throat and is manifested as Bahya (external) Sphota through utterance by the vocal organs and is capable of being heard by others. It is because of this nexus that we can, if we will, place ourselves in tune with the infinite Sphota (Sabda-Brahman), through the Vaikhari sound or Bahya-Sphota if we practice the necessary discipline.

Bhartrhari raised grammar to the level of a philosophical system: idam adyam pada-sthanam siddhi-sopana-parvanam, iyam sa moksamananam ajihma raja-paddhatih, “Grammar is the first step on the ladder to perfection, and is the straight royal path for those who talk about liberation” (1.16); asannam brahmanas tasya tapasam uttamam tapah, prathamam chandasam angam ahur vyakaranam budhah, “Grammar is the topmost austerity of the ascetics” (1.11).

Dr. Subrahmanyam remarks:

4\. He elucidated the concept of Patanjali that through the employment of Sadhu-Sabdas one would know the real form of Veda and thus get on track for attaining Dharma (this point is criticised by Somananda in Siva-drsti). \[...\]

8\. He construed the Vaiyakarana-siddhantas along with Advaita-vedanta and Veda-pramanikatva (authority of Vedas). He brought Sphota on a par with Apurva of Mimamsakas, Isvara of Naiyayikas, Pilu of Kanadas, Sunya of Bauddhas and Brahman of Vedantins.

Bhartrhari specifically talks about the last three phases of speech: vaikharya madhyamayas ca pasyantyas caitad adbhutam, aneka- tirtha-bhedayas trayya vacahparampadam (Vakya-padiya 1.143). But according to Dr. Subrahmanyam, Bhartrhari discusses Para Vak in verses 17 and 18 and in verses 112 to 115 of brahmakanda (the first chapter of Vakya-padiya). For example:

*atratita-viparyasah kevalam anupasyati \|*  
*chandasyas chandasam yonim atma chandomayim tanum \|\|*

**“The soul who has mastered grammar and is fit for the Vedas cons­tantly perceives the unique source of the Vedas, a source which is a form of the nature of the Vedas.” (Vakya-padiya 1.17)**

Bhartrhari’s Sphota theory is the ideal explanation of how the Maharishis cognized the Vedas in their trance:

While all this is true of us ordinary mortals, the great sages are credited with the power of cognizing the indivisible sphota directly, without going through the process of errors. Not only do they cognize it themselves, they also impart it to others. That is what Yaska has stated in his Nirukta I.20.

The first Rsis realised dharma, that is, they acquired it. It is implied that they acquired the Mantras also, without being taught by anybody. Their successors were of inferior calibre; and could neither realise the dharma nor acquire the Mantras by themselves. To them, the first Rsis imparted the Mantras by establishing the relation of teacher and pupil. This second batch of Rsis thus got the Mantras by listening to the words of their teachers. They are, therefore, Srutarsayah (Rsis through instruction). \[...\] That the Vrtti was influenced by the Nirukta in the interpretation of Vak. I.5 and 137 is shown by the fact that, in the explanation of the former stanza, the relevant passage from the Nirukta is actually quoted, and that in the explanation of the later stanza there is a reference to three kinds of Rsis. What the Vrtti says about the three kinds of Rsis is not identical with what the Nirukta says about them.

Bhartrhari’s theory of Sphota perfectly applies only to the Vedas because Bhartrhari’s Sphota is nitya (eternal), i.e. a word has an eternal set of given meanings—according to tradition, this idea was first formulated by Katyayana—and the Vedas convey archetypical meanings, not to mention that the words of the Vedas must be properly recited to achieve the desired effect, whereas in real life a sphota (flash of insight) does not always involve a meaning of an eternal nature.

Thus, Bhartrhari wanted to raise grammar to a philosophical system (darsana), and for that purpose he discussed the pramanas (means of obtaining valid knowledge):

In a regular darsanika work, there would be discussions about valid and invalid knowledge, prama and bhrama. But the Vakya-padiya is not a darsanika work. After all, it is the work of a grammarian; and although it does set forth a darsana as the view relating to the nature of the ultimate Reality and its manifestation just referred to, it shows that Bhartrhari is chiefly concerned with establishing the authority of Grammar. It can be authority only if it gives valid knowledge about something; and it is in this connection that Bhartrhari is led to make some observations on valid knowledge, and how it arises.

Moreover, Bhartrhari says Sanskrit is a divine language set in its ways, but he admits that over time foreign words became Sanskritized. Bhartrhari extended his theory of Sphota to language in general, and this is where his theory begins to collapse, for these reasons:

◊ Outside of the Vedas, there is no need to consider Pasyanti Vak, much less Para Vak;

◊ Poets invent words and derive some others in various ways, and so there is not always an eternal connection between a word and its meaning;

◊ In the scope of the Vedas, a Sphota concerns an archetypical meaning, whereas in poetry new ideas are invented all the time, thus a Sphota in poetry is not always nitya. Besides, even a wrong idea can be called sphota. So why bother calling a meaning Sphota, which is said to be sabda-brahma by nature? However, there is no doubt that Sarasvati, the goddess of language, can become manifest in the form of a special meaning in anyone’s words whenever she wants to.

## Philosophy Influences Poetic Theory

The Dhvanikara’s acceptance of Kumarila Bhatta’s tatparya, which implies the rejection of Bhartrhari’s Sphota theory, is an important, although neglected, event in the history of Kashmir Shaivism. The first documented evidence of the Kashmiris’ rejection of Bhartrhari’s theory is in the second chapter of Somananda’s Siva- drsti (c. 860 CE). Utpala, Abhinavagupta and other Kashmiris rejected Bhartrhari’s Sphota-vada. Abhinavagupta (c. 950-1020 CE) was Somananda’s great-grand-disciple.

## The Kashmiri Shaivite Tradition

![рис-005.jpg|625](<Versified History of Sanskrit Poetics/рис-005.jpg>)

The reason the Kashmiri Shaivites rejected Bhartrhari’s Sphota theory is that according to Bhartrhari, the phonemes of a word are unreal. The Kashmiri Shaivites cannot accept this because it implies that the world is unreal, whereas in their view the world is real, since it is a manifestation of Siva.

Bhartrhari’s Sphota is on the topic of vakya (sentence): The vakya- sphota is the meaning-bearer. Kumarila’s tatparya provided an ideal alternative to Bhartrhari’s theory because that tatparya is the literary function which accomplishes the overall sense of a sentence and because the Mimamsakas say the phonemes are real. The latter point is important for Kashmiris. For instance, Abhinavagupta states that the phonemes are manifestations of Siva. Dr. Raffaele Torella explains:

But there is something that keeps Abhinavagupta away from a whole-hearted acceptance of the whole of Bhartrhari’s conception: first of all, Bhartrhari’s dismissal of the phonemes and his considering them as pure abstractions. This must have seemed unacceptable to Abhinavagupta, in his position as a tantric master. He cannot ignore that practically any tantra belonging to the Saiva tradition deals with the phonemes, assigning them a central place both in ritual and speculation. What he says in the Isvara-pratyabhijna-vivrti-vimarsim, precisely addressing the Vaiyakaranas, sounds like a proud vindication: ‘For us, the “totality of sounds” is the supreme Lord himself, the goddess Matrka \[or the alphabet in the usual sequence\] - both distinct and not distinct \[from Him\] - is His Power, the eight alphabetic classes are the eight Powers of the Rudras, the fifty phonemes are the fifty Powers of the Rudras’. If Abhinavagupta intends to give space to the role of phonemes, this cannot but take place at the expense of the sphota doctrine, which in fact he totally ignores. Will this result in going closer to the MTmamsa? Why not? After all, both the MTmamsakas and the Saivas feel as their primary duty the defence and exegesis of the Sruti, as embodied in the Vedas for the former, in the Tantras for the latter.

All this enthusiasm of the Kashmiri poets for Kumarila Bhatta’s tatparya came to an abrupt halt when Mammata stopped inviting the Abhihitanvaya-vadins to the poetical party. He not only discarded the Drift, he indirectly pointed out that in one sense Kumarila Bhatta’s tatparya is the same as Bhartrhari’s Vakya- sphota: akanksa-yogyata-sannidhi-vasad vaksyamana-svarupanam padarthanam samanvaye tatparyartho visesa-vapur apadartho ’pi vakyarthah samullasatlty abhihitanvaya-vadinam matam. vacya eva vakyartha ity anvitabhidhana-vadinah, “The opinion of the Abhihitanvaya-vadTs is this: Although it is not the expressed meaning of the words, the tatparya artha (the Drift), whose form is a particularity, is the sense of the sentence and is apparent in the syntactical connection (the prose order) of the meanings of the words by the force of akanksa (mutual requirement of words), yogyata (congruity), and sannidhi (mutual proximity of words, i.e. uttered without delay) (tatparya artha = vakya artha = apadartha).

The Anvitabhidhana-vadis, however, say the expressed meanings of the words is the sense of the sentence (vacya artha = vakya artha)” (Kavya-prakasa 2.6 vrtti).

Mammata’s statement that Kumarila Bhatta’s tatparya is apadartha (not the meaning of the words taken at face value), that is, avacya (not literal), implicitly validates the grammarians’ opinion that the first perception of the meanings of the words of a sentence is unreal. For instance, in the sentence gaur anubandhyah, the phonemes of the word gauh do not reveal the actual meaning of the word. We must look at the case ending of its adjective to understand that here the word gauh is masculine, and so it means ox, not cow. Similarly, the individual perception of the phonemes of a word is unreal until they form a coherent whole: satyam yat tatra sa jatir asatya vyaktayah smrtah (Vakya-padiya 3.1.32). Bhartrhari stated that just as a word cannot only be understood as the sum total of individual phonemes (since the meaning of a word is understood from a dictionary, and so on), a sentence cannot be understood only by the meanings of the words in the sentence. The words must be linked by means of some function. Bhartrhari says the initial illusoriness of the meaning of a word in a sentence signifies that the phonemes are unreal, but Kumarila and Abhinava argue that the phonemes—the Sanskrit phonemes—are real nonetheless. Bhartrhari’s philosophy as such is not restricted to the Sanskrit language nor to Prakrit languages.

Abhinavagupta, however, says the meaning of a sentence obtained by the Drift is vacya (expressed): sabdavagataih padarthais tatparyenayo’rtha utthapyate sa eva vakyarthah, sa eva ca vacya iti (Locana 3.33). The Drift was ignored by Mammata, Visvanatha and Kavi Kamapura, although they mentioned it in passing. Mammata mentioned the Drift and wrote kesucit (according to some persons)—tatparyartho ’pi kesucit (Kavya-prakasa 2.6)— implying that he himself did not acknowledge it. Dr. Kane notes:

But it does not appear that Mammata entirely approved of this view. Otherwise he would not have said “kesucif”, but would have simply declared that tatparya is one of the functions. Our author also appears to hold views similar to Mammata.

Mammata propounded his own explanation of the tatparya, but he never explicitly applied it to poetics. He even contradicted himself on the topic. Thus, throughout his magnum opus Mammata accepted the Anvitabhidhana-vadins’ methodology of using the term vacya (literally expressed) to denote either the meaning of a sentence or the meaning of a single word. Regarding the former, commenting on his rule saksat sanketitam yo ’rtham abhidhatte sa vacakah (Kavya-pradlpa 2.7), he indicated that there is no need of the tatparya to explain the sentence gam anaya (bring a cow), which is a classic example in Anvitabhidhana-vada. But in the fifth chapter, Mammata sought to prove the validity ofthe function called Suggestiveness by demolishing Anvitabhidhana-vada, specifically by saying that the meaning of the sentence gam anaya is avacya (not literally expressed), hence tatparya, much less vyanjana, is not in the scope of the theory called Dirgha-vyapara-vada (any nondirect meaning can be explained as an extension of Denotation). Govinda Thakkura clarifies that according to Mammata, the meaning of the sentence gam anaya is avacya because that meaning is not sourced in a dictionary and the like: anvitabhidhana- naye tu padartha-samanyanvitah svarthah sanketa-visayah. gavadi-visesanvitanayanadi-rupas tv asanketita evety avacya eva vakyarthah (Kavya-pradpa 5.47). Nagesa Bhatta concurs: go- karmakanayanadi-viseso ’vacyah (Uddyota 5.47). But it could be argued that gam anaya is a set phrase, as in “to give punishment,” and so the meaning is literal, like a rudha word (a figurative word that has become literally expressive due to the profuseness of the usage).

For his part, to validate vyanjana, Visvanatha ignored Mammata and reiterated Abhinavagupta’s explanation that a rhetorical function (esp. abhidha and laksana) can only be used one time: viramya vyaparah sabda-karma-buddhy-adnam padarthavidbhir nisiddhah (Locana 1.4). The Dhvanikara used the tatparya twice.

Mammata’s tatparya is the real sense of the speaker’s words. In essence, in poetics Mammata’s tatparya is arrived at by rewording the sentence (the statement means to express more than what it says) and is exactly the same as the paryayokta ornament (circumlocution). And if Mammata’s tatparya is suggestive, it is classed as the suggestive factor called vakya-vaisistya (the suggestive specialty of the real statement) (Kavya-prakasa 3.21). Mammata’s tatparya was wrongly ignored by other poetical theorists—although Visvanatha accepted vakya-vaisistya (Sahitya- darpana 2.16)—because it explains the concept of paryayokta.

Another reason the Kashmiri Shaivites rejected Bhartrhari’s system is that it is based on only three phases of speech (Pasyanti, Madhyama and Vaikhari), whereas the Kashmiri Shaivites propound the quadripartition: Para Vac occurs before Pasyanti. Not only that, the Kashmiris say Bhartrhari is wrong in equating Sabda-Brahma with Pasyanti (or even with Para Vac). Dr. Raffaele Torella expounds:

We can detect three main targets in Somananda’s criticism:

1\. the identification of para-brahman with sabda-rupa- pasyanti-paravac,

2\. the claim of vyakarana to go beyond the narrow domain of grammar proper and constitute a world-view, and

3\. as a world-view, its preaching the unreality of manifested universe, just as within the field of linguistic speculation it upholds the basic unreality of sounds with respect to the sphota they are supposed to reveal.

It is apparent that we are in front of two competing world views.

Thus, in the preliminary of the second chapter of Siva-drsti, Utpala, the commentator, says Somananda aims at exalting Isvaradvaya- vada (non-difference between the world and God) over the Grammarians’ Sabda-Parabrahmadvaya-vada (non-difference between Sabda-brahma and Para-brahma): isvaradvaya-vada eva yuktiyukto, natu sabda-parabrahmadvaya-vada iti vaktum, vaiyakaranopeta-sabdadvaitam tavan nirakartum upakramamana aha (Siva-drsti 2.1 vrtti).

In Manjusa and in Sphota-vada, Nagesa Bhatta added Para Vak to Bhartrhari’s Sphota theory. Other works of note in the field are Sphota-tattva-nirupana by Sesa Krsna, Sabda-kaustubha by Bhattoji Diksita, and Vaiyakarana-bhusana by the latter’s nephew Kaunda Bhatta: “So far as the treatment of Sphota theory, Samasa- sakti, Dhatv-artha, Tin-artha, Ladesa, etc. is concerned, Nagesa has almost followed the line of Koundabhatta.”

On behalf of Grammarians, Nagesa Bhatta says the poetical theorists’ function called Suggestiveness must be acknowledged. But that does not invalidate Sphota-vada in any way.

Bhartrhari is not at fault for expounding the tripartition, because it is mentioned in the scriptures:
