In fact, things are more complex than they seem. In the Brahmanic tradition, which Bhartrhari refers to, there are traces of both a quadripartite system (cf. the famous passage from the Rgveda catvari vakparimita padani... and catvari srnga..., already quoted by the Nirukta (Parisista, XIII.7 and 9 respectively), and a tripartite one (cf. tisro vacas. in the

Rgveda; ghosim, jata-nirghosa, nirghosa/aghosa in the Mahabharata ).

Gaurinath Sastn remarks:

It is, however, surprising that though Punyaraja seems to differ from Bhartrhari in regarding Pasyanti as a manifestation of the Eternal Verbum and not as the Eternal Verbum itself, he does not make any comment either by way of elucidation or dissent on the scheme of manifestation of the Eternal Verbum as conceived by Bhartrhari. This warrants us in drawing the conclusion that there arose a difference of opinion in the school of the grammarian in later years

Dr. Subrahmnia Iyer adds:

It is quite possible that Bhartrhari may have intended to convey some correspondence of the three Kandas of the Vakya-padiya, dealing respectively with the Sabdatattva, Vakya, and Pada, to the three stages through which Vak passes, namely, pasyanti, madhyama and vaikhari. Helaraja definitely associates the third Kanda with the Vaikhari or trtiya vag-avastha.

Perhaps this explains why Dhvany-aloka consists of four chapters.

Further, Somananda says Bhartrhari is wrong because unreal words cannot possibly give rise to Sphota, which is real: sphotasyasatya- rupair hi padadyair vyangyata katham \| pasyantyah satya-rupaya asatyair vyangyata na ca \|\| (Siva-drsti 2.60). The debate regarding the reality of the phonemes is like the argument over whether a coin is made of the heads side or the tails side. It is made of both. During a recitation of Vedic sound by a proper speaker, the sound gradually becomes infused with transcendental potency. For instance, the Prana phase of Vedic sound, also called Para Vac, is imbued with material Prana and transcendental Prana, according to Visvanatha Cakravarti: prakrtaprakrta-prana-mayasya. In a proper recitation of the Vedas, the phonemes gradually become imbued with transcendental energy (Bhagavatam 11.12.18).

Nagesa Bhatta does not use the term “unreal”. He simply quotes Bhartrhari:

*pade na varna vidyante varnesv avayava na ca \|*  
*vakyatpadanam atyantam pravibhago na kascana \|\|*

**“Just as the letters themselves do not give the meaning of the word and just as the parts of a phoneme taken separately do not constitute the phoneme, so there is no use in analyzing the words separately from the sentence.” (Vakya-padiya 1.74)**

Kumarila Bhatta expresses the same basic idea: “The phonemes and the words are only means in achieving the sense of the sentence, like the flames of pieces of wood only serve to give heat.”

Moreover, Somananda, Utpala, Helaraja—Abhinavagupta’s teacher of Vakya-padiya—and others wrongly pointed out characteristic tenets of Advaita-vedanta in Bhartrhari’s philosophy. Dr. Gaurinath Sastn explains:

The third theory, which regards time as a divinity, differs from the second only in affiliating the time-force to the Absolute Brahman instead of the individual subject. \[...\]

According to the commentator the third theory is the theory of Bhartrhari. \[.\]

We have seen that in the transcendental plane the Eternal Verbum and Kala-sakti should be viewed as an uncompromising unity, that is, as one and the same principle, which differentiates itself into two aspects on the eve of creation. We have also seen that besides this Kala-sakti which is described as the Eternal Power of the Eternal Verbum, there lie in that plane innumerable other Powers, all belonging to the Eternal Verbum but mutally exclusive, and yet each of them identical with the Eternal Verbum in the same way as Kala-sakti is. It has been shown that the plurality of the Powers does not affect or contradict the unitary character of the Sternal Verbum in spite of the fact that they are held to be eternal and identical in essence with the Eternal Verbum. It should be carefully noted that at the pre-cosmic stage the Powers remain indistinguishable from the Eternal Verbum. \[...\] It will be our endeavour to study what exactly is meant by the grammarian when he asserts that the Eternal Verbum is the material cause of the phenomenal world. Does the grammarian mean that the Eternal Verbum transforms itself into the phenomenal world or dees he suggest that the Eternal Verbum is the changeless background to the stupendous panorama of the phenomenal world

The doctrines of real change (parinama) and appearance (vivarta) may be studied together. According to the former a cause undergoes a change and we have an effect. An effect, therefore, may be looked upon as subsisting in a subtler form in its cause. According to the latter, however, a cause does not undergo any change and yet we seem to cognize its effect. \[.\] It is contended by the exponents of the doctrine of parinama that like curd coming out of milk the world comes out of the Ultimate Principle and is as much real as the material cause of it. The most celebrated exponents of the doctrine ofparinama are the Sankhyaites according to whom the material cause of the world is Primordial Matter (Prakrti). It may be noted as well that the Yoga school of Patanjali, the Pasupatas, the Madhvas, the school of Nimbarka and the Vaisnava school of Bengal, all accept the view that Prakrti is transformed into the phenomenal world and thus subscribe to the doctrine of parinama. Similarly, Bhatta Bhaskara,the Pancaratra sects and others who declare that the Brahman changes into the material world, believe in the doctrime of parinama. Ramanuja, Snkantha, Bhaskara Raya and others who opine that the Brahman as determined by Prakrti is the material cause of the world, are also adherents to the doctrine of parinama.

The most outstanding exponent of the doctrine of vivarta is Sankara, according to whom the stupendous appearance of the phenomenal world is founded on the reality of the Brahman. \[•••\]

According to the Trika writers of Kashmir the universe is neither a parinama nor a vivarta of the Supreme Reality. In their opinion Consciousness (Caitanya) is the only reality and is all-embracing and all that we experience lies within it. Thus what is popularly called external is held to be a reflexion on Consciousness as on a mirror. The universe is an image within Consciousness. The manifestation of the universe is due to the unrestricted and spontaneous freedom of Consciousness and is a process of reflexion (abhasa). \[...\]

Patanjali, the author of the Vyakarana-mahabhasya, is of opinion that word is nothing but internal consciousness. He suggests that internal consciousness exists in the form of subtle speech and when it becomes manifest, it takes the form of word. Needless to say, Bhartrhari upholds the theory of Patanjali and seeks to explain its underlying implications.

Dr. Mithilesh Caturvedi observes: “Kaiyata says in his commentary on the Mahabhasya that he could cross the ocean of the Bhasya only with the help of the bridge constructed by Bhartrhari. Vitthala places him at the top of those who could reveal the secret of the Mahabhasya.” Caitanya Mahaprabhu’s explanation that all verbal roots are energies of Lord Krishna (Caitanya-bhagavata, madhya-khanda 1) is sourced in Vakya-padiya. Dr. Subrahmania Iyer remarks:

The main ideas of Bhartrhari regarding Brahman, the ultimate Reality, are given in the first four Karikas of Kanda I. There are many other Karikas where the main ideas are supplemented or elaborated. In fact, one can say that right through the Vakya- padiya, Bhartrhari has this ultimate reality at the back of his mind, even when he is dealing with what appear to be purely linguistic or grammatical topics. It runs like a thread right through his work and gives it a kind of unity. When he is speaking about jati or dravya, sadhana or kriya, dik or kala, he somehow connects it all with Brahman.

Gaurinath Sastn continues:

Let us now turn to the doctrines of change (parinama) and appearance (vivarta) to see how far the theory on which the grammarian bases his philosophy is in agreement with either of them. It is worthy of notice that Bhattoji-diksita in his Sabda-kaustubha writes that Bhartrhari, while dealing with the nature of word, has incidentally discussed the illusory creation of the objective world and kindred topics, and that this may very well be likened to the finding of a precious gem in course of a quest after an insignificant cowrie. \[...\]

Evidently, therefore, the philosophical system of the grammarian, in the opinion of Madhavacarya \[Vidyaranya\], is based on the doctrine of vivarta. \[.\] On the other hand, there is evidence to prove that as early as the time of Vacaspati, Jayanta-bhatta and Santaraksita there were at least two different schools of the philosophy of Sabda-brahman, one explaining it in the light of the doctrine of real change and another basing it on the doctrine of illusory appearance. Thus we find Vacaspati

Introduction, p.1. observing in the Nyaya-kanika that the philosophy of Sabda- brahman has been interpreted by exponents of the two schools of parinama and vivarta in their own ways. Jayanta-bhatta represents the grammarian’s philosophy as based on the doctrine of vivarta but is cautious enough to point out that there might be schools of thought which would interpret it from the viewpoint of the doctrine of parinama. Santaraksita again informs us through his Tattva-samgraha that a twofold interpretation of the philosophy of Sabda-brahman may be attempted. \[...\]

It appears to us, therefore, that Bhartrhari was not familiar with the difference in the connotations of the two terms which is so usual in later philosophical literature. That the term vivarta was used to convey an import which is expressed by the term parinama can be gathered even from the writings of Sankara himself who has used the term vivarta to explain the Sankhya view of the evolution of the universe. We therefore, conjecture that the term vivarta came to gather its peculiar sense of formal transformation or apparent self alienation in the writings of teachers of the Monistic Vedanta who came after Bhartrhari, and it is, therefore, nothing unusual that Bhartrhari’s position is sought to be explained in the light of either of the two doctrines of parinama and vivarta. With Bhartrhari there is no question of any marked distinction in the connotations of the terms parinama and vivarta. \[.\]

Both Punyaraja and Helaraja appear to explain the view of Bhartrhari from the standpoint of Absolute Monism as advocated by Sankara. Punyaraja identifies the Kala-sakti of the grammarian with the avidya in the system of Sankara \[.\]. Helaraja, however, has the courage of conviction to describe in unambiguous language the view of Bhartrhari in the light of Sankara’s Absolute Monism. \[.\] Though Bhartrhari has not a word to suggest that he recognizes avidya as a power of the

Eternal Verbum, Helaraja speaks not only avidya but also of avidya-sakti \[...\].

Somananda-natha in his Sivadrsti has surveyed the doctrine of Verbal Monism of the grammarian and criticized it in order to establish his own theory which, though a form of Monistic Idealism, yet accords to the phenomenal world a status of reality. According to him the grammarian regards Pasyanti as the Ultimate Reality in his system of philosophy beyond which there is nothing that enjoys a status superior to or higher than it. The grammarian describes Pasyanti as the transcendental consciousness in which the distinction between word and import, the knower and the knowable, vanishes and the diversity of objective realities does not appear. Somananda- natha, however, does not agree with the grammarian in thinking that this is the highest transcendental state which should be looked upon as the Ultimate Reality. He points out that Pasyanti is regarded as the immediate prius of madhyama in which temporal order and sequence (krama) manifests itself. In accordance with the law of homogeneity of cause and effect Pasyanti also should be supposed to be endowed with the latent power of embodying sequence, otherwise the sequential order in madhyama would be unaccountable. This obviously negates the claim of Pasyanti to be ranked as the Ultimate Reality, which is ex hypothesi, not compatible with the slightest trace of sequence —spatial or temporal. \[.\] Pasyanti owes its name to the fact that it surveys (^ drs) the entire universe in all its phases. \[.\]

Somananda-natha definitely says that in the opinion of the grammarian the transformations of Pasyanti into the objects of the world are all illusory and not real transformations.

It is, therefore, interesting to note that a celebrated teacher of Saivagama like Somananda-natha, who is held in high esteem by Abhinavagupta and others and whose authority is beyond question, does not interpret the doctrine of Bhartrhari in the light of the teachings of his own school. According to Utpaladeva, the author of the gloss on the Sivadrsti and worthy disciple of Somananda-natha, Bhartrhari is a champion of Verbal Monism according to which the universe is an illusory appearance. He represents Bhartrhari as upholding the view that the world-process proceeds as a result of the operation of avidya, which is neither real nor unreal (anirvacya) and hence does not present an opposing reality.

Somananda-natha flourished in the latter part of the 9th century A.D. Utpaladeva, who came immediately after Somananda- natha, his teacher, was in all probability well acquainted with the doctrine of vivarta as advocated by Sankara. It is not therefore in the least surprising that Utpaladeva and his teacher, too, would elucidate the grammarian’s philosophy in the manner of Sankara’s idealism which was current at that time. \[...\]

But we should not fail to point out that however much the later stalwarts might have tried to read Bhartrhari’s philosophical outlook in the light of their own favourite doctrines, it is extremely difficult to explain from their points of view some of the fundamental features of the grammarian’s philosophy. Thus if the philosophy of Bhartrhari is interpreted in the light of the doctrine of vivarta as sponsored by Sankara, the status accorded to Kala-sakti or, for the matter of that, to all other Powers (Kalas) cannot be explained with fidelity to Bhartrhari. That the Kala-sakti is ultimately real and has the same ontological status as the Eternal Verbum does not seem to admit of doubt. But Sankara would never accept the ultimate reality of any power (sakti) co-existing with the Absolute.

Dr. Subrahmnia Iyer comments:

It is with the help of this power called Kala that the Almighty creates the Cosmos in a particular order which is so vital to it, since without it there would only be confusion. Because of this, the Almighty himself gets the name of Kala, says Bhartrhari. As he puts it:

*jala-yantra-samavesa-sadrsibhih pravrttibhih \|*  
*sa kalah kalayan sarvah kalakhyam labhate vibhuh \|\|*  
*(VP III.9.14)*

\[...\] I have said nothing so far about Avidya-sakti. Bhartrhari does connect Kala with Avidya. He says that the first thing which happens in the state ofAvidya is the appearance of Kala:

*sakiy-aima-devaia-paksair bhinnam kalasya darsanam \|*  
*prathamam tad avidyayam yad vidyayam na vidyate \|\|*  
*(VP III.9.62)*

In the state of Vidya, that is, in Brahman, there is no place for Kala.

The above verse simply says that the differentiated perception of Time only occurs when Existence is in the state of Avidya. Gaurinath Sastn resumes:

Let us draw this chapter to a close by venturing a bold suggestion that Bhartrhari’s philosophy may be explained in the light of the doctrine of reflexion (abhasa) as sponsored by the Trika writers of Kashmir. We can cite a passage from the Vakya-padiya where Bhartrhari seems to entertain the view that the difference between the Eternal Verbum and the world is only a fiction conjured into existence by the operation of the Power lying in the Eternal Verbum—Bhartrhari does not clearly assert that the world also is an illusion. If the reality of the world is conceded by Bhartrhari and if again the identity of the world with Eternal Verbum is also maintained by him, we may be justified in hinting that Bhartrhari is the precursor of the doctrine of reflexion held by Trika writers. Further, the nature and character of the Eternal Verbum, the Kala-sakti and the multiple Kalas and their mutual relationship find a parallel in the concepts of Paramesvara, Vimarsa, and the different Saktis of the Trika system. The Trika system again is strictly monistic and concedes the reality of the world which is one with Paramesvara, the difference between the two appearing only to the ignorant. It may not be out of place to mention in this connexion that the high esteem and admiration in which Bhartrhari is held by all Trika writers also suggest the possibility that the Trika system of Indian philosophy owes an enormous debt to the writings of Bhartrhari.

Bhartrhari called the Vedantic monists by the name Trayy-anta- vedins. In doing so, he indicated that he did not believe that the universe is real in the highest sense: yatra drasta ca drsyam ca darsanam cavikalpitam, tasyaivarthasya satyatvam sritas trayy- anta-vedinah (Vakya-padiya 3.3.72). But he said the \[real\] Sakti of his Brahma is present in the world; Dr. Subrahmanyam translates and comments upon the verse cited by Gaurinath Sastn:

*118. sabdesv evasrita saktir visvasyasya nibandhani yannetrah pratibhatmayam bheda-rupah pratiyate*

Sum: The power which is based on Sabdas is the cause of (all transactions) in this universe. The universe which has a single intuition (pratibha) as its soul is perceived as manifold through the Sabda as the eye.

Com: Sabda is thc sole cause of the gamut of transactions across the globe. The entire world is in the form of Sabda and Artha, i.e. not different from the Sabda and the Artha, denoted by it. At this stage Vaiyakaranas believe that the so called Sakti (capacity) is nothing but the relation of expressive and expressed (or Vacya-Vacaka) between a Sabda and Artha. The entire transaction in the world is based on this relation. Sabda is the substratum of the transaction.

Notes: Pratibha is a unique type of intelligence. Its other form is the Vakyartha (verbal meaning). \[...\] In the outer world, the same thing is treated/understood/perceived differently by people. The same lady is considered by a lustful man as a thing of enjoyment, tiger etc. as something edible, parents as a daughter, her children as a mother and those who renounced the world as a dead body. The cause for such different considerations is the ‘Samskara’ (refinement) in their mind. Sabda is the very cause of all this.

Thus the essence of sphota is a flash of insight (pratibha). And that arises due to the specific subconscious impression (samskara, or vasana). The same is said about Suggestiveness: mukhyartha-badha-nirapeksa-bodha-janako mukhyartha- sambaddhasambaddha-sadharanah prasiddhaprasiddhartha- visayako vaktr-adi-vaisistya-jnana-pratibhady-udbuddhah samskara-viseso vyanjana (Parama-laghu-manjusa). Intuition often comes from the inner Soul (Paramatma):

Pratibha includes intelligence of a very high order, intuitive knowledge, the instinct of animals and birds, and even the spontaneous activities of newly born babies. This kind of knowledge is far more reliable. It comes from within. While speaking about it, Punyaraja reminds us of Kalidasa’s statement that, when in doubt, cultured people rely on the voice of their own conscience. It was an inner pratibha that told Dusyanta that Sakuntala was fit to be married to a Ksatriya.

The knowledge that one’s conscience gives is pratibha ; and everybody accepts it as authority. This pratibha arises in us in many ways. Among them, Bhartrhari recognizes six causes, and therefore six kinds of Intuition.

Ultimately, Sphota is Sabda in the highest sense (omkara, or sabda- brahma). In any other explanation of sphota, the term sphota denotes an archaic archetype upon which all types of meanings are built.

Moreover, in a strategic shift of opinion, Utpala adopted some of Bhartrhari’s views. Dr. Torella elucidates:

Somananda attacks it precisely because this is theoretically too close to the new Saiva darsana that he has set out to build. This could explain the total lack of fair play in his attitude to Bhartrhari, which resembles the fiery fightings between insiders rather than the cold and dismissal of a full outsider. By “total lack of fair play” I refer both to the unnecessary sarcastic remarks and the punctilious pointing out of seeming contradictions in terminology, which show a Somananda deliberately unwilling to catch the gist of Bhartrhari’s conception and expound it by doing justice to its boldness and originality. Somananda does not show any interest, not even a negatively critical one, in Bhartrhari, the epistemologist and grammarian, but only in his metaphysics of sabda-brahman.

Generally speaking, we know very little of what happened in the atelier of Indian philosophers, owing to the total lack of personal notes left by them, not to speak of “working” journals. For example, we know nothing of the inner developments which made Sankarananda abandon Saivism and embrace Buddhism (or viceversa), or of the possible intellectual wanderings of a Mandana Misra between Purva and Uttara Mimamsa. Apparently less dramatic but at least equally puzzling was the change of attitude of the Pratyabhijna school towards Bhartrhari, which took place very quickly in the span of only one generation and caused a difference between Somananda and Utpaladeva, the recognized founder of the Pratyabhijna and its systemizer, respectively, closely bound to each other by a direct guru-sisya relationship.

Two radically different world-views are at stake here: the depersonalized universe of the Buddhists, made of discrete and discontinuous realities tentatively connected in the ultimately unreal net of vyavahara — unreal insofar as it is the product of a “secondary” conceptual thought —, and the absolutely unitary universe of the Saivas, identified with and penetrated by a supreme Person, Siva, who runs through it like a golden thread unifying all the seeming multiplicity and dynamically transforming the apparently other into himself and himself into the other. Closely connected with Utpaladeva’s choice of establishing the Buddhists as the main opponents is his adoption of Bhartrhari as the main ally. At this point some questions may be asked: why Bhartrhari? and again: can he really be “used” against the Buddhists

What Utpala needed was a shared, if controversial, strong “philosophical” argument. The omnipervasiveness of language is an epistemological version of the omnipervasiveness of Siva, and at the same time calls for the integration into the spiritually dynamic Saiva universe. \[...\] The supreme Consciousness is the supreme Word, Pasyanti becomes a power of the supreme Lord. In this way, the formerly despised Bhartrhari is raised to the core itself of the Pratyabhijna. Did Utpaladeva accept the whole of Bhartrhari’s doctrine? I should say not. He accepted just what matched his own well-gauged requirements. Other very significant aspects of Bhartrhari’s thought are instead rejected, like the theory of sphota. Apparently, Utpaladeva did not propose his own answer to the crucial question “what is the meaning-bearer?”

## The Evolution of the Dhvani Theory

The Dhvani theory was reiterated by Mammata, who was followed by Visvanatha Kaviraja, Kavi Karnapura, Pandita-raja Jagannatha and other greats:

The labours, therefore, of all later writers, typified by Mammata, consisted generally in working out the details of the Dhvani theory and the scheme of Poetics standardised on its basis; and they spent all their fine scholastic powers in refining and explaining, but hardly in adding anything of abiding interest. No other work on Sanskrit Poetics has indeed exerted so much influence as the Dhvany-aloka, which brought to a focus the tentative efforts of earlier thinkers, and by its thoroughness and masterly exposition eclipsed all its predecessors, dominating, as it did, thoughts of generations of theorists even down to the present time.

However, there are major inconsistencies in the Dhvani theory propounded by the Dhvanikara. Even Anandavardhana’s expla­nations required modifications by Abhinavagupta and by Mammata:

Firstly, the Dhvanikara merely introduced the concept of Sugges­tiveness, in the form of tatparya. Anandavardhana, Abhinavagupta, and Mammata each changed the previous theorist’s methodology.

Secondly, the Dhvanikara often used the term rasa-adi. Depending on the context, this means either “rasadi-dhvani” (rasa, bhava, etc.) or “rasadi-dhvani, vastu-dhvani (implied idea), and alankara-dhvani (implied ornament).” The ambiguity was noted by Visvanatha Kaviraja: yat tu dhvani-karenoktam, kavyasyatma dhvanih iti tat kim vastv-alankara-rasadi-laksanas tri-rupo dhvanih kavyasyatma, uta rasadi-rupa-matro va. nadyah prehalikadav ativyapteh. dvitlyas ced om iti brumah, “The Dhvanikara says: “The soul of poetry is a dhvani” (Dhvany-aloka 1.1). Does he mean to say that dhvani, the soul of poetry, is either an implied idea, an implied ornament or a rasa-adi, or that dhvani, the soul of poetry, is only a rasa-adi ? The first option is incongruent, because there would be the overinclusion ofprahelika (conundrum, which involves an implied idea). If the second option is meant, then we say: Agreed.” (Sahitya-darpana 1.2)

Dr. Kane writes: “There is no single karika which expressly divides dhvani into vastu, alankara and rasadi.” (Kane (1998) p. 169). Anandavardhana was the first to clearly establish the theory that a dhvani can take the form of an implied idea or of an implied ornament: vastu-matram alankara-rasadayas ca (1.4 vrtti).

Thirdly, in Dhvany-aloka the methodology of slesa is convoluted. Abhinava says slesa is always implied: slesas ca nabhidha- vrtter aksiptah, api tv artha-saundarya-balad eveti sarvatha dhvanyamana eva slesah. (Locana 2.27). But Ananda says slesa can be literal (vacyena slesena, 2.21) (in what Mammata calls Udbhata’s slesabhasa, ref. Sahitya-kaumudl 10.133). If the double meaning is more excellent than the literal meaning in point of astonishment, it is called dhvani (specifically sabda-sakty-udbhava vastu-dhvani), not slesa. Moreover, a double meaning is deemed literal if the speaker reveals it. Ananda gives this example:

*vatse ma ga visadam svasanam uru-javam santyajordhva-pravrttam*  
*kampah ko va gurus te bhavatu bala-bhida jrmbhitenatra yahi \|*  
*pratyakhyanam suranam iti bhaya-samana-cchadmana karayitva*  
*yasmai laksmlm adad vah sa dahatu duritam mantha-mudham payodhih \|\|*

vatse—O child; ma—do not; gah—get (or go); visadam—despon­dency (or visa-adam—to the eater of poison); svasanam—sigh (or wind, Vayu); uru-javam—great speed (i.e. great trembling) (or Vayu, whose speed is great); santyaja—completely give up; urdhva-pravrttam—subsequent engagements (or Agni, whose usage goes upward); kampah—trembling (or kam-pah—Varuna, the protector of water); kah—what?; va—at all (or indeed); guruh— great (or spiritual master); te—of yours; bhavatu—there should be; bala-bhida— \[a yawn,\] which is a kind of power (or by Indra, the breaker of armies); jrmbhitena—with a yawn (or Indra, who is enlarged, i.e. puffed up); atra—here (or now); yahi—you should go on; pratyakhyanam—the respective naming; suranam—of gods; iti—in this way; bhaya—fear; samana—of appeasing; chadmana— with the pretext; karayitva—after making; yasmai—to whom; laksmlm—Laksmi; adat—it gave; vah—of all of you; sah—He; dahatu—may He burn; duritam—the dangers (evil) (“it goes (ita) in a bad way (dur)”); mantha—after the churning; mudham—she who was perplexed; payodhih—the ocean.

**“Child, do not be despondent. Completely give up your sighs, great shudder and subsequent preoccupations. Why should you have a great tremor at all? Go with a yawn here: It is a kind of power.” (Alternatively: “Child, do not go to Siva, a consumer of poison, nor to Vayu, who has great speed, nor to Agni, who goes high when used. You should have either Varuna, the master of water, or Brahma as a guru. You should go your own way, and so should Indra, who is puffed up.”) LaksmT was perplexed after the churning. May He to whom she was given by the Milk Ocean after it occasioned the names of gods under the pretext of alleviating her fear burn away your evil tendencies. (2.23)**

Here the second meaning is implied because it is not meant to be evident, inasmuch as the ocean was speaking in front of the gods, and so it is a dhvani. But because the poet revealed the implied double meaning, in the methodology of Dhvany-aloka it is classed as the slesa ornament: api tu slesalankara ity arthah (Locana 2.23). Visvanatha Kaviraja, however, would only say that the poetry is downgraded from first-rate to second-rate: yatra ca sabdantaradina gopana-krta-carutvasya viparyasah, “Second- rate poetry also occurs when the literary beauty constructed by a concealment is marred by another word” (Sahitya-darpana 4.14). Visvanatha follows Mammata’s methodology: A double meaning is called slesa when both meanings are literally applicable, and is called dhvani when one of the meanings is implied since it is not literally applicable in the context. Thus a slesa is always an expressed ornament and is only in the sphere of Denotation, by the maxim artha-bhedena sabda-bhedah, “There is a difference of words because of a difference in meaning” (Kavya-prakasa 9.84). Mammata, like Ananda, agrees with Sabara Svami that abhidha (Denotation) can only be used one time, but adds that in a literal pun each meaning has its own word (whereas Ananda thought that a paronomastic word consists of one word that has two meanings): A paronomastic word consists of two words that sound the same and that have united (hence the term slesa, ‘embrace’), and so no meaning is implied, since abhidha is used once for each word.

Still, Ananda went where no theorist had gone before and has gone since, by propounding the over-the-top concept of slesa-dhvani (implying a pun). His example is a verse by the master poet Magha:

*ramya iti praptavatlh pataka*  
*ragam vivikta iti vardhayantlh \|*  
*yasyam asevanta namad-vallkah*  
*samam vadhubhir valabhlr yuvanah \|\|*

**In that city the young men, accompanied by their brides, made use of the upper rooms. Those rooms were topnotch because they were charming and aroused love because they were isolated. And above them the thatch was stooping. (Sisupala-vadha 3.53)**

The implied pun is that the first half of the verse (the second sentence) could also modify the women if the word vadhubhih (with the brides) were in the same case ending as valabhlh (upper rooms of houses), because a simile between the women and the upper rooms is implied given that samam, a synonym of saha (with), can be punningly taken as an adverb (“in the same way”).

Fourthly, the Dhvanikara, Anandavardhana, Abhinavagupta and other ancients included Indication within Denotation. Mammata said that Indication is a completely separate function, in conformity with another statement of Anandavardhana: tad evam sabde vyavahare trayah prakarah—vacakatvam guna-vrttir vyanjakatvam ca (3.33 vrtti).

In that regard, Ananda’s terms for subcategories of Indication are peculiar: guna-vrttis tupacarena laksanaya cobhayasrayapi bhavati, “Guna-vrtti takes place either by upacara (metaphorical usage), by laksana (figurative usage), or by both” (3.33 vrtti). He used the term bhakti in the sense of upacara: upacara-matram tu bhaktih (1.14 vrtti). Mammata equated guna-vrtti with upacara— guna-vrttya upacarena (Kavya-prakasa 8.71 vrtti)—and turned it into a subcategory of laksana (Indication). Visvanatha coined the term gaunt (qualitative figurative usage): iyam ca guna-yogad gaumty ucyate. purva tupacaramisranac chuddha (Sahitya- darpana 2.10). Ananda greatly expounded upon guna-vrtti. Thus Dhvany-aloka is the first poetical treatise which includes a dissertation on the rhetorical functions. However, it is not systematic and is spread throughout the chapters.

Fifthly, Abhinava distinguished conventional figurative usage from purposeful figurative usage as follows: Only the latter has these three essential characteristics:

1\. The main meaning does not make sense,

2\. The indirect sense has some degree of connection with the main meaning, and

3\. There is an implied sense.

Following Mukula, Mammata said Indication, whether conventional or purposeful, has the first two characteristics, and reiterated that purposeful figurative usage is characterized by an implied sense (Kavya-prakasa 2.9).

Sixthly, the Dhvanikara, Ananda and Abhinava used the term vrtti for mukhya-vrtti (Dhvany-aloka 1.17) (a synonym of abhidha- vrtti) and guna-vrtti, but only used the term vyapara for the other functions. Mammata, however, used the term vrtti to denote the alliterations propounded by Udbhata, and used the term vyapara in the context of abhidha and so on.

Anandavardhana used the term vyanjakatvam. Abhinava inven­ted the term vyanjana (Suggestiveness). Visvanatha Kaviraja popularized the usage of the terms laksana-vrtti, tatparya-vrtti, and vyanjana-vrtti. Kavi Kamapura followed suit: vrtti-trayam tu, abhidha, laksana, vyanjaneti (Alankara-kaustubha 2.13).

Seventhly, Mammata used the terms abhidha-mula-dhvani (implied meaning founded on Denotation) and laksana-mUla-dhvani (implied meaning founded on Indication) instead of vivaksitanya- para-vacya-dhvani and avivaksita-vacya-dhvani. Kavi Kamapura used Mammata’s terms.

Eighthly, Mammata created the eight varieties of second-rate poetry based on the guidelines and examples in Dhvany-aloka. However, in Dhvany-aloka, meanings are divided in two categories: vacya (expressed) andpratiyamana (implied) (Dhvany-aloka 1.2). And an implied meaning has two subcategories: sphuta (clear) and asphuta (unclear): A sphuta implied meaning is either first-rate or second-rate. An asphuta implied meaning relates to third-rate poetry, where an implied sense might exist but is negligible. Mammata made an adjustment: A first-rate implied meaning is gudha (subtle) (in the category of laksana-mula), whereas agudha (Kavi Kamapura calls it sphuta) is a variety of a second- rate implied sense, and so is asphuta (hard to catch): agudham aparasyangam vacya-siddhy-angam asphutam (Kavya-prakasa 5.45). Still, Mammata said third-rate poetry is characterized by an implied sense which does not clearly stand out (asphuta): citram ifi gunalankara-yukfam. avyangyam ifi sphuta-prafiyamanarfha- rahitam (Kavya-prakasa 1.5).

Ninthly, Mammata expanded the list of suggestive specialties (vaisistya) (on the topic of arthi vyanjana) started by the Dhvani- kara, who mentioned avastha (condition, state of mind), desa (place), and kala (time).

*ahinaa-paoa-rasiesu pahia-samahaiesu diahesu \|*  
*sohai pasaria-gianam ninciam mora-vandanam \|\|  (Prakrit language)*

*abhinava-payodhara-rasitesu pathika-syamayitesu divasesu \|*  
*sobhate prasarita-grivanam nrttam mayura-vrndanam \|\|*

*abhinaya-prayoga-rasikesu pathika-samajikesu divasesu \|*  
*sobhate prasarita-grivanam nrttam mayura-vrndanam \|\| (double Sanskrit rendering)*

**The dance of the peacocks whose necks are outstretched is resplendent on the days when new rainclouds rumble. Those days appear gloomy (syamayitesu) to the travelers (in separation from their wives).**

**Alternatively: The dance of the peacocks whose necks are outstretched is resplendent on the days when the travelers, the spectators (samajikesu), are connoisseurs of theatrical repre­sentation. (3.43)**

Anandavardhana shows the verse to illustrate a combination of a dhvani (the second meaning of the verse) with both a simile (in syamayitesu, lit. “The days act like dark things”) and a metaphor (the travelers are spectators).

Alternatively, the verse illustrates the ornament of sound called bhasa-slesa (a Prakrit verse has a dual sense in Sanskrit), invented by Rudrata.

Moreover, in Dhvany-aloka, there are only eight kinds of artha- sakti-bhu dhvani (implied sense arisen by a word that can be changed without affecting implied sense). Mammata’s twelve kinds are essentially the same as those eight, but Pandita-raja Jagannatha followed Anandavardhana by only accepting eight kinds, saying that kavi-kalpita-vaktr-praudhokti-siddha (implied sense effected from a bold assertion of a speaker invented by the poet) is included in kavi-praudhokti-siddha (implied sense effected from a bold assertion of the poet).

## Miscellaneous Topics

In the second and third chapters, the Dhvanikara and Anandavardhana expound the manifold subdivisions of poetical categories in the Dhvani theory. The second chapter also features a disquisition on the gunas. In the third chapter is a lenghty discussion on the appropriateness of sounds and meanings with regard to the rasas. In addition, the three categories of poetry are defined. The fourth chapter mostly contains a technical discussion on creative intelligence and other considerations related to poets.

Ananda gave a list of mutually noncontradictory rasas, and another of mutually contradictory ones among which santa and raudra as well as santa and srngara are stated (3.18-19; 3.23). He says there is no contradictoriness between inherently contradictory rasas if one is primordial (angi) and the other secondary (anga) (3.24).

Mammata followed Dhvany-aloka. The details of modern Sanskrit poetics are in the present writer’s translation of Baladeva Vidyabhusana’s Sahitya-kaumudi, a remake of Kavya-prakasa.

All in all, the Dhvanikara propounded the Dhvani theory to provide a foundation for stating that the purport of a literary text should be rasa. In this way he took the Mimamsakas’ methodology one step further: According to them, the purport of the Vedas is dharma. That is, one should perform one’s duty: athato dharma-jijnasa, “Now, therefore, let us examine dharma” (Purva-mimamsa-sutra 1.1.1). Anandavardhana went further still: He not only acknowledged santa as a rasa, he stated that the purport of Mahabharata is santa because at the end of the narration of the Kuruksetra War, total dispassion is evoked in the readers, and this leads to santa, which is superior to all other rasas because, he says, liberation is the means to achieve God. One should feel God and should not be passionate about the material world: tasmat tasminn eva paramesvare bhagavati bhavata bhavita-cetasah, ma bhuta vibhutisu nihsarasu raginah (4.5 vrtti). Ananda did not clearly mention the sthayi of santa, but specified that the characteristic of santa-rasa is that it fosters a happiness which is the cause of the cessation of material desires: santas ca trsna-ksaya-sukhasya yah pariposas tal-laksano rasah pratiyata eva (3.26 vrtti). According to Abhinavagupta, this means Ananda says the sthayi of santa-rasa is trsna-ksaya (cessation of material desire), which Abhinava equates with nirveda (dispassion). Like Abhinavagupta, Mammata listed santa as the ninth rasa and said its sthayi is nirveda: nirveda-sthayi-bhavo ’sti Santo ’pi navamo rasah (Kavya-prakasa 4.35). Following Bharata Muni, Mammata also listed nirveda among the vyabhicari-bhavas (Kavya-prakasa 4.31). Thus Anandavardhana is the grandfather of modern poetics. He says he is the author of this verse:

*ya vyaparavati rasan rasayitum kacit kavinam nava*  
*drstir ya parinisthitartha-visayonmesa ca vaipasciti \|*  
*te dve apy avalambya visvam anisam nirvarnayanto vayam*  
*sranta naiva ca labdham abdhi-sayana tvad-bhakti-tulyam sukham \|\|*

**O You who repose on an ocean, to render the rasas relishable we are constantly depicting the world by making use of these two: Some new vision of poets which is endowed with literary functions, and a clever outlook due to which readers widen their eyes regarding meanings that are quite perfect. Yet we are tired. A happiness equal to devotional service to You was not achieved. (3.44)**

## 11. Bhatta Nayaka

Bhatta Nayaka belongs to the Rasa school. He was the first poetical rhetorician to criticize the Dhvani theory. He expounded his own version of the Dhvani theory, but his treatise is lost. Mammata cited Bhatta Nayaka’s views along with those of Lollata, Sankuka and Abhinavagupta on Bharata Muni’s rasa-sutra and thus immortalized him. Bhatta Nayaka was a pandit in the court of Avantivarman, the king who succeeded Anandavardhana’s patron. Dr. De writes: “...Bhatta Nayaka who is mentioned by Kahlana (5.159) as having flourished in the reign of Samkaravarman, son and successor of Avantivarman of Kashmir.”

Kalhana (also spelt Kahlana), the author of Raja-tarangini, greatly praised Bhatta Nayaka. Dr. Kane notes: “dvijas tayor nayakakhyo gaurisa-sura-sadmanoh \| caturvidyah krtas tena vag-devi-kula- mandiram \|\| (V.59) This refers to the time of Sankaravarman (883­902 A.D.).”

Regarding Bhatta Nayaka’s treatise, Dr. Kane comments:

I have drawn attention to the fact that the work was called Sahrdaya-hrdayaloka by Raghava-bhatta and in some colophons. We have further to notice that in his comment on the very first verse of the Natya-sastra, Abhinavagupta mentions Bhatta-Nayaka and his work called Sahrdaya-darpana. This raises the important question whether Bhatta-nayaka’s work was called Sahrdaya-darpana or Hrdaya-darpana.

\[T\]he Hrdaya-darpana was a work in verse and prose composed for establishing a theory of Poetics and for controverting the position of the Dhvany-aloka.

In his commentary on Kavya-prakasa, Candidasa referred to Bhatta Nayaka’s treatise: “Candidasa mentions a Dhvani-siddhanta- grantha \[written\] by himself. He also quotes a work called Sahitya- hrdaya-darpana, which may be Bhatta Nayaka’s lost Hrdaya- darpana.”

In Locana 1.5, Abhinavagupta twice calls the work “Hrdaya- darpana”. The information about Bhatta Nayaka’s treatise origi­nates from Abhinava’s citations in Locana and in Abhinava- bharati, often for condemnation. Mammata’s discourse on Bhatta

Nayaka’s opinion about rasa is sourced in Abhinava’s commentary on Natya-sastra. This is Bhatta Nayaka’s invocatory verse:

*namas trailokya-nirmana-kavaye sambhave yatah \|*  
*pratiksanam jagan-natya-prayoga-rasiko janah \|\|*

**Let us offer respects to Siva, the kavi expert in the making of the three worlds. Because of him, a person becomes a connoisseur of the usage of theatrical representation on the world stage. (Hrdaya-darpana**

Bhatta Nayaka criticized Anandavardhana’s Dhvani theory for two reasons: Nayaka says Suggestiveness is a function that relates to either the readers or the spectators, not to words. And secondly, he says only rasa-dhvani is the soul of poetry: Neither an implied idea (vastu-dhvani) nor an implied ornament (alankara-dhvani) should be included by the term dhvani in the statement that dhvani is the soul of poetry. Dr. Kane expounds:

The principal point on which he differs from the Dhvany- aloka is that he regards dhvani as transcending definition and as purely sva-samvedya. So he was a follower of those whom the Dhvani-karika says ‘kecid vacam sthitam avisaye tattvam Ucus tadiyam ’ \[1.1\] or as the Dhvany-aloka-vrtti says ‘kecit punar laksana-karana-salina-buddhayo dhvanes tattvam giram agocaram sahrdaya-hrdaya-samvedyam eva samakhyatavantah’. According to him rasa-carvana (or bhoga-krttva) is the soul of poetry and he is not prepared to admit dhvani in general as the soul of poetry. ‘dhvanir namaparo yo pii vyaparo vyanjanatmakah \| tasya siddhe pii bhede syat kavye ’msavaam na rupata \|\|’ (Locana).

The quotations cited above from Bhatta-Nayaka establish that the latter was concerned to show that dhvani means rasa only, that the Dhvani-kara is wrong in postulating vastu-dhvani and alankara-dhvani, that the principle of rasa apprehension cannot be explained in words and that the explanation of such verses as mama dhammia and attha ettha given by the Dhvany- aloka are not correct. Thus the Hrdaya-darpana dealt with rasa and in explaining it had naturally to deal with Bharata’s sutra ‘vibhavanubhava... ’.

Abhinavagupta cunningly remarked that Bhatta Nayaka turned out as a foremost supporter of the Dhvani theory: kim ca vastu- dhvanim dusayata rasa-dhvanis tad-anugrahakah samarthyata iti susthutaram dhvani-dhvamso ’yam. yad aha—krodho ’pi devasya varena tulyah, “Moreover, he favors rasa-dhvani, which implicitly substantiates the concept of vastu-dhvani, even though he denounces vastu-dhvani. This is such a nice demolition of the Dhvani theory! It as if illustrates the saying, “The curse of an angry sage is tantamount to a blessing”” (Locana 1.4). Dr. Triloki- natha Dvivedi notes that Bhatta Nayaka’s and Anandavardhana’s respective viewpoints are not very far apart: bhatta nayaka ka yah siddhanta dhvani-siddhanta se bahut dur nahin hai (Alankara- sarvasva, Triloki-natha Dvivedi (ed.) p. 29).

Moreover, Bhoja’s and Mammata’s definitions of poetry are reminiscent of Bhatta Nayaka’s standpoint: kavye dosabhava- gunalankara-mayatva-laksanena, “\[Rasa is felt by means of the function called bhavakatva (feeling), which,\] in poetry, is characterized by the fact that the poetry has literary qualities and ornaments and is faultless.” In the full citation, Abhinava shows that in Bhatta Nayaka’s methodology, the experience of the enjoyment of rasa is characterized by druti (melting), vistara (expansion), and vikasa (opening). Mammata expanded upon that: He used the term druti to explain the qualitative nature of the rasas of madhurya-guna and the term vistara (vistrti) to explain the qualitative nature of the rasas of ojas guna. Mammata also used the term dipt in reference to ojas. In addition, Pandita-raja Jagannatha equated vikasa with the qualitative nature of prasada- guna: gunanam caisam druti-dipti-vikasakhyas tisras citta- vrttayah kramena prayojyah, tat-tad-guna-visista-rasa-carvana- janya iti yavat, “The three states of mind called druti (melting), dipti (blazing) and vikasa (opening of the mind) are impelled by the respective gunas. This means those mental states are generated from the relishment of the rasa characterized by the corresponding guna (in the mind)” (Rasa-gangadhara, KM p. 54).

Further, Bhatta Nayaka explained the rise of rasa in oneself as a three-step process, which refers to his three functions: Dr. Sushil Kumar De expounds:

This school postulates three different functions of a word, namely abhidha (already admitted by the Mimamsakas and grammarians), bhavakatva and bhojakatva, and thus ascribes to a poem a threefold potency of its own, namely, the powers of denotation, of generalisation and of enjoyment. The abhidha is not merely the actual Denotation of a word, but is given an extended meaning so as to include laksana, or Indication, in its scope, thus embracing the two functions already analysed by previous speculation. It is meant probably that the Denotation (as postulated by Bhatta Nayaka) also gives to the expressed sense a metaphorical significance as the basis of Rasa. The bhavakatva (or rasa-bhavana), which, as Abhinavagupta suggests, is apparently derived from Bharata’s general definition of bhava, is described as the power of generalisation which makes the vibhavas as well as the sthayi- bhava, sensed in their general character without any reference to their specific properties. The vibhava, Sita, for instance, is understood through this power not as a particular individual but in the general character of a woman, and the sthayi-bhava (here Rama’s love towards her) is taken as love in general without any reference to the agent \[Rama\] or the object \[Sita\]. In this way the audience can appropriate the vibhavas, as well as the sthayi-bhava, as universal.

After the Rasa is thus generalised, comes its enjoyment. By the third function of bhojakatva, the sthayin is enjoyed in this general form, accompanied by the vibhavas, sensed also in a general form

Commenting on Kavya-prakasa, Narahari Sarasvati Tirtha elucidates:

*dosabhava-gunalankara-maye kavye catur- vidhabhinaya-rupe natye ca kavya-rupasya sabdasyabhidha bhavana tad-bhogi-krtir iti trayo vyaparah, abhidhanam kartr-vakya-bhuta-sabdarthalankaradi-visayam, bhavakatvam srngaradi-rasadi-visayam, bhojakatvam sahrdaya-visayatvam iti vivekah. \[...\] bhogena bhojakatva-vyaparenanubhava-smrti- vilaksanena.*

**“There are three functions of a word which is the form of poetry, when the poetry has qualities and ornaments and is faultless or when in a drama the four kinds of dramatic gestures are present: abhidha (Denotation), bhavana (feeling), and tad-bhogi-krti (it makes the poetry an enjoyment). The sphere of Denotation is an ornament of sound, and so on, which is a speaker’s sentence; the sphere of bhavakatva (a state of being that engenders feeling) is a rasa-adi; and the sphere of bhojakatva is a connoisseur. \[...\] Rasa is enjoyed by bhoga, the function called bhojakatva (it engenders enjoyment), which is different from an experience of day-to-day life and from a remembrance” (Bala-cittanuranjim 4.28).**

With the assistance of vibhava, anubhava, and vyabhicari-bhava, the second function turns the sihayl into rasa (the sthayi becomes relishable). The third function transforms that rasa into the rasa which is rapture. Experiencing this rapture is the goal sought by readers of poetry and by the spectators of a play. In Abhinava’s and Mammata’s methodology, those two functions are aspects of Suggestiveness. Though it is in the mind, the notion of sadharanya (generalization, and empathy), an aspect of Bhatta Nayaka’s second function expounded in the chapter on Mammata, applies to words when they are used as stimuli of rasa:

*saktir asti vibhavadeh kapi sadharani-krtau \|*  
*pramata tad-abhedena svam yaya pratipadyate \|\|*

**“The vibhavas and so on have some indescribable power to generalize, by means of which the perceivers think of themselves as non-different from a character.” (Bhakti-rasamrta-sindhu 2.5.103)**

When all the factors for making the sthayi-bhava turn into rasa are present, a catalyst, triggered by the reader’s predisposition, has to be accounted for. That is Bhatta Nayaka’s bhavakatva, whose essence is sadharani-karana (generalization, and empathy) (sadharanya).

In his introduction to Alankara-sarvasva, Ruyyaka sourced the origins of the concept of Dhvani in the theories of the ancient rheto­ricians. He mentioned Bhatta Nayaka: bhatta-nayakena tu vyangya- vyaparasya praudhoktyabhyupagatasya kavyamsatvam kathayata nyag-bhavita-sabdartha-svarupasya vyaparasyaiva pradhanyam uktam. tatrapy abhidha-bhavakatva-laksana-vyapara-dvayottirno rasa-carvanatma bhogapara-paryayo vyaparah pradhanyena visranti-sthanatayangi-krtah.

“By stating that the function which reveals an implied sense, a function obtained by the poet’s bold words, is an aspect of the poetry, Bhatta Nayaka stated the predominance of that very function, whose nature is such that it lessens the importance of sound and literal meaning. In addition, the function another synonym of which is bhoga; which is the soul of the relishment of rasa; and which arises after the two functions named abhidha and bhavakatva occur, was acknowledged by him as the most important poetical element in terms of being the place where the mind finds an exalted repose.” (Alankara-sarvasva)

Abhinava explained Bhatta Nayaka’s viewpoint by way of repudiating it:

*ananda iti rasa-carvanatmanah pradhanyam darsayan rasa-dhvaner eva sarvatra mukhya-bhutam atmatvam iti darsayati. tena yad uktam “dhvanir namaparo yo ’pi vyaparo vyanjanatmakah, tasya siddhe ’pi bhede syat kavye ’msavam na rupata” iti tad apahastitam bhavati. tatha hy abhidha-bhavana- rasa-carvanatmake ’pi try-amse kavye rasa-carvana tavaj jivita- bhuteti bhavato ’py avivado ’sti. yathoktam tvayaiva, “kavye rasayita sarvo na boddha na niyoga-bhak” iti tad vastv-alankara- dhvany-abhiprayenamsa-matratvam iti siddha-sadhanam. rasa- dhvany-abhiprayena tu svabhyupagama-prasiddha-samvedana- viruddham iti.*

**“By thus showing that in poetry the most important thing is the rasa, whose nature is a relishment, the Vrtti-kara illustrates that only a rasa-dhvani is the soul, meaning it is foremost every time it occurs. Consequently, this statement is repudiated: dhvanir namaparo yo ’pi vyaparo vyanjanatmakah, tasya siddhe ’pi bhede syat kavye ’msatvam na rupata, “Even if it were accepted for argument’s sake that Dhvani is an additional function and is the nature of suggestiveness, and that its varieties are proven, at the utmost it can only be a minor aspect of poetry and not its essential form” (Hrdaya-darpana). In other words, although poetry has three aspects: abhidha (Denotation), bhavana (feeling), and rasa- carvana (the relishment of rasa), only rasa-carvana is the life. Even you do not dispute this. For instance, you yourself stated: kavye rasayita sarvo na boddha na niyoga-bhak, “In poetry, everyone is an enjoyer; neither a knower nor a person enjoined” (Hrdaya- darpana). Therefore, to say that vastu-dhvani and alankara-dhvani are mere minor aspects is only stating the obvious. But if it should also signify rasa-dhvani, that would go against the above-stated fact acknowledged by you.” (Locana 1.1)**

Anandavardhana said that in the course of perceiving the rise of a rasa, the sequence of the functioning of Suggestiveness is unnoticed. The gist is that Suggestiveness, correlated with the reader’s predisposition, not only brings about the perception of an implied sense: It also gives rise to the relishment of it. This concept was first formulated by Bhatta Nayaka in a general way. Abhinavagupta correlated the concepts in a clear-cut fashion by subcategorizing the function of Suggestiveness: sa ca rasana- rupa pratitir utpadyate. vacya-vacakayos tatrabhidhadi-vivikto vyanjanatma dhvanana-vyapara eva, bhogi-karana-vyaparas ca kavyasya rasa-visayo dhvananatmaiva, “The perception (of rasa) that originates is the form of rasana. It is the exact same function called Suggestiveness, only it is the soul of Suggestiveness. It is entirely distinct from Denotation, which governs the vacya (the literal meaning), the vacaka (the sound that literally expresses that meaning), and so on (it is also distinct from Indication and the Drift). Bhatta Nayaka’s bhogi-karana-vyapara (the functional power that turns poetry into an enjoyment), whose scope is the relishment of poetry, is the exact same soul of Suggestiveness” (Locana 2.4).

The gist is that rasana is the function of rasa which propels the rasa that is “the relished sthayin” to the level of rapture. Abhinavagupta says the experience of rasa is also called carvana (relishment, lit. rumination), asvadana (relishment), and bhoga (enjoyment).

Bhatta Nayaka established a philosophical conclusion by saying that the ultimate experience of rasa is set in motion by a power of enjoyment. Abhinava named it rasana. Since Rupa Gosvami says that transcendental rasa has the nature of the highest bliss, and since Jiva Gosvami says “the highest bliss” signifies hladinl-sakti (the pleasure potency), Abhinavagupta’s rasana is the same as hladinl-sakti, which is either transcendental, material, or a mix of both, depending on the experiencer and the context. Jiva Gosvami explains that each transcendental potency has a respective material counterpart that bears the same name.

Abhinavagupta does not acknowledge any relishment outside the scope of the relishment of a rasa. He writes: rasenaiva sarvam jlvati kavyam, “Any poetry lives only by the rasa” (Locana 2.3). In the realm of the Dhvani theory, there are two main schools of thought: (1) Bhatta Nayaka, Abhinavagupta, Visvanatha and others say relishing poetry simply means relishing the rasa, and everything else, such as ornaments, implied ideas, and implied literary ornaments, is subservient to that rasa, in conformity with Bharata Muni’s statement: na hi rasadrte kascidarthahpravartate, “No meaning takes place without a rasa,” and (2) Mammata, Pandita-raja Jagannatha and others do not only exalt the rasa: They give great importance to ornaments, implied ideas, and so forth.

Therefore in poetics there are seven functions:

1\. Denotation (abhidha),

2\. Necessary connection (avina-bhava): the individual thing is indicated by the category; or a missing word is obviously understood, and so on,

3\. Indication (figurative usage) (laksana),

4\. Drift (the Abhihitanvaya-vadTs’ tatparya),

5\. Purport (Mammata’s tatparya, used in vakya-vaisistya (the special suggestiveness of the real statement) and in the modern paryayokta ornament, circumlocution),

6\. Bhatta Nayaka’s bhavakatvam, the catalyst that triggers the relishment of the poetry; it includes sadharanya (generalization and empathy), and

7\. Suggestiveness (vyanjana), which somewhat corresponds to Bhatta Nayaka’s bhavakatvam and bhojakatvam.

## 12. Rajasekhara

I J) ajasekhara wrote Kavya-mimamsa. As the title suggests, the treatise was meant to be a thorough exposition of poetics. Rajasekhara said he wrote the book for poets: vyakarot kavya-mmamsam kavibhyo rajasekharah \| (Kavya-mimamsa 1):

Later writers of Kavi-sikshas, like Ksemendra, Amara, Vinaya-candra and Devesvara, seem to have been indebted to the Kavya-mimamsa for some of the topics treated in their works.

Most of Kavya-mimamsa is now lost. In what is left of it, Raja- sekhara refers to upcoming portions of the book, which are not extant:

According to his own admission, the Kavya-mTmamsa was projected by Rajasekhara in 18 lengthy Adhikaranas each containing several Adhyayas; but unfortunately, the whole of this work is not found except the first, the Kavi-rahasya.

Similarly, at the very end of the eleventh chapter of Alankara- sekhara, Kesava Misra quotes two otherwise unheard-of verses about simile by attributing them to Rajasekhara.

Rajasekhara was patronized by King Mahendrapala (890-908 CE) and his son Mahipala (910-940 CE) who ruled the country of Madhyadesa (modern-day Uttar Pradesh) from its capital Kannauj (formerly Kanyakubja): “It is thus not unreasonable to assign a period of 880-920 A.D. to Rajasekhara.” In Kavya-mimamsa, Rajasekhara often calls himself Yayavariya (born in the Yayavara family):

Although Rajashekhara spent most of his time at Kanauj or Tripuri he must be regarded as one of the great writers of Maharashtra. According to Dr. Altekar, in a Banaras manuscript of one of Rajashekhara’s work he is described as the crest jewel of Maharashtra; he was a member of a family called Yayavara of Maharashtra and his wife Avantisundari was a princess of the Chahamana family.

Rajasekhara is also known as the writer of four dramas: Bala- ramayana, Karpura-manjari (in Sauraseni Prakrit), Viddha-sala- bhanjika and Bala-bharata (incomplete). He also wrote a maha- kavya called Hara-vilasa, mentioned by Hemacandra. The work, now lost, might be the source of several verses unaccounted for in Kavya-mmamsa:

In the two anthologies of Vallabhadeva and Samgadhara, we get a considerable number of verses ascribed to Rajasekhara. Of these, about 24 have been identified by Sten Konow in Rajasekhara’s four plays, but about 10 have not yet been traced in any of his known works, nor are they to be found in his Kavya-mmamsa.

Rajasekhara said he was a reincarnation of Bhartrmentha (author of Hayagriva-vadha): babhuva valmika-bhavah pura kavis tatah bhuvi bhartrmenthatam \| sthitah punar yo bhava-bhuti-rekhaya sa vartate samprati rajasekharah \|\| (Bala-ramayana 1.16). Dr. Kane says Rajasekhara is a name of Siva, “he on whose crest is the moon”:

One important question is whether Rajasekhara was a Brahmana or a Ksatriya. The name Rajasekhara (raja candrah sekhare yasya) means Siva (Candrasekhara being given by Amara as a synonym of Siva). He was said to be upadhyaya or guru of two kings of Kanoj. \[...\] Hence it should be held that Rajasekhara was a brahmana.

Ramaswami Sastri adds: “As the author of the Hara-vilasa, Raja- sekhara might be regarded to have been a staunch Saiva, but from the quotations in the Kavya-mimamsa in praise of Vishnu, it seems that he was not a sectarian.”

In the extant Kavya-mimamsa, Rajasekhara mentions general topics in passing. Dr. Kane writes: “This is a unique work, but it does not concern itself with the exposition of rasa, gunas or alankaras, and it is rather in the nature of a practical handbook for poets.”

Rajasekhara follows Rudrata’s fourfold classification of figures (vastava, aupamya, atisaya, artha-slesa) and his categorization of sabda-slesa as an ornament of sound (Kavya-mimamsa 1), but disagrees with Rudrata’s classification of kaku as an ornament of sound and reiterates Vamana’s ritis (Kavya-mimamsa 7). Bhoja copied Rajasekhara’s subdivisions of kaku and illustrations (Srngara-prakasa 7.131-135).

According to Rajasekhara, the knowledge ofpoetics forms a seventh Vedanga and a fifteenth branch of knowledge. As an example, he shows the famous verse about two birds in a tree (rendered in Bhagavatam 11.11.6). Ramaswami Sastri comments: “By this the superiority of Isvara is clearly brought out. In this way the knowledge of Alankara helps in correctly interpreting Vedic texts.” Pandita-raja Jagannatha says the verse features the atisayokti ornament (introsusception). Alternatively, since the introsusceptions are not for the sake of adding literary beauty to the respective subjects of the comparison (upameyas) (the soul and the Soul), the literary device is allegory, which falls in the category of aprastuta-prasamsa (indirect expression) (Sahitya-kaumudi 10.81 Commentary).

Rajasekhara defined the term sahitya (literature): sabdarthayor yathavat saha-bhavena vidya sahitya-vidya, “The science of literature is the science characterized by a proper togetherness of sounds and meanings” (Kavya-mimamsa 2). In other words: “Sahitya-vidya is the realization of the connections that exist between Sabda and Artha.” Bhoja elaborated upon that by naming twelve varieties of relations between sabda (sound, word) and artha (meaning). Following this statement of Bhoja, in Bhava- prakasana Sarada-tanaya defined sahitya and gave illustrations.

Rajasekhara invented the concept of Kavya-purusa (poetry repre­sented as a human) and matched various categories of poetic theory with the limbs of the Kavya-purusa. Kavi Kamapura did so too. Rajasekhara says the soul of the Kavya-purusa is rasa, and so did Kavi Kamapura. However, although Rajasekhara cites Anandavardhana on several topics, he does not mention Dhvani as an aspect of the Kavya-purusa, thus Rajasekhara is only classed in the Rasa school. He created an elaborate, mythological and far­fetched account of the Kavya-purusa, whom Rajasekhara imagines as a primeval being that married Sahitya-vidya and imparted the knowledge of poetics.

Rajasekhara derived the word kavi from the verbal root kav\[r\] varne (1A), by taking varna (to color, to change color) to mean varnana (to describe). However, no rule explains the addition of the suffix i after the verbal root. The sutra is: acah i, “The suffix i is added after a verbal root that ends in a vowel” (Unadi-sutra 4.140). The verbal roots that match this are ku sabde (to sound) and ku\[n\] sabde (to sound). In his commentary on that sutra, Ujjvala Datta interprets ku sabde to mean ku varne (Ramaswami Sastri (2010) Kavya-mmamsa, p. 143).

Rajasekhara says a nonenvious scholar is rare: sa punar amatsari jnata va viralah. (Kavya-mimamsa 4). Bana said the same about poets.

Yayavanya lists three kinds of kavis: (1) sastra-kavi (a master of scriptures), (2) kavya-kavi (a scholarly poet), and (3) ubhaya-kavi (both kinds of kavis). There are three kinds of sastra-kavis and eight kinds of kavya-kavis. In addition Rajasekhara enumerates the ten stages of a kavi: the sixth is mahakavi and the seventh is kaviraja.

Sisir Kumar Das says perhaps Rajasekhara is the only ancient Indian poet to acknowledge a woman for her contributions to his literary career. Dr. Sushil Kumar De explains: “He also quotes with respect the views of his wife Avantisundan of the Cahuana family, for whose pleasure, we know, he wrote his KarpUra-manjari (i.11) and who seems to have been an accomplished authoress.”

The Chauhan family is a clan that ruled parts of northern India in the medieval period. Rajasekhara cites the opinions of his wife about paka and so on. Dr. Kane writes: “No work of his wife Avantisundan has come down.” Ramaswami Sastri talks about the education of women in those days:

Rajasekhara’s views in this connection were very forward and liberal. He says that women too may become poetesses like men. Accomplishment is intimately connected with the soul, but does not depend upon the distinction of the sex. In his time daughters of princes and prime ministers, courtezans and wives of jesters were found well-versed in sciences, and poetesses too.

Moreover, in chapters twelve and thirteen Rajasekhara discusses plagiarism among poets. He says there are four categories of copied meanings, based on a difference in degree. Case in point, he adds that only he mentioned them, but in fact the first three categories were first stated by the Dhvanikara: samvado hy anya- sadrsyam tat punah pratibimba-vat \| alekhyakara-vat tulya-dehi- vac ca saririnam \|\| (Dhvany-aloka 4.12)

Rajasekhara says every poet is a thief, and every businessman is a trickster, but one who knows how to remain secretive flourishes without reproach: nasty acaurah kavi-jano nasty acauro vanig- janah \| sa nandati vina vacyam yo janati niguhitum \|\| (Kavya- mimamsa 11)

Bhoja cites verses of citra-kavya by specifying that Rajasekhara is the author. This is Rajasekhara’s verse for the dvi-srngataka diagram (“it twice meets the peaks”; crossroads):

*karasanja vasesam kha-gaurava sya kala-rasam \|*  
*samdhaya valayam sankam agaurim me vanatmaka \|\|*

**Dvi-srngataka**

![рис-006.jpg|404](<Versified History of Sanskrit Poetics/рис-006.jpg>)

The six syllables in the inner circle of the diagram denote the author’s name in the genitive case (“it belongs to”). kara-asanja—O you who make rays (or a hand) adhere; vasa- isam—to Siva, who has control; kha—in the sky; gaurava—O you who have venerability; sya—destroy; kala-rasam—the relishment of a fraction; samdhaya—after joining; bala-yam—which is attaining force; sankam—fear, doubt; agaurim—gloomy (“not bright”); me—my; vana—is in water; atmaka—O you whose body.

**O you whose rays penetrate the mind, O you who have venera- bility in the sky, O you whose body is in the lake of the heavens, grace me with the relishment of your crescent shape on almighty Siva and thus dispel my gloomy uneasiness: Cupid is gaining power. (Kavya-mlmamsa) (cited in Sarasvad-kanihabharana 2.313)**

In addition, Rajasekhara discusses poetic conventions at length (chapters 14-16). He says he prefers poetic conventions to objective reality: vastu-vrttir atantram kavi-samayah pramanam iti yayavariyah (Kavya-mmamsa 18). Notably, he says moonlight only occurs in the bright fortnight; sandalwood trees only exist in the Malaya Hills; couples of cakravaka birds become separated at night; cakora birds subsist on moonlight; blue lotuses only bloom at night; cuckoos coo only in spring; peacocks dance only in the rainy season; fame is white, and so is laughter; the teeth of lovers are red; and Siva has a crescent moon on his head.

The seventeenth chapter, called desa-vibhaga, mentions various regions, rivers, and mountains in the four quarters of India and the products peculiar to each, as well as the complexion of various people. In the eighteenth chapter, called kala-vibhaga, he mentions the seasons, winds, flowers, and birds, as well as actions appropriate to the seasons. Dr. Kane writes: “Hemacandra (Kavyanusasana pp. 126-130 and 130-135) and Vagbhata borrowed from him very largely, particularly chapters 17-18.” The reason for such an enthusiasm is that Kalidasa often gave elaborate details of the fauna and the flora in his descriptions of various regions, especially in Raghu-vamsa (4th, 6th, and 13th chapters) and in Megha-duta. This tradition was lost.

## 13. Mukula Bhatta

Back in Kashmir, the opponents of the Dhvani theory continued to have their say. Mukula Bhatta wrote Abhidha- vrtti-matrka. Dr. Kane comments:

He was the son of Bhatta Kallata and the teacher of Pratiharendu- raja. Bhatta Kallata flourished in the reign of Avantivarman (855-883 A.D.). \[...\] It follows that the Abhidha-vrtti-matrka should be assigned to the period 900-925 A.D.

Dr. Sushil Kumar De notes:

Adherents of other schools, such as Pratiharenduraja, who commented on Udbhata, or Gopendra Tippa Bhupala, who commented on Vamana, carry on the older tradition and do not fail to criticise the new theory.

Mukula Bhatta’s treatise is short: It consists of fifteen definitional verses (karikas) along with his elaborations. He expounds the theory that Indication (laksana-vrtti) is included in Denotation

(abhidha-vrtti). Mukula disagreed with the Dhvani school. He stated:

*laksana-margavagahitvam tu dhvaneh sahrdayair nitanatayopavarnitasya vidyata iti. disam unmilayitum idam atroktam. etac ca vidvadbhih kusagriyaya buddhya niripaniyam, na tu jhagity evasiiyitavyam ity alam ati-prasangena.*

**“It is thus understood that Dhvani, described by the venerable Sahrdaya as a new concoction, is included in Indication. This book is written to shed light on the topic. It can be explained by scholars with one-pointed concentration. Intelligent persons should not at once look down upon that truth. Enough of this digression.” (Abhidha-vrtti-matrka 11 vrtti)**

Mukula referred to the Dhvanikara by name elsewhere as well: evam-vidhe visaye ’tyanta-tiraskrta-vacyata sahrdayair angikriyate (11-12 vrtti).

Despite the small size of Abhidha-vrtti-matrka and despite his opposition to the Dhvani theory, Mukula Bhatta had a profound impact in Sanskrit poetics. Mukula established categories of figurative usage that were accepted by Mammata.

In addition, he made up the threefold rule of Indication, accepted by Abhinavagupta (Locana 1.1) and Mammata (KP 2.9):

(1) The main meaning does not make sense in the context;

(2) The indicated sense has a connection with the main meaning;

(3) Indication is either conventional or purposeful; the latter involves an implied meaning.

Mukula’s four categories of Denotation (jati, guna, kriya, yadrccha), as stated by Patanjali, and six categories of Indication were virtually copied by Mammata. The two diagrams below show the similarities between Mukula’s six categories of figurative usage and Mammata’s six varieties:

![рис-007.jpg|653](<Versified History of Sanskrit Poetics/рис-007.jpg>)

Mukula Bhatta subdivided purposeful figurative usage (prayojana- vati laksana) and conventional figurative usage (rudhi-laksana), but Mammata did not subdivide the latter. Visvanatha Kaviraja partly followed Mukula by subdividing it in almost the same way Mammata subdivided the former. In the second chapter of Kavya- prakasa, Mammata gave these examples of purposeful figurative usage:

1\. suddha upadana-laksana (pure Inclusive Indication) (no super­imposition and no qualitative usage): “The spears enter” (the spears enter along with the warriors who hold them) (the purpose, the implied sense, is that the warriors form a phalanx);

2\. suddha laksana-laksana (pure Exclusive Indication) (no superim­position and no qualitative usage): “The cowherd settlement is on the Ganges”;

3\. suddha saropa (pure superimposition) (no qualitative usage): “Ghee is longevity”;

4\. suddha sadhyavasana (pure introsusception) (no qualitative usage): “the longevity”;

5\. gauni saropa (qualitative superimposition): “The outsider is an ox”;

6\. gauni sadhyavasana (qualitative introsusception): “the ox”.

The second, third, and fifth examples are taken from Mukula. Mammata explained away Mukula’s other examples. Next, Mukula Bhatta expounded the types of connections that take place between the main meaning and the indicated meaning when the main meaning does not make sense. Mammata accepted most of those connections, but sometimes he renamed them. Mukula refers to a verse, ascribed to Bhartrmisra, where five connections are stated. Dr. Kane says Mammata cites the verse in his Sabda-vyapara- vicara. That verse was quoted by Abhinavagupta (Locana 1.1) and is also found in Agni Purana. For example, Mukula says the connection which explains the figurative usage in “The cowherd settlement is on the Ganges” is sambandha (relation). However, Mammata follows Patanjali and explains that example by the connection called samipya (nearness) (Kavya-prakasa 2.9). Mukula says there are many more types of connections: etac ca sarvam bahu-vyaktavyatvad iha na nirupyate (11-12 vrtti).

Furthermore, Mukula Bhatta mentioned three suggestive factors: vaktr (the speaker), vakya (the real meaning of the sentence) and vacya (the literal sense). Mammata reiterated all of them. This is Mukula’s example of an “indicated sense” (implied sense) which is understood because of the particular type of speaker (vaktr- vaisistya ):

*drstim he prativesini ksanam ihapy asmad-grhe dasyasi*  
*prayenasya sisoh pita na virasah kaupir apah pasyati \|*  
*ekakiny api yami satvaram itah srotas tamalakulam*  
*nirandhras tanum alikhantu jaratha-ccheda nala-granthayah \|\|*

**Dear neighbour, you’re a kind woman: Keep an eye on my house for a while. Usually my husband does not like to drink water from a well. Therefore I alone will quickly go to the riverbank where tamala trees abound. I don’t mind if the dense thorny bushes scratch my body. (Abhidha-vrtti-matrka) (Sad- ukti-karnamrta 541)**

The verse, composed by the poetess Vijja, is cited by Visvanatha Kaviraja as an instance of a svatah-sambhavi vastu that gives rise to a vastu-dhvani. The implied idea (vastu-dhvani) is that the speaker is going to meet her paramour and so she is using a pretext to explain away the nail marks that her lover will make on her body. tatrodaharanam (Abhidha-vrtti-matrka 7 vrtti).

## 14. Abhinavagupta

Abhinava-gupta (c. 950-1020 CE), one of the most famous Kashmiris, did not write a treatise on poetics, but his two commentaries had an immense impact in the field: He wrote Locana, a commentary on Dhvany-aloka, and Natya-veda-vivrti (Abhinava-bharatl), a commentary on Natya- sastra. Dr. Kane extols Abhinava:

Abhinavagupta is one of the most remarkable personalities of medieval India. He was a man of very acute intellect and was an encyclopedic scholar.

His teacher in Poetics was Induraja and in dramaturgy Tota. In these two branches his two works, viz. Locana and Abhinava-bharatl are monuments of learning, critical insight, literary grace and style. He has been followed by all subsequent eminent writers on these two subjects, except Mahima-bhatta.

Abhinavagupta was proficient in yogic practices, he believed that he had realized the Highest Reality (Siva) and was inspired by Siva to proclaim an easy way of Release out of compassion for less favoured people struggling to find spiritual enlightenment and peace. Even after having become blessed, for the sake of others he wrote works. At the end of the Pratyabhijna-vimarsini, Abhinava says that he has opened an easy and new way which former great teachers declared in the ‘Siva-drsti’; a man planting his feet on this path becomes perfect and one with Siva.

Bhatta Tauta (or Tota) wrote Kavya-kautuka, a work now lost. Abhinava reiterated Bhatta Tauta’s doctrine that santa is the highest rasa because it is conducive to liberation. Abhinava explained bhakti in these terms: isvara-pranidhana-visaye bhakti-sraddhe smrti-mati-dhrty-utsahanupraviste anyathaiva angam iti na tayoh prthag-rasatvena gananam.

“On the topic of devotion to God, bhakti and sraddha are subsumed in these vyabhicari-bhavas: smrti (remembrance), mati (thought­fulness based on the scriptures), dhrti (steadiness of the heart), and utsaha (perseverance), otherwise they are limbs of santa, thus neither one of those two is counted as a separate rasa” (Abhinava- bharati).

In this way, Abhinava implicitly accepts Sankaracarya’s standpoint that bhakti is only a means of attaining liberation.

Moreover, the Dhvanikara and Anandavardhana stated that a dhvani is either a rasadi-dhvani, a vastu-dhvani, or an alankara- dhvani, but Abhinava specified that a rasa-dhvani is primordial: sa ca rasadir dhvanir vyavasthita eva. na hi tac-chunyam kavyam kincidasti, “No poetry lacks a rasadi-dhvani” (Locana 2.3). In that respect, Visvanatha Kaviraja was Abhinava’s most loyal follower. Dr. De remarks:

Abhinavagupta in many places expresses himself unambiguously that the Rasa is in fact the essence of poetry; and, admitting that the unexpressed may also take the form of Vastu or Alankara, he thinks that these two forms of suggestion terminate ultimately in the suggestion of Rasa. We shall see that this opinion probably inspired the somewhat extreme theory ofVisvanatha that the Rasa alone constitutes the essence of poetry; but the considerations, which had wisely restrained the authors of the Dhvany-aloka from expressing it in clear terms, could not, as Jagannatha’s criticism of Visvanatha’s view shows, be easily put out of the way.

We find in the immediate followers of the system, however, not the extreme position of Abhinavagupta, but the theory and the scheme as finally outlined by Anandavardhana. With Anandavardhana, the Dhvani-theory, which was itself ancient, came to prevail; but with him also was evolved a more or less complete scheme of Poetics in which the divergent gleams of earlier thought and the accumulated stock of recognised ideas meet and are rationally adjusted. This scheme, with the concept of dhvani (especially rasa-dhvani) at its centre, was summed up and uttered in the concise form of a systematic text-book by Mammata, another Kashmirian, whose influence perhaps was not less potent than that of Abhinavagupta in raising it to almost exclusive authority in later times.

Dr. Keith observes:

Abhinavagupta went much further and declared that in reality all suggestion must be of sentiment, holding that in the long run suggestion of subject and figure reduced themselves to this. Visvanatha, author of Sahitya-darpana, followed his lead, but this never became the accepted doctrine, for the writers realized that, by attempting thus to limit suggestion, they would cut out a good deal of admitted poetry.

Furthermore, Abhinavagupta added to the Dhvanikara’s definition of connoisseur:

*yesam kavyanusilanabhyasa-vasad visadi-bhute mano-mukure varnaniya-tanmayi-bhavana-yogyata, te hrdaya- samvada-bhajah sahrdayah. yathoktam—yo 'riho hrdaya-samvadi tasya bhavo rasodbhavah, sariram vyapyate tena suskam kastham ivagnina.*

**“Those who have the capacity to attain identification with the subject of description, given that their mind-mirror has become clear by virtue of the practice of constantly taking interest in poetry, are the connoisseurs. The meanings speak to their hearts. For instance it is said: “An emotion that relates to a meaning which speaks to the heart gives rise to rasa. The body is pervaded by it like dry wood by fire” (Natya-sastra 7.7)” (Locana 1.1).**

This is the introductory verse in Locana:

*apurvam yad vastu prathayati vina karana-kalam*  
*jagad grava-prakhyam nija-rasa-bharat sarayati ca \|*  
*kramat prakhyopakhya-prasara-subhagam bhasayati tat*  
*sarasvatyas tattvam kavi-sahrdayakhyam vijayate \|\|*
