apurvam—not existing earlier; yat—which \[principle\]; vastu—an idea; prathayati—is spreading; vina karana-kalam—without a trace of the causes (i.e. fate or karmic reactions such as sukrti); jagat—the world; grava—a stone; prakhyam—equal to; nija-rasa—of its own rasas; bharat—from the profuseness; sarayati—causes to move; ca—and; kramat—sequentially; prakhya—from illumination (kavi- pratibha); upakhya—and the secondary designation (words); prasara—whose effusion; subhagam— \[an idea\] being lovely; bhasayati—causes to shine; tat—that; sarasvatyah tattvam— principle of Sarasvati; kavi-sahrdaya-akhyam—whose description is done by poets and by esthetes (or whose perception is properly done by poets and by esthetes); vijayate—is supereminent.

**The underlying principle of SarasvatT is supereminent. It is declared by poets and by other connoisseurs. Without a trace of the usual causality involved in the experience of worldly happiness and so on, it brings forth ideas previously unknown and, by the profuseness of its rasas, makes the stone-like world flow. It sheds light on a lovely meaning whose effusion occurred in sequence from the poet’s creative genius and the literary words. (Locana, mangalacarana)**

The underlying principle of Sarasvati is suggestive poetry: atha ca sarasvatyas tattvam dhvani-kavyam vijayate (Balapriya-tika). In Locana, Abhinava championed the Dhvani theory. Mammata reiterated many of his interpretations and illustrative examples. In addition, Mammata’s mangalacarana is based on Abhinavagupta’s above verse. Most likely, the name Locana was taken from these words of Anandavardhana: kim apy anyad eva sahrdaya- locanamrtam tattvantaram tadvad eva so ’rthah, “An implied meaning is something else: It is a distinct kind of principle that is nectar for the eyes (locana) of the connoisseurs” (Dhvany-aloka 1.4 vrtti). The Locana is not the only commentary on Dhvany-aloka:

Before the Locana, there existed a commentary on the Dhvany- aloka called Candrika, which was composed by someone who belonged to the same family to which Abhinavagupta belonged. The Locana cites it in many places and strongly condemns it.

The Locana signifies the third eye, which sees the implied sense. For instance, Appaya Diksita compares the three main literary functions to Siva’s three eyes. In that connection, Abhinava makes puns by way of glorifying his own commentary:

*kim locanam vinaloko bhati candrikayapi hi \|*  
*tenabhinavagupto ’tra locanonmilanam vyadhat \|\|*

**There may indeed be light (aloka), Enriched also by moonlight (candrika);**  
**Yet will it be resplendent without sight? (Locana) So has Abhinavagupta aright**  
**Provided his open eyesight!**  
**(Locana 1.19)**

Abhinavagupta referred to Candrika in this passage also: vibhaktataya na bhavyata ity arthah. anena vidyamana eva kramo na samvedyata ity uktam. tena yat sphotabhiprayenasann eva krama iti vyacaksate tat pratyuta viruddham eva, “Thus it is said that although there is a sequence between reading the words and understanding the sentence, the sequence is not perceived. Hence the commentator, who explains this passage as “nonexistent sequence, from the perspective of sphota,” is out of line” (Locana 1.11). In that regard, Abhinava relates an opinion that rasa is a form of sphota. That is true if the term rasa is taken in its meaning of rapture. But it is wrong in the meaning of rasa as “aesthetic delight”, because although both the perception of a rasa and a sphota have no sequence, by definition a sphota gives the meaning, whereas that type of rasa is a form of meaning (a rasa-dhvani is a particular vastu-dhvani).

Among all commentators on poetical treatises, Abhinavagupta was the wittiest. To prove Anandavardhana’s point that in any ornament, an implied sense is rarely first-rate, Abhinavagupta shows this verse as an example of the vyaja-stuti ornament (artful praise):

*kim vrttantaih para-grha-gataih kintu naham samarthas*  
*tusnim sthatum prakrti-mukharo daksinatya-svabhavah \|*  
*gehe gehe vipanisu tatha catvare pana-gosthyam*  
*unmatteva bhramati bhavato vallabha hanta kirtih \|\|*

**What is the use of talking about what happens in others’ homes? Still, innately talkative as I am, due to my nature from the south, I cannot remain silent. Alas, your beloved fame roams in every house, in marketplaces, in crossroads and in taverns as if she were inebriated. (Locana 1.13)**

According to Ruyyaka, the last sentence is a mix of implied praise and expressed praise, since the word kirti (fame, renown) is expressive of praise, and so Jayaratha, a commentator on Alankara- sarvasva, says the verse is a bad example, but Pandita-raja Jagannatha refutes Jayaratha’s verdict as follows: (1) In the first sentence, the expressed sense does not stand by itself insofar as there is a beginning of the samasokti ornament (concise statement) (see below) which amounts to an implied criticism, and (2) The paronomastic word vallabha (beloved) adds to the criticism: Firstly the word vallabha is taken as a noun (a beloved), and it forms a metaphor with fame: “Alas, fame, in the form of one of your beloveds, goes around as if she were inebriated.” Secondly, the word vallabha is taken as an adjective of fame: “Your dear renown goes around as if it were inebriated.”

The verse begins with an implied criticism (What is the use of talking about what others’ wives do?), ends with an expressed criticism, and culminates in an implied praise: “O king, you’re very famous.” The third sentence reveals the implied sense in the first. Therefore, what is prastuta (the subject matter) in the third sentence is aprastuta (not the subject matter) in the first. The samasokti ornament, where the aprastuta is implied from the prastuta, thus occurs in the first sentence, in reference to the paronomastic word grha (house; wife). In the end, Ruyyaka’s opinion stands, but it does not vitiate the example.

The opposite instance, where the criticism implied from the expressed praise does not completely invalidate the praise, is seen in Vijja’s verse (dhanyasi, “You are fortunate” etc.) cited earlier, in the section on Sanskrit poetesses. Moreover, in the verse quoted by Abhinava, the vyaja-stuti ornament is conjoined with an utpreksa ornament (fanciful imagination): “as if inebriated”, with the virodha ornament (semblance of a contradiction): “Fame roams”, and with an implied kavya-linga ornament: Fame is as if inebriated because it roams in taverns.

Abhinavagupta was a savant and a polymath. Dr. Mithilesh Catur- vedi writes:

In his Tantraloka, Abhinava refers to both Bhutiraja and Bhutiraja-tanaya as his teachers. \[...\] Helaraja, in his commentary on the Vakya-padiya, constantly refers to himself as Bhutiraja-tanaya. “If we accept Bhutiraja-tanaya, the teacher of Abhinavagupta, to be identical with the commentator on Vakya-padiyam, for the reason that Abhinava shows so deep knowledge of the Vakya-padiyam, we can definitely say that he lived in the tenth century CE in Kashmir.” \[...\] Helaraja was Abhinava’s teacher in dualistic-cum-monistic Saivism and thus a philosopher.

Abhinavagupta was the Sankara of poetics. In the West, Abhinava’s views are popular. Since he had an inclination toward monism, he did not carry on the true spirit of Anandavardhana, who clearly indicated, with his aforementioned verse that begins ya vyaparavati rasan rasayitum (Dhvany-aloka 3.44), that bhakti-rasa is superior to mundane rasa. Case in point, Abhinavagupta did not have the required predisposition to relish that type of rasa.

Abhinava completed over thirty-five works, the largest of which is Tantraloka, an encyclopaedic treatise on all the philosophical and practical aspects of Kashmir Shaivism, also called Pratyabhijna- sastra. In addition, he composed hymns such as Bhairava-stotra. Dr. Kane remarks:

The Tantraloka, a voluminous work (29 anihkas of which out of 37 occupy eleven volumes in the Kashmir Sanskrit Series), was composed before the Locana, which latter in its turn was followed by another voluminous work viz. the Abhinava- bharati on Bharata’s Natya-sastra. Besides these he composed other works. Therefore, it would not be quite wrong to assume that Abhinavagupta’s literary activity must have extended over 35 or 40 years i.e. from about 980 A.D. to about 1020 A.D.

The tradition is Kashmir says that Abhinavagupta accompanied by 1200 disciples entered a cave repeating the Bhairava-stotra and was seen no more (vide J.R.A.S. for 1910 p. 1334 at p. 1336 n. 1). Dr. Grierson states there that the cave is shown at Biru, ancient Bahurupa, 13 miles to the south-west of Srinagar.

## 15. Dhananjaya

Dhananjaya (c. 995 CE) wrote a famous treatise on drama: “The work is called Dasa-rupa or Dasa-rupaka because it is concerned with the representation of ten principal kinds of plays (called rupakas).” Dhananjaya calls his work Dasa- rupa. He explains that a drama is an imitation of situations. It is called rupa (a show) because it is seen, and is called rupaka for the same reason a metaphor is called rupaka: It is a representation (samaropa, lit. superimposition). The ten chief varieties of drama are: nataka, prakarana, bhana, prahasana, dima, vyayoga, samavakara, vithi, anka, and ihamrga. Dr. Kane comments:

Out of these, nataka and prakarana are most important and serve as the pattern (prakrti) on which the remaining kinds and other kinds of plays (such as the natika described by Bharata himself in chap. 20 verses 62-63 \[or 18.60\]) are constructed.

Further, Dhananjaya defines nrtya as a dance imbued with emotion, whereas nrtta is a dance based on rhythm and time (quick, moderate, or slow). The former is called marga (high style) and the latter desi (popular style). Each one assists dramaturgy and has two subcategories: lasya (gentle dance) and tandava (wild dance).

Dasa-rupaka consists of 277 karikas in four chapters. Dr. De says: The Dasa-rupaka of Dhananjaya, in its treatment of Drama­turgy, is apparently based on the time-honoured authority of Bharata ; but as Bharata’s huge compendium, both from the practical as well as theoretical point of view, is discursive and cumbersome with its load of histrionic and other matters, Dhananjaya attempts to sift the mass of details, and, limiting himself only to Dramaturgy, restates the general principles in the form of a practical, condensed and systematic manual. These features of the new contribution apparently obtained for it such reputation and currency that in course of time it seems to have superseded not only all other treatises on the subject but also the basic work of Bharata himself. Visvanatha, for instance, refers now and then to Bharata and gives one or two (mostly conventional) quotations from Natya-sastra, but in the main he bases his treatment of dramaturgic topics on Dhananjaya; while Vidyanatha admits, in the nataka- prakarana of his own work, his indebtedness to the latter, with the remark esa prakriya dasarupokta-rity-anusarena (p.131).

The illustrative examples are supplied by Dhanika in his com­mentary, called Avaloka. Dr. Kane explains the chronology:

Dhananjaya, the author of karikas, was son of Visnu and a member of the sabha of king Munja; while Dhanika also was the son of Visnu and therefore seems to have been the brother of Dhananjaya. \[...\] Therefore the Dasarupa must have been composed between 974 to 996 A.D. \[.\] As Dhanika quotes a verse from the Nava-sahasanka-carita the commentary must have been composed not earlier than 1000 A.D.

Munja, also called Vak-patiraja, was the seventh ruler of the Paramara dynasty of Malwa. Munja was Bhoja’s uncle.

After an invocation to Ganesa, Dhananjaya follows up with another invocation by making a pun on the word dasa-rupa:

*dasa-rupanukarena yasya madyanti bhavakah \|*  
*namah sarvavide tasmai visnave bharataya ca \|\|*

**Obeisances to all-knowing Vishnu and Bharata, whose esthetes take pleasure because of the images of the ten forms (or whose esthetes take pleasure by means of worldly imitations which are the ten kinds of theatrical representations). (1.2)**

Dhananjaya followed Bhatta Nayaka’s methodology. Visvanatha Cakravarti says the term bhavaka (esthete)—used in the above verse—is a synonym of bhavuka (Bhagavatam 1.1.3). He adds that the term refers to Bhatta Nayaka’s system. Dr. Sivaprasada Dvivedi says Dhananjaya did not adhere to the Dhvani theory. Later opponents of the Dhvani theory are Mukula Bhatta, Kuntaka, and Mahima-bhatta. Dhanika too opposed the Dhvani theory. Visvanatha Kaviraja cited him: yac ca dhanikenoktam, tatparyavyatirekac ca vyanjakatvasya na dhvanih, “Dhanika said, “Dhvani is not related to suggestiveness because it is not entirely distinct from the purport” (Kavya-nirnaya)” (Sahitya-darpana 5.1). This indicates that Bhatta Nayaka followed the Dhvanikara’s theory that suggestiveness is nothing but the tatparya (Drift + Purport). Dhananjaya (arthopaksepakaih sucyam, 1.52, etc.) and Dhanika (aksipyamanopama-cchayalankarah, Avaloka 1.1) used the terms upaksepaka and aksepya instead of vyanjaka and vyangya.

Dhananjaya treats of rasa in the fourth chapter of his work. Dr. De writes: “In the fourth Prakasa we have an exposition of its peculiar theory of Rasa in which, not the relation of Vyangya-vyanjaka but that of Bhavya-bhavaka is posited, after Bhatta Nayaka, between Rasa and Kavya.” Dr. Kane notes:

We learn from Dhanika’s comment (on IV.37) that he wrote a work called Kavya-nirnaya from which he quotes seven verses. He seems to have held views somewhat similar to those of Bhatta Nayaka, when he says (on IV. 37) ‘na rasadlnam kavyena saha vyangya-vyanjaka-bhavah kim tarhi bhavya- bhavaka-sambandhah \| kavyam hi bhavakam \| bhavyah rasadayah \|’ (Kane (1998: 246)).

Poetry is bhavaka (it causes feelings to arise) (ref. Dhanika’s words kavyam hi bhavakam) only if the spectators or the readers have the required predisposition, which arises from a previous experience in real life. Dhananjaya used the terms bhavaka and bhavya thus:

*ramyam jugupsitam udaram athapi nlcam*  
*ugram prasadi gahanam vikrtam ca vastu \|*  
*yadvapyavastu kavi-bhavaka-bhavyamanam*  
*tan nasti yan na rasa-bhavam upaiti loke \|\|*

**“There is no subject matter—whether delightful, disgusting, elevated, lowly, cruel, humane, obscure, or adapted—nor a subject matter made to be felt by the poet’s power of conveying feeling that cannot facilitate the rise of rasa in a person.” (4.79)**

In defining rasa, Dhananjaya said that the sthayl relished because it is made to be felt (bhavita) by meanings expressive of vibhava, anubhava and vyabhicarl is called rasa: padarthair indu-nirveda- romancadi-svarupakaih \| kavyad vibhava-sancary-anubhava- prakhyatam gataih \|\| bhavitah svadate sthayl rasah sa pariklrtitah (4.43-44). In Bhatta Nayaka’s system, the relation between the sthayl and the vibhavas etc. is bhavya-bhavaka, whereas the relation between Rasa and the relished sthayl is bhojya-bhojaka.

Dhananjaya referred to Nayaka’s concept of sadharanya (empathy):

*vacya prakaranadibhyo buddhi-stha va yatha kriya \|*  
*vakyarthah karakair yukta sthayl bhavas tathetaraih \|\|*  
*rasah sa eva svadvyatvad rasikasyaiva vartanat \|*  
*nanukaryasya vrttatvat kavyasyatat-paratvatah \|\|*  
*drastuh pratltir vrldersya-raga-dvesa-prasangatah \|*  
*laukikasya sva-ramanl-samyuktasyeva darsanat \|\|*

**“Just as the contextual verb, whether uttered or merely present in the mind, becomes the essential meaning of the sentence when combined with declined words, so the sthayi-bhava combined with other bhavas is the essence of a play. It is called rasa since it has become relishable. And that is mostly because esthetes are present, not because of the characters’ deeds nor only because the poetry aims at arousing rasa. In terms of shame, jealousy, passion, and hatred, a spectator should feel the same way he or she would feel in real life upon seeing their lover with another.” (Dasa-rupaka 4.35-37)**

Further, Dhananjaya does not negate that an actor can truly relish the emotions and meanings in the poetry: kavyartha-bhavanasvado nartakasya na varyate (4.40).

In subsequent treatises on poetics, Dhananjaya and Dhanika were often taken to be the same person. Visvanatha Kaviraja quotes a verse which he says was composed by Dhanika: yad uktam dhanikena, "na catirasato vastu duram vicchinnatam nayet, rasam va na tirodadhyad vastv-alankara-laksanaih” (Sahitya-darpana 6.63). The verse is Dasa-rupaka 3.29. Similarly, Rupa Gosvami states: danadi-trividham viram varnayantahparisphutam, dharma- viram na manyante katicid dhanikadayah, “Dhanika and others do not consider dharma-vira while clearly dividing the heroes in three categories, beginning from dana-vira ” (Bhakti-rasamrta-sindhu 4.3.61). Dhananjaya said there are three kinds of heroes: daya-vira, rana-vira (yuddha-vira), and dana-vira. Dr. De remarks:

The suggestion that the author and the commentator of Dasa-rupaka are one and the same person, chiefly on the ground of the apparent similarity of names and identity of patronymic, as well as the inadvertant attribution of a verse of Dhananjaya’s to Dhanika in some later works like the Sahitya- darpana need not be seriously considered. Jacobi, however, supports this suggestion by pointing out that there is no separate mangalacarana to the commentary. This hypothesis, however, cannot altogether get rid of the fact that Dhananjaya and Dhanika are indeed distinguished by some later writers. For instance, Vidyanatha, in his numerous references to the Dasa-rupaka, cites the Karika-verses and never from the commentary, although his commentator, Kumarasvamin, falls in one place into the error of attributing one of Dhananjaya’s verses (ii.23b) to Dhanika.

Another topic of interest in Dasa-rupaka is Dhananjaya’s disqui­sition on the categories of rasa. He mentioned bhakti:

*priti-bhakty-adayo bhava mrgayaksadayo rasah \|*  
*harsotsahadisu spastam antarbhavan na kirtitah \|\|*

**“The bhavas such as priti and bhakti and the rasas such as mrgaya (hunting) and aksa (gambling) are not expounded because they are clearly included in harsa (joy), utsaha (zeal) and so on” (4.77).**

Dhananjaya made three categories of srngara-rasa: ayogo viprayogas ca sambhogas ceti sa tridha (4.58 in Hall’s edition). Dhananjaya specifies that purva-raga is not a type of separation per se because the lovers haven’t met, therefore vipralambha has two broad categories: ayoga (absence of meeting) and viprayoga (separation).

Dhananjaya did not expound santa-rasa at all. In the context of the sthayi-bhavas he wrote: samam api kecit prahuh pustir natyesu naitasya, “Some speak of sama (even-mindedness) (the sthayi of santa). In dramas there is no enhancement of this one” (4.33). According to him, the denouement only relates to the first three goals of life: karyam tri-vargas tat suddham ekanekanubandhi ca (1.16).

In santa-rasa in real life, the world is already seen as a stage: “All the world’s a stage. And all the men and women merely players. They have their exits and their entrances, And one man in his time plays many parts, His acts being seven ages.” (As You Like It, by William Shakespeare)

## 16. Kuntaka

Kuntaka (c. 1000 CE) wrote Vakrokti-jivita (the life of poetry is poetic expression). He calls his treatise Kavyalankara. Dr. Kane notes:

Though the karikas thus appear to have been meant to be called Kavyalankara, the whole work has been referred to by later writers as Vakrokti-jivita.

The book consists of four chapters, 183 karikas, and 517 verses in the elaborations. Most of the examples are taken from other authors. In modern editions, the third and fourth chapters are incomplete. Dr. Sushil Kumar De writes:

Kuntaka is better known in Alankara literature under the descriptive designation of the Vakrokti-jivita-kara from the peculiar name of his work Vakrokti-jivita, which itself is so called because of its central theory that vakrokti is the ‘soul’ or essence of poetry. The work had been known only through quotations and references until it was edited from two imperfect MSS by the present writer.

Kuntaka’s date is fixed approximately by his quotation from the dramatist Rajasekhara, on the one hand, and by Mahima- bhatta’s citation of Kuntaka and his work, on the other. Mahima-bhatta flourished, as we shall see, towards the end of the 11th century. We may, therefore, place Kuntaka between the middle of the 10th and the middle of the 11th. As this date falls in with the known dates of Abhinavagupta (whose latest date is 1015 A.D.), we may take Kuntaka as a contemporary of this commentator on Anandavardhana. Although Abhinava refers to various views about vakrokti held before his time, it is remarkable that he never alludes to the Vakrokti-jivita- kara who, as his title rajanaka indicates, was probably a Kashmirian, and whose work, if written before Abhinava’s time, ought not to have been, from its important nature and content, thus entirely ignored by a rival theorist.

Like Dandi’s and Bhamaha’s, Kuntaka’s vakrokti (poetic expres­sion) is a twist on the usual mode of expression in day-to-day life in order to produce a certain striking effect or an imaginative turn of speech. It thus differs from Rudrata’s vakrokti (ambiguous speech). Kuntaka, sometimes called Kuntala, did not accept the Dhvani theory. Kuntaka detailed vakrokti by recategorizing Anandavardhana’s categories of implied meanings into categories of vakrokti. The so-called Vakrokti school is simply a revised Alankara school post-Dhvani-theory. This is Kuntaka’s definition of poetry:

*sabdarthau sahitau vakra-kavi-vyapara-salini \|*  
*bandhe vyavasthitau kavyam tadvid-ahlada-karini \|\|*

**“Poetry is sounds and meanings together, positioned in a construction which abounds in the roundabout usage of poets and which makes the delight of those who know poetry.” (Vakrokti- jivita 1.7)**

To distinguish poetry from nonpoetical works, Kuntaka adds that in poetry the togetherness of sounds and meanings is a specific togetherness, which signifies that they give resplendence to one another.

In the Dhvani theory, the rasa-dhvani, as well as the alankara- dhvani, is alankarya (what is to be embellished). Kuntaka, however, says the sounds and the meanings are alankarya. In that context, Kuntaka defines vakrokti:

*ubhav etav alankaryau tayoh punar alankrtih \|*  
*vakroktir eva vaidagdhya-bhangi-bhanitir ucyate \|\|*

**“Both of these are what is to be embellished. And what embellishes them is vakrokti, a wording with a witty twist.” (1.10)**

Here Kuntaka says vakrokti is an alankara in the broad sense of “embellishment”. It does not mean figure of speech, therefore Visvanatha Kaviraja is wrong in criticizing Kuntaka’s theory that “Vakrokti is the life of poetry” because Kuntaka says vakrokti is an alankara. Moreover, Kuntaka derives this term alankara in the instrumental voice, “that by means of which sound and meaning are embellished,” whereas Vamana used the same derivation to explain the term alankara which means “figure of speech”.

Anandavardhana reworded the ancients’ vakrokti as ukti-vaicitrya, or bhaniti-vaicitrya (amazingness of expression). Mammata and others used the term vaicitrya in that way. It only refers to ornaments, not to an implied sense: kim ca vaicitryam alankara iti (Kavya-prakasa verse 383 vrtti).

Kuntaka expounds:

*vakroktih prasiddhabhidhana-vyatirekim vicitraivabhidha. kidrsi, vaidagdhya-bhangi-bhanitih, vaidagdhyam vidagdha-bhavah kavi-karma-kausalam tasya bhang! vicchittih, taya bhanitir vicitraivabhidha vakroktir ucyate.*

**“Vakrokti is an amazing denotation entirely distinct from well- known manners of denoting things. What is it like? It is vaidagdhya- bhang!-bhaniti (a wording with a witty twist). Wittiness is expertise in the work of a poet. Vakrokti is a wording with a witty twist, i.e. with the strikingness of poetic expertise, thus vakrokti is an amazing denotation of things” (1.10 vrtti).**

Dr. Kane comments:

Kuntaka’s definition of vakrokti as ‘vaidagdhya-bhangi- bhanitih’ seems to be borrowed from someone like Avanti- sundan ‘vidagdha-bhaniti-bhangi-nivedyam vastuno rupam na niyata-svabhavam iti avantisundar!’ (Kavya-m!mamsa p. 46). The word vidagdha has been used from ancient times as opposed to vidvat and means ‘versed in belles lettres, proficient in poetic or clever speech’. Vide Dhvany-aloka ‘prasiddhis ceyam asty eva vidagdha-vidvat-parisatsu’ etc. (4.5) (p. 300); Dhvany-aloka p. 250 ‘vidagdha-parisatsu’ (3.33). In Malati- madhava (I.) when Makaranda hears the double-meaning words ‘raman!ya esa vah sumanasam samnivesah etc.’ he ejaculates ‘aho vaidagdhyam’.

Dr. Sushil Kumar De writes:

Kuntaka then explains that the Vakrokti charms us by the skill of the poet, and is therefore called vaidagdhya-bhang!- bhaniti. It rests ultimately on the conception (pratibha) of the poet, or on his skill (kausala), or on an act of imagination on his part, which is termed kavi-vyapara or kavi-karman. parisad. Avantisundari is cited in Kavya-mimamsa as saying: vidagdha-bhaniti- bhang!-nivedyam vastuno rupam na niyata-svabhavam \[“An idea should be communicated with the twist of a witty expression. The form of an idea is not fixed in its nature”\].

Kuntaka does not exactly define this kavi-vyapara, which is the ultimate source of poetry, perhaps because he is conscious of the fact that it is in its nature undefinable; but he analyses it elaborately, and distinguishes and classifies its function in six different spheres, namely, in the arrangements of letters (varna), of the substantive and terminal parts of a word (pada-purvardha and pada-parardha), of a sentence (vakya), of a particular topic (prakarana), and of the composition as a whole (prabandha). He devotes nearly the whole of his work, with the exception of the introductory portion of the first chapter, to the definition, classification and illustration of these varieties of kavi-vyapara-vakrata, which thus form the different categories into which poetic speech may be analysed. It is clear from this brief exposition that Kuntaka cannot admit as poetry a composition involving mere svabhavokti, which he takes to be a plain description without the requisite strikingness.

In other words, Kuntaka divides vakrokti in the above six categories. The first category, varna-vinyasa-vakrata (poetical placement of phonemes) is a fancy term for anuprasa (alliteration). However, Kuntaka does not acknowledge yamaka (word rhyme). For the most part, Kuntaka subsumes dhvani into his pada-purvardha- vakrata. It has many subvarieties: rudhi-vaicitrya-vakrata, upacara-vakrata, paryaya-vakrata, and so on on. Ruyyaka wrote about Kuntaka: upacara-vakratadibhih samasto dhvani-prapancah svikrtah, “The entire elaboration of implied meanings is included in upacara-vakrata and so on” (Alankara-sarvasva, introduction). Dr. De explains:

It follows from the prominence given by Kuntaka to Vakrokti in poetry that all ideas of Dhvani and Rasa should be comprehended in certain aspects of vakrata. \[...\] The idea of Dhvani is included partly in rudhi-vaicitrya-vakrata. \[. \] vyavasthanat. (2.3 vrtti); yamakam nama ko ’py asyah prakarah paridrsyate \| sa tu sobhantarabhavad iha natipratanyate \|\| (2.7)

Other aspects of Dhvani are ackowledged in upacara-vakrata. \[...\] From Kuntaka’s treatment it appears that he takes upacara in the sense of a supposed or fancied identification of two objects, however distinct, on the basis even of the slightest resemblance. As such, therefore, it is admittedly involved in figures like metaphor (rupaka) and forms the basis of metaphorical expression generally. This would come under the comprehensive domain of transferred expression known as laksana, and would be included by Dhvani-theorists under laksana-mula-dhvani, i.e. suggestion based on transference or Indication. Kuntaka would thus belong to that group of writers regarding whom the Dhvani-kara says that they do not deny the existence of dhvani but regard it as bhakta (bhaktam ahus tam anye), i.e. depending on a transference of sense or Indication.

In the third chapter of his work, dealing with vakya-vakrata, he discusses how poetry may be made charming by delineating appropriate Rasas.

Kuntaka takes up the rasavat topically under vastu-vakrata. \[.\] But he allows Rasa to play the greatest part in what he calls prabandha-vakrata, i.e. in vakrata occurring in the composition as a whole which, he thinks, must be accomplished chiefly by the aid of pleasing Rasas.

Kuntaka used the term rasa-vakrokti in his definition of prasada- guna. In that regard, Bhoja said that in poetry words are classed in three broad categories: (1) vakrokti (poetic expression, i.e. when an ornament is predominant), (2) rasokti (when a rasa is predominant), and (3) svabhavokti (when Bhoja’s gunas are predominant). Among them, rasokti is the best. Further, Dr. Kane writes:

According to Jayaratha and the Ekavali (p. 51), the Vakrokti- jivita was included among those who belong to the Bhakti- vadi school referred to in the hrst karika of the Dhvany-aloka (bhaktam ahus tam anye). But this is not accurate.

For example, Kuntaka shows this verse to illustrate poetry:

*samrambhah kari-kita-megha-sakaloddesena simhasya yah*  
*sarvasyaiva sa jati-matra-vihito hevaka-lesah kila \|*  
*ity asa-dvirada-ksayambuda-ghata-bandhe py asamrabdhavan*  
*yo ’sau kutra camatkrter atisayam yatv ambika-kesari \|\|*

**A lion’s ferocity that arises because a fragment of a cloud resembles an insect-like elephant takes place merely by the nature of the species of lion and is only a whim. Ambika’s lion is not ferocious even when the Earth-supporting­elephant-like clouds of final annihilation assemble, therefore on what occasion might her lion bring about an incredible astonishment? (Vakrokti-jivita, illustration 1.28)**

In his explanation of the verse, Kuntaka hints that he accepts the methodology of the Dirgha-vyapara-vadins.

Dr. Sushil Kumar De summarizes the issue:

The general scheme of Poetics outlined by the Dhvani school, in spite of the loopholes that may be detected in the doctrinal edifice, is accepted as canonical by all important writers coming after Anandavardhana. Here and there an isolated theorist arose who dared to question the general creed, but he was at once put down as a heretic and condemned to neglect and oblivion. The immediately following systems of the Vakrokti-jivita-kara and the Vyakti-viveka-kara were, in spite of their able and ingenious efforts, unable to supplant the Dhvani theory; and, finding no strong adherents, themselves languished and died out. These views are taken notice of by later writers only for the purpose of refuting them. Bhatta Nayaka. judging from the long quotations from his lost work in Abhinavagupta and others, seems to have made a greater impression; but even he does not appear to have been very successful. All these writers, no doubt, accept the concept of a suggested sense, but when they endeavour to explain it in a different way, they could hardly find a patient hearing.

It seems, therefore, that the exponents of the different theories approach ultimately the same standard, albeit through different avenues of thought, and agree in holding that vaicitrya or camatkara (in Alankara or Rasa) must be finally subjected to the taste of the sahrdaya.

In addition, Kuntaka developed his own system of riti. He rejected the designations “Vaidarbhi” etc. and propounded three styles: Sukumara, Vicitra and Madhyama. The third one is a mix of the first two. Each style has four gunas, which have the same names but are differently defined: madhurya, prasada, lavanya, and abhijatya. Each style has two more gunas in a general way: aucitya (1.53-54) and saubhagya (1.55-56): Those two relate to a verse as a whole. Kuntaka discusses the topic of inappropriateness and cites a verse from Kalidasa to illustrate it (puram nisadadhipateh, Raghu-vamsa) (1.57).

In the third chapter, Kuntala discussed ornaments of meaning, which constitute his vakya-vakrokti. Dr. Kane expounds:

He criticizes the definitions and examples of preyah and urjasvin given by Udbhata, Bhamaha and Dandi. \[...\] He finds fault with the threefold division of dlpaka given by Bhamaha \[...\]. He goes on examining many other figures and elucidates them in his own way, such as rupaka, aprastuta-prasamsa, paryayokta, vyaja-stuti, utpreksa, atisayokti and about 20 more figures.

## 17. Agni Purana

This Purana as it is nowadays is not the work of Vyasa. Chapters 336 to 346 of the Agni Purana treat of poetics and drama. In particular, chapter 338 shortly delineates the doctrine of rasa. However, no illustrative example is given on any topic: “Agnipurana is later than Bharata, Bhamaha, Dandi, the Dhvany-aloka and probably Bhoja and has no claim to be regarded as an original work on the Alankara-sastra.” Dr. De writes:

The date of this apocryphal work, which is counted as one of eighteen Mahapuranas is uncertain ; but there is enough evidence to show that the Alamkara-section in it is chiefly a compilation by a writer, who was himself no great theorist but who wanted to collect together and present a workable epitome, conforming in essentials to the teachings of no particular system, yet gathering its material from all sources.

The modern Agni Purana was compiled sometime after Dhvany- aloka because the compiler of the Purana was aware of the Dhvani theory, though he did not agree with it. He followed Bhamaha’s and Udbhata’s opinion. The Agni Purana propounds the literary functions of the Old School of poetics (abhidha, laksana, gauni), but although the Purana acknowledges the concept of dhvani in ornaments, it does not correlate it with a literary function. Moreover, Dr. Kane remarks:

Therefore it can be argued that the portion on Poetics in the Agni Purana is not much later than the Dhvany-aloka. The latter work, it will be seen, was composed in the latter half of the 9th century. It is further to be noted that two verses (apare kavya-samsare etc. and srngari cet kavih etc.) occur in the Agni Purana (338. 10-11 = 339. 10.11 of Anan. ed.) and in the Dhvany-aloka (p. 278). In the latter these verses are introduced with the words tatha cedam ucyate and so it is argued that the Dhvany-aloka is merely quoting from another work. \[...\] Abhinava expressly ascribes the authorship of one of the two verses to Anandavardhana in his comment on the Natyasastra VI.36-37 \[...\]. Therefore I am of the opinion that the Agnipurana not only knew the Dhvani theory but actually borrowed two verses from the Dhvanyaloka.

Many verses in the Agni Purana and in Bhoja’s Sarasvati- kanthabharana are alike. Sushil Kumar De says Agni Purana was compiled before Bhoja’s treatise was written, whereas Dr. Kane says the opposite; he comments upon Bhoja’s Sarasvati- kanthabharana:

The first karika in the fifth pariccheda (raso ’bhimano ’hankarah srngara iti giyate) bears a close resemblance to certain verses of the Agnipurana (338.1-4) quoted above on p. 8. Similarly, Sara. ka. II. 2, 39,75 are much the same as the Agnipurana 341.18-19, 21 and 342.10. Dr. De in J.R.A.S. 1923 pp. 537-549 holds that Bhoja borrows from the Agnipurana. I demur to his conclusion. He is wrong as to the verse srngan cet found in Sara. ka. 5.3 and Agni-pu. 338.11, as shown above on pp. 7-8.

However, Dr. Kane is inconsistent in this matter:

There is a certain symmetrical arrangement in everything that Bhoja treats of, as in the sixteen dosas and 24 figures of sabda, artha and ubhaya, the six varieties of riti, vrtti, mudra, etc. He stands almost alone in regarding upama, aksepa, samasokti, apahnuti and several others as figures of both sabda and artha. In this he probably follows the Agnipurana (vide chap. 344) or some other prior work.

As in the case of Dandi and Bhamaha, perhaps Bhoja and the compiler of the Purana had the same sources. In the preface to his publication of Agni Purana (Calcutta: Firma KLM, 1976), Suresh Mohan Bhattacharya states:

Though the Purana draws upon almost all the earlier Alankarikas, it does not however follow in its standpoint the tenets of any individual school of Poetics. It deals with the established or conventional analysis of poetry, but its treatment is often uncritical and occasionally unintelligible. \[...\] \[It\] does not attempt to establish a new system of speculation, nor does it present any new theory; but it possesses some characteristics peculiar to itself and sometimes differs from the views of the established schools in some notable features. This deviation is probably due to the influence on it of an entirely different tradition, which is now lost to us and which appears also to have been exploited by some later writers headed by Bhoja.

According to Agni Purana, the experience of rasa depends on the conceit of thinking of oneself as a man or as a woman. In the Purana, the theory of rasa is that bliss is inherent in Brahma; the manifestation of bliss conveys relishment (rasa) in the form of astonishment; the first manifestation of Brahma is the ego; ego gives rise to conceit; conceit occasions rati, the sthayi of srngara; and when rati is enhanced by the blend of appropriate vibhavas, vyabhicari-bhavas, and so on, it is called srngara. The writer of Agni Purana thus indicates that srngara is the topmost rasa, whereas Abhinavagupta propounded that santa is the highest rasa.

In this regard, Bhoja follows the Agni Purana, but uses the term srngara in a higher, metaphysical sense: He indicates that the words rasa, abhimana (conceit), ahankara (ego), and srngara are synonymous. According to Bhoja, the propensity to relish rasa originates from a predisposition; rasa is a unique cause of the origination of all one’s qualities; and if the poet habitually enjoys aesthetics (srngarin = rasika ), automatically the poetry is relishable. The last sentence, taken from Anandavardhana, is also cited in Agni Purana: srngari cet kavih kavye jatam rasa- mayam jagat \| sa eva vita-ragas cen nirasam sarvam eva tat \|\| (Dhvany-aloka 3.43 vrtti) (Agni Purana 338.10).

In the Purana and in Bhoja’s works, the definitions of ornaments are based on Dandi’s and Bhamaha’s treatises: “The borrowings from Bhamaha and Dandin by the Purana are extensive. \[...\] The Agni-purana takes no less than 160 passages from Dandin.”

In addition, the Purana and Bhoja’s works mention the concept of ubhaya alankara (ornament of both sound and meaning). However, the respective lists differ. Mammata accepted that concept, but only for punar-uktavad-abhasa (semblance of redundancy).

In Agni-purana, the gunas are:

- Seven sabda-gunas: slesa, lalitya, gambhirya, saukumarya, udarata, satya, and yaugiki,
- Six artha-gunas: madhurya, samvidhana, komalatva, udarata, praudhi, and samayikata, and
- Six sabdartha-gunas: prasada, saubhagya, yatha-samkhya, prasastyata, paka, and raga.

The ornaments are:

♦ Nine sabda alankaras: chaya, mudra, ukti, yukti, gumphana, vako-vakyam, anuprasa (the Purana includes yamaka in anuprasa), citra-kavya, and duskara, with many details concerning subcategories for each one;

♦ Eight artha alankaras: svarupa (svabhava), sadrsya (which has four varieties: upama, rupaka, sahokti, and arthantara- nyasa), utpreksa, atisaya, vibhavana, virodha, hetu and sama;

♦ Six ubhaya alankaras: prasasti, kanti, aucitya, sanksepa, yavad-arthata and abhivyakti.

The eighteen kinds of simile (upama) comprise most of Dandi’s subvarieties.

In Agni-purana, the distinction between gunas and alankaras is slight, like in Dandi’s and Vamana’s methodologies. According to the compiler of the Purana, a literary quality is that which is conducive to a great splendor in the poetry (yah kavye mahatim chayam anugrhnaty asau gunah, 345.3) whereas an ornament is an attribute that makes the resplendence of the poetry (kavya-sobha- karan dharman alankaran pracaksate, 341.17) (copied from Kavyadarsa 2.1).

Visvanatha Kaviraja was the first poetical theorist to refer to Agni Purana: vag-vaidagdhya-pradhane ’pi rasa evatra fivitam, “Although in poetry the main thing is cleverness in the wording, only a rasa is the life in it” (Agni Purana 336.29) (Sahitya-darpana 1.2). This is the other reference quoted by Visvanatha:

*naratvam durlabham loke vidya tatra ca durlabha \|*  
*kavitvam durlabham tatra saktis tatra ca durlabha \|\|*

**In the world, taking birth as a man is a privilege. In addition, knowledge is acquired with difficulty. Moreover, becoming recognized as a poet is hard to achieve. Over and above that, poetic ability is hard to come by. (Agni Purana 336.3) (Sahitya- darpana 1.2)**

The verse features the sara ornament (climax). Regarding the verse, Dandi, Bhamaha and Vamana used the term pratibha (creative intelligence) instead of sakti (ability). In this matter, Rajasekhara states two schools of thought: Anandavardhana, who used both terms interchangeably, says sakti is superior to vyutpatti (having much related knowledge). Rajasekhara says a kavi must have both. According to Vamana, creative intelligence is sufficient: kavitva-bijam pratibhanam (Kavyalankara-sutra 1.3.16). Dandi stated that natural creative intelligence, much flawless and traditional knowledge, and effortful perseverance are the causes of the excellence of poetry.

Rajasekhara went in the details: He said samadhi (concentration) and abhyasa (practice) give rise to sakti, the most important cause of poetry, and sakti is the driving force ofpratibha and vyutpatti.

Bhatta Tauta, Abhinavagupta’s teacher of Natya-sastra, defined pratibha in this way: prajna nava-navonmesa-salini pratibha mata, “Pratibha is an intellect that abounds in ever fresh brilliancy” (cited by Ksemendra in Aucitya-vicara-carca 35).

Abhinava writes: pratibha apurva-vastu-nirmana-ksama prajna. tasya viseso rasavesa-vaivasya-sundara-kavya-nirmana- ksamatvam, “Pratibha is an intellect capable of inventing unique ideas. Its specialty is the capacity to create beautiful poetry, on account of the poet’s upsurge of rasa” (Locana 1.6).

According to Mahima Bhatta, pratibha is the intellectual capacity of the poet whose mind is fixed in contemplation on words and meanings conducive to the rasa. That intellectual function arises at once from the contact with the soul and is equated with Siva’s third eye because it makes things in the three worlds seem like they are present before one’s eyes: rasanuguna-sabdartha-cinta-stimita- cetasah \| ksanam svarupa-sparsottha prajnaiva pratibha kaveh \|\| sa hi caksur bhagavatas trfiyam iti giyate \| yena saksat-karoty esa bhavams trailokya-vartinah \|\| (Vyakti-viveka 2.117-118)

Rudrata said that vyutpatti is the discernment between propriety and impropriety and arises from the knowledge of grammar, of the ways of the world, and so on. Rajasekhara agreed with Rudrata, without acknowledging him. The Agni Purana, however, has a different methodology:

*vyutpattir durlabha tatra vivekas tatra durlabhah \|*  
*sarva-sastram avidvadbhir mrgyamanam na sidhyati \|\|*

**“Vyutpatti (having much related knowledge) is harder to come by than sakti (ability), and viveka (discernment) is harder to achieve than vyutpatti. The scriptures looked into by those who have little knowledge do not become fruitful.” (Agni Purana 336.4)**

In addition, Dr. Kane points out that a distinction should be made between Agni Purana and Vahni Purana:

The commentary of Mahesvara and that on Vidyabhusana quoted above apparently make no distinction between Agni- purana and Vahnipurana. But there is a Vahnipurana that is different from the extant Agnipurana as Eggeling’s Catalogue of India Office Sanskrit mss. part 6 pp. 1294 ff clearly shows.

## 18. Bhoja

King Bhoja ruled from circa 1005 to circa 1055 CE. He wrote Sarasvafi-kanthabharana and Srngara-prakasa. He was the king of Malwa, a region that corresponds to modern­day districts of western Madhya Pradesh and of south-eastern Rajasthan. Ujjain is a prominent city in the Malwa region. Bhoja shifted his capital from Ujjain to Dhara. Avanti was one of the sixteen great kingdoms of circa 600 BCE mentioned in Anguttara Nikaya, an ancient Buddhist text. The capital of Avanti was Ujjain (Ujjayini). Candragupta \|\| (380 CE-415 CE), one of the most powerful emperors of the Gupta empire in northern India, conquered Ujjain; he was widely renowned as a patron of Sanskrit learning. Kalidasa lived in Ujjain: It is one of the oldest and most renowned seats of learning, and has a rich academic and cultural heritage. According to tradition, Krishna and Balarama studied here under the guidance of Sandipani Muni. In the Mauryan period, starting from the 4th century BCE, students from all over the world came to Ujjayini in pursuit of knowledge.

Dr. Sushil Kumar De writes: “Kahlana states (vii.259) that king Bhoja of Dhara was the true friend of poets; and it is possible that he had himself literary predilections. He was son and successor of Sindhuraja and nephew of Munja-vakpatiraja.”

Dr. Kane expounds upon the chronology:

According to the Bhoja-prabandha, there was a prophecy that Bhoja would reign for 55 years. Bhoja’s uncle Munja was slain by Tailapa between 994 and 997 A.D. and Munja was succeeded by his brother Sindhuraja or Sindhula also styled Navasahasanka. An inscription of Jayasimha the successor of Bhoja dated Samvat 1112 (1055-56) A.D. settles this dispute about the date of Bhoja.

However, V. Raghavan states: “Bhoja might have assumed reigns of Government about 1010 A.D. or somewhat later. \[...\] He died sometime after 1062 A.D.” 796 Dr. Kane notes:

Bhoja is credited with having composed 84 works on almost all sciences of medieval India by Ajada quoted by Dr. Raghavan in note 2 on p. 5. Dr. Raghavan appears to treat with ridicule those who hold that these works cannot all be the compositions of Bhoja and that several of them must have been composed by those whom Bhoja patronized (pp. 5-6 of Raghavan’s vol. I).

Still, Dr. Kane points out that Bhoja was often at war:

Bhoja waged protracted wars with neighboring kings \[.\]. Some of Bhoja’s works are very voluminous. He wrote Sarasvati-kanthabharana (on Poetics and also on grammar). His Samarangana-sutradhara (about 7000 verses) has been published in the G.O.S.

Most likely, Sarasvati-kanthabharana and other works under Bhoja’s name were composed by pandits patronized by Bhoja:

Actually Bhoja had with him a rich academy of eminent scholars of all the branches of learning. Rather there was available a marvelous galaxy of poets, aestheticians and other expert scholars in Bhoja’s university called Sarasvati- kanthabharana, ruins of which are still available at Dhara.

Similarly:

The most important information contained in these plates is regarding the migration of Brahmanas from various parts of the country to Malwa where they were recipients of donations at the hands of the Paramara prince. In several instances the donees seem to have migrated all the way from Bengal

Sir Monier-Williams thought that Bhoja is not the author of the poetical treatise called Sarasvail-kanihabharana. Under that listing, he wrote: “generally ascribed to Bhoja, but probably written by some Pandit during or after the reign of that king, in the end of the eleventh century A.D.” (Monier-Williams Dictionary). A verse of Sarasvati-kanthabharana has Bhoja’s name in it as a vocative: jaya jaya jaya sriman-bhojaprabhati vibhavari (2.239). Similarly, the example of sabda-guna praudhi cited ahead refers to Bhoja in the third person, and this example of artha-guna praudhi refers to Bhoja in the second person: tvad-vaktrendu-vilokanakula-dhiya dhatra tvadiyam sriyam, niksipya pratirajakesu vidusam laksmya tvam apuritah (illustration 1.122).

## SarasvatT-kanthabharana

Bhoja belongs to the Rasa school, but he did not adhere to the Dhvani theory. Another particularity of this school, headed by Lollata, Sankuka, and Bhatta Nayaka, is the equal importance of rasa, guna, and alankara and the absence of dosa. This is Bhoja’s definition of poetry:

*adosam guna-vat kavyam alankarair alankrtam \|*  
*rasanvitam kavih kurvan kirtim pritim ca vindati \|\|*

“The poet who makes faultless poetry that has a guna, an alankara and a rasa obtains fame and pleasures.” (1.2)

Bhoja’s definition is an improvement on the definition of poetry in Agni Purana. In Sahitya-darpana (1.2), Visvanatha Kaviraja quotes the above and criticizes it for the same reasons he disagrees with Mammata’s definition. Visvanatha says the notions that the poetry should be faultless and should have both a guna and an alankara are not invariable. However, Bhoja’s system of gunas is unique.

Sarasvatl-kanthabharana consists of 631 karikas and 1564 examples in five chapters: (I) Definition of poetry; sixteen faults in a declined word (pada-dosa), sixteen faults in a sentence (vakya- dosa), and sixteen faults in the sense of the sentence (vakyartha- dosa); twenty-four sabda-gunas and twenty-four artha-gunas; on occasion a dosa is a quality, (II) Twenty-four ornaments of sound (sabda alankara), (III) Twenty-four ornaments of meaning (artha alankara), (IV) Twenty-four ornaments of both sound and meaning (ubhaya alankara), and (V) Rasa and a panoply of related topics.

Many of Bhoja’s examples are written in Prakrit. On the whole, Bhoja’s innovative spirit in the chapters on gunas, sabda alankara, and rasa is striking at first, but upon a closer examination it becomes apparent that he created too many categories, which he created for the sake of symmetry.

## Sources

Both in the karikas and in the examples, Bhoja profusely copied previous authors. Dr. Kane remarks:

The SarasvaU-kanihabharana quotes over 1500 examples from former poets and therefore is valuable for the chronology of Sanskrit literature. But, as much earlier works like the Kavyalankara-sutra-vrtti of Vamana, the Dhvany-aloka and Locana have become available to all, its importance is now much less than in the days of Aufrecht. It draws upon Kalidasa and Bhavabhuti at every step. Besides the above it quotes Abhidhana-mala, Kadamban, Kama-sastra, Chalita- rama, Jaimini, Tapasavatsaraja, Dhvany-aloka, Bana, Bhatti,

Bharata, Bhamaha, Bharavi, Maha-bharata, Ratnavali, Rajasekhara, Ramayana, Rudrata, Vikranta-sudraka, Veni- samhara, Sisupala-vadha.

Verse 12 of Caura-pancasika by Bilhana, who lived in the eleventh century, is illustration number 1.195 in Sarasvati-kanihabharana. Dr. Sushil Kumar De comments: “We have not based any chronological inference on this, because Bihlana’s authorship of the work is not beyond question.”

The Sarasvati-kanthabharana is very similar to Agni Purana. Dr. De expounds:

The same reverence to Bharata and Dandin is shown throughout; and in fact, Dandin is estimated to have supplied Bhoja with more than two hundred unacknowledged quotations. At the same time, Bhoja very freely incorporates definite verses and illustrative stanzas from most of his well-known predecessors, especially from Bhamaha, Vamana, Rudrata and Dhanika. He even appropriates Karikas from the Dhvany-aloka, although he does not accept its theory. His huge compilation, like its prototype the Agni-purana, in more or less cyclopaedic in scope and eclectic in spirit, and represents apparently one of the several forms of arranging the teachings (with the exception of ignoring the dhvani theory) of earlier schools in the light of a different tradition, of which another form is perhaps preserved, to a certain extent, in the two Jaina Vagbhatas. But in some of the main points, similarity of his treatment to the Agni-purana is obvious. \[...\]

Apart from this fact of literal similarity, which, however, is not conclusive, there is a striking coincidence, as we shall see presently, of treatment, as well as agreement of views on fundamental points, which is more than merely accidental. It is not suggested that Bhoja is directly copying from the Agni- purana or the Purana copying directly from Bhoja; it is quite possible that they exploit in common an unknown source. But there is hardly any doubt that they follow a common tradition which is different in many respects from that of the Kashmirian writers.

A comparative study of Bhoja’s Sarasvafi-kanthabharana and the Alankara section of the Purana would, in our opinion, indicate that \[...\] there might be no question of direct mutual borrowing, but both were drawing upon a common source, and that the more elaborate and systematic Bhoja was probably chronologically later. If the Purana- compiler was later and took from Bhoja, it would be strange indeed that he should present as undeveloped and unsystematic what was already developed and systematic in his presumed source. It would hardly make any difference if the Purana-compiler is proved later than Bhoja, but as our available evidence is at best uncertain, it would be better to leave the question open.

Most likely, a common source was Rajasekhara’s Kavya-mimamsa. In addition, Rajasekhara mentions Syamadeva and Mangala as previous authorities (Kavya-mimamsa 4 and 5). According to Ramaswami Sastri, Syamala is Syamilaka, the author of Pada- fadifaka.

The author of Agni Purana mentions the word kavya-mimamsaka— ye vyufpaffadina sabdam alankarfum iha ksamah \| sabdalankara- namnas fan kavya-mimamsaka viduh 11 (Agni Purana 341.17)—and Bhoja has a similar verse:

*ye vyufpaffadina sabdam alankarfum iha ksamah \|*  
*sabdalankara-samjhas fe jheya jafy-adayo budhaih \|\| (Sarasvafi-kanthabharana 2.2).*

## Gunas

Bhoja’s twenty-four sabda-gunas and twenty-four artha-gunas have the same names, but the definitions differ. He incorporated Vamana’s ten qualities of sound and ten qualities of meaning, but Bhoja does not define all of them in the same way. Among those, the main dissimilarities are: sabda-guna prasada, sabda-guna samadhi, artha-guna madhurya, and artha-guna udarata.

Mammata vehemently demolished Vamana’s system of gunas. Mammata must also have had Bhoja in mind, since taking time to analyze a verse in consideration of forty-eight gunas is impracticable.

Bhoja’s twenty-four sabda-gunas are: slesa (coalescence of words), prasada (using words in their well-known sense), samata (not deviating from the type of phonemes), madhurya (the words are not compounded and are not in coalescence), saukumarata (no usage or almost no usage of hard phonemes), artha-vyakti (clarity of the meaning of the whole sentence), kanti (gracefulness of the construction, owing to alliteration), audarya (the usage of hard phonemes), udattata (exalted yet simple adjectives), ojas (many compounds), aurjitya (coalescence of words with harsh phonemes), preyas (an expression of affection said with cleverness), susabdata (proficiency in the usage of nouns and verbs), samadhi (superimposing an attribute on another, such as attributing functions of living entities to inert things) (Kuntaka included this in his upacara-vakrata), sauksmya (an additional sense of a verb is implied with regard to the difference between the active voice and the passive voice), gambhirya (implied sense), vistara (elaboration), sanksepa (conciseness), sammitatva (use of the absolutely necessary words, neither more nor less, to convey the intended sense, i.e. balance of sound and sense), bhavika (the statement is built upon the prominent vyabhicari-bhava of the speaker), gati (heigthening effect and lowering effect, one after the other, such as the mandakranta meter) (the same as Vamana’s sabda-guna samadhi), riti (no lack of symmetry), ukti (cleverness of a reply, i.e. not giving a direct answer), and praudhi (topmost stage of eminence).

Bhoja’s sabda-guna praudhi is based on the concept of paripaka (also called paripaka or simply paka) (ripeness, maturity). He expounds it in the chapter on rasa: The relishment of a verse is one of three kinds:

1\. Reading the verse is like eating ripe grapes (mrdvika-paka): There is no relishment at the outset, but there is relishment afterward,

2\. Reading the verse is like eating coconut (narikela-paka): There is relishment at the beginning and at the end, and

3\. Reading the verse is like eating a mango (amra-paka): The relishment gradually increases.

Rajasekhara had propounded nine kinds ofpaka (Kavya-mimamsa 5). Bhoja’s three kinds are the highest in Rajasekhara’s methodology. Those three are also listed in Agni Purana, which lists paka as a sabdartha-guna (quality of both sound and meaning).

Regardingpaka, Vamana wrote: guna-sphutatva-sakalyam kavya- pakam pracaksate, “They say kavya-paka occurs when all the gunas are clearly manifest” (Kavyalankara-sutra 3.2.15). Vamana and others favored sound over meaning: That theory is called Sausabdya. Bhoja echoed that theory in the definition of his sabda- guna susabdata: vyutpattih sup-tinam ya tu procyate sa susabdata (1.73). According to Vamana, sabda-paka (ripe choice of words) is this: The words are so well chosen that they cannot be changed, even for synonyms (Kavyalankara-sutra 1.3.15).

Rajasekhara favored the viewpoint of his wife, Avantisundan: She says Vamana’s above definition of sabda-paka is only the absence of poetic ability, since all the various expressions of great poets in reference to the same object are ripe, therefore, she opines, paka consists of a composition suitable to the development of rasa. She adds: “In my opinion, when the manner of stringing sound and meaning together with regard to guna (quality), alankara (ornament), riti (style of compounding) and ukti (cleverness of expression) is relished by cultured persons, that is vakya-paka.”

The concept of artha-paka (ripeness of meanings) occurred later in the history of poetics; it was invented by Vidyadhara and Vidyanatha:

Vidyadhara admits only what is called artha-paka above; but he alludes to the other theories which say that paka consists of pada-vyutpatti (Mangala) or of pada-parivrtti-vaimukhya (Vamana). Vidyanatha calls this last sayya, and accepts and defines paka as depth of sense. Bhoja would call it praudhi and enumerate it as a sabda-guna.

Vidyanatha used the term sayya (repose) instead of sabda-paka. The commentator Kumara Svamin explains this as a friendship between the words. Perhaps Vidyanatha’s usage of the term sayya is sourced in a verse cited by Vamana. Vidyanatha accepts

Bhoja’s twenty-four sabda-gunas just as Bhoja defines them, but he says paka, the depth of meaning, is that which goes to the heart. Vidyanatha acknowledges two kinds ofpaka: The ripeness of grapes and the ripeness of coconut. He likens the ripeness of grapes to a verse where the rasa is spread throughout, and the ripeness of coconut to a verse where the rasa (especially srngara) is relished below the surface meaning. Vidyanatha specifies that the kinds ofpaka denote the categories of the relishment of rasa, and he as well correlates it with praudhi-guna. Anandavardhana, however, applied the notion of paka to the poets themselves: paripakavatam kavinam rasadi-tatparya-virahe vyapara eva na sobhate, “For the poets who have full maturity, no literary function appears resplendent in the absence of a purport such as a rasa” (Dhvany-aloka 3.43 vrtti).

This verse is Bhoja’s example of sabda-guna praudhi (topmost stage of eminence). He says the verse illustrates narikela-paka (ripeness like that of a coconut):

*abhyuddhrta vasumati dalitam ripurah*  
*ksipta-kramam kavalita bali-raja-laksmih \|*  
*atraika-janmani krtam yad anena yuna*  
*janma-traye tad akarotpurusah puranah \|\|*

**The Earth was uplifted, the chests of enemies were ripped apart, and the opulence of the best offerings of tribute (or King Bali’s resplendence) was turned into a morsel. What the ancient Purusa did in three lifetimes was done by this young man (Bhoja) in one, with a change in the sequence. (1.98)**

Bhoja’s twenty-four artha-gunas are: slesa (a nice sequence of ideas) (the same as Vamana’s artha-guna slesa; Bhoja gives the same example), prasada (clear manifestation of the sense) (this is already included either in sabda-guna prasada or sabda-guna artha-vyakti), samata (no lack of symmetry) (this is the same as sabda-guna riti), madhurya (no excessiveness in expressions of anger and so on), saukumarata (no harshness) (this is already included in artha-guna madhurya), artha-vyakti (straightforward mention of the nature of things) (this is the same as the jati ornament of meaning), kanti (a blazing rasa), audarya (eminence of opulence) (Dandi’s second variety of udatta alankara), udattata (sublime intention) (Dandi’s first variety of udatta alankara), ojas (only the speaker knows the real sense: viparita-laksana, irony, reverse figurative usage), aurjitya (the speaker has an arrogant ego, i.e. a trace of urjasvin), preyas (pleasing comparisons exalt what is intended to be achieved, like comparing nectar and so on to the lover’s lips), susabdata (using good synonyms instead of displeasing words), samadhi (indirect expression of the intended sense), sauksmya (subtle sense) (already included in sabda- guna gambhirya), gambhirya (depth of sense with regard to the scriptures), vistara (elaboration) (not different from sabda-guna vistara), sanksepa (conciseness) (not different from sabda- guna sanksepa), sammitatva (equality between word and sense: just the right number of words) (not different from sabda-guna sammitatva), bhavika (speaking with a hidden intention), gati (one meaning is implied from another) (not different from sabda-guna gambhirya), riti (sequence of actions), ukti (the intended sense is said in a roundabout way) (included in artha-guna samadhi), and praudhi (roundabout mode of expression) (others calls this the paryayokta ornament).

Although in his definition of poetry Bhoja states the concept of rasa, he follows Vamana by including the concept of “blazing rasa” in his artha-guna kanti (1.81). Moreover, based on his example, Bhoja’s sabda-guna gambhirya corresponds to Anandavardhana’s sabda- sakti abhidha-mula dhvani. According to Bhoja, the designation sabda-guna only means the quality is mostly external whereas the name artha-guna means the quality is mostly internal: bahyah sabda-gunas tesu cantaras tv artha-samsrayah (1.61). Bhoja says there are three kinds of gunas: tri-vidhas ca gunah (1.60). His third kind is called vaisesika (special). It occurs when a literary blemish becomes a quality according to the context: vaisesikas tu te nunam dosatve ’pi hi ye gunah (1.61).

## Ornaments

Bhoja’s twenty-four ornaments of sound are: jati (language), gati (verse, prose, or both, and druta, etc.), riti (style of compounding), vrtti (mode), chaya (shadow), mudra (sign), ukti (statement: affirmative (vidhi), negative (nisedha), with alternatives (vikalpa), parisankhya, etc.), yukti (wilful syntactical connection), bhaniti (statement: possible, impossible, amazing, etc.), gumphana (stringing together), sayya (repose), pathiti (kaku, etc.), yamaka (word rhyme), slesa (pun), anuprasa (alliteration), citra (citra- kavya, (picture poetry), vako-vakya (dialogue), prahelika (riddle), gudha (hidden: kriya-gudha, karaka-gudha, etc.), prasnottara (question and answer), adhyeya (worth studying), sravya (worth hearing), preksya (worth seeing), and abhiniti (dramatical gesture).

Vako-vakya is also seen in Agni Purana. Bhoja subsumed Rudrata’s vakrokti (ambiguous speech) in his vako-vakya (illustration 2.348). Visvanatha Kaviraja referred to vako-vakya in his explanation that a fable is a subvariety of aprastuta-prasamsa.

The count of twenty-four ornaments of sound is misleading. Many of the above are not ornaments proper. For instance, Bhoja included Dandi’s aslh ornament in his sravya (illustration 2.358). Chaya has six varieties: Bhoja defines it as an imitation of some particular kind of utterance: anyoktmam anukrtis chaya saptha sad-vidha (2.39); An example of his chekokti-cchaya (an imitation of the statement of a clever person) is “Obeisances to the beast of man who is not subjugated by his beloved’s face which has wide blue eyes and playful eyebrows”: yo hi dlrghasitaksasya vilasa-lalita- bhrunah \| kanta-mukhasyavasa-gas tasmai nr-pasave namah \|\| (illustration 2.38). The instances of the Dvaraka queens’ speaking in the madness of separation from Krishna fall in the category of his unmattokti-cchaya (illustration 2.40). Bhoja’s mudra, which has six varieties, includes the concepts of laksana-mula dhvani, padamsa-dhvani, and artha-sakti abhidha-mula dhvani. Bhoja’s sayya ornament simply consists in introducing some idea which is out of context: sayyety ahuh padarthanam ghatanayam parasparam \| sa prakrantena kasmimscid aprakrantena kutracit \|\| (2.54). Bhoja’s examples of preksya consist of a description of the Rasa dance. His abhimti (abhinaya), also called citrabhinaya, is the same as Bharata Muni’s dramaturgical ornament called citrabhinaya. Bhoja’s prahelika and prasnottara are subsumed in the uttara ornament by some other writers. Bhoja lists uttara separately, as an ornament of meaning.

Bhoja lists six kinds of riti, as an ornament of sound: Vaidarbhi, Pancali, Gaudiya, Avantika, Latiya, and Magadhi. He defines his regional riti, Avantika, as a style between the Pancali and the Vaidarbhi, which means the sounds are not harsh and each compound consists of two to four words: antarale tu pancall- vaidarbhyor yavatisthate \| savantika samastaih syad dvi-trais tri- caturaih padaih \|\| (2.32).

Bhoja mentions six vrttis, which, for the most part, he defines in terms of a combination of the phonetic construction (soft or hard) and the meaning (soft or hard) (Rudra and Vidyanatha correlated the types of meaning with rasas). The vrttis are: Kaisiki (sweet meaning and sweet sounds), Arabhati (forceful meaning and forceful sounds), Bharati (sweet meaning and both sweet and forceful sounds), Sattvati (forceful meaning and both sweet and forceful sounds), Madhyama Kaisiki (sweet meaning and forceful sounds) and Madhyama Arabhati (forceful meaning and sweet sounds). In modern poetics, neither of those six terms is used.

Bhoja’s system of alliteration is very elaborate. At first he lists six basic kinds: sruti, vrtti, varna, pada, namokti, and lata (2.72). His sruti anuprasa has three kinds: gramya, nagara, and upanagara (2.73 vrtti). His gramya variety has four kinds. The upanagara variety of Bhoja’s sruti anuprasa (2.75) is the origin of Visvanatha Kaviraja’s sruti anuprasa (alliteration of phonemes which belong to the same place of pronunciation in the mouth).

Bhoja lists twelve kinds of vrtti anuprasa, based on a geographical region: karnati (repetition of phonemes of ka-varga), kauntali (repetition of phonemes of ca-varga), kanki (repetition of phonemes of ta-varga), kaunkani (repetition of phonemes of ta-varga), bana-vasika (repetition of phonemes of pa-varga), dravini (repetition of y, r l, v), mathuri (repetition of s, s, s), matsi (repetition of phonemes of two or three vargas), magadhi (repetition of phonemes two by two), tamra-lipika (repetition of n and n)), audri (repetition of a compound consonant of the same phoneme), and paundri (repetition of a compound consonant of distinct phonemes) (2.79). Most of those alliterations are mentioned in Agni Purana.

Afterward, Bhoja lists another set of twelve kinds of vrtti anuprasa involving various kinds of combinations: gambhTra, ojasvinT, praudha, madhura, nisthura, slatha, kathora, komala, misra, parusa, lalita, and mita (2.85). The madhura variety consists in the repetition of anusvara (m, n, n). The kathora variety consists of the repetition of phonemes of ka-varga and of combinations between phonemes of ka-varga and r The komala variety is the repetition of single and short r and single and short n. Of those twelve kinds, five are mentioned in Agni Purana, but the definitions differ from those of Bhoja. He said that according to some authorities, the latter twelve vrttis are not entirely distinct from the gunas nor from the vrttis such as Kaisiki: iti dvadasadha vrttih kaiscidya kathiteha sa, na gunebhyo na vrttibhyo prthaktvenavabhasate (2.87).

Bhoja’s varna anuprasa has twelve categories (2.89-91). This is his example of garbha varna anuprasa (repetition of phonemes with a phoneme added between the repetition):

*kalam kapala-malankam ekam andhaka-sudanam \|*  
*vande vara-dam isanam sasanam puspa-dhanvanah \|\|*

**I praise Siva. He is Time, has a garland of skulls, is unique, killed Andhaka, gives boons, and is the punisher of Cupid. (2.204)**

The above instances of garbha anuprasa are as follows: (1) In “kalam kapala,” the letters k and l are repeated, but the letter p was inserted, (2) In “kam ekam,” the letter e intervenes, (3) In “vande vara-da,” the letters v and d are repeated, but r intervenes, and (4) In “sanam sasana,” the letter s intervenes.

Bhoja’s section on citra is voluminous. He lists six kinds:

(1) varna-citra (verses of one consonant, etc.),

(2) sthana-citra (the usage of only guttural phonemes, etc., like in sruti anuprasa),

(3) svara-citra (alliteration of certain short vowels or certain long vowels),

(4) akara-citra (picture poetry: the syllables of a verse fit in a dia­gram) (known nowadays as citra-kavya),

(5) gati-citra (procedure: diagrams of squares), and

(6) bandha-citra (other kinds of akara-citra).

Bhoja admits that he copied Rajasekhara’s verse for the eight­petalled lotus diagram, Rajasekhara’s verse for the dvi-srngataka diagram, Magha’s verse for the drum diagram (muraja) and Magha’s verse for the wheel diagram (cakra).

Bhoja shows examples of verses of four kinds of consonants (one type of consonant per line) (Sisupala-vadha 19.3), of three kinds of consonants (Kavyadarsa 3.93), of two kinds of consonants (Sisupala-vadha 19.66), and of one kind of consonant (Kiratarjumya 15.15). Bhoja gives many examples of alliteration of vowels: Most of them are taken from Kavyadarsa. In this example of varna-citra, only the syllables of the musical notes are used (sa, ri, ga, ma, pa, dha, ni):

*sa mamari-dhamam nidhanini*  
*sama-dhama dhani-dhama-sadhini \|*  
*manini sa-garimapapapa-pa*  
*sapaga sama-samagamasama \|\|*

**She casts my enemies away. She has the treasures. She has the power of conciliation. And she effects the splendor of rich people. She is highly revered, has weighty dignity, and protects sinless persons. She has a river and unites with Narayana (sa­ma). She is incomparable. (2.265)**

In the following verse, all the thirty-three consonants of the Sanskrit alphabet occur in sequence:

*kah khagaughan acic-chauja jhas jno ’tauthld adan dha-nah \|*  
*tathodadhin papharbabhir mayo ’rilv-asisam sahah \|\|*

kah—who?; khaga—of birds (or kha-ga—of things that go in the sky, i.e. the three flying fortresses named Tripura); ogha—a multitude; an—he manifests; acit—inert matter; cha—that cuts through; ojah—he has the power; jhas—he consumes; jnah—he is learned; ata—those who move (at gatau + pac-ader a\[c\]); oth— \[Arjuna,\] who fully strikes down (a\[n\] + uth upaghate + kvip); id—he praises (id stutau + kvip); adam—in such a way that there is no fire; dha—is a drum; nah—he whose ornament; tatha— and (“in that way”); uda-dhin—water receptacles; papharba—he filled; abhih—fearless; mayah—Maya; ari—enemies; lu—that cut (annihilate) (lU\[n\] chedane + kvip); asisam—of blessings; sahah—capable.

**Who manifested Tripura, has power that splits matter, is a consumer, is learned, praised Arjuna when there was no fire, has a drum as an ornament, filled a pond, and is fearless? He is Maya Danava. He is able to give blessings for the destruction of enemies. (2.263)**

The above also illustratesprasnottara (question and answer).

These are Bhoja’s twenty-four ornaments of meaning: jati (i.e. svabhavokti), vibhavana, hetu, ahetu (mentioned by Dandi in his subvarieties of hetu), suksma, uttara, virodha, sambhava, anyonya, parivrtti, nidarsana, bheda (vyatireka), samahita (Mammata’s samadhi), bhranti (bhrantiman), vitarka, milita, smrti, bhava, pratyaksa, anumana, agama (apta-vacana), upamana, arthapatti, and abhava.

Bhoja lists many subvarieties. He turned the six pramanas (valid means of obtaining knowledge) acknowledged by the Purva- mimamsakas into ornaments (the last six on the list), although the poetic figure called anumana was first stated by Rudrata. Anumana was accepted by Mammata and others. Ruyyaka, Visvanatha and Jagannatha also accepted arthapatti (presumption). In that regard, at first the Naiyayikas accepted four pramanas: pratyaksa (direct perception), anumana (inference), upamana (comparison), and sabda (scriptural testimony, in which apta- vacana may be included). The Vaisesikas say sabda is inherent in anumana. The Prabhakara school of Mimamsa added arthapatti. The Bhatta school of Mimamsa added anupalabdhi (a synonym of abhava: perception of the absence of a thing) for a total of six.

As a poetic theorist of the Old School, Bhoja subsumed the concept of dhvani in several ornaments, one of which is the suksma ornament, invented by Dandi. This is Bhoja’s illustration of the akara variety (an involuntary sign) of suksma (subtle hint):

*sa yuni tasminn abhilasa-bandham*  
*sasaka salmataya na vaktum \|*  
*romanca-laksyena sa gatra-yastim*  
*bhittva nirakramad arala-kesyah \|\|*

**That well-behaved woman with curly hair was unable to talk about the intricacy of her longing for that youthful man. Under the guise of goose bumps, it passed through her slender frame and burst forth. (3.50) (Raghu-vamsa 6.82)**

By the mention of the word laksya (under the guise of), the verse also features the modern apahnuti ornament (poetic denial). Mammata and others only accept Dandi’s first variety of suksma, called ingita (gesture), where a hint is voluntarily intended to be expressed, and define the akara variety in a different way (a suggestive drawing).

Often, the name of an alankara in Bhoja’s system is the same in Mammata’s yet the usage differs, not to mention the subvarieties. For instance, Bhoja says the bhrantiman ornament exists to some degree in milita, which has four varieties: pihita, apihita, tad-guna, and atad-guna: milite bhrantiman astiti bhranty-anantaram milita- laksanam aha. vastv-antara-tiraskaro vastuna militam smrtam \| pihitapihite caiva tad-gunatad-gunau ca tat \|\| (3.41). In this way, Bhoja keeps the count of ornaments of meaning at twenty-four.

Bhoja’s twenty-four ornaments of both sound and meaning are: upama, rupaka, samya, samsaya, apahnuti, samadhi, samasokti, utpreksa, aprastuta-prasamsa, tulya-yogita, lesa, sahokti, samuccaya, aksepa, arthantara-nyasa, visesa, parikara, dipaka, krama, paryaya, atisayokti, slesa, bhavika, and samsrsti.

The above ornaments do not fit in this category at all, except when slesa is involved. Bhoja seeks to resolve the contradiction by stating that his ornaments of sound are mostly external, his ornaments of meaning are mostly internal, and his ornaments of both sound and sense are both external and internal: sabdarthobhaya-samjnabhir alankaran kavisvarah \| bahyan abhyantaran bahyabhyantarams canusasati \|\| (2.1).

Bhoja says the drstanta ornament (exemplification) where the comparison between the two sentences is expressed, by using a word such as iva (like), is called the drstantokti variety of his samya ornament: ivady-aprayoge drstantalankarah, ivadi-prayoge tu drstantoktih (illustration 4.56 vrtti). The samya ornament had been created by Rudrata to account for a simile where the comparison involves an action, since Vamana’s simile only concerns qualities. This illustrates the nisedhe vakra prapancokti variety (an elaboration expressive of a negation, stated with a roundabout mode of expression) of Bhoja’s samya ornament (sameness):

*tad-vaktram yadi mudrita sasi-katha tac cet smitam ka sudha*  
*tac-caksur yadi haritam kuvalayais tas ced giro dhin madhu \|*  
*dhik kandarpa-dhanur bhruvau ca yadi te kim va bahu brumahe*  
*yat satyam punar-ukta-vastu-virasah sarga-kramo vedhasah \|\|*

**If her face is seen, talks about the moon are postponed. If she smiles, who cares about nectar? If her eyes are seen, blue lilies are surpassed. If she speaks, fie on honey. And if her eyebrows are in motion, shame on Cupid’s bow. Why should we talk much? Truly, Brahma’s method of creation is not repetitive. (4.72) (Rajasekhara’s Viddha-sala-bhanjika)**

Visvanatha Kaviraja cites the above as an example of the p rati pa ornament (reverse simile) (Sahitya-darpana 10.87).

## Rasa

Bhoja expanded the topic of rasa. In this regard, Bharavi had nicely drawn a distinction between real love and shallow love.

Bhoja was the first poetical rhetorician to expound upon that. He lists twelve varieties of love (prema): nitya (constant), naimittika (temporary), samanya (ordinary), visesavan (special), pracchanna (covert), prakasa (manifest, i.e. understood by a confidante), krtrima (artificial, for a reason), akrtrima (not artificial, i.e. unconditional), sahaja (natural, i.e. originating from a previous life), aharya (incidental, i.e. occurring as a result of the lover’s deed), yauvana-ja (born of youthfulness), and visrambha-ja (born of intimacy) (illustrations 5.321-332). Bhoja does not say where prema fits in his theory at large. Later, Singabhupala (Rasarnava- sudhakara 2.109) and Rupa Gosvami classed prema as the stage of love after rati: syad drdheyam ratih prema (Ujjvala-nilamani 14.59). Bhoja defines nitya-prema (constant love) as love that does not vanish even when the woman is separated from her lover: prema-prakaresu viprayogadibhir apy avinasimyo nityah (5.321).

Bhoja lists eight kinds of rati (the sthayi-bhava of srngara): naisargiki (natural), samsargikl (the vaisayiki variety experienced in separation), aupamaniki (arisen by a similitude in another), adhyatmiki (soul to soul), abhiyogiki (arisen by a gesture such as a sidelong glance), samprayogiki (increased by contact, i.e. the woman exhibits mana), abhimaniki (arisen from conceit), and vaisayiki (related to one or more of the five sensory objects: sound, touch, form, taste, odor) (illustrations 5.80-90). Bhoja’s example of the ‘sound’ variety of vaisayiki rati was shown in the preamble, in the section on Sanskrit poetesses. This is Bhoja’s example of aupamaniki rati (affection arisen by a similitude of the beloved in another):

*api janaka-sutayas tac ca tac canurupam*  
*sphutam iha sisu-yugme naipunonneyam asti \|*  
*nanu punar iva tan me gocari-bhutam aksnor*  
*abhinava-satapatra-srimad asyam priyayah \|\|*

**This year, with some wit one can clearly deduce a similarity between Sffa and the two boys. Is My beloved’s face, resplendent like a fresh lotus, as if present before My eyes again? (5.81)**

This is Bhoja’s example of abhimaniki rati (arisen from conceit):

*iyam gehe laksmir ayam amrta-vartir nayanayor*  
*asav asyah sparso vapusi bahulas candana-rasah \|*  
*ayam bahuh kanthe sisira-masrno mauktika-sarah*  
*kim asya na preyo yadi param asahyas tu virahah \|\|*

**At home, this LaksmT is an abode of nectar for my eyes. Her touch on my body feels like an abundance of sandalwood paste. Her arm on my neck is a cool and soft pearl necklace. Is there anything about her that is not pleasing? There is. Separation from her is highly intolerable. (5.85)**

Moreover, Bhoja lists twelve rasas. To Bharata Muni’s eight rasas, Bhoja adds santa, preyas, udatta and uddhata. Bhoja’s purpose in adding four rasas is that he matches the dhira-santa hero with santa-rasa, the dhira-lalita hero with preyo-rasa (kindness), the dhirodatta hero with udatta-rasa (being a keeper of moral standards), and the dhiroddhata hero with uddhata-rasa (boastfulness). Rupa Gosvami equates the dhira-santa hero with the dharma-vira hero, thus he classes the dhira-santa hero in vira- rasa (Bhakti-rasamrta-sindhu 4.3.55).
