Bhoja said dhrti (steadfastness), sneha (affection), mati (thoughtfulness), and garva (overweening pride) are the sthayi- bhavas of santa-rasa, preyo-rasa, udatta-rasa and uddhata-rasa respectively (Sarasvati-kanthabharana, illustrations 5.74-78 vrtti). Singabhupala criticized him: bhojenokta sthayino ’nye garvah sneho dhrtir matih \| sthasnur evoddhata-prayah santodatta-rasesv api \|\| tatra sneho rater bhedo stri-pumsecchatmakatvatah \| anye posasahisnutvan naiva sthayi-padocitah \|\| (Rasarnava-sudhakara 2.157-158). In Srngara-prakasa, however, Bhoja said the sthayiof santa is sama and the sthayi of udatta-rasa is ego. Therein Bhoja said udatta is a synonym of urjasvin.

According to Bhoja, the gunas called preyas, bhavika and aurjitya are upgraded to the status of alankara if they have eminence, and are then called preyas, rasavat, and urjasvin. Bhoja accepted Dandi’s and Vamana’s principle that a literary quality (guna) is an alankara in the broad sense of embellishment. Bhoja added that the rasas as well are alankaras in the broad sense. This is similar to Anandavardhana’s statement: vyanjakatvam ca yathokta-carutva- hetum vyangyam vina na vyavatisthate, “Suggestiveness involves an implied sense which is a cause of literary beauty” (Dhvany- aloka 3.33 vrtti).

Although Bhoja’s other treatise on poetics, Srngara-prakasa, implies by its name a profound dissertation on love, the disquisition on rasa in the fifth chapter of Sarasvati-kanthabharana is thorough. In treatises on poetics, Sarasvati-kanthabharana is cited more often than Srngara-prakasa. For instance:

*na vina vipralambhena sambhogah pustim asnute \|*  
*kasayite hi vastradau bhuyan rago ’nusajyate \|\|*

**Without separation, the rendezvous of lovers is not nourished. When a garment is dipped in a reddish dye many times, the red color increases. (Sarasvati-kanthabharana 5.52) (Sahitya- darpana 3.213) (Ujjvala-nilamani 15.3)**

Rupa Gosvami refers to Bhoja’s twofold classification of mana (pique): sa-hetu (with a cause) and nirhetu (without a cause or without a valid cause). Rupa Gosvami says that his two categories of mana (irsya-mana, pranaya-mana) are the same as Bhoja’s categories (Ujjvala-nilamani 15.100-103) (Sarasvafi- kanthabharana, illustrations 5.177-178). Rupa Gosvami also cites Sarasvafi-kanthabharana in Ujjvala-nilamani 15.102. Bhoja added ceta (servant) to the list of the companions of a hero: hina-patrani sesani pithamardo vidusakah \| vita-cetau patakas ca sakhyas caisamparigrahah \|\| (Sarasvafi-kanthabharana 5.121) (ref. Rupa Gosvami’s Ujjvala-nilamani 2.3).

In addition, Bhoja innovated by stating four categories ofsambhoga- srngara (the reunion after each type of vipralambha): sa cafurdha, prathamanuraganantarah, mananantarah, pravasanantarah, karunanantarah (illustration 5.186 vrtti).

## Srngara-prakasa

Bhoja’s Srngara-prakasa consists of 36 chapters, called prakasas (illuminations). It is the largest work in Sanskrit poetics. It treats of both poetics and dramaturgy. This treatise is an encyclopedia: It is filled with examples from famous works. It was most likely written by a different team of scholars patronized by Bhoja, although there are many points of resemblance between the two treatises. The main difference is that Srngara-prakasa expounds grammatical topics at length.

Professor V. Raghavan (1908-1979) edited and translated Bhoja’s Srngara-prakasa. For this work and his commentary, he won the Sahitya Akademi Award for Sanskrit in 1964. It was later published as volumes 53 and 54 of the Harvard Oriental Series in 1998. Here, however, Rewa-prasada Dwivedi’s edition of Srngara-prakasa (root text) is being used. Rewa-prasada Dwivedi says Srngara- prakasa contains 7358 verses: 6117 of them are in Sanskrit; the number of karikas is 1108.

The contents of each chapter are as follows:

(I) Definitions of kavya: Bhoja reiterates Bhamaha’s definition of poetry: tat punah sabdarthayoh sahityam amananti. tad yatha “sabdarthau sahitau kavyam” iti (Srhgara-prakasa 1.13 vrtti); Definitions of sabda (“that by the utterance of which a meaning is perceived”) and artha (“that which is made to be perceived by a word”); Twelve subdivisions of sabda (prakrti, pratyaya, upaskara, upapada, pratipadika, vibhakti, upasarjana, samasa, pada, vakya, prakarana, prabandha), twelve subdivisions of artha (kriya, kala, karaka, purusa, upadhi, pradhana, upaskarartha, pratipadikartha, vibhakty-artha, vrtty-artha, padartha, vakyartha), and twelve types of relation between word and sense (in poetry) (abhidha, vivaksa, tatparya, pravibhaga, vyapeksa, samarthya, anvaya, ekarthi-bhava, dosa-hana, gunopadana, alankara-yoga, rasaviyoga); The details about the first four subdivisions of sabda;

(II) The details about the middle four subdivisions of sabda (pratipadika, vibhakti, upasarjana, samasa);

(III) The details about the last four subdivisions of sabda (pada, vakya, prakarana, prabandha);

(IV) The details about the first four subdivisions of artha (kriya, kala, karaka, purusa);

(V) The details about the middle four subdivisions of artha (upadhi, pradhana, upaskarartha, pratipadikartha);

(VI) The details about the last four subdivisions of artha (vibhakty- artha, vrtty-artha, padartha, vakyartha);

(VII) The details about the first four types of relation between word and sense (i.e. the powers of a word) (abhidha, vivaksa, tatparya, pravibhaga): Abhidha has three subdivisions: mukhya, gaum, laksana (7.1). Kaku is included under vivaksa. Dhvani is a type of tatparya: Bhoja says that the purport (tatparya) in general language is called dhvani (implied sense) in poetics: tatparyam eva vacasi dhvanir eva kavye (1.5). Bhoja follows the Dirgha-vyapara- vadins: yat-paras sabdah sa sabdartha iti tatparyam (7.162 vrtti). His tatparya has three varieties: abhidhiyamana (expressed), pratiyamana (perceived), and dhvani-rupa (implied sense) (7.162 vrtti). Pravibhaga is the separation of the constituent grammatical elements: pade vakye prabandhe vasyaitavatah sabdasyayam artho ’sminn arthe cayam etavan sabda iti sabdarthayor mithah sambandhitayaprthaktvenavadharanam pravibhagah (7.209);

(VIII) The details about the middle four types of relation between word and sense (i.e. the characteristics of a sentence): vyapeksa, samarthya, anvaya, and ekarthi-bhava;

(IX) Dosa-hana (three categories of blemishes: pada-dosa, vakya- dosa, vakyartha-dosa) and gunopadana: The twenty-four sabda- gunas and twenty-four artha-gunas along with the examples are the same as those in Sarasvati-kanthabharana. The gambhirya sabda-guna is the occurrence of an implied sense. Here also there is a third category called dosa-guna (sometimes a so-called fault turns out as a quality);

(X) Alankara-yoga: The same twenty-four ornaments of sound, twenty-four ornaments of meaning, and twenty-four ornaments of both sound and meaning as those in Sarasvati-kanthabharana. The section on citra-kavya is shorter (Srngara-prakasa 10.133­138), although Bhoja highly values it: vinayena vina ka srih ka nisa sasina vina, vina yamaka-citrabhyam kidrsiva vidagdhata, “What is wealth without good conduct? And what is night without the moon? Indeed, what would poetical cleverness be like without yamaka and citra-kavya?” (10.164);

(XI) Rasaviyoga: Bhoja lists twelve rasas and matches the dhira-santa hero with santa-rasa, etc. (11.61-65) like he did in Sarasvati-kanthabharana; Guna-sankara, rasa-sankara, alankara-sankara, guna-rasa-sankara, gunalankara-sankara, and rasalankara-sankara; The rasas in the prabandhas (two types: preksya-prabandha, sravya-prabandha);

(XII) Dramaturgy and sixty-four kavya-laksanas;

(XIII) Overview of dharma-srngara (bharati vrtti, paurastya pravrtti, pancali riti, svakiya nayika, dhirodatta nayaka), artha- srngara (gaudiya riti, audramagadhi pravrtti, arabhati vrtti, sarvah nayikah, dhirodhatta nayaka), kama-srngara (vaidarbhi riti, daksinatya pravrtti, kaisiki vrtti, sarvah nayikah, dhira-lalita nayaka), and moksa-srngara (latiya riti, avantya pravrtti, sattvati vrtti, svakiya nayika, dhira-santa nayaka); Dissertation on fifty- one bhavas, including the eight types of rati;

(XIV) Subcategories and examples of forty-eight bhavas;

(XV) Alambanas of rati (of the sthayi of srngara);

(XVI) Uddipanas of rati;

(XVII) Anubhavas; Ritis (Pancali, Gaudiya, Vaidarbhi, Latiya), vrttis (Bharati, Arabhati, Kaisiki, Sattvati), and pravrttis (Paurastya, Audramagadhi, Daksinatya, Avantya);

(XVIII) Elaboration on dharma-srngara;

(XIX) Elaboration on artha-srngara;

(XX) Elaboration on kama-srngara;

(XXI) Elaboration on moksa-srngara (ref. chapter 13); The sub­divisions and qualities of lovers and ladyloves;

(XXII) Anuraga (sixty-four kinds) (only for dharma-srngara, artha-srngara and kama-srngara),

(XXIII) Four types of vipralambha (prathama anuraga, mana, pravasa, karuna) and the corresponding four types of sambhoga (prathama anuraga antara, mana anantara, pravasa anantara, karuna anantara);

(XXIV) Elaboration on vipralambha;

(XXV) Elaboration on prathama anuraga;

(XXVI) (wanting in both editions);

(XXVII) Sanketa;

(XXVIII) The procedures for a tryst (abhiyoga-vidhi): The qualities and actions of messengers, etc.;

(XXIX) Dispatching a messenger, rebuking a messenger, etc.; (XXX) Elaboration on mana;

(XXXI) Elaboration on pravasa;

(XXXII) Elaboration on karuna-vipralambha;

(XXXIII) Elaboration on sambhoga;

(XXXIV) Elaboration on prathama anuraga anantara sambhoga; (XXXV) Elaboration on the three other types of sambhoga;

(XXXVI) Further elaboration on the four types of sambhoga.

Dr. Mithilesh Caturvedi comments:

A careful study of Bhoja’s Srngara-prakasa and Helaraja’s commentary reveals that there are some strikingly similar passages in the two works. It seems that some material of Helaraja’s commentary has been incorporated by Bhoja in his work. It is well-known that Bhoja tried to give his work an encyclopaedic character and included in it whatever he read from other sources. Not only has he frequently quoted from the Vakya-padiya but he has also utilized the Vrtti on the Vakya-padiya. Therefore there is good reason to believe that Bhoja borrows from the commentary of Helaraja and that is the reason for the close similarity found in some passages of the two works. Bhoja’s date is 996-1051 CE.

From the viewpoint of poetics, the main difference between Srngara-prakasa and SarasvaU-kanihabharana is the topic of moksa-srngara (chapter 21). The SarasvaU-kanihabharana only mentions the first three in passing (with the names dharmodarka, arthodarka, kamodarka}. dharmartha-kamodarkas ca prema- samparka-bhaktayah (5.125) (illustrations 450-452). The category called moksa-srngara includes the love experienced by a self­realized person for his wife. However, there is no trace of rasa in Bhoja’s examples of moksa-srngara. The type of lover Bhoja attributes to moksa-srngara is the same he attributes to santa- rasa. It seems that Bhoja created this category of srngara simply to account for the love between saintly persons, for the love between gods, and for the love between higher divinities, as in the love between Siva and Parvati described by Kalidasa in Kumara- sambhava.

At the outset of the treatise, Bhoja says the ancients listed ten rasas—Bharata Muni’s eight in addition to vatsala and santa— whereas he says srngara is the only Rasa (or the main rasa) since only it provides great relishment. In that regard, Krishna Kavi writes:

*atha bhoja-mpadmam matam atra prakasyate \|*  
*raso vai sa iti srutva rasa eka prakirtitah \|\|*  
*ato rasah syac chrngara eka evetare tu na \|*  
*dharmartha-kama-moksakhya-bhedena sa catur-vidhah \|\|*

“Henceforth the opinion of King Bhoja and of others is stated: In reference to raso vai sah, “God is Rasa” (Taittiriya Upanisad 2.7), one rasa is proclaimed, therefore rasa is one: srngara. The others are not so. Srngara has four varieties: dharma, artha, kama, and moksa” (Mandara-maranda-campu, KM edition p. 107).

Bhoja denies a multiplicity of rasas. He says srngara is the only Rasa: na hi bahavo rasah, api tv eka eva srngaro rasa ity agrato ’pi prabandhena pratipadayisyate (Srngara-prakasa 11.67 vrtti). Dr. Kane remarks:

We saw above (p. 248) that Bhoja developed in the Smgara- prakasa the theory (adumbrated in S.K.A.) that rasa is only one, that poetry is beautiful because of its presence, that the one rasa may be called srngara and is identified with abhimana and ahankara, that it pervades the soul of man owing to the impressions made on the soul in many births and that it is the one cause from which spring many good characteristics of the soul (raso ’bhimano ’hankarah srngara iti giyate \| yo ’rthas tasyanvayat kavyam kamaniyatvam asnute \|\| visistadrsta-janmayam janminam antaratmasu \| atma-samyag-gunodbhuter eko hetuh prakasate \|\| Sarasvati- kanthabharana 5.1-2). What Bhoja means by srngara being identified with ahankara is practically the same as holding that rasa realization is ananda-maya and brahma-sahodara. When Bhoja says that srngara is the only rasa he gives a different and philosophic significance to that word from what it ordinarily has viz. the love of man and woman. He keeps the two meanings apart.

In this context, the term rasa means “astonishing bliss”. For instance, Visvanatha relates Narayana Pandita’s opinion that there is only one rasa, astonishment: adbhutam evaha krti narayano rasam (Sahitya-darpana 3.3): This is the purport of Bhoja’s above disquisition on srngara.

In keeping with the tradition of Agni Purana, Bhoja also says srngara is a specific trait of the ego. He adds that srngara exists in the soul: atma-sthitam guna-visesam ahankrtasya srngaram ahur iha fivitam atma-yoneh \| tasyatma-sakti-rasaniyataya rasatvam yuktasya yena rasiko ’yam iti pravadah \|\| (Srngara- prakasa 1.3). The purport might be that the soul is love, but Bhoja’s philosophical stance in this regard is simply that moksa-srngara involves the ego whereas a liberated soul has no ego: ity-adi-yogya- cetaso ’bhimanah sa moksa-srngarah ity ucyate. tan-nivrttau ca asyahankara-virahan moksa eveti, yavad ahankaravams tavad ayam moksa-srngari, virahitahankaras tu mukta eveti (Srngara- prakasa 21.4 vrtti). Rather, Bhoja says lust is the primary goal of life: dharmartha-kama-laksanas tri-vargah purusarthah (Srngara- prakasa 22.1); tatrapi dharmartha-srngarayor hetu-bhutatvat kama-srngara eva phala-bhutatvat pradhanam (Srngara-prakasa 22.2 vrtti). In essence, Srngara-prakasa is an elaboration on Kama- sutra. Bhoja indicates that he took inspiration from Vatsyayana’s work: evam artham ca kamam ca dharmam capy acaran narah \| ihamutra ca nihsalyam atyantam sukham asnute \|\| (Kama-sutra 1.2.39) (Srngara-prakasa 22.1).

Bhoja’s example of rati which becomes srngara-rasa is Dandi’s example of the rasavat ornament:

*mrteti pretya sangantum yaya me maranam matam \|*  
*saisavanti maya labdha katham atraiva fanmani \|\|*

**\[Hearing the rumor that his beloved Vasava-datta had burned, Vatsaraja exclaims:\]**

**She passed away, therefore I think I should die to meet her again, in the afterlife. How could I possibly see that woman of Avanti once more in this life? (Kavyadarsa 2.280) (Srngara- prakasa 11.49)**

Bhoja’s standpoint that srngara-rasa is topmost was practically implemented by his entourage as well. For instance, this is Mammata’s example of the udatta ornament (exaggerated statement of opulence):

*muktah keli-visutra-hara-galitah sammarjambhir hrtah*  
*pratah prangana-simni manthara-calad-balanghri-laksarunah \|*  
*durad dadima-bija-sankita-dhiyah karsanti keli-suka*  
*yad vidvad-bhavanesu bhoja-nrpates tat tyaga-lilayitam \|\|*

**“Fallen from necklaces that snapped during amorous play, the pearls, reddened by the lac on the feet of sixteen-year-old girls slowly exiting at the edge of the courtyard in the early morning, are swept with brooms. The domesticated parrots pick them up thinking they are pomegranate seeds. What happens in the domiciles of the savants of King Bhoja acts like a pastime of the life of renunciation.” (Kavya-prakasa verse 505)**

The verse also features the bhrantiman ornament (mistaken perception): The parrots mistake the pearls from pomegranate seeds. It seems that Bhoja’s kingdom had a distinct reputation: Ruyyaka shows this verse, copied by Visvanatha, as an example of the vaidharmya variety of the prativastupama ornament (contrasted similarity between two sentences):

*cakorya eva caturas candrika-pana-karmani \|*  
*vinavantir na nipunah sudrso rata-narmani \|\|*

**“Only female cakora birds are expert in drinking moonlight. Except the women of Avanti, pretty-eyed women are not skilled in sexual humor.” (Alankara-sarvasva, KM pp. 74-75) (Sahitya- darpana 10.50)**

Dr. Kane speaks of Bhoja’s demise:

Bhoja suffered from a long illness and died in the midst of wars with Bhima, king of Gujarat and Kalacuri Karna, king of Tripuff (Prabandha-cintamani, Tawney’s tr. p. 4). The Sukrta- sankirtana (II. 16-18) narrates Bhoja’s defeat by king Bhima, and the Vadnagarprasasti of Kumarapala (1151 A.D.) in E.I. vol. I p. 293 speaks of Dhara being devastated by the cavalry of Bhima.

Dr. De writes:

We know that he fought with Calukya Jayasimha III between 1011 and 1019 A.D., and with the latter’s successor Somesvara (1042-1066 A.D.) who, according to Bihlana, took Dhara by storm and forced Bhoja to flee. Bihlana himself speaks of Bhoja as a contemporary whom he did not visit though he might have done so.

An important offshoot of Srngara-prakasa is Bhava-prakasana by Sarada-tanaya (13th century). Also called Bhava-prakasa and Bhava-prakasika, it is a treatise on dramaturgy and rasa: “Sarada- tanaya’s Bhava-prakasana, which deals with the same subject, constitutes really a summary of the important chapters of Bhoja.”

## 19. Rudra Bhatta

I J) udra-bhatta (eleventh century) wrote Srngara-tilaka. He says he centers on the topic of rasa in the context of poetry whereas Bharata discoursed on rasa with regard to dramaturgy: prayo natyam prati prokta bharatadyai rasa-sthitih \| yatha-mati mayapy esa kavyam prati nigadyate \|\| (1.5)

Rudra composed most of his illustrations. This verse incidentally illustrates the vinokti ornament (description of a thing in the absence of another):

*yaminrvenduna mukta narrva ramanam vina \|*  
*laksmir iva rte tyagan no van! bhati nirasa \|\|*

**Like the night without the moon, like a woman without a lover and like having wealth without self-restraint, words lacking a rasa are not resplendent. (1.6)**

Rudra’s treatise consists of three chapters: (I) The nine rasas, overview, the qualities of a lover, the four types of lovers (anukula, daksina, satha, dhrsta), the three companions of a lover (plthamardo vitas ceti vidusaka iti tridha, 1.30), the types of ladyloves, the eight states of ladyloves (abhisarika, etc.), (II) Vipralambha, the ten stages of vipralambha, the six means for pacifying a woman in a pique, (III) Elaboration on hasya-rasa and so on; incompatibility between rasas; the vyabhicari-bhavas; and the four vrttis (Kaisiki, Sattvati, Arabhati, Bharati).

This is the invocatory verse:

*srngari girijanane sa-karuno ratyam pravlrah smare*  
*btbhaiso ’sthibhir utpham ca bhaya-krn murtyadbhutas tungaya \|*  
*raudro daksa-vimardane ca hasa-krn nagnah prasantas cirad*  
*ittham sarva-rasasrayah pasupatir bhuyat satam bhutaye \|\|*

**He is in love with ParvatT, felt pity for Rati, was too much of a warrior for Cupid, is loathsome with his skull ornaments, is frightful with his snakes, is awe-inspiring with his tall body, was furious in killing Daksa, evokes ridicule by being naked, and has been peaceful for ages. May Siva, who thus embodies all the rasas, increase the prosperity of the righteous. (Srngara- tilaka 1.1)**

Rudra Bhatta combined poetics and erotics. Over the centuries, Srngara-tilaka became a mine of information for a host of other works on the topic of rasa. As in Srngara-prakasa, in Srngara- tilaka the line of reasoning is that ethics lead to prosperity, prosperity to love, and love gives rise to happiness, therefore srngara is the topmost form of enjoyment (rasa): dharmad artho ’rthatah kamah kamat sukha-phalodayah \| sadhlyan esa tat-siddhyai srngaro nayako rasah \|\| (1.20).

In essence, Rudra’s Srngara-tilaka is an elaboration of the chapters on rasa in Rudrata’s Kavyalankara. Rudra Bhatta gave illustrative examples. Another difference is that Rudra redefined Bharata’s vrttis to make them applicable in poetry by correlating them with rasas, but they overlap. His Kaisiki is a construction of madhurya- guna for srngara, hasya, and karuna (3.38-39). His Arabhati is a construction of ojas guna for raudra, bhayanaka, and blbhatsa (3.40-41). The Sattvati mostly consists of harsa and ascarya and is for vlra, raudra, adbhuta, and santa; in the Sattvati, the meanings are not too subtle and the sounds are pleasant to hear: natigudhartha-sampattih sravya-sabda-manorama \| vlre raudre ’dbhute sante vrttir esa mata yatha \|\| (3.43). The Bharati is for exalted persons such as a king, a god or the Lord: pradhana- purusa-praya sad-vakrokti-nirantara \| bharatlyam bhaved vrttir vlra-hasyadbhutasraya \|\| (3.44).

The anthologies often confuse Rudra with Rudrata, but all historians on poetics say the two are distinct. For instance, Rudra mentions nine rasas, in contrast to Rudrata’s ten. Srngara-tilaka 1.21-22 is almost the same as Kavyalankara 12.4-5, and Srngara-tilaka 1.51 is almost identical with Kavyalankara 12.31. And both Rudra and Rudrata say ladyloves are divided in three categories: svaklya (the wife), paraklya (unmarried woman; or another’s wife), and vesya (courtezan). Rudrata does not exalt the courtezans whereas Rudra-bhatta speaks favorably of them. Dr. Kane notes:

Compare Rudrata 12.39 (sarvangana tu vesya samyag asau lipsate dhanam kamat \| nirguna-guninos tasya na dvesyo na priyah kascit II) with Srngara-tilaka 1.62-63 (samanya vanita vesya sa dravyam param icchati \| nirgune ’pi na vidveso na rago ’sya guniny api \|\| tat-svarupam idam proktam kaiscid brumo vayam punah I). The Srngara-tilaka winds up by saying about courtesans ‘sarvasvam etas tad aho smarasya (1.69).’

The word kaiscit in the Srngara-tilaka is very suspicious. It almost seems certain that Srngara-tilaka refers to Rudrata’s words. \[...\]

The only alternative is to suppose that one of the works is based on the other. Taking all the above circumstances together I think that Rudra is later than Rudrata, elaborates the dicta of Rudrata with illustrations, bases his Srngara-tilaka on the Kavyalankara and flourished between 950-1100 A.D.

According to Dr. Kane, Hemacandra (Kavyanusasana, KM p. 110) was the first poetical rhetorician to cite Srngara-tilaka (1998: 159).

## 20. Ksemendra

He was a polyhistor at the court of King Ananta of Kashmir (1028-1063 CE). Ksemendra was the author of a plethora of works on different subjects. In poetics, he is known for his Aucitya-vicara-carca and Kavi-kanthabharana. In addition, he is famous for Brhat-katha-manfari and so on.

Owing to Aucitya-vicara-carca, Ksemendra is renowned as the head of the Aucitya school. There is no official follower of this school. In other treatises, appropriateness shines by its absence in the topic of dosa (literary blemish). Ksemendra’s discourse on appropriateness centers on rasa:

*aucityasya camatkara-karinas caru-carvane \|*  
*rasa-fivita-bhutasya vicaram kurute ’dhuna \|\|*

**“Now let us examine appropriateness: It is the life of rasa. Appropriateness brings about astonishment in the relishment of literary beauty.” (Aucitya-vicara-carca 3)**

Dr. Kane expounds:

His contribution to Poetics was meagre and he did not exert any appreciable influence over the Alankara-sastra. In his Suvrtta- tilaka (divided into three vinyasas) he makes very interesting remarks upon metres, gives directions as to their employment and points out in what metre certain poets excelled e.g. Abhinanda in anustup, Panini in upajati, Bharavi in vamsa- stha, Kalidasa in mandakranta, Ratnakara in vasanta-tilaka, Bhavabhuti in sikharini Rajasekhara in sardula-vikridita.

\[...\] In the Aucitya-vicara-carca he simply develops what the Dhvany-aloka had laid down (in III. 7-14 and pp. 174-186) and which the Dhv. had summarized in the verse: anaucityad rte nanyad rasa-bhangasya karanam \| prasiddhaucitya-bandhas tu rasasyopanisat para \|\| \[3.10-14 vrtti\].

\[...\] In the Brhat-katha-manjari he tells us that he learnt Sahitya from Abhinavagupta: ‘srutvabhinava-guptakhyat sahityam bodha-varidheh I’. He was originally a Saiva but was converted to the Vaisnava faith in later life by Somacarya. He calls himself Vyasa-dasa in almost all works.

\[.\] The Aucitya-vicara-carca and Kavi-kanthabharana were composed by him in the time of king Ananta \[.\]. King Ananta ruled in Kashmir from 1028 to 1063 A.D. and crowned his son Kalasa in 1063. \[.\] As he was a pupil of Abhinavagupta whose literary activity lay between 980-1020, Ksemendra must have been born about 990 A.D. and died sometime after 1066 A.D.

Ksemendra says appropriateness is the life of poetry:

*kavyasyalam alankaraih kim mithya-ganitair gunaih \|*  
*yasya jivitam aucityam vicintyapi na drsyate \|\|*

**“Even after looking into it, if appropriateness, the life of poetry, is not perceived in the poetry, what is the use of the poetry’s ornaments and qualities, which are thus falsely counted?” (Aucitya-vicara- carca 4).**

Except rasa, Ksemendra does not take interest in dhvani. His epilogue of five verses aside, Aucitya-vicara-carca consists of thirty-nine definitional verses along with illustrations and expla­nations. The thirty-nine karikas are the ten introductory karikas and the twenty-nine karikas that expound the twenty-seven categories.

To dissect appropriateness, Ksemendra divides poetry in twenty­seven categories, and for each one provides both good examples and bad examples from the works of classical poets and from his own. Those categories are: pada (declined word), vakya (sentence), prabandhartha (the sense in a multitude of sentences), guna (literary quality), alankara (ornament), rasa (esthetic relish), kriya (action), karaka (meaning of a case ending), linga (gender), vacana (number), visesana (modifier), upasarga (prefix), nipata (particle, such as ca and va), kala (time), desa (place), kula (group of persons; lineage), vrata (vow), tattva (a description of someone or of something), sattva (the description of someone’s power), abhipraya (intention), svabhava (nature), sara-sangraha (a summary of the essence of a topic), pratibha (the poet’s creative intelligence), avastha (situation; condition owing to age), vicara (consideration), nama (name), and asirvada (blessing) (Aucitya- vicara-carca 8-10).

Ksemendra specifies that such categories are infinite (Aucitya- vicara-carca 39). As an example of inappropriateness in srngara- rasa, Ksemendra shows this verse by Kalidasa:

*varna-prakarse sati karnikaram*  
*dunoti nirgandhataya sma cetah \|*  
*prayena samagrya-vidhau gunanam*  
*paranmukhl visva-srjah pravrttih \|\|*

**Translation:**

**When its color and shape became eminent, the karnikara flower pained the mind due to its lack of scent. When the required set of qualities is almost there, usually the ways of the creator become adverse.**

**Versified translation:**

**How sighed the spirit o’ver that loveliest flower**  
**That boasts no fragrance to enrich its dower !**  
**For Nature, wisest mother, oft prefers**  
**To part more fairly those good gifts of hers.**  
**(Kumara-sambhava 3.28)**

Ksemendra comments:

*atra kevala-karnikara-kusuma-varnana- matrena vidhatr-vacyata-garbhenaiva prastuta-srngaranupayogina tad-uddipana-vibhavocitam na kincid abhihitam.*

**“Here no suitable uddipana of srngara-rasa whatsoever is denoted by the mere description of just the karnikara flower (a yellow trumpet flower that grows in a tree). That description contains criticism toward the creator and is not useful for srngara-rasa, the actual topic” (Aucitya-vicara-carca 16).**

Occurrences of criticism toward fate or toward the creator are classed in Ananda’s and Mammata’s irsya variety of vipralambha. Other examples are Bhagavatam 10.31.15 and 10.39.19, but here the context is not vipralambha. Moreover, the verse features the arthantara-nyasa ornament (corroboration). There is also the punar- uktavad-abhasa ornament (seeming redundancy): vidhi (Brahma) and visva-srk (creator of the world) are synonymous in one sense, but here vidhi is used in a different sense (the requirement).

Next, Ksemendra shows this verse by the same author to illustrate appropriateness in srngara-rasa:

*balendu-vakrany avikasa-bhavad*  
*babhuh palasany atilohitani \|*  
*sadyo vasantena samagatanam*  
*nakha-ksataniva vana-sthalinam \|\|*

**Translation:**

**Since they had not opened, the very reddish palasa blossoms were curved like a crescent moon. They were splendid. At a cursory look, they seemed to be nail marks made by the spring­lover on the woodland-ladyloves.**

**Versified translation:**

**There from the tree Palasa blossoms spread,**  
**Curved like the crescent Moon, their rosiest red, With opening buds that looked as if young Spring Had pressed his nails there in his dallying. (Kumara-sambhava 3.29)**

Ksemendra comments: atra parvatya paramesvarasyabhilasa- srngare vaksyamane prathamam uddipana-vibhava-bhutasya vasantasya varnanayam kamukadhyaropena vana-sthali- lalananam kutila-lohita-palasa-kalikabhir nava-sangama- yogya-nakha-ksatany utpreksitani paramam aucitya-carutam pratipadayanti, “On account of the curved and reddish palasa blossoms, the nail marks, fitting occurrences on a new meeting, of women in the forms of the woodland are fancifully imagined by means of the superimposition of a lover. Given that the romance, consisting of deep longing, between Parvati and Siva is going to be stated, mentioning such nail marks at first, in the description of spring, an uddipana, implements the highest beauty of appropriateness” (Aucitya-vicara-carca 16).

In the above verse, the appropriateness is in the form of ornaments: upama (simile) and utpreksa (fanciful imagination). Herein lies Ksemendra’s contribution to poetics. He showed that a sthayi- bhava can be raised to the level of rasa (relishment) simply by the use of ornaments, without the need to portray vibhava, anubhava or vyabhicari. This is expounded in the section on Jagannatha.

Further, Ksemendra equated an unhappy ending (such as bathos) with inappropriateness, due to a lack of poetical resplendence (Aucitya-vicara-carca 16; 34). By contrast, this is his example of an appropriate usage of santa-rasa:

*bhoge roga-bhayam sukhe ksaya-bhayam vitte ’gnibhubhrd-bhayam*  
*dasye svami-bhayam gune khala-bhayam vamse kuyosid-bhayam \|*  
*mane mlani-bhayam jaye ripu-bhayam kaye krtantad bhayam*  
*sarvam nama bhave bhaved bhayam aho vairagyam evabhayam \|\|*

**In enjoyment, there is fear of disease. In happiness, there is fear it is going to cease. When one is wealthy, there is fear the government will burn it. In addition, employees fear their employer. And when someone displays a quality, such as compassion, there is fear bad people will take advantage of it. In a respectable family, there is fear a daughter will become depraved. When people are highly respected, they fear the respect will decrease. There is fear of enemies even in victory over them. As regards the body, there is fear of death. Everything in material life involves some degree of fear. But, lo and behold, dispassion is fearlessness. (Ksemendra’s Catur- varga-sangraha) (cited in Aucitya-vicara-carca 16)**

The composition is enhanced by the yamaka “bhave bhave” in the fourth line, and so on. Dr. Keith gives details about Ksemendra’s other poetical treatise:

Ksemendra is a better critic than a poet. The Kavi- kanthabharana discusses the possibility of becoming a poet, the issue of borrowing on a small or large scale, and the legitimacy of doing so in the case of the epic and similar works, the charm of poetry with illustration of its ten aspects, the defects and excellencies with regard to sense, sound, or sentiment, and the various arts which a poet ought to be familiar with.

Ksemendra is often confused for Ksemeraja. Dr. Sushil Kumar De elucidates:

Peterson proposed, against the opinion of Buhler, who appears to have left the question open, the identification of Ksemendra with Ksemaraja, the Saiva philosopher of Kashmir, who was a pupil of Abhinavagupta, and who wrote, among numerous other works, a commentary on the Siva-sutra and on Abhinavagupta’s Paramartha-sara. Stein supports this identification, but Peterson himself appears to admit later on that his own theory is doubtful. In his Aucitya- vicara, Ksemendra pays homage to Acyuta or Visnu; but we know that he was, like his father, a Saiva in his youth but was converted afterwards into Vaisnavism, as he himself indicates, by Somacarya. \[...\] We know nothing, on the other hand, of Ksemaraja’s genealogy or personal history. But we are told at the end of the Brhat-katha-manjari that Ksemendra learnt sahitya from Abhinavagupta, while Ksemaraja at the end of his Svacchandoddyota (as well as in the colophon to his Stava- cintamani) is described as sisya of the same great philosopher. It is worth noting, however, that while Ksemendra’s surname Vyasadasa is given in all his works (with the exception of his Kala-vilasa), it does not occur in any of Ksemaraja’s philosophical treatises.

## 21. Mahima Bhatta

Mahima-bhatta (c. 1020-1060 CE) was another Kashmiri who opposed the Dhvani theory. His treatise is called Vyakti-viveka (the discernment regarding Suggestiveness). In poetics, at first the term vyakti was used specifically with regard to the “manifestation” of an implied sense. Over time, the term vyakti became a synonym of vyanjana (Suggestiveness).

According to Mahima Bhatta, word and sense cannot be suggestive (vyanjaka): Rather, the suggestiveness relates to the mind, therefore it is a form of inference. Mahima Bhatta’s sole purpose was to establish that an implied sense is arrived at by inference. For the most part he was an adherent of Sankuka’s viewpoint: “He seems to have followed Sankuka in regarding even rasa as inferred.”

There are three chapters in Vyakti-viveka. In the first one, he argues that dhvani is included in anumana (inference). In the second, he expounds inappropriateness; there are two varieties: (1) Inappropriate meaning (also called antaranga anaucitya), such as the improper usage of a vibhava, anubhava or vyabhicari in the manifestation of a rasa—that topic had already been expounded by Anandavardhana—and (2) Inappropriate word (also called bahiranga anaucitya): The occurrence of a literary fault. In the third chapter he gives forty examples to illustrate the inclusion of dhvani in anumana. The work includes 146 explanatory verses (sangraha-slokas).

In the first chapter, he finds ten faults in the Dhvani-karika: kathita dhvani-laksmaniti dasa dosah (1.23). Then Mahima sets forth his own methodology. He says an implied sense is an inferred meaning and figurative usage too is a form of inference. In that regard he says there are two forms of Indication (laksana, also called bhakti): padartha (the meaning of a word) and vakyartha (the meaning of a sentence). Dr. Kane explains:

The position of the Vyakti-viveka-kara is that he does not dispute that rasa is the soul of poetry, but the point on which he lays stress is that the essence of poetry (viz. rasa etc.) is grasped by anumana and not by an independent power of words such as vyanjana.

His own position is that words have a single power (abhidha), that the suggested sense (pratiyamana) is conveyed by the expressed sense through the process of inference (anumana) and that word and sense are not vyanjaka.

So it will be noticed that, according to his view, sabda has only two senses: vacya and anumeya ; the laksana of other writers will be included under anumana. He says that in such verses as ‘suvarna-puspam prthivim cinvanti purusas trayah ’ (example of avivaksita-vacya-dhvani in Dhv. p. 58), ‘patyuh siras-candra-kalam anena’ (Dhv. p. 267), ‘evam vadini devarsau’ (Dhv. p. 124), the suggested sense is really inferred: atra hi sarvatra sulabha vibhutayah suradmam ity ayam artho ’numiyata ity etad vitanisyate (Vyakti-viveka p. 9). As vacya sense and pratlyamana sense stand in the relation of linga and lingin the process is anumana: ‘vacya-pratlyamanayor vaksyamana-kramena linga-lingi-bhavasya samarthanat sarvasyaiva dhvaner anumanantar-bhavah samanvito bhavati tasya ca tad-apeksaya maha-visayatvat’ (Vyakti-viveka p. 12) \[...\]. He says that in many instances of Dhvani cited in the Dhvany-aloka the ultimate vyangya sense is not suggested by the expressed sense but between the two one or more inferences intervene (as in ‘vaniaaa hatthi-danta’ Dhv. p. 157). In gaur vahikah, the ultimate sense is arrived at by anumana; as the two cannot in reality be identical, one comes to the conclusion that they possess similar qualities: tasmad yo ’yam vahikadau gavadi-sadharmyavagamah sa tattvaropanyathanupapatti- parikalpito ’numanasyaiva visayah na sabda-vyaparasyeti sthitam (p. 24). The same reasoning the Vyakti-viveka applies to gangayam ghosah. It asserts, by using dhvani-karikas themselves with a slight turn of expression, that dhvani is identical with bhakti ‘bhaktya bibharti caikatvam rupabhedad ayam dhvanih \| na ca navyapty-ativyaptyor abhaval laksyate taya \|\| suvarna-puspam ity-adau na cavyaptih prasajyate \| yatah padartha-vakyarthayor bhedad bhaktir dvidhodita \|\| atasmims tat-samaropo bhakter laksanam isyate \| arthantara- pratity-arthah prakarah so’pi sasyate \|\|’ (Vyakti. p. 26; compare Dhvani-karika 1.17). He opposes (pp. 27-28) the views of those who think that there is a single pervasive power of words which conveys what is called the vacya sense and the implied sense and who rely upon the instance of an arrow. He controverts the position of the Vakrokti- fivita (karika 1.7-8 sabdarthau sahitau vakra.) and says that if what is conveyed by the striking mode of speech adopted by the poet is different from the plain expressed sense, then vakrokti also is included like dhvani under anumana (p. 28). He denies that words have any other power than abhidha \[...\]. He ridicules the Dhvani-kara for not giving a definition of kavya in general and for dilating upon the two varieties of it, dhvani and guni-bhuta-vyangya, in the absence of a general definition: ‘kim ca kavyasya svarupam vyutpadayitu-kamena matimata tal-laksanam eva samanyenakhyatavyam... yat tu tad anakhyayaiva tayoh pradhanetara-bhava-kalpanena prakara-dvayam uktam tad aprayofakam eva \|’ (p. 32).

The major poetical rhetoricians argued against the Anumana- vadins. Sankuka lived in the first quarter of the ninth century; Anandavardhana attempted a refutation of his standpoint. In short, Anandavardhana said the relation between a meaning and its implied sense is not invariable, whereas in anumana the linga always implies a lingin, like smoke always reveals the presence of fire. In addition, in poetics the lingin (the implied sense) is not the source of the linga (the revealer). Dr. Sushil Kumar De writes:

The process of inference in poetry by which the unexpressed may be thus reached is presumably the ordinary process of syllogistic reasoning, which consists in the invariable concomitance (vyapti) of the middle (linga) and the major (lingin) terms. The Dhvani or suggested sense is the lingin, and its suggestors (viz. word and sense) are apparently its linga. The invariable concomitance is ascertained in three ways, viz. by anupalabdhi (non-cognition), tadatmya (identity) and tad- utpatti (causation). In reply to Mahima-bhatta’s position, it has been shown that none of these means of proving a syllogism is applicable to establishing the invariable concomitance between the linga sabdarthau and the lingin dhvani.

In a Vedic inference, the reason must be a universal rule. To counter that, Mahima-bhatta coined the term kavyanumiti (poetical inference). But even then the issue of an absence of invariable causality in deriving an implied sense in poetics was not solved.

In addition to Anandavardhana’s retort, Mammata said anumana is inapplicable in poetics to begin with because the validity of a speaker’s assertion in the verse itself—when some character is quoted—needs to be proven in order to have a first premise.

Mahima Bhatta says that whenever a sthayi is enhanced by appropriate vibhavas and so on, or by acting techniques, the rasa is inferred, and the two factors necessary for a logical conclusion, namely vyapti (invariable concomitance, e.g. where there is smoke there is fire) and paksa-dharmata (existence of the attribute in the subject, e.g. there is smoke on the mountain), are met. Sankuka said that in a drama the spectators infer the character’s rasa in the actor. Sankuka and Mahima Bhatta’s explanations are in line with Bharata Muni’s rasa-sutra, but Visvanatha Kaviraja states that Mahima Bhatta used the term rasa only with regard to a sthayi that has become manifest by vibhavas, anubhava and vyabhicari, whereas the rasa everyone is interested in is rapture yet the latter is not inferrable. Visvanatha says there is no invariable concomitance between perceiving the existence of a rasa in a text or in a play and being moved by the rasa. In effect, Visvanatha agrees with Mahima Bhatta’s viewpoint.

Moreover, at the beginning of the experience of rasa, there is no doubt that a certain degree of inference is involved in perceiving an implied meaning, such as the sthayi-bhava, but this kind of inference is based on the predisposition. Therefore it is not like the inference used in philosophy. In essence, an implied meaning can be an assumption, whereas a meaning obtained by inference must be certain, otherwise there is no point in using the term inference: Anumana is one of thepramanas (a means of acquiring knowledge). The fivefold syllogism in Vedanta is well-known. In addition, Visvanatha Kaviraja writes: anumanam nama paksa- sattva-sapaksa-sattva-vipaksa-vyavrttatva-visistal lingal lingino jnanam, “Inference is the knowledge of the lingin derived from a linga, characterized by paksa-sattva (related to the thing under discussion), sapaksa-sattva (functioning in relation to something connected to the thing under discussion), and vipaksa-vyavrttatva (inconsistent with something opposite to the thing under discussion)” (Sahitya-darpana 5.4).

For his part, Kavi Karnapura refutes Anumana-vada by saying that since an inference involves a formal syllogism, each implied sense would have to be proved that way, therefore the process of Suggestiveness is more convenient.

Mimamsakas and Logicians are derided in poetics because perceiving a meaning in the scope of srngara-rasa involves intui­tion, which occurs on the strength of a predisposition. The required predisposition is essential on the topic of rasa, but Mahima Bhatta omitted it, and that is the main problem in his system. Bhatta Nayaka had filled that gap in the refutations of the Dhvani theory by using the concept called sadharanya (generalization, identification), but Mahima Bhatta ignored him out of vanity: “Mahima-bhatta, who had a similar object of combating the Dhvani theory, claims entire originality for his own treatment by boasting that he had never looked into the Darpana at all.”.

Mahima Bhatta cites this verse by Anandavardhana to illustrate that a rasa is always inferrable:

*patyuh siras-candra-kalam anena*  
*sprseti sakhya parihasa-purvam \|*  
*sa ranjayitva caranau krtaslr*  
*malyena tam nirvacanam jaghana \|\|*

**As ParvatT was applying lac to her feet, her girlfriend jokingly said: “To prove that you put your feet on his head, touch his crescent moon with them.” ParvatT then hit her with a garland without saying a word. (Dhvany-aloka 3.40) (Vyakti-viveka 1.20 vrtti, TSS edition p. 9)**

Mahima Bhatta comments that here many vyabhicari-bhavas evoke Parvati’s love for Siva.

However, another problem with Anumiti-vada regards the vyabhicari-bhavas: It is not always possible to always point out precisely which ones occur. In this matter, above Mahima Bhatta uses the word adi (and so on). Mahima Bhatta only concerned himself with inferring the rasa. Next, he gives another example of an inferred rati:

*evam vadini devarsauparsve pitur adhomukhl \|*  
*llla-kamala-patrani ganayamasa parvatl \|\|*

**While Narada was telling her father that she should marry Siva, ParvatT lowered her face and counted the petals of her play lotus. (Kumara-sambhava 6.84) (Dhvany-aloka 2.22) (Vyakti- viveka 1.20 vrtti, TSS p. 10)**

There is no hard-and-fast rule that one particular vyabhicari-bhava is inferred from this verse. Abhinavagupta says the vyabhicari- bhava is bashfulness (arthantaram iti lajjatmakam, Locana 2.22). Parvati experienced a rise of autsukya (eagerness, longing): She was overjoyed (harsa) to the point of being simple-minded.

In the second chapter, Mahima Bhatta expounds five literary faults: vidheyavimarsa (improperly considered predicate), prakrama- bheda (broken sequence), krama-bheda (lack of sequence), paunaruktya (useless repetition), and vacyavacana (the improper usage of an ambiguously double-meaning word). Mammata reiterated most of Mahima’s methodology on this topic:

Further, in the seventh ullasa the Kavya-prakasa seems to follow the vyakti-viveka very closely in pointing out dosas. If this is the case as appears very likely, then Mahima-bhatta flourished between 1020 and 1050 A.D.

The first fault vidheyavimarsa is treated of in pp. 37-58. He takes the verse samrambhah kari-kita-megha \[...\] cited in the Vakrokti-jivita (I. p. 17) as a faultless piece of poetry and shows that it contains three cases of vidheyavimarsa. The first is that the compound (nan-samasa) asamrabdhavan is improper, the second is that the relative pronoun in yo’sau has no corresponding demonstrative pronoun (sah) in the verse, and the third is that the compound ambika-kesari is improper, as the word ambika, being a member of a compound, is subordinate and the sense also is therefore subordinate and not at once perceived as principal (while Ambika is really the principal object of adoration to the poet). He suggests (on p. 57) how the verse should be read to avoid these faults.

Moreover, Ruyyaka is the author of the commentary on Mahima Bhatta’s treatise:

Even his commentator does not appear to possess much sympathy for his somewhat extreme view, and Mahima-bhatta is rather unique in having no followers in later literature. The commentator referred to has been identified with some reason with Ruyyaka.

Jayaratha distinctly ascribes the commentary on the Vyakti- viveka to Ruyyaka: ‘vacyasya pratiyamanena tadatmya-tad- utpatty-abhavadi neha pratanyata iti vyakti-viveka-vicare hi mayaivaitad vitatya nirnitam iti bhavah’ .

Furthermore, Rewa Prasada Dwivedi remarks: “Therefore, one other great rhetorician, Mahima-bhatta, came forward with his theory—“Metre too is an alankara of poetry” (Vyakti-viveka, Chapter \|\| Page 181, 235 in my edition). It is, of course, a reality. That is why even an ordinary statement creates an illusion of poetry if versified like the Samskrta lexicons and other versified topics. One would be aware of the fact that music survives in prose too, since words can never be separated from the sound, and all that is svara or musical touch.”

Kavi Kamapura says the anumana ornament involves three factors: paksa (the thing under discussion), sadhya (the idea to be proved) and sadhana (or hetu, linga) (the proof). In usage, however, a word such as “therefore” often signifies the anumana ornament. It only involves the proof of a stated idea, not the inference of a rasa.

(Alankara-kaustubha 8.224-225)

## 22. Mammata

Mammata (c. 1030-1100 CE) wrote Kavya-prakasa, the bible of Sanskrit poetics, sometime between 1050 and 1100 CE. The ending ta in his name indicates that Mammata was a Kashmiri. The word mamma is the Prakrit rendering of the Sanskrit marma (vital part; secret, mystery). Mammata revolutionized poetry, not by propounding a new theory, but by including all aspects of poetical theory into one treatise and by fine-tuning everything. In short, he systemized the Dhvani theory, perfected the definitions of ornaments of the Alankara school and provided outstanding citations as examples. Dr. Sushil Kumar De explains why Mammata’s magnum opus has been popular:

The Kavya-prakasa, consisting of ten Ullasas, traverses the whole field of Sanskrit Poetics (with the exception of dramaturgy) in only 143 Karikas and about 620 illustrations derived from various sources. As it combines the merit of fulness with that of conciseness, it became one of the classic works of Sanskrit Poetics and Rhetoric which has always maintained a great authority and popularity throughout India. It sums up and explains in the succinct form of a brilliant text­book all the previous speculations on the subject, becoming in its turn the starting point of endless exegetic works and text­books. As such it occupies a unique position in the history of Sanskrit Alankara literature.

There is hardly any other technical work in Sanskrit which has been so much commented upon as the Kavya-prakasa, and no less than seventy different commentaries and glosses will be found noticed in the various reports, catalogues and journals relating to Sanskrit MSS. They count as their authors not only independent and notable writers on Poetics like Ruyyaka and Visvanatha, but also men having other literary interests, like the Naiyayika Jagadisa and Narasimha Thakkura, the grammarian Nagoji Bhatta, the Mimamsaka Kamalakara Bhatta, the Vaisnava Baladeva Vidyabhusana, as well as the Tantrika Gokulanatha.

Dr. Kane notes:

The work is divided into ten ullasas and comprises as usual three parts, the karikas, the vrtti and the examples, all of which are taken from other works (except probably a few simple examples under upama, vyatireka, etc.). \[...\] Though much of Mammata’s treatment is based upon the works of his predecessors, such as the Dhvany-aloka, Udbhata, Bhamaha, Rudrata (from whose work about 30 verses are quoted), Vamana, Abhinavagupta, yet he is a man of independent views and his respect for these ancient authorities does not preclude him from criticizing them when occasion demands.

Mammata was a man of great erudition and vast reading. He seems to have been a profound student of grammar also. \[.\] He was styled Rajanaka, which is a title borne by Kashmirian brahmanas even now. It means ‘almost a king’. \[.\] Except the Bhagavad-gita there is hardly any other work in classical Sanskrit that has so many commentaries on it.

Before composing Kavya-prakasa, Mammata wrote Sabda- vyapara-vicara, also named Sabda-vyapara-paricaya, where he expounded the rhetorical functions (abhidha, laksana, vyanjana). He also discussed that topic in the second chapter of his masterpiece.

This is Mammata’s definition of poetry: tad adosau sabdarthau sa-gunav analankrtlpunah kvapi, “Poetry is faultless sounds and meanings which have a literary quality and an ornament, although sometimes there is no ornament” (Kavya-prakasa 1.4). Mammata specifies that if there is no ornament, the text must have a first-rate rasa-dhvani in order to be called poetry.

Kavi Karnapura found fault with that definition: “tad adosau sabdarthau sa-gunav analankrtl punah kvapi” iti laksanam “kuranga-nayana” ity-adav api paryaptam bhavati, sa- gunalankara-nirdosa-sabdarthatvat, “Mammata’s definition is overinclusive because it also applies to a compound such as kuranga-nayana (doe-eyed woman), since it has a quality (madhurya-guna) and an ornament (simile) and is faultless” (Alankara-kaustubha 1.7).

Therefore Visvanatha Kaviraja commented: tad adosav iti karikayah phalitarthah asvadatmakam vakyam kavyam iti, “The resultant meaning of Mammata’s definition is: “A relishable vakya is poetry”” (Kavya-prakasa-darpana 1.4). A vakya (statement, lit. sentence) must have these three characteristics: akanksa (mutual requirement of words), yogyata (congruity) and sannidhi (proximity). Visvanatha thus established a middle ground between Mammata’s definition and his own, stated ahead (p. 546).

Mammata’s definition is wide enough to include third-rate poetry, where a rasa is not essential. Mammata respected old school poetry by turning Anandavardhana’s third category of poetry into a category of poetry proper, whereas Anandavardhana did not acknowledge it as real poetry.

Mammata invented three ornaments: ete ca rasavad-ady- alankarah. yadyapi bhavodaya-bhava-sandhi-bhava-sabalatvani nalankarataya uktani tathapi kascit bruyad ity evam uktam, “These are the ornaments beginning from rasavat. Although bhavodaya, bhava-sandhi, and bhava-sabalya were not listed as ornaments by earlier poetical theorists, something had to be said, thus they are mentioned that way” (Kavya-prakasa, verse 123 vrtti); Mammata showed with examples that when either bhavodaya, bhava-sandhi or bhava-sabalya is second-rate—meaning it is a subsidiary aspect of another rasa—it should be classed as an alankara (ornament), not as a vyabhicari-bhava. Ruyyaka and Visvanatha implemented this methodology by naming them “the bhavodaya ornament” and so forth in their respective chapters on ornaments.

In addition, Mammata gave some prominence to the concept of bhakti (devotion) by including it in the deva-visaya subcategory of the sthayi-bhava called rati (affection), but as such Mammata implied that bhakti cannot reach the level of rasa. Further, in explaining the subcategories of rati, Mammata included the concept of vatsalya (parental affection) with the wordputra (son): adi-sabdan muni-guru-nrpa-putradi-visaya (4.35).

## Four Theories of Rasa

Mammata relates four opinions—those of Lollata, Sankuka, Nayaka, and Abhinavagupta—regarding Bharata Muni’s rasa- sutra (Natya-sastra 6.32). Those four were Kashmiris; Lollata, Sankuka and Abhinavagupta commented on Natya-sastra, and in his Hrdaya-darpana Nayaka commented on Bharata’s rasa-sutra. Mammata drew from Abhinava’s Locana and from Abhinava’s paraphrase of the opinions of those three in Abhinava-bharati. Dr. Kane remarks: “The important questions are: ‘where does rasa reside,’ ‘what the nature of rasa is’ and ‘how it is evolved and realized’.” This is Mammata’s disquisition:

## Lollata

*uktam hi bharatena, vibhavanubhava-vyabhicari-samyogad rasa-nispattih. etad vivrnvate. vibhavair lalanodyanadibhir alambanoddipana-karanai raty-adiko bhavo janitah anubhavaih kataksa-bhujaksepa-prabhrtibhih karyaih pratiti-yogyah krtah vyabhicaribhir nirvedadibhih sahakaribhir upacito mukhyaya vrttya ramadav anukarye tad-rupatanusandhanan nartake ’pi pratiyamano rasa iti bhatta-lollata-prabhrtayah.*

**Bharata said: vibhavanubhava-vyabhicari-samyogad rasa- nispattih, “The effectuation of rasa occurs from the blend of vibhava, anubhava, and vyabhicari-bhava” (Natya-sastra 6.32). They expound this.**

**Bhatta Lollata and his followers say: A sthayi-bhava which is: (1) brought to light by vibhavas, the causes: an alambana such as a young woman and an uddipana such as a flower garden, (2) rendered capable of being perceived by means of anubhavas, i.e. the effects such as a sidelong glance and a brisk gesture with the arms, (3) enhanced by vyabhicari-bhavas, the assistants such as nirveda (self-disparagement), and (4) perceived, by the main literary function (mukhya vrtti), in the character that is portrayed, such as Rama, and even in the actor because he takes interest in being the form of that character, is the rasa.(Kavya-prakasa 4.28)**

Dr. Kane explains:

Briefly put, Lollata’s view is as follows: Rasa in the primary sense belongs to the hero, Rama etc. (i.e. Rama loves Sita and the dramatist describes this love in appropriate words). The spectator ascribes to the actor, on account of the latter’s clever acting, the same mental attitude that belonged to Rama and the spectator’s apprehension of imputed love in the actor brings to him delight. This is the meaning of the words vibhava... msa-nispattih. This view does not treat of rasa as a matter of the spectator’s aesthetic appreciation of the inner meaning of the representation. All that Lollata means is that the spectator is delighted by the fact that the actor cleverly represents by his acting that he is Rama himself, feels the same love that the historic or legendary person (Rama) felt towards the heroine. The spectator is charmed by this. \[...\] Here real rasa (srngara) is produced in Rama and therefore this view is called utpatti- vada.

Lollata is of the opinion that in a drama the locus of the rasa is the characters (anukarya) and the actors (anukartr). Abhinavagupta points out that Lollata’s viewpoint is the standard interpretation of Bharata’s sutra and was already present in seed form in the works of the ancients such as Dandin: sa cobhayor api, anukarye anukartary api canusandhana-balat iti. cirantananam cayam eva paksah. tatha hi dandina svalankara-laksane ’bhyadhayi “ratih srngaratam gata rupa-bahulya-yogena” \[Kavyadarsa 2.281 \] iti "adhiruhya param kotim kopo raudratmatam gatah ” \[Kavyadarsa 2.283\] ity-adi ca (Abhinava-bharati 6.32). Dr. Sushil Kumar De expounds:

Lollata, in explaining Bharata’s sutra, took the vibhava as the direct cause (karana) of Rasa, which therefore is an effect (anukarya or utpadya), and the term nispatti of Bharata should be explained as utpatti or pusti. The Rasa, found in characters like Rama, is attributed to the actor, who imitates the characters in form, dress and action, and thereby charms the spectator. Mammata and his followers make this interpretation of Lollata’s view more clear by saying that the permanent mood or sthayin is directly connected (mukhyataya vrttya = saksat sambandhena) with the hero like Rama, but it is recognised as existing in the actor through a clever imitation of the original character, this imitation being apparently the source of the charm to the spectator. The Rasa, therefore, resides in the hero; but the objection is that it is not clear how a mental state which belongs to the hero can be transferred to the actor, and how the spectator can be charmed by a feeling which does not exist in him.

## Sankuka

*rama evayam ayam eva rama iti na ramo ’yam ity auttara-kalike badhe ramo ’yam iti ramah syad na vayam iti rama-sadrso ’yam iti ca samyan-mithya-samsaya-sadrsya-pratitibhyo vilaksanaya citra-turagadi-nyayena ramo ’yam iti pratipattya grahye nate, seyam mamangesu sudha-rasa-cchata supura-karpura-salakika drsoh \| manoratha-srir manasah sanrm pranesvari locana-gocaram gata \|\|*  
*daivad aham adya taya capalayata-netraya viyuktas ca \|*  
*avirala-vilola-jaladah kalah samupagatas cayam \|\|*  
*ity-adi-kavyanusandhana-balac chiksabhyasa-nirvartita- sva-karya-prakatanena ca natenaiva prakasitaih karana- karya-sahakaribhih krtrimair api tathanabhimanyamanair vibhavadi-sabda-vyapadesyaih samyogad gamya-gamaka- bhava-rupad anumiyamano ’pi vastu-saundarya-balad rasaniyatvenanyanumiyamana-vilaksanah sthayitvena sambhavyamano raty-adi-bhavas tatrasann api samajikanam vasanaya carvyamano rasa iti sri-sankukah.*

**Sn Sankuka states: When an actor is comprehended with the notion “He is Rama” like children think that a picture of a horse is the horse—such a notion is entirely distinct from: (1) A perception of sameness: “Rama is he. He is Rama,” (2) A perception of falsehood, at another time, when there is an act expressive of danger: “He’s not Rama,” (3) The perception of a doubt: “Is he Rama or not?” and (4) A perception of similarity: “He is similar to Rama”— and when the affection (rati), or the like, that the actor portrays is imagined as the sthayi and is being relished, although it is not really in the actor, by the spectators because of their predisposition (vasana), that affection, or another sthayi, is the rasa.**

**The actor gives expression to the causes, effects and auxiliaries by the display of his art. He refined his skills through instruction and practice by virtue of taking interest in poetry. For instance:**

**“On My limbs she is a mass of nectarous rasa. She is like a cosmetic pencil of camphor that nicely permeates both eyes. She is a beauty, the embodiment of My heart’s desire. That mistress of My life used to cross the path of My sight. Now, due to fate, the time of thick unsteady dark clouds has come: Alas I am separated from that woman of fickle and wide eyes.”**

**Although these causes, effects and auxiliaries are artificial, the spectators do not consider them artificial. The sthayi is inferred because of its connection with those three, which are called vibhava, anubhava and vyabhicari. By the mode of gamya-gamaka (indicated and indicative), those three cause the inference of the sthayi. Although thus inferred, the sthayi is, by virtue of being relishable due to the beauty of the story, different from other objects of inference. (Kavya-prakasa 4.28)**

The very first step in the occurrence of aesthetic enjoyment is the willful suspension of disbelief. Dr. Kane writes:

Sankuka thinks that rasa is a matter of inference. The actor who has been well trained in the art of gesticulation cleverly simulates the actions of real heroes and the spectator apprehends for the moment the actor as non-different from the real hero and infers love (of Rama etc.) from the anubhavas, vyabhicari- bhavas presented by the actor and mentally contemplates such love and relishes it. Here rasa is no doubt spoken of in relation to the spectator; but it is said to be a matter of inference due to clever imitation (anukarana-rupo rasah). It would be noticed that Sankuka speaks of rasa from the standpoint of the spectator. It is his view that rasa is inferred by the spectator. The sthayi-bhava in the original hero is inferred to exist in the actor (though not actually existing in him) on account of vibhavas cleverly represented by him in his acting, so as to give rise to the notion that the actor experiences feelings identical with those of the hero and makes the spectator forget for the time being the difference between the actors and the characters they represent. This inferred mood possesses peculiar charm entirely different from ordinary perceptions and inferences. Hence the realisation of rasa by the spectator is a logical inference.

Dr. De notes:

Lollata’s view does not deal with Rasa as a matter of the spectator’s feeling. Sankuka, on the other hand, thinks that the

Rasa is not produced as an effect, but inferred by the spectator, and the inferred feeling is relished by him as Rasa. \[...\] The realisation of Rasa, therefore, is a process of logical inference, and the nispatti of Bharata’s sutra is explained as anumiti, the vibhavas standing to Rasa in the relation of anumapaka or gamaka to anumapya or gamya.

In his explanation of Sankuka’s opinion, Abhinavagupta does not mention the concept of vasana (predisposition). Moreover, the historians mention the date of Sankuka. Dr. Kane writes:

Sankuka has probably to be identified with the poet Sankuka, author of Bhavanabhyudaya, mentioned in the Raja-tarangini (IV705) ‘ kavi-budha-manah-sindhu- sasankah sankukabhidhah \| yam uddisyakarot kavyam bhuvanabhyudayabhidham \|\|’. This would assign him to about 840 A.D.

Dr. De says:

To Sankuka are also ascribed several verses in the anthologies of Sarnga-dhara, Jahlana and Vallabha-deva,—which indicates that there was also a poet of the same name. Kahlana mentions (iv.703-5) a poet Sankuka and his poem Bhuvanabhyudaya. The reference is to the time of Ajitapida, whose date is given as 813 A.D. by Cunningham and 816 A.D. by S. P. Pandit. If our Sankuka is identical with this poet, then he may be assigned to the first quarter of the 9th century.

The problem with Sankuka’s theory is that inferring the sthayi is not equivalent to relishing it.

## Nayaka

na tatasthyena natma-gatatvena rasah prafiyate notpadyate nabhivyajyate, api tu kavye natye cabhidhato dvitiyena vibhavadi- sadharam-karanatmana bhavakatva-vyaparena bhavyamanah sthayl sattvodreka-prakasananda-maya-samvid-visranti- satattvena bhogena bhujyate iti bhatta-nayakah.

Bhatta Nayaka holds this opinion: There is no such thing as a “rasa” perceived in the character, nor a rasa perceived in the actor, nor a rasa perceived as something that goes to oneself, nor is there a rasa that is either effected or roused. Rather, what happens in poetry and in dramaturgy is that a sthayi felt by means of the function called bhavakatvam (a state of being that engenders feeling)—which is the second one, after Denotation, and whose nature is to generalize the vibhavas and the characters’ emotions—is enjoyed as bhoga (enjoyment), whose nature is a mental repose in sheer awareness composed of bliss which is a manifestation from an upsurge of sattva (good vibrations, and sattva-guna). (Kavya-prakasa 4.28)

Pandita-raja Jagannatha explains that according to Bhatta Nayaka, the clause “There is no such thing as a rasa that goes to oneself” signifies that the relishment a spectator feels is distinct from that of the character, since the causes are not the same: bhatta-nayakas tu, tatasthyena rasa-pratitav anasvadyatvam. atma-gatatvena tu pratyayo durghatah, sakuntaladinam samajikan praty avibhavatvat (Rasa-gangadhara, KM p. 23).

Visvanatha Kaviraja explains the sense of “upsurge of sattva”: rajas-tamobhyam asprstam manah sattvam ihocyate ity ukta- prakaro bahya-meya-vimukhatapadakah kascanantaro dharmah sattvam. tasyodreko rajas-tamasau abhibhuya avirbhavah. atra ca hetus tatha-vidhalaukika-kavyartha-parisilanam, “Sattva is a particular mental attribute which makes one indifferent to external objects, by the dictum: “In this regard, a mind untouched by either rajo-guna or tamo-guna is called sattva (Sarasvati-kanthabharana 5.20).” Sattva manifests by constantly taking interest in the meanings of extraordinary poetry” (Sahitya-darpana 3.2-3).

The concept of sadharam-karana (generalization of situations; stereotyping the characters; empathy), expounded by Bhatta Nayaka, originates from Bharata Muni: tatrastau bhavah sthayinah, trayastrimsad vyabhicarinah, astau sattvika iti bhedah. evam ete kavya-rasabhivyakti-hetava ekonapancasad bhavah pratyavagantavyah. ebhyas ca samanya-guna-yogena rasa nispadyante, “There are forty-nine bhavas. The rasas are effected from these ones by a connection with the quality of being generic” (Natya-sastra 7.7). Dr. Sushil Kumar De elucidates:

To state it briefly and without any technicality, there is in the mind a latent impression of feelings which we once went through (or which we acquired from previous births), and this is roused when we read a poem which describes similar things. By universal sympathy or community of feeling we become part and parcel of the same feeling and imagine ourselves in that condition. Thus the feeling is raised to a state of relish, called rasa, in which lies the essence of poetic enjoyment. It will be noticed that these theorists presuppose latent impression of experience (vasana) and universal sympathy (sadharanya or sadharam-karana). Those who have not experienced the feeling of love, for instance, and have therefore no impression of experience left in them, as well as those who have no sense of community of human feelings, can never relish Rasa. The vasana, we are told, is natural (naisargiki) and may have been left in our mind through the samskara of previous births, but it may also be acquired by study and experience. The writers on Poetics, therefore, are merciless in their satire on dull grammarians and old Mimamsakas, to whom such relish of Rasa is denied, and they declare unanimously that the rasika alone is capable of realising the rasa; for Rasa is not an objective entity which can reside in the hero or the actor, but a subjective condition realised by the reader’s own capacity of aesthetic enjoyment. Thus a degree of culture, experience and aesthetic instinct is demanded in the critic, the rasika or sahrdaya, in conformity with this subtle conception of poetry.

It will be noticed that these different theories about Rasa, though applied to drama and poetry, are yet generally tinged with the doctrines of the various schools of Indian philosophy. Lollata, it is clear, is a Mimamsaka who believes in the far- reaching function of the Denotation of a word and thinks that it is capable of expressing all other implied or suggested sense in the shape of the Rasa. Sankuka, on the other hand, is a Naiyayika or logician who would demonstrate the Rasa by means of syllogistic reasoning. He believes that the implied Rasa can be reached by the logical process of inference from the expressed sense, although he has to admit that the inferred mood is cognised differently from the objects of ordinary inference, being sensed by the spectator through the force of its exquisite charm. In Bhatta Nayaka we mark a further development. In his theory there is not only a transition from what may be called the objective to the subjective view of Rasa, and an understanding that the whole phenomenon should be explained in terms of the spectator’s inward experience, but also the fact that Bhatta Nayaka in his peculiar theory of aesthetic enjoyment (bhoga) is substantially following the teachings of the Samkhya philosophers.

According to Bhatta Nayaka, therefore, Rasa consists in the sthayi-bhava or the permanent mood, experienced in a generalised form in poetry and drama through the powers of abhidha and bhavakatva, and enjoyed by a blissful process, known as bhoga, till it is raised to a state of pleasurable relish, which is not worldly (a-laukika) but disinterested and which is akin to the philosophic meditation of Brahma. \[...\] This comes about through the predominance of the sattvika-guna in both cases

Commenting on Bhatta Nayaka’s theory, Abhinava points out that there is no need, as there is no authority, for assuming the two powers of bhavakatva and bhogi-karana, for they are implicitly included in the idea of rasa-vyanjana and its ultimate asvada.

Bharata’s dictum kavyarthan bhavayantiti bhavah \[Natya- sastra 7.1\] implies that bhavakatva is an inherent capacity of all bhavas, as the means of bringing into consciousness the sense of poetry, the term sense indicating here the principal Sense consisting ofthe relish of Rasa. Hence the sthayin, together with the vyabhicarin, being bhavas themselves, bring into existence through this inherent power the extraordinary relishable sense of poetry, cognised in a general or impersonated form. In this way, the sthayin may be regarded as the bhavaka or nispadaka of Rasa; and this so-called bhavakatva, according to Abhinava, consists in nothing more than a suitable use of Guna and Alankara (samucita-gunalankara-parigrahatmakam) for the ultimate purpose of awakening Rasa through the suggestive power of word and sense. Thus partially admitting bhavana or bhavakatva but explaining it somewhat differently, Abhinava turns to the other power assumed as bhoga or bhogi-karana by Bhatta Nayaka. \[...\] Abhinava thinks that the bhoga supposed by Bhatta Nayaka is nothing more than the asvada or relish of Rasa, based on permanent moods like rati etc., and made possible by the suggestive power of poetry. It falls naturally, therefore, within the domain of suggestion and need not be taken as a separate function (bhogi-karana-vyaparas ca kavyatmaka-rasa visayo dhvananatmaiva).

## Abhinavagupta

*loke pramadadibhih karanadibhih sthayy-anumane ’bhyasa- patavavatam kavye natye ca tair eva karanatvadi-pariharena vibhavanadi-vyaparavattvad alaukika-vibhavadi-sabda- vyavaharyair mamaivaite satror evaite tata-sthasyaivaite, na mamaivaite na satror evaite na tata-sthasyaivaite iti sambandhi- visesa-svikara-parihara-niyamanadhyavasayat sadharanyena pratitair abhivyaktah samajikanam vasanatmataya sthitah sthayi raty-adiko niyata-pramatr-gatatvena sthito pii sadharanyopaya- balat tat-kala-vigalita-parimita-pramatrta-vasonmisita- vedyantara-samparka-sunyaparimita-bhavena pramatra sakala- sahrdaya-samvada-bhaja sadharanyena svakara ivabhinno ’pi gocari-krtas carvyamanataika-prano vibhavadi-jlvitavadhih panaka-rasa-nyayena carvyamana pura iva parisphuran hrdayam iva pravisan sarvangmam ivalingan anyat sarvam iva tirodadhat brahmasvadam ivanubhavayan alaukika-camatkara-kari srngaradiko rasah. sa ca na karyah vibhavadi-vinase ’pi tasya sambhava-prasangat, napi jnapyah siddhasya tasyasambhavat, api tu vibhavadibhir vyanjitas carvamyah. karaka-jnapakabhyam anyat kva drstam iti ced na kvacid drstam ity alaukikatva-siddher bhusanam etan na dusanam. carvana-nispattya tasya nispattir upacariteti karyo ’py ucyatam. laukika-pratyaksadi-pramana-tatasthyavabodha- sali-mita-yogi-jnana-vedyantara-samsparsa-rahita-svatma- matra-paryavasita-parimitetara-yogi-samvedana-vilaksana- lokottara-sva-samvedana-gocara iti pratyeyo ’py abhidhiyatam. tad-grahakam ca na nirvikalpakam vibhavadi-paramarsa- pradhanatvat, napi sa-vikalpakam carvyamanasyalaukikananda- mayasya sva-samvedana-siddhatvat, ubhayabhava-svarupasya cobhayatmakatvam api purva-val lokottaratam eva gamayati na tu virodham iti srimad-acaryabhinavagupta-padah.*

**The venerable master teacher Sn Abhinavagupta states:**

**A sthayi-bhava which was present, as a predisposition, in the spectators who have proficiency by virtue of a habit in inferring a sthayi-bhava in the world by means of a young woman and so on and which, in poetry and in drama, is roused as follows by a young woman and so on, is a rasa, such as srngara.**

**In ordinary parlance, a woman, a garden, and so on are called causes and so on (effects and auxiliaries). In poetry and in drama, however, they are designated by the words vibhava, anubhava, and vyabhicari, which are otherworldly inasmuch as they have the functions called vibhavana and so on by giving up their being causes, etc., in the worldly sense.**

**In addition, they are perceived by sadharanya (generalization, empathy). This means the readers or the spectators do not limit themselves either by denying particular connections, as in: “These situations and emotions do not relate to me, these ones do not relate to an enemy, nor do these ones relate to the third party,” or by assuming that some connections are restrictive in another way, such as “These ones only relate to me, these ones only to an enemy, and these ones only to the third party.”**

**Though it exists in terms of belonging to particular competent persons and though it is non-different as if it were one’s own form (a soul), the rasa is brought in the scope of cognizance, by means of sadharanya, by a perceiver who is the recipient of the tidings of all the connoisseurs and in whom, by the force of sadharanya, the bhava is not limited, has no connection with something else that was known, and is expanded since the state of being a perceiver, which is limited, melted away at that time.**

**The sole life of the rasa is its being relished. It lasts as long as the vibhavas and so on have life: It is relished like a beverage.**

**While vibrating as if it were vibrating right in front, penetrating as if it were penetrating the heart, embracing as if it were embracing all the limbs, and as if making all else disappear, rasa creates otherworldly astonishment as though it were causing the realization of the bliss of Brahma.**

**Moreover, rasa is not an effect, something produced by vibhava, anubhava and vyabhicari as instrumental causes, because if it were an effect it would continue to exist even after the vibhavas and so on cease to exist. Nor is it something to be made known by the vibhavas and so on, since its existence is already established. (Rasa cannot be made known because the perception of it is inseparable from its existence.) Rather, it is implied by the vibhavas and so on and is potentially relishable. In case someone thinks: “Has a cause which is different than both a karaka (a direct agent) and a jnapaka (informative element) ever been admitted?”, the answer is: No, yet this unprecedentedness only confirms the transcendental nature of rasa.**

**Still, rasa could be said to be effected: The rasa is figuratively said to be an effectuation (nispatti) on account of the effectuation of the relishment.**

**In addition, it might even be said that rasa is knowable, in the sense that it is cognizable: Rasa is in the range of one’s super- sensory awareness. Such an awareness is different from direct worldly perception and other means of acquiring knowledge. It is also distinct from a yogi’s limited experience of trance, a state between trance and worldly awareness, and from a yogi’s deep cognition that only culminates in the self and that is void of all thought.**

**Moreover, grasping the rasa is not an experience that consists of a non-differentiation, because for the most part it involves taking interest in the vibhavas and so on. Nor is it an experience that involves a differentiation, since what is being relished as extraordinary bliss depends on the awareness of it. The fact that it is neither the former nor the latter and yet partakes of the nature of both is not contradictory. Rather, as before it only proves its transcendental nature. (Kavya-prakasa 4.28)**

## Two Meanings of Rasa

Bharata Muni propounded two meanings of the term rasa. The first one refers to his rasa-sutra and denotes aesthetic relishment whereas the second one denotes rapture. Lollata’s and Sankuka’s explanations relate to the rasa-sutra alone, whereas Bhatta Nayaka and Abhinavagupta explain the two meanings of the term rasa in one take. For instance, Abhinava says that according to Nayaka, the scope of bhavakatvam is the perception of a rasa and the like: nanuktam bhatta-nayakena \[...\] tatrabhidayakatvam vacya- visayam, bhavakatvam rasadi-visayam, bhogakrttvam sahrdaya- visayam iti trayo ’msa-bhUta vyaparah. (Locana 2.4)

The two meanings of the word rasa are: (1) A sthayi-bhava that has become relishable: yatha narendro bahu-jana-parivaro ’pi sa eva nama labhate nanyah sumahan apipurusah, tatha vibhavanubhava- vyabhicari-parivrtah sthayi bhavo rasa-nama labhate, “A sthayi- bhava surrounded by vibhavas, an anubhava and a vyabhicari is called rasa (aesthetic delight), like only a king is called king although some other man too might be a very great personality and have a big entourage” (Natya-sastra 7.8), and (2) Rapture (full-fledged relishment), where the bliss is a variation of the soul’s bliss: yo ’rtho hrdaya-samvadi tasya bhavo rasodbhavah, sariram vyapyate tena suskam kastham ivagnina, “An emotion that relates to a meaning which speaks to the heart gives rise to Rasa. The body is pervaded by it like dry wood by fire” (Natya-sastra 7.7). This is the ultimate meaning of the saying: The mind is not a vessel to be filled, but a fire to be kindled. (Plutarch)

After the sthayi has reached the stage of rasa, the rasa turns into Rasa (rapture) when there is an outstanding vastu-dhvani (implied sense). In that regard, Abhinavagupta invented the function called rasana: sa ca rasana-rupa pratitir utpadyate. vacya-vacakayos tatrabhidhadi-vivikto vyanjanatma dhvanana-vyapara eva, “The perception (of rasa) that originates is the form of rasana. It is the exact same function called Suggestiveness, only it is the soul of Suggestiveness” (Locana 2.4).
