He expounds: sa ca rasana na pramana-vyaparo na karaka-vyaparah. svayam tu napramaniki sva-samvedana-siddhatvat. rasana ca bodha-ripaiva kintu bodhantarebhyo laukikebhyo vilaksanaiva, upayanam vibhavadmam laukika-vailaksanyat. tena vibhavadi-samyogad rasana yato nispadyate ’tas tatha-vidha-rasana-gocaro lokottaro ’rtho rasa iti tatparyam sitrasya.

“Rasana is a function that has no proof, nor is it a function that is an active force. It itself, however, is not devoid of proof, because it can be proven by one’s experience of it. Rasana is simply a form of cognizance, but is obviously distinct from other, worldly types of cognizance, since the vibhavas and so on, the means, are distinct from the worldly means. Consequently the purport of Bharata Muni’s sitra is this: Since rasana has become effected from the blend of vibhavas and so on, an extraordinary meaning in the scope of rasana becomes Rasa (rapture)” (Abhinava-bharati 6.32).

Abhinava takes the vibhavas as instrumental causes (nimitta- karanam), according to Govinda Thakkura, but Abhinava and Lollata each uses the term rasa in a different sense. Lollata’s interpretation follows Bharata’s sitra to the letter. According to Kavi Kamapura, the sthayi is the inherent cause; the two vibhavas, namely the alambanas and the uddipanas, are instrumental causes; and an anubhava, as well as a vyabhicari, is a noninherent cause. The analogy is this: The sthayi is the threads; the vibhavas are the spinning wheel (or the shuttle); and the anubhava and the vyabhicari are the combining of the threads to make the cloth. In Nyaya, there are three kinds of causes: karanam tri-vidham, samavayy-asamavayi-nimitta-bhedat. (Tarka-sangraha 3.26)

In Abhinava’s interpretation, the Rasa, rapture, self-manifests: There is a relishment of a certain implied sense which acts as the catalyst that propels aesthetic delight to the level of rapture: This process of causation is not automatic. Therefore in truth rasana is as if an active force in the sense that it opens the door to the bliss of the soul so that it can enter the mind. Abhinava hinted at that: tatra vighnapasaraka vibhava-prabhrtayah, “In this matter, the vibhavas and so on remove the covering” (Abhinava-bharatl6.32). Dr. Sushil Kumar De notes:

The idea of Vedantin’s Moksa, which consists of a condition, not to be produced but to be made manifest by the removal of enveloping obstacles, finds an analogy in the idea of the manifestation of Rasa, implied in its abhivyakti, which consists not in the expression of anything new but in the revealing of something already existing. The brahmasvada is likened to the rasasvada because in both cases the intimate realisation comes after the limitations of the ego-centric attitude are transcended, and all separate existence is merged in the unity or harmony realised.

In day-to-day life, the immediate effect of relishment is an intensity; in poetry its immediate effect is an indolence of the mind and senses; and in dramaturgy or in a good movie its effect is a combination of mental intensity and indolence of the senses.

A similar process of the removal of the covering occurs in the experience of laughter: The mind is thrown off balance because it agreeably reads or hears or sees something highly unexpected; thereafter the natural joy of the soul enters the consciousness. Children are happy by nature because their egos have not expanded and do not get in the way of the innate joy of the soul.

Similarly, in the state between rasa (aesthetic delight) and Rasa (rapture), the bliss of the soul filters into the mind. Transcendental consciousness (cit) drizzles into the mind as Rasa, just like in The Matrix movies there is a rain of script on a computer monitor (the Matrix code).

The rasas can reach the state of rapture in day-to-day life. This is laukika Rasa. As regards drsya-kavya, however, the rapture of adbhuta-rasa arises while watching a great sci-fi thriller, the highest degree of laughter (hasya) is achieved by watching an excellent comedian on stage, and so on. But for the most part, the soul’s bliss imbued with srngara is the Rasa achieved by means of reading poetry. Santa-rasa proper occurs in trance when on the one hand the soul concentrates on Paramatma and does not lose awareness of itself, and on the other Paramatma reciprocates.

## Ornaments of Meaning

**Milita (indistinct)**

*apanga-tarale drsau madhura-vakra-varna giro*  
*vilasa-bhara-manthara gatir ativa kantam mukham \|*  
*iti sphuritam angake mrga-drsah svato lilaya*  
*tad atra na madodayah krta-pado ’pi samlaksyate \|\|*

**Her eyes are tremulous at the edges. Her words have sweet and tricky sounds. Her gait is graceful and languid. And her face has a glow. All this spontaneously and sportively manifests in the tender body of that doe-eyed woman, therefore no sign of drinking is perceptible in it. (verse 546)**

**Apahnuti (poetic denial)**

*bata sakhi kiyad etat pasya vairam smarasya*  
*priya-viraha-krse ’smin ragi-loke tatha hi \|*  
*upavana-sahakarodbhasi-bhrnga-cchalena*  
*prati visikham anenottankitam kalakutam \|\|*

**How amazing, sakhi, look at this: Cupid harbors ill will against lovers emaciated due to the pang of separation: He applied poison, under the false appearance of bumblebees hovering in mango trees in the courtyards, to his arrows.**

Mammata elaborates: atra hi na sa-bhrngani sahakarani, api tu sa-kalakutah sara iti pratitih, “Here the perception is: “These are not mango trees with bees: These are arrows with poison”” (verse 431 vrtti).

**Paramparita-rupaka (one metaphor causes another)**

*vidvan-manasa-hamsa vairi-kamalasankoca-dipta-dyute*  
*durgamargana-nila-lohita samit-svikara-vaisvanara \| satyapriti-vidhana-daksa vijaya-prag-bhava-bhima prabho*  
*samrajyam vara-vira vatsara-satam vairincam uccaih kriyah \|\|*

**O king, you are the swan on the Manasa Lake minds of scholars. You are the torrid sun that minimizes the enemies’ prosperity (or the sun, which does not close the enemies’ lotuses). You are Siva, who does not seek the shelter of forts (or Siva, who seeks Durga). You are Agni, who accepts battle (or Agni, who accepts fuel). You are Daksa, who implements truth (or Daksa, who is displeased with SatT). And you are bhlma (terrifying) in feeling victorious beforehand (or BhTma, whose elder brother is Arjuna). O great warrior, may you rule the kingdom for one hundred years of Brahma. (verse 425)**

The verse is unique because it features paronomastic one- word metaphors that justify a corresponding metaphor: (1) Superimposing manasa in the sense of “Manasa Lake” unto the same word manasa in the sense of “mind” (the mind is a Manasa Lake) is the cause of superimposing a swan unto the king (the king is a swan), (2) Superimposing vairi-kamalasankoca in the sense of “it does not close the enemies’ lotuses” unto the same word vairi-kamala-sankoca in the sense of “it minimizes the enemies’ prosperity” is the cause of superimposing a sun unto the king, (3) Superimposing durga-margana in the sense of “seeking Durga” unto durgamargana in the sense of “not seeking forts” is the cause of superimposing Siva unto the king, (4) Superimposing samit-svikara in the sense of “accepting fuel” unto samit-svikara in the sense of “accepting battle” is the cause of superimposing Agni unto the king, (5) Superimposing saty-aprlti-vidhana in the sense of “he is displeased with Sati” unto satya-priti-vidhana in the sense of “he implements truth” is the cause of superimposing Daksa unto the king, and (6) Superimposing vijaya-prag-bhava in the sense of “whose elder brother is Arjuna” unto vijaya-prag- bhava in the sense of “feeling victorious beforehand” is the cause of superimposing Bhima unto the king.”

Thus each implied metaphor is a second-rate alankara-dhvani in the category of second-rate poetry called vacya-siddhi-anga (an aspect in the accomplishment of the literal sense).

**Yamaka**

Mammata’s eight examples of yamaka (repetition of sound with a difference in meaning) are mostly taken from Rudrata and Ananda- vardhana:

*1*  
*sannari-bharanomayam aradhya vidhu-sekharam \|*  
*sannaribha-rano ’maya tatas tvam prthivlm jaya \|\|*

sat—good; narl—women; bharana—who supports; uma—Uma; ayam— \[Siva,\] who goes to (or whose is the place, i.e. the shelter of); aradhya—after worshiping; vidhu-sekharam—Siva (“on whose crest is a moon”); sanna—are dead; ari—of the enemies; ibha—the elephants; ranah— \[you,\] in whose battle; amaya—O you who are devoid of Maya (or O you who have no deceit); tatah—after that; tvam—you; prthivlm—the Earth; jaya—should conquer.

**O disillusioned king: In battle, the enemies’ elephants collapse. Having worshiped Siva, who shelters Uma, the supporter of virtuous women, and on whose crest a moon abides, conquer the Earth. (Kavyalankara 3.5)**

*2*  
*vinayam eno nayatasu-khadina*  
*vina yamenonayata sukhadina \|*  
*maha-jano ’diyata manasad aram*  
*mahaja-nodi yata-manasadaram \|\|*

vina—without; ayam—this; enah—a crime; nayata— \[by Yama,\] who is leading (i.e. taking away); asu-khadina—\[by Yama,\] who habitually causes the life airs to be eaten; vina—a special man (visista-nr) (or because of Garuda (a bird, vi )У, yamena—by Yama; unayata— \[by Yama,\] who is diminishing \[others\]; sukha-adina— in a happy way and so on; maha-janah—a great person; adiyata— was given (i.e. was given up); manasat—from the heart; aram— quickly; maha—to festivals; aja—those who go; nodi—who impels; yata-manasa—to those by whom the mind is controlled; adaram—in such a way that there is deference (or yatamana-sada- ram—in the manner of giving (ram) despondency (sada) (krsna- viraha) to those who are making efforts).

**A great person was given up by Yama, who happily diminishes others while taking them away and who habitually causes their life airs to be devoured. This special man, who had not committed a crime, used to inspire festivalgoers: He had an immediate profound respect from the heart for those who control their minds. (Kavyalankara 3.15)**

*3*  
*sa tv aram bharato ’vasyam abalam vitataravam \|*  
*sarvada ranam anaisid avan alasam asthitah \|\|*

*sattvarambha-rato ’vasyam avalambita-taravam \|*  
*sarva-darana-manaisi davanala-sama-sthitah \|\|*

sah tu—that same one (the king); aram—to a multitude of enemies; bharatah—on account of a burden; avasyam—necessarily; abalam—not an army; vitata—was expansive; aravam—in such a way that the noise; sarvada—always; ranam—a battle; anaislt—he brought; avan—he was not going; alasam—idly; a-sthitah—he who abides in Vishnu (or not stationary); sattva—with power; arambha—of a beginning; ratah—fond; avasyam— \[the multitude,\] which could not be subjugated; avalambita—was clung to; taravam—\[the multitude,\] by which the state of being a tree (i.e. the condition of not bending); sarva— everything; darana—from his tearing apart; mana—respect; esl—he desires; dava-anala—a conflagration; sama—is equal to; sthitah—he whose standing.

**He always brought a fight to the enemies when it was necessary, since they were a burden, and the noise was tumultuous then. Although they were not an army, they could not be subjugated: They stuck to firmness. He was a king who abided in Vishnu and was fond of a beginning with power. Desiring respect by tearing apart everything, he was not moving idly. His presence was akin to a conflagration. (Kavyalankara 3.18-19)**

These two verses form one yamaka. In yamaka and in citra- kavya, sometimes the grammatical rules are bent: Here the letters v and b are used interchangeably, and the anusvara becomes m (in “avalambita-taravam ” which is the same sound as “abalam vitataravam”).

In addition, sa tva, in the first verse, changed to sattva in the second, by the unwritten rule that when the letter t is followed by a consonant, another t can be added. The reason is that the sound is roughly the same. The reverse is often seen: When two t’s are followed by a consonant, one t is optionally deleted, as in the word satra in Bhagavatam 1.1.4, which means sattra (sacrificial session).

*4*  
*ananta-mahima-vyapta-visvam vedha na veda yam \|*  
*ya ca mateva bhajate prayate manave dayam \|\|*

ananta-mahima—with infinite glory; vyapta-visvam—her, by whom the world is pervaded; vedhah—Brahma; na veda—does not know; yam—whom; ya—who; ca—and; mata iva—like a mother; bhajate—worships; prayate—who is dutiful; manave—to a man; dayam—compassionate.

**She is compassionate to a dutiful man. She is like a mother, and pervades the world by her infinite glory. Brahma worships her though he does not understand her. (Devi-sataka)**

*5*  
*yad-anato ’ya-danato nayatyayam na yaty ayam \|*  
*sivehitam sive hitam smaramitam smarami tam \|\|*

yad-anatah—who bows to whom; aya—of good fortune; danatah—because of the gift; naya—of morals; atyayam—the destruction; na yati—does not get; ayam—this \[person\]; siva- ihitam—desired by Siva; sive—in the matter of auspiciousness; hitam—beneficial; smara-amitam—who is unattained by Cupid; smarami tam—I remember her.

**A person who bows to her never loses his morals, because she gives good fortune. She is desired by Siva, is beneficial in terms of auspiciousness, and is not approached by Cupid. I remember her. (Devi-sataka)**

*6*  
*sarasvati prasadam me sthitim citta-sarasvati \|*  
*sara svati kuru ksetra-kuruksetra-sarasvati \|\|*

sarasvati—O Sarasvati; prasadam—grace; me—to me (or my); sthitim—presence; citta—of my mind; saras-vati—in the river; sara—attain \[grace\]; sv ati—nicely and eminently (su = susthu) (ati = atisayena); kuru—make \[your presence\]; ksetra—is a field; kuruksetra—of Kuruksetra; sarasvati— O you because of whom the wisdom.

**O SarasvatT, you because of whom the wisdom of Kuruksetra is a field of knowledge, be pleased with me and become beau­tifully and eminently present in the river-like flow of my mind. (Devi-sataka)**

*7*  
*sasara sakam darpena kandarpena sa-sarasa \|*  
*saran navana bibhrana nabibhrana saran nava \|\|*

sasara—went (went out); sakam—with; darpena—who is proud; kam-darpena—with Cupid (“he makes Brahma proud” (Uddyota)); sa-sarasa—\[autumn,\] which has cranes and lotuses (an ekasesa compound); saram—arrow (or sarad—autumn); nava—are new (because the roads are mud-free); anah—\[autumn,\] during which the carts; bibhrana—while fostering; na—not; abibhrana—not having (or na a-vi-bhrana—she has no absence of sounds of birds); saram—rush (a type of reed) (or sarad—autumn); nava— youthful.

**Autumn, a time when cranes and lotuses abound and the carts look new, went out with proud Cupid. Youthful autumn fosters Cupid’s arrows, but it is not that she does not have reeds of her own. (Kavyalankara 3.35)**

This is a mirror yamaka. Such a yamaka is not seen in Kavi Kamapura’s examples. Moreover, Kavi Kamapura took inspiration from this verse in writing his astounding sarva-yamaka verse of two consonants, beginning sasara sa (Alankara-kaustubha 7.66).

*8*  
*madhupa-raji-parajita-manim- jana-manah-sumanah-surabhi-sriyam \|*  
*abhrta varita-varija-viplavam sphuiita^tamra^tatamra-vanam jagat \|\|*

madhupa—of bees; raji—on account of a multitude; parajita— are won over; manim-jana—of the ladies in mana; manah— \[the flowers,\] due to which the minds; sumanah—at which time the flowers (or because of flowers); surabhi-sriyam—the resplendence of spring (or surabhi sriyam: surabhi—\[the world,\] fragrant, sriyam—resplendence); abhrta—fostered; varita—is prevented; vari-ja—of lotuses (“born from water”); viplavam—in which the ruination; sphutita—are manifest (in bloom); tamra—coppery red; tata—and expansive; amra-vanam—in which the forests of mango trees; jagat—the world.

**The forests have expansive, reddish mango trees in bloom, and the lotuses in the woodland are prevented from decaying. The world fosters the resplendence of spring, so that the flowers, along with the bees, win over the minds of the girls in mana. (Ratnakara’s Hara-vijaya)**

Kavi Kamapura would call this a madhya yamaka (ayamaka in the middle of each line).

## The Two Authors of Kavya-prakasa

Mammata passed away while writing Kavya-prakasa. There was much turmoil in Kashmir around the turn of the century: Kalasa ruled from 1063 to 1089; and Harsa ruled from 1089 to 1101, when he was murdered by feudatory landlords known as damaras. In 1099, Kashmir was ravaged by plague, flood and famine, as well as by lawlessness on a large scale. Many commentators, such as Ruyyaka and Manikyacandra, say Kavya-prakasa was begun by one writer and completed by another. Only Rajanaka Ananda, whose commentary is dated 1665 CE, is explicit on the topic:

*krtah sri-mammatacarya-varyaih parikaravadhih \|*  
*granthah sampuritah sesam vidhayallaka-surina \|\|*

**“Mammata Acarya wrote the book up to the parikara ornament. The rest was completed by Allaka Sun.” (Kavya-prakasa-nidarsana)**

King Arjunavarman (c. 1215 CE), who commented on Amaru- sataka, which contains verses seen in Kavya-prakasa, says Alaka was also involved in the seventh chapter.

Bhimasena, in his commentary on Kavya-prakasa called Sudha- sagara, praises Mammata:

*sabda-brahma sanatanam na viditam sastraih kvacit kenacit*  
*tad-devi hi sarasvatl svayam abhut kasmira-dese puman \|*  
*srimaj-jaiyata-gehini-sujatharaj janmapya yugmanujah*  
*srlman-mammata-samjnayasrita-tanum sarasvatim sucayan \|\|*  
*maryadam kila palayan siva-purim gatva prapathyadarat*  
*sastram sarva-janopakara-rasikah sahitya-sutram vyadhat \|*  
*tad-vrttim ca viracya gudham akarot kavya-prakasam sphutam vaidagdhyaika-nidanam arthisu catur-varga-pradam sevanat \|\|*  
*kas tasya stutim acaret kavir aho ko va gunan veditum*  
*saktah syat kila mammatasya bhuvane vag-devata-rupinah \|*  
*sriman kaiyata auvvatau hy avarajau yac-chattratam agatau*  
*bhasyabdhim nigamam yatha-kramam anuvyakhyaya siddhim gatau \|\|*

**“Transcendental sound is eternal. It is not cognized by anyone at any time through the scriptures. Sarasvati, the presiding deity of it, appeared in person in the form of a man in the land of Kashmir. The younger one of twins took birth from the splendid womb of Jaiyata’s wife. To hint at Sarasvati, by whom a body was assumed with the name Mammata, and to follow etiquette, he went to Benares and respectfully learned the scriptures. He was a rasika who benefited everyone. He composed the karikas of Kavya- prakasa and a profound elaboration on them. That book is the primary cause of cleverness and bestows the four goals of life to those who want them, after serving it. Ah! Which poet can praise him? And who is able to understand the qualities of Mammata, the form of the presiding deity of words who has come to Earth? His two younger brothers, Kaiyata and Uvvata, became teachers. The former commented upon the ocean of the Bhasya and the latter on the Vedas. Both persons achieved success” (Sudha-sagara, opening verses).**

According to Dr. Siva-Sankara Avasthi, Uvata lived in Avanti under the patronage of King Bhoja. In that regard, Mammata’s example of the udatta ornament (verse 505)—cited earlier, in the section on Srngara-prakasa—speaks of Bhoja, and that suggests a connection between Mammata and Uvata. Thus Mammata might have composed some verses while writing the karikas, and Alaka filled the blanks. Udatta (Kavya-prakasa 10.115) occurs before parikara (10.118). Ganganatha Jha relates this story:

At the same time there is no reason to believe that the author of the Kavya-prakasa lived earlier than the eleventh century A.C.; for he quotes a verse in his 10th Chapter from Bhoja, who reigned in the earlier half of that century ; for a tradition has it that his younger brother Uvata attended the court of this very Bhoja at his capital Avanti for some time; and he was probably the medium of the quotation.

Dr. Kane observes:

About the personal history of Mammata we know practically nothing. Bhimasena in his Sudha-sagara (Ch. S.S.) says that Mammata was the elder brother of both Kaiyata (author of Mahabhasya-pradipa) and Uvata (author of bhasya on Rk- pratisakhya), that he was the son of Jaiyata and, though born in Kashmir, studied at Benares and taught his brothers. But this account furnished by an author who wrote six centuries after Mammata (in 1672-73 A.D.) seems to be more or less fanciful and based probably on the similarity of sounds in the three names. We know from Uvata’s bhasya on the Rk-pratisakhya that he was a son of Vajrata (and not of Jaiyata) and a native of Ananda-pura. Uvata wrote his Vajasaneya-samhita-bhasya while Bhoja was reigning (bhoje rajyam prasasati). There is therefore nothing improbable in Mammata being a brother of Uvata, but he cannot then be the brother of Kaiyata, whose father was Jaiyata.

## 23. Ruyyaka

Ruyyaka was the last Kashmiri giant. His protege, Mankha, was the last well-known Kashmiri poet. Ruyyaka is famous I V^for his Alankara-sarvasva (everything about ornaments). He and Mammata exerted equal influence on Visvanatha Kaviraja. Moreover, Ruyyaka was the first to comment on Kavya-prakasa:

The commentary of Manikyacandra is expressly dated Samvat 1216 = 1159-60 A.D. The exact date of Ruyyaka’s commentary is not known, but we know from other sources that Ruyyaka flourished in the second and third quarters of the 12th century. The earliest dated MS from Jesalmere appears to have been copied in 1158 A.D.

The Kavya-prakasa-sanketa of Manikya-candra (composed in 1159-1160) refers to the Alankara-sarvasva several times. Therefore the Alankara-sarvasva was composed sometime between 1135-1150 A.D.

In addition, Alaka commented on Ruyyaka’s treatise:

This Alata or Alaka is supposed to be the same as Rajanaka Alaka who wrote a commentary on Ruyyaka, and is quoted by Ratnakantha as such. \[...\] This will make the two writers commentators on each other’s text ; and if this were so, we may naturally expect a reference to this fact by Ruyyaka, who otherwise alludes to the dual authorship of the Kavya-prakasa, but does not mention the name of Allata as the continuator.

Ruyyaka was the son of Tilaka, who wrote a commentary on Udbhata’s Kavyalankara-sara-sangraha. Udbhata and Mammata equally influenced Ruyyaka.

Dr. Kane expounds:

The Alankara-sarvasva of Ruyyaka—This is a standard work on figures of speech. The author is a staunch advocate of the dhvani school and briefly summarises the views of Bhamaha, Udbhata, Rudrata, Vamana, the Vakrokti-jivita, Vyakti-viveka and Dhvanikara on the essence of poetry. He then deals with punar-uktavad-abhasa, chekanuprasa, vrtty- anuprasa, yamaka, latanuprasa, citra and about 75 figures of artha beginning with upama. He defines more figures than Mammata and his treatment (in the 86 sutras and the vrtti thereon) is generally more elaborate than the latter. \[...\] The work is divided into three parts; first come the sutras (in prose) defining the figures, then the vrtti and the examples, all of which are cited from previous works. \[.\] He frequently cites the views of Udbhata, and Jayaratha tells us that the author of the Sarvasva generally follows the views of Rajanaka Tilaka who wrote a work called Udbhata-viveka or -vicara. \[.\] It is further to be noted that the definitions of several alankaras are the same in both Kavya-prakasa and Alankara-sarvasva e.g. citra, kavya-linga, vyajokti, uttara, milita, samadhi and that about 76 illustrations are the same in the 10th ullasa of Mammata and in the Sarvasva.

Inspired by Rudrata’s classification of ornaments, Ruyyaka established a sequence of his own: For the details, consult the appendix in the present writer’s translation of Bhakti-rasamrta- sesa. Before or after defining each ornament, Ruyyaka explained why he chose to so place that ornament in his sequence. Visvanatha Kaviraja followed Ruyyaka’s sequence for the first twenty-five ornaments. Jagannatha did so for the first fifty-five, except three ornaments.

Moreover, Ruyyaka invented two ornaments: vicitra and vikalpa. He created several subvarieties of ornaments, most of which were accepted by Visvanatha and Jagannatha.

Dr. Sushil Kumar De notes:

He shows, however, a remarkable degree of insight and independence of judgment which distinguishes him from his predecessor. \[...\] His views on this matter have been accepted as authoritative by such important later writers as Visvanatha, Vidyadhara, Vidyanatha and Appayya Diksita.

Throughout his elaborations, Ruyyaka repeatedly emphasized the importance of Kuntaka’s vicchitti (literary charm). Dr. De writes:

It cannot be said, however, that Ruyyaka was a follower of the Vakrokti-jivita-kara, for Ruyyaka himself declares his own adherence to the Dhvani theory; and, in spite of his borrowing from Udbhata and Kuntaka, he cannot by any means be directly affiliated with the Alankara school.

This is Ruyyaka’s example ofthe old-school nidarsana (illustration):

*cudamani-pade dhatte yo ’mbare ravim agatam \|*  
*satam karyatitheyiti bodhayan grha-medhinah \|\|*

**To inform householders about showing hospitality to good persons, the Eastern Mountain puts on its head the sun arriving in the sky. (Alankara-sarvasva, KM p. 76)**

The verse also features a twist on the variety of atisayokti characterized by the simultaneous occurrence of the cause and its effect: The arrival of the sun in the sky is the cause of—and is the same as—the eastern horizon’s act of putting the sun on its head. The purpose of this variety of atisayokti is to express the quickness of the efficacy of the cause.

The main difference between Ruyyaka’s and Mammata’s metho­dologies is the topic of slesa (double meaning). Like Mammata, Ruyyaka repudiated Udbhata’s dogma that a slesa lessens the operation of any accompanying figure, but on the main Ruyyaka revived Udbhata’s interpretations of slesa. Ruyyaka says slesa is threefold in two ways: (A) sabda-slesa, which corresponds to sabhanga-slesa (a different word is formed by a different sound), involves a difference in the Vedic accent, (B) artha-slesa, which corresponds to abhanga-slesa, does not involve a difference in Vedic accent, and (C) ubhaya-slesa (both sabhanga-slesa and abhanga-slesa). This third one is Ruyyaka’s innovation in poetic theory: Visvanatha accepted it: punas tridha sabhango ’bhangas tad-ubhayatmakah (Sahitya-darpana 10.12). Still, on the whole Visvanatha dismantled Ruyyaka’s methodology of slesa (Sahitya- darpana 10.12) like Mammata demolished Udbhata’s. Jagannatha, however, revived Ruyyaka’s system, except that he did not mention Vedic accents.

Ruyyaka’s slesa (pun: literal double meaning) has three categories:

- Each meaning is prakaranika (contextual),
- Both are aprakaranika (not contextual) or
- One meaning is prakaranika and the other aprakaranika.

The second one is Ruyyaka’s innovation in poetic theory and occurs in the tulya-yogita ornament (same connection with the attribute). Ruyyaka stated that the first two categories can also be classed in the tulya-yogita ornament whereas the third one overlaps the dipaka ornament.

Ruyyaka’s example of the third category of slesa is a slesopama (simile based on a literal double meaning):

*svecchopajata-visayo ’pi na yati vaktum*  
*dehiti margana-satais ca dadati duhkham \|*  
*mohat samutksipati jlvanam apy akande*  
*kastam manobhava ivesvara-durvidagdhah \|\|*

**Darn, the king is like Cupid. Although Cupid, the flower archer, chooses his object of pursuit (svecchopajata-visaya), he never goes to that person to say “Here I am in embodied form” (dehiti = dehl iti). Rather, Cupid torments the person with hundreds of arrows (margana), and after causing stupefaction (mohat) Cupid unexpectedly wrecks that person’s life (jivanam). The witless king, whose objects of pleasure are obtained at will (svecchopajata-visaya), never says “Distribute the goods” (dehiti = dehi iti). Rather, he pains others with hundreds of requests (margana), and causelessly wastes drinking water (jivanam) out of ignorance (mohat). (Alankara-sarvasva, KM p. 96)**

As regards these three categories of slesa, Jagannatha follows Ruyyaka. Mammata and Visvanatha reject Ruyyaka’s third category, but Ruyyaka is not wrong, because Mammata and others say the subject of comparison (upameya) is always the subject of description (the prakaranika, also calledprastuta andprakrta) and the standard of comparison is always aprakaranika (noncontextual), and so in their methodology the paronomasia upon which a simile is based should be classed as a dhvani (implied meaning), not as a slesa (literal double meaning), but in usage they say it is slesa. Mammata and others appear to be inconsistent, but Bhatta Nayaka stated that in a simile, the meanings are only literal (contextual).

Ruyyaka wrote many other works in the field of poetics. In particular, he composed a huge poetical treatise called Sahitya- mimamsa. He refers to it in Alankara-sarvasva. It consists of eight chapters. Therein Ruyyaka amalgamates the methodologies of Dandi, Udbhata, Rajasekhara, Bhoja and Kuntaka and adds new theory. Kumara Svamin, the commentator on Vidyanatha’s Pratapa-rudriya, mentions the work: prapancitam ca sahitya- mimamsayam (Ratnapana 1.10). Dr. Kane gives the details:

In the Tri. S. Series a work called Sahitya-mimamsa was published in 1934, the edition being based on a single ms. \[...\] The work is a large one. \[...\] About six hundred verses are quoted from numerous sources in this work, out of which one hundred are prakrit. It is divided into eight prakaranas \[.\]. A brief summary is given here. I. Salutation of vacya and vacaka (which stand for Para and Apara Brahma), enumeration of the topics to be discussed in the work viz. eight topics of vrtti, vivaksa, tatparya, pravibhaga, vyapeksana, samarthya, anvaya, aikarthya (these eight are called sahitya); 4 topics that set off sahitya (i.e. sahitya-pariskara) viz. dosa-tyaga, gunadhana, alankara-yoga and rasanvaya; four kinds of Kavi viz. sat- kavi, vidagdha-kavi, arocaki-kavi, satrnabhyavaharaka-kavi; three kinds of rasika viz uttama, madhyama, adhama (i.e. sattvika, rajas and tamasa); II. definition of vrtti (as padanam vyaparah), which is threefold: mukhya, laksana, gauni; definitions of these three; definitions of vivaksa, pravibhaga (into prakrti and pratyaya, vakya, maha-kavya), vyapeksana (akanksa), samarthya (bheda, samsarga and ubhaya), anvaya (paraspara-grathana), aikarthya (eka-vakyata) and their examples; these eight constitute sahitya (sahitya is language and grammar and not poetics), difference between sahitya and kavya (the latter is sahitya with four pariskaras, dosa-tyaga etc.); III. Dosas \[...\] IV. Gunas of kavya, sabda-gunas being bahya and artha-gunas being abhyantara; ten gunas (slesah prasadah samata madhuryam sukumarata \| artha-vyaktir udaratvam ojah-kanti-samadhayah II); their definitions and illustrations; V. definition of alankara \[...\] VI. Rasa, its causes (bija), nature, co-operating elements (sahakari) and whatever else is useful for the elucidation of Rasa are dealt with here; bhavas are pradhana and apradhana; pradhana-bhavas are the eight called sthayins, apradhana-bhavas are bahya (eight called sattvika) and 33 abhyantara (called vyabhicarins); enumeration of these, their definitions and examples; Rasa expounded; eight rasas enumerated by the ancients; Santa rasa enumerated by some, its sthayi-bhava being dhrti ; \[...\] VII. The fourfold equipment of the poet (sramah sarva-kala-viksa niyogas tasya silanam \| sa klesah karanodyogah pratibha bhasvati matih \| prajna nava-navonmesa-salini pratibheti va I); kavi is four kinds, sat-kavi who wields vaidarbhi style (such as Valmiki and Kalidasa), vidagdha-kavi who is bent on vakrokti (such as Vyasa and Bana), arocaki-kavi who sticks to arthalankaras (such as Magha and Bharavi), satrnabhyavaharaka-kavi who writes in the Gaud! style and is after slesa, citra and yamaka (such as Sivabhadra); \[.\] characteristic descriptions of the ladies of several countries and their complexions; pravrttis called avantya, daksinatya, paurastya and audra-magadha; various festivals and sports of different countries and in different seasons; the six pramanas; VIII. The reader who relishes kavya secures the highest pleasure (idrsam bhavayan kavyam rasikah paramam sukham \| prapnoti kala-vaisamyad gunatas tri-vidho ’pi san II); the Veda (in Rg. X.71.2 saktum iva...) and the Uttara-rama-carita (avirbhuta-jyotisam IV.18) state that the most auspicious glory resides in the words of poets and unparalleled pleasure is the reward of revolving the meaning of a good poem in the mind.

\[.\] On pp. 145-146 are quoted three verses about the dress of the ladies of Gauda, Mahodaya and Avanti which occur in Rajasekhara’s Kavya-mimamsa (pp. 8-9). The most important thing is that the Kavya-prakasa is quoted twice. \[.\] The Vakrokti-jivita appears to have exerted a great influence over the Sahitya-mimamsa. \[...\] On p. 117 the verses speaking of the six kinds of vakratva are quoted from the Vakrokti-jivita (I.19-21), the same examples are cited \[...\]. Dr. Raghavan on ‘Srngara-prakasa’ vol. I. pp. 88-103, shows that the Sahitya- mimamsa follows the Srngara-prakasa, though it differs from it in some respects. He also doubts (pp. 99-100) whether it is the work of Ruyyaka.

The most important characteristics of the Sahitya-mimamsa are two, viz. that it does not speak of the vyanjana function of words at all, but of tatparya-vrtti which gives rise to the realization of rasa (apadartho’pi vakyartho rasas tatparya- vrttitah I p. 85). Secondly, it treats of only a few arthalankaras and includes such figures as samasokti, aprastuta-prasamsa, sahokti under vakratva. It does not appear to accept the theory of the Srngara-prakasa when it says ‘visistadrsta-janmana atma-gunodbhuti-hetor anadi-vasana-rupasyahankarasya ca rasatvam aikyam ca nisiddham asmabhih \| na tu kuta- sthatma-svarupasyanandasyaika-rupasya bhedo vaktum na sakyate ity-adi I’ (p. 161).

The above characteristics of the Sahitya-mimamsa create a difficulty. A Sahitya-mimamsa was the work of Ruyyaka author of the Alankara-sarvasva, as stated by himself. The Sarvasva was a staunch advocate of the Dhvani theory and the vyanjana function, as stated on p. 16 (asti tavad vyangya- nistho vyanjana-vyaparah). It also enumerates about 75 arthalankaras beginning with upama and including samasokti, aprastuta-prasamsa, rasavat, urjasvi, preyah. The only way in which this contradiction can be explained is by supposing that the Sahitya-mimamsa was composed by him when the author was comparatively young and under the influence of the Vakrokti-jivita, while the Alankara-sarvasva was composed when he was of mature intellect and had come completely inder the influence of the Dhvany-aloka and Abhinavagupta.

Mankha assisted Ruyyaka in the making of Alankara-sarvasva:

It is probable that Mankhaka, who was a pupil of Ruyyaka, took great pains to spread the fame of his master’s work and in editing it afresh made some additions. It is probably in this way that a few verses from the Sri-kantha-carita of Mankha (II.49 on p. 25, and V.23, VI.16 and X.10 on pp. 114-115) got into the Alankara-sarvasva (i.e. the master appears to quote from his pupil’s work).

## 24. Hemacandra

Hemacandra Suri (1088-1172 CE) wrote Kavyanusasana. He wrote the vrtti (elaboration), which he calls Alankara- cudamani, and the commentary, which he calls Viveka.

Like most of his other works, Kavyanusasana is a compilation that displays his encyclopedic erudition. Hemacandra was a polymath. Dr. Sushil Kumar De summarizes Hemacandra’s contribution:

Hemacandra wrote voluminous works on many branches of Sanskrit learning, such as grammar (Siddha-hemacandra Sabdanusasana, Linganusasana, Dhatu-parayana), prosody (Chandonusasana), lexicon (Abhidhana-cintamani, Anekartha-sangraha, Nighantu-sesa, and Desi-nama-mala), besides works on Jaina Sastra. His stupendous learning justifies his sobriquet Kalikala-Sarvajna. His Kavyanusasana in eight chapters has the merit of comprehending all topics of Poetics, including a brief reference to Dramaturgy. In spite of occasional differences Hemacandra borrows freely from Bharata, Anandavardhana, Abhinavagupta, Mammata and Rajasekhara. Its want of any striking originality perhaps stood on the way of its being accepted as an authoritative work. It exercised little influence on later writers and is scarcely ever quoted.

His Anekartha-sangraha dictionary, commonly known as Hema- kosa, mostly follows Medim-kosa and is highly authoritative. In addition, Dr. Belvalkar states: “To illustrate the rules of his grammar, Hemachandra has composed a poem, resembling the Bhattikavya, which is known as Dvy-asraya-mahakavya. ”

Hemachandra rose to prominence under the reign of Siddharaja (fl. 1092-1141) and was an advisor to his successor Kumarapala (1143-1173). His influence on Kumarapala resulted in the Jain religion becoming the official religion of Gujarat, and animal slaughter was banned. \[...\] Hemachandra, following the earlier Gopala (c. 1135), presented an earlier version of the Fibonacci sequence. It was presented around 1150, about fifty years before Fibonacci (1202).

Furthermore, Hemacandra copied Anandavardhana’s example of avivaksita-vacya-dhvani (implied sense based on figurative usage):

*suvarna-puspam prthivlm cinvanti purusas trayah \|*  
*suras ca krta-vidyas ca yas ca janati sevitum \|\|*

**Three types of men pluck the golden-flowered Earth: A heroic combatant, an accomplished scholar, and a man who knows how to serve. (Dhvany-aloka 1.13) (Kavyanusasana, KM p. 45)**

Hemacandra paraphrases Abhinavagupta’s explanation that here the figurative usage suggests the excellence of those three types of persons.

Dr. Kane writes:

The one merit ofthe work is that in the vrtti and the commentary he cites about 1500 examples from various authors. \[.\] Hemacandra is the brightest star in the galaxy of Jain writers. He was a voluminous writer and wrote on numerous branches of study.

He was born on the Full-Moon day of Kartika in samvat 1145 (1088 A.D.), he was initiated in samvat 1150 (1093 A.D.), he became a suri or acarya in samvat 1166 (1109 A.D.) and died at the age of 84 in samvat 1229 (1173 A.D.). \[...\] From the fact that Hemacandra (on p. 109) mentions Mammata by name \[.\] and from the fact that he wrote the Kavyanusasana after the Sabdanusasana and makes no mention of Kumarapala in the Kavyanusasana it may be said that he composed it about 1140 A.D.

Dr. Belvalkar adds:

Hemachandra, who was now an octogenarian, soon felt his end drawing near, and he boldly set out to meet it by means of prayopavesana \[abstaining from food and awaiting in a sitting posture the approach of departure\]. He was 84 at the time of his death. Kumarapala died only six months after him. With their deaths the glories of the Jain empire also came to an end, after a brief existence of unparalleled brilliancy.

## 25. Sridhara Svami

In his commentary on Bhagavata Pumna, Sridhara Svami revealed the true nature of bhakti: It can reach the state of rasa. Sridhara Svami’s dates and place of birth are uncertain. He lived before the second half of the thirteenth century CE because Jiva Gosvami says that Citsukha’s commentary on a verse of Bhagavatam reflects Sridhara Svami’s opinion. Everyone is agreed that Citsukha lived around 1220 CE. Further, Prabhat Mukherjee writes:

The Vishnusvami and Sri Cults in Orissa—From the eleventh century A.D., Puri became a centre of the Vishnusvami cult which was founded by Devatanu Vishnusvami. Sridhar Svami, and Lakshmidhar, the author of Srinama Kaumudi, belonged to this sect. They lived at Puri at an uncertain date. Sridhar is famous for his Bhavartha Dipika commentary ofthe Bhagavata, in which he has quoted the opinion of Vishnusvami in two places (I.7.6 and III.12.2). According to tradition, Sridhar’s home was in Northern Orissa. There is a family at Mareijna near Remuna in Balasore, which claims to be the descendants of Sridhar Svami. But the family records, supporting such a claim, are now lost.

The sectarian Mantras of the Vishnusvami sect are, “Om Rama-Krishnaya namah” and “Om Rama-Krishna Hari.” It is to be noticed that the name of Rama precedes the name of Hari. The Mantra of sixteen namas (consisting of 8 Hari, 4 Rama, and 4 Krishna words) prevailed in Orissa, even before the Chaitanya Age. The names of Rama were placed before the names of Krishna. Later on, Krishna turned the tables. Jagannatha Dasa, the author of the Oriya Bhagavata, has followed the interpretations of Sridhar Svami. This fact has been acknowledged in the last canto of Jagannatha’s book.

Similarly, Dr. Bhagavan Panda lists Sridhara Svami among the reputed scholars of Orissa, but some say Sridhara Svami was born in Gujarat before the time of Ramanuja. However, by most accounts Laksmidhara belonged to Sankaracarya’s disciplic succession.

Sridhara Svami was a Mayavadi who converted to Vaishnavism. His Vaishnava guru is said to be Paramananda Tirtha, whom he seems to implicitly refer to in his invocatory verse in his commentary on Bhagavad-gita.

New Delhi: Asian Educational Services, pp. 38-39.

Sridhara Svami also wrote Atma-prakasa, a commentary on Visnu Purana. Another well-known commentary on this scripture is Visnu-cittlya, by Visnucitta: He lived from 1097 to 1197 CE. He was a grand-disciple of Acarya Ramanuja. The two commentaries are very similar: Perhaps both authors used the same older commentary as a source. In the opinion of the present writer, who translated the fifth canto of Visnu Purana, Sridhara Svami copied Visnucitta, because the former adds to the latter. For example, consult their commentaries on verses 5.1.10; 5.1.51; and 5.7.46.

Sridhara Svami expounded the highest philosophy. For example:

*tvat-kathamrta-pathodhau viharanto maha-mudah \|*  
*kurvanti krtinah kecic catur-vargam trnopamam \|\|*

**Some accomplished persons who are greatly joyful while sporting in the ocean of nectar topics about You render the four goals of life insignificant like straw. (Bhavartha-dipika 10.87.21) (quoted in Bhakti-rasamrta-sindhu 1.1.40)**

Caitanya Mahaprabhu extolled Sridhara Svami:

*sridhara-svami-prasade ‘bhagavata’ jani \|*  
*jagad-guru sridhara-svami ‘guru’ kari’ mani \|\|*

**“I know Bhagavatam by the grace of Sridhara Svami. I consider that he, the spiritual master of the universe, is a guru” (Caitanya- caritamrta 3.7.133).**

In his commentary on the third verse of Bhagavatam, Sridhara Svami explained that the word amrta-drava-samyuta signifies that the Bhagavatam, the fruit of the tree of the Vedas, is a fruit endowed with the rasa which is a form of the highest bliss. He linked this understanding with the scriptural statement: raso vai sah, “The Lord is rasa” (Taittiriya Upanisad 2.7). He said Bhagavatam is a form of rasa and should be savored by the rasikas, those who are conversant with rasa (rasikah = rasa-jnah). In his explanation of the word a-layam (up to and including liberation), he established the philosophical conclusion that drinking the nectar which is Bhagavatam should not stop, even when one has achieved liberation.

In his commentary on this famous verse, Sndhara Svami expounded upon bhakti-rasa:

*mallanam asanir nrnam nara-varah strmam smaro murtiman*  
*gopanam sva-jano ’satam ksiti-bhujam sasta sva-pitroh sisuh \|*  
*mrtyur bhoja-pater virad avidusam tattvam param yoginam*  
*vrsninam para-devateti vidito rangam gatah sagrajah \|\|*

**In the battle arena, Krishna, accompanied by His elder brother, was perceived by the people there as follows: To the wrestlers He was a thunderbolt, to the men of Mathura He was the best of men, to the women He was Cupid in person, to the cowherds He was their relative, to the unrighteous kings He was their punisher, to His parents He was their child, to Kamsa He was his own death, to ignorant people He was the Universal Form, to the yogis He was the Absolute Truth, and to the Vrsnis He was their topmost Deity. (Bhagavatam 10.43.17)**

Sridhara Svami comments:

*tatra srngaradi-sarva-rasa-kadamba- murtir bhagavan. \[...\] malladisv abhivyakta rasah kramena slokena nibadhyante, raudro ’dbhutas ca srngaro hasyam viro daya tatha. bhayanakas ca bibhatsah santah sa-prema-bhaktikah.*

**“At that time, the Lord was the form of all the rasas, beginning from srngara. Toward Him the wrestlers had raudra-rasa, the men had adbhuta-rasa, the women had srngara-rasa, the cowherds had hasya-rasa, the impious kings had vira-rasa, His parents had daya (compassion, pity) (vatsalya), Kamsa had bhayanaka-rasa, the ignorant people, who saw Him as Virat, had bibhatsa-rasa, the yogis had santa-rasa, and the Vrsnis had prema-bhakti-rasa. ” (Bhavartha-dipika 10.43.17)**

Sridhara Svami thus established bhakti as a rasa proper (prema- bhakti-rasa), but he did not include other rasas within it. That was Vopadeva’s contribution. For the most part, above Sridhara Svami simply matched the other types of people with Bharata Muni’s rasas. Only karuna-rasa is absent.

In Rupa Gosvami’s methodology, the repartition is different. Jiva Gosvami explains:

*kim calaukika-rasa-vidam pracinanam api matanusarena sidhyaty asau rasah. tatra samanyatah sri- bhagavan-nama-kaumudi-karair darsitah. tasya visesatas tu santadisu pancasu bhedesu vaktavyesu sri-svami-caranair mallanam asanir ity-adau te pancaiva darsitah. strinam srngarah. samavayasam gopanam hasya-sabda-sucita-narma- maya-sakhya-sthayi sakhya-mayah preyan. tatas tan-mate gopanam sridamadinam ity evarthah. pitror dayapara-paryaya- vatsalya-sthayi vatsalah. yoginam jnana-bhakti-mayah santah. vrsninam bhakti-maya iti. tatha samanya-priti-maya-rasas ca nrnam darsitah. tatradbhutatva-nirdesas ca sarvasyaiva rasasya tat-pranatvat santatvadi-vaisistyabhave tad eva nirdistam iti. yathaha dharmadattah, rase saras camatkarah sarvatrapy anubhuyate, tac-camatkara-saratve sarvatrapy adbhuto rasah, tasmad adbhutam evaha krti narayano rasam.*

**“Bhakti-rasa is proven in accordance with the opinions of ancient scholars on the topic of transcendental rasa. Among them, it was illustrated in a general way by the venerable author of Sri- bhagavan-nama-kaumudi In the details, however, the five rasas, beginning from santa, should be stated (the main ones in Rupa Gosvami’s system). Sridhara Svami showed those five in the verse that begins mallanam asani. The women had srngara-rasa. The cowherd boys had preyas, which consists of friendship (sakhya) and whose sthayi is a friendship imbued with jokes: This signifies humor (hasya). His two parents had vatsala, whose sthayi is vatsalya, another synonym of daya. The yogis had santa-rasa, which consists of jnana and bhakti. The Vrsnis had rasa consisting of bhakti. It is also illustrated that the men had a rasa imbued with affection for the Lord in a general way. Moreover, it is said that the men had astonishment because it is the life of every rasa. When there is no specific rasa, only that one is pointed out. For instance, Dharmadatta said: “When there is relishment, the essence, astonishment, is perceived everywhere. Therefore Pandit Narayana says there is only one rasa: adbhuta” (cited in Sahitya-darpana 3.3)” (Priti-sandarbha 110).**

Baladeva Vidyabhusana cites the Bhagavatam verse as an instance of the ullekha ornament (angles of description) (Sahitya-kaumudi 11.17). In the chapter on literary faults, he paraphrased Sndhara Svami’s interpretation in this way: Although Krishna is the object of all the rasas, there is no contradiction because the rasas are not mundane.

In Rupa Gosvami’s methodology, if the person who is a subject (asraya) of a rasa related to Krishna has no connection with Him, that is a type of semblance of bhakti-rasa called anurasa (Bhakti- rasamrta-sindhu 4.9.33). And any rasa where Krishna’s enemy is a subject is called aparasa, another kind of bhakti-rasabhasa (Bhakti-rasamrta-sindhu 4.9.38).

In propounding his concept of dasya-bhakti-rasa (mood of service to God), Rupa Gosvami said it was called prema-bhakti-rasa by Sridhara Svami. According to Rupa Gosvami, Sridhara Svami thus implied that it is the highest rasa. Rupa Gosvami added that Laksmidhara, in his Nama-kaumudi, listed dasya as a subcategory of the ancients’ sthayi-bhava called rati (whereas in Rupa Gosvami’s methodology, any sthayi-bhava of bhakti is called rati). In addition, Rupa Gosvami specified that dasya-rasa was described as a form of santa-rasa by Sudeva and others. Mammata had implicitly included dasya in the subcategory of rati called devadi-visaya, but in his methodology it cannot reach the level of rasa.

## Supplement on Laksmidhara

Laksmidhara is also famous for his Advaita-makaranda and for his commentary on Sankaracarya’s Saundarya-lahari. He was not a strict follower of Sankara because in Advaita-makaranda he expounded that the soul is not different from Brahma, whereas the Acarya says a soul is an upadhi (extrinsic attribute) of Brahma. P. Thirugnanasambanda writes:

Lakshmidhara, the author of the Advaita-makaranda, a prakarana work on Advaita Vedanta, has to his credit two other works, namely, a commentary on Srimad Bhagavata and Bhagavan-nama-kaumudi dealing with nama-samkirtana as a means of attainment of purusharthas and with the meaningfulness of the Puranas. This is evident from the author’s own statement in the latter work which is as follows:

*yena bhagavata-vyakhya kritamrita-tarangini*  
*advaita-makarandas cha so’karon nama-kaumudim*

\[...\] Sri S. Srikantha Sastri states that Lakshmidhara was the son of Simhala, sister of Sri Vidyaranya and that he was probably identical with the patron of the Kannada Poet Madhura in the time of Devaraya I (1406 A.D.).

\[.\] From the above facts it appears that Lakshmidhara, the author of Advaita-makaranda, son of Narasimha and disciple of Anantananda Raghunatha assigned to the 15th century by the editor of Vani Vilas publication is different from the Lakshmidhara of Cherukuru family who flourished in the court of Tirumalaraya of Vijayanagara in the latter half of the 16th century.

The work bears a felicitous name, Advaita-makaranda, which as the author himself describes towards the end of the work, is sweet like the honey collected from the autumnal lotus (Sarad- ambhoja-sambhrita), capable of delighting the bees, viz., those learned in the sastras (vidvad-bhringah). ‘Advaitam’ is Brahman and ‘makaranda’ is rasa and the title gives the subject-matter of the work, the nature of Brahman that is identical with rasa, ‘raso vai sah’. The nature of Brahman can be known only by ‘anubhava’ as the sweetness of honey is experienced only by one who tastes it and not by one who listens to an exposition about its nature.

The work contains twenty-seven verses dealing with the nature of Brahman that is not different from the soul. These verses are commented upon by Svayamprakasayati, disciple of Kaivalyananda Yogindra, in a lucid and authoritative manner. The author invokes the blessing of his ishtadevata Sri Krishna, the Blissful and Eternal (anantananda Krishna), a term which can be taken to make an oblique reference to his teacher Anantananda Raghunatha \[...\]. The central thesis of this work is ‘brahmaivaham’.

## 26. Vag-bhata I

Vag-bhata (twelfth century) wrote Vag-bhatalankara. He was a Jain from Gujarat. He accepts the ancients’ ten gunas. He mentions thirty-five ornaments of meaning and expounds on citra-kavya, vakrokti, anuprasa and yamaka. Vagbhatalankara briefly touches on all the topics of poetics, except the Dhvani Theory and dramaturgy. It was the first simple treatise on poetics. Dr. Kane notes:

There are two Vag-bhata’s in Alankara-sastra. This is the first. The work is not an elaborate treatise. It is divided into five paricchedas, which contain 260 verses. Most of the verses are in the Anustubh metre \[...\]. All the examples cited in the work appear to be the author’s own. \[.\] He cited (as pointed out by Col. Jacob, JRAS 1897 p. 309) six verses which occur in the Nemi-nirvana-kavya, the author of which is a Vag-bhata. \[.\] The editors of the K.M. series show from the Prabhavaka- caritra of Prabha-candra (p. 205) that Vag-bhata was living in samvat 1179 and 1213 (i.e. 1123 and 1156 A.D.). Therefore, Vag-bhata flourished in the first half of the 12th century and his Kavyalankara was written between 1125-1143 A.D.

Vag-bhata illustrates the parisankhya ornament (answer with an exclusion):

*yatra vayuh param caurah paura-saurabha-sampadam \|*  
*yuvanas ca krta-krodhad eva bibhyur vadhu-janat \|\|*

**In such a place, the wind is the only thief—a thief that steals the affluence of the citizens’ fragrance—and young men only fear young women who are in a pique. (Vag-bhatalankara 4.142)**

Here this question is implied: “What is a nice city?” and the exclusion of other possibilities are implied: the exclusion of other kinds of thieves and of other kinds of fear.

This is Vag-bhata’s example of ekavali (modified series):

*desah samrddha-nagaro nagarani ca sapta-bhumi-nilayani \|*  
*nilayah salila-lalana lalanas catyanta-kamaniyah \|\|*

**A real country is a place where there is a prosperous city. Such a city is one where there are seven-story mansions. A real mansion is one where there are sexy women. And a sexy woman is a woman who is sweet to a high degree. (4.136)**

## 27. Vag-bhata II

This Vag-bhata wrote Kavyanusasana. His purpose in writing the book was to make a short yet complete treatise. He endorses Mammata’s concept of three gunas. He says rasa is the life of poetry: atah kavyasya prana-bhutan rasan aha (Kavyanusasana, KM p. 53). He disserts on sixty-three literary ornaments, in which some of Rudrata’s old figures reappear. He refers to Anandavardhana’s Dhvany-aloka for a disquisition on Dhvani. Dr. Sushil Kumar De comments on the books of the two Vag-bhatas:

The object of these Jaina manuals (though there is nothing specifically Jaina in them) appears to have been the presentation of a popular and easy epitome of the subject, allaying themselves to no particular school or system, but following the traditional notions in a spirit of eclecticism, without critically systematising them in the light of a central theory. In this respect, they bear a close resemblance to the alankara section in the Agni-purana and the Sarasvati-kanthabharana of Bhoja, whose definition of poetry is forcibly recalled by that of the older Vagbhata quoted above.

Dr. Kane writes:

The author was a Jain. \[...\] He was the son of Nemikumara and is to be distinguished from Vag-bhata I who was the author of the Vag-bhatalankara, as he himself mentions the latter: ‘dandi-vamana-vagbhatadi-pranita dasa kavya-gunah I vayam tu madhuryaujah-prasada-laksanas trin eva gunan manyamahe’ (Kavyanusasana-vrtti p. 31). \[...\] There is no originality in the work. He largely borrows from the Kavya- mimamsa of Rajasekhara, the Kavya-prakasa and other works and quotes examples contained in other works e.g. he quotes under yamaka the verse rambharama which is Vag- bhatalankara IV.30 and Nemi-nirvana-kavya VII.50. \[.\] Therefore he is later than 1150 A.D. He probably flourished in the 14th century.

This is Vag-bhata’s example of pankti-yamaka (each line sounds the same). The speaker addresses Nemi:

*rambharama kur abaka-ka-mala-*  
*ram bharama kurabaka-kamala- \|*  
*rambha ramakurabaka kamala-*  
*rambha-ramakura-baka-kamala \|\|*

rambha—have plantain trees; arama—in which the gardens; kuh— the Earth; abaka—which has few cranes (a = isat); ka—water; mala—it has; aram—intensely (aram = alam); bhara-ama—it gets a weight (from the verbal root am); kurabaka-kamala—of kurabaka flowers and of lotus flowers; arambha—it has beginnings; rama—is splendid; aku-ravaka— O you whose sounds are not contemptible (ka is added without a change in meaning); kamala- rambha—are Laksmis and Rambhas; rama—are beautiful; akura— charming (“they do not contemptibly shine”); baka—are rogues (in a figurative sense, since the crane is a bird of great cunning); ka­mala—on which the women (“they have happiness”).

**On Earth, the parks include banana trees and the ponds have few cranes. The Earth is splendid: It eminently bears the weight of mountains and is lovely with kurabaka flower buds and lotus blossoms. O you of splendid sounds, on Earth the women are beautiful: They are LaksmTs and Rambhas. They are charming rogues.**

Commenting on this verse in Vag-bhatalankara, Simhadeva-gani says that for the purpose of yamaka the cesura after the second line is not taken in consideration. The meter is bhramara-vilasita. Further, sometimes the last letter of the first line (or third line) of a verse is part of the yamaka in the second line (or in the fourth line).

## 28. Jayadeva

Jayadeva (c. 1200-1250 CE) wrote Candraloka. He lived in Bihar, and called himself Piyusa-varsa Jayadeva (he rains nectar) (1.2; 10.5-6). He is not the well-known Jayadeva who wrote Glta-govinda, because he was born in Odisha and flourished during the reign of Laksmana-sena (ruled 1178-1204 CE).

Candraloka consists of 350 verses in ten chapters. Jayadeva composed all his examples. It is the first simple and complete treatise on poetics—Vag-bhata \|\| probably lived after him—and is the most famous among the lesser-known works on poetical theory.

In its own right, the Candraloka (C.A.) became as popular as the Kavya-prakasa (K.P.):

Like the K.P., which was read everywhere, the C.A. in its time and among its circle was a highly popular work and was regarded as an ideal manual which can be placed in the hands of the beginners and of those who wanted shortcuts in the subject.

The chapter on ornaments is by far the most voluminous: It expounds around ninety ornaments of meaning, not to mention the subvarieties, for a total of 111, and it is the basis of other works, such as Appaya Diksita’s Kuvalayananda and Baladeva Vidyabhusana’s Kavya-kaustubha.

For the most part, Jayadeva’s methodology is this: He states the definition in the first half of a verse and gives one example in the second half. For instance:

*alankarah parikarah sabhipraye visesane \|*  
*sudhamsu-kalitottamsas tapam haratu vah sivah \|\|*

**The parikara ornament is the usage of a highly purposeful adjective: May moon-crested Siva take away your burning afflictions. (5.39)**

Sometimes Jayadeva’s example is the definition itself:

*avrtta-varna-stabakam stava-kandankuram kaveh \|*  
*yamakam prathama dhurya-madhurya-vacaso viduh \|\|*

avrtta—repeated; varna—of letters; stabakam—\[a yamaka,\] in which there is a bunch; stava—of praise; kanda—of the root; ankuram—the sprout; kaveh—of a poet; yamakam—a yamaka (“like a pair”); prathamah—the first ones; dhurya—who are leaders; madhurya—have sweetness; vacasah—whose words; viduh—they know.

**The best persons, those who are leaders and whose words are sweet, know that a yamaka includes a bunch of repeated letters and is the beginning of the praise of a poet. (5.8)**

The yamakas are “stabakam stava-kan” and “ma dhurya- madhurya”. In the first one, the repetition of the anusvara is the letter n before d, since before d an anusvara optionally becomes n.

Jayadeva slightly modified the interpretations of several ornaments, such as parikara and parinama, and invented some others, notably purva-rupa (previous form), parikarankura (significant epithet), praharsana (great joy), anuguna (enhancement of one’s quality, sambhavana (high-flying possibility), and atyukti (hyperbole). He reiterated the ornaments invented by Ruyyaka.

In Kavya-kaustubha, Baladeva Vidyabhusana followed Jayadeva’s methodology of ornaments. In his commentary on Kavya-prakasa, Nagesa Bhatta rejected some of Jayadeva’s ornaments, such as vikasvara, oftentimes by subsuming them in some other ornament. Those dubious ornaments are not found in Sahitya- kaumudi, where Baladeva Vidyabhusana added a chapter to the text of Kavya-prakasa to treat of the best ornaments of Jayadeva and of Visvanatha.

Candraloka is easy to read. The meanings are not profound. Dr. Keith writes: “Jayadeva’s Candraloka is no more than a convenient manual of figures with happy illustrations, on which (c. 1600) Appaya Diksita the polymath based his Kuvalayananda. ” Nonetheless, Jayadeva’s methodology is original and thorough. He accepts the Dhvani theory, but does not make it the central aspect of his system. This is his definition of poetry:

*nirdosa laksana-vati sa-rtir guna-bhusana \|*  
*salankara-rasaneka-vrttir vak kavya-nama-bhak \|\|*

**“Faultless words that have a kavya-laksana, a riti, a guna, an ornament, a rasa, and a vrtti of alliteration obtain the designation ‘poetry’.” (1.7)**

In this regard, with another brilliant yamaka he criticizes Mammata:

*angikaroti yah kavyam sabdarthav analankrti \|*  
*asau na manyate kasmad anusnam analam krti \|\|*

**“Some accomplished scholar accepts that sounds and meanings devoid of an ornament are poetry. Then why does he not think that fire has no heat?” (1.8)**

Siva-prasada Bhattacarya explains the general contents of Baladeva Vidyabhusana’s Kavya-kaustubha (K.K.) by way of explaining the methodology in Candraloka:

The case of the K.K. drawing in upon the C.A. is a clear one. \[...\] The K.K. has affiliated itself to the C.A., esp. in chaps. I (Kavya-laksana), VI (Dosa), IX (Alankara) which correspond readily with chaps. I, \|\| and V of the C.A. respectively. In broad outlines chaps. \|\| (Abhidha-vrtti), III (Rasa-bhava), IV (Guna), V (Rlti), VII (Dhvani), VIII (Madhyama-kavya) cover the same ground respectively as chaps. I and IX, VI, IV (latter half), VI (latter half), VII and VIII of the C.A. Both the works are in the nature of short and simple practical manuals—the Mandara-maranda-campu of a later age coming very near to them though of a more ambitious type—and do not deal in controversial issues or theories. The K.K. however is written in the Karika-vrtti-udaharana pattern, the fashionable form of Alankara nibandhas and was intended as a handy work for students in general and not for advanced specialists.

There is, however, one fundamental difference. The C.A. does not explicitly regard the Dhvani-kavya as uttama or first-rate nor the guni-bhuta-vyangya to be madhyama-kavya or second- rate poetry. Its treatment thereof is apparently for purposes of imparting fulness and not to indicate the essential nature of the concept. Even its characterisation of vyanjana (sammukhyam vidadhanayah sphutam arthantare girah \| kataksa iva lolaksya vyaparo vyanjanatmakah \|\| (VII.2) is that of the tatastha who admires but is not convinced of its intrinsic merit. Jayadeva’s description of laksana (iyam alankara-bijataya sthita, IX.16), his winding up of his Alankara work with the treatment of abhidha (chap. X.) his characteristic retort (angikaroti yah kavyam sabdarthav analankrti \| asau na manyate kasmad anusnam analam krti \|\| I.8) betray his affinities with the old Alankara school, which, as Anandavardhana points out, stake everything on abhidha-vrtti. The K.K., true to its salt of Bengal Vaisnavite tradition cannot accede to such a view of alankaras suppressing rasas or emerging thereover—indeed with Baladeva, alankaras come in connection with what with Mammata he regards as the adhama or the citra-kavya, not even of the madhyama as is the case with the bulk of later rhetoricians including the great Jagannatha. Baladeva, however, does not push the consequences of such a view to their extreme limits. His rather half-hearted admission and inadequate treatment of the rasa-dosas is a pointer to his real motive in writing the K.K. It was out and out his intention to write an easy work on the lines of the C.A.

Jayadeva reiterates Rudrata’s methodology of ritis and vrttis (Candraloka 6.21-26). In the fourth chapter, he accepts Bharata Muni’s ten gunas and defines some of them differently: Jayadeva’s slesa is this: The description has a meaning that poetically stands in opposition. His prasada is the modern prasada, which corresponds to Bharata Muni’s artha-vyakti. The samata is the uniformity of short compounds with the same kind of letters. His samadhi is simply the greatness of a meaning which causes the readers’ body to erupt in goosebumps. The madhurya is a charming repetition of sounds. His two subdivisions of ojas are the same as Vamana’s first two categories of artha-guna ojas. The saukumarya is, as he admits, simply the absence of harsh sounds. And his udarata is, in his own words, clever only because it is not rustic. He adds that kanti-guna is subsumed in srngara-rasa and artha- vyakti in prasada.

In the third chapter, Jayadeva expounds ten kavya-laksanas, taken from Bharata Muni. Jayadeva’s definitions and examples are in parentheses: (1) aksara-samhati (few words say much) (it is almost like the parikarankura ornament) (“Sauri, the hero, was followed by the lover of Usa”), (2) sobha (resplendence) (a fault is repudiated because of a quality: “People uselessly criticize this world, where Krishna is revered”), (3) abhimana (conceit, i.e. the negation of an implied sense: “If this is the moon, why is it harsh?”), (4) hetu (cause, i.e. various possibilities are negated: “This is not the moon; this is not the blazing sun; rather it is the submarine fire arisen from the ocean”), (5) pratisedha (negation; it is almost like vibhavana, an effect without the usual cause) (“Fighters do not fall in battle, rather they fall because of the movements of women’s eyebrows”), (6) nirukta (etymology, i.e. a double meaning: “Due to these deeds, O king, you truly are dosakara (a moon, or a mine of faults)”), (7) mithyadhyavasaya (double unreality) (this was classed as an ornament by Appaya Diksita, who renamed it mithyadhyavasiti; Baladeva Vidyabhusana included it in Sahitya-kaumudi), (8) siddhi (effectuation, a form of tulya-yogita: “Both of you are renowned: You because of an army and an ocean because of the mass of water”), (9) yukti (trickery: “You, O king, are some sort of cloud because you rain gold”), and (10) karya (effect: “The moon rises to dispel the pique of beautiful women”).

Jayadeva covers the literary faults in chapter 2, the rasas, ritis and vrttis in chapter 6, Suggestiveness and the categories of dhvanis in chapter 7, first-rate poetry and second-rate poetry in chapter 8, and figurative usage in chapter 9.

In chapter 10, Jayadeva expounds Denotation. At first he says a word is used simply because it denotes an attribute: dharmam kancit puraskrtya prayah sabdah pravartate \| yayartham spastam acaste sabdas tam abhidham viduh \|\| (10.1). He lists six kinds of literal words: A word denotes either the category, a quality, an action, a possession, a name, or else a word is constructed in a special way: jatya gunena kriyaya vastu-yogena samjnaya \| nirdesena tatha prahuh sad-vidham abhidham budhah \|\| (10.2).

Examples of the first five are: go (cow, bull), nila (blue), pacaka (cook), dandi (one who has a stick), and dittha (a person named Dittha): gaur nilah pacako dandi ditthah kamsa iti kramat \| (10.3ab). The sixth category is his contribution to poetical theory. To illustrate it, he says the word ‘Kamsa’ in this sentence is literally denoted: kam samhinasti kamsarir naram ca kam samasritam, “Toward whom or what is Kamsari hostile? He is hostile to the man who is Kamsa (lit. kam sam asritam, “the kam which accompanies sa”)” (10.3). This is the prasnottara ornament. As a pun: “Kamsari is also hostile to Naraka (lit. naram ca kam samasritam, “the nara who fully accompanies ka”).”

Piyusa-varsa Jayadeva is also the author of a play called Prasanna- raghava. Therein he writes:

*na brahma-vidya na ca raja-laksmis*  
*tatha yatheyam kavita kavinam \|*  
*lokottare pumsi nivesyamana*  
*putriva harsam hrdaye karoti \|\|*

**“This poetic skill of scholarly poets gives joy to the heart like giving one’s daughter in marriage to a highly qualified man does. Neither trance in Brahma nor kingly opulence can compare to it.” (Prasanna-raghava, prastavana 23)**

In Sanskrit at large, logical reasoning is strictly applied. Sanskrit poetics is no exception: Speculating about a meaning that is either incongruent in context or not based on a grammatical rule is out of the question. Studying Sanskrit gives maturity: The language is scientific. Therefore it is fitting that Jayadeva, an innovator in poetics, was also an accomplished Logician:

From the Prasanna-raghava it appears that he was a great logician also (nanu ayam pramana-pravino ’pi sruyate \| ... sutra-dharah—yesam komala-kavya-kausala-kala-lilavati bharati tesam karkasa-tarka-vakra-vacanodgare ’pi kim hiyate \|\| I.18). \[...\] The Alankara-sekhara of Kesava Misra (p. 17) speaks of a poet Jayadeva Pandita who vanquished by his logical subtlety the pandits at the court of the king of Utkala.

## 29. Vopadeva

Vopadeva (thirteenth century) wrote Mukta-phala, a treatise solely on the topic of bhakti-rasa. He was the first to base an understanding of rasa entirely on Bhagavatam.

He thus brought to light subdivisions of bhakti, and showed that the nine rasas can take the form of bhakti-rasa. Vopadeva substantiated his statements by citing approximately eight hundred verses from Bhagavatam.

Hemadri wrote the commentary on the Mukta-phala, called Kaivalya-dipika. In text 4.3.54 of his magnum opus (BRS), Rupa Goswami mentions Vopadeva. There are major differences in methodology, but in Bhakti-rasamrta-sindhu Rupa Gosvami must have used Vopadeva’s selection of Bhagavatam verses as a source of inspiration for his examples. In Ujjvala-mlamani, Rupa Gosvami acknowledged that in Mukta-phala Vopadeva had discussed the love that the Dvaraka queens felt in separation from Krishna. Vopadeva cited the verses beginning from kurari vilapasi (Bhagavatam 10.90.15) in the section on vipralambha (Mukta-phala 12.72 etc.). Rupa Gosvami invented the term prema- vaicittya (Ujjvala-nilamani 15.147).

In his commentary on the first verse of Gopi-gitam, Visvanatha Cakravarti wrote: atra sloke prati-padam dvitiyaksarasyaikyam tatha prathamaksara-saptamaksarayos ca. evam anyesv api slokesu prayah kvacit kvacid asti tac ca muktaphala-tika-karair vivrtam, “In this verse, the consonant in the second syllable of each line is the same, and so are the consonants of the first and seventh syllables. For the most part, this occurs here and there in other verses as well. And that was explained by the writer of the commentary on Mukta-phala” (Sarartha-darsini 10.31.1). Vopadeva cited the verse (Mukta-phala 12.21). But Hemadri did not mention all the noteworthy details.

The name Vopadeva seems to be a corruption of Gopadeva which later became Bopadeva. Vopadeva and Hemadri were two royal pandits in Devagiri (modern-day Daultabad, 11 kms north-west of Aurangabad) in Maharashtra. The famous Ellora Caves are only 16 kms away from Devagiri-Daultabad.

Dr. Katre writes:

Hemadri, the celebrated author, principally of works of Dharma- shastra, and popularly known in Maharashtra as Hemadpant, was the son of Kamadeva, and grandson of Vasudeva of vatsa- gotra, and flourished during the reigns of Mahadeva (A. D. 1260-70) and Ramachandra (A. D. 1271-1309) and was minister to both of them. His most famous compilation is the (1) Chatur-varga-chintamani which is an inexhaustible mine of information in Dharma-shastra, voluminous in extent and all-comprehensive in its nature. Besides this, he is also the author of (2) a commentary on Shaunaka’s Pranava-kalpa, (3) Kaivalya-dipika, a commentary on Mukta-phala by Bopadeva, (4) Shraddhakalpa according to the rules of Katyayana and (5) Ayurveda-rasayana, a commentary on Ashtanga-hridaya of Vaghbhata. As minister of the Yadava king Mahadeva he was in charge of the imperial records at Devagiri. Bopadeva, the author of Mukta-phala, was one of Hemadri’s proteges in the court of the Yadavas, and was the son of a physician named Keshava and a pupil of Dhanesha. From the internal evidence regarding parentage, he appears to be identical with the author of Mugdhabodha, a new system of Sanskrit grammar. This is one more illustration of the fact that linguistic study was a vital aspect of Maharashtrian scholarship which has continued unabated from the time of the great Varttika-kara.

For some reason, the German scholar Max Muller thought that Vopadeva is the author of the Bhagavatam. Vopadeva was a prolific writer:

Besides the Mugdha-bodha, Kavi-kalpa-druma, and its commentary—the Kamadhenu— Bopadeva has written the Mukta-phala and Hari-lila-vivarana, (both dealing with the Bhagavata Purana), a medical work called Sata-sloki, and a treatise on Dharma-sastra.

In Mugdha-bodha-vyakarana, Vopadeva became the first gram­marian to consistently refer to the Lord:

Another feature which we notice in this grammar for the first time is its religious element. In the choice of examples illustrating his rules, Bopadeva has taken care to use wherever possible the names of Hari, Hara, and other gods. Bopadeva is here equally partial to Hari, Hara, or Rama; but later writers have outdone him in this respect.

Vopadeva’s methodology inspired Jiva Gosvami: In Hari- ndmdmrta-vyakarana, he renamed Panini’s grammatical terms by using the Lord’s names. Most of Jiva Gosvami’s examples center on the Lord. Jiva Gosvami mentioned details of Vopadeva’s grammatical theories from Mugdha-bodha-vyakarana several times.

The reason scholars who lived after Panini bothered to write their own grammatical treatises was to facilitate the learning of Sanskrit. Dr. Belvalkar writes:

The difficulty in understanding Panini comes from the very circumstance which Panini himself perhaps considered his real advance over all his predecessors, namely his attempt to economise expression where conceivably he could do so without being misunderstood. Why Panini should have elected to strain all his nerves to bring about a result which a student of grammar is often likely to regard as the curse of his lot is more than we can say.

## The Major Grammatical Treatises Post-Astadhyayi

**Author** **Date** **Name** **Region of popularity**   Sarvavarman 100 CE Katantra- vyakarana (Kalapa) Kashmir, Bengal, Tibet   Devanandin (Pujyapada) 500 Jainendra- vyakarana Jain communities   Candragomin 600 Candra-vyakarana Tibet, Indian Buddhist communities   Sakatayana 850 Sakatayana- sabdanusasana Jain communities   Bhojaraja 1030 Sarasvati-kanthabharana Malwa   Hemacandra 1140 Sabdanusasana Gujarat and other Jain communities   Vopadeva 1250-1275 Mugdha-bodha- vyakarana Maharashtra   Kramadisvara 1250-1275 Sanksipta-sara- vyakarana Bengal   Anubhuti- svarupacarya (or Narendracarya) 1275 Sarasvata- vyakarana (Sarasvati- prakriya) Bihar, Varanasi, Malwa, Uttar Pradesh, Nepal, Tibet   Padmanabha Bhatta 1350-1375 Saupadma- vyakarana (Supadma- vyakarana) Mithila (Videha), Bengal   Ramacandra 1400-1450 Prakriya-kaumudi Varanasi   Jiva Gosvamin 1570 Hari-namamrta- vyakarana Bengal and Vrindavan   Bhattoji Diksita 1600 Siddhanta- kaumudi Varanasi, all of India

Bhattoji Diksita was a Maharashtrian, therefore he must have taken inspiration from Vopadeva’s Mugdha-bodha-vyakarana.

In the Sandarbhas as well Jiva Gosvami referred to Vopadeva: “vedah puranam kavyam ca prabhur mitram priyeva ca, bodhayandd hi prahus tri-vrd bhagavatam punah” iti mukta- phale hemadri-kara-vacanena ca, “The contents of this verse are partially from the statements of Hemadri in Mukta-phala: “They say the Vedas, the Puranas, and poetry make one understand like a master, like a friend and like a wife respectively. However, the Bhagavatam does so like all three”” (Tattva-sandarbha 26.2).

The verse is in Vopadeva’s Hari-Ulamrta (1.9), sometimes called Hari-lila-vivarana: In twelve chapters, he composed a total of 126 verses to summarize each chapter of Bhagavatam. In the above verse, the first sentence originates from Abhinavagupta (Locana 3.14; 3.30) and was first cited by Mammata (Kavya-prakasa 1.2).

Before writing his commentary on Mukta-phala, Hemadri composed Caturvarga-cintamani, an encyclopedic work on dharma. The five chapters are divided as vrata, dana, tirtha, moksa and parisesa respectively. In Tattva-sandarbha, Jiva Gosvami refers to that book several times. For instance:

*hemadrer vrata-khande, “stn-sudra-dvijabandhunam trayl na sruti-gocara, karma-sreyasi mudhanam sreya evam bhaved iha, iti bharatam akhyanam krpaya munina krtam” iti vakyam sri- bhagavatlyatvenotthapya bharatasya vedartha-tulyatvena nirnayah krta iti. tan-matanusarena tv evam vyakhyeyam bharatarthasya vinirnayah. vedartha-tulyatvena visisya nirnayo yatreti.*

**“In his Catur-varga-cintamani, Vrata-khanda (1.28), Hemadri cites the following verse from Bhagavatam, “Out of compassion, the great sage thought it wise to do something that would enable even those who are ignorant of how to act for their own benefit to achieve the ultimate goal of life. Thus he compiled the great historical narration called the Mahabharata for women, workers, and friends of the twice-born because they do not have access to the Vedas” (Bhagavatam 1.4.25). Hemadri uses this verse to demonstrate that the Mahabharata is as valuable as the Vedas. Consequently, the phrase bharatartha-vinirnayah, “Bhagavatam establishes the meaning of the Mahabharata” (Garuda Purana, cited in Tattva-sandarbha 21.1) should be explained, in accordance with this view, as saying that Bhagavatam is the literature in which the Mahabharata’s message is conclusively defined and is shown to be equal to that of the Vedas.” (Tattva-sandarbha 22.5)**

Jiva Gosvami continues:

*yad eva ca hemadri-granthasya dana- khande purana-dana-prastave matsya-puraniya-tal-laksana-dhrtya prasastam. hemadri-parisesa-khandasya kala-nirnaye ca kali- yuga-dharma-nirnaye kalim sabhajayanty aryah ity-adikam yad- vakyatvenotthapya yat pratipadita-dharma eva kalav angl-krtah.*

**“The Bhagavatam is also extolled in the Dana-khanda section of Hemadri’s Catur-varga-cintamani. His chapter entitled “Giving Puranas in Charity” praises the Bhagavatam by noting that it possesses the defining characteristics of a maha-purana specified in the Matsya Purana (53.20-22). In the Parisesa-khanda of Catur- varga-cintamani, in the Kala-nirnaya section, where Hemadri defines the appropriate religion for Kali-yuga, he quotes the Bhagavatam verse beginning kalim sabhajayanty aryah (“Those who are advanced in knowledge are able to appreciate the essential value of this age of Kali. Such enlightened persons revere Kali-yuga because in this fallen age all perfection of life can easily be achieved by the performance of sanklrtana.” 11.5.36). In this way he recognizes as appropriate for this age only the religious principles established in Bhagavatam.” (Tattva-sandarbha 23.2).**

Jiva Goswami’s manner of naming the speaker of Bhagavatam verses cited in the Sandarbhas is modeled on Hemadri’s procedure: In Kaivalya-dipika, at the end of each commentary he writes that the verse quoted by Vopadeva was spoken by so and so to so and so.

## The Purpose of Writing the Mukta-phala

In his opening verse, Vopadeva explains the scheme of the treatise:

*visnum pancatmakam vande bhaktyastadasa-bhedaya \|*  
*sanga-vargonavimsatya bhaktair navabhir asritam \|\|*

**“With the eighteen divisions of bhakti and the nineteen series of aspects of bhakti, \| extol Vishnu, who has five forms. He shelters the nine types of devotees.” (Mukta-phala 1.1)**

Based on Vopadeva’s introductory verses, Hemadri says that Vopadeva was not satisfied with the five topics discussed in Caturvarga-cintamani—vrata, dana, tirtha, moksa and parisesa— and therefore in Mukta-phala Vopadeva set out to describe Vishnu, of subdivisions of bhakti, of bhakti-rasa, and of devotees. Hemadri gives various derivations of the name Mukta-phala. Among them, he says mukta means liberation (muc + kvip + tap). Muktaphala is a suitable result for liberated souls (mukta-aphala) (a = samyak).
