In a cryptic manner, Vopadeva hints at his motive for writing the Mukta-phala, revealed above by Hemadri; Vopadeva’s fourth introductory verse implies the uttara ornament (the question “By which book are the subdivisions of bhakti and so on described?” is implied from this answer):

*mukta-phalena granthena sad-bhagavata-suktina \|*  
*bhakti-khyaty-ambuna mugdha-markandeya-sisu-sriya \|\|*

**“By the book entitled Mukta-phala, so called because it is the result (phala) in the form of a pearl (mukta). That pearl issued from the eminent oyster which is the Bhagavatam in the ocean of the renown of bhakti on which there is the splendor of baby Vishnu because of whom Markandeya was fascinated.” (Mukta-phala 1.4)**

Somewhat might think, “Other gems and other treatises exist, so what is the use of this?” Vopadeva answers:

*mukta-phalam su-khacita-sphuta-bhakti-bheda-*  
*pratyaksa-rajita-lasat-pada-padmaragam \|*  
*hemadri-sambhava-suvarna-nivesa-ramyam*  
*kanthe kurudhvam avarundham apurva-laksmim \|\|*

mukta-phalam—fruit-like pearls (or the Mukta-phala) (or the psychoactive cobra lily plant); su-khacita—nicely inlaid (or sukha- cita—easily cited); sphuta—clearly; bhakti-bheda—whose type of division (or whose categories of devotion); pratyaksa-rajita—is refulgent when perceived by the senses (or praty-aksara—in every syllable; ajita—of Ajita); lasat-pada—\[a ruby,\] whose resting place is shining; padmaragam—\[pearls,\] because of which a ruby (or lasat—shining; pada-padma-ragam—it it is love for the lotus feet); hema-adri—is Sumeru (“the golden mountain”) (or Hemadri); sambhava—whose origination; suvarna—of gold (or su-varna—of nice phonemes); nivesa—because of the placement; ramyam—beautiful; kanthe—on the neck (or in the throat); kurudhvam—all of you should make (put); avarundham—; apurva—unprecedented; laksmlm—resplendence.

**\[First interpretation:\]**

**Put the Mukta-phala on the path of your vocal cords. In the Mukta-phala, the categories of bhakti are clearly defined and were cited with ease. The Mukta-phala includes love for the splendid lotus feet of Ajita in every syllable and is beautiful with the placement of nice phonemes originating from Hemadri. Thus it has an unprecedented resplendence.**

**\[Second interpretation:\]**

**Put a string of berry-like pearls on your neck. They enhance the splendor of nicely inlaid rubies that are refulgent when seen up close and that were nicely chiseled. Such pearls are beautiful with an arrangement of gold, which originates from Sumeru, and thus have an unprecendented resplendence. (Mukta-phala 1.5)**

## Sequence of Topics

The Mukta-phala consists of nineteen chapters. Vopadeva’s method is this: He writes a few lines of theory and then substantiates it with many verses of Bhagavatam. Hemadri provides the verse numbers. His commentary is far more voluminous than Vopadeva’s writing.

The topics in the treatise are: (I) Visnu-laksana-bhedah (definition of and forms of Vishnu), (II) Visnu-rupam (Vishnu’s form), (III) Visnor avatara-rupam (Vishnu’s Incarnations), (IV) Visnor adhisthana-rupam (Vishnu’s form for rulership), and visnor mahima (God’s glory), (V) Visnu-bhakter laksanam bhedas ca (definition of bhakti and its subdivisions) and visnu-bhakter adhikari-bhedah (the types of persons qualified for bhakti), (VI) Visnu-bhakti- mahima (the glory of bhakti), (VII) Visnu-bhakty-anga-varga- prakaranam (series of aspects of bhakti), (VIII) Visnu-sravanam, and visnu-kirtanam, (IX) Visnu-smaranam, (X) Visnu-sravana- kirtanam, and visnu-smarana-kirtnanam, (XI) Visnu-bhaktasya laksanam bhedas ca (characteristics and categories of devotees), visnu-bhaktanam hasya-rasah (the devotees’ mood of humor), and visnu-bhaktanam sambhoga-srngarah (the devotees’ mood of love in meeting), (XII) Visnu-bhaktanam vipralambha-srngarah (the devotees’ mood of love in separation), (XIII) Visnu-bhaktanam karuna-rasah (the devotees’ mood of lamentation), (XIV) Visnu- bhaktanam raudra-rasah (the devotees’ mood of inflamed anger), (XV) Visnu-bhaktanam bhayanaka-rasah (the devotees’ mood of fear), (XVI) Visnu-bhaktanam bibhatsa-rasah (the devotees’ mood of disgust), (XVII) Visnu-bhaktanam santa-rasah (the devotees’ mood of peacefulness), (XVIII) Visnu-bhaktanam adbhuta-rasah (the devotees’ mood of wonderment), and (XIX) Visnu-bhaktanam vira-rasah (the devotees’ mood of heroism).

Vopadeva writes:

*sa navadha bhaktah nava-vidhatve hetum aha, bhaktiti. bhaktir vihitavihita ca, bhakti-rasasyaiva hasya- srngara-karuna-raudra-bhayanaka-bibhatsa-santadbhuta-vira- rupenanubhavat. iti mukta-phale bhaktanam laksanam bhedas ca. vyasadi-vivarnitasya visnor visnu-bhaktanam va caritasya nava- rasatmakasya sravanadina janitas camatkaro bhakti-rasah.*

**“A devotee is classed in one of nine categories, since bhakti-rasa is experienced in the forms of hasya, srngara, karuna, raudra, bhayanaka, bibhatsa, santa, adbhuta, and vira. Bhakti-rasa is defined as the astonishment produced by hearing, remembering, etc., the deeds of either Vishnu or His devotees, as described by Vyasa and others. Those deeds comprise the nine rasas. ” (Mukta- phala 11.1)**

In the first chapter, Vopadeva says God has five modes of being: One of them is His formless nature, and the four others are these forms: Brahma, Visnu, Siva, and Purusa. Vopadeva mostly uses the term ‘Purusa’ in the sense of ‘Narayana’ (Garbhodaka-sayi Visnu). According to Vopadeva, the forms of the Purusa consist of sattva- guna with a trace of rajas and tamas whereas Vishnu’s form is made of sattva-guna without any rajas or tamas. Jiva Gosvami refuted Vopadeva and set forth the viewpoint that in Bhagavatam the word sattva is used in one of two ways: asuddha-sattva (sattva- guna ) and suddha-sattva (transcendental existence). Jiva Gosvami quoted Vopadeva as regards the first option.

In the second chapter, Vopadeva describes Vishnu’s form: He cites Bhagavatam verses 10.89-52-57, about Maha-Visnu. He also quotes verses regarding a meditation on Vishnu’s limbs.

In the third chapter, he lists forty Avataras (some of them are mentioned twice): Varaha, Kapila, Catuhsana, Narada, Nara- Narayana, Prthu, Rsabha, Hayagnva, Matsya, Kurma, Nrsimha, Hari (Vopadeva cites verses about Vishnu as the deliverer of Gajendra (2.7.15-16) and verse 11.4.19), Vamana, Hamsa, Manvantaresa, Dhanvantari, Mohini, Parasurama, Sri Rama, Sri Krsna, Vyasa, Buddha, Kalki, and Manvantara Avataras: Yajna, Hari, Vaikuntha, Ajita, Kurma, Vamana, Sarvabhauma, Rsabha, Visvaksena, Yogesvara, Brhadbhanu, and others.

Vopadeva says the Kali-yuga Avatara is black and cites the famous verse that begins krsna-varnam tvisakrsnam (Bhagavatam 11.5.32). On this topic, Rupa Gosvami listed forty-one Avataras

(Laghu-bhagavatamrta 1.4.27) and reiterated Vopadeva’s opinion that in Kali yuga the Avatara is black. However, the entire Gaudiya Vaishnava faith rests on the aforesaid verse because it forecasts the Appearance of Caitanya Mahaprabhu: Jiva Gosvami made the connection.

In the fourth chapter, Vopadeva discusses Vishnu’s form as Paramatma.

Notably, in the fifth chapter Vopadeva establishes eighteen subdivisions of bhakti. For the most part, he cites one verse of Bhagavatam for each subdivision. At the outset, he states the axiom: tasmat kenapy upayena manah krsne nivesayet, “Therefore one must think of Krishna by any means” (Bhagavatam 7.1.32) (Mukta- phala 5.1). That is Vopadeva’s definition of bhakti. The means are the categories stated in Bhagavatam 7.1.30. Here Hemadri cites Sridhara Svami. Hemadri adds that the word “therefore” optionally signifies “since only the Lord gives liberation (kaivalya ).” At first, Vopadeva subdivides those categories in two: vihita (ordained) (vaidhi) and avihita (not ordained):

## Supplement on Madhusudana Sarasvati

In Bhakti-rasayana, MadhusUdana Sarasvati (c. 1500-1600 CE) expounded Vopadeva’s philosophy though he never mentioned Vopadeva:

*nava-rasa-militam va kevalam va pum-artham*  
*paramam iha mukunde bhakti-yogam vadanti \|*  
*nirupama-sukha-samvid-rupam asprsta-duhkham*  
*tam aham akhila-tustyai sastra-drstya vyanajmi \|\|*

**“For the pleasure of all, I here explain bhakti-yoga, the path of devotion to Mukunda, by looking at the scriptures. Bhakti is the highest goal of life. Either bhakti is conjoined with one of the nine rasas or it occurs by itself. It is a form of incomparable happiness and awareness, untouched by sorrow.” (Bhakti-rasayana 1.1)**

In his commentary on Bhagavad-gTta, called Gudhartha-dTpika, Madhusudana followed Sridhara Svami’s opinion that bhakti is not fully transcendental (sa-guna). In addition, he reiterated Vopadeva’s classification of bhakti as suddha, karma-misra and jnana-misra. According to tradition, the path of jnana (trance) is only open to those who have the four requisites. Madhusudana accepted this and added that bhakti is open to all, but ideally one should be hard-hearted in terms of refraining from undue sense gratification and soft-hearted toward God.

Madhusudana Sarasvati says bhakti is all about the melting of the heart. This is his definition of bhakti: drutasya bhagavad- dharmad dhara-vahikatam gata, sarveso manaso vrttir bhaktir ity abhidhiyate, “When the mind has melted due to the practice of bhagavad-dharma, the resultant mindset which conveys an unbroken stream of awareness of God is called bhakti.” (Bhakti- ras ay ana 1.3)

Madhusudana Sarasvati often cites the Bhagavatam. Based on the first canto therein, he mentions twelve stages of bhakti: (1) Serving the greats, (2) Becoming the recipient oftheir mercy, (3) Developing faith in the values emphasized by the greats, (4) Hearing about Hari’s qualities, (5) The rise of a sprout of affection, (6) Being established in one’s nature as a soul, (7) Increase of divine love, (8) Manifestations of love, (9) Becoming fixed in the practice of bhagavad-dharma, (10) Acquiring the qualities of the greats and those of the Lord, and (11) Attaining the topmost stage of love.

Following Sndhara Svami, Vopadeva implicitly concluded that bhakti can reach the level of rasa—although most poetical rhetoricians said that bhakti, classed as deva-visaya rati, cannot possibly become rasa. Both Jiva Gosvami and Madhusudana Sarasvati reiterated this and specified that only devotion to demigods applies to the ancients’ methodology. Madhusudana is also famous for his Advaita-siddhi, where he refutes Madhvacarya’s Dvaita-vada.

Visvanatha Cakravarti often favorably referred to Madhusudana Sarasvati, for instance in his commentary on Bhakti-rasdmrta- sindhu 1.2.148 and in his commentary on Bhagavad-gita (4.6­9; 4.36; 5.9; 7.7; 8.18; etc.). Madhusudana was born in Bengal. According to tradition, Vallabhacarya entrusted his son Vittalanatha (b. 1516 CE) in the care of Madhusudana for his studies.

Svami Gambhirananda, who translated Gudhartha-dipika, dis­courses on Madhusudana:

The details of Madhusudana’s life and work given here are mostly based on what is available in Swami Sanatanadeva’s Hindi translation of the Gudhartha-dlpika (pub. Chaukhamba Sanskrit Sansthan, Benares; 1983) and to some extent on P.M. Modi’s introduction to his English translation of Siddhanta- bindu (pub. Vohra Publishers & Distributors, Allahabad).

His ancestor, Rama Misra Agnihotri, is believed to have migrated from Kannauj (in Uttar Pradesh) in AD 1194 to escape religious persecution by the foreign invaders. Coming away to Bengal, he settled in the village Unasiya (in Kotali- pada, district Faridpur, now in Bangladesh). \[...\] The third son, Kamala-nayana, born in about AD 1490 (according to some) and the brightest of them, received the name Madhusudana Sarasvati when he embraced monasticism in later life.

While a boy, Madhusudana was taught Sanskrit grammar, poetry, etc., by his father who was himself renowned for his scholarship. Some say that Madhusudana renounced home when he was merely ten years and travelled all the way to Navadvip (in West Bengal) to meet Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu, who was famous then as an embodiment of intense love for God. But, as destiny would have it, at that time Sri Caitanya was elsewhere in India spreading his message of bhakti. Disappointed, no doubt, but not disheartened, Madhusudana nevertheless stayed on there waiting for Sri Caitanya’s return. And in the meanwhile, studying under the guidance of Mathura-natha Tarka-vagisa, the then foremost professor of Nyaya, he mastered that philosophy. At the same time, he also deeply imbibed the devotional teachings of Sri Caitanya with which Navadvip was vibrant.

After thorough studies at Navadvip, and still unable to meet Sri Caitanya even after a long time, Madhusudana proceeded to Kasi (Varanasi) in search of a teacher of Advaita philosophy. \[...\]

Madhusudana left behind three eminent disciples—Balabhadra Bhattacarya, Sesa-govinda and Purusottama Sarasvati. The first of these wrote a commentary called Siddhi on Madhusudana’s Advaita-siddhi. The second, also known as Krsna Pundita, was from Maharashtra and the teacher of the famous grammarian Bhattoji Diksita; he wrote a commentary on Sri Sankaracarya’s Sarva-Vedanta-Siddhanta-Sarasangraha. The last, Purusottama Sarasvati, was a monk and wrote an exposition of his guru’s well-known work Siddhanta-bindu.

Some additional facts about the barely known life of Madhusudana found in the books referred to (pp. 13-14, f.n.) are noteworthy: He stayed for several decades at Gopala Mafha on the Catuhsasthi Ghat (popularly known as the Causasthi Yogini Ghat) in Benares. A historically important event at Benares in those days has been recorded by Prof. J.N. Farquhar: One of the notorious practices of the Muslim priests, ‘as good Muslims’, was to frequently ‘attack and kill’ the Hindus, lay and monastic, especially at pilgrim centres such as Benares. Those priests were protected by a faulty law that exempted them from any legal punishment! So the hapless Hindus approached Madhusudana to do something to stop this injustice. Since he was well known at the durbar of Emperor

Akbar (who ruled between 1556-1605), he met the Emperor through Raja Birbal and narrated to him the religious atrocities at Benares, etc. As a solution, the Emperor suggested that Madhusudana should organize a militant band of sannyasins to defend Hinduism and its followers. At the same time he promulgated a law that thenceforth the Hindu sannyasins too, like the Muslim priests, were outside the purview of legal action. Thus was born at the hands of Madhusudana the much respected, and feared, Naga sect of Vedantic sannyasins. The recruits into it were mostly from the Ksatriya caste. They lived in monasteries called akhadas, lit. gymnasiums, and were trained in the martial arts. Despite these great contributions, Madhusudana, it seems, was hounded out of Benares by the pandas (Hindu priests at pilgrim centres) during his later years for some unclear reasons. As a result he had to go away to Haridvar where, it is believed, he passed away at the ripe age of 107 (in AD 1697 \[i.e.1597\], according to some).

## 30. Vidyadhara

Vidyadhara (c. 1300) wrote Ekavali. The striking feature of the treatise is that he explained the name of each ornament with regard to the etymology. In his notes on Sahitya-darpana, Dr. Kane often cited Vidyadhara in that regard. Moreover, Dr. Kane wrote:

The peculiarity of this work is that all the examples are composed by Vidyadhara himself and contain panegyrics of his patron, king Narasimha of Utkala (or Orissa).

The Rasarnava-sudhakara of Singha-bhupala (about 1330 A.D.) refers to the Ekavali ‘utkaladhipateh srngara- rasabhimanino narasimha-devasya cittam anuvartamanena vidyadharena kavina badham abhyantari-krtosi \| evam khalu samarthitam ekavalyam anena’ (p. 206 of Trivandrum ed.) and on pp. 258 and 277 Singha-bhupala quotes Prasanna-raghava ; therefore the Ekavall must have been composed between 1285-1325 A.D.

Mallinatha’s Tarala is the sole commentary on Ekavall. Mallinatha is the renowned commentator on the maha-kavyas. He flourished in the mid-fourteenth century. Moreover, for the most part the Ekavall is based on Mammata’s treatise, chapter by chapter:

The agreement is as under—

**Ekavall, unmesas** **Kavya-prakasa, ullasas**   1 1 and 5 (latter part)   2 2 and 3   3 4   4 5   5 8   6 7   7 9   8 10

Though embracing the same subjects as the Kavya-prakasa, it is simpler than it and may be read with advantage by the student who wishes to master the harder work of Mammata.

In the treatment of laksana the author admits like the Vedantins and some Naiyayikas jahad-ajahat-svartha laksana, which is not admitted by Mammata. \[...\] The fifth unmesa treats of Gunas \[...\] and concludes with the Rltis. \[...\] In the classification and treatment of figures, Vidyadhara mostly follows Rajanaka Ruyyaka, the author of Alankara-sarvasva.

Vidyadhara followed Mammata regarding most of the ornaments and incorporated ornaments invented by Ruyyaka. For instance, Vidyadhara accepted Mammata’s interpretation of slesa, but as regards paryayokta he favored Ruyyaka’s explanation. Regarding the above table, Mammata’s chapter six, on third-rate poetry, is automatically covered by Vidyadhara in his treatment of ornaments of sound and of ornaments of meaning (Chs. 7-8). This is Vidyadhara’s example of vicitra (amazing) (for getting the intended result, one does something contrary to the usual means of obtainment):

*malinayitum khala-vadanam vimalayati*  
*jaganti deva kirtis te \|*  
*mitrahladam kartum*  
*mitraya druhyati pratapo ’pi \|\|*

**O king, your fame purifies the world to sully the mouths of backbiters. And your effulgence rivals the sun (mitra) to delight your friends (mitra). (Ekavali 8.39) (cited in Kuvalayananda 94)**

## 31. Vidyanatha

Vidyanatha (c. 1300 CE) wrote Prataparudra-yaso- bhusana, often called Pratapa-rudriya for short. Vidyanatha wrote all the examples in honor of his patron, King Prataparudra \|\| (ruled 1289-1323 CE) of the Kakati family in Warangal (Telangana). Dr. Sushil Kumar De comments: “Its nine prakaranas cover almost the same ground as the ten paricchedas of Visvanatha’s Sahitya-darpana. Like Vidyadhara, Vidyanatha follows Mammata in general, but prefers Bhoja in the matter of

Gunas and Ruyyaka in the matter of poetic figures.” Kumara Svamin, the son of Mallinatha, wrote the commentary on Pratapa- rudriya, called Ratnapana. Since Kumara Svamin cites Sahitya- darpana, he is younger than Visvanatha Kaviraja. This is Vidyanatha’s example of vicitra:

*prataparudra-nrpater agre duran naresvarah \|*  
*avarohanti hastibhyas tan arodhum anargalam \|\|*

**In the presence of King Prataparudra, other kings alight from their elephants from afar to rise to new heights of joy. (Pratapa- rudriya 8.162)**

In Vidyanatha’s and Vidyadhara’s treatises, on the one hand the theory is interesting. For instance, in his commentaries on the maha-kavyas, Mallinatha cites them:

The date of Mallinatha, author of the Tarala commentary on the Ekavali, has been fixed at the end of the 14th century by Bhandarkar and Trivedi. He must have written his commentary after a certain time had elapsed from the composition of the original text ; for from sloka 6 it appears that the Ekavali was not studied for some time because it had no commentaries. He is identical with Kolacala Mallinatha Suri (Pedda Bhatta) who is the well-known scholiast and commentator on the five standard Maha-kavyas of Kalidasa, Bharavi, Bhatti, Sriharsa and Magha, in some of which he quotes from the Ekavali itself.

Vidyanatha, in his turn, is quoted extensively but anonymously for definitions of poetic figures by Mallinatha in the latter’s many commentaries on the different Kavyas. This gives us the same broad limits to his date as to that of Vidyadhara ; and other considerations make it probable that he was contemporaneous with the latter.

But on the other, the great majority of examples in Pratapa-rudrlya and in Ekavall are not on a par with those in first-class treatises, where praising a king is not a continuous occurrence.

At the other end of the spectrum, Mankha, a Kashmiri poet, only associated with other literati; he never paid tribute to a king. His work is not tarnished by the constant glorification of a monarch. In his Srlkantha-carita (25.5-8-9) he exclaimed: “How fortunate am I that Sarasvati, Goddess of Speech, willful though she may be, has prompted me to praise no one but Siva. Away with those whose speech, though immersed in Sarasvati, Goddess of Speech (bathed in the river Sarasvati), dirties itself like a drunken woman with the filth of praise given to kings. The vision belonging to Sarasvati is befouled by a poet when rendered subservient to kings.”

Dr. Kane expounds upon the Pratapa-rudrlya:

This work is very popular in Southern India. The work contains three parts, karikas, vrtti and illustrations. All the examples are composed in honour of the Kakatiya king of Telangana, Prataparudradeva (also called Virarudra or Rudra), whose capital was ekasila (Orangal or Warangal) \[just east of Hyderabad\] ‘prataparudradevasya gunan asritya nirmitah \| alankara-prabandho ’yam santah karnotsavo ’stu vah \|\|’ I.9. In this respect it resembles the Ekavall. The work has 9 prakaranas on nayaka, kavya, nataka, rasa, dosa, guna, sabdalankara, arthalankara, misralankara. \[...\] In the third prakarana, while illustrating the requirements of a nataka, he exhibits a model drama called Prataparudra-kalyana.

Prataparudradeva was the son of Mahadeva and Mummudi or Mummudamba, who was the daughter of Rudramba. This Rudramba was known as Rudra and ruled at Ekasila after her father Ganapati. Prataparudradeva is said to have routed

Sevana of the Yadava family (i.e. Ramadeva of Devagiri, 1271-1309 A.D.). From this fact and the information supplied by epigraphic records it follows that Prataparudradeva ruled in the 14th century and was captured in 1323 A.D. by Muhammad Tughlak’s armies. Therefore, the Prataparudra-yaso-bhusana was composed in the first quarter of the 14th century.

## Sequence of Topics

In the first chapter, Vidyanatha expounds the topics of lover (nayaka) and ladylove (nayika) in eighty verses by refining Dhananjaya’s ideas. In the second chapter he paraphrases Mammata’s definition of poetry: gunalankara-sahitau sabdarthau dosa-varfitau, gadya- padyobhaya-mayam kavyam kavya-vido viduh, “Those who know poetry say it consists of either prose, prosody, or both, and is faultless sounds and meanings endowed with a literary quality and with an ornament” (Pratapa-rudriya 2.1). Vidyanatha says the life of poetry is the might of an implied sense: sabdarthau murtir akhyatau fivitam vyangya-vaibhavam (2.2). He reiterates Mammata’s categories of poetry and discourses on dhvani.

Vidyanatha does not agree with Mammata’s rebuttal of Vamana’s gunas. Firstly, he illustrates Bharata Muni’s styles called Kaisiki, Arabhati, Bharati, and Sattviki (Pratapa-rudriya 2.15-26). He defines them along the lines of Bhoja’s explanations, in terms of being categories of expressed meanings, which relate to specific rasas: The Kaisiki Vrtti (very soft meanings) is for srngara and karuna, the Arabhati (very hard) is for raudra and bibhatsa, the Bharati (somewhat soft) is for hasya, santa, and adbhuta, and the Sattviki (somewhat hard) is for vira and bhayanaka.

And secondly, Vidyanatha expounds three ritis in conformity with Vamana’s interpretations: They only relate to sabda (sound, word). Kumara Svamin says this distinguishes the ritis from the vrttis.

Vidyanatha’s Vaidarbh! is a composition where the words are not too compacted (in Devanagari script), they are not too difficult to understand, and there is no long compound (2.27). His Gaud! is the same as Vamana’s: a composition that has ojas guna and kanti-guna (2.30). His Pancal! is a mix of Vaidarbh! and Gaud!: pancala-ritir vaidarbhi-gaudi ity ubhayatmika (2.32). In this regard, Visvanatha Kaviraja implicitly referred to Vidyanatha’s opinion: anye tv ahuh, “gaud! dambara-baddha syad vaidarbhi lalita-krama, pancali misra-bhavena lati tu mrdubhihpadaih” (Sahitya-darpana 9.5).

By contrast, in Ekavali Vidyadhara followed Bhoja by stating that the Pancal! is devoid of ojas and kanti and is characterized by compounds of five or six words. Visvanatha voiced that opinion as well, though he says it originates from a certain Purusottama. In poetical theory, the topic of R!ti gave rise to the most divergence of opinion.

The third chapter of Pratapa-rudriya was another source of inspiration for Visvanatha since it treats of dramaturgy. Dr. De comments:

Although based avowedly on Dhananjaya’s Dasa-rupaka, this chapter is one of the important later contributions to the subject of Dramaturgy, and a great interest attaches to its inclusion of a model drama illustrative of all its characteristics and eulogistic of the author’s patron Prataparudra.

In the fourth chapter, instead of enumerating the usual list of ten, Vidyanatha lists twelve stages of love: caksuh-priti (love at first sight), manah-sanga (engrossment), sankalpa (always desiring to be with the lover), pralapa (mentioning the lover’s qualities), jagara (sleeplessness), karsya (emaciatedness), arati (having no interest for anyone else or anything else), lajja-tyaga (lack of bashfulness), samjvara (fever), unmada (craziness), murcchana (fainting), and marana (death, i.e. losing the will to live) (4.109-110).

In the sixth chapter, Vidyanatha reiterates Bhoja’s twenty-four gunas, but he does not make a distinction between sabda-guna and artha-guna. In Vidyanatha’s system, a dhvani is categorized in accordance with Mammata’s methodology and is also classed in gambhlrya-guna. Vidyanatha makes a pun on the title of Mammata’s magnum opus: caturvimsatir ete syur gunah kavya-prakasakah, “These twenty-four literary qualities bring out the poetry” (6.3). Similarly, Kumara Svamin quotes Rudra Bhatta: tad uktam rudra- bhattena—yo hetuh kavya-sobhayah so ’lankarah prakirtyate, guno ’pi tadrso jneyo dosah syat tad-viparyayah, “An ornament is the cause of the resplendence of the poetry. Even a guna should be known to be like that. A literary fault is the opposite” (Ratnapana 6.40).

Vidyanatha agreed with Mammata’s interpretation of slesa. Further, to some extent Vidyanatha followed Ruyyaka’s classi­fication of figures in specific categories: (1) karya-karana-virodha- prastavad asangatir ucyate (8.159); (2) vakya-nyaya-mulalankara- prastavad vikalpa ucyate (8.240).

## 32. Singa-bhupala

Singa-bhupala (c. 1330 CE) composed Rasarnava-sudhakara.

His name is sometimes spelled Singha-bhupala. The original word is simha (lion): In the old days, in Prakrit and sometimes in Sanskrit, the letters x and s were interchangeable. He ruled in Rachakonda (Telangana) after the Kakati dynasty ended. His treatise centers on dramaturgy, and for that purpose, he says, he discourses on the topic of raxa because raxa is the life of a play: rasotkarso hi natyasya pranas tat sa nirupyate \| vibhavair anubhavais ca sattvikair vyabhicaribhih \|\| amyamanah svadutvam sthayibhavo rasah smrtah \| (1.58-59)

For the theory, Singa-bhupala cites Natya-sastra, Srngara- prakasa, Sarasvati-kanthabharana, Bhava-prakasana, and so on. His illustrative examples are outstanding: He cites many classical authors, mostly Kalidasa. In addition, quite often Singa-bhupala shows his own verses. In his chapter on drama, he quotes from numerous plays.

When the Kakati rule ended, Mallinatha’s parents migrated to Rachakonda. From the colophons of Sanjlvanl (Mallinatha’s commentaries on three works of Kalidasa), it is known that Singabhupala honoured Mallinatha with the title of Mahamahopadyaya, and Mallinatha’s son with the title of Mahopadyaya. Did Mallinatha write Rasarnava-sudhakara?

The treatise consists of three chapters: (I) Definition of rasa, the types of lovers and ladyloves and their emotions, etc., three ritis, ten gunas, four vrttis (Bharati, Satvati, Kaisiki and Arabhati), and the eight sattvika-bhavas, (II) The thirty-three vyabhicari-bhavas, the eight rasas, and rasabhasa, and (III) Dramaturgy.

Singa-bhupala’s invocatory verse incidentally illustrates a yatha-sankhya alankara-dhvani (implied parallelism):

*srngara-vira-sauhardam maugdhya-vaiyatya-saurabham \|*  
*lasya-tandava-saujanyam dampatyam tad bhajamahe \|\|*

**I revere a certain married couple in which there is the friendship of srngara-rasa and vira-rasa, the fragrant companionship of innocent simplicity and assertive boldness, and the harmonious coexistence of graceful dancing and wild dancing. (Rasarnava- sudhakara 1.1)**

Dr. Sushil Kumar De expounds:

Singa-bhupala, whose name is also given as Singa-dharanisa, Singa-raja or Singa-mahipati has been identified by Sesagiri Sastri with Singama Nayadu, raja of Venkatagiri who ruled, on the authority of a biographical sketch of the Rajas of Venkatagiri, about 1330 A.D. This date is probable, as Mallinatha (on Kumara i.25, iti bhUpalah = Rasarnava i.181) as well as Kumara-svamin, quotes our author. The introductory verses of the Rasarnava-sudhakara, attributed to this South Indian prince, show that he belonged to the Recarla dynasty, and ruled over the country lying between the Vindhyas and Srisaila, of which Rajacalam (Racakonda) was the hereditary capital. \[...\]

The Rasarnava appears to be mainly based on previous works like Bhoja’s Srngara-prakasa (Bhoja cited 57, 69, 149, 168, 190) and Sarada-tanaya’s Bhava-prakasana (cited pp. 139, 169, 202), although it draws directly on Bharata, Rudrabhatta (cited pp. 29, 30, 87), the Dasa-rupaka and other authors and works on Rasa and Dramaturgy.

Siva-prasada Bhattacarya remarks:

It is also to be noted that the Rasarnava-sudhakara, which is stated to be one of the two works whose authors really saw the Srngara-prakasa, was a well-known work in Bengal as much as the Bhava-prakasana of Sarada-tanaya. Rupa Gosvamin in the Ujjvala-nilamani, Jiva Gosvamin in his commentary thereon and in the Nataka-candrika and very likely Kavikarnapura used these works. Bhoja’s ideas and terminology—his fourfold classification of sambhoga—srngara into samksipta, samkirna, sampanna and samrddhimat are what are utilised and elaborated in the Ujjvala-nTlamani.

In Nataka-candrika, Rupa Gosvami expounded the art of dramaturgy. He says Nataka-candrika is based on Natya-sastra and on Singabhupala’s Rasarnava-sudhakara.

The abovementioned four terms used by Rupa Gosvami—tan purva-ragato manat pravasa-dvayatah kramat \| jatan samksipta- sankirna-sampanna-rddhimato viduh \|\| (Ujjvala-nilamani 15.191)—are sourced in Rasarnava-sudhakara (2.221), but they originate from Sarasvatl-kanthabharana: sa sanksipto thia sanktrnah sampurnah samyag-rddhiman \| anantaropadistesu rasa- bhogesupapadyate \|\| (5.84); prathamanuraganantare sambhogah sanksiptah \[...\] sa eva manantare sanktrnah \[...\]pravasanantare sampurnah \[...\] karunanantare samrddhah (illustrations 5.275­278). Visvanatha Kaviraja followed Bhoja, but Rupa Gosvami modified the fourth type of vipralambha by replacing karuna with distant pravasa (Ujjvala-ntlamani 15.184). In conformity with Vopadeva, Rupa Gosvami added prema-vaicittya to poetical theory; Jiva Gosvami says the meeting after prema-vaicittya makes a fifth variety of sambhoga.

In Srngara-prakasa, Bhoja used similar terms in different ways: 1. sanksipto bhogah sattavasthayam, 2. sankirno bhogah abhivyaktavasthayam, 3. sampurno bhogah anubandhavasthayam, 4. samyag-bhogah prakarsavasthayam iti (36.1).

The inclusion of mana (pique) in poetical theory originates from Rudrata. Bharata Muni had implied the concept of mana by stating a ladylove’s conditions called khandita and kalahantarita. Following Singabhupala (2.128-139), Rupa Gosvami said that although rosa is one of three types of krodha, rosa is actually an additional vyabhicari-bhava of srngara-rasa. In effect Rupa Gosvami equated mana with the vyabhicari-bhava called rosa (anger), in conformity with Singabhupala: sapatni-hetuko roso vipralambheprapancyate (2.140).

Moreover, Rupa Gosvami’s verse 2.4.3 of Bhakti-rasamrta-sindhu is exactly the same as Rasarnava-sudhakara 2.3.

Rupa Gosvami’s six types of hasya-rati (humor)—smita (slight smile: the teeth are not seen and the eyes and cheeks express joy), hasita (joyful smile: the teeth are slightly visible), vihasita (laughing sounds are heard and the teeth are visible), avahasita (high laughter: the nose swells and the eyes squint), apahasita (higher laughter, with tears in the eyes), and atihasita (the highest laughter: laughter combined with slapping the hands and bending the body) (Bhakti-rasamrta-sindhu 4.1.14-26)—are sourced in Singhabhupala’s treatise: prakrti-vasat sa ca sodha smita-hasite vihasitavahasite ca \| apahasitatihasitake jyesthadnam kramad dve dve \|\| (Rasarnava-sudhakara 2.229)

Rupa Gosvami’s list of Krishna’s qualities is based on the list of a lover’s qualities (Sarasvati-kanthabharana 5.122-123) (Rasarnava-sudhakara 1.61-72).

For the topic of rasabhasa, Rupa Gosvami took inspiration from the corresponding section in Singabhupala’s treatise (illustrations

2.496-497) regarding a woman loving more than one man and a man loving his beloveds equally (Bhakti-rasamrta-sindhu 4.9.13­17). Singabhupala says there is no overlap with the definition of the daksina lover because the daksina lover treats his ladyloves equally. Rupa Gosvami implicitly agrees with him: yad va— nayikasu apy anekasu tulyo daksina ucyate (Ujjvala-mlamani 1.34). But Visvanatha Kaviraja and Kavi Kamapura disagree with Singabhupala: esu tv aneka-mahilasu sama-rago daksinah kathitah (Sahitya-darpana 3.35); sama-rago daksinas tu sarvasu (Alankara-kaustubha 5.83).

Quoting Sarada-tanaya, Singabhupala adds that too much hasya in srngara is a form of rasabhasa: tatha ca bhava-prakasikayam (6.16-20)—srngaro hasya-bhuyisthah srngarabhasa iritah \| (2.263 vrtti).

Rupa Gosvami’s twenty emotional ornaments of women (Ujjvala- nilamani 11.2-5) are sourced in Rasarnava-sudhakara 1.190-208. Bhoja gave the general idea. Other references of Rasarnava- sudhakara in Rupa Gosvami’s treatise are: Ujjvala-nilamani 5.25; 10.41; 10.59; 10.64; 10.101-103; 11.7; and 13.45. Sometimes Rupa Gosvami calls the book Rasa-sudhakara.

Singabhupala says rati has six stages: ankura-pallava-kalika- prasuna-phalabhoga-bhag iyam kramatah \| prema manah pranayah sneho rago ’nuraga ity uktah \|\| (2.109), in accordance with Sarada-tanaya: tatha ca bhava-prakasikayam (16.17): iyam ankurita premna manat pallavita bhavet \| sa-koraka pranayatah snehat kusumita bhavet (Rasarnava-sudhakara 2.157 vrtti); Rupa Gosvami agrees, although he places sneha before mana (UN 14.59).

Of all the methodologies of gunas which involve ritis, Singa- bhupala’s is the most perfect. He says the Vaidarbhi is the soft riti, and the Gaud! is the harsh riti. His Pancali is a mix of both: sa misra saiva pancali (1.240). Kavi Kamapura’s Pancali is the same, but he adds Lati, which he says is the soft riti, whereas the Vaidarbhi is sweet. Their Pancali is an imperfect Vaidarbhi.

Singabhupala’s Vaidarbhi includes ten gunas. His definitions make sense: His gunas are Vamana’s sabda-gunas, with these exceptions: His prasada is Vamana’s artha-guna prasada, his madhurya consists of relishable sounds and meaning (tan madhuryam bhaved yatra sabdarthe ca sphuto rasah, 1.234), the udarata is Vamana’s artha-guna udarata, the kanti is a not-too-far-fetched lovely meaning (loka-sthitim anulanghya hrdyartha-pratipadanam, kantih syat, 1.237-238), and the samadhi is Vamana’s artha-guna samadhi.

Singabhupala shows this verse by Kalidasa, from Raghu-vamsa 3.17, to illustrate the vyabhicari-bhava called harsa (joy) (2.324); it also exemplifies the adhika ornament (exceeding):

*nivata-padma-stimitena caksusa*  
*nrpasya kantam pibatah sutananam \|*  
*mahodadheh pura ivendu-darsanad*  
*guruh praharsah prababhuva natmani \|\|*

**King DilTpa felt great joy upon drinking the beautiful face of his son Raghu. The king’s eyes were as motionless as two lotuses in a breezeless place. Like the ocean swelling upon seeing the moon, the king could no longer contain the joy in his body.**

## 33. Visvanatha Kaviraja

Visvanatha was a Vaishnava and an accomplished poet. He wrote Sahitya-darpana (c. 1350). It is a masterpiece. In universities, it almost has the same status as Kavya- prakasa. Dr. Sushil Kumar De states:

As a suitable and complete manual of Poetics, including a treatment of the dramatic art, it has always held its popularity as one of the most convenient textbooks on the subject as a whole.

This is Visvanatha’s famous dictum: vakyam rasatmakam kavyam, “A statement whose soul is a rasa is poetry” (Sahitya-darpana 1.3). Visvanatha defined a vakya (a statement, i.e. one or many sentences: a bunch of words that have akanksa, mutual requirement, yogyata, congruity, and sannidhi, mutual proximity). In addition, he broadly defined the term rasa: rasyate iti rasa iti vyutpattya bhava-tad- abhasadayo ’pi grhyante, “By the derivation: rasyate iti rasah, “It is relished, thus it is a rasa,” the sthayi-bhavas, and rasabhasa, bhavabhasa, and so on, are included if they are relishable on the occasion” (Sahitya-darpana 1.3). In that way Visvanatha follows both the Dhvanikara, by rejecting third-rate poetry as genuine poetry—kavyam dhvanir guni-bhuta-vyangam ceti dvidha mata (Sahitya-darpana 4.1)—, and Abhinavagupta, by interpreting the word dhvani in the Dhvanikara’s dictum kavyasyatma dhvanih only as a rasadi-dhvani.

Visvanatha cited Pandit Narayana’s opinion that there is only one rasa, astonishment; he invented an amazing subvariety of apahnuti, and so on, but on the whole Visvanatha copied Mammata’s and Ruyyaka’s methodologies. Dr. Kane expounds:

Beyond a few scraps of information gathered from his own works, we know very little about the personal history of Visvanatha. He came from a brahmana family that had distinguished itself by learning. His great-great-grand-father was Narayana, who appears to have been a learned man and to have written a work on Rhetoric. His father was Chandrasekhara, who was a poet and a scholar. His verses are often quoted by Visvanatha. Visvanatha mentions by name two works of his father, viz. the Puspamala (on VI.25) and Bhasarnava which dealt with the characteristics of Sanskrit, Sauraseni, Maharastri and other Prakrit dialects. As Visvanatha explains certain Sanskrit expressions by Uriya equivalents in his commentary on the Kavya-prakasa, he appears to have been an inhabitant of Orissa. The father of Visvanatha and Visvanatha himself appear to have held some important office at the court of a king, probably of Kalinga. Both of them are styled Sandhi-vigrahika-Mahapatra.

Visvanatha was a Vaisnava as is made clear by the colophon at the end of the first Pariccheda and the last verse of the Sahitya-darpana. He was a poet and quotes his own verses in Sanskrit and Prakrit at every step, when illustrating the canons of Rhetoric. He composed a number of works, besides the Sahitya-darpana, of which the following are mentioned in the latter:—I. a maha-kavya in Sanskrit, called Raghava-vilasa (under III.222-224); \|\| Kuvalayasva-carita, a kavya in Prakrit (III.149); III. Prabhavati-parinaya, a Natika (III.58); IV. Chandrakala, another Natika (III.96); V. Prasasti-ratnavali, a Karambhaka in sixteen languages (VI.337). After composing the Sahitya-darpana, he wrote two other works, a kavya called Narasimha-vijaya and a commentary on the Kavya-prakasa called Kavya-prakasa-darpana. Candidasa, who wrote a commentary on the Kavya-prakasa, was the younger brother of Visvanatha’s grand-father.

The question of Visvanatha’s date does not present much difficulty. \[...\] From these two circumstances it follows that the Sahitya-darpana was composed at some time between 1300 A.D. and 1384 A.D.

## The Kings of Orissa

Most likely, the Pandit Narayana who was Visvanatha’s ancestor was patronized by the same king who patronized Vidyadhara, the author of Ekavall. P.V. Kane writes:

Visvanatha quotes the words of a writer called Dharmadatta, who was a contemporary of Narayana, the grand-father (great­great-grand-father ?) of Visvanatha and was vanquished by him in the court of king Narasimha of Kalinga. Whether Narayana was the grandfather or great-great-grand-father of Visvanatha would make not much difference. Many kings of Kalinga bore the name Narasimha. Besides, there is a good deal of confusion about the dates of their accession. As a ms. of the Sahitya- darpana is dated in 1384 A.D. Narasimha IV is certainly not the king at whose court Narayana lived, because Narasimha IV came to the throne at some time between 1373 A.D. and 1411 A.D. Narasimha III also is out of question, as the date of his accession is somewhere between 1328 A.D. and 1361 A.D. It is likely that Narasimha \|\| is the king referred to. The date of his accession falls between 1270 A.D. and 1303 A.D.; he is also styled Kavipriya in his inscriptions, which makes it probable that he patronized many learned men. If Narayana was really the great-great-grand-father of Visvanatha, then the king may have been Narasimha I, the date of whose accession is somewhere near 1253 A.D.

The modern state of Odisha consisted of two regions: Kalinga and Utkala. Kalinga, in the south and in the west of modern Odisha and in northern parts of Andhra Pradesh, formed the largest part of the old Odisha. Utkala (“beyond Kalinga”) was located in the northern and eastern parts of Odisha. However, it seems that in those days they were not kingdoms governed by separate rulers. In addition, four more kings were called Narasimha. Dr. Trivedi discourses on Vidyadhara:

The age in which the poet lived can be settled approximately from the internal evidence the work affords. As stated before, the illustrative stanzas are all composed to glorify king Nrsimha or Narasimha, king of Kalinga or Utkala. It is therefore certain that the poet Vidyadhara flourished in the reign of this king; for no poet can eulogize a king in such magniloquent terms unless he were his patron. The question therefore turns upon the settlement of the age of the king Narasimha. In the long list of kings of Orissa given by Mr. Robert Sewell in his ‘Sketch of the Dynasties of Southern India’ Appendix VII., pp. 64 to 69, eight kings bearing the name Narasimha are mentioned as under:—

Narasingh Deva B.C. 421-306   Narasingh Kesari A.D. 1013-1024   Languliya Narasingh A.D. 1237-1282   Kesari Narasingh A.D. 1282-1307   Pratab Narasingh A.D. 1307-1327   Kapil Narasingh A.D. 1329-1330   Narasingh Jana A.D. 1549-1550   Narasingh Deva A.D. 1628-1653

The copper-plate inscriptions of Nrsimha-deva IV and Nrsimha-deva \|\| of Orissa published in the Journal of the Asiatic Society of Bengal, Vol. LXIV, Part I, 1895 and Vol. LXV, Part I, 1896, are the latest source of information regarding kings of Utkala.

\[...\] Thus neither Languliya Narasingh of Mr. Sewell nor Nrsimha I of inscriptions could have been the patron of Vidyadhara. These considerations make it clear that Vidyadhara must have flourished in the reign of either of the two remaining Narasimhas. Kesari Narasingh (1282-1307) or Pratap Narasingh (1307-1327) of Mr. Sewell, or Narasimha \|\| of inscriptions, and that the Ekavali was composed in the beginning of the fourteenth century.

It is well known that King Narasimha I built the Konark Temple. Furthermore, Dr. Bhandarkar gives two other possible dates for each of the four Narasimhas. He adds that there existed three kings named Vira-Bhanudeva: Vira-Bhanudeva I ruled after Narasimha I, and so on. Dr. Bhandarkar notes:

The list of the princes who ruled over Orissa given by Sir W.W. Hunter and Mr. Sewell is based on the chronicle of the Jagannatha Temple and like other productions of the kind contains a great deal that has no surer foundation than fancy or imagination, mixed especially in the later portion with much that is historically true.

That Narasimha \|\| was the Narasimha of the Ekavali is rendered highly probable, or I might say, certain by the fact that in the inscriptions of Narasimha IV he is in one place called kavi-priya or “favourite of poets” and in another kavi- kumuda-candra “the Moon that made the night lilies in the shape of poets expand.” This description applies to the hero of the Ekavali, both because he was chosen for his panegyric by Vidyadhara and because he must have patronized him and others like him.

## The Meaning of Sahitya-darpana

Commenting on Kavya-mimamsa, Dr. Kane expounds:

These passages establish that sometime before 900 A.D. (when Rajasekhara flourished) the word sahitya came to be used in the sense of ‘the science of Poetics’. How much earlier it was employed in that sense it is difficult to say. The word sahitya seems to be derived from sahita (meaning ‘together’). When poetry came to be defined as ‘sabdarthau sahitau kavyam, ’ the science of poetic criticism that propounded this definition was naturally called sahitya. \[...\] In order to constitute real kavya, the sahitya of sabda and artha is required to possess peculiar charm.

The notion of togetherness can also refer to other concepts, such as slesa, yamaka, implied meanings, alliteration, and rasa: By Bharata Muni’s dictum, the togetherness of sthayi-bhava, vibhava, anubhava and vyabhicari-bhava is rasa.

At a cursory look, the name Sahitya-darpana (a mirror of literature) resembles Dandi’s Kavyadarsa (a mirror of poetry). Other meanings of the title Sahitya-darpana are:

- The pride of literature;
- It causes the pride of literature;
- A mirror of the togetherness \[of sounds and meanings\];
- Pride because of the togetherness \[of poetry and dramaturgy in the book\];
- A mirror of rasa (“a state of being beneficial”: sahitya as derived from sa-hita).

## The Derivation of the Term srngara

In plain terms, the derivation is: srngam rcchati, “It attains (or achieves) srnga. ” The breakup of the word srngara is srnga-ara, where ara is a participial form made by applying vrddhi to the verbal root r gatau prapane ca (to go, attain) (1P), by the usual rule: karmany an, “The suffix a\[n\] is applied after the second word in a compound when the first word is the object of that verb” (Astadhyayi3.2.1). The meanings of the word srnga are: “horn” (the bony protuberance of certain mammals), “the main thing”, and “peak”: kuto ’stri sikharam srngam (Amara-kosa 2.3.4); srngam pradhanya-sanvos ca (Amara-kosa 3.3.26).

According to Visvanatha, srngara-rasa is so called because it achieves srnga, the breakthrough manifestation of Cupid \[in a woman\] which is caused by the arrival of Cupid: srngam hi manmathodbhedas tad-agamana-hetukah \| uttama-prakrti-prayo rasah srngara isyate \|\| (3.183).

Visvanatha’s dissertation on rasa, including a discourse on lovers and ladyloves, is voluminous, is partly based on Rasarnava- sudhakara and was the main source of inspiration for Rupa Gosvami’s Ujjvala-nilamani. In the section on lovers and ladyloves in his chapter on rasa in Alankara-kaustubha, Kavi Kamapura largely drew from Visvanatha’s exposition.

**Vastu-dhvani**

Visvanatha’s analyses are sharp. Sometimes it may be argued that he went overboard. For instance, he analyzes this verse by denying an occurrence of slesa (literal double meaning):

*sat-paksa madhura-girah*  
*prasadhitasa madoddhatarambhah \|*  
*nipatanti dhartarastrah*  
*kala-vasan medini-prsthe \|\|*

sat-paksah—whose wings are eminent (or whose side (allies) is eminent); madhura-girah—whose sounds are sweet (or who speak sweetly); prasadhita-asah—by whom the directions are adorned (or by whom the directions are put under control); mada-uddhata- arambhah—whose efforts (flying upward) exceed the usual measure out of joy (or whose efforts are monstrous due to self-conceit); nipatanti—fly down (or will fall); dhartarastrah—geese (or the sons of Dhrtarastra); kala-vasat—under the influence of the

**\[First interpretation:\]**

**The beautiful-winged geese cry sweetly and adorn the direc­tions. They extravagantly fly upward out of joy, by the influence of the season, and land on the ground.**

**\[Second interpretation:\]**

**The sons of Dhrtarastra are sweet talkers and have eminent allies. They conquered the cardinal directions. And their undertakings are dreadful due to self-conceit. On account of fate, they will fall dead upon the ground. (Vem-samhara 1.6).**

As the title suggests, Vem-samhara is a play centered on Duhsasana’s brutal act of dragging Draupadi by the hair. The context, in preceding verses, is a description of autumn. In his explanation, perhaps Visvanatha is at fault for not taking the larger context in consideration: atra sarad-varmanaya prakaramena dhartarastradi-sabdanam hamsady-arthabhidhane niyamanad duryodhanadi-rupo ’rthah sabda-sakti-mulo vastu-dhvamih. iha ca prakrta-prabandhabhidheyasya dvitlyarthasya sUcyatayaiva vivaksitatvad upamanopameya-bhavo na vivaksita iti nopama- dhvanir na va slesa iti sarvam avadatam.

“In this verse, the meanings ofdhartarastra and so on as Duryodhana and so on are implied ideas (and not literal double meanings) arisen by the power of the words, because there is a restriction that only the meanings of ‘swan’ and so on should be expressed since the context is a description of autumn. In addition, since the second meaning (the sons of Dhrtarastra) is only meant to suggest the actual subject matter of the book, a relation of similitude is not meant to be stated. Thus, there is no implied simile, nor is there slesa. Now everything is clear” (10.12). If the double meanings were taken as a slesa, automatically a simile would be implied.

## The Sweetness of Dr. Kane

P.V. Kane wrote notes on the first, second, and tenth chapters of Sahitya-darpana. He included this work in the first publication of his History of Sanskrit Poetics, in 1923. Subsequently it was reprinted as a separate publication, called The Sahitya-darpana. Therein Dr. Kane was critical of Visvanatha, as if Pandita-raja Jagannatha’s rebukes of Appaya Diksita had come back to life and taken a new form. For instance, Dr. Kane writes:

In explaining the application of his definition of parinama to the verse, the author appears to have broken down completely. \[...\] Hence the definition ofparinama as given by Visvanatha does not apply to the verse. The definition of Ekavall applies.

Further in this regard, Visvanatha begins his book with a trenchant attack on Mammata’s definition of poetry. Dr. Kane comments:

As to these objections one cannot help saying that Visvanatha is here over-fastidious and is perhaps actuated by the desire of making a show of his erudition by pouring ridicule upon a famous predecessor. This much must be said in favor of Mammata, that his definition has the great merit of being simple and easily understood. His definition is good enough for all practical purposes.

## The Differences Between Sahitya-darpana and Kavya-prakasa

Visvanatha adopted Mammata’s methodology, but there are major differences: (1) Visvanatha does not acknowledge Mammata’s third variety of poetry, (2) He made up eighty varieties of figurative usage, in contrast to Mammata’s thirteen varieties, (3) Visvanatha expounded upon a definition of a sentence (taken from Tarka- sangraha), (4) He added vatsalya to the list of rasas, saying it was approved by Bharata Muni, (5) He included a chapter on dramaturgy, (6) He wrote a chapter on riti, whereas Mammata ignored the topic by including the styles of compounding and the type of phonemes within the methodology of gunas, (7) Visvanatha added categories of alliteration (sruti anuprasa and antya anuprasa), and (8) In the chapter on ornaments of meaning, Visvanatha mostly followed Ruyyaka.

Compared to Mammata, Visvanatha is weak in some areas: (A) His sections on yamaka and citra-kavya contain only one example each, although Mammata’s examples are copied from other works, and (B) His section on first-rate poetry is shorter than Mammata’s. However, Visvanatha gives more details on the topic of rasa, such as subdivisions of lovers and ladyloves.

Visvanatha propounded the notion that the love of a married woman for a lover is a kind of rasabhasa. As an example of srngara-rasabhasa, Visvanatha shows a verse, which he says is his own, where a married gopi is in love with Krishna and is embraced by Him (Sahitya-darpana 3.266).

In this matter, Jiva Gosvami supported Visvanatha: jara- bhava-mayah sangamas ca sadaiva sopadravas tasmad asau paryavasana-purusarthatve tat-tac-chastra-sammato na syat, “A meeting imbued with the mood of paramours is always associated with outrage. Therefore the scriptures do not approve of it, since it does not turn out as a goal of life” (Krsna-sandarbha 178).

Jiva Gosvami added:

*nanu \[...\] jarah papa-patih samau iti trikanda-Sesadi-darsanena namapi tasya ninda-garbham eva labhyate, natyalankara-sastrayos tu tasya nyak-karas ca sruyate. yad uktam tat-tan-matam sangrhya sahitya-darpane upanayaka- samsthayam.*

**“Someone might think: “By looking at definitions such as the one in Tri-kanda-sesa: jarah papa-patih samau, “Jara (paramour, lit. he who causes old age) and papa-pati (paramour, lit. he whose master in sin) are synonymous” (Tri-kanda-sesa 2.6.10), even the name involves censure. Plus, such a person is treated with contempt in Natya-sastra and in treatises on poetics. In consideration of that opinion, in Sahitya-darpana it is said: upanayaka-samsthayam (when there is the presence of a paramour)... (3.263)” (Locana- rocam 1.21).**

Further, on the whole Visvanatha cited many of his own compo­sitions. In addition, Visvanatha’s writing style is clear. By contrast, sometimes Mammata’s style is obscure. Dr. Kane says this about Visvanatha:

Beside the brilliance of Anandavardhana, Mammata and Jagannatha his light appears dim. Still the work of Visvanatha has some merits of its own. Its greatest merit is that it presents in the compass of a single work, a full and complete treatment of the science of rhetoric in all its branches. Most writers on sahitya, such as Dandin, Mammata and Jagannatha, leave out the treatment of dramaturgy. The Sahitya-darpana, however, contains a thorough disquisition on the technicalities of the dramatic art and forms, together with the Natya-sastra of Bharata and the Dasarupa of Dhananjaya, a triumvirate in the domain of the Sanskrit drama.

Another merit of the work is that it is written in a simple and flowing style. The reader is often hampered in going over the Kavya-prakasa of Mammata by the author’s studied efforts at brevity. Jagannatha frightens the student by his flowery language, his subtle reasoning and his scathing criticism of his predecessors. Visvanatha, although he displays here and there a love for hair-splitting, is generally clear in expression. He is, however, more or less a compiler and not an original writer. \[...\] He is not happy in the innovations that he introduces and is sometimes wrong in what he says. In spite of these blemishes, his work forms an easy and suitable introduction to Sanskrit sahitya.

Dr. De writes: “The Kavya-prakasa has not been so often printed in Bengal as it has been in other provinces of India where it is perhaps much more extensively studied; for in Bengal Visvanatha’s Sahitya-darpana appears to be a more popular textbook.”

In the seventeenth century, a disciple of Jiva Gosvami did a remake of Sahitya-darpana, called Bhakti-rasamrta-sesa since it treats of all the poetic theory left out of Bhakti-rasamrta-sindhu, where Rupa Gosvami only discourses on rasa. Bhakti-rasamrta-sesa covers all the topics discussed in Sahitya-darpana except rasa and dramaturgy. All the definitions of poetical concepts were taken verbatim from Sahitya-darpana. The illustrations include Visva- natha’s best examples as well as verses from Gopala-campu, Alankara-kaustubha and Govinda-lllamrta.

## 34. Bhanu Datta

Bhanudatta (c. 1450-1500 CE) wrote Rasa-manjan (flower bud of rasa) and Rasa-tarangim (river of rasa). He was the finest flower of the Rasa school. He composed all the examples in his treatises, which have the value of outstanding literary works. Bhanu-datta says he was born in Videha (Mithila, Bihar): videha-bhuh (Rasa-manjarl 138). He traveled south-west in search of patronage:

A closer approximation of Bhanudatta’s date is possible if any inference is permissible from the mention of Nijama- dharani-pala in the Rasa-manjari. It is suggested that the Nizam referred to as ruler of Devagiri by Ananta Pandita’s commentary is Ahmad Nizam Shah, who obtained possession of Daulatabad (Devagiri) sometime between 1499 and 1507 A.D. and founded the Nizam Shahi dynasty of Dekkan.

In Rasa-tarangim, Bhanu Datta discusses rasa and the various factors that go in producing it (sthayi-bhava, vibhava, anubhava, sattvika-bhava, vyabhicari-bhava). In addition, he clearly distin­guishes santa-rasa from mundane rasa, thus implicitly categorizing santa as a rasa exclusively in the mode of goodness (sattva-guna): citta-vrttir dvidha, pravrttir nivrttis ca. nivrttau yatha santa-rasah, tatha pravrttau maya-rasa iti pratibhati, “There are two modes of thinking: pravrtti (engaging in material activity) and nivrtti (refraining from worldly activity). Santa-rasa is to nivrtti what maya-rasa is to pravrtti” (Rasa-tarangini, ch. 7). Dr. Raghavan remarks:

The acceptance of santa gave rise in later times to another controversial rasa called maya. Just as there is the possibility of depicting the santa-rasa with psychological, religious and metaphysical concepts like Jnana, Bhakti, Sama, Dama, Samtusti, etc., there is also the possibility of depicting the maya-rasa by showing the jlvatma enmeshed in samsara as a result of mithya-jnana or avidya, with characters such as Kama, Krodha and Lobha. Even as santa is the rasa of the state of nivrtti, maya is the rasa of the state of pravrtti. In a philosophical drama, the rasa from which the hero escapes into the santa, is maya.

Dr. Ananta-sarovara Dasi comments: “This refers to allegorical dramas where the characters are abstract qualities. Srila Kavi

Karnapura also used that allegorical style in his Caitanya- candrodaya-nataka, which seems to have been modeled along the lines of the Prabodha-candrodaya of Kesava Misra.”

Dr. Sheldon Pollock expounds the topic:

Clearly, these are core questions not just of literature but of human existence: the very capacity to distinguish aesthetic from pragmatic emotion, even to respond to aesthetic emotion, is one of the things that make people cultured, perhaps even human. And they are questions that took Indian scholarship by storm in the late tenth century, transforming Indian aesthetic thought once and for all time.

At least this is what most scholars believe. In fact—and to register this fact is to record a historical truth, and not of course to denigrate the profound insights of the innovators—many later Indian literary theorists appear to have been entirely indifferent to the new ideas originating in Kashmir. Bhanu- datta is most certainly one of them throughout his exposition in the “River of Rasa.” His are largely the old concerns of how literature creates emotion, the concerns of, say, King Bhoja, the great encyclopedist who synthesized the “normal science” of aesthetics in the mid-eleventh century. Only rarely does Bhanu depart from the classical doctrine—hence his close dependence on the Natya-sastra—and the few times he does so, he reveals that he is far more a poet than a thinker. (His distinction between “ordinary” and “extraordinary” rasa— which differentiates between a rasa that arises for a character from normal contact with the underlying object and a rasa that arises for a character in dreaming, imagining, or witnessing a mimetic representation—does mark a noteworthy if undeveloped advance.) It is for the poetry we should enter into the “River of Rasa,” not the science—though of course having the science clearly in our heads, as Bhanu makes it very convenient to do, is the only way to fully engage with the poetry.

In Rasa-manjari, Bhanudatta used the term vyangya (implied) on several occasions; the commentator Badannatha Sarma says this could signify that Bhanudatta acknowledges Suggestiveness, the fourth literary function in the Dhvani theory.

At any rate, as the foremost representative of the Rasa school, Bhanudatta implicitly emphasized Abhinava’s and Visvanatha’s dictum, in line with Bharata and Bhoja, that rasa is the soul of poetry.

Over and above that, Bhanudatta masterly applied the precept that an ornament enhances the rasa. In this regard, Anandavardhana said everyone knows that ornaments are a cause of literary beauty: alankaro hi carutva-hetuhprasiddhah (Dhvany-aloka 2.5 vrtti) and added: alankaro hi bahyalankara-samyad anginas carutva-hetur ucyate, “Owing to a similarity with a bodily ornament, a literary ornament is so called because it adorns the angi (“the predominant element in the text”, a first-rate rasa)” (Dhvany-aloka 2.17 vrtti).

Visvanatha Kaviraja followed Anandavardhana. According to Visvanatha, by definition an ornament adorns the rasa: sabdarthayor asthira ye dharmah sobhatisayinah \| rasadin upakurvanto lankaras te ’ngadadi-vat \|\| (Sahitya-darpana 10.1)

The Rasa-manjari was written before the Rasa-tarangirii  and mostly treats of the types of nayaka (lover, lit. leader) and nayika (ladylove, lit. female leader):

The Rasa-manjari is a somewhat smaller treatise than the Rasa-tarangim and their topics are somewhat different. The Rasa-manjari deals with nayikas and their varieties (about two-thirds of the work are taken up by this subject), the sakhi of the nayika, dUti, nayakas (in srngara) and their varieties, the friends of the nayaka (viz. plthamarda, vita, ceta, vidusaka), the eight sattvika-gunas (stambha etc.), two varieties of srngara and ten stages of vipralambha.

Bhoja in Srngara-prakasa, Rudra-bhatta in Srngara-tilaka, and Singa-bhupala in the first chapter of Rasarnava-sudhakara had expounded these topics.

Bhanudatta says the sight of the lover occurs in one of three ways: svapna-darsana (seeing a dream), citra-darsana (seeing a picture), and saksad-darsana (seeing in person). This illustrates svapna- darsana:

*muktaharam na ca kuca-gireh kankanam naiva hastat*  
*karnat svarnabharanam ayi va nitavan naiva tavat \|*  
*adya svapne bakula-mukulam bhusanam sandadhanah*  
*ko’yam cauro hrdayam aharat tanvi tan na pratimah \|\|*

**This time, he did not remove my pearl necklace from the mountains of my breasts, nor did he take the bangles from my forearms, nor did he take off my golden earrings. This time, sakhi, he crept in my dream, wearing bakula buds, and stole my heart. What a thief! I can’t believe it. (Rasa-manjari 134)**

This is Bhanudatta’s example of saksad-darsana:

*cetas cancalatam tyaja priya-sakhi vride na mam pidaya bhratar munca drsau nimesa bhagavan kama ksanam ksamyatam barham murdhni karnayoh kuvalayam vamsam dadhanah kare so’yam locana-gocaro bhavati me damodarah sundarah \|\|*

**O mind, give up your restlessness. O bashfulness, my dear friend, don’t bother me. O brotherly eyelids, leave my eyes alone. O almighty Cupid, hold on a second. Let beautiful Damodara stay in the range of my sight: He has a peacock feather on the head, lotuses on the ears, and a staff in the hand. (Rasa-manjari 136)**

The enumeration in the last sentence constitutes the ullekha ornament (angles of description). The following verse is Bhanu Datta’s example of a sulky adhira-madhya ladylove. A girl addresses her lover, who cheated on her:

*jatas te nisi jagaro mama punar netrambuje sonima*  
*nispitam bhavata madhu pravitatam vyaghurnitam me manah \|*  
*bhramyad-bhrnga-ghane nikunja-bhavane labdham tvaya sriphalam*  
*pancesuh punar eva mam hutavaha-kruraih saraih krntati \|\|*

**You stayed awake all night, yet the redness is in my eyes. You quaffed that intoxicating nectar, yet only my mind is whirling. You obtained bael fruits in that pleasure grove filled with buzzing bees, but it is I who was hit hard: Cupid pounded me with firelike fierce arrows. (Rasa-manjari 13)**

The verse is cited by Visvesvara Pandita as an example of the asangati ornament (dislocated cause and effect) (Alankara- kaustubha, KM p. 366).

Moreover, Dr. Kane says a work called Alankara-tilaka is also attributed to Bhanu Datta although the author does not mention his name (1998: 309). The Alankara-tilaka is a complete treatise on poetics that mostly follows Sarasvati-kanthabharana. In addition,

Bhanudatta wrote a book called Gita-gaurisa, an imitation of Gita- govinda:

As a Maithili writer, it is not surpising that he was acquainted with the Gaudiya Jayadeva’s well-known lyric, and tried to emulate it with a similar work on Siva and Gauri.

The Gita-gaurisa appears to have been modelled on Jayadeva’s Gita-govinda which, like Kalidasa’s Megha-duta, gave birth to numerous imitations in later times. Even a cursory examination of these two works will show the close connexion between them; and it is remarkable that not only the general scheme, but even the verses in some chapters of Bhanudatta’s poem correspond in metre with those of Jayadeva’s.

Dr. Pollock dilates upon Bhanudatta’s fame:

Bhanu-datta is perhaps the most famous Sanskrit poet— certainly the most famous Sanskrit poet of early modern India—whom no one today has heard of. Although accorded little more than a footnote in standard Indian literary histories, the two texts edited and translated in this edition, the “Bouquet of Rasa” (Rasa-manjari; on types of female and male characters in poetry) and the “River of Rasa” (Rasa-tarangini; on Sanskrit aesthetics) attracted an astonishing amount of interpretive attention from the sixteenth to the eighteenth century, including commentaries from a dozen of the period’s most celebrated scholar-exegetes. No other Sanskrit poet exercised anything remotely approaching Bhanu-datta’s influence on the development of the Hindi literary tradition between 1600 and 1850, the “Epoch of High Style” (riti- kala). No literary work, at least of the non-religious, lyrical sort, made a bigger impact than the “Bouquet of Rasa” on the new art of miniature painting that burst onto the Indian scene in the late sixteenth century. When Abu al-Fazl, the leading intellectual at the court of Akbar, presented a review of the arts and sciences of the Hindus to the Mughal emperor in the 1590s, he turned in part to the work of Bhanu to describe the nature of literature. And two centuries later, when the first Europeans began to study Sanskrit, this poet’s works, among others now more celebrated, were presented to them as exemplary by their Indian teachers.

Bhanu-datta’s extraordinary influence was not the result of any truly revolutionary break-through he achieved on the conceptual plane. It was due, rather, to his consummate skill in summarizing the thousand-year-long tradition of Indian aesthetic theory more clearly and engagingly than any one had previously and, more important, to his talent for crafting illustrative verses of far higher literary caliber than anyone had offered before him.

## 35. Rupa Gosvaml

Rupa Gosvami (1489-1564 CE) authored Bhakti-rasamrta- l\\ sindhu, Ujjvala-riilamani, and Nataka-candrika. In Bhakti- rasamrta-sindhu (1541 CE), Rupa Gosvami perfected the methodology of bhakti-rasa. He made a clear distinction between material rasa and transcendental rasa. The treatise is a revolution in the world of poetic theory because it systematically explains the concept of transcendental energy in the form of bhakti-rasa.

In practical terms, this energy can be experienced during sankirtana (chanting or simply hearing the hare krsna mantra in the company of expert musicians and singers).

Rupa Gosvami’s system of bhakti-rasa consists of two groups: One main group of five rasas (santa, dasya, sakhya, vatsalya, srngara), in ascending order of importance, and one secondary group of seven rasas (Mammata’s nine minus santa and srngara). Rupa Gosvami says he classes those seven as rasas only in deference to Bharata Muni because, according to Rupa Gosvami, in truth those seven are vyabhicari-bhavas in the scope of those five.

In bhakti-rasa, santa is the first stage whereas srngara is the highest: In this srngara-rasa, God is a lover and His damsels have transcendental bodies.

Rupa Gosvami said that if the bliss of Brahma were directly experienced over a period of one parardha (50 years of Brahma’s life span), it still would not equal a drop ofthe ocean ofthe happiness of bhakti (Bhakti-rasamrta-sindhu 1.1.38). In that regard, Jiva Gosvami shows verses of Bhagavatam (4.9.10 and 3.15.48) which establish that bhakti-rasa is more blissful than the bliss of Brahma (Priti-sandarbha 62).

Rupa Gosvami’s definition of pure bhakti (BRS 1.1.11) is an elaboration on this verse:

*ananya-mamata visnau mamata prema sangata \|*  
*bhaktir ity ucyate bhisma-prahladoddhava-naradaih \|\|*

**“According to Bhisma, Prahlada, Uddhava and Narada, love in which the possessiveness is only directed at the Lord is called bhakti.” (Bhakti-rasamrta-sindhu 1.4.2)**

Rupa Gosvami shows this verse to describe Krishna’s buffalo horn. It also illustrates yamaka (word rhyme):

*taravali venu-bhujangamena*  
*taravalila-garalena dasta \|*  
*visanika-nada-payo nipiya*  
*visani kamam dvi-guni-cakara \|\|*

taravali—Taravali; venu— \[in the form\] of the flute; bhujangamena—by the snake; tara—of a high note; avalila—\[is in the form\] of the play; garalena—\[the snake,\] whose poison; dasta—\[being\] bitten; visanika—of a small horn; nada—\[in the form\] of the sound; payah—milk; nipiya—after drinking; visani— the poisons; kamam—the love; dvi-guni-cakara—doubled.

**The gopi named TaravalT was bitten by the flute snake, whose poison is the playfulness of a high note. When she drank the milk in the form of the sound of His horn, the poison doubled her passion. (2.1.374)**

According to tradition, drinking milk aggravates the effect of poison. Further, this is the example of hasa (the sthayi-bhava of hasya-rasa):

*maya drg api narpita jarati dadhni tubhyam sape*  
*vadhus  tava nirargala tad api me mukham jighrati \|*  
*prasadhi tad imam mudha cchalita-sadhum ity acyute*  
*vadaty ajani dutika hasita-rodhane na ksama \|\|*

**“\[Seeing that Jatila, Radha’s mother-in-law, was going to another village, a confidante at once organized a secret meeting between Radha and Krishna in Jatila’s house. Jatila came back sooner than expected, saw those two kissing, and began to scold Radha. To deceive Jatila, Krishna said:\]**  
**“Old lady, I swear to you, I did not even look at the yogurt in your house. Your daughter-in-law is boldly sniffing My mouth to make sure. You should teach Her good manners. She wrongfully accused Me, a good person, of theft.” When Krishna said this, the confidante could no longer contain her outburst of laughter. (2.5.54)**

The themes in Ujjvala-nilamani (verses translated by Kusakratha and commentaries translated by Bhanu Svami), are mostly based on Bhanu-datta’s Rasa-manjan. At the beginning of the treatise, Rupa Gosvami writes:

*mukhya-rasesu pura yah samksepenodito rahasyatvat \|*  
*prthag eva bhakti-rasa-rat sa vistarenocyate madhurah \|\|*

**“Madhura-rasa, one of the primary rasas, was briefly described in Bhakti-rasamrta-sindhu because of its confidential nature. Now this king of all bhakti-rasas is described here in detail.” (1.2)**

This is similar to Bhanu Datta’s motive for writing Rasa-manjari. Keeping in mind that erotics makes poetry relishable, in Ujjvala- nilamani Rupa Gosvami discoursed upon the various categories of ladyloves as well as their emotions and so on, and applied those concepts to bhakti-rasa. Dr. Sushil Kumar De says Ujjvala- nilamani is an erotico-religious treatise: “With the exception of the Ujjvala-nilamani, which attempts to bring erotico-religious ideas to bear upon the general theme of Rasa, these specialised treatises have, however, very little importance from the speculative point of view ; and as they belong properly to the province of Erotics rather than Poetics, treatment of them should be sought elsewhere.”

In the tradition of Sanskrit poetics, the study of treatises on love (kama-sastra) was deemed necessary: “Without a study of erotics, Sanskrit poetry cannot be appreciated.”

In this matter, Dr. Kane observes:

The great Vaisnava movement inspired by Sri Caitanya (1486-1533 A.D.) produced an erotico-mystical technique. \[...\] The work Ujjvala-nilamani applies to the work and also to Sri Krsna who is srngara incarnate and who is described as ghana-mla. It also suggests that the work Ujjvala-mlamani arose out of the previous work Bhakti-rasamrta-sindhu. Jiva Gosvami in his commentary on Introduction verse 2 makes it clear that even when the Ujjvala-mlamani is meant to expound srngara explicitly in relation to Sri Krsna, it is not meant that it should be laid bare anywhere and before anybody like other works.

Rupa Gosvami says that what is called illicit and secret love and is ordinarily condemned is the highest pinnacle of srngara and that the condemnation applies only to ordinary mortals and not to a completely perfect avatara (Krsna) who took to an incarnation to give a taste of mystic love to his devotees.

Rupa Gosvami established philosophical conclusions on diverse topics, such as paraklya-bhava:

*laghutvam atra yatproktam tat tu prakrta-nayake \|*  
*na krsne rasa-niryasa-svadartham avatarini \|\|*

**“The abovementioned shortcoming of the material paramour does not apply to Krishna. He, the source of Avataras, descended to this world to relish the exudation of rasa. ” (Ujjvala-nilamani 1.21)**

In this way Rupa Gosvami states his disagreement with Visvanatha Kaviraja. Still, in Bhakti-rasamrta-sindhu, on other topics Rupa Gosvami agreeably cited verses from Sahitya-darpana, and so did Jiva Gosvami in his commentary thereon. At the outset of Nataka- candrika, however, Rupa Gosvami said that for the most part he did not accept Visvanatha’s chapter on dramaturgy because it deviates from Bharata Muni’s methodology.

Rupa Gosvami wrote many literary works. Poets are poets, but the question whether Rupa Gosvami was a superexcellent poet or a supramundane poet does not explain his glory: He alone is able to open the door of the heart and insert a meaning in there before we know it, so that we can ruminate over it. Rupa Gosvami’s compositions are: Hamsaduta, Uddhava-sandesa, Dana-keli- kaumudi (dated 1495), Vidagdha-madhava (dated 1532), Lalita- madhava, Utkalika-vallari, Govinda-virudavali, Stavamala, and Padyavali (inclusive of the poems of many others and compiled by Jiva Gosvami). His other works are: Upadesamrta, Mathura- mahima, Krsna-janma-tithi-vidhi, Radha-krsna-ganoddesa-dipika, Laghu-bhagavatamrta, and Prayuktakhyata-manjari.

## 36. Jiva Gosvami

Jiva Gosvami (1513-1598 CE) wrote Priti-sandarbha. He solidified Rupa Gosvami’s contribution to poetic theory by strengthening the underlying principles in his guru’s methodology. Jiva Gosvami had done the same in a general way in Durgama-sangamani, a commentary on Bhakti-rasamrta-sindhu, and on Locana-rocani, a commentary on Ujjvala-nilamani. Jiva Gosvami was Rupa Gosvami’s nephew:

The genealogical table of Sanatana Gosvami, Rupa Gosvami and Vallabha Gosvami can be traced back to the twelfth century Sakabda, when a gentleman of the name Sarvajna appeared in a very rich and opulent brahmana family in the province of Kamata. He had two sons, named Aniruddhera Rupesvara and Harihara, who were both bereft of their kingdoms and thus obliged to reside in the highlands. The son of Rupesvara, who was named Padmanabha, moved to a place in Bengal known as Naihati, on the bank of the Ganges. There he had five sons, of whom the youngest, Mukunda, had a well behaved son named Kumaradeva, who was the father of Rupa, Sanatana and Vallabha. Kumaradeva lived in Fateyabad, an area bordering Baklacandradvipa in East Bengal (now Bangladesh). The present-day village of Prembagh, which lies near Ramshara in the Jessore district of Bangladesh, is said by many to be the site of Kumaradeva’s house. Of his many sons, three took to the path of Vaisnavism. Later, Sri Vallabha and his elder brothers Sri Rupa and Sanatana came from Candradvipa to the village in the Maldah district of Bengal known as Ramakeli. It is in this village that Srila Jiva Gosvami took birth, accepting Vallabha as his father.

Jiva Gosvami uses the term priti in the general sense of bhagavat- prlti (affection for the Lord). It means the same as bhakti. It corresponds to Mammata’s and Visvanatha’s deva-visaya rati, except that Jiva Gosvami substantiated Vopadeva’s and Rupa Gosvami’s standpoint that bhakti can reach the level of rasa. Rupa Gosvami uses the term priti as a synonym of dasya-rati.

Jiva Gosvami states:

*kim ca laukikasya raty-adeh sukha-rupatvam yatha-kathancid eva vastu-vicare duhkha-paryavasayitvat. tad uktam svayam bhagavata “sukham duhkha-sukhatyayah duhkham kama-sukhapeksa” iti.*

**“Even though from an ordinary perspective the mundane sthayi- bhavas are forms of happiness one way or another, upon careful consideration they are not so, since they culminate in unhappiness. The Lord Himself said it: “Real happiness is to transcend material happiness and unhappiness, and real misery is to be implicated in searching for sexual pleasure” (Bhagavatam 11.19.41)” (Priti- sandarbha 110).**

Madhusudana Sarasvati said the same and added that the trifling, mundane rasas are like fireflies compared to the sun-like bhagavad- rati that has become rasa.

In essence, Jiva Gosvami states that after all, the immediate goal of life is the obtainment of happiness and the cessation of unhappiness; the happiness derived from bhakti totally eclipses unhappiness. The reason for that is the occurrence of transcendental potency in the experience of bhakti-rasa. Jiva Gosvami adds that, as in the case of the mundane rasas, a particular subconscious impression is required, so that affection for the Lord can rise to the level of rasa: purusa-yogyata ca sri-prahladadmam iva tadrsa-vasana (Priti- sandarbha 110).

Jiva Gosvami indited literary works, such as Madhava-mahotsava and Sankalpa-kalpadruma. In addition to the six Sandarbhas, he wrote a treatise on grammar, Hari-namamrta-vyakarana, which supersedes all other Sanskrit grammars: It is more complete than Panini’s Astadhyayi and is more thorough than Bhattoji Diksita’s Siddhanta-kaumudi. Hari-namamrta was translated by Matsya Avatara Dasa and edited by the present writer. Jiva Gosvami also wrote two commentaries on Bhagavatam—Laghu-vaisnava-tosani and Krama-sandarbha—and a commentary on Brahma-samhita.

Among his literary works, Gopala-campu is a poetical masterpiece. Therein, on occasion he paraphrased Visvanatha’s examples of ornaments in Sahitya-darpana. To illustrate the theory expounded by Visvanatha, the author of Bhakti-rasamrta-sesa often showed such verses by Jiva Gosvami. According to Matsya Avatara Dasa, Gopala-campu is similar to Bhatti-kavya in the sense that all the rules of grammar, though already written and explained with examples in Hari-namamrta-vyakarana, are illustrated therein. These verses from Gopala-campu exemplify ornaments:

**Arthantara-nyasa (corroboration)**

*srimad-gopa-nrpena nutana-tanujatasya viksakrte*  
*pragrya eva nimantrita vraja-janah sarve tu tatrayayuh \|*  
*yarhy ambhoja-vanakarah sva-kusuma-vrata-prakasa-pratha-*  
*vyaptah syat kim u tarhi satpada-ganan akarayaty atmana \|\|*
