**Nanda invited the best persons to see the child and they all came. In addition, many who were uninvited came to see the child. When a lotus pond is filled with lotuses, does it not attract bees by itself? (Gopala-campu 1.5.5)**

**Vibhavana (an effect without a normal cause)**

*krsna-bhru-yugalam tad dhanur-anukrd api sphurac citram \|*  
*yat khalu vinapi banam tam api radham svayam jayati \|\|*

**Imitating his bow, Krishna’s brows are astonishing, since even without arrows they automatically win Radha over. (Gopala- campu 2.34.54)**

**Apahnuti (poetic denial)**

*tvat-kirtya svetitah kamso ’py etat krsna mrsoditam \|*  
*tat-sparsas tasya nasty eva kintu tad-bhiti-vaikrtam \|\|*

**Krishna, Kamsa became white due to Your fame. Actually that’s not true. He is untouched by it. Rather, he is terrified of you. (Gopala-campu 1.33. 21)**

Gopala-campu culminates in a description of the marriage of Radha and Krishna (Gopala-campu 2.35). Jiva Gosvami wrote the book to promote Svakiya-vada (the two lovers must be married to each other).

But on occasion Jiva Gosvami denied that the love between Krishna and the gopis is illicit. Jiva Gosvami implicitly validated parakiya-bhava (the mood of paramours) with regard to Krishna: svecchaya likhitam kincit kincid atra parecchaya, “Here something is written out of my own desire, and something is written out of others’ desire” (Locana-rocani 1.21). The purport is that the love between Krishna and the gopis is svakiya from the viewpoint of tattva (the truth), since the gopis have transcendental bodies and thus have the same nature as Krishna, whereas it is parakiya from the viewpoint of rasa (i.e. imitating the ways of mortals). At the end of his grammatical treatise Jiva Gosvami expressed his desire to be the friend of Gopala Dasa in this life and in the next. Matsya Avatara Dasa explains:

There is a book named Sadhana-dipika which was written by Radha-krsna dasa, a disciple of the famous Haridasa Gosvami who was the chief sevaka of the Radha Govinda deities and who requested Krsnadasa Kaviraja to write Caitanya- caritamrta. At the end of the ninth chapter of that book some details about Gopala dasa are mentioned.

To summarize what is mentioned there: Gopala dasa was a dear disciple of Jiva Gosvami, hailing from a vaisya family. It was under the sway of his request that Jiva Gosvami established the svakiya-rasa in some of his works like Gopala-campu and

Krsna-sandarbha, and in his Ujjvala-nilamani-tika. Being a direct disciple of Rupa Gosvami and a recipient of his potency and instructions, Jiva Gosvami personally accepted only the parakiya-rasa, but to cater to certain disciples like Gopala dasa he seemingly supported the svakiya-rasa.

For example, in the mangalacarana of Gopala-campu, a book which contains many descriptions of the svakiya-rasa, Jiva Gosvami clearly dedicates the book to Gopala-dasa by saying sri-gopala-gananam gopalanam pramodaya / bhavatu samantad esa namna gopala-campur ya (“May this book entitled Gopala-campu bring about the pleasure of the gopalas in the group of Sri Gopala”).

However, at the end of the section in Krsna-sandarbha that establishes svakiya-rasa, we find that Jiva Gosvami begs forgiveness from the Lord for promoting such a faulty conception. He says: yad etat tu maya ksudra-tarena taralayitam / ksamatam tat ksama-silah sriman gokula- vallabhah (“May the beloved Lord of Gokula, who is forgiving by nature, forgive insignificant me for my fickleness”).

And in his Ujjvala-nilamani-tika he frankly admits that his writing about the svakiya-rasa is prompted by the will of others. It is not his own viewpoint. He says there: svecchaya likhitam kincit kincid atra parecchaya (“Some parts in this commentary have been written out of my own will and other parts have been written out of another’s will”).

Keeping all this in mind, learned Vaisnavas overlook such sections in Jiva Gosvami’s works, knowing that at heart he never once deviates from the teachings of Rupa Gosvami.

## 37. Kavi Karnapura

Kavi Karnapura (1524-1576 CE) wrote Alankara- kaustubha. Other than the topic of rasa, he followed Mammata to the letter: He paraphrased Mammata’s definitional verses. Even his sequence of ornaments is the same as the one in Kavya-prakasa. He did not acknowledge the ornaments propounded by Ruyyaka and other moderns.

Kavi Karnapura composed all his examples. He is also the author of Caitanya-candrodaya-nataka, Ananda-vrndavana-campu, Sri-krsnahnika-kaumudi, and Gaura-ganoddesa-dipika. But unlike Visvanatha Kaviraja’s modus operandi in Sahitya-darpana, Kavi Karnapura’s verses in Alankara-kaustubha are unique compositions.

Dr. Sivaprasada, who wrote a Sankrit commentary on Alankara- kaustubha, states: “Kavi Karnapura was a name to conjure with in Bengal Vaisnava circles.” In his commentary on Ujjvala- nilamani, Visnudasa, a disciple of Rupa Gosvami, often cited Alankara-kaustubha.

However, Kavi Karnapura’s fame in Bengal was as big as it was little outside of it. He was ignored by most Indian literati. Matsya Avatara Dasa and the present writer co-translated Alankara- kaustubha. It is one of the best treatises on Sanskrit poetics. In all fairness, it is not inferior to Jagannatha’s Rasa-gangadhara. And in point of skill and originality in examples, among complete works on poetical theory it is topmost.

This is Kavi Karnapura’s example of the suggestiveness of onomat­opoeia:

*asam rasa-vilasa-lasya-laharim asvadya vadya-cchalat*  
*ta dhik ta dhig itiprabhasya murajah svar-nartakir nindati \|*  
*te na na ga ri ma dha ma iti muhuh patha-svaroccaranat*  
*tasam hanta jugupsate bhagavati vani ca gana-kraman \|\|*

**Relishing the waves of the gopis’ dancing in the Rasa dance, the muraja drum, on the plea of being a musical instrument, resounds with the beat ta dhik ta dhik and thus rebukes the female dancers of heaven. And by repeating the gopis’ phrase “te na na ” and their notes “ga ri ma dha ma, ” SarasvatT, the goddess of language, rebukes the Gandharvas’ style of singing.**

Kavi Karnapura elucidates: atra te na na iti pathah. ga ri ma dha ma iti gandhara-rsabha-madhyama-dhaivata-punar-madhyama iti tana-visesa-svarah, tabhyam te nana-vidho yo ’garima tenadhama ity artho vyajyate.

“Here, te na na is the phrase, and ga ri ma dha ma, that is, gandhara, rsabha, madhyama, dhaivata and again madhyama, are the notes of a certain euphonic series. By articulating this phrase and these notes, the implied meaning is: “They, the Gandharvas, are lower on account of many types of inferiority (agarima = nicatva)” (te na na ga ri ma dha ma iti = te nanagarimadhamah iti).” (Alankara- kaustubha 2.43). The words ta dhik ta dhik as well are a double meaning: “Fie on them. Fie on them” (tah dhik tah dhik).

Kavi Kamapura is so called either because he fills the ears (with rasa) or because he is an ear ornament (karnapura) for the connoisseurs. His given name was Paramananda-dasa (Caitanya- caritamrta 3.12.45). At a young age Kavi Karnapura, the son of Sivananda Sena, received Caitanya Mahaprabhu’s blessing: sivananda yabe sei balake milaila mahaprabhu padangustha tara mukhe dila, “When Sivananda introduced the child to Mahaprabhu, He put His big toe in the child’s mouth” (CC 3.12.50). Caitanya Mahaprabhu affectionately called Paramananda-dasa by the name Puri-dasa (CC 3.12-47-49).

Kavi Karnapura composed this verse at seven years of age and recited it to Mahaprabhu (CC 3.16.75):

*sravasoh kuvalayam aksnor*  
*anjanam uraso mahendra-mani-dama \|*  
*vrndavana-ramaninam*  
*mandanam akhilam harir jayati \|\|*

**He is the blue lilies on the gopis’ ears, the eyeliner on their eyes, and the necklace of sapphires on their chests. He is all their ornaments. Hari is glorious. (cited in CC 3.16.74).**

In the gopls’ minds, those three things are uddipanas (stimuli). Kavi Karnapura shows the verse as an example of mala-rUpaka (a series of metaphors) (Alankara-kaustubha 8.77). Everyone was astonished that a seven-year-old boy could compose such a beautiful verse in Sanskrit. According to tradition, Svarupa Damodara named him Karnapura because he thus suffused (pura) the devotees’ ears.

This is Kavi Karnapura’s example of the second-rate implied sense called sphuta (obvious) (Mammata calls it agudha

*drsta bhagavatah krpapy upagata tesam sthitam taih samam*  
*jnatam vastu viniscitam ca kiyata premnapi tatrasitam \|*  
*jlvadbhir na mrtam mrtair yadi punar martavyam asmadrsair*  
*utpadyaiva na kim mrtam bata vidhe vamaya tubhyam namah \|\|*

**I saw the Lord’s devotees and obtained their mercy. I was with them. I understood the real thing that was ascertained by them as the essence of all. I used to sit among them with so much love. If persons like us don’t die while we’re in a good condition, and moreover if we’ll have to die in a miserable state, then why don’t we just die after taking birth? Alas, O cruel fate, I offer my respects to you. (4.3)**

Moreover, Kavi Karnapura invented a category of poetry: uttamottama-kavya (superexcellent poetry), where either one first- rate implied sense gives rise to another or a first-rate implied sense occurs and both the sounds and the meanings create a feeling of wonder.

Previously, only poetry that contains a first-rate implied sense was ranked highest (uttama-kavya). By the skill displayed in his illustrations, Kavi Kamapura raised the standards of poetry.

Kavi Karnapura’s definition of poetry is: kavi-van-nirmitih kavyam, “A poet’s verbal composition is poetry” (Alankara-kaustubha 1.8). He avoids circular reasoning by defining the word kavi, not only in the sense of poet, but also in terms of an intelligent and learned person (since the words kavi, vidvan, pandita, and so on are synonymous; Amara-kosa 2.7.5): He says a kavi is someone who has the innate propensity, is expert in all the scriptures, and relishes rasa. And if the kavi has creative intelligence, then he or she is first-class.

## Yamaka

Kavi Kamapura is the king of yamaka (word rhyme). He shows thirty excellent examples of different varieties. This illustrates a madhya-yamaka (a yamaka in the middle of each line):

*madana-sangara-sanga-rasakula*  
*bhava viharini harini madhave \|*  
*kusuma-raji-viraji-vibhusand*  
*madhupa-raga-paraga-paracita \|\|*

**Your ornaments appear splendid with flower decorations. You are smeared with a flower pollen that delights bees. Hey playful girl, while Madhava is stealing your heart, become absorbed in the bliss of union. (7.60)**

This illustrates an ady-anta-madhya-yamaka (a yamaka at the beginning, middle, and end of each line):

*maso maso maricyah sa-madhura-madhura-preyasT-preya-sima-*  
*vrnda vrndavana-srir upavana-pavana-bhrantir abhranti-ramya \|*  
*nandanandagra-kandah smara-samara-samo vyuha-harTha harTsangT*  
*sangTia-devya ahar ahar aharad rasa-radham sa radham \|\|*

**The moonrays were emitting much light. Vrndavana was so beautiful that it deserved to be filled to its limits with sweet loving girls. The movement of the breezes in the groves was pleasant on account of their carefulness (the breezes were thinking: “It is appropriate for us to move slowly in these groves of Vrndavana”). It was at this time that Krishna, who is the foremost cause of Nanda’s bliss, who wears a garland, and who is fond of music, took away Radha. She daily brings the Rasa dance to perfection. Krishna appeared beautiful in the battle of Cupid while disposing of Cupid’s soldiers. (7.61)**

This is an antadi-yamaka (a yamaka at the beginning of each line and another at the end of each line):

*na manam adhehi manasy adah syadah*  
*subham subhamyoh syati devi te ’vite \|*  
*aho aho-ratra-krtarusa rusa-*  
*yaso yasoda-bhuvi vidyate ’dya te \|\|*

**Beautiful girl, you have such a good reputation. Don’t let pique stay in your heart, for that impulse will destroy your good fortune. How amazing, even now you remain shielded by your anger, which causes you pain day and night. By now the news of your bad temper must have reached Yasoda’s son: Your reputation will suffer. (7.62)**

This is an example of sarva-yamaka (each line is a yamaka and each line is the same):

*sasara sa sa-sarasa-*  
*sa-sara-sasa-sara-sa \|*  
*sasarasasa-sarasa*  
*sa sarasasa-sara-sa \|\|*

sasara—wandered (from the verbal root sr gatau); sa— She (Radha); sa-sarasa—with a lotus \[in Her hand\]; asa—of complete bewilderment (as\[u\] ksepane); sara—which causes the attainment (sr gatau); sasa—of sleepiness (sas\[u\] svapne); sara—the power; sa—who destroys (i.e. puts to shame) (so ’nta-karmani); sasa— become sleepy (stunned); arasa—sound nicely (ras\[a\] sabde); asa—shine (i.e. appear beautiful) (as\[a\] dlptau); samsa—Radha, because of whom the cakravaka birds; sah—He (Krishna); samsa— of the cranes; asa—of the sitting (as\[a\] upavesane); sara—the firmness; sa—who destroys (i.e. belittles) (so ’nta-karmani).

**Radha and Krishna stroll together in a forest. Her movements put to shame the bewildering power of sleep. Radhika holds a lotus flower and belittles the pose of the cakravaka birds. Upon seeing Her, these cakravakas cry, become stunned, and look resplendent. (7.64)**

## Citra-kavya

Kavi Kamapura’s section on citra-kavya is unique. He and Rupa Gosvami (Stavamala) raised the standards of picture poetry. This verse with two yamakas illustrates the umbrella diagram:

*tanutam tamtam radha-*  
*krsnayos carita-srutih \|*  
*hrt-tapanam sudha-sindhu-*  
*dhara tam nu tatam nuta \|\|*

tanutam—the littleness; tanutam—may it cause; radha-krsnayoh— of Radha and Krishna; carita—of the deeds; srutih—the hearing; hrt—of the heart; tapanam—of the afflictions; sudha—of nectar; sindhu—of the ocean; dhara—the flow; tam—that \[hearing\]; nu— (a particle used out of respect); tatam—which is expanded; nuta— you all should praise.

**May the hearing of Radha’s and Krishna’s pastimes, which conveys the flow of an ocean of nectar, dispel the afflictions of the heart. All of you should praise a prolonged hearing of that sort. (7.83)**

![рис-010.jpg|600](<Versified History of Sanskrit Poetics/рис-010.jpg>)

Kavi Kamapura’s section on varna-citra (verses of few consonants) rivals Rupa Gosvami’s (in Stavamala). This is a verse where each line has only one consonant:

*sam-slh sasi sasasasam*  
*papo 'papapa-pah papih \|*  
*lolo lalala lila-lim*  
*yayayam yo ’yaya yayau \|\|*

**The moon is not awake to my happiness. It has suddenly shifted to another direction. The wicked moon withers sinless girls like us and frustrates our desires. Krishna thirsts for gopis. He wanted a girl who will embrace Him during play. He must be having union with such a girl by now, and surely that girl will not leave Him. (7.99)**

This is Kavi Kamapura’s verse of one consonant:

*na nana nanino ’nena*  
*nananenananam nu nuh \|*  
*nunam nonan nrn anunan*  
*anu na nun-nun nunnimh \|\|*

na—the man (the Purusa); nana—many; na—not; aninah—He has no master (or He other than whom there is no master); anenah— is sinless; nana—various; anena—by Him; ananam—the life; nu—obviously; nuh—of a living entity; nunam—indeed; na—not; unan—tiny (i.e. humans); nrn—persons; anunan—not tiny (i.e. demigods); anu—directed toward; na—not; nut—praise; nut—one who dispels; nu—certainly; unninih—constantly leads upwards.

**The Supreme Person is not manifold. Obviously, He has no master and is free from sin. Indeed, He created this variegated universe and is the life of every living being. Certainly, He never prevents praise directed at exalted individuals nor even at insignificant people. Is He not the one who is a constant uplifter? (7.100)**

## Rasa

The fifth chapter of Alankara-kaustubha treats of rasa and corresponds to Rupa Gosvami’s Bhakti-rasamrta-sindhu and Ujjvala-mlamani. This is an example of srngara-rasa:

*mrdu-spandam lila-kara-kisalayotkampam udayat*  
*prasunesu krida-vivasa-muditali-vraja-sukham \|*  
*amandi-kurvanam kim api kala-kantha-dhvani-kalam*  
*siseve radhangam harir atha vasantanilam iva \|\|*

**\[First interpretation:\]**

**Hari served Radha’s body as if a springtime breeze was taking place. A springtime breeze moves slowly, makes for a pastime (lila-kara), causes lotuses to shake (kisalaya-utkampa) and, while intensifying the expertise (kala) of the cuckoos’ chirping (kalakantha-dhvani), increases the joy of delighted bees who are absorbed in playing in flowers (krida-vivasa-mudita-ali).**

**\[Second interpretation:\]**

**Hari served Radha’s body, which was like a springtime breeze. Her body moved slowly on the flowers, and there was a tremor in it because of the lotus which is a mine of pastimes (lila-akara- kisalaya-utkampa). While raising the standard of the art (kala) of moaning (kala-kantha-dhvani) in the helpless state of taking pleasure (krida-vivasam), it increased the joy of the sakhis who had woken up (udita-ali). (5.31)**

An example of kissing the lips (adhara-pana):

*madhvikacamanotsave kutukinor anyonya-danta-cchadav*  
*anyonyena krtopadamsa-racanau sri-radhika-krsnayoh \|*  
*ksunnau ca dvija-kutmalair abhavatam aksunna-laksmi-bharau*  
*pitau carunitau babhuvatur aho premno vicitra gatih \|\|*

**The lips of Radha and Krishna, who were jovial during the festivity of tasting sweet wine, concocted each other’s amuse- bouches. The lips, broken by the bud-like teeth, achieved an unbroken splendor. In addition the lips were drunk, and became reddened. Wow! How amazing is the main course of love! (5.46)**

This illustrates prema-rasa (true love):

*preyams te ’ham tvam api ca mama preyasiti pravadas*  
*tvam me prana aham api tavasmiti hanta pralapah \|*  
*tvam me te syam aham iti ca yat tac ca no sadhu radhe*  
*vyavaharo nau na hi samucito yusmad-asmat-prayogah \|\|*

**Radha, if I were to say “I am Your sweetheart and You are Mine,” that would only be chatter. And the words “You are My life and I am Yours” are simply prattle. Even saying “You belong to Me and I to You” is not right. The terms “You” and “I” are not proper usage between Us. (5.27)**

In his methodology, Kavi Kamapura divides rasa in three broad categories: material, transcendental, and a semblance: prakrtaprakrtabhasa-bhedad esa tridha matah (5.13). He says Bhoja added prema and vatsalya for a total of eleven rasas: bhojas tu vatsalata-premabhyam ekadasa rasan acaste, vatsalye mama- karah, premani citta-dravas ca sthayi (Alankara-kaustubha 5.4). Kavi Kamapura agrees with Bhoja and adds bhakti-rasa for a total of twelve rasas. In Alankara-kaustubha, bhakti-rasa corresponds to Mammata’s deva-visaya rati and to Rupa Gosvami’s santa-rasa or dasya-rasa.

In Kavi Karnapura’s prema-rasa, the sthayi-bhava is citta-drava (melting of the heart, i.e. sneha) (5.4). He says some theorists consider the relationship between Radha and Krishna to be only srngara-rasa. In that case, he says, prema (love) is an aspect of srngara (erotic). His own opinion, however, is that prema-rasa is the basis of all the rasas, so that in the above verse srngara is an aspect of prema.

Kavi Karnapura’s statement that Bhoja added prema as a rasa is a mystery. Rewa-prasada Dwivedi comments on Bhoja’s concept of srngara:

For this kind of approach to the term srngara two categories are involved ‘mundane and supermundane’ or ‘mundane and transcendent’— laukika and alaukika and lokottara or divya so to say. The latter one is fixed for the divinity alone like Siva and Siva, Sri Krsna and Radha, etc. At this level the erotic sense of Kumara-sambhava etc. is quite appropriate.

Still, Bhoja’s moksa variety of srngara includes both categories. Moreover, Bhoja stated that the srngara which is based on the soul is the only Rasa. Perhaps Kavi Karnapura renamed the metaphysical srngara. However, Kavi Karnapura does not provide a citation and Bhoja nowhere gives a list of eleven rasas. In both treatises, Bhoja lists the traditional eight and adds four: santa, preyas, urjasvin (or udatta), and uddhata (SK 5.164) (Srngara-prakasa 11.61 vrtti).

There is another explanation. Jiva Gosvami states that Bhoja and others list preyas and vatsala. He cites Bhoja as regards preyas and Visvanatha as regards vatsala. In Sarasvati-kanthabharana, Bhoja says vatsala is an integral aspect ofpreyas, and sneha is the sthayi of preyas: atra vatsala-prakrter dhirataya lalita-nayakasya priyanubhavad utpannah sneha-sthayi-bhavo \[...\] nispannah preyan itipratiyate (illustration 5.74 vrtti). And most likely, Bhoja knew that Udbhata’s example ofpreyas is an instance of vatsala. In Srngara-prakasa, Bhoja mentioned vatsala in passing, in the list of the ancients’ ten rasas. Concerning Kavi Karnapura, Dr. Raghavan writes:

He accepts the eight rasas of Bharata, the santa and the vatsalya. To these ten he adds two more, prema and bhakti. Prema is the name he gives to the madhura-rasa, the divine srngara between Krsna and the gopis. He considers citta- drava as its sthayi. According to him, this love is not srngara. He also records the view of some who hold srngara as the rasa between Radha and Krsna and says that, in that case, prema will be the anga of that srngara. But, according to himself, prema is the angi; srngara, its anga. This prema, Kavi Karnapura considers as Love Supreme within which every other rasa comes. This view of prema will make it the basic Love which, Bhoja also says, lies at the root, as mula-prakrti, of rati and priti.

Thus Professor Raghavan, who translated Srngara-prakasa, traces Kavi Karnapura’s usage of prema-rasa to Bhoja’s disquisition on preyo-rasa, only stated in Sarasvati-kanthabharana: atra vatsala-prakrter dhirataya lalita-nayakasya priyanubhavad utpannah sneha-sthayi-bhavo visaya-saukumaryatma-prakrty- adibhih uddipana-vibhavaih uddipyamanah samupajayamanaih moha-mati-dhrti-smrty-adibhih vyabhicari-bhavair anubhavais ca prasamsadibhih samsrjyamano nispannah preyan iti pratiyate. rati-prityor api cayam eva mula-prakrtir isyate (SK, illustration 5.74 vrtti). Here Bhoja says preyas should also be considered the root of rati and priti. The difference between rati and priti is this, according to Dandi and Bhoja: Priti (love) is a form of rati (a man’s love for his beloved, or vice versa) which does not involve sex. Perhaps Kavi Karnapura misread “preyan vatsalas ca” in

Jiva Gosvami’s text as “prema vatsalas ca”. Or else he changed the term preyas to prema. Therein Jiva Gosvami cites this illustration ofpreyas from Bhoja: yad eva rocate mahyam tad eva kurutepriya, iti vetti na janati tat-priyam yat karoti sa, “My beloved does what appeals to me. Whether she knows this or not, she does what I like” (Sarasvail-kanthabharana. illustration 5.74) (Srngara-prakasa 11.63; 12.7). In Srngara-prakasa as well, Bhoja said the sthayl of preyas is sneha: sneha-prakrtih preyan (11.65).

Bhoja obliquely referred to prema as a rasa: asrayo yasya raty-adih premader upajayate, visayo yatra yosadau so’sya janmadhigacchati , “The man whose rati, etc., of his prema, etc., is both the foundation of his feelings for a woman and the object of the woman’s love has a life” (SK 5.35). Bhoja mentioned twelve varieties of prema.

Kavi Karnapura’s prema is the same as Singabhupala’s prema, one of the stages after rati (affection in the scope of srngara). Singabhupala defines it: saprema bheda-rahitamyunoryad bhava- bandhanam, “Prema is the love between a young woman and a young man which involves no disrupture” (Rasarnava-sudhakara 2.110). Similarly, Rupa Gosvami defines prema as love that does not dwindle even in the midst of difficulty: sarvatha dhvamsa- rahitam saty api dhvamsa-karane \| yad-bhava-bandhanam yunoh sa prema parikirtitah \|\| (Ujjvala-nilamani 14.63). Singabhupala gives this example:

*rathanganamnor iva bhava-bandhanam*  
*babhuva yat prema parasparasrayam \|*  
*vibhaktam apy eka-sutena tat tayoh*  
*parasparasyopari paryaciyate \|\|*

**“The love between Dilipa and Sudaksina resembled the love of two cakravaka birds. Although it was partitioned by their love for their son, it kept increasing above it.” (Raghu-vamsa 3.24)**

Singabhupala comments that although their love for their son was a potential cause of the disrupture of their love, their love was not disrupted: atra bheda-karane suta-snehe saty api sudaksina- dilipayoh rater apariharena bheda-ratitvam \[bheda-rahitvam\] (Rasarnava-sudhakara, illustration 2.382 vrtti).

This raises the question whether the love between two souls is real.

Lust is what makes you keep wanting to do it, even when you have no desire to be with each other. Love is what makes you keep wanting to be with each other, even when you have no desire to do it. (Judith Viorst

However, those three rhetoricians do not agree about the position prema should have in the sequence of the stages of love. Singabhupala’s sequence is: rati, prema, mana, pranaya, sneha, raga, and anuraga (Rasarnava-sudhakara 2.109). Rupa Gosvami’s sequence is: rati, prema, sneha, mana, pranaya, raga, anuraga, and mahabhava (Ujjvala-mlamani 14.59). Kavi Karnapura says the sequence is: rati, bhava (this bhava is the first alankara among the twenty alankaras of srngara), purva-raga, raga, anuraga, pranaya, prema, sneha, and maha-raga (AK 5.10).

Most likely, at the time of writing Alankara-kaustubha, Kavi Kamapura knew Rupa Gosvami’s works, since he seemingly referred to him: kaiscit sakhibhih saha yuddham udahriyate, tat tu lila-visesa iti prakrte na likhyate. “Some eminent scholar illustrates vira-rasa by describing a fight between Krsna and His friends (Bhakti-rasamrta-sindhu 4.3.6-8). But that is only a particular type of pastime, and so it is not emphasized in this discourse.” (Alankara-kaustubha 5.16). Kavi Karnapura said that Rupa-manjan, in Goloka Vrndavana, appeared as Rupa Gosvami (Gaura-ganoddesa-dipika 180). He glorified Rupa Gosvami in yet another eminent way with this sweet-sounding verse:

*priya-svarupe dayita-svarupe*  
*prema-svarupe sahajabhirupe \|*  
*nijanurupe prabhur eka-rupe tatana rupe*  
*sva-vilasa-rUpe \|\|*

**Lord Caitanya expanded in Rupa, a unique form, a form of His manifestations for pastimes. Rupa was in conformity with Him: Rupa’s nature was cherished, Svarupa was dear to him, Rupa had the nature of pure love, and was naturally very beautiful. (Caitanya-candrodaya-nataka 9.143) (cited in Caitanya-caritamrta 2.19.121)**

Not counting Rupa Gosvami’s works, Alankara-kaustubha is one of four Gaudiya Vaishnava treatises on poetic theory. The three others are: Bhakti-rasamrta-sesa, and Baladeva Vidyabhusana’s Sahitya-kaumudi and Kavya-kaustubha. In Bhakti-rasamrta-sesa and in Sahitya-kaumudi, the respective authors abundantly copied the examples in Alankara-kaustubha. The illustrations in Kavya- kaustubha are simple.

## 38. Kesava Misra

Kesava Misra (c. 1570 CE) wrote Alankara-sekhara. For the most part, the treatise is a rehash of old ideas. He follows Dandi’s methodology of subdivisions of metaphors. The particularity of this work is that he attributes the authorship of the karikas to Gautama Buddha, whom he calls Sauddhodani. According to Kesava Misra, Sauddhodani defined poetry in this way: kavyam rasadi-madvakyam srutam sukha-visesa-krt, “Poetry is a vocal statement that has a rasa, and so on, and that produces a special delight” (Alankara-sekhara 1.1). Kesava Misra says poetry is a statement that has either a rasa, an ornament, or both.

Dr. Kane comments:

Whether Sauddhodani is the name of an author or whether the karikas were composed by some Buddhist writer and were subsequently ascribed to Sauddhodani (a name of Bhagavan Buddha) cannot be determined. The work very largely draws upon the Kavyadarsa, Kavya-mimamsa, the Dhvany-aloka, the Kavya-prakasa, Vag-bhatalankara, Bhojaraja and quotes Sn-pada (an otherwise unknown author on alankara) very frequently.

Kesava Misra tells us in the Introduction and at the end that he wrote the Alankara-sekhara at the instance of king Manikyacandra son of Dharmacandra. This Dharmacandra was a son of Ramacandra, a scion of the family of Susarma, who routed a Kabila (Afgan) king of Delhi. According to Cunningham (Arch. Survey of India vol. V. p. 160) Manikyacandra, king of Kangra, succeeded Dharmacandra in 1563 and ruled for about ten years. Hence the Alankara- sekhara was composed in the latter half of the 16th century.

Kesava Misra divides his work in twenty-two chapters grouped under eight headings, called gems: upakrama-ratna, dosa-ratna, guna-ratna, alankara-ratna, varnaka-ratna, kavi-sampradaya- ratna, kavi-samarthya-ratna, and visrama-ratna (Alankara- sekhara, KM p. 83). Kesava Misra only expounds fourteen ornaments of meaning. Dr. Sushil Kumar De continues:

This is followed by a curious chapter, entitled varnaka-ratna, in which are detailed the upamanas appropriate for describing a damsel, her complexion, hair, forehead, eyebrows etc. It goes on to give practical hints as to how poets should describe the physical characteristics of the hero, mentions words which convey the idea of similarity, details the conventional usages of poets (kavi-samaya), as well as the topics for description (such as the king, the queen, a town, a city, a river etc.) and the way of describing them, the colours of various objects in nature, words that convey numerals from one to one thousand, certain tricks of words such as bhasa-sama (where a verse reads the same in Sanskrit as in Prakrit), samasya-purana, the nine Rasas, the kinds of hero and heroine, the different Bhavas, the Dosas of Rasa, and lastly, the arrangement of letters favourable to each Rasa.

The chapter on samasya-purana (19) only deals with the proper association of ideas that a poet should keep in mind. Kesava Misra’s poetical concept called gatagata is simply a mirrored type of alliteration (18.1). Moreover, Kesava Misra acknowledges vyanjana-vrtti (Sugges-tiveness) (3.1) but does not illustrate many subdivisions of Dhvani.

In chapter seven he propounds five sabda-gunas and in chapter eight four artha-gunas. The five sabda-gunas are: sanksepa (concise wording), udatta (great adjectives), prasada (ease of understanding), ukti (implied meaning) and samadhi (attributing sentience to nonsentient entities).

The four artha-gunas are: bhavikatva (the speaker obliquely conveys her intention), susabdatva (not using an inauspicious word in denoting an inauspicious meaning), paryayokti (the same as Mammata’s paryaya) and sudharmita (a substantive is inferred from its adjectival nouns) (a form of paryayokta, circumlocution). This illustrates sudharmita:

*ayam udayati mudra-bhanjanah padmininam*  
*udaya-giri-vanall-bala-mandara-puspam \|*  
*viraha-vidhura-koka-dvandva-bandhur vibhindan*  
*kupita-kapi-kapola-kroda-tamras tamamsi \|\|*

**That breaker of the seals of lotuses is on the rise: It is the newly blown reddish mandara flower in the big forest in the Eastern Mountain; it is reddish like the middle of the cheeks of an angry ape; and as it dispels darkness it becomes the friend of couples of cakravaka birds dejected due to the pang of separation. (KM p. 22) (example of Lati riti in Sahitya-darpana 9.4)**

This is Kesava Misra’s example of the virodhabhasa ornament (semblance of a contradiction):

*muktanam kama-das tusto rusa kamam dahann api \|\|*  
*api jnana-maya sthanur yas tam isam stuvmahi \|\|*

**Though he angrily turned Cupid (kama) to ashes, he is self­content and fulfills the desires (kama) of liberated souls. Let us praise that god Sthanu though he is transcendent. (Alankara- sekhara, KM p. 35)**

Siva is called Sthanu (lit. post) because during his austerities he remains motionless like a tree trunk. This is the example of the sara ornament (climax):

*visayesu tavad abalas tasv api gopyah svabhava-mrdu-vacah \|*  
*madhye tasam api sa tasya api saci-viksitam kim api \|\|*

**Of all things of beauty, women are second to none. Of all women, gopis who speak softly by nature are foremost. Of them, She is the most eminent. And the best thing about Her is some crooked sidelong glance. (Alankara-sekhara, KM p. 35**

## 39. Appaya Dlksita

Appaya Diksita wrote Vrtti-varttika, Kuvalayananda and Citra-mimamsa. He was born in a Brahmana family in Tamil Nadu. He was a polymath who wrote one hundred and four books. A Shaivite, he is also known as an acarya of Advaita-vedanta. His name is also written Appayya and Appa.

Appaya Diksita’s date of birth is a subject of controversy. Dr. Kane says his dates are 1554-1626 CE. He adds that some say his dates are 1520-1593, but he refutes this on the grounds that Appaya and Jagannatha must have been contemporaries for some time since in his books Jagannatha vehemently insults Appaya (Kane, 1998: 319-320). Pandit Bhattasri Narayana Sastri says Appaya’s dates are approximately 1587-1659 CE, considering the well-known fact that Appaya passed away at the age of 72 and that he must have been involved in the famous quarrel with Jagannatha after the latter came to Benares following the imprisonment of Shah Jahan.

In Vrtti-varttika, Appaya expounds three literary functions: Denotation (abhidha) with its three subcategories (rudhi, yoga, yoga-rudhi) and the factors that narrow down possible literal meanings (samyoga etc.); Indication (laksana) along the lines of Mammata’s methodology—including saropa and sadhyavasana— but he follows Visvanatha by subdividing gaunl laksana into nirudha (conventional usage) and phala (it has an implied sense) (KM edition p. 15); and Suggestiveness (vyakti).

Kuvalayananda is a treatise on ornaments of meaning. It includes all of Jayadeva’s ornaments of meaning. Appaya Diksita admits that he copied Jayadeva’s definitional verses in that regard. He added examples to Jayadeva’s definitions and invented ornaments for a total of 124 ornaments. The word kuvalaya signifies a blue lily that opens at night. In the last verse of the treatise he poetically explains the relation between the names Kuvalayananda (the lilies’ delight), Candraloka (the sight or light of the moon), and Sarad- agama (“the arrival of autumn”: the commentary on Candraloka composed by Pradyotana Bhatta in 1583):

*candraloko vijayatam sarad-agama-sambhavah \|*  
*hrdyah kuvalayanando yat-prasadad abhud ayam \|\|*

**“The sight of the moon is glorious and is caused to be that way by the arrival of autumn. By the clearness of both, blue lilies have a lovely delight.”**

**Alternatively: “Glorious is Candraloka, because of which the Sarad-agama came into being. Owing to the clarity of them, this lovely Kuvalayananda occurred.” (Kuvalayananda 172)**

**Atyukti (hyperbole)**

*rajan saptapy akuparas tvat-pratapagni-sositah \|*  
*punas tvad-vairi-vanita-baspa-purena puritah \|\|*

**The seven oceans dried up due to the heat of your fiery intensity, O king, but they became full again by the flow of tears of your enemies’ wives. (Kuvalayananda 163)**

**Parikarankura (significant epithet)**

*phanindras te gunan vaktum likhitum haiyayadhipah \|*  
*drastum akhandalah saktah kvaham esa kva te gunah \|\|*

**Sesa is able to describe your qualities, KartavTryarjuna is able to write about your qualities, and Indra is able to see your qualities, but where on one hand am I, an insignificant being, and where on the other are your qualities? (Kuvalayananda 63)**

Parikarankura is actually implied here because the sense is that Sesa has a thousand mouths, KartavTryarjuna has a thousand arms, and Indra has a thousand eyes: phanindra ’ ity-adi-visesya-padani sahasra-vadanady-abhipraya-garbhani (63 vrtti). The verse ends with the visama ornament (disparity).

**Vyaja-stuti (artful praise)**

*ardham danava-vairina girijayapy ardham sivasyahrtam*  
*devettham jagati-tale smara-harabhave samunmilati \|*  
*ganga sagaram ambaram sasikala nagadhipah ksma-talam*  
*sarvajnatvam adhisvaratvam agamat tvam mam ca bhiksatanam \|\|*

**O king, half of Siva was taken by Vishnu and his other half by ParvatT. Given that the Earth thus lost the presence of Siva, the Ganges went to the ocean, the crescent moon to the sky, the king of snakes to Patala, omniscience and lordship to you, and mendicancy to me. (Kuvalayananda 71)**

Appaya Diksita often propounded novel details in the theory regarding ornaments. On occasion he strayed from the beaten path by not following Mammata’s methodology of ornaments. With all the ornaments and the little details they added, Piyusa- varsa Jayadeva and Appaya Diksita created their own world of ornaments.

In his commentary on Rasa-gangadhara, Nagesa Bhatta often defended Appaya Diksita. In his commentary on Kavya-prakasa, however, at the end of almost every section on an ornament, Nagesa Bhatta refuted ornaments propounded by Jayadeva and Appaya and sometimes those only propounded by the latter. For instance, Nagesa said pihita is included in suksma. At the end of the section of vyajokti, he rejected these ornaments invented by Appaya: gudhokti, because it has a first-rate implied sense; chekokti, because it does not embellish anything; yukti since it is the same as Mammata’s asambandhe sambandha variety of atisayokti (a connection when there is no connection); and mithyadhyavasiti for the same reason (Uddyota on Kavya-prakasa verse 521).

Jagannatha disregarded some of them too. For instance, he rejected Appaya’s prastutankura ornament (the prastuta (subject of description) implies another prastuta) (Kuvalayananda 67): etena “dvayohprastutatveprastutankura-namanyo lankarah” iti kuvalayanandady-uktam upeksamyam (Rasa-gangadhara, KM p. 407).

On occasion, Nagesa Bhatta went too far. For instance, he rejected Jayadeva’s and Appaya’s sambhavanam, accepted by Jagannatha. Nagesa says it is the same as Mammata’s variety of atisayokti where the word “if” is used. But in truth it is distinct because in sambhavana no similarity is intended to be expressed.

Nagesa wrongly says this example of sambhavana by Appaya is an atisayokti: “If Sesa were the speaker, your qualities could be worded” (Kuvalayananda 126).

In Citra-mimamsa, Appaya Diksita stayed closer to the tradition. Dr. Kane says Appaya wrote it after writing Kuvalayananda. As the name suggests, it is a dissertation on Mammafa’s third category of poetry. Appaya defines it: yad avyangyam api caru tac citram, “Poetry which is beautiful though it has no implied sense is citra (amazing)” (Citra-mimamsa, KM p. 5). Appaya subdivides citra in three categories: sabda-citra (amazing because of an ornament of sound), artha-citra (amazing because of an ornament of meaning), and ubhaya-citra (amazing because of both). He says that for the most part sabda-citra is not very relishable and so the poets do not focus much on it. Therefore, he adds, his Citra-mimamsa is actually an Artha-citra-mimamsa. In this book, he begins with two examples of first-rate poetry, two examples of second-rate poetry, and only gives additional details about these twelve ornaments of meaning: upama, upameyopama, ananvaya, smarana, rupaka, parinama, sandeha, bhrantiman, ullekha, apahnuti, utpreksa, and atisayokti.

**Apahnuti**

*ankam ke’pi sasankire jalanidheh pankam pare menire*  
*sarangam katicic ca sanjagadire bhu-cchayam aicchan pare \|*  
*indau yad dalitendranila-sakala-syamam dari drsyate*  
*tat sandram nisi pitam andha-tamasam kuksi-stham acaksmahe \|\|*

**Some suspect it is a mark. Others think it is the mud of a dry ocean. Some say it is a deer, and others want it to be the Earth’s shadow. The darkish spot on the moon resembles a split section of a sapphire. A hollow is seen there, but we say the dense darkness of the night was drunk by the moon and is now located in its belly. (Citra-mimamsa, KM p. 83) (Kuvalayananda 26)**

On this topic, the master poet Snharsa wrote:

*hata-saram ivendu-mandalam*  
*damayanti-vadanaya vedhasa \|*  
*krta-madhya-bilam vilokyate*  
*dhrta-gambhira-khanl-kha-mlima \|\|*

**“To make Damayanti’s face, the Creator took the best part of the moon. For this reason, a hole is seen in the middle of the lunar orb, as though its essence is gone. The bluish darkness of \[the lake of\] the sky has now filled the vast hollow.” (Naisadha-carita 2.25)**

**Ullekha**

*akrsam kucayoh krsam vilagne*  
*vipulam caksusi vistrtam nitambe \|*  
*adhare ’runam avirastu citte*  
*karuna-sali kapali-bhagadheyam \|\|*

**May Siva’s good fortune, abounding in compassion, appear in my mind. That good fortune is plump on the breasts, thin at the waist, wide in the eyes, large on the hips, and red on the lips. (Citra-mimamsa, KM p. 81) (Kuvalayananda 23)**

In this verse, a parinama alankara dhvani also occurs because Parvati is compared to good fortune—here the parinama-dhvani begins as an introsusception (atisayokti)—and because the good luck is said to have Parvati’s qualities. Therefore the standard of comparison (upamana), good luck, needs to assume the identity of the subject of the comparison (upameya), Parvati, to make sense of the literal meanings. The parinama (modification) is implied because Parvati, the upameya, is implied.

## 40. Pandita-raja Jagannatha

Pandita-raja Jagannatha wrote Rasa-gangadhara. In the pantheon of Sanskrit poetics, he is a grandmaster revered as a patriarch. He flourished between 1620 and 1665 CE. He was a Vaishnava, but for the most part of his life he lived in Delhi and in Agra under the patronage of the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan. Jagannatha’s poetry is as amazing as the Taj Mahal. In the Kavya- mala edition of Rasa-gangadhara, the editor Pandit Durga-prasada indicates that Shah Jahan gave Jagannatha the title “Pandita- raja”. But Shah Jahan was not Jagannatha’s first patron:

He also seems to have lived under the protection of Nawab Asaf Khan (d. 1641), brother of Nur Jahan and a nobleman in the court of Shah Jahan, in whose praise he wrote his Asapha- vilasa and who is also referred to in verses quoted in his Rasa-gangadhara (p. 166 sudhiva van! ; 457 yuktam tu yate, referring to Asaf’s death). In the latter work, there is also a reference in a verse (p. 521) to Nuradina which is apparently the Sanskritised form of one of the names of Jahangir (1605­1627), Shah Jahan’s father. Shah Jahan came to the throne in 1628 A.D., and was thrown into prison in 1658 A.D. In his Jagad-abharana Jagannatha eulogises king Jagat-simha of Udaipur (1628-1654) and in his Pranabharana king Prana- narayana of Kamarupa (1633-1666); but they are essentally identical works which have been utilised, with certain change of names and addition of verses, to eulogise two patrons. It seems, therefore, Jagannatha enjoyed the patronage of four rulers, Jahangir, Shah Jahan, Jagat-simha and Prana-narayana at different periods of life.

After Aurangzeb usurped the throne in 1658, Jagannatha went to Mathura. Subsequently, he went to Varanasi.

Like in Kavya-prakasa, a revolution occurred in Rasa-gangadhara: Pandita-raja Jagannatha took poetics to the next level by polishing every angle of poetical theory. The Rasa-gangadhara is popular among scholars because Jagannatha was very learned; because his mind was sharp—he wrote elaborately perfect definitions (without the fault of ativyapti, overinclusion, which he pointed out in Mammata’s definitions of simile, metaphor, etc.), facilitated by his use of the sutra style (the definitions are only in prose, not in verse), and quoted and refuted any dubious opinion of a poetical theorist or of a commentator by way of expressing his own, sound opinions—and because he composed all his examples, which show skill and originality. In addition, he is the only poetical theorist to always illustrate alankara-dhvani (implied ornament), in the chapter on ornaments, whenever applicable.

Jagannatha was born around 1590 CE in Tailanga (Telangana), a region formerly in Andhra Pradesh: Since 2014, Telangana, where Vidyanatha lived, is a state separate from Andhra Pradesh. According to Durga-prasada, Jagannatha’s father, Perubhatta, studied from various scholars in Varanasi; Jagannatha mostly learned from him. Jagannatha mentioned his father: sarva- vidya-dharo yah. pasanad api piyusam syandate yasya lilaya, tam vande peru-bhattakhyam laksmi-kantam maha-gurum, “I extol the erudite supermaster called Perubhatta, the husband of Laksmi. His poetry even makes stones melt into ambrosia” (Rasa-gangadhara, opening verses 2-3).

At the outset of his Manorama-kuca-mardana, Jagannatha indicates that he also studied from Sesa Viresvara Pandita, who had taught his father. This diagram by Durga-prasada shows the connection between the greats in Varanasi in those days (KM edition, Introduction, p. 6):

![рис-011.jpg|500](<Versified History of Sanskrit Poetics/рис-011.jpg>)

Nagesa Bhatta wrote Marma-prakasa, a commentary on Rasa- gangadhara. In his invocatory verse, he bows to Gangadhara, his teacher. Jagannatha mentions Gangadhara in another one of his books. Har Dutt Sharma says the Gangadhara mentioned by Jagannatha is the same as the Gangadhara who was Nagesa’s teacher.

The Caukhamba publication ofRasa-gangadhara, in three volumes, contains a thorough and outstanding Sanskrit commentary, which fills the numerous crater-like holes and other gaps in Nagesa Bhatta’s annotations. Dr. Shankarji Jha remarks:

Fourthly, Pandita Badannatha Jha’s Sanskrit commentary namely Candrika has won a good name for itself and the author both. Fifthly, Pandita Madana Mohana Jha has produced an elaborate Hindi commentary which is quite successful. His Hindi commentary has been published together with the Sanskrit commentary of the late Pt. Badannath Jha. Nowadays, the edition of the Rasa-gangadhara along with the commentaries of the Jha-brothers is well-acclaimed throughout India. Undoubtedly, it can be opined that among all the exisiting commentaries on the Rasa-Gangadhara, the same of the Jha-brothers is the best-reading and best-selling. Untill quite recently, one of the “Jha-brothers”, Pt. Madana Mohana Jha was gracing the world, living in his native village Nawani, in the district Madhubani of Bihar and the author had a proud privilege to meet him personally and seek his blessings,

According to Caukhamba publishers and in conformity with the colophons at the end of the commentaries, Badannatha Jha wrote the Sanskrit commentary in the first anana of Rasa-gangadhara whereas Madana Mohana Jha wrote both the Sanskrit commentary for the rest of the treatise and the Hindi translation. Under the name Badannatha Sarma, Badannatha Jha also wrote a commentary on Bhanudatta’s Rasa-manjari.

Furthermore, Jagannatha’s illustrative examples center either on his wife, on the Ganges, on the king, on Siva (rarely), or on Krishna, therefore his poetry has a distinct charm. Another particularity is that, other than verses about Krishna, his poetry never relates to love outside of wedlock. His descriptions of the gopls ’ love for Krishna are far from being graphic. On that topic, Jagannatha criticized the well-known Jayadeva for going to extremes: jayadevadibhis tu gita-govindadi-prabandhesu sakala-sahrdaya- sammato ’yam samayo madonmatta-matangajair iva bhinna iti na tan-nidarsanenedammtanena tatha varnayitum sampratam, “The etiquette agreed upon by all connoisseurs was broken in compositions such as Glta-govinda by authors such as Jayadeva, who are like elephants maddened by rut. It is improper for modern poets to compose that way by following their example” (Rasa- gangadhara, KM p. 52). The etiquette is the unspoken agreement that poets should neither describe the intimate rapport between Radha and Krishna nor those between Parvati and Siva, who are everyone’s parents so to speak.

In Shah Jahan’s court, Jagannatha married a Muslim woman, named Lavanga-lata or Lavangi for short. This resulted in a heated rivalry between him on one side and Appaya Diksita and Bhattoji Diksita on the other. Because of that marriage, Bhattoji Diksita, a friend of Appaya, uttered the supreme insult to Jagannatha: he called Jagannatha a mleccha (someone outside the Vedic fold). Jagannatha retaliated in his books. In Rasa-gangadhara in particular, Jagannatha fired on all cylinders, and thus produced a gem of Sanskrit culture. Therein he often heavily rebuked

Appaya Diksita regarding the latter’s viewpoints on several topics in poetics. By “fate”, modern editions of Rasa-gangadhara are incomplete: The last verse is not whole. Jagannatha shows the verse as an example of a subvariety of his uttara ornament where a question and its answer are in the same clause, as a pun:

*kim kurvate daridrah*  
*ka saravati dhara manojnatara \|*  
*ko ’pavanas tri-lokyam*  
*(...) II*

**What do poor people do (kim kurvate)? (They do bad things: kim-kurvate.) Which land has the essence (ka saravati) and is very charming? (A land that has a pond: kasara-vati.) In the three worlds, which person is impure (ko ’pavana)? (Someone who stays angry: kopavana = kopa-avana). (RG, KM p. 522)**

Jagannatha completed his magnum opus and some pages were lost. The proof is that in his commentary on the arthapatti ornament, Nagesa Bhatta writes: “This example is actually either the sambhavana ornament, which is going to be mentioned, or the atisayokti used with the meaning ofyadi (if),” yet the sambhavana is not seen in any edition of Rasa-gangadhara. Moreover, on the last page of the book, Nagesa Bhatta’s commentary ends abruptly as well: There is no colophon, although after each section on an ornament, a specific mention marks the end of the commentary. Similarly, in his section on the anumana ornament, Jagannatha himself refers to the unmilita ornament, which he says “is going to be described,” yet it is not found in modern editions of his treatise.

The title Rasa-gangadhara has several meanings, such as “The lips are like the flowing Ganges.” Jagannatha intended to hint at a connection between his treatise and his wife:

*kavyatmana manasi paryanaman pura me*  
*piyusa-sara-sarasas tava ye vilasah \|*  
*tan antarena ramani ramaniya-sile*  
*ceto-hara sukavita bhavita katham nah \|\|*

**O you of a pleasing character, how will my good poetry be charming and attractive to the mind in the absence of those moves of yours, which, sweet like the essence of nectar, at once transformed themselves into verses in my mind? (Bhamini- vilasa 3.10**

Badannatha Jha says the title Rasa-ganga-dhara means either “It has a Ganges of relishment” or “It is like Siva in terms of explaining the rasas”. Other scholars say the derivation is: rasa-rupam gangam dharati iti rasa-gangadharah, “Siva sustains the liquid Ganges; or the book is so called because it contains a Ganges River of relishment.” The word ganga-dhara is a name of Siva: By sustaining on his head the descent of the Ganges, he was instrumental in Bhagiratha’s successfully bringing the Ganges from heaven to Earth. Still, Jagannatha’s illustrations rarely center on Siva. Jagannatha uses the term anana (face) to denote a chapter, therefore some scholars, such as Sesaraja Sarma and Dr. Sushil Kumar De, speculate that Jagannatha wrote a very large treatise:

In conformity to a pun in the word gangadhara in the title, the work was apparently planned to consist of five heads (anana) or chapters, of which we have got only one complete and another incomplete chapter.

Compared to complete treatises on poetics, the missing aspects in Rasa-gangadhara are guni-bhuta-vyangya (second-rate poetry) and sabda alankara (ornaments of sound, including citra-kavya). To think that the treatment of those topics was lost is not reasonable because in all the major treatises on poetics they are treated before a disquisition on ornaments of meaning. Another proof is that although Jagannatha discourses on dosa (literary blemish), he only discusses rasa-dosas (KM p. 50) and upama-dosas (KM p. 191). In addition, Jagannatha does not accept that yamaka, citra-kavya, a verse of one consonant, and so on are poetry because, he says, they are only an embellishment of sound. Therefore the original version of Rasa-gangadhara was only slightly longer than the modern one.

Jagannatha expounded seventy ornaments of meaning (artha alankara) in this order: upama, upameyopama, ananvaya, asama, udaharana, smarana, rupaka, parinama, sa-sandeha, bhrantiman, ullekha, apahnuti, utpreksa, atisayokti, tulya-yogita, dipaka, prativastupama, drstanta, nidarsana, vyatireka, sahokti, vinokti, samasokti, parikara, slesa, aprastuta-prasamsa, paryayokta, vyaja-stuti, aksepa, virodha, vibhavana, visesokti, asangati, visama, sama, vicitra, adhika, anyonya, visesa, vyaghata, karana- mala, ekavali, sara, kavya-linga, arthantara-nyasa, anumana, yatha-sankhya, paryaya, parivrtti, parisankhya, arthapatti, vikalpa, samuccaya, samadhi, pratyamka, pratipa, praudhokti, lalita, praharsana, visadana, ullasa, avajna, anujna, tiraskara, lesa, tad-guna, atad-guna, milita, samanya, and uttara.

For the most part, Jagannatha followed Ruyyaka’s sequence of ornaments. Ruyyaka grouped similar ornaments together and explained their common element. Jagannatha did so as well, yet briefly. By looking at Ruyyaka’s sequence, the ornaments left to be expounded after uttara are: suksma, vyajokti, vakrokti, svabhavokti, bhavika, udatta, rasavat, preyas, urjasvin, samahita, bhavodaya, bhava-sandhi, bhava-sabalata, samsrsti, and sankara.

Jagannatha states that he wants his treatise to eclipse all others:

*nimagnena klesair manana-jaladher antar udaram*  
*mayonnito loke lalita-rasa-gangadhara-manih \|*  
*harann antardhvantam hrdayam adhirudho gunavatam*  
*alankaran sarvan api galita-garvan racayatu \|\|*

**By deeply plunging within the ocean of contemplation, with hardship I have brought the charming jewel called Rasa- gangadhara to the world. It has reached the hearts of virtuous and knowledgeable persons while dispelling internal darkness. May this jewel render all previous Alankaras prideless. (mangalacarana 4)**

As it stands, Rasa-gangadhara supersedes Sahitya-darpana in point of originality, with the exception of the topic of dramaturgy. Jagannatha himself says he is the author of all his examples: nirmaya nutanam udaharananurupam kavyam mayatra nihitam na parasya kincit \| kim sevyate sumanasam manasapi gandhah kasturika-janana-sakti-bhrta mrgena \|\| (RG, mangalacarana 6). However, he took inspiration from other poets:

A verse in the Rasagangadhara, “Her eyes are not just white and black but made of nectar and poison.Why else, when they fall on a man, would he feel at once so strong and weak?” is almost certainly adapted from an earlier poem in Brajbhasha, and a verse of the great poet of the preceding generation, Bihar! lal, corresponds to one found in the Bhamim-vilasa. These examples are likely to be the tip of an iceberg.

Bhamim-vilasa is a collection of verses on various topics. Many examples in Rasa-gangadhara are also in Bhamim-vilasa. Har Dutt Sharma says that according to Nagesa Bhatta, Jagannatha wrote Bhamim-vilasa before Rasa-gangadhara and so it served as a storehouse from which Jagannatha drew his examples.

In his Sanskrit commentary on Bhamim-vilasa, Har Dutt Sharma mentioned which verses in Bhamim-vilasa are also in Rasa- gangadhara. By comparing texts, Har Dutt Sharma has shown that the respective ideas in four verses of Bhamim-vilasa were copied from Sambhu Mahakavi’s Anyokti-mukta-lata (c. 1090 CE) and that the ideas in three other verses were taken from Rudra Nyaya Vacaspati’s Bhava-vilasa (c. 1600 CE). However, only two of those seven verses from Bhamim-vilasa are in Rasa- gangadhara. In addition, as a proper example Jagannatha copied an entire verse from Ruyyaka without naming him (cudamani- pade etc., RG, KM p. 345). Moreover, as is often the case in Kavi Karnapura’s Alankara-kaustubha, sometimes the theme of a verse which illustrates an ornament is based on a corresponding verse by Mammata. However, none of those instances is a stain on Jagannatha’s reputation, because what Jagannatha meant to express is that, unlike Anandavardhana, Mammata, Visvanatha and Appaya, he did not cite scores of verses composed by other authors.

On the whole, Pandita-raja Jagannatha gave detailed explanations. Throughout his treatise and particularly in his definition of poetry,

Jagannatha showed his erudition in Logic. Dr. Shankarji Jha writes:

The special character of the Rasa-Gangadhara is that the author has been greatly influenced by the Nyaya School of Indian Philosophy especially in style and structure. Such a fusion of Philosophy and Literature is rare in the realm of Sanskrit-learning. It is really striking that being a great scholar of Grammar and Philosophy etc., he had not only the poetic bent of mind, but also a poetic genius of high order.

In that matter, Pandita-raja Jagannatha criticized Appaya Diksita for using the term kaimutika (“how much more so”) to explain the scheme of the arthapatti ornament (presumption). Jagannatha says that in kaimutika-nyaya the other meaning is lesser to some degree: What is to be accounted for (the upapadya) is within the scope of the explanatory reason (the upapadaka). Jagannatha says that in arthapatti, what is to be accounted for can be on a par with the explanatory reason, and sometimes it can exceed the scope of the explanatory reason. This is Jagannatha’s example of arthapatti where the statement to be substantiated is within the scope of the explanatory reason:

*udumbara-phalanlva brahmandany atti yah sada \|*  
*sarva-garvapahah kalas tasya ke masaka vayam \|\|*

**Who are we mosquitos compared to Time? It eradicates all arrogant pride and constantly consumes entire universes as if they were figs. (RG, KM p. 486)**

Jagannatha gives an example of arthapatti where the statement to be substantiated is on a par with the explanatory reason:

*lila-lunthita-sarada-pura-dhiyam asmadrsanam pura*  
*vidya-sadma-vinirgalat-kana-muso valganti ced balisah \|*  
*adya svah phaninam sakunta-sisavo dantavalanam sasah*  
*simhanam ca sukhena murdhani padam dhasyanti sala-vrkah \|\|*

**If fools are jumping, having stolen tidbits issued from SarasvatT’s storehouse, right in front of people like us, who playfully looted the knowledge in SarasvatT’s kingdom, then today or tomorrow young birds will easily step on the heads of snakes, rabbits will comfortably step on the heads of elephants, and puppies will happily step on the heads of lions. (KM p. 485)**

The above verse also illustrates a mala arthapatti (a series of presumptions). To construct arthapatti, Jagannatha often uses an “if” clause and a “then” clause. The “if” clause is the explanatory reason. This is another example of that subvariety:

*tavagre yadi daridryam sthitam bhupa dvijanmanam \|*  
*sanaih savitur apy agre tamah sthayasty asamsayam \|\|*

**O king, if in front of you Brahmanas remain poor, then in front of the sun darkness will gradually take place for sure.**

Nagesa Bhatta says Jagannatha’s usage of an “if”’ clause constitutes either the sambhavana ornament (assumption) or the yadi variety of atisayokti. Jayadeva invented the sambhavana ornament. Appaya Diksita says sambhavana is the same as Mammata’s yadi variety of atisayokti. However, an “if” clause does not constitute the sambhavana ornament if that clause does not involve high­flying imagination. This is Jayadeva’s example of sambhavana: “If pearls sprinkled with water that was made pure by being placed in a container with quartz produces a creeper, then its flowers could be compared to your fame.” Moreover, based on Mammata’s, Visvanatha’s and Kavi Kamapura’s examples of the yadi variety of atisayokti, an “if clause” is not an atisayokti if no similarity is intended to be expressed.

This is Jagannatha’s example of arthapatti where the statement to be substantiated exceeds the scope of the explanatory reason:

*yadi te caranambujam hrda*  
*vahato me na hato vipad-ganah \|*  
*atha canda-karena mandite*  
*dina-madhye ’pi jitam tamo-ganaih \|\|*

**O Lord, if the troubles of this individual who is holding Your lotus feet in his heart do not go away, then even in the middle of the day adorned by the sun Your lotus feet have been defeated by a mass of darkness. (KM p. 485)**

## Definition of Poetry

Jagannatha’s definition is: ramanlyartha-pratipadakah sabdah kavyam, “Sound that conveys a lovely idea is poetry.” This is a throwback to the Sausabdya theory, although citra-kavya verses of one type of consonant, etc., which are a main aspect of this theory, are implicitly excluded by Jagannatha. He expounds: ramanlyata ca lokottarahlada-janaka-jnana-gocarata, “In this regard, loveliness is the fact of being in the scope of an awareness that generates an extraordinary delight” (RG, KM p. 4). Owing to implications of the usage of the word jnana in Nyaya—sarva-vyavahara-hetur guno buddhir jnanam, sa dvi-vidha smrtir anubhavas ca (Tarka-sangraha 3.68), hence Bhatta Nayaka pointed out that the experience of rasa is neither a remembrance (smrti) nor an experience of day-to-day life (anubhava)—Jagannatha then changes jnana (awareness, knowledge) to bhavana (contemplation): karanam ca tad- avacchinne bhavana-visesah punah-punar-anusandhanatma, “The cause of such an extraordinary delight is a distinct contemplation whose nature consists of continuously taking interest in the meaning” (RG, KM p. 4). Jagannatha continues by thus making subtle references to Nyaya philosophy.

Thereafter, Jagannatha follows the tradition of demolishing the tradition: He rejects Mammata’s definition of poetry—tad adosau sabdarthau sa-gunav analankrtl punah kvapi, “Poetry is faultless sounds and meanings which have a literary quality and an ornament, although sometimes there is no ornament (in which case there must be a rasa)” (Kavya-prakasa 1.4)—on the grounds that the word artha (meaning) has no place in such a definition due to a lack of proof, because in life people say such things as “Poetry is recited aloud”, “The sense is understood from the poetry”, and “The poetry was heard but the meaning was not grasped.” Jagannatha thus begs the question, because in such expressions the word poetry is used in a figurative sense. But Jagannatha refuses to ackowledge it; he says there is no solid proof that the word poetry can refer to sabda and artha together. Jagannatha contradicts himself because in his second example of third-rate poetry, shown ahead, he says the verse is third-rate poetry because the sounds (sabda) and the expressed meanings (vacya = vacya artha) equally generate astonishment: atra vrtty-anuprasa- pracuryad ojo-guna-prakaSakatvac ca sabdasya, prasada-guna- yogad anantaram evadhigatasya rupakasya hetv-alankarasya va vacyasya camatkrtyos tulya-skandhatvat samam eva pradhanyam (RG, KM pp. 20-21).

In Mammata’s term sabdarthau, the word sabda refers to either an ornament of sound, phonemes of madhurya-guna or phonemes of ojas guna, and the term artha refers to either an ornament of meaning or any type of meaning, but Jagannatha only refers to Nyaya philosophy: vakyartha-jnanam sabda-jnanam. tat-karanam sabdah, “The knowledge of the meaning of the sentence is called sabda-jnana. The means to arrive at that knowledge is the words (sound)” (Tarka-sangraha 7.5). To demolish Mammata’s definition, Jagannatha takes the term sabda therein in the sense of “word” rather than “sound” and argues with logic that the expression “word and sense” is incongruent. He says the term poetry used in reference to both sabda and artha could only be valid by the principle of either vyasajya-vrtti (poetry exists in word and meaning, as an undivisible whole) or pratyeka-paryapta (poetry exists in word, and poetry exists in meaning). Jagannatha says the first option is inapplicable because all that could be said is something like “The sentence of the verse is not poetry.” He says the second option is inapplicable too because in the same verse there would be poetry with regard to words and poetry with regard to meanings. Nagesa Bhatta, however, supports Mammata: tenanupahasariiya-kavya-laksanam prakasoktam nirbadham (Marma-prakasa). Besides, Jagannatha uses the term sabdarthau in his definition of uttamottama-kavya, cited ahead (p. 616).

Afterward, Jagannatha intends to finish off the rest of Mammata’s definition: Jagannatha says there is no universal rule that poetry must contain either a guna or an alankara. He says that in sentences such as “The moon has risen” and “The sun has set”, various implied meanings can be construed—based on the context, on the speaker, on the person addressed, on the time, etc.—therefore those two factors are inadequate (avyapti). Jagannatha says there is no reason why such isolated sentences cannot be taken as poetry. Jagannatha adds that in poetics there is no agreement about the distinction between guna and alankara nor about the types of gunas. Here also Jagannatha begs the question: Mammata specified his usage of the terms guna and alankara, and everyone knows that Kavya- prakasa is the bible of poetics.

Jagannatha adds that the term adosau (faultless) in Mammata’s definition is faulty because in day-to-day life one might say “The poetry is faulty” (by Mammata’s definition, what is faulty cannot be called poetry): dustam kavyam iti vyavaharasya badhakam vina laksanikatvayogac ca (RG, KM p. 7). However, in his commentary on Kavya-prakasa, Govinda Thakkura says the negative particle in adosau has the sense of “slight”: nano ’Iparthalvat. alpatvasya catrasphutatva eva visramat (Kavya-pradlpa 1.4). Visvanatha had mentioned it, but then, he says, the meaning would be “Sounds and meanings that are slightly faulty are poetry,” and in that way faultless sounds and meanings are not included in the definition: nanv isad-arthe nanah prayoga iti cet tarhi Isad-dosau sabdarthau kavyam ity ukte nirdosayoh kavyatvam na syat (Sahitya-darpana 1.2). Therefore adosau signifies isad-dosav api, “even if the sounds or the meanings are slightly faulty,” such as the occurrence of few minor sounds of ojas guna in the context of madhurya or the occurrence of a minor fault such as apusta (irrelevant). But that wording does not fit well in the meter. All this nit-picking at Mammata’s definition is pointless, by the maxim: pradhanyena vyapadesa bhavanti, “Designations are made according to the majority of cases” (Kavya-prakasa verse 123 vrtti) (RG, KM p. 396). Sounds and meanings devoid of a big fault, and so on, are poetry.

In the definition, Visvanatha says Mammata is wrong in using the adjective sa-gunau, because a guna suggests a rasa, therefore it should be said sa-rasau. Mammata says sometimes a guna takes place although there is no rasa. Even though Visvanatha accepts and illustrates this, he says it is unacceptable because there is no rasa. Thus Visvanatha shows verses which illustrate his theory but do not fit in his definition of poetry.

Subsequently, Jagannatha attacks Visvanatha’s definition: yat tu rasa-vad eva kavyam iti sahitya-darpane nirnitam, tan na, vastv- alankara-pradhananam kavyanam akavyatvapatteh, “The dictum in Sahitya-darpana ‘A statement that has a rasa is poetry’ is wrong because by that axiom, poetry which essentially consists of an idea or of an ornament could not be classed as poetry” (RG, KM p. 7).

## Four Categories of Poetry

Like Kavi Kamapura, Jagannatha propounded four kinds of poetry: tac cottamottamottama-madhyamadhama-bhedac caturdha (RG, KM p. 9). However, they are respectively different. Jagannatha gave new life to old-school poetry. What he calls uttamottama- kavya (superexcellent poetry) is called uttama-kavya (first-rate poetry) by everyone else. His definition is: sabdarthau yatra guni- bhavitatmanau kam apy artham abhivyanktas tad adyam (RG, KM p. 9). For example:

*sayita savidhe ’py anisvara*  
*saphali-kartum aho manorathan \|*  
*dayita dayitananambujam*  
*dara-milan-nayana niriksate \|\|*

**Although her bridegroom is next to her on the bed, she simply stares at his beautiful face and is unable to break the ice.**

The verse features a first-rate rati of srngara: atralambanasya nayakasya, savidha-sayanaksiptasya rahah-sthanader uddipanasya ca vibhavasya, tadrsa-niriksanader anubhavasya, trapautsukyades ca vyabhicarinah samyogad ratir abhivyajyate (RG, KM p. 10). Jagannatha also hints at this by using the viyogini meter (also called sundar). Jagannatha thus implicitly created a new category of vipralambha: the feeling of separation in the presence of the lover (viz. example of pravasa in Appendix II, p. 706) (of which prema-vaicittya would be a subcategory), even though Jagannatha did not subdivide vipralambha because he did not see any distinct particularity among Mammata’s categories: imam panca-vidham prancah pravasadibhir upadibhir amananti. te ca pravasabhilasa-virahersya-sapanam visesanupalambhan nasmabhih prapancitah (RG, KM p. 35).

Jagannatha’s second-rate poetry is an implied sense that is technically third-rate (second-rate in Mammata’s system) but is upgraded because it is very astonishing: yatra vyangyam apradhanam eva sac camatkara-karanam tad dvitiyam (RG, KM p. 17). Jagannatha’s definition is wanting (ref. apradhanam) because it excludes the category of Mammata’s second-rate poetry called tulya-pradhanyam, where the implied sense and the literal meaning are equally astonishing. He illustrates his second-rate poetry:

*raghava-viraha-jvala-santapita-sahya-saila-sikharesu \| sisire sukham sayanah kapayah kupyanti pavana-tanayaya \|\|*

**In the winter, the monkeys comfortably taking rest at the top of the Sahya Mountain which is scorched by the fire of separation felt by Rama became angry at the son of the wind god.**

Here the implied sense is that Rama’s fire of separation ceased after Hanuman told Him good news about Sita and therefore the mountain cooled down. Although this implied meaning is technically second-rate since it makes sense of the literal meaning “The monkeys became angry at Hanuman,” the verse is upgraded because the implied sense is subtle: atra janaki-kusalavedanena raghavah sisiri-krta iti vyangyam akasmika-kapi-kartrka- hanumad-visayaka-kopopapadakataya gunibhutam api durdaiva- vasato dasyam anubhavad raja-kalatram iva kam api kamaniyatam avahati (RG, KM p. 17).

*Jagannatha’s third-rate poetry is the same as Mammata’s second- rate poetry: yatra vyangya-camatkarasamanadhikarano vacya- camatkaras tat trtiyam. \[...\] anayor eva dvitiya-trtiya-bhedayor jagarUkajagaruka-gunibhuta-vyangyayoh pravistam nikhilam alankara-pradhanam kavyam (RG, KM p. 19). This is Jagannatha’s example of third-rate poetry where the implied sense is not more astonishing than the expressed sense:*  
*yatha yamuna-varnane— tanaya-mainaka-gavesana-lambi-krta-jaladhi-jathara-pravista- himagiri-bhujayamanaya bhagavatya bhagirathyah sakhi.*

**The Yamuna was the friend of the godly Ganga, which looked like Himalaya’s arm that had stretched to the depth of the ocean in order to fetch his son Mainaka. (Jagannatha’s Yamuna- varnana)**

According to Vedic lore, only Mainaka, the son of Himavat and Menaka, retained his wings when Indra clipped those of other mountains. Here the implied sense is that the Ganges is whitish. But it is less astonishing than the literal sense, the utpreksa ornament (fanciful assumption): atrotpreksa vacyaiva camatkrti-hetuh. svaitya-patala-tala-cumbitvadinam camatkaro lesataya sann apy utpreksa-camatkrti-jathara-nilinah (RG, KM p. 19).

Jagannatha criticized Mammata for subdividing third-rate poetry into artha-citra (amazing because of the meanings) and sabda-citra (amazing because of the sounds). According to Jagannatha, artha- citra generates more astonishment than sabda-citra, therefore the two categories cannot be on a par. Jagannatha redefined Mammata’s third-rate poetry in two ways: (A) sama-pradhanye tu madhyamataiva, “When the sounds and the meanings equally generate astonishment, the poetry is classed as average” (second- rate poetry in Mammata’s system and third-rate in Jagannatha’s system) (Jagannatha copies Kavi Karnapura) (RG, KM p. 20), and (B) yatrartha-camatkrty-upaskrta sabda-camatkrtih pradhanam tad adhamam caturtham, “Fourth-rate poetry, the lowest, is that in which the amazingness of the sounds is predominant and is assisted by the amazingness of the meanings” (RG, KM p. 19).

This is Jagannatha’s example of third-rate poetry where the sounds and the meanings equally generate astonishment:

*ullasah phulla-pankeruha-patala-patan-matta-puspamdhayanam*  
*nistarah soka-davanala-vikala-hrdam koka-smantimnam*  
*utpatas tamasanam upahata-mahasam caksusam paksa-patah*  
*sanghatah ko’pi dhamnam ayam udaya-giri-prantatah pradurasit*

**Some particular mass of splendor made its appearance at the top of the Eastern Mountain. The mass is the joy of greedy bees which hover over newly-opened night lotuses; it is the deliverance of the female cakravaka birds whose hearts are disturbed by the fire of separation; it is the removal of darkness; and it is a partisan of the eyes whose festival had ceased.**

Here the sounds and the meanings are equally astonishing. The sounds produce wonder because of alliteration and because of ojas guna (the quality of vigorous sounds). Plus, the meanings which are the metaphors, optionally interpreted as the hetu ornament (a cause is expressed in terms of being identical with its effect), are amazing, especially because the verse is not too difficult to understand (this is prasada-guna, an artha-guna according to Vamana and Jagannatha): atra vrtty-anuprasa- pracuryad ojo-guna-prakasakatvac ca sabdasya, prasada-guna- yogad anantaram evadhigatasya rupakasya hetv-alankarasya va vacyasya camatkrtyos tulya-skandhatvatsamam eva pradhanyam (RG, KM pp. 20-21).

This verse illustrates fourth-rate poetry where the amazingness of the sounds is predominant and is assisted by the amazingness of the meanings:

*mitratriputra-netraya trayi-satrava-satrave \|*  
*gotrari-gotraja-traya go-tratre te namo namah \|\|*

**Let us offer repeated obeisances to the Lord: The sun and the moon are His eyes, He is the foe of the enemies of the Vedas, He protects the gods, and He herds cows. (RG, KM p. 19)**

## Features of Rasa-gangadhara

Jagannatha’s magnum opus is a masterpiece with regard to these themes of poetics: vyabhicari-bhava, guna, rasa, alankara-dhvani, and artha alankara. Compared to Mammata, Jagannatha shows few examples of categories of first-rate implied sense, but he illustrates all the vyabhicari-bhavas whereas Mammata only gives one example in addition to those of bhava-sandhi and the like. This is Jagannatha’s example of garva vyabhicari-bhava-dhvani (implied overweening pride):

*a mulad ratna-sanor malaya-valayitad a ca kulat payodher*  
*yavantah santi kavya-pranayana-patavas te visankam vadantu \|*  
*mrdvika-madhya-niryan-masrna-rasa-jhari-madhUri-bhagya-bhajam*  
*vacam acaryatayah padam anubhavitum ko ’sti dhanyo mad-anyah \|\|*

**Let expert writers of poetry from the base of Mount Meru in the north to the shore of the ocean along the perimeter of the Malaya Hills in the south doubtlessly say whether anyone beside me is fortunate enough to have the status of a grandmaster of words that abound in the sweetness of a flow of smooth juice of ripe grapes. (KM p. 84)**

Moreover, Jagannatha pointed out that among the vyabhicari- bhavas, sometimes one is a cause of another, or an effect of yet another, and so on.

Jagannatha implicitly accepted Vamana’s twenty gunas: He clearly defined and exemplified them, and said that according to other scholars, they are included in Mammata’s three gunas. For the details about Jagannatha’s discourse on the specific guna in each rasa and about his examples of Vamana’s gunas, consult the present writer’s translation of Sahitya-kaumudi (ch. 8).

Pandita-raja Jagannatha disagreed with Mammata’s opinion that the term guna figuratively applies to sounds and meanings that evoke sweetness and so on. Jagannatha said they literally evoke sweetness and so on, even if there is no rasa of sweetness and so on (whereas Mammata says a guna is actually only a rasa-guna, the quality inherent in the relishment of a rasa, and the nature of the sounds is supposed to reflect that). Jagannatha thus supported Vamana. Mammata propounded the aforesaid notion of figurative usage at first, and gave the alternative explanation, which applies when there is no rasa, later on.

On the whole, Jagannatha emphasized the importance of accepting the system established by Bharata Muni and by Anandavardhana. Jagannatha acknowledged nine rasas because, he said, that is in accordance with Bharata Muni. Jagannatha said santa should be acknowledged as a rasa in dramaturgy as well.

Jagannatha slightly differs from Mammata on the topic of subdivisions of rati (affection). Jagannatha classifies affection for either a guru, a demigod, or a son as a thirty-fourth vyabhicari- bhava. But he adds that actually the count is unaltered since some vyabhicari-bhavas are included in others, so that one way or another the count can be adjusted to the traditional thirty- three. Jagannatha does not accept that vatsalya can become a foundational mood (sthayin), let alone a rasa. However, he follows Mammata by categorizing affection for God as a rati proper, not as a vyabhicari-bhava. For instance, he criticized Mammata’s example of adbhuta-rasa by stating that bhakti is predominant therein, consequently the adbhuta-rasa is second-rate and so the rasavat ornament takes place. Thus in Mammata’s and Jagannatha’s methodologies, bhakti is classed in deva-visaya rati. For instance:

*bhavad-dvari krudhyaj-jaya-vijaya-dandahati-dalat-*  
*kintas te kita iva vidhi-mahendra-prabhrtayah \|*  
*vitisthante yusman-nayana-paripatotkalikaya*  
*varakah ke tatra ksapita-mura nakadhipatayah \|\|*

**O Murari, Brahma, Siva and others wait at the gate of Vaikuntha in the hope of receiving Your glance, but they are driven away like flies by Jaya and Vijaya who become angry and dash their divine headgears with their sticks. Ha! In that place, who are those lowlifes that preside over heaven?**

prakarsakatvenasya guni-bhutatvat. \[...\] ittham casya rasalankaratvam ucitam (RG, KM pp. 42-43).

Jagannatha classifies the above as a first-rate rati-bhava-dhvani. Jagannatha does not dispute that bhakti can reach the level of rasa, but he cannot find a place for it as such in the methodology since the patriarchs only acknowledged nine rasas, therefore he feels compelled to follow Mammata and to class it only as a sthayi-bhava limited in scope. (Here Jagannatha is too modest. His example of the tiraskara ornament incidentally illustrates bhakti-rasa; ref. my translation of it in my commentary on Sahitya-kaumudi, p. 933.) Jagannatha says bhakti-rasa cannot be included in santa-rasa because anuraga is incompatible with vairagya.

Jagannatha ingeniously added four subcategories of vira-rasa to the well-known four (dana, daya, yuddha, dharma): satya-vira (hero of virtue), panditya-vlra (hero of learning), ksama-vira (hero of tolerance), and bala-vira (hero of strength). Jagannatha was an example of panditya-vlra:

*api vakti giram patih svayam*  
*yadi tasam adhidevatapi va \|*  
*ayam asmi puro hayanana-*  
*smaranollanghita-vanmayambudhih \|\|*

**Even if Brhaspati argues, or even if SarasvatT herself speaks, I who have crossed the ocean of words by remembering HayagrTva am here to give a reply afterward. (KM p. 41)**

In life, a man must be a vira one way or another. Vira-rasa is the most important rasa in the life of a man.

Further, Pandita-raja Jagannatha is the only poetical rhetorician to fully illustrate the concept of implied ornament (alankara-dhvani). He does so at the end of a section on an ornament. This is his example of upama-dhvani (implied simile):

*vimalataram atigabhiram*  
*supavitram satattva-vat surasam \|*  
*hamsavasa-sthanam*  
*manasam iha sobhate nitaram \|\|*
