**“In this world, the Manasa Lake (manasa), the residence of swans (hamsa), is continuously resplendent. It is very clear, exceedingly deep, and superbly pure. It has the nature of things (satattva-vat) and has nice water (su-rasa).”**

**The contextual meaning is: “In this world, a heart (manasa) which is the residence of Hamsa is continuously resplendent. It is very clean, exceedingly deep, and superbly pure. It is endowed with the Absolute Truth (satattva-vat) and is aesthetical (su-rasa)” (RG, KM p. 186).**

The implied simile is that such a heart is like the Manasa Lake.

Jagannatha’s methodology of slesa differs from Mammafa’s. Jagannatha subdivided slesa like Ruyyaka did: (1) Each meaning is prastuta (contextual), (2) Both are aprastuta (not contextual) or (3) One meaning is prastuta and the other aprastuta. This is Jagannatha’s example of the third one; the verse illustrates slesopama (simile based on paronomasia):

*alam hi mam paridirna-gatrah*  
*samapitah phalguna-sangamena \|*  
*atyantam akanksita-krsna-vartma*  
*bhismo mahatmajani magha-tulyah \|\|*

**BhTsma, the great soul, became similar to the month of Magha. Indeed, BhTsma was very self-conceited and his body was pierced through and through (and Magha is the month when the bodily limbs are harrowed by heaps of snow: himam-paridirna- gatrah). BhTsma was finished as a result of an encounter with Arjuna (and Magha ends by the contact of the month of Phalguna). BhTsma intensely desired the path of Krishna (and Magha is a month in which fire (krsna-vartma, “whose path is black”) is highly needed). (KM p. 392)**

Jagannatha mentions the three schools of thought regarding slesa. Whenever slesa occurs in conjunction with an ornament,

1\. The slesa is considered to be more important than the ornament, and so the text is only classed as a slesa,

2\. The slesa and the ornament are equally predominant, therefore the ornament is said to be conjoined with slesa, and

3\. The slesa is considered to be less important than the ornament, consequently the text is only called by the name of the ornament. Udbhata was the leader of the first school. Jagannatha adopted the intermediate school. Mammata and Visvanatha acknowledged the validity of the second school, but preferred the third school.

Jagannatha agrees with Ruyyaka in categorizing abhanga-slesa and sabhanga-slesa in the category of ornament of meaning.

In addition, Jagannatha paraphrases Ruyyaka’s disapproval of Mammata’s principle that “Abhanga-slesa and sabhanga-slesa are ornaments of sound because each meaning needs to be ascribed its own word (since by Abhinavagupta’s rule Denotation can only be used once for each word) and because in sabda-slesa it is the sound that causes the most wonder (one sound has two words and two meanings),” since by the logic: pratyartham sabda-nivesah, “One word is used for each meaning,” even artha-slesa would have to be considered an ornament of sound inasmuch as one meaning is used twice.

Jagannatha expounded ornaments absent in Mammata’s treatise: asama, udaharana, vicitra, praudhokti, lalita, praharsana, visadana, ullasa, avajna, anujna, tiraskara, and lesa. Not all the concepts expressed by them deserve a categorization as an ornament. This is Jagannatha’s example of the asama ornament:

*bhuvana-tritaye ’pi manavaih*  
*paripurne vibudhais ca danavaih \|*  
*na bhavisyati nasti nabhavan*  
*nrpa yas te bhajate tula-padam \|\|*

**Though the three worlds are filled with men, gods, and wicked beings, O king, no one will ever be equal to you, no one is equal to you, and no one has ever been equal to you. (KM p. 211).**

The asama ornament is almost the same as an elliptical simile characterized by the ellipsis of the upamana. This is Jagannatha’s example:

*yasya tulam adhirohasi*  
*lokottara-varna-parimalodgaraih \|*  
*kusuma-kula-tilaka campaka*  
*na vayam tam jatu jammah \|\|*

**O campaka, best of flowers, we do not know anything that could be compared to you in terms of emanating an extraordinary color and fragrance. (KM p. 165)**

According to Jagannatha, although this verse does not involve a similarity, it is not the asama ornament because in the future there might be something that will resemble a campaka flower, therefore in that sense the verse culminates in some sort of possible similarity. By contrast, the asama ornament is characterized by the complete negation of any comparison. Jagannatha himself says asama is an implied ananvaya ornament (self-comparison): sarvathaivopama-nisedho 'samakhyo ’lankarah \|\| ayam cananvaye vyangyo ’pi tac-camatkaranugunataya rupaka-dlpakadav upameva na prthag-alankara-vyapadesam bhajate. vacyatayam tu svatantryena camatkaritaya prthag-vyapadesa-bhak (RG, KM p. 210).

Jagannatha propounds the udaharana ornament because according to him the expressed similarity between a generality and a particular is not in the scope of a simile. For instance:

*amita-guno ’pi padartho dosenaikena nindito bhavati \|*  
*nikhila-rasayana-rajo gandhenogrena lasuna iva \|\|*

**Even a thing that has immense qualities is belittled only because of one fault, like garlic, the king all rejuvenators, is depreciated because of the terrible odor. (RG, KM p. 213)**

Another example:

*upakaram eva kurute vipad-gatah sad-guno nitaram \|*  
*murccham gato mrto va nidarsanam parado ’tra rasah \|\|*

**A person with eminent qualities continues to assist others even while undergoing hardship. An illustration is this regard is mercury, whether calcined or weakened.**

Jagannatha says the verse is optionally classed as the drstanta ornament (exemplification): drstanto va (RG, KM p. 214). Nagesa Bhatta altogether rejects Jagannatha’s udaharana ornament. Nagesa cites the above verse and says it is nothing but arthantara- nyasa (corroboration). Jagannatha takes the first sentence as a particular instance whereas Nagesa takes it as a generality.

Jagannatha’s examples of praharsana and tiraskara were shown in the present writer’s translation of Sahitya-kaumudl (ch. 11). Jagannatha’s visadana, copied from Appaya Diksita, is a twist on the visama ornament. His lesa ornament is the combination of Rudrata’s two varieties of lesa: A quality is described as a fault, and some other fault as a quality.

In addition, Jagannatha accepted Ruyyaka’s subcategories of ornaments and created subcategories. For instance, his arthapatti has twenty-four subvarieties—catur-vimsati-bheda (RG, KM p. 485)—he expanded parikara; and he made eight subvarieties of simile by applying therein all eight varieties of metaphor.

Jagannatha was a harsh critic, but he rarely mentioned the source when he took material from another author. Jagannatha implies that the asama ornament is seen in a treatise called Alankara- ratnakara: etena \[...\] ity atrasamalankaro ’yam upamatirikta iti vadanto ’lankararatnakaradayah parastah (RG, KM p. 165). Nagesa Bhatta cites the same and mentions Ratnakara instead: etenasamalankaro ’yam upamatirikta iti ratnakarady-uktam apastam (Uddyota on Kavya-prakasa verse 400). Jagannatha often referred to a certain Ratnakara (KM pp. 202, 207, 209, 211, 221, 225, 281, 313, 480, 492). Dr. Sushil Kumar De remarks:

An anonymous Alankara-ratnakara is mentioned in Burnell 54a (Kashmir Rep. App. ii no. 228, p. cxxviii.); but Buhler describes a work of that name by Sobhakara-mitra, son of Trayisvara-mitra. Peterson informs us that the Kashmirian poet Yasaskara extracted some sutras on Alamkara from a work called Alankara-ratnakara by Sobhakara-mitra, and illustrated them in his Devi-stotra by composing verses in praise of Devi, as the opening words of the latter work themselves show. The work of Yasaskara in Stein is for this reason called Alamkarodaharana-samnibaddha Devi-stotra. The Ratnakara of Jagannatha undoubtedly refers to this Alankara-ratnakara of Sobhakara-mitra; for the citation from Ratnakara at p. 202 is the same as sutra 11 (as given in Peterson i p. 78). Jayaratha criticises (pp. 41, 52) the Kashmirian Sobhakara who deviates from Ruyyaka. Jagannatha says (p. 281) that Appayya Diksita follows Alankara-ratnakara.

## Criticism

On occasion, after stating his definition of an ornament Jagannatha compares it with other theorists’ definitions. For instance, he said Mammata’s definition of upama (simile) is not too pretty because it is overinclusive. Jagannatha criticized Vidyanatha’s definition of upama for the same reason. Jagannatha also disapproved of Mammata’s definition of metaphor, and Appaya Diksita did so too. Mammata wrote in the karika style. On the whole, Jagannatha’s definitions of ornaments are perfect especially because the sutra style favors elaborate definitions. The karika style is cumbersome because in the elaboration the author needs to clarify the definition, and so the purpose of writing concisely in verse form is defeated by the repeated usage of the words in the elaboration. The sole purpose of writing in the karika style is to show off one’s skill in writing tersely in verse form.

Jagannatha says a simile is defined as “a beautiful similarity that adorns the meaning of the sentence; “literary beauty” means astonishment is generated; and astonishment is a special kind of bliss whose existence is proven by the connoisseurs’ experiences in their hearts.” According to Jagannatha, ideally an ornament should be a cause of the loveliness of an implied sense, the soul of poetry. Jagannatha says a simile is an ornament in one of five ways. It adorns either: (1) a vastu-dhvani (implied idea), (2) an alankara-dhvani (implied ornament), (3) a rasa, (4) an expressed vastu, or (5) a expressed alankara. This also applies to other ornaments.

Jagannatha’s definition falls short of establishing a distinction between a simile and a metaphor. He should have stated that in a simile the similarity is expressed (vacya) whereas in a metaphor it is figuratively stated (gauna). In that line of thought, elsewhere he said the difference between a simile and a metaphor is that the latter does not involve a word of comparison: yayor ivadi-sabda- prayoge upama tayor ekatranyarope rupakam iti niyamat (RG, KM p. 239).

Jagannatha adds that his definition of simile is not meant to exclude the pratipa ornament (reverse simile) nor the upameyopama ornament (reciprocal comparison) because a simile occurs in them as well, in the sense that both of them are really subcategories of simile. Nagesa Bhatta says astonishment differentiates a literary simile from an ordinary one: camatkarity anena “gaur iva gavayah” ity-ader vyavrttih. vakyarthopaskarakam iti alankara- samanya-laksana-praptam (Uddyota).

Moreover, Jagannatha was not too happy with Mammata’s usage of the term samasokti in “the samasokti variety of aprastuta- prasamsa” since samasokti and aprastuta-prasamsa are poles apart.

Jagannatha’s other targets include Ratnakara, Srivatsa-lanchana (on the topic of vira-rasa) (KM p. 39), Vamana (on the topic of visesokti), Jayaratha (several times) and Ruyyaka (many times). Jagannatha even rejected one of Anandavardhana’s example of rupaka-dhvani, by saying it is only an instance of an implied bhrantiman ornament. However, perhaps Anandavardhana was not aware of the concept of bhrantiman, invented by Rudrata.

Mammata’s demolition of Udbhata’s categorization of slesa and thrashing of Vamana’s methodology of gunas were kind gestures compared to Jagannatha’s verbal abuses of Appaya Diksita. For example, Jagannatha rebuked Appaya’s opinion that there is no rupaka in a particular verse, and in so doing called him dirgha- sravas (widely famous) (or long-eared, like a donkey).

Oftentimes Jagannatha’s criticism of Appaya Diksita is not justified. Jagannatha himself proved it: On at least three occasions, he criticized Appaya’s illustrative verse (on gunibhuta-kavya, luptopama, vyaja-stuti), and after a long explanation of his disapproval Jagannatha said that on second thought Appaya could be right! Dr. Shankarji Jha comments on Jagannatha’s treatise:

“Even P. J. is not logical on every point while refuting the views of Appaya Diksita.” (Jha (1998) p. 187)

Furthermore, Jagannatha says the bhrantiman ornament only consists of an erroneous perception done by an animal. Kavi Karnapura does not agree with this. Jagannatha illustrates bhrantiman:

*kanaka-drava-kanti-kantaya*  
*militamramam udiksya kantaya \|*  
*capala-yuta-varida-bhraman*  
*nanrte cataka-potakair vane \|\|*

**Seeing Rama with His beloved STta, lovely with a radiance that resembles a flow of molten gold, the young cataka birds danced in the forest because they mistakingly perceived a cloud with lightning.**

Jagannatha gives another example:

*adharam bimbam ajnaya mukham abjam ca tanvi te \|*  
*kiras ca cancarikas ca vindanti paramam mudam \|\|*

**Slender woman, the parrots and the bees achieve the topmost joy by completely assuming that your netherlip is a bimba fruit and your mouth a lotus. (KM p. 270)**

Jagannatha explains that there is no ullekha ornament (angles of description) in the above verse because there is more than one object of erroneous perception (the netherlip and the mouth). Jagannatha defines ullekha: ekasya vastuno nimitta-vasad yad anekair grhitrbhir aneka-prakarakam grahanam tad ullekhah (RG, KM p. 270). He illustrates it:

*narair vara-gati-pradety atha suraih svakiyapage-*  
*ty udaratara-siddhi-dety akhila-siddha-sanghair api \|*  
*hares tanur iti srita munibhir asta-sangair iyam*  
*tanotu mama sam tanoh sapadi santanor angana \|\|*

**May Santanu’s wife quickly expand the aupiciousness of my body. People take shelter of her by thinking she bestows liberation, the gods by knowing she is their own river, all the perfected beings by believing she is the bestower of more honorable perfections, and wise renunciants by realizing she is Hari’s body. (KM p. 271)**

Jagannatha’s example of ullekha-dhvani is mixed with a bhrantiman dhvani (rather a bhrantimad-alankara-dhvani):

*smayamanananam tatra tam vilokya vilasinim \|*  
*cakoras cancarikas ca mudam varataram yayuh \|\|*

**Her face was smiling and she was playful. Seeing her at that time, the cakora birds and the bees felt even more joyful.**

Here the following is implied: To the cakora birds her face is a moon, and to the bees her face is a lotus. This is a double bhrantiman dhvani, and is also an ullekha-dhvani because there are two subjects and only one object of erroneous perception (the face): atra dhvanyamanaya ekaika-grahana-rupaya bhrantya tad-ubhaya-samudayatma ullekhah sankirnah (RG, KM p. 277). Jagannatha is the only poetical theorist to depict an ullekha with only two subjects in the repartition.

Sometimes Jagannatha’s interpretations are deep, if not far-fetched. Jagannatha illustratesparinama (modification):

*ahina-candra lasatananena jyotsnavati capi suci-smitena \|*  
*esa hi yosa sita-paksa-dosa tosaya kesam na mahi-tale syat \|\|*

**She is a full moon by her shining face, and has moonlight by her radiant smile. Who on Earth does not derive satisfaction from this woman who is a night in the bright fortnight?**

Jagannatha comments: atra sarvesam eva tosaya syad ity anena virahi-jana-tosa-janakatvam api labhyate. tac caropyamana-sukla- paksa-rajanyah svatmana badhitam, yosa-rupena tu sangacchata iti bhavati parinamah, “Indeed, everyone derives satisfaction from her. It follows that a person who is feeling the pang of separation obtains relief that way, but this idea is blocked by the very nature of the standard of comparison, a night in the bright fortnight (since a full moon increases the pang): It makes sense only if the moon is the woman (instead of the woman being the moon). That constitutes parinama” (RG, KM p. 249).

The difference between metaphor and parinama is that in the latter the standard of comparison needs to assume the nature of the subject of comparison to make sense of the action attributed to the standard of comparison: visayi yatra visayatmatayaiva prakrtopayogi na svatantryena sa parinamah \|\| atra ca visayabhedo visayiny upayujyate, rupake tu naivam iti rupakad asya bhedah (RG, KM p. 248).

Jagannatha illustrates the vyaja-stuti ornament (here praise is implied from the criticism):

*urvim sasati mayy upadrava-lavah kasyapi sa syad iti*  
*praudham vyaharato vacas tava katham deva pratimo vayam \|*  
*pratyaksam bhavato vipaksa-nivahair dyam utpatadbhih krudha*  
*yad yusmat-kula-koti-mula-puruso nirbhidyata bhaskarah \|\|*

**O king, how can we possibly believe you when you boldly say: “As long as I rule on Earth, no one will ever be in trouble,” because owing to your anger the sun, the founder of your dynasty, was pierced by the huge bundle of deceased enemies that were going through it on their way to heaven? (KM p. 417)**

Moreover, in Mammata’s dipaka, one thing is contextual and the other is not, whereas in tulya-yogita all the things are either contextual or noncontextual. In practice, however, the difference between those two ornaments is hard to make. Kavi Karnapura simplified the issue: In dipaka he does not speak of eitherprastuta or aprastuta: karakaikye kriya bahvyo vyatyaye ’pi ca dipakam (Alankara-kaustubha 8.130). Pandita-raja Jagannatha, however, made matters worse. He criticized Mammata’s definition of dipaka. Mammata says dipaka has two varieties: karaka-dipaka (one noun is connected with many verbs) and kriya-dipaka (one verb is connected with many nouns): According to Mammata, the concepts of prastuta and aprastuta only apply to kriya-dipaka. Jagannatha, however, says those concepts also apply to karaka- dipaka. Not only that, he gives an example of an action which is both contextual and noncontextual (!):

*vasu datum yaso dhatum vidhatum ari-mardanam \|*  
*tratum ca madrsan rajann ativa nipuno bhavan \|\|*

**O king, you sir are expertly able to give wealth, to bestow fame, to arrange for a crushing defeat of the enemy, and to protect individuals of my type.**

Here Jagannatha says that since there clearly is a speaker (not to mention a vocative), the two actions of giving wealth and of protecting the speaker are contextual; the action of crushing the enemy is non-contextual; and the action of bestowing fame is both contextual and non-contextual.

Jagannatha turned poetics into a set of mathematical formulas. On some other occasions he showed his love for hair splitting:

*nitaram parusa saroja-mala*  
*na mrnalani vicara-pesalani \|*  
*yadi komalata tavangakanam*  
*atha ka nama kathapi pallavanam \|\|*

**If the softness of your limbs is felt, then lotuses are forever rugged and lotus stems are not worth a consideration, not to mention new leaves.**

The verse features a vyatireka-dhvani (implied contrast), but Jagannatha shows the verse to illustrate the variety of aprastuta- prasamsa where a cause is understood from its effect: atra pallavadi- tiraskarena karyena tad-anganam saukumaryatisayah karanam, “Here the stated effect is the depreciation of new leaves and so on, and the cause understood from that is the supereminence of the softness of her limbs” (RG, KM p. 405). By construing a difference between “the softness of her limbs” and “the supereminence of the softness of her limbs” in terms of considering the former to be non-contextual and the latter to be contextual, Jagannatha emulates Ruyyaka and Visvanatha, two notorious hair-splitters: Their verse illustrative of this subcategory is followed by a similar interpretation (indur lipta ivanjanena...) (Alankara-sarvasva, KM p. 105) (Sahitya-darpana 10.59).

## Jagannatha and Nagesa

Jagannatha is a giant in the field of poetics, and Nagesa is a giant in the field of grammar. Each one is also a master in the other field. Dr. Shankarji Jha remarks:

Unlike the other original Sanskrit texts, the Rasa-gangadhara has few commentaries on it, perhaps because of its quality as being both the latest and profound. The oldest commentary on the Rasa-gangadhara is Guru-marma-prakasa by Nagesabhatta a noted writer on Indology. This commentary of Nagesa- Bhatta on the Rasa-gangadhara is too short, and its primary aim seems to be the refutation of the tenets produced in the Rasa-gangadhara. In fact a commentary primarily aims at deciphering the true import of the original in a lucid style, and in this job NagesaBhatta is quite unsuccessful. It appears that owing to the personal bias against Panditaraja Nagesa-Bhatta has commented upon the Rasa-Gangadhara, as Nagesa Bhatta comes from the lobby of Appaya Diksita and has to answer the refutation of Appaya Diksita’s tenets made by Panditaraja.

At the end of his book, however, Dr. Shankarji Jha contradicts himself: “To me, Nagesa’s critique on the R.G. is undoubtedly satisfactory, as at certain places it helps in making a reader understand the purport of the terse lines of P. J. to some more extent.” (1998: 187)

In Rasa-gangadhara, on several occasions Jagannatha went overboard in criticizing Appaya Diksita, and Nagesa Bhatta corrected Jagannatha. For instance, Jagannatha said Appaya is wrong in using the word puratah, because according to Jagannatha the word puratah can only be made by adding the suffix tas\[il\] after the word pura (town). Jagannatha says the proper form is purah, made by applying the suffix as\[i\] after pur, a replacement ofpurva by Astadhyayl 5.3.39, and he quotes Kalidasa to show the usage of purah. However, Nagesa Bhatta points out that first of all the suffix tas\[il\] is inapplicable after pura (since tasil is applied after either a sarvanama or bahu, by Astadhyayi 5.3.7). Nagesa says the word puratas is proper: He gives three explanations of its formation. Firstly, puratah is a replacement. Secondly, pura is made with the suffix pac-adi a\[c\] (Astadhyayi 3.1.134), and the suffix \[a\]tas\[uc\] is applied after it, because that is implied as a possibility in Astadhyayi5.3.28. Thirdly, the suffix \[k\]a is added to the verbal root pur agra-gamane by Astadhyayi 3.1.35; then tas\[i\] is appended. In this way, and by citing Kalidasa and Bhavabhuti, Nagesa demonstrates that Appaya Diksita is not at fault.

Jagannatha’s mistake is not as bad as Visvanatha’s blunder of writing a word of comparison in his example of an elliptical simile characterized by the elision of the standard of comparison (Sahitya- darpana 10.20) (since a word of comparison is always placed after a standard of comparison). Dr. Kane comments: “It must be said that these remarks of Visvanatha are quite wrong” (Kane (1995) The Sahitya-darpana, p. 100).

Jagannatha is the only poetical theorist to point out that the Grammarians and the Alankarikas have different viewpoints in terminology. He states the two schools of thought: The Grammarians say the word iva and other words of comparison are dyotakas (suggestive of similitude), whereas the Logicians say they are vacakas (expressive of similitude). However, there is no fundamental difference. The Alankarikas, the poetical theorists, follow the Logicians in this regard. As a grammarian, Nagesa Bhatta says a word of comparison is a dyotaka, i.e. it suggests that the thing before it is the standard of comparison: iva-sabdas tu tad- gatopamanatva-dyotaka iti bodhyam (Mahabhasya-pradipoddyoia 2.1.55).

On that topic, Jagannatha finds fault with Appaya Diksita for classing the expression “patu-patur devadattah” (Devadatta is as if clever) in the category of dharma-lupta upama (elliptical simile where the attribute in common was elided). Jagannatha says that Appaya is wrong in interpreting the repetition “patu-patu” as a vacaka because Patanjali and Kaiyata say it is a dyotaka, therefore the repetition in patu-patu should be classed in the category of vacaka-dharma-lupta upama (elliptical simile where the attribute in common and the word of comparison were elided). Nagesa

Bhatta says that according to Jagannatha the reduplication itself is not a vacaka since it does not literally express the similarity. Nagesa says the grammarians’ dyotaka is the same as the poeticians’ vacaka. He says the reduplication in patu-patu is a dyotaka and thus expresses the comparison. Here Jagannatha is partly wrong because he makes a distinction between dyotaka and vacaka, and partly right due to Appaya Diksita’s classification: The elision of the word of comparison (iva) in patu-patu—which means patur iva “as if clever” in the sense of “not quite clever” (patu-patuh, patuto nyuna-guna ity arthah, Hari-namamrta-vyakarana 1038)— is the same as the elision of a word of comparison in the double usage of the suffix namul, which Appaya, following Mammata, classes as vacaka-lupta. However, Visvanatha classes the usage of namul only in the category of dharma-lupta (Sahitya-darpana 10.19), since namul conveys the sense of comparison, by the rule: upamane karmani ca (Astadhyayl3.4.45).

InMarma-prakasa, Nagesa Bhatta clarified Jagannatha’s explanation of theparinama ornament as follows: vayam tu brumah, upamana- vacyatvena dyotakasyapi bodhakatvanapayena nasti vacaka-lopa iti tad-asayad abodha-mulakam iti cintyam idam. (Marma-prakasa KM pp. 170-171) pratiyogikabhedo rupakam, upameya-pratiyogikabhedah parinamah, “We say: In metaphor, the subject of comparison is not different from the standard of comparison, whereas in parinama the standard of comparison is not different from the subject of comparison” (Marma-prakasa, RG KM p. 248). In Uddyota, however, Nagesa followed Mammata and quoted Jagannatha’s definition ofparinama to refute it; Nagesa reasons that in parinama the eminence of the subject of comparison is not enhanced and so there is no embellishment to speak of. Further in that regard, this is Jagannatha’s introductory verse:

*smrtapi tarunatapam karunaya harantl nrnam*  
*abhangura-tanu-tvisam valayita satair vidyutam \|*  
*kalinda-giri-nandinl-tata-sura-drumalambinl*  
*madiya-mati-cumbini bhavatu kapi kadambini \|\|*

**Simply by being remembered, some new cloud dispels burning afflictions. It usually abides near a heavenly tree on the Yamuna’s shore and is surrounded by hundreds of lightning flashes whose radiance is constant. May that cloud kiss my intelligence. (RG, mangalacarana)**

The verse begins with a parinama-dhvani: The standard of comparison (the cloud) needs to assume the nature of the subject of the comparison (Krishna) to accomplish the meaning “is surrounded by hundreds of lightning flashes (gopls) (this is an atisayokti ornament).” The parinama is implied because the upameya, Krishna, is implied. However, Nagesa Bhatta does not accept the parinama ornament, therefore he says the verse features a commixture of vyatireka (a contrast between the Krishna cloud and a normal cloud) and atisayokti (introsusception: Krishna is a cloud). But as an example of atisayokti, Jagannatha reworded the sentence: mamasu haratu sraman atitamam tamala-drumah, “May the tamala tree quickly dispel my fatigue.” A tree does so simply by providing shade, therefore in this sentence it makes perfect sense to attribute that action to its subject, the tree. The universal axiom is that a special rule (apavada) supersedes the general rule (utsarga), consequently only the most specific definition applies to a set of words whenever applicable: parinama is more specific, i.e. intricate, than either atisayokti or vyatireka.

Nagesa does not explain the sense of “may it kiss” (may it come in contact with). The verse is sourced in Bhamim-vilasa: Har Dutt Sharma paraphrases Nagesa and says it means “May it resplendently abide in my heart.” That constitutes the paryayokta ornament (circumlocution), and it is implied because Krishna, the doer of the action, is implied. But since a cloud cannot be in the body, the same parinama-dhvani occurs, but this time it is implied by the implied paryayokta. Or else, at first the same parinama-dhvani is carried over to that sentence, so that Krishna is superimposed on the cloud to make sense of the action of kissing, and then the paryayokta is implied from that (“May He kiss my intelligence” has the sense of “May He abide in my mind”). This dual possibility—paryayokta- dhvani or parinama-dhvani—constitutes a samsaya aspadata sankara-dhvani (being in the scope of a doubt: “Is this implied ornament occurring or is that implied ornament occurring?”).

Moreover, Nagesa Bhatta defended Ruyyaka when Jagannatha said that Ruyyaka’s example of nidarsana is actually a vakyartha- rupaka (RG, KM p. 343). Nagesa Bhatta’s approach led Pandit Mathura-natha Sastn, who published Rasa-gangadhara and Marma-prakasa along with his own commentary, to vehemently criticize Nagesa Bhatta on several occasions. Dr. Shankarji Jha remarks:

Through this passage, it is evident that Pt. Mathuranatha Sastn had not a good opinion about the performance of Nagesa. He has collected a number of such points, where he has shown the lapses in the commentary of Nagesa. No doubt, he is right in his job, but his rustic and absurd language toward Nagesa- bhatta hurt the feelings of the scholars.

For instance: In the explanation of his verse that begins unmulitah saha madena, an example of mala-sahokti cited in Appendix II, Jagannatha says the nidarsana ornament is included therein: sahoktir nidarsananupranita ca (RG, KM p. 364). Commenting on this, Nagesa says the nidarsana is a vakyartha-nidarsana, but Mathura-natha Sastn retorted that the verse features padartha- nidarsana, not vakyartha-nidarsana, and proceeded to deride Nagesa’s entire commentary on the treatise. In response, Madana-Mohana Jha cited Purusottama Caturvedi’s disapproval of Mathura-natha’s manner of rebuking Nagesa Bhatta, especially since Nagesa is a savant highly revered by all Sanskrit scholars. Nonetheless, Madana-Mohana Jha says he agrees with Mathura- natha’s opinion on the issue.

## Twelve Theories of Rasa

Pandita-raja Jagannatha gives eleven interpretations of the term rasa (poetic delight). Most likely, Jagannatha says there are eleven theories in reference to the title of the treatise: The eleven Rudras are a form of Siva. The twelfth theory is Jagannatha’s own, added as a subvariety of the first. Jagannatha shows the theories in decreasing order of importance:

(1) Abhinavagupta, Mammata, Visvanatha, and Jagannatha. The details are in the chapter on Mammata. In this theory, Jagannatha says the meaning of Bharata Muni’s rasa-sutra is: vibhavanubhava-vyabhicaribhih samyogad vyanjanad rasasya cid- ananda-visista-sthayy-atmanah sthayy-upahita-cid-anandatmano va nispattih svarupena prakasanam ity adye, “The effectuation, i.e. the manifestation as its true nature, of rasa—which signifies that its essence is either “the sthayi characterized by cid-ananda ” (in Abhinava’s opinion) or “cid-ananda enhanced by the sthayf” (in Jagannatha’s opinion)—occurs on account of the suggestive connection with vibhavas (subject, object, and stimuli), anubhava (bodily reaction) and vyabhicari (transient emotion)” (RG, KM p. 28).

Abhinavagupta himself writes:

*na cayam rasadir arthah “putras te jatah” ity ato yatha harso jayate tatha, napi laksanaya, api tu sahrdayasya hrdaya-samvada-balad vibhavanubhava-pratitau tan-mayl-bhavanenasvadyamana eva rasyamanataika-pranah siddha-svabhava-sukhadi-vilaksanah parisphurati.*

**“Rasa is not something comparable to the joy a new father feels when he hears “Your child is a boy”, nor does it occur as a form of figurative usage. Rather, it is simply relished by a connoisseur by the process of tan-mayi-bhava (becoming absorbed) when the heart responds to poetic descriptions in the forms of vibhavas and anubhavas. The essence of this aesthetic emotion is that it is relished. Rasa is thus distinct from empirical joy and other such emotions whose nature is settled.” (Locana 1.4)**

In Locana, Abhinavagupta used the term tan-mayi-bhava, whereas in Abhinava-bharati he only mentioned sadharanya, and added that sometimes only the vibhavas are predominant, and so on, although ideally all three (vibhava, anubhava, vyabhicari) should be equally predominant. And for that purpose, he says, dramaturgy is best and a lengthy composition is second-best: ayam atra sanksepah, \[...\] sadharanl-bhuta santana-vrtter ekasya eva va samvido gocara- bhuta ratih srngarah. sadharanl-bhavas ca vibhavadibhir iti. tatra vibhava-pradhanyena sadharani-bhavo yatha \[.\]. kintu sama-pradhanya eva rasasvadasyotkarsah. tac ca prabandha eva bhavati. vastutas tu dasa-rupaka eva. yad aha vamanah (6.32).

Dr. Satyavrata Singh explains the term sadharam-krti in Sahitya- darpana 3.9 as tan-mayi-bhavana. Commenting on Abhinava’s words varnanlya-tanmayl-bhavana-yogyata in Locana, Rama- saraka equates tan-mayl-bhavana with the process of identification: varnanlyeti, varnanlyam nayakadi-vibhavadi, tan-mayl- bhavanasya tat-tadatmyapatti-rupasya yogyata samarthyam ity arthah (Balapriya on Locana 1.1). Visvanatha Kaviraja interprets Mammata’s word vasana (predisposition) in the latter’s paraphrase of Sankuka’s theory as tan-mayl-bhava-dayinl dhl (a frame of mind that gives the tan-mayl-bhava): anumlyamano raty-adir bhavah, tada rama-tadatmyena pratlte nate samajikanam preksanam vasanaya tan-mayl-bhava-dayinya dhiya carvyamanah punah punar anumlyamano rasa iti srl-sankuka-nama kascid acarya iti sambandhah (Kavya-prakasa-darpana 4.28). However, Sesaraja Sarma explains Candidasa’s usage of the term tan-mayi-bhava in this context as akhanda-buddhi-svarupa-bhava (being completely absorbed) (Candrakala-tika 4.14).

Jagannatha gives this analogy: As a previously covered light is uncovered and sheds light on the things near it, so the soul both illumines (enlivens) the sthayi-bhava which is mixed with the vibhavas and so on and manifests itself: yatha hi saravadina pihito dipas tan-nivrttau sannihitan padarthan prakasayati svayam ca prakasate, evam atma-caitanyam vibhavadi-samvalitan raty-adin (RG, KM p. 22).

Jagannatha gives a slightly different version of the “main theory of rasa”, held by Abhinava and others. This abstract is Jagannatha’s own theory:

*yadva vibhavadi-carvana-mahimna sahrdayasya nija-sahrdayata-vasonmisitena tat-tat-sthayy-upahita-sva- svarupanandakara samadhav iva yoginas citta-vrttir upajayate, tan-mayi-bhavanam iti yavat. anando hy ayam na laukika- sukhantara-sadharanah, anantahkarana-vrtti-rupatvat.*

**“There is another explanation: Like a yogi in trance, a state of mind is produced on the strength of the relishment of the vibhavas and so on. The relishment occurs by the own connoisseurship of the connoisseur. The state of mind is the bliss of the soul, the soul being enhanced by the corresponding sthayi. This means one becomes transcendental bliss (or one becomes rasa)” (RG, KM pp. 22-23).**

nanubhuyate, kalantare tu prakaranadi-paryalocanaya bhavann apy asau na kavya-vyapadesam vyahantum isah, tasyasvada-matrayattatvat” iti (Sahitya- darpana 4.14).

(2) Bhatta Nayaka. The details were given in the chapter on Mammata. Jagannatha says the only difference between “the main theory” and Bhatta Nayaka’s theory is the function called bhavakatva: matasyaitasya purvasman matad bhavakatva- vyaparantara-svikara eva visesah. bhogas tu vyaktih. bhoga- krttvam tu vyanjanad avisistam. anya tu saiva saranih (RG, KM p. 25). This means the terminology is different. Bhavakatva is twofold: sadharanya (generalization, stereotyping, empathy) and bhavana (contemplating on the meaning such as a rasa). Another difference between Abhinava and Nayaka is that the latter does not mention vasana (predisposition): Even in his paraphrase of Nayaka’s viewpoint, Jagannatha does not mention the concept of predisposition. It is included in sadharanya.

In Bhatta Nayaka’s theory, Bharata Muni’s rasa-sutra means: vibhavanubhava-vyabhicarinam samyak sadharanatmataya yogad bhavakatva-vyaparena bhavanad rasasya sthayy- upahita-sattvodreka-prakasita-svatmananda-rupasya nispattir bhogakhyena saksat-karena visayi-krtir iti dvitiye, “On account of a proper contemplation (samyoga = samyak yoga)—“proper” means its essence is sadharanya (generalization and identification)—, by the function called bhavakatva, of vibhavas and so on, the rasa is brought in the scope of cognizance by the ultimate direct mode of perception called bhoga (enjoyment). The rasa is the form of the soul’s bliss made manifest by an upsurge of sattva-guna that relates to the sthayin” (RG, KM p. 28).

(3) The moderns. When the characters are not divinities, a spectator can completely identify with a character and imagine in themselves the nature of the character’s sthayin. It involves a voluntary disregard of the character’s qualities: Such is the nature of generalization, but Jagannatha specifies that the spectator attributes faults to the character in order to facilitate the total identification.

The gist is this:

*navyas tu “kavye natye ca kavina natena ca prakasitesu vibhavadisu vyanjana-vyaparena dusyantadau sakuntaladi-ratau grhltayam anantaram ca sahrdayatollasitasya bhavana-visesa-rupasya dosasya mahimna kalpita- dusyantatvavacchadite svatmany ajnanavacchinne sukti-kasa- kala iva rajata-khandah samutpadyamano ’nitvacamyah saksibhasyah sakuntaladi-visayaka-raty-adir eva rasah.”*

**“In poetry and in drama, at first Dusyanta’s love for Sakuntala, for instance, is understood by the function called Suggestiveness when the vibhavas and so on are manifested by the actor. Thereafter arises in a spectator a voluntary illusory mistake due to the propensity to enjoy. That mistake is the form of a particular way of feeling: The spectator thinks he is Dusyanta and thus clouds himself with ignorance. Then the spectator feels the character’s sthayi toward the other, such as Dusyanta’s love for Sakuntala. That sthayi which has come into being is called the rasa. It is felt in a directly perceivable way like seeing silver in mother-of-pearl and is thus false and otherwise indescribable” (RG, KM p. 25).**

In this theory, Bharata’s rasa-sutra means: vibhavanubhava- vyabhicarinam samyogad bhavana-visesa-rupad dosad rasasyanirvacaniya-dusyanta-raty-ady-atmano nispattir utpattir iti trtiye, “The origination of rasa, whose essence is the indescribable sthayi of Dusyanta, et al., occurs because of the fault which is a particular way of contemplating upon the vibhavas and so on.” (RG, KM p. 28)

Visvanatha Cakravarti gives examples:

*atha kadacit satam madhye ramayana-pathe hanumatah samudra-langhanam agatam tac chrutva tatrasthah kascit sahrdaya-bhaktas tadrsa- rasavesena lajja-sankocadikam anaveksya svayam api samudra- langhanartham sabha-madhye cukurda. drsya-natye ’pi kascid dasaratha-rupa-dhari sahrdaya-natah ramo vanam jagameti srutva dasarathasya bhavavesena svayam api pranan tatyajeti loke mahati prasiddhir asit.*

**“During a recitation of Ramayana among respectable persons, sometimes a sympathetic devotee, hearing that Hanuman jumped over the ocean, becomes absorbed in that mood, gives up all sense of shame and leaps through the audience as if to cross the ocean. Or in a drama, sometimes a sympathetic actor who plays the role of Dasaratha gives up his life upon hearing that Rama went to the forest. Such well-known occurrences are heard of from time to time.” (Bhakti-sara-pradarsini 2.5.101)**

(4) Others. This theory is the same as the third one, except that Inference replaces Suggestiveness and a spectator feels either one or all of the following: (A) I have love for Sakuntala, a love particularized by my having Dusyanta’s state of mind, (B) I am Dusyanta, which means I have love for Sakuntala, and (C) I have Dusyanta’s state of mind and I have love for Sakuntala.

In the fourth theory, Bharata’s rasa-sutra means: vibhavadmam samyogaj jnanad rasasya jnana-visesatmano nispattir utpattir iti caturthe, “The origination of rasa whose nature is a special awareness occurs from the awareness of the vibhavas and so on.” (RG, KM p. 28)

The inferential sign (linga = hetu) is the actor’s play. Pandit Badannatha Jha explains: At first the spectator thinks the actor is Dusyanta. Then the spectator infers from the actor’s play that he is in love with Sakuntala. Afterward the spectator identifies with Dusyanta: This means the spectator does not exactly think he is Dusyanta; rather he thinks he is Dusyanta in the way portrayed by the actor. Thus the voluntary mistake occurs after the inference: atra mate purvam dusyantatvena jnate nate cestaya sakuntala- rater anumanam, pascat tadrsa-dusyantena sahatmanas tadatmyavagahi prag-uktam tri-vidham manasam jnanam eva rasa iti saram (Candrika). Another possibility is that the spectator identifies with an implied character in the play, a character whose behavior is implied from the circumstances.

(5) Lollata. In a drama, the rasa, meaning the sthayi, which belongs to Dusyanta, for instance, is directly felt in a straightforward way by completely superimposing it on the actor, who is expert in showing his skills. The spectators think: “He is Dusyanta and loves Sakuntala” and so on. The sthayi is called the rasa. As before, the sentiment is extraordinary in the character and is more or less normal in the actor.

In Lollafa’s theory, Bharata’s sutra means: vibhavadinam sambandhad rasasya raty-ader nispattir aropah iti pancame, “There is a superimposition of the rasa, i.e. of the sthayi, due to the connection between vibhavas, anubhava and vyabhicari” (RG, KM p. 28).

(6) Sankuka. When the actor is perceived as the character, the character’s sthayi is inferred in the actor because the fake vibhavas etc. on stage are not taken to be fake and is called rasa. For instance, the real Dusyanta is not on stage. The inference arises because all the necessary components are present and thus exclude the possibility of another means of knowing. Dr. Jha expounds:

It means to say that during a theatrical performance, there exist not only Paksa, Sadhya and Hetu, viz. actors, sthayins and gestures respectively, but also the accessories like the stage, curtain, footlights and the like. In this circumstance, how can one say only the inferring of Rasa and not the direct perception of the other things? The knowledge of the stage, curtain etc. can be derived from the direct perception (pratyaksa) at that very time. In reply to this possible objection, P. J. says:

*bhinne visaye ’numiti-sanKigtya balavattvat \|\|*

That is, it is mandatory to accept that in case of the presence of two or more separate sets of the factors (Samagns), relevant to the separate kinds of perception like Pratyaksa, Anumana and others, that of the Anumana (inference) is the most powerful, and thus, it is obstructive to all other perceptions. Thus, the above confusion does not take place, and Anumana is accepted here without any hindrance. It is interesting to note that P. J. does not say any anomaly in this tenet, but Pandita Badarinatha Jha does so stating:

*paroksa-jnanasya acamatkaritvam catra pakse ’nici-byam \|\|*

Pt. Jha is of the view that an inferred knowledge is regarded to be Paroksa—indirect; that is held to be devoid of sublimity (Camatkara) in the case of Poetic enjoyment. Hence, this tenet propounding Rasa through Anumana is not acceptable because of being indirect perception and losing the sublimity. \[... if tan-mayi-bhava is not involved.\]

In Sankuka’s theory, Bharata’s sutra means: vibhavadibhih krtrimair apy akrtrimataya grhitaih samyogad anumanad rasasya raty-ader nispattir anumitir natadau paksa iti sesa iti sasthe, “The rasa, meaning the sthayl is inferred in the actor because of an inference by means of fake vibhavas and so on which are not taken to be fake.” (RG, KM p. 28). (In the fourth theory, empathy occurs by depreciating the nature of the character. But Mammata includes this too in Sankuka’s theory.)

(7) vibhavadayas trayah samudita rasah iti katipaye, “Some say: When the three—vibhava, anubhava, and vyabhicari— occur together, there is rasa” (RG, KM p. 28). Here Bharata’s sutra means: vibhavadlnam trayanam samyogat samudayad rasa-nispatti rasa- pada-vyavaharah iti saptame, “The usage of the word rasa occurs on account of the rise of those three together.”

(8) trisu ya eva camatkari sa eva raso ’nyatha tu trayo ’pi na, iti bahavah. \[...\] vibhavadisu samyag yogac camatkarat ity astame. tad evam paryavasitas trisu matesu sutra-virodhah, “Many say: “Among those three, the one which is astonishing is the rasa, otherwise those three are not taken into account.” In the eighth theory, the rasa-sutra means: “The usage of the word rasa occurs on account of the proper connection, i.e. the astonishment, among those three.” The next three theories are not in conformity with Bharata’s sutra” (RG, KM p. 28).

(9) bhavyamano vibhava eva rasah ity anye, “Others say: A vibhava which is constantly contemplated upon is rasa.” (RG, KM p. 28)

(10) anubhavas tatha tatha, ititare, “Yet others state: An anubhava which is constantly contemplated upon is rasa.” (RG, KM p. 28)

(11) vyabhicary eva tatha tatha parinamati iti kecit, “Some say: A vyabhicari which is constantly contemplated upon turns out as rasa.” (RG, KM p. 28)

Rudrata and Bhoja acknowledge the eleventh theory in the sense that a vyabhicari-bhava becomes rasa by the blend of vibhavas, anubhava, and another vyabhicari. At a cursory look, the eleventh theory seems to be in conformity with the rasa-sutra, given that Bharata Muni omitted the word sthayi-bhava therein, but Bharata obliquely forbids it: tatha vibhavanubhava-vyabhicari- parivrtah sthayi bhavo rasa-nama labhate (Natya-sastra 7.8).

Among the eleven theories, in the first two the term rasa means rapture and in the last nine it means aesthetic delight. An example of a vyabhicari-bhava that turns into aesthetic delight is in Kalidasa’s verse cited at the end of the chapter on Singabhupala. In that regard, Mammata pointed out that in Bharata’s rasa-sutra, the suggestiveness of a vyabhicari-bhava, etc., can be replaced by the suggestiveness of an aspect of a word (padamsa) and so on: padaika-desa-racana-varnesv api rasadayah (KP 4.43).

In Mammata’s methodology, sometimes a padamsa implies an ornament, and that implied ornament raises the sthayi to the level of rasa (aesthetic delight). Therefore, since an implied ornament thus enhances the sthayi, it should be acknowledged that an expressed ornament as well is able to effect that. In Kalidasa’s verse, the vibhavas, the anubhava, and the ornaments (expressed and implied) contribute to raise the vyabhicari-bhava to the level of aesthetic delight. In terms of evoking a rasa, an ornament has the force of a vyabhicari-bhava. This marks a distinction between kavya-rasa and natya-rasa. Abhinava sums it up by saying that the sthayi turns into rasa simply because of some particular type of appropriateness: tena sthayi-pratltir anumiti-rupa pracya, na rasah, ataeva sutre sthayi-grahanam na krtam, tatpratyuta salya- bhutam syat. kevalam aucityad evam ucyate sthayi rasl-bhuta iti. aucityam tu tat-sthayi-gatatvena karanaditaya prasiddhanam adhuna carvanopayogitaya vibhavaditvavalambanat. (Abhinava- bharatl 6.32). Anandavardhana wrote: prasiddhaucitya-bandhas tu rasasyopanisat para, “A literary construction based on a well- known appropriateness is the highest secret teaching for the relishment of a rasa” (Dhvany-aloka 3.14). This was expounded by Ksemendra.

## The Last Great Sanskrit Poet

Pandit Durga-prasada says Jagannatha composed thirteen works: (1) Amrta-laharl, eleven verses in praise of Yamuna, (2) Asafa- vilasa, in praise of Nawab Asaf Khan, (3) Karuna-lahari, sixty verses in praise of Krishna, (4) Citra-mmamsa-khandanam, a repudiation of Appaya Diksita’s Citra-mlmamsa, (5) Jagad- abharanam, a description of Dara, a son of Shah Jahan, (6) Ganga- laharl, also called Plyusa-laharl, (7) Pmnabharanam, fifty-three verses in praise of Prana-Narayana (a king of either Kamarupa or Nepal), (8) Bhamini-vilasa (the play of the woman who is beautiful due to anger: 2.72), a work in four chapters that totals 376 or 254 verses, depending on the edition; the first chapter is a miscellaneous collection of verses; the second centers on his wife, the third on lamentation due to her death, and the fourth on offering oneself to Krishna, (9) Manorama-kuca-mardanam, a work on grammar that refutes Bhattoji Diksita’s Praudha-manorama, (10) Yamuna- varnanam, (11) Laksmi-lahari, a poem of forty-one verses in praise of Laksmi, (12) Sudha-lahari, a short poem of thirty verses in praise of the sun god, and (13) Rasa-gangadhara. (RG, KM Introduction, pp. 3-4)

Dr. Shankarji Jha remarks:

After the confinement of Shaha-jahan, Panditaraja came to Kas! or Varanasi and led a scholarly life for several years. Thus, Panditaraja may have resorted to heavenly abode sometime in 1670, and a long period of 12 years seems to be sufficient for composing valuable treatises like Rasa-Gangadhara, and the like. Thus he may safely be placed in between 1590-1670.

Undoubtedly, Appaya Diksita and Panditaraja were simultaneously alive for a few years, for we have certain proofs to this effect. One proof is found in the form of a verse according to which we are informed that in the presence of Appaya Diksita etc. Panditaraja refuted the tenets of Bhattojidiksita in his work “Manorama-kuca-mardana” in the revenge of his insult done by Bhattoji-diksita, who called Panditaraja a “Mleccha” (Mean) in a congress of scholars. Panditaraja with utmost patience, then proved his “Mlecchatva” (meanness), when he rubbed the breasts of his daughter-like work, namely, “Manorama” or “Praudha-Manorama”, (i.e. refuted the tenets of the work Manorama) before the hosts of great scholars like Appaya Diksita etc., that is, they could not do anything in reply to the refutation made by Panditaraja. This verse runs thus:

*drpyad-dravida-durgraha-graha-vasanmlistam guru-drohina*  
*yan mleccheti vaco ’vicintya sadasi praudhe ’pi bhattojina \|*  
*tat satyapi tam eva dhairya-nidhina yat sa vyamrdnat kucam*  
*nirbadhyasya manoramam avasayann apy appayadyan sthitan \|\|*

**About this verse pandita Madana Mohan Jha opines that it is cited in the preface of the work “Siddhanta-lesa-sangraha” of “Kumbhakona” edition (Tamil-nadu state).**

Perhaps Rasa-gangadhara was a work in progress: Jagannatha might have composed the bulk of it in Shah Jahan’s court.

J. M. Nallasami Pillai explains the circumstances that led Jagan- natha to write Manorama-kuca-mardana:

Bhattoji was a pupil of Sesha Krishna Dikshita, and a co­student of the latter’s son Viresvara, who was, in addition, Jagannatha’s master. Krishna Dikshita had written a commentary called Prakriya-prakasa on the grammatical work of Prakriya-kaumudi. Bhattoji, in his well-known work named Manorama seriously attacked the commentary of his teacher.

Jagannatha was very much enraged at this ingratitude of a pupil to a preceptor and to the father of his own guru. He also disliked Appaya for the support he rendered to his adversary. He was once insulted in open assembly by Bhattoji. Henceforth he commenced his crusade against the two professors who made common cause with each other.

In Hari-namamrta-vyakarana, sometimes Jiva Gosvami found fault with Prakriya-kaumudi: prakriya tu cintya (HNV 406; 438). Jiva Gosvami also referred to Sesa Krsna’s commentary: iti krsna- panditasya prakriya-tikayam (HNV 379 vrtti on anid-gana). Sesa Krsna was a pupil of Madhusudana Sarasvati.

Pandita-raja Jagannatha was the last great poet in Sanskrit culture in general: “The modern poetry, except in the hands of a few geniuses like Jagannatha, tends to be loose and inchoate.” In truth the last master poet was Visvanatha Cakravarti (c. 1630-1725).

Jagannatha was the last ofthe touring poets. Before being patronized by Shah Jahan, Jagannatha traveled in search of employment. Dr. Pollock expounds:

In his literary oeuvre and in the course his life took,

Jagannatha marks a point of historic break in the history of Sanskrit literary culture. His movements as a professional writer traveling in quest of patronage from region to region and court to court—from Andhra to Jaipur and Delhi, and from Udaipur to Assam—show that the transregional space that Sanskrit literature had occupied during the two preceding millennia persisted well into the seventeenth century despite what are often represented as discontinuities in the political environment with the coming of the Mughals in the preceding century. In the same way, Jagannatha’s life as a court poet, and much of the work that he produced in that capacity (like his panegyrics to the kings of Udaipur, Delhi, and Assam), was no different from the lives and works of poets centuries earlier. His masterpiece of literary analysis, the Rasa-gangadhara (The Ganga-Bearer (Siva) of aesthetic emotion), participates as a full and equal interlocutor in a millennium-long debate on the literary and shares the same assumptions, procedures, and goals.

Yet Jagannatha marks a historical end point in a number of important ways. If it can be said that his ontogeny recapitulated the phylogeny of Sanskrit literary culture, this was probably the last such case; we know of no later poet who circumambulated the quarters of Sanskrit’s cosmopolitan space. While we should not exaggerate his artistic power, still, no later poet produced literary works that achieved the wide diffusion of his Rasagangadhara and of his collection of poems, the Bhamim- vilasa (Play of the beautiful woman). His literary criticism is rightly regarded as the last original contribution to the ancient conversation; thereafter all is reproduction. \[...\]

\[H\]e is described as a Brahman, belonging to a family hailing from the bastion of orthodoxy and tradition in the Venginadu region of Andhra Pradesh, who fell in love with a Muslim woman and met his death—whether in despair or repentance or defiance the legends are unclear—by drowning in the Ganga at Varanasi.

Something very old died when Jagannatha died, but also something very new. What was new in his literary oeuvre had much to do with his social milieu, the Mughal court of Shahjahan (r. 1626-1656), where he was a client of both Prince Dara Shukoh and the courtier Asaf Khan. The sometimes startling intellectual and social and aesthetic experiment that marked this world marked Jagannatha, too. What it meant for Sanskrit, Persian, and vernacular poets to gather in a common cultural space in Shahjahanabad \[Old Delhi\] is an unstudied question. But Jagannatha’s oeuvre suggests two important areas of innovation, one in the relationship between Sanskrit and both vernacular and Persian literature, the other in the kind of subjectivity that could find expression in literature.

Shah Jahan himself was half-Hindu: His mother was Manavati (Mughal name: Taj Bibi Bilqis Makani), the tenth daughter of King Udai Singh \|\| of Marwar. She was the third wife of Jahangir (r. 1605-1627), Shah Jahan’s father.

Jagannatha was a great man also in the sense that his poetry advocates dharma (moral codes), yet his personal dharma was not in line with the dharma of the society of that time. Jagannatha’s least-noted praiseworthy aspect is that he was a Vaishnava. The depth of his heart can be fathomed only from this perspective.

Moreover, in his life Jagannatha suffered the loss of his wife (Bhamim-vilasa 3.1-19) and of their son, but in Rasa-gangadhara his feelings center more on the Lord than on his wife and others. Thus Rasa-gangadhara contains many verses of pure bhakti-kavya. He was the last renowned non-mainstream Vaishnava. He and Anandavardhana implicitly taught that bhakti is the highest rasa, yet they could not find a proper place for it in their methodologies, much like Suggestiveness is in the mind, not in the scope of words per se.

Jagannatha’s life is shrouded in mystery. Pandit Madana-mohana

Jha relates hearsay which, he says, must have some truth: After his studies in Benares, Jagannatha went to Jaipur and opened a Sanskrit school there (but Jaipur was founded in 1727). One day, a Kazi from Delhi came; in his presence Jagannatha refuted Muslim scriptures. The Kazi returned to Delhi and praised Jagannatha in the emperor’s court. Then the emperor (either Jahangir or Shah Jahan) invited Jagannatha to Delhi. Eventually, Jagannatha married the daughter of the emperor. Much later, after Aurangzeb had usurped the throne, Jagannatha went to Benares with her and was insulted by Appaya Diksita and other Hindu pandits there and was thus excommunicated by Hindu society.

Pandit Madana-mohana Jha relates the well-accepted rumor that Jagannatha wrote Ganga-laharl during his last days in Benares. According to tradition, Appaya Diksita and Bhattoji Diksita refused to allow Pandita-raja to be reintroduced in the Brahmana community, and so in the end Jagannatha composed Ganga-laharl, saying that if he is pure, let the Ganges rise and take him away. Dr. Shankarji Jha writes:

Inasmuch as he was a great literary doyen, he won wide- spread fame within and without Varanasi. As the last scene of his life-play, the story goes, he was reciting his most charming self-composed hymns in praise of the holy river Ganga, while sitting on her bank, and, to the utmost astonishment of all the nearby public, the holy Ganga being overwhelmed with his soul-stirring hymns, rose upwards and submerged Panditaraja

## 41. Krishna Kavi

Krsna Sarma wrote Mandara-maranda-campu. The pub­lishers of the Kavya-mala series (number 52, 1895 CE) name him Sri Krsna Kavi. The author is widely known by that name, but the colophon at the end of the first chapter says the work was authored by Krsna Sarma and Candradeva Sarma. The colophons and the last verse state that the authors resided in Guhapura (some unknown place). In his index, Dr. Kane writes:

Mandara-maranda-campu of Krsna Sarman and of Candradeva Sarman in eleven bindus. An extensive compilation for serving as a handbook for poets. Later than 1600 A.D. Deals with metres, slesa, yamaka, citra-bandhas, nataka and other rupakas and their angas, nayaka, nayika, rasa, vrttis, alankaras etc.

Krsna Sarma wrote all his examples. His treatise contains few original ideas, and in the theory he rarely deviated from the beaten path, but overall the treatise is remarkable.

His definition of poetry is: salankara-gunau kavyam sabdarthau dosa-varjitau, “Faultless sounds and meanings that have a literary quality and an ornament constitute poetry” (KM p. 186). He says sounds and meanings are the body of poetry, and reiterates Kuntaka’s and Vidyanatha’s statement that the life of poetry is the power of an implied sense: sanram tasya sabdarthau jivitam vyangya-vaibhavam (KM p. 187).

He follows Appaya Diksita’s threefold classification of third-rate poetry: sabda-citram cartha-citram ubhayam ceti tat tridha (KM p. 187).

In that regard, Krishna Kavi’s section on citra-kavya is elaborate. This is his example of the snake diagram:

*sri-ramo harmya-dhama sa tata-sumahima-srl-nato jna-prabhutah*  
*sugriva-pritaye tat-sahajam ayam amum bha-lasat-sayakena \|*  
*payan mam bhubhrd-lso vanam iha mihira-vrata-badhady-abhave*  
*tasyayann ajnaya yamam asam adhi-sukho ’initasyaridhara \|\|*

**May SrT Rama, the king of kings, protect me. He went to the forest by his father’s order although other elders in the city were not objecting to His presence. He has a lovely radiance. Brahma and other glorious beings of wide renown bow to Him: He is great with intelligentsia. To please SugrTva, He disposed of Valin, his sibling, with an arrow blazing with splendor. Though He is very blissful, He took to the unhappy path of austerity. When He is made high-spirited, He lets fly His trail-forming cakra.**

To fit the diagram, mihira-vrata in the third line should read mihiri-vrata. The word mihira means either sun, cloud, or wise man: mihirah surya-vrddhayoh (Medinl-kosa); mihiro ’rke ’mbude buddhe (Hema-kosa 3.630). The sense of mihiri-vrata is “a multitude of assemblies,” where the nominal base mihirin (assembly) is derived as “in which there are wise men”.

**The Snake**

![рис-012.jpg|600](<Versified History of Sanskrit Poetics/рис-012.jpg>)

This is the example of the zigzag diagram (go-mutrika-bandha):

*bhaje radha-varam kanja-mukham bhakta-ruci-vratam \|*  
*vraje badhaharam kunja-sukham vyakta-suci-smitam \|\|*

**I revere Radha’s lover: He has a lotus face. The devotees continuously take pleasure in Him. In Vraja, the fun in a kunja brings trouble and is the reason a smile due to Eros becomes apparent. (KM p. 54)**

**Zigzag**

![рис-013.jpg|600](<Versified History of Sanskrit Poetics/рис-013.jpg>)

The themes in the chapters sire: (I) Meyers, (II) The; essence (sara), (III) Slesa, (IV) Yamaka, (V) Citra-kavya, (VI) Gupti, (VII) Dramaturgy, (VIII) Nayaka, srngdra-ndyika, and the four vrttis (Kaisiki, Arabhati, Sattviki, Bharati), (IX) Rasa and its constituents, (X) Ornaments of sound, ornaments of meaning (including lesser- known ones such as lalita), categories of first-rate implied sense, categories of second-rate implied sense, and (XI) Miscellaneous topics.

The second chapter of the work is a campu (a story in verse and in prose). It consists in twenty-eight verses. The purpose of the chapter is to illustrate that a renowned personality is the primary cause of the brilliance of the poet and of the poetry. The commentator explains that here the author follows Vidyanatha.

The story in the campu involves Madhvacarya and Vyasa, and revolves around Krishna.

Krishna Kavi’s examples of ornaments are simple. He nicely defined paryayokta (circumlocution) and also followed Ruyyaka’s and Visvanatha’s interpretation of paryayokta: The contextual subject matter is an effect implied from the stated cause, which is equally contextual by the force of it. For instance: “Krishna, today that slender girl fell to the ground and stopped breathing.” His third kind ofparyayokta is the same as Kesava Misra’s bhavikatva-guna (under a pretext, the speaker conceals her intention).

This is the example of asangati (dislocated cause and effect): krsne bibhrati bhu-bharam vinamra jana-maulayah, “When Krishna supports the weight of the world, the heads of people bend” (KM p. 133). This illustrates parivrtti (exchange):

*pritim dattva sarojaksi jagrhe kamino manah*  
*tulasi-majarim ekam dattva bhejur hareh krpam*  
*dattva sudha-muco vacah kavir bheje kapardikam \|\|*

**A lotus-eyed woman gives affection and steals the hearts of men. A devotee offers one tulasi bud and receives Hari’s mercy. A poet provides words that effuse nectar and reaps pennies. (KM p. 138)**

In the eleventh chapter, these topics are treated (at length): (1) Synonyms of numbers, (2) The gana scheme, in prosody, (3) The faults (kavya-dosa), (4) Vidyanatha’s twenty-four literary qualities defined without examples: Nine of those are artha-gunas and the rest are sabda-gunas, (5) The three literary functions (abhidha, laksana, vyanjana), the restrictive factors in Denotation, and the suggestive specialties, (6) Sayya and paka: Krishna Kavi copies Vidyanatha’s interpretations of those two (KM p, 182, p. 187), (7) Rupaka-bhasa (language in a play), (8) Thirteen rasa-dosas and exceptions thereof, (9) The purpose ofpoetry (he follows Mammata), the definition of poetry, two categories of poetry (maha-kavya, upakavya), eighteen characteristics of a maha-kavya; upakavya is manifold, such as: akhyayika, katha, cakravalaka, bhogavali, virudavali, taravali, visvavali, ratnavali; definitions of those, (10) The convention of poets (kavi-samaya): Lists of things to describe in a given place or situation; lists of white things, red things, etc., crooked things, sharp things, heavy things, sweet things, etc., and (11) The categories of padarthas (jati, guna, dravya, kriya).

In the fourth chapter, Krishna Kavi illustrates a triple literal meaning:

*dhvastaghalinibaddhoru-gunalinihate bhave \|*  
*gatam hares tanuh padau caritrani sada hrdi \|\|*

**Once material life has been overcome, may Hari’s form, feet and deeds always go to your heart: They dispose of lowly groups and abound in correlated great qualities. (KM p. 43)**

In relation to tanuh (body), the words dhvastaghalmibaddhoru- gunalinihate are separated as: dhvasta-agha-ali nibaddha-uru- guna-ali nihate. With regard to padau (two feet), those words are separated in the same way, by taking the nominal base to be ali instead of ali. Both mean ‘multitude’. In agreement with caritrani (deeds), however, the separation is: dhvastaghalini baddhoru- gunalini hate.

That triple pun illustrates Visvanatha’s category of slesa called ubhayatmaka (both abhanga, pun achieved by not breaking up the syllables, and sabhanga, pun achieved by breaking up the syllables): punas tridha sa-bhango’bhangas tad-ubhayatmakah (Sahitya-darpana 10.12).

In the above verse, the verb gatam is the imperative tense atmanepada in the singular, dual or plural. The verbal root is ga\[n\] gatau (to go). In the singular, the suffix is tam. In the dual it is atam. And in the plural it is antam. The n of antam is deleted by the rule: a-ramanya-varnadante-antam-antanam nasya harah, “When ante, antam, or anta comes after a phoneme other than a short a, the n is deleted” (Hari-namamrta-vyakarana 317) (atmanepadesv anatah, Astadhyayl 7.1.5). The master poet Sriharsa too composed a triple slesa (on the word sruti-gamitaya and on the verb vyatibhate):

*api loka-yugam drsav api*  
*sruta-drsta ramam-guna api \|*  
*sruti-gamitaya dama-svasur*  
*vyatibhate sutaram dharapate \|\|*

**“O king, the respective families of Damayanti’s parents add resplendence to each other (vyatibhate) because everyone has heard about their renown (sruti-gamitaya); her eyes add resplendence to each other because they extend to the ears (sruti-gamitaya); and her womanly virtues, whether they were simply heard of or realized in her presence, add resplendence to one another because they are in conformity with the scriptures (sruti-gamitaya)” (Naisadha- carita 2.22). The atmanepada in vyatibhate is obtained by the rule: kartari karma-vyatihare (Astadhyayi 1.3.14).**

## 42. Visvesvara Pandita

Visvesvara Pandita (first half of the eighteenth century) wrote Alankara-kaustubha, published in the Kavya-mala series. It only treats of ornaments of meaning. It thus differs from Kavi Karnapura’s book of the same name. Visvesvara expounded about seventy ornaments. His selection of examples makes his book valuable. He was an independent thinker who lived in Uttar Pradesh. On occasion he refuted the views of Visvanatha, of Appaya Diksita, and of Pandita-raja Jagannatha.

Visvesvara shows this verse to illustrate the bhavika ornament (seemingly present occurrence):

*tam tasya svara-sankramam mrdu-girah slistam ca tantri-svanam*  
*varnanam api murchanantara-gatam taram virame mrdum \|*  
*hela-samyamitam punas ca calitam  ragad dvir-uccaritam*  
*yat satyam virate ’pi gita-samaye gacchami srnvann iva \|\|*

**Although in truth the song had stopped, while going home I as if still hear it, the sequence of his notes, the soft words, the intertwined sounds of the lute, the high notes in yet another murchana, the soft sounds in the break, the smooth subduing of the voice, then the departure from the melody and the repeated utterance. (Mrc-chakatika 3.5)**

Visvesvara Pandita elaborates: atra gita-virame ’pi tasya sravana- rupa-saksat-karas carudattenoktah. smarananavaccheda- rupa-karyena drdha-samskaradhayakataya tasyatiramaniyatve tatparyam, “In this verse, the direct experience of hearing, even though the song had ceased, is expressed by Carudatta. By the effect, the nonspecification of a remembrance (there is no smrti vyabhicari-bhava), the sense culminates in the idea that the song was highly delightful in terms of being a cause of a strong mental impression.” (Alankara-kaustubha, KM p. 335)

## 43. Baladeva Vidyabhusana

Baladeva Vidyabhusana (eighteenth century) wrote Kavya- kaustubha and Sahitya-kaumudi. Kavya-kaustubha is a short treatise on poetics, with simple examples: For the most part, in Kavya-kaustubha Baladeva followed Jayadeva’s methodology. Concepts propounded by Visvanatha and Appaya are also seen therein.

In Sahitya-kaumudi (1.6), Baladeva reiterated Mammata’s defini­tion of poetry, but in Kavya-kaustubha he paraphrased Kavi Karnapura’s critique of the same definition: adosau salankarau sabdarthau kavyam iti tu kuranga-nayanety atrativyaptam tadrsa- sabdartha-rupatvat (Kavya-kaustubha 1.10).

This is Baladeva Vidyabhusana’s definition of poetry: kavina nirmitam vakyam kavyam. camatkara-kara-gadya-padyatmana racitam kaver vakyam kavyam, “A text composed by a kavi is kavya. This means a poet’s statement, written in the form of either prose or prosody, that causes astonishment is poetry” (Kavya- kaustubha 1.4).

This is Baladeva’s own example of yamaka (word rhyme):

*ayata sarad aho*  
*sara-daho manmathah prakharah \|*  
*sarati sarah kalahamsi*  
*kalaham simantim tyajati \|\|*

ayata—has come; sarad—autumn; aho—whether; sara— because of arrows; dahah—a heat; manmathah—related to Cupid; prakharah—harsh; sarati—goes; sarah—to a lake; kalahamsi—a female goose; kalaham—a quarrel; simantini—a woman (“she has a parting in her hair”); tyajati—gives up.

**Has autumn arrived? There is a heavy internal heat caused by Cupid’s arrows, the female swans are going to the lakes, and women have stopped arguing. (Kavya-kaustubha 9.4)**

His Sahitya-kaumudi, translated by the present writer, is a remake of Kavya-prakasa: Baladeva Vidyabhusana copied Mammata’s karikas (definitions) and selected the illustrative examples from the canon of Vaishnava literature. Baladeva added an eleventh chapter, which includes the best ornaments from Visvanatha’s Sahitya- darpana and from Jayadeva’s Candraloka.

Baladeva composed verses in this treatise too. In the section on citra-kavya, this is his example of the necklace diagram:

*kuru taruni rusam nopatapa-prapanne*  
*bhaja nija-vijanam tara-hara-sphuranti \|*  
*stana-kanaka-nagau sata-pata-prataptam*  
*tanum anu tanutam bhava-sabalyavattam \|\|*

**Girl, do not be angry at Me. I am feeling the pain. You are resplendent with a necklace of pure pearls. Go to our secret meeting place. The two golden mountains of your breasts should cause the body, heated by a repeated fall of happiness, to experience a friction of emotions. (9.43)**

## The soul is Rasa

Although Sahitya-kaumudi is Baladeva Vidyabhusana’s “commen­tary” on Kavya-prakasa and Kavya-kaustubha is his “commentary” on Candraloka, and although in Sahitya-kaumudi he rewrote Mammata’s vrtti by taking inspiration from Snvatsa-lanchana’s commentary called Sara-bodhini, Baladeva Vidyabhusana is a master of poetical theory in his own right because he clearly established the philosophical conclusion that the soul is Rasa: atmaivanandamse vibhavadibhir bhagnavaranas tad-vyanjita- raty-ady-avacchinnas tat-sannibhas ca rasah, “The soul whose covering of its aspect of bliss is shattered by the vibhavas and so on is the Rasa, which is particularized by the sthayi, implied by those ones, and which is like that bliss.” (Sahitya-kaumudi 4.10) (KM p. 31). This Rasa is a once-in-a-lifetime epiphany.

Bhatta Nayaka, Abhinavagupta and Visvanatha said the bliss of relishing Rasa is like the bliss of the soul. Pandita-raja Jagannatha said the bliss of relishing Rasa is the bliss of the soul: “Transcendental consciousness (cit) (the soul’s awareness) whose covering is shattered and which is particularized by the sthayi is the Rasa (cid eva rasah).” Thus Pandita-raja Jagannatha lived up to his title. Baladeva Vidyabhusana changed the term citto atma, but the general idea is the same, since the soul is sat-cid-ananda. Dr. Jha observes:

And, in this state, a perceiver feels raso ’ham, “I am Rasa” or “Rasa is I”, and thus identifies himself with Rasa. According to the Vedantic theory, a soul is the very person in the form of light and bliss, and such indeed is Rasa. Furthermore, this unique experience cannot take place until and unless the cover of ignorance on the Soul is removed. \[...\] Through the combination of the trinity of Vibhava etc. the revealed state of Sthayin is Rasa. bhagnavarana-cid-visisto raty-adih sthayi bhavo rasa iti sthitam. vastutas tu vaksyamana-sruti-svarasyena \[arthat raso vai sa ity-adi\] raty-ady- avacchinna bhagnavarana cid eva rasah. (RG, KM pp. 22-23).

Vamana said that an implied sense can be a cause of samadhi. Jagannatha gives two scriptural statements to prove that Rasa is transcendental. Firstly, the highest bliss is attainable by the intelligence. And secondly, since God is Rasa, by the dictum raso vai sah, it follows that the souls are particles of Rasa. This explains Krishna’s statement in Bhagavad-gita:

*ascarya-vat pasyati kascid enam*  
*ascarya-vad vadati tathaiva canyah \|*  
*ascarya-vac cainam anyah srnoti*  
*srutvapy enam veda na caiva kascit \|\|*

**“Some see the soul as amazing, some describe the soul as amazing, some hear of the soul as amazing, whereas others cannot understand the soul even after hearing about it.” (2.29)**

Philosophy is the basis of Sanskrit poetics, and poetics thus explains philosophy. Things have come full circle.

Commenting on the verse, Baladeva Vidyabhusana says the word ascarya-vat can be interpreted in three ways: (1) As a modifier of the object of the verb, (2) As an adverb, or (3) As a modifier of the subject of the verb. In the first option, the sense is:

“Someone sees the soul, which is as if amazing.” The second option is: “Someone sees the soul in a way that is as if amazing.” Sankaracarya gives an example of the third option: “One who sees the soul is, as it were, marvelous.” The soul is as if amazing, not amazing, like Brahman is said to be nirvisesa (without a material attribute), because in Sanskrit rhetoric, words do not literally apply to a transcendental entity.

Vedanta philosophy states that a soul is transcendental:

♦ mamaivamso fiva-loke fiva-bhutah sanatanah, “In the world of living beings, My spark which is a soul is eternal” (Gita 15.7);

♦ ubhaya-vyapadesat tv ahi-kundala-vat, “But, because of both kinds of statements (bheda and abheda), Brahman and the souls are like a snake and its coil” (Vedanta-sutra 3.2.27);

♦ amso nana-vyapadesad anyatha capi dasa-kitavaditvam adhiyata eke (Vedanta-sutra 2.3.41);

♦ vifnanam brahma ced veda, tasmac cen na pramadyati, sarire papmano hitva sarvan kaman samasnute, “If one knows that the vifnana-maya purusa (a soul) is transcendental, and if one makes no big mistake in life, one sheds off all sins upon giving up the body and fulfills all one’s desires” (Taittiriya Upanisad2.5).

Abhinavagupta defines bliss (ananda) as follows: anando nirvrty- atma camatkarapara-paryayah, “Bliss is the life of joy and is a synonym of astonishment” (Locana 1.1). In short, the equation is: Bliss + Astonishment = Rasa. Bliss inherently involves some degree of astonishment, but when the astonishment goes through the roof, by the force of an over-the-top implied sense, the combination of the soul’s bliss and the astonishment is called Rasa. This is the spiritual counterpart of Einstein’s formula: E = mc2. The world revolves on Rasa. Its presence is felt everywhere, all the time. Even seemingly dry dealings like business transactions between people take place because of the persons’ rasa (mojo) (shadow effect of Rasa), since feelings dependent on appropriateness, trickery, and ego are involved.

Siva-prasada Bhattacarya says Baladeva Vidyabhusana was familiar with Rasa-gangadhara:

It is to be noted that the Bengal Vaisnavas generally, like the Jainas, were admirably informative, assimilating and adapting. Baladeva using the K.A. of Appaya Diksita and knowing the views of Jagannatha was no exception.

Perhaps this explains why Baladeva, like Jagannatha, says Bharata mentioned nine rasas — “navaiva rasah, pare tu bhavah” iti svatantrecchena munina paribhasanat (Sahitya-kaumudi 4.42)— even after citing Mammata’s quotation that Bharata listed eight rasas: astau natye rasah smrtah \[Natya-sastra 6.15\] (Kavya- prakasa 4.29) (Sahitya-kaumudi 4.11).

Baladeva Vidyabhusana wrote many other prominent works, including Govinda-bhasya (commentary on Vedanta-sutra) and Vaisnavanandim (commentary on the tenth canto of Bhagavatam).

Thus the soul is Rasa. People unconsciously equate rasa with passion when they say “Follow your passion” and the like. Everyone automatically and unknowingly seeks to realize that the soul is Rasa. For that purpose, those who are in the mode of tamo-guna use narcotics, those in the mode of rajo-guna have intercourse, and those in the mode of sattva-guna practice meditation, perform sankirtana, develop the Buddhist concept of feeling unconditional love for all beings, and so on. The rapture obtainable by means of poetry can be achieved by those who are in the mode of sattva- guna with a touch of rajo-guna. Music and other art forms are implicitly based on the fact that the soul is Rasa.

Rasa is the most fundamental principle of the universe. In the highest sense, the term Rasa is a synonym of Paramesvara (God): raso vai sah, “God is Rasa” (Taittiriya Up. 2.7). Hence Rasa is the substratum of Brahman too, given that Brahman is an aspect of God: anadi mat-param brahma (Bhagavad-gita 13.13).

According to the patriarch of modern poetics, ultimately the feeling of rasa (aesthetic delight) is meant to attract us to the path of dharma (moral ethics). Anandavardhana wrote: srngara-rasangair unmukhl-krtah santo hi vineyah sukham vinayopadesan grhnanti. sad-acaropadesa-rUpa hi natakadi-gosthi vineya-jana-hitartham eva munibhir avatarita, “The learners readily accept instructions of moral conduct only when the poetry caught their attention by means of aspects of srngara-rasa. Poetry, including dramaturgy, in the form of instructions about moral conduct was introduced by Bharata Muni and others only for the benefit of the learners, that is, those who deserve to be taught.” (Dhvany-aloka 3.30 vrtti)

Other instances of the manifestations of the soul in life should be looked into, such as intuition, extraordinary ability all of a sudden, a little miracle, and trance in meditation. In the first volume of the series Srimad Bhagavatam: A Symphony of Commentaries on the Tenth Canto, in the appendix on the second chapter I prove from scriptural texts that there are two types of life force (prana) in the body: normal and supernormal. The latter is the vehicle of the soul. Bruce Lee (1940-1973 CE) was known to access the supernormal aspect of the life force at will. Bruce Lee used to say, “Don’t think. feel.” The study of poetry increases our quotient of emotional intelligence (EQ).

There are two kinds of Bhakti Rasa outside the scope of literature: Either the senses are involved (the full bliss of sankirtana) or only the mind is involved. Both are out of this world (alaukika). The latter is induced by prayer (the Yoga of dejection) and is the ultimate form of love of Krishna (krsna-prema-rasa): the blend of nectar and poison: visamrte ekatra milana (Caitanya-caritamrta 2.2.51): This type of Bhakti Rasa is exactly the same as the vyabhicari- bhava called mrti (“death”, not desiring to live), the tenth and final stage of separation from the Lord, in its form of full-fledged relishment, and is depicted in the Bhagavatam verse 10.32.1. For more details on this type of love of God, consult my book Srimad Bhagavatam: A Symphony of Commentaries on the Tenth Canto: The Rasa-lila. Moreover, my articles on nirvisesa, savisesa, the supernatural life force, the Unified Theory of Vedanta, etc., can be downloaded from my Academia page: independent.academia.edu/ CharlesFilion.

## Afterword

## Einstein’s Three Stages of Religion

Albert Einstein (1879-1955) was the most famous scientist of the twentieth century. He is renowned for his Relativity Theory and for winning the Nobel prize of physics in 1921.
