But he also wrote several essays on religiosity. Five of them, composed between 1930 and the early 1950s, were published in his book Ideas and Opinions. In an article Einstein composed for the New York Times in 1930, he listed humankind’s three stages of religion: (1) Religion of Fear, (2) Moral Religion, and (3) Cosmic Religious Feeling. He expounds:

With primitive man it is above all fear that evokes religious notions — fear of hunger, wild beasts, sickness, death. Since at this stage of existence understanding of causal connections is usually poorly developed, the human mind creates illusory beings more or less analogous to itself on whose wills and actions these fearful happenings depend. Thus one tries to secure the favor of these beings by carrying out actions and offering sacrifices which, according to the tradition handed down from generation to generation, propitiate them or make them well disposed toward a mortal. In this sense I am speaking of a religion of fear.

... The social impulses are another source of the crystallization of religion. Fathers and mothers and the leaders of larger human communities are mortal and fallible. The desire for guidance, love, and support prompts men to form the social or moral conception of God. This is the God of Providence, who protects, disposes, rewards, and punishes; the God who, according to the limits of the believer’s outlook, loves and cherishes the life of the tribe or of the human race, or even of life itself; the comforter in sorrow and unsatisfied longing; he who preserves the souls of the dead. This is the social or moral conception of God.

... The truth is that all religions are a varying blend of both types, with this differentiation: that on the higher levels of social life the religion of morality predominates.

Common to all these types is the anthropomorphic character of their conception of God. In general, only individuals of exceptional endowments, and exceptionally high-minded communities, rise to any considerable extent above this level. But there is a third stage of religious experience which belongs to all of them, even though it is rarely found in a pure form: I shall call it cosmic religious feeling. It is very difficult to elucidate this feeling to anyone who is entirely without it, especially as there is no anthropomorphic conception of God corresponding to it.

The individual feels the futility of human desires and aims and the sublimity and marvelous order which reveal themselves both in nature and in the world of thought. Individual existence impresses him as a sort of prison and he wants to experience the universe as a single significant whole. The beginnings of cosmic religious feeling already appear at an early stage of development, e.g., in many of the Psalms of David and in some of the Prophets. Buddhism, as we have learned especially from the wonderful writings of Schopenhauer, contains a much stronger element of this.

The religious geniuses of all ages have been distinguished by this kind of religious feeling, which knows no dogma and no God conceived in man’s image; so that there can be no church whose central teachings are based on it. Hence it is precisely among the heretics of every age that we find men who were filled with this highest kind of religious feeling and were in many cases regarded by their contemporaries as atheists, sometimes also as saints. Looked at in this light, men like Democritus, Francis of Assisi, and Spinoza are closely akin to one another.

... I maintain that the cosmic religious feeling is the strongest and noblest motive for scientific research.

While it is true that scientific results are entirely independent from religious or moral considerations, those individuals to whom we owe the great creative achievements of science were all of them imbued with the truly religious conviction that this universe of ours is something perfect and susceptible to the rational striving for knowledge. If this conviction had not been a strongly emotional one and if those searching for knowledge had not been inspired by Spinoza’s Amor Dei Intellectualis, they would hardly have been capable of that untiring devotion which alone enables man to attain his greatest achievements.

Einstein’s main source of inspiration was Spinoza’s philosophy:

New York’s Rabbi Herbert S. Goldstein asked Einstein by telegram: “Do you believe in God? Stop. Answer paid 50 words.” In his response, for which Einstein needed but twenty- five (German) words, he stated his beliefs succinctly: “I believe in Spinoza’s God, Who reveals Himself in the lawful harmony of the world, not in a God Who concerns Himself with the fate and the doings of mankind.”

Spinoza (1632-1677) was a Dutch philosopher. Hegel said, “You are either a Spinozist or not a philosopher at all.” Spinoza’s teachings coincide with Vedanta philosophy: Max Muller noted the similarities between Vedanta and the system of Spinoza: “the Brahma, as conceived in the Upanishads and defined by Sankara, is clearly the same as Spinoza’s “Substantia”.” The 19th-century German Sanskritist Theodore Goldstucker wrote that Spinoza’s thought was

... a western system of philosophy which occupies a foremost rank amongst the philosophies of all nations and ages, and which is so exact a representation of the ideas of the Vedanta, that we might have suspected its founder to have borrowed the fundamental principles of his system from the Hindus, did his biography not satisfy us that he was wholly unacquainted with their doctrines... We mean the philosophy of Spinoza, a man whose very life is a picture of that moral purity and intellectual indifference to the transitory charms of this world, which is the constant longing of the true Vedanta philosopher... comparing the fundamental ideas of both we should have no difficulty in proving that, had Spinoza been a Hindu, his system would in all probability mark a last phase of the Vedanta philosophy.

Spinoza expounded pantheism, though it was first outlined in the hymn ofRg-Vedacalled Purusa-sUkta. For example:purusaevedam sarvam, “The entire universe is God” (Rg-Veda 10.90.2). The word pantheism is made from the Greek roots pan (all) and theos (God). But the Vedic version of pantheism involves a personal-like God within, as Paramatma, and personal manifestations of God both inside and outside the universe.

Furthermore, the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy states:

At its most general, pantheism may be understood positively as the view that God is identical with the cosmos, the view that there exists nothing which is outside of God, or else negatively as the rejection of any view that considers God as distinct from the universe.

... There are several different ways to think about pantheism. (1) Many of the world’s religious traditions and spiritual writings are marked by pantheistic ideas and feelings. This is particularly so for example, in Hinduism of the Advaita Vedanta school, in some varieties of Kabbalistic Judaism, in Celtic spirituality, and in Sufi mysticism. (2) Another vital source of pantheistic ideas is to be found in literature, for example, in such writers as Goethe, Coleridge, Wordsworth, Emerson, Walt Whitman, D.H. Lawrence, and Robinson Jeffers. Although it should be added that, far from being limited to high culture, pantheistic themes are familiar, too, in popular media, for example in such films as Star Wars, Avatar, and The Lion King.

. Spinoza, the most famous of all modern pantheists starts from the necessary existence of something he calls ‘substance.’ By this he means that which exists wholly in its own right, that whose existence does not depend upon anything else. The notion of ‘the Absolute’, or wholly unconditioned reality, as it figures in the philosophies of Schelling, Hegel, and the British Idealists may be considered a related development of the same philosophical starting point. In both cases the reasoning runs that this necessary being must be all-inclusive and, hence, divine.

. For Spinoza the claim that God is the same as the cosmos is spelled out as the thesis that there exists one and only one particular substance which he refers to as ‘God or nature’; the individual thing referred to as ‘God’ is one and the same object as the complex unit referred to as ‘nature’ or ‘the cosmos.’

... Even Spinoza suggests that the highest stages of knowledge consist in a form of intuitive insight, which transcends mere reasoning or conceptual knowledge in that it enables us to grasp the essence of individual things. Part of what he calls ‘the intellectual love of God’, such scientia intuitiva is itself assigned a salvific role in Spinoza’s thought; it is the path to human blessedness.

11\. Personal

Einstein was a pantheist but rejected any notion of a personal God. (Einstein 2010, 325)

... Spinoza’s God is an “infinite intellect”, (Ethics 2p11c) all knowing, (2p3) and capable of loving both Himself—and us, insofar as we are part of His perfection. (5p35c) And if the mark of a personal being is that it is one towards which we can entertain personal attitudes, then we should note too that Spinoza recommends amor intellectualis dei (the intellectual love of God) as the supreme good for man (5p33). \[.\] Moreover, while we may love God, we need to remember that God is really not the kind of being who could ever love us back. “He who loves God cannot strive that God should love him in return,” says Spinoza (5p19).

. A small number of pantheistic thinkers have attempted to develop more genuinely personal senses of immortality. For example, Spinoza controversially claims that “The human mind cannot be absolutely destroyed with the body, but something of it remains which is eternal” (Ethics e5p23). Josiah Royce, in his early Absolute Idealist phase, attempted to argue that if our finite will, which in this life is never quite satisfied, is itself but a part of a greater infinite will that is eternally satisfied, then that can only mean that we must find our share of that satisfaction “in a life that is not this present mortal life” (Royce 1906, 147).

The connection between God and us is rasa, in one way or another. The connection is intermittent. Moreover, God communicates indirectly: paroksam mama capriyam (Bhagavatam 11.21.35).

Pantheism appealed to Einstein, but he would rather call himself an agnostic:

Scientific research can reduce superstition by encouraging people to think and view things in terms of cause and effect. Certain it is that a conviction, akin to religious feeling, of the rationality and intelligibility of the world lies behind all scientific work of a higher order... This firm belief, a belief bound up with a deep feeling, in a superior mind that reveals itself in the world of experience, represents my conception of God. In common parlance this may be described as “pantheistic”.

My position concerning God is that of an agnostic. I am convinced that a vivid consciousness of the primary importance of moral principles for the betterment and ennoblement of life does not need the idea of a law-giver, especially a law-giver who works on the basis of reward and punishment.

In response to a question about whether or not he defined himself as a pantheist, Einstein wrote:

Your question is the most difficult in the world. It is not a question I can answer simply with yes or no. I am not an Atheist. I do not know if I can define myself as a Pantheist. The problem involved is too vast for our limited minds. May I not reply with a parable? The human mind, no matter how highly trained, cannot grasp the universe. We are in the position of a little child, entering a huge library whose walls are covered to the ceiling with books in many different tongues. The child knows that someone must have written those books. It does not know who or how. It does not understand the languages in which they are written. The child notes a definite plan in the arrangement of the books, a mysterious order, which it does not comprehend, but only dimly suspects. That, it seems to me, is the attitude of the human mind, even the greatest and most cultured, toward God. We see a universe marvelously arranged, obeying certain laws, but we understand the laws only dimly. Our limited minds cannot grasp the mysterious force that sways the constellations. I am fascinated by Spinoza’s Pantheism. I admire even more his contributions to modern thought. Spinoza is the greatest of modern philosophers, because he is the first philosopher who deals with the soul and the body as one, not as two separate things.

On the one hand, the soul is the witness (saksi): jagrat svapnah susuptam ca gunato buddhi-vrttayah, tasam vilaksano jivah saksitvena viniscitah, “Wakefulness, dreaming and deep sleep are the three functions of the mind, on account of the three modes of Nature. The soul is distinct from these functions and is thus ascertained as a witness” (Bhagavata Purana 11.13.27). But on the other, the ego is infused by the consciousness of the soul: karanam cid-acin-mayah, “The ego consists of real consciousness and material consciousness” (Bhagavatam 11.24.7). Sndhara Svami explains: cid-acin-mayah, cid-abhasa-vyaptatvad ubhaya-granthi- rupa iti, “The term cid-acin-maya means the ego is a knot of both, in the sense that the ego is pervaded by the soul” (Bhavartha-dipika 11.24.7). It’s as though the soul separated itself into two. That is as if amazing. Those two (soul, and ego + soul) are the components of the inner dialogue.

Further, Einstein also wrote:

The most important human endeavor is the striving for morality in our actions. Our inner balance and even our very existence depend on it. Only morality in our actions can give beauty and dignity to life. To make this a living force and bring it to clear consciousness is perhaps the foremost task of education. The foundation of morality should not be made dependent on myth nor tied to any authority lest doubt about the myth or about the legitimacy of the authority imperil the foundation of sound judgment and action.

Robert Goldman quotes Einstein as stating, “I have always believed that Jesus meant by the Kingdom of God the small group scattered all through time of intellectually and ethically valuable people.”

## Synchronicity

Ultimately, pantheism also involves the notion of synchronicity, not to mention that all souls are connected by the collective consciousness, or the collective unconscious, as Carl Jung (1875­1961) calls it. Moreover, Jung coined the word “synchronicity” to describe “temporally coincident occurrences of acausal events.”

Carl Jung’s belief was that, just as events may be connected by causality, they may also be connected by meaning; events connected by meaning need not have an explanation in terms of causality. Jung defines synchronicity as a meaningful coincidence inexplicable by chance.

On Feb. 25, 1953, in a letter to Carl Seelig, the Swiss author and journalist who wrote a biography of Albert Einstein, Jung wrote, “Professor Einstein was my guest on several occasions at dinner \[...\]. These were very early days when Einstein was developing his first theory of relativity \[...\]. It was he who first started me on thinking about a possible relativity of time as well as space, and their psychic conditionality. More than 30 years later the stimulus led to my relation with the physicist professor W. Pauli and to my thesis of psychic synchronicity.” Pauli had won the Nobel Prize in physics in 1945.

Carl Jung popularized the idea of unus mundus (one world), the concept of an underlying unified reality from which everything emerges and to which everything returns. Jung, in conjunction with the physicist Wolfgang Pauli, explored the possibility that his concepts of archetype and synchronicity might be related to the unus mundus—the archetype being an expression of unus mundus; synchronicity, or “meaningful coincidence”, being made possible by the fact that both the observer and connected phenomenon ultimately stem from the same source, the unus mundus.

A close associate of Jung, Marie-Louise von Franz stated towards the end of her life that the concept of synchronicity must now be worked on by a new generation of researchers.

Thus, the very first line of the Bhagavata Purana can be interpreted with a pun on the word arthesu (in things, or in meanings): janmady asya yato ’nvayad itaratas carthesu, “\[We meditate on Him\] from whom the creation, the continuation and the destruction of the universe take place because of His connection (anvayat) in meanings (arthesu) and (ca) because He is altogether distinct (itaratah) from them” (Bhagavatam 1.1.1).

Events connected in meaning do not necessarily occur at the same time. Everyone knows that sometimes there is a “sign” of something that is going to happen, or there is a sign that what happened to oneself is good or bad. There are man-made symbols and archetypal symbols. The study of poetry gives us a feel for symbolic usage and thus enables us to read the signs in life, to make our hearts receptive, and to express ourselves in metaphorical language. The term “poetic justice” is an offshoot of this understanding.

Among the arts, music best facilitates a taste of Rasa. The full- fledged Rasa, experienced by reading poetry, is unexcelled, though very rarely achieved, but the state where Rasa filters into the consciousness, by highly relishing the poetry, is attainable every now and then. At any rate, art gets our mojo going. That is rasa. Therefore Einstein wrote:

How can cosmic religious feeling be communicated from one person to another, if it can give rise to no definite notion of a God and no theology? In my view, it is the most important function of art and science to awaken this feeling and keep it alive in those who are receptive to it.

## Appendix I

## The Best of Bhartrhari’s Three Centuries

Bhartrhari (c. 50 BCE) wrote three centuries: Niti-sataka, Srngara-sataka, and Vairagya-sataka. He is not the Bhartrhari who wrote Vakya-padiya: Many Indian scholars say the writer of the three centuries was a king of Ujjain in the first century BCE and the elder brother of Vikramaditya. The Bhartrhari who wrote Vakya-padiya flourished circa 600 CE. Dr. Belvalkar notes:

This gives us 650 A.D. as the lower limit for Chandragomin. The upper limit is supplied by a vrtti on the Chandra sutras, \[...\] This gives us 470 as the approximate date for Chandragomin. This result is further confirmed by the fact that Vasurata, the preceptor of Bhartrhari, acknowledged Chandracharya (Chandragomin) as his master. Chandragomin must have lived therefore at least two generations before the author of the Vakyapadiya.

According to Encyclopedia Britannica, however, the author of the three centuries also wrote Vakya-padiya:

Bhartrihari, (born 570? ce, Ujjain, Malwa, India—died 651?, Ujjain) Hindu philosopher and poet-grammarian, author of the Vakyapadiya (“Words in a Sentence”) \[...\]. Of noble birth, Bhartrihari was attached for a time to the court of the Maitraka king of Valabhi (modern Vala, Gujarat), where most likely his taste for sensuous living and material possessions was formed.

\[...\] Three of the works attributed to Bhartrihari are titled shataka (“century”): the Shringara (love)-shataka, Niti (ethics and polity)-shataka, and Vairagya (dispassion)-shataka.

Vettam Mani gives yet a different account of the literary Bhartrhari: “Bhartrhari was the son of Vidyasagara, a great brahmin scholar who lived in Pataliputra. There is a legend about the birth of Bhartrhari in Uttara Bharata.” (Puranic Encyclopedia, p. 124). One day, Vidyasagara went to Kalinga, became exhausted and took rest on the doorstep of some house:

When he was fit for travel he started to go but Mandakini objected and requested him to marry her. Vidyasagara did not agree to it and she took him to the King and told him all that had happened. Finding Vidyasagara to be one with great erudition and good manners he decided that Vidyasagara should marry his daughter (a Ksatriya), daughter of his minister (a brahmin), daughter of Kulapati (a vaisya), and also Mandakini (a Sudra). There was an injunction in those days that a brahmin should marrya Sudra only after having married from all the higher castes. The decision of the King surmounted this difficulty for Vidyasagara to marry the sudra girl, Mandakini. Marriages were all conducted in order. The King’s daughter bore the name Kalavati, the minister’s Malati and Kulapati’s Sumangali. Each delivered a son. The brahmin boy was named Vararuci, the Ksatriya boy, Vikramaditya, the Vaisya boy, Bhatti and the Sudra boy, Bhartrhari.

2\) Kingship. When the King of Kalinga became old he gave the kingdom to Vidyasagara and whenVidyasagara died all his other sons made Bhartrhari the King.

Thereafter Vettam Mani relates the famous mango story. In the end, Vettam Mani mentions the three centuries but not Vakya-padiya.

**Because of not knowing the burning nature of it, a moth might fall in an intense fire if it wants to. Owing to ignorance, a fish might eat the bait on a hook if it wants to. Yet we do not renounce material objects, interwoven in the net of ether, though we have an understanding in this matter. Ha! Such is the profound greatness of bewilderment.**

*38*  
*vyaghriva tisthati jara paritarjayanti*  
*rogas ca satrava iva praharanti deham \|*  
*ayuh parisravati bhinna-ghatad ivambho*  
*lokas tathapy ahitam acaratiti citram \|\|*

**Like a tigress, old age is threatening to pounce. Diseases assail the body like enemies do. Life is ebbing like water from a leaking pot. Yet, how strange, people keep doing unbeneficial things.**

*50*  
*ksanam balo bhutva ksanam api yuva kama-rasikah*  
*ksanam vittair hinah ksanam api ca sampurna-vibhavah \|*  
*jara-jirnair angair nata iva vali-mandita-tanur*  
*narah samsarante visati yamadham-yavanikam \|\|*

**A human is like a theatrical performer:**  
**Having become a child for a short duration,**  
**One turns into a youth, but not forever,**  
**And relishes sensory gratification.**  
**For some time, one is devoid of affluence,**  
**Later, for a trice**  
**One becomes replete with opulence.**  
**At the end of life,**  
**The body is adorned with wrinkles and with limbs old.**  
**Then one goes behind the curtain to Yama’s abode.**

*84*  
*mahesvare va jagatam adhisvare*  
*janardane va jagad-antar-atmani \|*  
*na vastu-bheda-pratipattir asti me*  
*tathapi bhaktis tarunendu-sekhare \|\|*

**I do not perceive a real difference between bhakti to Mahesvara, the overlord of the worlds, and bhakti to Janardana, the inner Soul of the universe. Still, \|**  
**am devoted to him who is youthful and has the crescent moon on his head.**

*85*  
*sphurat-sphara-jyotsna-dhavalita-tale kvapi puline*  
*sukhasinah santa-dhvanisu rajanisu dyu-saritah \|*  
*bhavabhogodvignah siva siva sivety ucca-vacasah*  
*kada yasyamo ’ntargata-bahula-baspakula-dasam \|\|*

**On nights when the sounds are peaceful, when shall we who are afflicted by the snake of material life sit comfortably somewhere on a bank on the Ganges’ shore where the ground is whitened by an intensely radiating moonlight and become overwhelmed by tears that penetrate the heart while exclaiming “Siva Siva Siva”?**

## A Verse of Vakrokti by Ratnakara

The Kashmiri poet Ratnakara popularized the vakrokti ornament (ambiguous speech). Here is an example:

*tvam me nabhimato bhavami sutanu svasrva avasyam matah*  
*sadhuktam bhavata na me rucita ity atra bruve ’ham punah \|*  
*mugdhe nasmi nameruna nanu citah preksasva mam patu vo*  
*vakroktyeti haro himacala-bhuvam smerananam mukayan \|\|*

**Parvati: You’re not dear to me (me nabhimatah = me na abhimatah).**

**Siva (thinking she said me nabhi-matah, “A relative of mine thinks highly of you”): ’Tis true, slender one. My mother-in­law thinks highly of me.**

**Parvati: You said that nicely. But I don’t like you (na me rucitah).**

**Siva (thinking she said nameru-citah): I have this much to say about that, simple woman: I don’t have nameru flowers. Look at me.**

**May Siva, who silenced the smiling mouth of Himalaya’s daughter with equivoque in this way, protect you all.**

**(Vakrokti-pancasika)**

## Appendix II

## Illustrative Examples by Pandita-raja Jagannatha

The best examples were shown in the present writer’s translation of Sahitya-kaumudi, in chapters 10 and 11. Not counting Jagannatha’s verses mentioned earlier in this book, the rest of Jagannatha’s best examples are shown henceforth:

## Deva-rati bhava-dhvani

*na dhanam na ca rajya-sampadam*  
*na hi vidyam idam ekam arthaye \|*  
*mayi dhehi manag api prabho*  
*karuna-bhangi-tarangitam drsam \|\|*

**Перевод:**

**O Lord, becoming rich does not matter to me; I do not seek kingly opulence nor do I thirst for knowledge. I only want one thing: Send a wave of Your merciful glance on me.**  
**(Rasa-gangadhara, Kavya-mala edition p. 97)**

## Vipralambha

*avirbhuta yad-avadhi madhu-syandini nanda-sunoh*  
*kantih kacin nikhila-nayanakarsane karmana-jna \|*  
*svaso dirghas tad-avadhi mukhe pandima ganda-yugme*  
*sunya vrttih kula-mrga-drsam cetasi praduraslt \|\|*

**Перевод:**

**When Krishna’s unique luster which exudes nectar and which knows the magic for attracting everyone’s eyes became conspicuous, the long sighs in the mouths of the doe-eyed gopis, as well as the paleness on their cheeks and a void in their mental functions, made their appearance. (KM pp. 34-35)**

**Комментарий:**

Commenting on the above verse, Pandit Badarinatha Jha says the verse features the variety of atisayokti where the cause and its effect occur simultaneously. The purpose of this variety is to express the quickness of the efficacy of the cause.

## Pravasa-vipralambha

*nayanancalavamarsam ya na kadacitpura sehe \|*  
*alingitapi josam tasthau sa gantukena dayitena \|\|*

**Перевод:**

**Though embraced by her lover, who intended to go to a distant place, she who could never bear the contact of his sidelong glance prior to their marriage remained silent. (KM p. 35)**

## Karuna-rasa

*apahaya sakala-bandhava- cintam udvasya guru-kula-pranayam \|*  
*ha tanaya vinaya-salin katham iva para-loka-pathiko ’bhuh \|\|*

**Перевод:**

**Dear son, you abounded in humility. You gave up thinking about all your friends and relatives and put aside your love for your elders. Alas, why did you travel to the next world? (KM p. 35)**

## Santa-rasa

*malayanila-kalakutayo*  
*ramam-kuntala-bhogi-bhogayoh \|*  
*svapacatmabhuvo nirantara*  
*mama jata paramatmani sthitih \|\|*

**Перевод:**

**My outlook toward the Malaya wind and poison, toward the braid of a pretty woman and the body of a snake, and toward an outcaste and Brahma continuously takes place with regard to the inner Soul. (KM p. 35)**

## Raudra-rasa

*navocchalita-yauvana-sphurad-akharva-garva-jvare*  
*madiya-guru-karmukam galita-sadhvasam vrscati \|*  
*ayam patatu nirdayam dalita-drpta-bhubhrd-gala-*  
*skhalad-rudhira-ghasmaro mama parasvadho bhairavah \|\|*

**Перевод:**

**\[His meditation broken by hearing the sound of the breaking of Siva’s bow, Parasurama said to himself:\]**

**Let my dreadful axe, which consumed the blood coming out of the split necks of haughty kings, mercilessly fall on whomever dauntlessly broke my guru’s bow. The fever of overweening pride of that culprit sprang up because of fresh youth.(KM p. 36)**

## Yuddha-vira-rasa

*rane dinan devan dasa-vadana vidravya vahati*  
*prabhava-pragalbhyam tvayi tu mama ko ’yam parikarah \|*  
*lalatodyaj-jvala-kavalita-jagaj-jala-vibhavo*  
*bhavo me kodanda-cyuta-visikha-vegam kalayatu \|\|*

**Перевод:**

**\[Rama speaks:\] Hey ten-faced Ravana, you’re puffed because of your prowess since you made the gods miserable in battle and put them to flight, but I don’t need an armor to fight with you. Only Siva, who consumes the entire universe by the might of the blaze arising from his forehead, should feel the velocity of the arrows shot from My bow. (KM p. 40)**

## Dana-vira-rasa

*kiyad idam adhikam me yad dvijayarthayitre*  
*kavacam amaraniyam kundale carpayami \|*  
*akarunam avakrtya drak krpanena niryad-*  
*bahala-rudhira-dharam maulim avedayami \|\|*

**Перевод:**

**\[Karna speaks to people who are perplexed by his intention to return to Indra, begging with the attire of a Brahmana, two of his war implements:\]**

**The unattractive cuirass and earrings I am offering to the desirous Brahmana are somewhat superfluous in my case. I would even nonchalantly and quickly cut off my head with a sword and offer it while the blood is profusely gushing.**

**Комментарий:**

According to Jagannatha, Karna’s pride and his remembrance of his illustriousness in terms of having the sun god as a father are two sancari-bhavas implied from the word me (in my case), which is an arthantara-sankramita-vacya dhvani (an implied meaning in regard to which the literal sense changes to another sense: “in my case” means “in the case of powerful me”). In the Battle of Kuruksetra, Arjuna defeated Karna after Indra retrieved those two gifts.

## Daya-vira-rasa

*na kapota bhavantam anv api*  
*sprsatu syena-samudbhavam bhayam \|*  
*idam adya maya trm-krtam*  
*bhavad-ayuh-kusalam kalevaram \|\|*

*na kapotaka-potakam tava*  
*sprsatu syena manag api sprha \|*  
*idam adya maya samarpitam*  
*bhavate carutaram kalevaram \|\|*

**Перевод:**

**\[King Sivi was widely renowned for his unselfishness. Agni and Indra decided to test him. Agni took the form of a dove and Indra that of a hawk. The dove went to Sivi and sought protection. Sivi said:\]**

**All right, dove, have no fear of the hawk. Today I shall render my body insignificant like grass so that you may live long. \[Then the hawk came. Sivi said:\] Hawk, even your thoughts should not touch this young dove. Let me offer this beautiful body of mine to you. (KM pp. 39-40)**

**Комментарий:**

According to The Puranic Encyclopedia, which refers to chapter 197 of the vana-parva of Mahabharata, at first the hawk told Sivi that to save the dove Sivi would have to cut from his right thigh a body mass equal in weight to that of the dove. The king began to put his flesh in the scale, but the dove was heavy. In the end, the king put his whole body in the scale. Then the hawk flew away; Agni assumed his original form and told the king everything.

## Dharma-vira-rasa

*sapadi vilayam etu rajya-laksmir*  
*upari patantv athava krpana-dharah \|*  
*apaharatutaram sirah krtanto*  
*mama tu matir na manag api dharmat \|\|*

**Перевод:**

**\[Yudhisthira speaks to someone who was proposing the idea that the enemy should be overcome by immoral means:\]**

**Let the opulence of the kingdom at once come to nil, or let swords fall on my head, or let personified death decapitate me— my mind will not even slightly deviate from moral principles. (KM pp. 40-41)**

## Adbhuta-rasa

*caracara-jagaj-jala-sadanam vadanam tava \|*  
*galad-gagana-gambhiryam viksyasmi hrta-cetasa \|\|*

**Перевод:**

**\[Yasoda speaks:\] Seeing Your mouth, my mind is blown away. Your mouth is the substratum of the network of all things, and in it the vastness of outer space vanishes. (KM p. 42)**

## Hasya-rasa

*sri-tata-padair vihite nibandhe*  
*nirupita nutana-yuktir esa \|*  
*angam gavam purvam aho pavitram*  
*katham na va rasabha-dharma-patnyah \|\|*

**Перевод:**

**\[A boy speaks: \] This is the new theory propounded in the book written by my venerable father: “The front part of a cow is pure.” For that matter, why not say that the front part of the chaste wife of a donkey is pure? (KM p. 43)**

## Bhavodaya

*viksya vaksasi vipaksa-kamini-*  
*hara-laksma dayitasya bhamini \|*  
*amsa-desa-valayi-krtam ksanad*  
*acakarsa nija-bahu-vallarim \|\|*

**Перевод:**

**Upon noticing the mark of a rival ladylove’s necklace on her lover’s chest, the beautiful woman at once withdrew her creeper-like arm, which had become like a large bracelet on his shoulder.**

**Комментарий:**

A rise of anger is implied: rosodayo vyangyah (KM p. 103). In addition, the word bhamini (beautiful woman; vixen) suggests the rise of anger. Jagannatha equates rosa with the vyabhicari-bhava called amarsa (indignation).

Moreover, Jagannatha says krodha, a sthayi-bhava, and amarsa both denote anger; the difference is based on the nature of object of the anger. Therefore he equates amarsa with mana (pique). Rupa Gosvami, however, says that although rosa is one of three types of krodha, rosa is actually an additional vyabhicari-bhava of srngara-rasa. In effect Rupa Gosvami equates rosa with mana (pique).

## A svatah-sambhavi alankara occasions a vastu-dhvani

*nadanti mada-dantinah parilasanti vaji-vrajah*  
*pathanti virudavalm ahita-mandire vandinah \|*  
*idam tad-avadhi prabho yad-avadhi pravrddha na te*  
*yuganta-dahanopama nayana-kona-sona-dyutih \|\|*

**Перевод:**

**O king, on the enemies’ properties, ruttish elephants trumpet, horses look great, and the bards recite hymns so long as the cosmic-fire-like splendor of the redness of your eyes does not occur.**

**Комментарий:**

Here the simile suggests the idea that the enemies’ affluence will come to nil right when the king’s anger will take place. According to Jagannatha, this implied idea is first-rate because it is outstanding although technically it is second-rate since it is an aspect of the speaker’s affection for the king.

## A kavi-praudhokti-siddha vastu occasions a vastu-dhvani

*tad-avadhi kusali purana-sastra-*  
*smrti-sata-caru-vicarajo vivekah \|*  
*yad-avadhi na padam dadhati citte*  
*harina-kisora-drso drsor vilasah \|\|*

**Перевод:**

**The discernment originating from a resplendently careful study of hundreds of Puranas and smrti scriptures is in good condition so long as the flirtation of the eyes of a fawn-eyed woman does not find a place in the mind.**

**Комментарий:**

Jagannatha explains:

*atra kamini-drg-vilase cetasi padam arpitavati vivekasya nasti kusalam iti vastuna drg-vilasa-kartrka- padarpanasya loka-siddhatvabhavat kavi-praudhokti-nispannena sunisanne tasmin ka kusala-carca vivekasyeti vastu vyajyate.*

**“Discernment is not in good condition when the dalliance of a beautiful woman’s eyes finds a place in the mind. That is the first idea. It is effected by the poet’s bold assertion because in real life there is no such thing as the flirtation of eyes that goes in the mind and finds a place to stay. The idea implied from that is: When that sort of flirtation is predominant in the mind, what at all can be said about the stability of the discernment?” (Rasa-gangadhara, KM p. 136).**

Jagannatha’s so-called implied sense is not “implied”. Rather, it is only the purport (tatparya) because it is simply a rewording of the verse.

## A kavi-praudhokti-siddha vastu occasions an alankara-dhvani

*sahankara-surasuravali-karakrsta-bhraman-mandara-*  
*ksubhyat-ksiradhi-valgu-vici-valaya-sri-garva-sarvamkasah \|*  
*trsna-tamyad-amanda-tapasa-kulaih sanandam alokita*  
*bhumi-bhusana bhusayanti bhuvanabhogam bhavat-kirtayah \|\|*

**Перевод:**

**O king, O ornament of the Earth, your fame, blissfully seen by the renunciants afflicted by thirst, adorns this planet. Your fame dispels the pride of the splendor of the Milk Ocean’s charming waves that occurred during the churning by means of Mandara Mountain which was rotated by the rope in the hands of the conceited gods and Daityas.**

**Комментарий:**

Here the vastu (idea) is the literal meaning of the verse. Jagannatha says the alankara-dhvani is an implied bhrantiman ornament (mistaken perception) (they mistook his fame for milk): atra kirteh sanandalokanena vastuna kavi-kalpitena dugdha-bhrantis tapasa- gata vyajyate (RG, KM p. 137). Alternatively, the verse suggests this implied utpreksa ornament (fanciful assumption): They think, “His fame is as good as milk, so it’s as if good enough to drink.”

## Luptopama (elliptical simile)

*kope ’pi vadanam tanvi tulyam kokanadena tu \|*  
*uttamanam vikare ’pi napaiti ramamyata \|\|*

**Перевод:**

**Slender woman, when you’re angry your face looks like a red lotus. Even when the best things undergo a modification, their loveliness does not go away. (KM p. 166).**

**Комментарий:**

The attribute of redness was elided from the first sentence: Her angry face is red like a kokanada lotus. This elliptical simile is technically called arthi vakya-gata dharma-lupta upama. Here the simile is part of the arthantara-nyasa ornament (corroboration).

## Upameyopama-dhvani

*gambhiryematimatrema mahimna paramema ca \|*  
*raghavasya dvitiyo ’bdhir ambudhes capi raghavah \|\|*

**Перевод:**

**Owing to an immeasurable profundity and an eminent great­ness, an ocean is second to Rama, and Rama is second to an ocean.**

**Комментарий:**

Jagannatha explains: dvitiya-sabdasya sadrsya-visiste sakty- abhavad vyaktir eva, “Suggestiveness occurs here because the word dvitiya (second) does not literally express a similarity” (KM p. 202).

## Ananvaya (self-comparison)

*krta-ksudraghaughan atha sapadi santapta-manasah samuddhartum santi tri-bhuvana-tale tirtha-nivahah \|*  
*api prayascitta-prasarana-pathatita-caritan naran urikartum tvam iva janani tvam vijayase \|\|*

**Перевод:**

**In the three worlds, many holy places exist to swiftly deliver people who committed minor sins and whose minds are afflicted. However, O Mother Ganges, you are like yourself: You resplendently abide to accept men whose deeds are out of the scope of the path of the implementation of atonement. (Ganga-lahari) (RG, KM p. 204)**

*ramayamanah sri-ramah sita sita-manorama \|*  
*mamantah-karane nityam viharetam jagad-guru \|\|*

**Перевод:**

**Rama is like Rama, and STta is enchanting like STta. May these two gurus of the world forever take pleasure in my mind. (KM p. 205)**

## Ananvaya-dhvani

*nagebhyo yantinam kathaya tatininam katamaya*  
*puranam samhartuh suradhuni kapardo ’dhiruruhe \|*  
*kaya va sri-bhartuh pada-kamalam aksali salilais*  
*tula-leso yasyam tava janani diyeta kavibhih \|\|*

**Перевод:**

**Tell us, O Mother Ganges: Out of many rivers emanating from mountains, by which river have Siva’s matted locks been ascen­ded, or by which river have Vishnu’s lotus feet been bathed, so that poets might allow a fraction of a comparison to you? (KM p. 210)**

## Smarana

*kvacid api karye mrdulam*  
*kvapi ca kathinam vilokya hrdayam te \|*  
*ko na smarati naradhipa*  
*navanitam kim ca sata-kotim \|\|*

**Перевод:**

**Upon seeing that your heart is sometimes soft and sometimes hard, O king, who would not remember butter and a thunder­bolt? (KM p. 224)**

*santy evasmis jagati bahavah paksino ramya-rupas*  
*tesam madhye mama tu mahati vasana catakesu \|*  
*yair adhyaiksair atha nija-sakham niradam smarayadbhih*  
*smrty-arudham bhavati kim api brahma krsnabhidhanam \|\|*

**Перевод:**

**There are many beautiful birds in this world, yet of those I have a great predilection for the cataka birds because when I see them they remind me of their friend, the cloud, hence some incredible Brahma named Krishna finds its way into my mind. (KM p. 221)**

## Eka-desa-vivarti Rupaka (partial overall metaphor)

*bhava-grisma-praudhatapa-nivaha-santapta-vapuso*  
*balad unmulya dran nigadam aviveka-vyatikaram \|*  
*visuddhe ’sminn atmamrta-sarasi nairasya-sisire*  
*vigahante duri-krta-kalusa-jalah sukrtinah \|\|*

**Перевод:**

**Virtuous persons whose bodies are scorched by the very torrid heat of the summer of material life and who have shaken off the mesh of sinful reactions forcefully and quickly pull out the fetters of nondiscernment and plunge into the pure nectar-lake, which has the coolness of desirelessness, of the soul.**

**Комментарий:**

Jagannatha says the implied metaphor is: Those virtuous individuals are elephants: atra sahacarair nigadadi-rupakaih sukrtisu gaja- rupakam aksipyate (RG, KM p. 232). Jagannatha mentions two kinds of eka-desa-vivarti rupaka, (1) The implied metaphor is the main metaphor, (2) The implied metaphor is a minor metaphor. The above illustrates the first kind. This is an example of the second kind:

*rupa-jala cala-nayana nabhy-avarta kacavali-bhujaga \|*  
*majjanti yatra santah seyam tarum-tarangim visama \|\|*

**Перевод:**

**Good men immerse themselves in the formidable river of a young woman in which there is the water of bodily beauty; fickle eyes; a whirlpool in the form of the central hollow; and snakes in the form of braids.**

**Комментарий:**

Jagannatha says the necessarily obtained metaphor is that a woman’s eyes are fish: purvam tu kaveh samarthyatvenabhimatasya rupakasyaksepah, iha tu samarthakatvenabhimatasya nayanayor mina-rupakasyeti visesah (RG, KM p. 232). Alternatively, the verse shows the fault called nyuna-pada (missing word) because in the standard of comparison the equivalent for the eyes is not stated. Jagannatha mentions that fault: bimba-pratibimba-bhave dharmamam upamanopameya-gatanam nyunadhikyam (RG, KM p. 191). Baladeva writes: sadharmya-gata nyunata nyuna-padata (Sahitya-kaumudi 10.267).

## Rupaka-dhvani

*kasturika-tilakam ali vidhaya sayam*  
*smeranana sapadi silaya saudha-maulim \|*  
*praudhim bhajantu kumudani mudam udaram*  
*ullasayantu parito harito mukhani \|\|*

**Перевод:**

**SakhT, in the evening put a musk tilaka on your forehead and, with a smiling face, visit the top of the palace immediately afterward: Let the night lotuses experience a full development as an exalted merriment, and let the front part of the directions shimmer. (KM p. 246).**

**Комментарий:**

The above verse also features a yamaka in “mudam uda” and a cheka anuprasa in “arito harito. ”

*timiram haranti haritam purah sthitam*  
*tirayanti tapam atha tapa-salinam \|*  
*vadana-tvisas tava cakora-locane*  
*parimudrayanti saraslniha-sriyah \|\|*

**Перевод:**

**Young woman of cakora-bird-like eyes, the effulgence of your face dispels the gloom in the front part of the directions and removes the renunciants’ woes. It takes away the resplendence of day lotuses.**

**Комментарий:**

Jagannatha comments: ihapi vadanam candra iti gamyate, “Here also it is implied that the face is a moon” (RG, KM p. 246).

## Niscayanta Sandeha

*capala jaladac cyuta lata va*  
*taru-mukhyad iti samsaye nimagnah \|*  
*guni-nihsvasiiaih kapir mams!*  
*niranaisid atha tam viyoginiti \|\|*

**Перевод:**

**Immersed in doubt: “Either a lightning flash fell from a cloud or a creeper descended from a tree,” Hanuman, an intelligent monkey, concluded from the heavy sighs that there was a woman separated from her husband. (KM p. 258)**

## Sandeha-dhvani (implied poetical doubt)

*tire tarunya vadanam sa-hasam*  
*nire sarojam ca milad-vikasam \|\|*  
*alokya dhavaty ubhayatra mugdha*  
*maranda-lubdhali-kisora-mala \|\|*

**Перевод:**

**Seeing the young woman’s smiling face on the shore and a open lotus on the water, the silly young bees, greedy for nectar, zoom to both.**

**Комментарий:**

The bees wonder: “Is a lotus this one or that one?”: atra kamala- dharmiko ’bhedena samsargena puro-varti-vyakti-dvaya- prakarakah kamalam idam idam veti bhramara-gatah samsayo vyangyah (RG, KM p. 260).

## Ullekha-dhvani

*analpa-tapah krta-koti-papa*  
*gadaika-sirna bhava-duhkha-jirndh \|*  
*vilokya gangam vicalat-tarangam*  
*ami samastah sukhino bhavanti \|\|*

**Перевод:**

**Those who are greatly afflicted, those who committed millions of sins, those who are rent by a major disease, and those who are withered by the unhappiness of material life become happy upon seeing the Ganges, whose waves go in special ways.**

**Комментарий:**

Jagannatha elaborates: atra purvardhodlritanam caturnam vilokana-kartrnam sukhitvoktya kramena tapa-papa-roga-bhava- ndsakatva-prakdrakdni grahanany aksipyante, “By the mention that the four kinds of onlookers become happy, these four types of understanding are implied sequentially: The Ganges ends the affliction of greatly afflicted people; the Ganges ends the sinful reactions of sinners; the Ganges ends the disease of diseased persons; and the Ganges ends the distress of material life of those who are so withered” (KM p. 277).

*bhasayati vyoma-gata*  
*jagad akhilam kumudinir vikasayati \|*  
*kirtis tava dharani-gata*  
*sagara-sutayasam aphalatam nayate \|\|*

**Перевод:**

**In the sky, your fame makes the entire world radiant and makes white lilies open. On Earth, your fame renders the endeavor for King Sagara’s sons useless.**

**Комментарий:**

This is implied: In the sky, Shah Jahan’s fame is a moon, and on Earth it is an ocean. This constitutes a sankara of ullekha-dhvani and rupaka-dhvani, according to Jagannatha. There is an ullekha- dhvani because the same thing, fame, is described differently with regard to different objects (locations). The fame of Shah Jahan is white (pure) like moonlight. In addition, Shah Jahan’s fame renders the ocean useless in the sense that his fame is expansive. It is also a vyatireka-dhvani (implied contrast): The ocean of his fame is vaster than any other ocean. Thus the second sentence of the verse constitutes the paryayokta ornament (circumlocution). It is based on a well-known fact (prasiddhi-vaisistya): Bhagiratha brought the Ganges from heaven for the purpose of purifying the ashes of the sixty-thousand sons of King Sagara (Bhagavatam 9.9.11). After Bhagiratha led the river to the ocean, he called the ocean sagara in honor of his ancestor Sagara (Monier-Williams’ Dictionary) (Mahabharata): sagarasya rajno yam iti sagarah (Sabda-kalpa- druma).

## Apahnuti (poetic denial)

*smitam naitat kintu prakrti-ramamyam vikasitam mukham brute mudhah kumudam idam udyat-parimalam \|*  
*stana-dvandvam mithya kanaka-nibham etat phala-yugam lata ramya seyam bhramara-kula-namya na ramam \|\|*

**Перевод:**

**This is not a smile, but a natural and lovely opening of a flower. Only a simpleton would call this a face; it is a fragrant lotus. That pair of breasts is sheer illusion: It is actually a pair of fruits that have the luster of gold. She is a ravishing creeper that deserves to be served by bees; she is not a beautiful woman. (KM p. 278)**

*syamam sitam ca sudrso na drso svarupam*  
*kintu sphutam garalam etad athamrtam ca \|*  
*no cet katham nipatanad anayos tadaiva*  
*moham mudam ca nitaram dadhate yuvanah \|\|*

**Перевод:**

**The eyes of a beautiful-eyed woman are not black and white. Rather they clearly are both poison and nectar. If they are not so, then why do young men always feel stupefaction and joy when her two eyes fall on them? (KM p. 278)**

*vadane vinivesita bhujangi*  
*pisunanam rasana-misena dhatra \|*  
*anaya katham anyathavalldha*  
*nahi jivanti jana manag amantrah \|\|*

**Перевод:**

**The creator placed a snake in the guise of a tongue in the face of slanderous backbiters, otherwise why do people lacking advice stop living? They are licked by it. (KM p. 279)**

*stanantar-gata-manikya-vapur bahir-upagatam \|*  
*mano ’nuragi te tanvi manye vallabham iksate \|\|*

**Перевод:**

**Slender girl, I think that your passionate heart (or red heart) sees the beloved. It has come out in the form of the large ruby between your breasts.**

**Комментарий:**

Here the perception is: “This is not a large ruby; it’s your heart.” In this verse as well, utpreksa is the foundation. In Visvanatha’s methodology, however, the wording “This is not a large ruby; it’s your heart” constitutes the niscaya ornament (certainty) because the standard of comparison is negated and the subject of the comparison is established in its place. Thus niscaya is the exact opposite of apahnuti. And alternatively the verse features a niscaya-dhvani. Optionally, the verse is simply a metaphor.

## Utpreksa

*viyoga-vahni-kunde ’smin hrdaye te viyogini \|*  
*priya-sanga-sukhayeva muktaharas tapasyati \|\|*

**Перевод:**

**Girl who feels the pang of love: On your heart, a boiler heated by the fire of separation, your pearl necklace is undergoing austerity as if for the happiness of an encounter with the lover.**

**Комментарий:**

As a double meaning, the pearl necklace (mukta-hara) has given up eating (muktahara = muktah aharo yena sah).

Jagannatha offers a tongue twister as another example of utpreksa (fanciful assumption):

*nayanendindirananda-mandiram milad-indiram \|*  
*idam indlvaram manye sundarangi tavananam \|\|*

**Пословный перевод:**

nayana—\[in the form\] of eyes; indindira—of bumblebees; ananda—of the bliss; mandiram—the house; milad-indiram— \[the face,\] in which resplendence (indira = laksml = srl = sobha); idam—this; indivaram—a lotus; manye—I think (a word expressive of utpreksa); sundara-angi—O woman with a beautiful body; tava—your; ananam—face.

**Перевод:**

**Beautiful girl, I think that your splendrous face, the hive of bliss for the bees of your eyes, is a lotus. (KM p. 304)**

## Slesa-mula Utpreksa

*kapola-palim tava tanvi manye*  
*lavanya-dhanye disam uttarakhyam \|*  
*vibhati yasyam lalitalakayam*  
*manohara vai sravanasya laksmih \|\|*

**Перевод:**

**Slender woman blessed with beauty, I think that your cheek, on which are charming curls (alaka) (or on which is the charming Alaka city, Kuvera’s capital), is the cardinal direction called the north. Indeed (vai), your cheek is resplendent with the delightful beauty (laksmi) of the ear (sravana) (or with the delightful wealth (laksmi) of Vaisravana). (Bhamim-vilasa 2.9)**

**Комментарий:**

Vaisravana is a name of Kuvera (Amara-kosa 1.1.72). Kuvera is the presiding deity of the north. Further, in his magnum opus Jagannatha rewrote the verse by referring to the king’s daughter: vibhati yasyam lalitalakayam manohara vai sravanasya laksmih, kapola-palim tava tanvi manye narendra-kanye disam uttarakhyam (RG, KM p. 305).

## Padartha-nidarsana

*aganyair indradyair iha parama-punyaih paricito*  
*jagaj-janma-sthana-pralaya-racana-silpa-nipunah \|*  
*prasarpat-piyusambudhi-lahari-lila-vilasito*  
*drg-antas te mandam mama kalusa-vrndam dalayatu \|\|*

**Перевод:**

**O Lord, in this world You are perceived by countless and highly meritorious persons, such as Indra, You are expert in the craft of fashioning the creation, the continuation and the destruction of the world, and You are resplendent with the playful waves of a wide Nectar Ocean. May Your sidelong glance extinguish my dark thoughts.**

**Комментарий:**

Here the nidarsana is a special type of metaphor (His sidelong glances are playful waves) in the sense that the metaphor is not implied as a first-rate implied meaning, since neither the upamana (standard of comparison) nor the upameya (subject of the comparison) is implied or directly expressed: atra drg-antambudhi- lahari-lilayor asraya-bhedad bhinnayor api sadrsya-mulas tadrupyabhimanah. aropo va drgante lahari-lilayah (RG, KM p. 341). The verse also features this first-rate implied metaphor: Each one of His eyeballs is the Nectar Ocean (the Milk Ocean).

*panau krtah panir ila-sutayah*  
*sa-sveda-kampo raghu-nandanena \|*  
*himambu-mandanila-vihvalasya*  
*prabhata-padmasya babhara sobham \|\|*

**Перевод:**

**\[This describes their wedding:\] Rama placed STta’s hand in His. Perspiring and trembling, her hand assumed the resplendence of a lotus agitated by snow flakes and by a mild breeze at dawn. (KM p. 341)**

**Комментарий:**

Here the perspiration and the trembling of Sita’s hand reflects the agitation of a lotus occasioned by cold dew drops and by a gentle breeze. Padartha-nidarsana is so called because it illustrates the meaning of a word (pada-artha) (the padartha is either the upamana or the similar attribute of the upamana).

## Sahokti

*bahu manyamahe rajan na vayam bhavatah krtim \|*  
*vipadbhih saha diyante sampado bhavata yatah \|\|*

**Перевод:**

**We do not think much of your deeds, O king, because you give wealth along with problems.**

**Комментарий:**

Here the sahokti is combined with vyaja-stuti (purva kartr- sahoktih, iyam tu karma-sahoktir vyaja-stuti-samvalita, RG, KM p. 358) and with slesa (literal double meaning): “Riches are given (diyante) by you, and so are problems.” That is, “Problems are ended (diyante) by you.” The verbal roots are \[du\]da\[n\] dane (to give) and do avakhandane (to destroy) respectively.

## Mala-sahokti

*unmulitah saha madena balad balarer*  
*utthapito bala-bhrtam saha vismayena \|*  
*nilatapatra-mani-danda-ruca sahaiva*  
*panau dhrto giridharena girih punatu \|\|*

**Перевод:**

**May Govardhana Hill cause a purification. The mountain was uprooted by Krishna, and so was Indra’s pride, by force. The mountain was raised by Krishna, and so was the amazement of powerful beings. Govardhana was held on His hand, and so was the splendor of a dark umbrella and of a jewelled handle.**

**Комментарий:**

In the verse, sahokti occurs three times. Each one is conjoined with the variety of atisayokti where the cause and its effect occur at the same time: Indra’s pride was uprooted at the same time that Krishna uprooted the mountain. The amazement of powerful beings went up at the same time that Krishna lifted the mountain. And the splendors of a dark umbrella and of a jewelled handle, the effects, occurred at the same time that holding Govardhana, the cause, took place. This third sahokti also features padartha- nidarsana (a metaphor where the upamana and the upameya are separately placed in a verse). It occurs twice: The splendor of a dark umbrella is superimposed on Govardhana Hill (Govardhana Hill was a dark umbrella), and the splendor of a jewelled handle is superimposed on His forearm (His forearm was a jewelled handle) (either His hand was the handle or the existence of the forearm is the purport of the mention of the hand): atra mlatapatra- mani-danda-ruco giri-dharanottara-kalikatvad uttarardha-gata paurvaparya-viparyayanupranitaiva sahoktir nidarsananupranita ca. purvardha-gate tu prakara-dvayenapi sambhavatah (RG, KM p. 364).

## Vinokti-dhvani

*na yabhyam alidha parama-ramaniya tava tanuh \|*  
*ayam tu nyak-karah sravana-yugalasya tri-pathage*

**Перевод:**

**Комментарий:**

The implied vinokti is twofold: Eyes are not resplendent without having seen the Ganges, and ears are not resplendent without having heard the tumult of the Ganges’ waves. Jagannatha adds that the verse features an anugnahya-anugnahakata sankana (facilitated and facilitator) between a bhava-dhvani (affection for the Ganges) (ganga-visaya-rati-dhvani), and vinokti-dhvani.

## Samasokti

*utsange tava gange*  
*payam payam payo 'timadhurataram \|*  
*samitakhila-srama-bharah*  
*kathaya kadaham ciraya sayitahe \|\|*

**Перевод:**

**O Ganga, tell me, when will I rest in peace for a long time? The whole burden of my exertion will be relieved by continuously drinking your sweeter-than-sweet water (or milk) in your depth (or on your lap).**

**Комментарий:**

This is samasokti (concise statement) because a noncontextual meaning (the rapport between a boy and his mother) is implied from the contextual topic (the dealings between the speaker and the Ganges) and because of an implied similarity: On account of gender and paronomastic modifiers, the behavior of the noncontextual meaning is superimposed unto the behavior of the contextual topic: atra sisu-janam-vrttantabhedena sthitah prakrta-vrttantah (RG, KM p. 377).

## Ruyyaka’s Samasokti

**Комментарий:**

Visvanatha and Jagannatha accept Ruyyaka’s fourfold classification of samasokti, which is based on the permutations between the mode of being of a thing from day-to-day life and the mode of being of a thing pertaining to some science. This example by Jagannatha illustrates the superimposition of the mode of being of a thing in a branch of science (suffixes, in grammar) on the mode of being of another thing in a branch of science (Brahma, in Vedanta):

*guna-vrddhlpare yasmin naiva stah pratyayatmake \|*  
*budhesu sad iti khatam tad brahma samupasmahe \|\|*

**Перевод:**

**“We revere Brahma, known as sat among the wise (in om tat sat). Brahma is of the nature of consciousness and is transcendental. The gunas and an increase do not occur in it.” Alternatively: “We revere transcendental sound (brahma = sabda-brahma) in the form of satr and sanac (yasmin = satr-sanaj-rupe). Guna and vrddhi never occur after them (pare = paratah vartamane). They are of the nature of suffixes and, among grammarians, are known as sat.”**

**Комментарий:**

In samasokti, the main nouns are not paronomastic. Thus, in the second interpretation, the noun brahma is used in a different shade of meaning, yet the difference is not drastic enough to be considered slesa (literal paronomasia) because by definition

Brahma is twofold in that way: brahma sabda-rupam artha-rupam cety arthah (Marma-prakasa, KM p. 384); dve brahman!veditavye sabda-brahma param ca yat I sabda-brahmani nisnatah param brahmadhigacchati \|\| (Visnu Purana 6.5.64)

The following verse is an example of the superimposition of the behavior of a scientific thing unto the behavior of a day-to-day thing: Jagannatha ingeniously superimposes the concept of the tat- purusa compound unto a man (purusa). Thus Jagannatha fittingly illustrates samasokti with paronomastic modifers in reference to a type of compound (samasa):

*parartha-vyasangad upajahad atha svartha-paratam*  
*abhedaikatvam yo vahati guna-bhutesu satatam \|*  
*svabhavad yasyantah sphurati lalitodatta-mahima*  
*samartho yo nityam sa jayatitaram ko’pi purusah \|\|*

**Перевод:**

**Some particular man is supereminent. He, completely giving up being dedicated to his own interest (svartha-parata) (or it gives up being solely focused on its very own meaning) because he is devoted to benefiting others (parartha-vyasanga) (or because of a close connection with the sense of the other), constantly entertains the notions of non-difference and oneness (abhedaikatvam) (or it carries the notion of oneness on account of non-difference) even in regard to inferior beings (guna- bhuta) (or in regard to the secondary thing). In his heart (antar) naturally shines a charming and elevated greatness (lalitodatta- mahima) (or its end, antah, which has the charming greatness of the udatta accent, is resplendent). He is always competent (samartha) (or it is always connected in sense).**

**Комментарий:**

Jagannatha says the double meanings refer to Patanjali’s commentary on Panini’s rule: samarthah pada-vidhih (Asiadhyay! 2.1.1). In this verse, the noun purusa (man) is not paronomastic because on the side of grammar the corresponding concept is purusa-sabda (a word such as “purusa ” in a tat-purusa compound).

The details are as follows: When a word such as purusa is combined with a word such as rajan to make the tat-purusa compound raja- purusa (the king’s man), compounding is possible because the two words are connected in sense (samartha) and because neither has an adjective outside the compound. The word purusa gives up its very own meaning (svartha-parata) because it is closely connected in sense (parartha-vyasanga) with the word rajan. This mutual suitability produces a new overall meaning, technically called ekarthi-bhava. In a tat-purusa compound, the first word is secondary (guna). It can be either singular (the king’s man), dual (the two kings’ man) or plural (the kings’ man): The actual number is unknown because the case ending was deleted in the formation of the compound, consequently the first word is supposed to have a number generally and not particularly. The technical name assigned to such a number is called abhedaikatva-sankhya. Moreover, in Vedic Sanskrit, a tat-purusa compound takes the udatta accent on the last syllable, by the rule: samasasya (Astadhyayi 6.1.223) (Siddhanta-kaumudi 3734).

## Abhanga Slesa

*kara-kalita-cakra-ghatano*  
*nityampitambaras tamo-’ratih \|*  
*nija-sevi-jadya-nasana-caturo*  
*harir astu bhutaye bhavatam \|\|*

**Перевод:**

**\[First interpretation:\]**

**May Hari exist for your well-being. He by whom the placement of the cakra is done on the hand (kara-kalita-cakra-ghatana) always has a yellow garment (pttambara). He is the enemy of ignorance (tamo-’rati). He is clever in ending the inertia of those who serve Him.**

## Sabhanga Slesa

*sambhuty-artham sakala-jagato visnu-nabhi-prapannam yan-nalam sa tribhuvana-gurur veda natho virincih \|*  
*dheyam dhanyalibhir atitaram sva-prakasa-svarupam padmakhyam tat kim api lalitam vastu vas tustaye ’stu \|\|*

**Пословный перевод:**

sambhuti-artham—for the sake of the origination (or for the sake of the complete prosperity); sakala-jagatah—of the whole world; visnu-nabhi-prapannam—it begins from Vishnu’s navel (or visnuna abhiprapannam—attained closeby by Vishnu; or visnu-nabhi-prapannam—it has attained the central point of Vishnu); yat-nalam—the stem of which \[lotus\] (or yat—since; na—not; alam—able); sah—that \[well-known\]; tribhuvana—of the three worlds; guruh—teacher; veda—he knows; na—not; atho— completely (or veda-nathah—the master of the Vedas); virincih— Brahma (“he creates”); dheyam—it should be meditated upon; dhanya-alibhih—by fortunate bees (or dhani-alibhih—by lady friends of rich people); atitaram—very much; sva-prakasa—is a self-manifestation; svarupam—whose nature; padma—as a lotus (or padma—Laksmi); akhyam—known; tat—that; kim api—some (i.e. remarkable); lalitam—charming; vastu—entity; vah—of you all; tustaye—for the satisfaction; astu—may it be.

**Перевод:**

**\[First interpretation:\]**

**May some incredibly lovely entity known as a lotus exist for your satisfaction. Brahma, the guru of the three worlds and the master of the Vedas, does not fully know its stem. That lotus begins from Vishnu’s navel and takes place for the sake of the origination of the whole world. The nature of that lotus is a self-manifestation. The lotus should be intensely meditated upon by fortunate bees.**

**\[Second interpretation:\]**

**Since Brahma, the guru of the three worlds and the master of the Vedas, is unable to effect the complete prosperity of the whole world, may some incredibly lovely entity called Padma exist for your satisfaction. She is near Vishnu. Her nature is a self-manifestation. She should be intensely contemplated upon by the female friends of rich people. (KM p. 391)**

**Комментарий:**
