## Appendix III (747)

## Mythology in Hinduism

Hinduism is often labeled as mythology. On the one hand, it cannot be denied that there is mythology in Vedic literature. For instance, nowadays in accordance with the Solar Nebula Theory, we know that the solar nebula, a cloud of interstellar gas and dust, condensed to form the sun and the planets of the solar system. However, the Bhagavata Purana states that Lord Varaha lifted the Earth globe from the Garbhodaka Ocean (Bhagavatam 2.7.1). In such contexts (2.7.1; 3.13.31; 3.18.2; etc.), that narrative is not described as an allegory: We are made to believe that it is a fact.

Similarly, in accordance with the Giant Impact Hypothesis, we are almost certain that about 4.5 billion years ago a gigantic collision between Earth and a protoplanet about half the size of Earth created a disk of molten rock, gas and debris that consolidated to form the moon. And therefore the moon goes away from the Earth at the rate of 3.78 centimeters (1.5 inches) per year. However, the Vedic belief is that the moon originates from the Milk Ocean; the Mahabharata states that the Moon god appeared from the Milk Ocean. The Vaishnava poets refer to the relation between the moon and the Milk Ocean: navadvlpe sacl-garbha-suddha-dugdha- sindhu, tahate prakata haila krsna purna indu, “Like a full moon, in Navadvipa, Krishna took birth from the Milk Ocean of Saci’s womb” (Caitanya-caritamrta 1.4.272); ekampunar alam abhavad apurvam, ajani vidhur bata yad itah purvam, “The moon arose after the churning of the Milk Ocean, but Krishna arose before the churning of the Milk Ocean” (Gopala-campu, verse 1.4.30). Some see the myth as an allegory. Nonetheless, in the context of the Churning, the Bhagavatam does not refer to the moon in any way (Bhagavatam 8.8). The Visnu Purana makes a distinction: tatah sltamsur abhavaj jagrhe tam mahesvarah, “Next the moon arose: Siva took it” (his crest is a crescent moon) (Visnu Purana 1.9.96).

Albert Einstein remarks that mythology is a form of symbolism: “It is this mythical, or rather this symbolic, content of the religious traditions which is likely to come into conflict with science.”

In addition, there are many obscure statements in Bhagavatam. For instance, the Bhagavatam says that from the Earth’s perspective the moon is farther than the sun. Several Vaishnava scholars clarified the matter. Richard L. Thompson writes:

The Bhagavatam verse 5.22.8 says that the moon is 100,000 yojanas above the sun, and this is often taken as a highly unscientific statement. However, it makes perfect sense from the point of view of the planisphere interpretation. The sun and the moon both require planes above the earth plane, but this has nothing to do with their distances from the earth globe.

On the other hand, the existence of the soul cannot be denied. The soul, the self, is real. It is cognizable, and the scriptures describe the process of transcendental meditation, the means to realize this. Only the Vaishnavas are in line with Vedic scriptures. In the West, monists such as Sankaracarya and Abhinavagupta are held in higher esteem that Vaishnavas, but Sankaracarya rejects part of Vedanta- sutra, a canonical text of Vedanta philosophy, by arguing that Vyasa is mistaken. In his commentary on: yatha ca taksobhayatah, “\[The soul is a doer\] in two ways, like a carpenter (by volition and through instruments: transcendental senses)” (Vedanta-sutra 2.3.38) (or 2.3.40), he writes: yat tuktam sastrarthavattvadibhir hetubhih svabhavikam atmanah kartrtvam iti tan na, “It was stated with several reasons, beginning from sastrartha-vattvat (“The soul is a doer, because this doership is as if the purpose of the scriptures” Vedanta-sutra 2.3.31), that the doership of the soul is inherent: That is wrong” (Sariraka-bhasya 2.3.38). For a refutation of Sankaracarya’s disapproval, consult my introduction in Sahitya- kaumudi.

Vedic poetry consists of Ramayana, Mahabharata, the Puranas, and poetical works based on bhakti. By the logic of fighting fire with fire, Vedic poetry pulls the mind, like pulling a wet garment made of cotton: The mind is stretched as if it were a wet T-shirt so that afterwards, in its normal state, it achieves the desired shape. Thus, the Bhakti works of Sanskrit Poetics dispel illusion by propounding better, poetical types of illusion. Poetry softens our hearts so they can be molded in the shape of higher values. Much like the experience of Rasa depends on the willful suspension of disbelief, the experience of bhakti-rasa is contingent on the belief that the Bhagavata Purana is a flawless scripture of divine origin. The theory regarding the transcendental nature of God’s names is indeed divine. To up the ante, the writers of the Bhagavatam contradicted the statement in Mahabharata and in Visnu Purana, which are widely regarded as authoritative texts, that Krishna’s body was burned after He passed away. The writers added that Krishna and Balarama learned the sixty-four arts, while studying at the school of Sandipani Muni (Bhagavatam 10.45.36) (ref. p. 92 above). The Bhagavatam was written sometime after 300 BCE, because it mentions Dhana Nanda, Chanakya, and Chandragupta Maurya (12.1.8-12). Yogamaya is the energy of divine illusions.

## Appendix IV

## Comparisons Between Sanskrit Poetics and English Poetics

In English poetics, figures of speech originate from the ancient Greeks’ classical rhetoric, whereas in Sanskrit poetics the figures originate from dramaturgy. Classical rhetoric, one of the seven liberal arts, is the art of persuasion. In Rhetoric, Aristotle mentioned three modes of persuasion: It is achieved by ethos, the speaker’s personal character; by logos, logical reasoning; and by pathos, the stirring of emotion in the hearers. Pathos corresponds to rasa. In a political speech, literary devices are important. In Rhetoric, Aristotle (384-322 BCE) remarked: “It is metaphor above all else that gives clearness, charm, and distinction to the style.” Aristotle also wrote Poetics.

The seven liberal arts are the trivium (grammar, logic, and rhetoric) and the quadrivium (arithmetic, geometry, astronomy, and music). Philosophy unites all seven. The tradition of first learning those three subjects was established in ancient Greece whereas the quadrivium was added in the Middle Ages. Poetics was studied as an offshoot of rhetoric: In Aristotle’s time, rhetoric and poetics were two aspects of the study of performance on stage. Aristotle wrote Politics and many other works. He taught Plato and was also the tutor of Alexander the Great, who made an incursion in India in 326 BCE.

In Sanskrit culture, political science and economics are based on Kautilya’s Artha-sastra (c. 300 BCE). To succeed, politicians and poets must be crooked in their manner of expression. And in day­to-day life, everyone needs to outfox the opposition.

In India, the status of Natya-sastra is akin to that of Aristotle’s Poetics in the West. There are obvious differences but also noteworthy similarities:

Bharata expounds the detailed physical movements and gestures of the actors, a topic ignored by Aristotle. \[...\] Moreover, both Aristotle and Bharata contend that the aim in drama is to convey certain emotions to the audience. However, Aristotle confines his discussion of the arousal of emotion by tragedy to a few remarks (for example, his contention that tragedy should arouse pity and fear for the purpose of catharsis and his claim that even hearing the basic plot outline should arouse these emotions). Bharata, on the other hand, develops a detailed taxonomy of emotion and emotional expression

Aristotle’s Poetics consisted of two parts: Only the first part— tragedy—has been recovered. The lost second part discussed comedy. Bharata Muni’s discourse on rasa is more elaborate than pity, fear, and humor. In addition, Bharata expounded meters, types of ladyloves, varieties of emotions, and music. In both works, a play more or less culminates in a moral. Aristotle’s Poetics also treats of lyric poetry and epic poetry. However, Aristotle’s main objective was to bring about catharsis:

A Catharsis is an emotional discharge through which one can achieve a state of moral or spiritual renewal or achieve a state of liberation from anxiety and stress. Catharsis is a Greek word and it means cleansing. \[.\] Originally, the term was used as a metaphor in Poetics by Aristotle to explain the impact of tragedy on the audiences. He believed that catharsis was the ultimate end of a tragic artistic work and it marked its quality. He further said in Poetics:

“Tragedy is an imitation of an action that is serious, complete, and of a certain magnitude; . . . through pity \[eleos\] and fear \[phobos\] effecting the proper purgation \[catharsis\] of these emotions” (c. 350 BCE, Book 6.2).

For example: “Here’s to my love! \[Drinks\] O true apothecary! Thy drugs are quick. Thus with a kiss I die. \[Falls\]” (Romeo and Juliet, by Shakespeare):

In “Romeo and Juliet”, Romeo commits suicide by drinking the poison that he erroneously thinks Juliet had tasted too. The audience usually finds themselves crying at this particular moment for several reasons. Primarily because losing a loved one is a feeling that all of us share. Watching or reading such a scene triggers the memories of someone we have lost (either by death or by mere separation) and because we are able to relate to it, we suddenly release the emotions that we have been repressing.

**Function of Catharsis: Dramatic uses**

In dramatic art the term catharsis explains the impact of tragedy, comedy or any other form of art on the audience and in some cases even on the performers themselves. Aristotle did not elaborate on the meaning of “catharsis” and the way he used it in defining tragedy in the Poetics (1449b21-28).

In Sanskrit poetics, catharsis corresponds to a sublime form of sadharanya (empathy). Comedy best causes catharsis. A Comedy, for example Kandarpa-keli, is called prahasana, where the six kinds of hasya must be used: sad-vidho hasya eva tu (Dasa-rupaka 3.50). In Sanskrit dramaturgy, a Comedy is very rare, and there is no such thing as a “Tragedy.” Every play must end on a good note.

Moreover, according to Aristotle and other Greek rhetoricians, rhetoric has five canons or established principles. These principles outline the systems of classical rhetoric:

Invention: To discover the available means of persuasion. Arrangement: To select and assemble the argument effectively. Style: To present the argument cogently and eloquently.

Memory: To speak extemporaneously.

Delivery: To effectively use voice, gestures, text, and images.

After the Middle Ages, the list of seven liberal arts evolved:

In the Renaissance, the Italian humanists, who in many respects continued the grammatical and rhetorical traditions of the Middle Ages, rechristened the old Trivium with a new and more ambitious name: Studia humanitatis, and also increased its scope. They excluded logic and added to the traditional Latin grammar and rhetoric not only history, Greek, and moral philosophy (ethics), but made poetry, once a sequel of grammar and rhetoric, the most important member of the whole group.

Nowadays the term rhetoric also denotes the science of all literary uses of language in prose or verse, including the figures of speech. Scholars of classical Western rhetoric divided figures of speech in two main categories: schemes and tropes. Schemes—from the Greek schema, form or shape—are figures of speech characterized by an artful deviation from the ordinary arrangement of words, whereas a trope—from the Greek tropos, turn—is an artful deviation from the ordinary or principal signification of a word. For the most part, a trope is any literary or rhetorical device that consists in the use of words in other than their literal sense (Webster’s Dictionary).

Examples of tropes that do not consist of figurative usage are: simile, rhetorical question, and onomatopoeia.

During the Renaissance, English scholars meticulously enumerated and classified figures of speech. Henry Peacham, in his The Garden of Eloquence (1577), enumerated 184 different figures of speech. The count continued to increase. Professor Robert DiYanni writes: “Rhetoricians have catalogued more than 250 different figures of speech, expressions or ways of using words in a nonliteral sense.” A figure of speech is also called rhetorical figure, figure of style, or simply figure:

The Greeks called them “schemes”, a better word than “figures”, because they serve as persuasive tricks and rules of thumb. While Shakespeare had to memorize more than 200 of them in grammar school, the basic ones aren’t hard to learn. Figures of speech change ordinary language through repetition, substitution, sound, and wordplay. They mess around with words—skipping them, swapping them, and making them sound different.

According to Kenneth Burke (1897-1993), in rhetoric the four master tropes are metaphor, metonymy, synecdoche, and irony. In addition, simile, hyperbole and personification are often used.

In summary, the categories of schemes are: (1) Structures of balance, (2) Change in word order, (3) Omission, and (4) Repetition.

The categories of tropes are: (A) Reference to one thing as another, (B) Wordplay and puns, (C) Substitutions, (D) Overstatement/ Understatement, and (E) Semantic inversions.

The three concepts of ethos, logos and pathos also apply in poetics. In classical rhetoric, “The personality of the orator outweighs the issues.” Similarly, in poetry quite often the readers think that the text must be relishable since the author is renowned. In poetry, logos corresponds either to figurative usage or to the Dhvani theory at large. And pathos is the power of a literary device to evoke emotion in the readers.

Aristotle is famous for saying “Probable impossibilities are to be preferred to improbable possibilities.” With regard to the requirements of art, a probable impossibility is to be preferred to a thing improbable and yet possible. In short, Probable Impossibility refers to a situation that is impossible to happen in the real world, but is probable in the universe of imaginary events. For example: Fish raise families, are able to talk, and set out on a journey, etc. Improbable Possibility refers to a situation that is a possibility in the real world, but is extremely unlikely. For instance, James Bond winning every poker game.

By extension, in Sanskrit poetics the kavi-praudhokti variety (the poet’s bold assertion) of implied meaning is more astonishing than the svatah-sambhavi variety (naturally possible in day-to-day life).

**Technical Differences Between English Poetics and Sanskrit Poetics**

(I) Sanskrit poetics involves a high degree of paronomasia: Many words have many meanings. By nature, speech in Sanskrit involves phonetic combinations conducive to puns. Many new words can be formed etymologically, by adding some suffix after a verbal root. And a compound, especially a bahuvrihi, can be derived in various ways. But a new word cannot be formed by joining truncated words. Moreover, in English a double meaning is a double meaning, but in Sanskrit a double meaning is either literal (slesa) or implied (dhvani).

(II) In Sanskrit, there is a methodology for analyzing an implied meaning, especially because a first-rate implied sense is considered the soul of poetry.

(III) In Sanskrit, the same word cannot be an object of repeated figurative usage, unlike a metaleptical word such as Bollywood.

(IV) In Sanskrit, the categories of lovers and of ladyloves have been systemized to a high degree. This detailed categorization causes predictability and thus limits the scope of the characters. Still, Sanskrit culture makes it clear that love involves relishing the nature of the other person, not just the looks.

(V) In a typical Sanskrit drama, the Hero and other primary characters speak in Classical Sanskrit, often in verse (a drama is a campu of sorts), whereas the Heroine and minor characters speak in a Prakrit language, even in the same conversation. But Rupa Gosvami let Paumamasi, a female character, speak Sanskrit.

(VI) The Hindu drama is very structured. In the introduction, the playwright must follow the rules regarding the specific types of intro. Afterward, there are five artha-prakrtis (the elements of the plot: bya (seed of the storyline), bindu (drop, i.e. development), pataka (incidental episode), prakan (minor incidental episode) and karya (denouement)), which correspond to the five avasthas (the stages of action: arambha (commencement), yatna (endeavor), prapty-asa (prospect of success), niyatapti (some success) and phalagama (consummation)). The five sandhis (mukha, pratimukha, garbha, avamarsa and nirvahana) combine an artha-prakrti with its corresponding avastha. The sandhis have subdivisions which total sixty-four. For example, the mukha-sandhi combines the bya and the arambha and has twelve subdivisions, which can be used out of sequence, yet the playwright must, according to Dhanika, use at least these six subdivisions: upaksepa-parikara-parinyasa- yukty-udbheda-samadhananam avasyam bhaviteti (Avaloka 1.27).

(VII) In Sanskrit, many ornaments are based on an implied similarity or on some implied meaning.

(VIII) In Sanskrit, many ornaments are based on a contrast or on an apparent contradiction: vyatireka, vibhavana, visesokti, visama, virodhabhasa, asangati, vyaghata, atad-guna.

(IX) Similarly, many ornaments are characterized by a series: karana-mala, mala-dipaka, ekavali, sara.

(X) Sanskrit poetics features citra-kavya (picture poetry, etc.).

(XI) In Sanskrit, most poetical theorists do not value alliteration of a vowel (assonance).

(XII) In a metaphor of Sanskrit poetics, the standard of comparison must not be far-fetched. Therefore, what is called metaphor in English is classed either as rupaka (metaphor), atisayokti (introsusception), virodha (contradiction), utpreksa (conceit: fanciful assumption), or simply poetic expression. In Sanskrit, not all metaphorical usage falls under the heading of metaphor. In English, there are thirteen types of metaphors. A submerged metaphor is either a rupaka- dhvani (implied metaphor) or an atisayokti (introsusception).

(XIII) In Sanskrit poetics, the simile of English poetics can be classed in one of many ornaments, depending on the wording: upama, upama-dhvani, utpreksa, nidarsana, apahnuti, prativastupama, malopama, rasanopama, ananvaya, anyonyopama.

(XIV) Sanskrit poetics contains many allusions to mythology. Symbolism is profound. Many philosophical concepts are inferred as a foundation. Notably, the concepts of the soul (Atman) and of God (Brahma), whether He is within (Paramatman) or without (Paramesvara, Bhagavan), are central. In addition, Vaishnava literature propounds the difference between material energy and transcendental energy. The histories, sometimes called mythology, are the sugar coating meant to facilitate the understanding of those subtle truths of life. English literature too aims at soul-searching. And supernatural powers mastered by Buddhists, and others, are sometimes referred to.

(XV) In Sanskrit culture, for the most part the ultimate principle is that true happiness is derived internally, not from objects: visaya vinivartante niraharasya dehinah, rasa-varjam raso pyasyaparam drstva nivartate, “When a person restricts the senses, the sensory objects go away, but not the taste for them. Yet upon realizing the Absolute (or a higher thing), even that taste goes away. (Bhagavad­gita 2.59). In poetics, to experience Rasa the readers must have a pure heart, abounding in sattva-guna (goodness), so that sattvika- bhavas (feelings, or good vibrations) can arise. The sattvika-bhavas are so called because they originate from sattva (a mind devoid of both rajo-guna, the mode of action/ passion, and tamo-guna, the mode of lethargy or ignorance): rajas-tamobhyam asprstam manah sattvam ihocyate (Sarasvate-kanthabharana 5.20); sattvad asmat samutpanna ye ye bhavas te tu sattvikah (Bhakti-rasamrta- sindhu 2.3.2). Aside from literary embellishments, enjoying good old literature often means relishing descriptions that reveal the amazing nature of a character. This emphasizes that in life the nature and the education of a person matter as much as their looks. By contrast, nowadays in English cinematography, Rasa is most often derived externally, from technological advancement: Great astonishment and pleasure are obtained by becoming aware of innovations in technology: Special effects, as well as technology used by the characters themselves, are an integral part of a great movie. A major offshoot of this is the genre called science-fiction, utterly absent in Sanskrit literature. At any rate, reading literature entices us to speak in metaphorical terms, to develop humor, and so on.

(XVI) Comic strips are popular in India too. They are more properly called graphic strips, or graphic novels. Only in the English language is the word comics used to denote such strips: Pre-nineteenth-century strips were seldom intended to be comical. The terms comics and comic strip became established about 1900 in the United States, when all strips were meant to be comic. The French term is bande dessinee. Graphic strips became popular some time after the invention of the printing press by Johannes Gutenberg in 1439 CE. Still, I have seen color strips (citra-katha) dating from the sixteenth century at the City Palace Museum in Udaipur (Rajasthan).

(XVII) Of the ten major kinds of dramaturgic plays in Sanskrit, the nataka is the most popular. In it, by definition the rasa must be either vira (heroism) or srngara (romance): eko raso ’ngikartcvyoo virah srngara eva va (Dasa-rupaka 3.30). Similarly, in English movies, action thrillers, which are the equivalent of vira-rasa, are very prominent. The natural attraction for such movies shows that in life, by nature the primary Rasa of a man is vira, and srngara should be subservient to that. In Ramayana, for example, the vira- rasa between Rama and Ravana is predominant, and the love, whether in meeting or in separation, between Sita and Rama is secondary. In Mahabharata too, where the apex is the Kuruksetra War, vira-rasa is predominant for the most part. In regard to vira- rasa, Jagannatha’s eight kinds of vira are worthy of consideration (p. 623). Over the past decades, women have become ‘heroes’ (vira). For instance, women too become learned in their field of knowledge (panditya-vira) and outfox one another.

(XVIII) In English culture, and by extension in English literature, the concepts of right and wrong are based on the law of the majority, whereas in Sanskrit culture, for the most part they are founded on the Vedic concept of moral ethics (dharma).

(XIX) In English dramaturgy (especially in movies), the concept of horror combines the Sanskrit concepts of bhaya-rasa (fear) and bibhatsa-rasa (disgust) and takes them to the next level.

(XX) Sometimes ojas guna (vigor) corresponds to cacophony in English:

“Beware the Jabberwock, my son! The jaws that bite, the claws that catch! Beware the Jubjub bird, and shun the frumious Bandersnatch!” (Lewis Carroll)

In Sanskrit literature, vigor is expressed in sound by long com­pounds and by certain types of phonemes and phonetic combi­nations. Richard Nordquist expounds upon forcefulness in English literature by citing this:

Demetrius’s On Style (c. 3rd or 2nd Century BC)—Forcefulness: “\[F\]orcefulness demands brevity and terseness: short phrases instead of clauses, for “length destroys vehemence” (241). Even when we use periods, and a succession of periods can be forceful, they must be short, not more than two clauses, and with clear, well marked endings. Rhetorical devices such as antithesis, paromoiosis, balanced clauses and so on must be avoided as incompatible with strong emotion, but discordant combinations of sound, hiatus, a jerky and forced, unnatural order of words, lack of connectives, all these can contribute to forcefulness which requires a histrionic delivery.”

(XXI) In English, euphony involves the use of long vowels, of harmonious consonants such as l, m, n, r, and soft ‘f ’ and ‘v’ sounds, and of soft consonants or semi-vowels: w, s, y, and th or wh. In Sanskrit, madhurya-guna (sweetness) mostly comes alive by the use of nasal sounds (m, n, n). There is no ‘f ’ sound. The letter l is used for softness.

(XXII) In Sanskrit, a literary composition should end in madhurya (sweetness, or melting), by the maxim: madhurena samapayet, “One should end on a sweet note,” whereas in English literature anything goes. The construction of madhurya-guna is also used for santa-rasa:

*visvadrica bhuvanam akhilam bhasate yasya dhamna*  
*sarvesam apy aham ayam itipratyayalambanam yah \|*  
*tam prcchanti sva-hrdaya-gatavedino visnum anyan*  
*anyayo ’yam siva siva nrnam kena va varnaniyah \|\|*

**Those who do not know that God is in their hearts ask others about Him, by whose all-pervading splendor the universe revolves and who is the object of their perception “I am He.” Alas, who could possibly explain this indecorum of people? (Rasa-g angadhara, example of the vicitra ornament, KM p. 453)**

## Appendix V

## Tribute to Kalidasa

Kalidasa was the greatest Indian playwright. Yet there are few verifiable facts about his life. Based on the descriptions of the flora in his works, some pandits opine that Kalidasa was born and raised in Kashmir. According to tradition, as a young man Kalidasa was a simpleton: The woman who became his wife was a learned princess who was tricked into marrying him. Later, challenged by his wife, he studied poetry and became a great poet.

There was a king who had an erudite daughter. When he told her that the time had come for her to get married, she said she would marry a man who could defeat her in a debate. The pandits, wanting to take revenge on her, suggested a young man for the task. This man, they said, would only engage in mute debates. Thus, the debate between the princess and Kalidasa began.

The princess showed him one finger, meaning the Absolute Truth is one. Kalidasa, a dullard in his early youth, thought that she wanted to poke him in the eye, so he showed her two fingers. She conceded the point, thinking that Sakti is indeed the counterpart of Siva. Next, she showed him her open hand, meaning there are five elements. But Kalidasa, thinking she wanted to slap him in the face, put his fist in front of him. Again she conceded the point, thinking that Kalidasa meant the five elements are nothing without being united. Thus, the two became married, but after the wedding she realized that Kalidasa was a fool, so she kicked him out of the house. He went to a temple dedicated to Kali. The goddess was pleased by his entreaty and granted him profound wisdom. Incidentally, in the name Kalidasa, the word Kali optionally becomes Kali within a name, by the rule: ny-apoh samjna-chandasor bahulam (Astadhyayi 6.3.63). When he returned to the house, his wife asked: asti kascid vag-visesah, “Do you have anything special to say?” Hence the great Kalidasa wrote three books starting with those words: Kumara-sambhava begins with asti, Megha-duta with kascit, and Raghu-vamsa with vak. Needless to say, his wife edited his books.

Kalidasa’s life was as epic as his works. His demise too was poetic. According to the legend, he went to visit his friend Kumaradasa (c. 500 CE), the prince of Ceylon. He is the author of Janaki-harana. Kumaradasa showed a half verse to his retinue and told them that he would give great wealth to anyone who could properly add the second half to complete the verse. This is the thirty-third of the sixty-four arts, called samasya-puranam (filling a verse). The first half is this:

*kamale kamalotpattih*  
*sruyate na ca drsyate \|*

**The origination of a lotus (or of lotuses) in a lotus has never been heard of nor seen anywhere else.**

At night, Kalidasa went to see a courtesan. She had heard about the enigma. She told him the words, and Kalidasa immediately found the answer:

*bale tava mukhambhoje*  
*katham indivara-dvayam \|\|*

**Girl, how is it that two lotuses are in your lotus face?**

The courtesan, greedy for the reward, killed Kalidasa and hid his body. The next day, Kumaradasa gave her the prize. But after a few days, he ordered a search for Kalidasa. His body was found. In one version of the story, Kumaradasa placed Kalidasa’s body on the funeral pyre and entered the fire too.

Kalidasa’s Abhijnana-sakuntala is based on a true story, found in Mahabharata. India is called Bharata-varsa (the country of Bharata) in honor of Bharata, the son of Dusyanta and Sakuntala. Bharata is a distant ancestor of the Kauravas and Pandavas. In Sanskrit culture, pandits know this verse about Kalidasa:

*kavyesu natakam ramyam tatra ramya sakuntala \|*  
*tatrapi ca caturtho ’nkas tatra sloka-catustayam \|\|*

**Of all types of poetic works, a play is the best. Among plays, Sakuntala is foremost. In it, the fourth act is most excellent. And therein, four verses are outstanding.**

The heroine is Sakuntala, daughter of the sage Visvamitra and the celestial courtesan Menaka. Abandoned at birth by her parents, Sakuntala, so-called because she was cared for by birds (sakunta-la = sakuntair lalita), is brought up in the hermitage of the sage Kanva. One day, while Kanva was away on a pilgrimage, Dusyanta, king of Hastinapura, goes hunting in the forest. He meets Sakuntala, is fascinated by her, courts her in royal style, and marries her by the Gandharva rite. Before returning to the capital, he gives her a ring, so that when she goes to see him there he can recognize her and grant her a place as a queen in his court. These are the four verses:

*yasyaty adya sakuntaleti hrdayam samsprstam utkanthaya*  
*kanthah stambhita-baspa-vrtti-kalusas cinta-jadam darsanam \|*  
*vaiklavyam mama tavad idrsam idam snehad aranyaukasah*  
*pidyante grhinah katham nu tanaya-vislesa-duhkhair navaih \|\| 4.6 \|\|*

**Kanva thinks:**  
**Today Sakuntala will depart for her bridegroom’s abode, Hence my heart is touched by yearning,**  
**My voice is impeded by a downpour of tears I try to hold, And my sight is blurred by worrying.**  
**If I, a renunciate residing in the forest,**  
**Am so disconcerted due to fervor,**  
**How can parents not be harrowed by the tempest Of separation from their daughter?**

*susrusasva gurun kuru priya-sakhT-vrttim sapatnT-jane*  
*bhartur viprakrtapi rosanataya ma sma pratTpam gamah \|*  
*bhuyistham bhava daksina parijane bhagyesv anutsekinT*  
*yanty evam grhinT-padam yuvatayo vamah kulasyadhayah \|\| 4.18 \|\|*

**Kanva speaks to Sakuntala:**  
**Serve the elders; behave like a dear friend**  
**To your co-wives; don’t go near your husband**  
**When you’re angry, even if you were offended;**  
**With your entourage be very open-minded;**  
**And fortunate people should not be berated.**  
**Thus does a maiden become a good wife, Whereas a sullen girl is a curse of life.**

*abhijanavato bhartuh slaghye sthita grhinT-pade*  
*vibhava-gurubhih krtyais tasya prati-ksanam akula \|*  
*tanayam acirat pracTvarkam prasuya ca pavanam*  
*mama virahajam na tvam vatse sucam ganayisyasi \|\| 4.19 \|\|*

**Abiding in the praiseworthy status**  
**Of the wife of a man of noble descent,**  
**In his deeds replete with greatness**  
**You will be absorbed in every moment.**  
**And as the sun is delivered by the eastern skies, A son, a blessing, from you will arise.**  
**Dear daughter, my sorrow of separation You will have no occasion to reckon.**

*bhutva ciraya caturanta-mahT-sapatnT*  
*dausyantim apratiratham tanayam nivesya \|*  
*bhartra tad-arpita-kutumba-bharena sardham*  
*sante karisyasi padam punar asrame ’smin \|\| 4.20 \|\|*

**Having become, with the Earth, the emperor’s co-wife for an era, And having secured the future of your son by Dusyanta, A son whom no chariot warrior can face,**  
**You may return to this place**  
**To live in peace with your husband,**  
**Who to him will have entrusted the household, a burden.**

*artho hi kanya parakiya eva*  
*tam adya sampresya parigrahituh \|*  
*jato mamayam visadah prakamam*  
*pratyarpita-nyasa ivantar-atma \|\| 4.22 \|\|*

**Kanva thinks:**  
**A daughter is another man’s treasure.**  
**To her husband today she is given.**  
**Now I feel a calm and sacred pleasure, As though I have redirected a loan from heaven.**

End of Act Four

## Glossary

A

Ananda — bliss, joy. It denotes either transcendental bliss or material bliss, according to the context (see Sac-cid-ananda).

Anubhava — an effect, specifically any bodily reaction triggered by seeing a vibhava or by experiencing a vyabhicari-bhava. The word anu means pascat (it occurs afterward). By definition, an anubhava is that which reveals the emotion in the person’s heart: anubhavo bhava-bodhakah (Amara-kosa 1.7.21) (rendered in Bhakti-rasamrta-sindhu 2.2.1).

Asraya — (1) refuge, shelter, (2) the person who is the subject of the feeling for the other person. The asraya (subject) is the correlative of the visaya (object). Both constitute the alambana aspect of vibhava. For example, in the sentence “Radha loves Krsna,” Radha is the asraya and Krsna the visaya.

B

Bhagavatam — the Bhagavata Purana.

Bhakti (bhakti-yoga) — service to God, devotional service. The nine primary types of bhakti are: sravanam, kirtanam, smaranam, pada-sevanam, arcanam, vandanam, dasyam, sakhyam, and atma- nivedanam.

Bimba — An Indian “fruit” which becomes red when ripe. It is the size of a thumb or of a little finger. The redness of the lips of a woman are compared the redness of a ripe bimba fruit. Notably, the master poet Snharsa wrote:

*adharam khalu bimba-namakam*  
*phalam asmad iti bhavyam anvayam \|*  
*labhyate ’dhara-bimbam ity adah*  
*padam asya radana-cchadam vadat \|\|*

Although the word adhara-bimbam (“her lips are like a bimba fruit,” by the derivation adharo bimbam iva) is expressive of the splendor of DamayantT’s lips, a more suitable derivation is: adharam bimbam asmat, “The bimba fruit is less eminent than this” (Naisadha-carita 2.24). The latter derivation is a bahuvrihi compound where the word adhara is an indeclinable word meaning ‘lower’. In like manner, Kavi Karnapura states: sarvany etany adharayatity adharah, “The lips are called adhara because they make everything else lower in point of sweetness” (Alankara- kaustubha 3.5).

Brahma (Brahman) — the Absolute Truth, the all-pervasive aspect of God which is the ultimate substratum of all souls (not to be confused with Brahma, the creator in Hinduism).

C

Cinmaya — transcendental (“made of cit”).

Cit — transcendental consciousness; spirit.

Cit-sakti — the Lord’s internal potency (as contrasted with Maya, the material energy); synonyms are Acintya-sakti, Para sakti, Svarupa-sakti, and Yogamaya.

D

Dasa — a servant.

G

Gandharva — the celestial beings in the higher planets who are especially noted for their expertise in singing and in music.

Gopa — a cow herder (esp. in Vrindavan).

GopT — (1) female cow herder, (2) a cowherd girl who loves Krsna. GosvamT (Gosvamin) — a title (lit. “master of his senses”).

Guna — quality. However, the term “three gunas ” denotes the three modes of material nature: sattva-guna (goodness), rajo-guna (action / passion), and tamo-guna (ignorance, darkness).

H

HladinT-sakti — The form of Cit-sakti which governs the ananda aspect (bliss, pleasure). The Sandhini-sakti governs the sat aspect (transcendental existence), and the Samvit-sakti the cit aspect (cognitive faculty).

J

Jiva (or jlvatma) — a soul. A soul is transcendental (sat-cid- ananda), just like Brahma.

K

Krsna — God in the form ofYasoda’s son; He is equal to Narayana in terms of Godhood, but is the foremost manifestation of God from the viewpoint of rasa (relishment). According to some Hindu astronomers, Lord Krsna was born on July 18, 3228 BCE and passed away on February 18, 3102 BCE (the start of Kali Yuga). There is disagreement about the exact dates, yet everyone agrees that Krsna passed away thirty-five years after the Kuruksetra War.

L

Laksmi — the consort of Narayana. She is the presiding deity of wealth. She is also called Sri.

Lila — a pastime; amusement, fun, sport.

M

Madhura-rasa (or Madhurya-rasa) — a synonym of srngara-rasa (romance).

Mana — pique, huffiness.

Mathura — the city where Lord Krsna was born, located between Delhi and Agra (Uttar Pradesh, India), about twelve kilometers from Vrindavan.

N

Narayana — God’s form in Vaikuntha, in the mood of majestic opulence.

Nayaka — lover: the protagonist. There are four kinds of nayakas (dhlra-lalita, etc.). Romance (srngara-rasa) must at least be an aspect.

Nayika — ladylove. A ladylove is the nayaka’s woman, but she is not always a heroine (protagonist). Conversely, a heroine in an English drama is not called a nayika if she does not display the mood of romance (srngara-rasa).

Nirguna — transcendental; without the three gunas.

P

Paramatma — the Soul (Supersoul), the form of God situated in the hearts of all as a witness and as a giver of intuition.

Prema — (1) love, (2) transcendental love (in the context of bhakti): When Krsna-prema makes its appearance in the heart of a devotee, that love is like poison and nectar mixed together: sei prema yanra mane, tara vikrama sei jane, visamrte ekatra milana (Caitanya-caritamrta 2.2.51).

R

Radha — She is a Gopi married to Abhimanyu and is Krsna’s foremost ladylove in Vrindavan.

Rama — (1) Ramacandra, the husband of Sita, (2) Balarama, Krsna’s elder brother.

Rasa — relishment. There are several technical meanings:

(1) In classical poetics, there are nine rasas (srngara, love, romance; hasya, humor, laughter; karuna, lamentation; raudra, rage; vira, heroism; bhayanaka, fear; bibhatsa, disgust; adbhuta, astonishment; and santa, saintly peacefulness). In bhakti, however, there are five main rasas (Santa, dasya, sakhya, vatsalya, and srngara) and seven secondary ones (hasya, adbhuta, vira, karuna, raudra, bhayanaka, and bibhatsa). Quite often, the name of a rasa is mentioned instead of its corresponding sthayi-bhava, that is, sometimes the term rasa means sthayi-bhava;

(2) A sthayi-bhava implied by vibhavas (causes), anubhava (effect, physical reaction), and vyabhicari-bhava (transient emotion) is called rasa (aesthetic delight) in the sense that it has become relishable (Bharata Muni’s rasa-sutra, pp. 95 and 459 above);

(3) When the relishment of that rasa (the sthayi-bhava thus implied) is augmented by an extraordinary implied meaning, it becomes rasa in the sense of ‘aesthetic rapture’ (ref. p. 471 above). The pleasure in that state is directly derived from the bliss of the soul: raty-ady-avacchinna bhagnavarana cid eva rasah (Pandita­raja Jagannatha, Rasa-gangadhara, KM p. 23): atmaivanandamse vibhavadibhir bhagnavaranas tad-vyanjita-raty-ady-avacchinnas tat-sannibhas ca rasah (Baladeva Vidyabhusana, Sahitya-kaumudi 4.10). There are two broad varieties of Rasa: laukika (material) (in day-to-day life) and alaukika (transcendental) (aesthetic rapture, and bhakti-rasa). The rapture in the state of bhakti-rasa is partly brought about by the transcendental energy: yatra tu bhagavad- ratir eva vibhavadi-sambhinna rasas tatra rater hladim-samvid- vrtti-bhutatvat tad-alambanadnam ca jnana-sukhatmakatvat, hasadinam api raty-anugrhitatvat tatha-bhuta-rasa-rupata susiddhaiva (Sahitya-kaumudi 4.10). Further, aesthetic delight turns into rapture because of an upsurge of sattva: sattvodrekad akhanda-sva-prakasananda-cin-mayah (Sahitya-darpana 3.2): hrdi saiivojjvale badham svadate sa raso matah (Bhakti-rasamrta- sindhu 2.5.132). In the case of the Rasa of the soul, the term sattva means “good vibrations” (vibrations in the form of sattva-guna), a state where the mind is untouched by either rajo-guna or tamo- guna. This sattva (good vibes) is the same as the sattva which gives rise to sattvika-bhava and to anubhava. In the case of bhakti-rasa (the Rasa of the soul mixed with transcendental energy), sattva denotes both sattva (the vibes) and suddha-sattva (transcendental consciousness).

Rasika — (1) a refined person (lit. “one who has good taste”), someone who has mastered the art of living; (2) someone who has swagger; (3) a person who is able to imbibe and relish the feelings or meanings portrayed in literature: synonym of Sahrdaya (a connoisseur of literature, lit. someone who has a heart).

Rati — (1) Affection; (2) In classical poetics, the type of sthayi- bhava characterized by love; (3) In bhakti, a synonym of bhava (sthayi-bhava) (bhava-bhakti).

S

SakhT — female friend (in usage, this word denotes a woman who is a friend of another woman).

Sancari-bhava — a synonym of vyabhicari-bhava (transient emotion).

Sat-cid-ananda (proper spelling: sac-cid-ananda) — transcen­dental. A Sanskrit idiom which literally means, “what is real (sat = satya), transcendentally conscious (cit), and bliss (ananda).” These three concepts are not separate, rather they are united: Transcendence is the one essence of sat, cit, and ananda.

Sattvika — of the nature of sattva-guna.

Sattvika-bhava — one of the eight sattvika-bhavas: stambha

(being stunned), sveda (perspiration), romanca (horripilation), svara-bheda (faltering voice), vepathu (trembling), vaivarnya (a change in the complexion, often due to separation), asru (tears), and pralaya (loss of consciousness, owing to happiness; or total devastation).” (Sahitya-darpana 3.135) (Bhakti-rasamrta-sindhu 2.3.16). The sattvika-bhavas are so called because they arise from sattva (good vibes): krsna-sambandhibhih saksat kincid va vyvadhanatah, bhavais cittam ihakrantam sattvam ity ucyate budhaih. sattvad asmat samutpanna ye ye bhavas te tu sattvikah (Bhakti-rasamrta-sindhu 2.3.1-2). Because they are bodily reactions too, the eight sattvika-bhavas are classed in the category of anubhava. The difference between the two is that an anubhava involves volition. The similarity between the two is that both arise from sattva (good vibrations). There is no set number of anubhavas. Sri — (1) a name of Laksmi, (2) splendor, beauty, (3) an honorific, lit. “endowed with splendor” (sri = sr-yukta).

Srngara-rasa — romance, love. It has two categories: sambhoga (meeting) and vipralambha (separation).

Sthayi-bhava (also called sthayT) — foundational mood. Each rasa has its corresponding sthayi-bhava. In classical poetics, the nine sthayi-bhavas are as follows (in sequence with the nine rasas mentioned above): rati (affection), hasa (humor), soka (sorrow), krodha (anger), utsaha (great zeal), bhaya (fear), jugupsa (disgust), vismaya (wonder), and nirveda (total dispassion).

Svadhina-bhartrka — an amorous woman who controls her man.

U

Uddipana — stimulus: anything that inflames the sthayi-bhava, such as the time, the place, a quality, a living being, and an object.

V

Vaisnava (Vaishnava) — a devotee of Lord Visnu.

Vedanta (Uttara-mimamsa) — the philosophy of the Upanisads, lit. “the end or conclusion of the Vedas.” The Upanisads constitute the fourth and final part of each Veda. Snharsa eminently alludes to Vedanta philosophy in the following verse. The context is this: At Damayanti’s svayamvara ceremony, Indra, Agni, Yama and Varuna disguise themselves as Nala. He too is present. Damayanti wants to choose him as her bridegroom:

*saptum prayacchati na paksa-catustaye tam*  
*tal-labha-samsini na pancama-koti-matre \|*  
*sraddham dadhe nisadha-rad-vimatau matanam*  
*advaita-tattva iva satya-tare pii lokah \|\|*

**She was in doubt as to who was the real Nala. Given that the set of four alternatives was not giving an opportunity to be sure, she was unable to be sure about the fifth alternative, even though it had provided some certainty. In like manner, given that the four philosophical theories are varieties of opinion, people are not sure about the doctrine of nonduality, even though it is very true. (Naisadha-carita 13.36)**

The above refers to two verses of Gaudapada-karika (asti nasty asti nastiti nasti nastiti vapunah... kotyas catasrah...). Thus, if the topic is whether the soul exists after the demise of the body, the four alternatives are:

1. It exists.
2. It does not exist.
3. It both exists and does not exist.
4. It is neither existent nor nonexistent.

In verse 21.88, Sriharsa calls Buddha vidhuta-koti-catuska (unconcerned with the four alternatives) and advaya-vadin (believer in nondualism). In other words, on this topic, Sunyavada is the same as Sankaracarya’s philosophy: mano-vacam agocaram brahma, “Brahman is beyond the purview of mind and words.” In the opinion of Anandagiri, however, the topic of the karikas of Sankaracarya’s parama-guru relates to whether there is a soul in the body, and so he says Sankaracarya implies that the first alternative is held by the Vaisesikas, the second by the Vijnanavadin Buddhists, the third by the Jains, and the fourth by the Sunyavadin Buddhists. (Handiqui, K.K. (1956) (2nd ed.) Naisadha-carita of Sriharsa, Puna: Deccan College, p. 530)

Vibhava — the determinants of Rasa. There are two kinds: alambana (the foundation: asraya and visaya) and uddipana (stimuli). Vibhava is the cause of anubhava, the effect. Vyabhicari- bhava accompanies an anubhava. When those three are present in a text, a sthayi-bhava is implied by them and turns into rasa (aesthetic delight).

Visaya — (1) topic, (2) object of sensory perception, (3) the person who is the object of the other person’s feeling: The visaya is the correlative of the asraya (subject).

Vyabhicari-bhava — transient emotion: An emotion that rises from and merges back into the sthayi-bhava like waves in an ocean. Theoretically, the vyabhicari-bhavas are thirty-three in number, but some of them have subcategories.

## Sanskrit Pronunciation Guide

**The vowels are pronounced as follows:**

a — as in but

f — as in creed

a — as in far

1 — as in cool run

i — as in insure

e — as in they

i — as in pique

ai — as in aisle

u — as in bush

o — as in holy

u — as in rule

au — as in owl

r — as in crib

or as in crush

**The consonants are pronounced as follows:**

**Gutturals (pronounced from the throat)**

k — as in kite

kh — as in khan

g — as in glove

gh — as in mug house

n — as in song

**Palatals (pronounced with the middle of the tongue against the palate)**

c — as in chair

ch — as in staunch heart

j — as in jelly

jh — as in hedgehog

n — as in gang

**Cerebrals (pronounced with the tip of the tongue about an inch behind the teeth)**

t — as in tent

th — as in tent hill

d — as in red

dh — as in red home

n — as in money

**Dentals (pronounced with the tongue behind the teeth)**

t — as in tennis

th — as in toe

d — as in doctor

dh — as in odd house

n — as in nurse

**Labials**

(pronounced with the lips)

p — as in paul

ph — as in uphill

b — as in bow

bh — as in bob high

m — as in moist

**Semivowels**

y — as in yes

r — as in rook

l — as in lobby

v — as in video

(when v follows a consonant,

it sounds like swan)

Pronunciation Guide

**Sibilants**

s — as in shine

s — as in hush

s — as in sweet

**Aspirate**

h — as in house

**Anusvara**

m — as in song

**Visarga**

h — a final h-sound;

ih is pronounced almost like ihi

**Conjuncts**

jn — as in dig yonder
